How should one know that external objects do not truly exist, but that only internal consciousness arises appearing as external objects? (Answer:
Because a real self and real dharmas cannot be apprehended.

△ Second, the specific explanation through interrogation and response, which has two parts: first, the refutation of the grasping at a self (*ātman*); second, the refutation of the grasping at phenomena (*dharma*).

Within the first [part], there are three sections: first, posing a hypothetical question to introduce the topic; second, the actual refutation of the characteristics of the self; third, answering questions to resolve potential difficulties. Now, the first [section].
How is it that a real self cannot be found?

△ Second, the actual refutation of the characteristics of the self has three parts: first, an account of the refutation of the attachments held by the non-Buddhists and the Hīnayānists; second, the establishment of formal logic (*pramāṇa*) to reveal *vijñaptimātratā*;
third, the concluding judgment regarding innate and conceptual [grasping]. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, the individual refutation of the three theories of the six teachers.
Second, the specific refutation of the three views of the Hinayana; third, the general refutation by means of consciousness, faculties, and objects. The first [section] has two parts:
first, the presentation of their views; second, the refutation. Now, the first [part].

The various conceptions of a self are, in brief, of three kinds. First, there is the conception that the essence of the self is eternal and all-pervasive, equal in extent to space, yet performs actions in every location and experiences pleasure and pain.
Second, there is the conception that although the essence of the self is eternal, its extent is not fixed, expanding and contracting according to the size of the body.
Third, there is the conception that the essence of the self is eternal and extremely subtle, like a single atom.
Because it functions within the body to perform activities, there are three types of grasping:
the first is the grasping held by the Vaiśeṣikas, who posit the agent as the self (*ātman*); and the Sāṃkhyas, who posit the experiencer as the self.
The second is the grasping held by those such as the Ahrīkas and the Nirgranthas. The third is the grasping held by Paśupati and the Vyāsa...
This concludes the exposition of their calculations; thus they are called the "Six Teachers and Three Calculations. Part Two: Refutation, which is divided into three sections.
First, the refutation of permanence and omnipresence; second, the refutation of indeterminacy; third, the refutation of extreme subtlety. Now, the first section.

The first [position] is initially unreasonable. Why is this? If one maintains that the self is eternal, omnipresent, and equal in extent to space, it should not experience suffering, pleasure, and so forth in accordance with the body.
Furthermore, because it is eternal and omnipresent, it should be devoid of movement; how then could it follow the body to perform various karmic actions?
This first refutes the notion of impermanence and omnipresence by taking the experiencer as the agent.
Since movement constitutes action, that which lacks movement and transition cannot perform action.
Furthermore, regarding the self that is asserted [by you], are all sentient beings identical or distinct? If one says they are identical (to a single self), then...

If one sentient being performs an action, all sentient beings should likewise perform that action; if one sentient being experiences the fruit [of karma], all sentient beings should likewise experience that fruit;
and if one sentient being attains liberation, all sentient beings should likewise attain liberation. In this case, the world would lack established distinctions, which would lead to a great error.
If, on the other hand, it is said that the self-essence (*ātman*) of each sentient being is distinct, then [the self of] the various sentient beings...

Because [the self] is omnipresent, its substance would necessarily be intermingled. Furthermore, since the "self" (ātman) belonging to all sentient beings is omnipresent in every location, when one sentient being performs an action and another receives the fruit thereof, there would be no difference between the locus of that [action] and the locus of the selves of all sentient beings;
consequently, it would follow that [the fruit] is produced by and experienced by all sentient beings.
This further refutes the arguments for the permanence and omnipresence of the self by examining whether its essence is identical or distinct [from the aggregates].
If it is argued that there is no such fault because the agent and the experiencer each have their respective domains, this is also logically untenable;
for it would be irrational for karma, its fruit, and the body to be conjoined with various selves such that they belong to one and not to another.
One might fear that the opponent will offer this defense: "Although my substance (*ātman*) is indeed all-pervasive, the agent and the experiencer each have their own specific domains;
therefore, there is no case of one acting and another experiencing, nor does the fault of [one person] being named for all actions and experiences apply. To this, we now state the refutation:
This is also not logically tenable. For if the substance of the self were pervasive, then karma, its fruit, and the body would necessarily [be shared] with all sentient beings.

The nature of the self is conjoined [with the body]. If it still belongs to this [body] and does not belong to that [other body], then because there is partial belonging, it cannot be called "pervasive";
for the principle of the self being omnipresent would be inconsistent with such a state.
Furthermore, when one sentient being attains liberation, all sentient beings should likewise attain liberation, for the Dharma that is cultivated and realized is the same for all.
Because the self-essence of all sentient beings is conjoined, if one acts, all act;
if one experiences, all experience. Likewise, if one is liberated, all should be liberated.
Since acting, experiencing, and liberation would each have their own distinct ownership, the principle of being eternal and omnipresent cannot be established. △

Next, the refutation of the "indeterminate" [self] is also irrational. Why is this? If the essence of the self were eternal, it should not undergo expansion and contraction in accordance with the body.
Since it does indeed expand and contract, it would be like the air within a flute; thus, it could not be eternal. Furthermore, since the self conforms to the size of the body...
It should be analyzed just as the body is; how, then, can one maintain that the essence of the self is a single unity? Therefore, what they say is like the play of children.
The words and their meaning are both clearly manifest; there is no need for further explanation. △ Next, the refutation of the [self] as being subtle:
the latter view is also irrational. Why is this? (As it has been said: "If my measure is as small as a single atom, how could I cause a large body to move throughout its entirety?
If it is argued that although the essence of the self is small, it moves rapidly through the body like a whirling firebrand, appearing to be all-pervasive—
As for that which moves, it is the self as it is grasped; it is neither unitary nor permanent. Because all things involve coming and going, they are neither permanent nor unitary.
First, it was refuted that a small self could cause a large body to move. Next, by refuting coming and going, it is shown that [the self] is neither permanent nor unitary:
because it sometimes goes and sometimes comes, it is not permanent; because the one who goes is not the same as the one who comes, it is not unitary. This concludes the initial specific analysis.
The refutation of the three propositions of the six heretical teachers is complete. △ Second, the specific refutation of the three propositions of the Hīnayāna has two parts:
first, the presentation of their propositions; second, the refutation and censure thereof. Now, for the first:
furthermore, the self they grasp has three types: first, identical with the aggregates (*skandha*); second, separate from the aggregates; third, [neither] with nor separate from the aggregates.
It is neither identical with nor separate from [the aggregates].

These three are all non-Buddhist views that merely attach themselves to the Buddha-dharma. △ Second, the refutation and rejection has three parts: first, the refutation of identity with the aggregates;
second, the refutation of separation from the aggregates; third, the refutation of being neither identical nor separate. Now, the first.
First, the position that the self is identical to the aggregates is logically untenable. For the self would then be like the aggregates—neither permanent nor unitary.
This is the general refutation: because the aggregates arise and perish, they are impermanent; because there are five aggregates, they are not one.
Furthermore, internal forms are certainly not a real self, just like external forms, because they possess substantiality and resistance.
Below, this will be refuted specifically; first, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is refuted as being non-self. "Internal forms" refers to the five sense organs and the body;

"external forms" refers to the five sensory objects. This body is a provisional construction formed from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and it is [identical in nature] to the external four great elements and the five sensory objects.

There is no difference. Since that which possesses material obstruction can be analyzed, how could it be clung to as a self? The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The physical body is the subject (*dharmin*);
it is certainly not a real self, this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because it possesses material obstruction. The example (*udāharaṇa*) is: like external matter.
The mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) are likewise not a real self, for they do not persist in a constant continuum and depend upon various conditions.

This refutes the four aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as being the self. "Mind" refers to the eight consciousnesses, which are the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
"Mental factors" refer to the fifty-one mental concomitants, which constitute the three aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations. [This includes] the first six consciousnesses...
Furthermore, the associated mental factors (*caitta*) do not all persist in a constant succession. Eye-consciousness arises depending on nine conditions;

ear-consciousness arises depending on eight conditions; nose, tongue, and body consciousnesses arise depending on seven conditions; and mind-consciousness arises depending on five conditions. Therefore, they are not a real self (*ātman*).
Although the seventh and eighth consciousnesses persist in a constant succession, they too depend on three or four conditions.
They arise, yet they are not a real self (*ātman*). However, since other vehicles (yānas) fundamentally do not know that the seventh and eighth consciousnesses exist, they are not discussed here.

For now, we merely refute their false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that the six consciousnesses—the mind-kings (*citta-rāja*)—and the mental factors (*caitta*), such as sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*), constitute the self.

The formal inference (*prayoga*) is as follows: The mind and its mental factors are the subject (*dharmin*); they are definitely not a real self, this is the thesis (*pakṣa*); [the reason is] because... [the logical mark (*hetu*)].
It is said: [The self] does not exist as a constant continuity because it depends upon various conditions, just like sound and so forth.
Other formations and other forms are likewise not a real self, for they lack the nature of cognition, just like space and so forth.
This further refutes that the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and the matter included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*) are not the self.

Although these dissociated formations and the matter of the sphere of mental objects lack physical form, they are nonetheless not of the nature of cognition. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The remaining formations and the remaining matter are the subject (*dharmin*);
they are certainly not the real self, according to our tenet (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because they are not of the nature of cognition. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like space.
The refutation of the self as identical with the aggregates is concluded. Next, the refutation of the self as separate from the aggregates:
the principle that a self exists apart from the aggregates is likewise untenable, for it would then be like space, devoid of both action and experience.

Since the self as it is grasped is already separate from the five aggregates, it is neither form nor mind; it should therefore be like empty space, unable to perform actions and unable to receive retribution.
Furthermore, how could one possibly call empty space the "self"? △ Third, refuting [the view that the self] is neither identical to nor separate [from the aggregates].
Furthermore, the claim that it is neither [conditioned nor unconditioned] is also logically untenable.

Since you admit that the self is established in dependence upon the aggregates, yet maintain that it is neither identical to the aggregates nor distinct from them, it must—like a jar and the like (which are established in dependence upon a lump of clay, being neither identical to nor distinct from the clay)—be a merely conventional phenomenon rather than a real self.

Moreover, since it cannot be described as either conditioned or unconditioned, it likewise should not be described as either "self" or "non-self. Therefore, the real self as conceived by them [is untenable].

This is not established. First, he sets forth a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) as follows: "The self (*ātman*) as it is conceived by them—neither identical to nor distinct from the aggregates—is the subject (*dharmin*). It is certainly not a real self; this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is:

'because it is admitted to be established in dependence upon the aggregates. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like a jar and so forth. Subsequently, he further [establishes] existence by means of non-existence.

This is refuted by way of illustration. For if [the self] were identical to the five aggregates, it would be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); if it were separate from the five aggregates, it would be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Now, since it is not identical to the aggregates, it cannot be said to be conditioned; and since it is not separate from the aggregates, it cannot be said to be unconditioned.
Since it cannot be described as either conditioned or unconditioned, how could it possibly be said to be either "self" or "non-self"? And yet...
Is it not also erroneous to cling to the existence of a real self? This concludes the second section: the specific refutation of the three views of the Hīnayāna. △ Third:

A general refutation of the three [factors]—consciousness, faculties, and objects. 1. Refutation by means of the presence or absence of deliberation; this is a refutation by means of consciousness (*vijñāna*). 2. Refutation by means of the presence or absence of function;

this is a refutation by means of the faculties (*indriya*). 3. Refutation by means of whether the object of perception (*ālambana*) is real or not; this is a refutation by means of the objects (*viṣaya*).
Refutation. First:
Furthermore, regarding the substantially existent self-entity that you maintain, does it possess volition or is it devoid of volition?
If it possesses volition, it must be impermanent, because it does not possess volition at all times. If it is devoid of volition, it must be like empty space.
It cannot perform actions, nor does it receive results; therefore, the "self" as you maintain is logically untenable in both respects.

First, there is a dual interrogation; next, a specific refutation; finally, a summary conclusion—all of which may be understood accordingly. △ Second, the refutation based on the presence or absence of activity, which is specifically a refutation based on the sense faculties.
Furthermore, regarding the substantially existent self-entity that you assert: does it possess activity or is it devoid of activity?
If it possesses activity, then like hands, feet, and so forth, it must be impermanent. If it is devoid of activity, then like a rabbit’s horn and the like, it cannot be a real self.
Therefore, the self you assert fails to be established under either alternative.

This also involves a twofold interrogation, a specific refutation, and a summary conclusion, which may be understood accordingly. △ Third, the refutation based on whether the object of perception exists or not; that is, the refutation based on the sense-objects (*viṣaya*).
Furthermore, regarding the substantially existent self-body (*ātman*) that you grasp: is it the object of perception for the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*)? If it is not the object of the view of self...
Regarding the object of focus: how do you know that there truly exists a self?

If this were the object of the view of self, then the one who possesses the view of self should not be subsumed under the category of cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*), because they would be knowing [the object] as it truly is.

If that were the case—that is, if it were indeed true and non-distorted—why then do those who cling to a self disparage all the authoritative scriptures (*āgama*) and so forth that they themselves believe in, while praising the view of self?
Regarding "no-self," it is said that those who possess the view of no-self can realize nirvāṇa, whereas those who cling to the view of self sink into the cycle of birth and death.
How could a false view lead to the realization of nirvāṇa? Or how could right view cause one to sink into the cycle of birth and death?
Furthermore, first one should generally challenge [the opponent] with this, and subsequently refute them specifically. First, the refutation:
if it were not the object of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), then since it would not be an object at all, how could its existence be known? This is easily understood. Next, the refutation:

if it were the object of the view of self, then the view of self, as a result, would perceive a real self and thus would not be a distortion (*viparyāsa*). Since the view of self is not [such a thing...]
If this were inverted, it would follow that right view should instead become wrong, and the doctrine of non-self would conversely become a false view.
How could a false view of non-self be praised in the supreme teachings as that which realizes nirvāṇa?

And how could the correct view of self be reviled in the supreme teachings as that which causes one to sink into the cycle of birth and death? This concludes the initial section refuting external [opponents].
The refutation of the minor [proponent's] tenets is complete. △ Second, establishing the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to reveal that there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*):
Furthermore, all views of a self do not take a real self as their object, because they possess an object of cognition (*ālambana*), just like other cognitions that take other things as their objects.

This first refutes the subjective cognition (*ālambaka*) by means of a valid inference (*pramāṇa*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The subject (*dharmin*) is "all views that grasp at a self.
The thesis (*sādhya*) is "they necessarily cannot take a real self as their object. The reason (*hetu*) is "because they possess an object of cognition (*ālambana*).

The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is "like a mind that takes other phenomena as its object. For all other minds that take objects, they can only take the appearance (*nimitta*) manifested by themselves as their object.
[It is] determined that [the mind] cannot take external phenomena as its object;

thus, all current attachments to the view of self likewise can only take the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) transformed by itself as their object, falsely conceptualizing it as a self. How could there truly be a real self existing externally to the mind?
Yet the view of self is indeed able to take that as its object.
That which is the object of the view of self is certainly not a real self, because it is an object, just like all other phenomena.

This further refutes the object of cognition (*ālambana*) by means of true inference (*pramāṇa*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The object of my visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is a subject (*dharmin*).
It is definitely not a real self (*ātman*), according to our thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is the object of my visual consciousness. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is:

like the other five sense-objects (*viṣaya*), such as visible form (*rūpa*) and so forth. For these five sense-objects, such as visible form, are merely the objects of the five consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*).
The objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) that is transformed [by consciousness] does not exist as a real object external to the mind.

Now, this grasped "real self," being the object-condition (*ālambana*) of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), is likewise merely the objective aspect transformed by that very view of self. How could there truly be a real self?

Question: Suppose an opponent does not admit the existence of objective aspects consisting of form (*rūpa*). In that case, would the supporting example (*dṛṣṭānta*) not incur the fault of being non-existent (*asiddha*)?
[This would incur] the fault of neither [of the two parties] establishing [the reason]. Answer:

Even if the opponent does not admit that there is the form-aspect (nimittabhāga), the fact that the five objects of the external realm are subject to transformation and impermanence can still serve as a common example (dṛṣṭānta) for the lack of a real self.

Therefore, my view does not take a real self as its object; rather, it takes the various aggregates manifested by internal consciousness as its object. Following one's own deluded sentiments, various conceptualizations arise.
First, by refuting the subjective perceiver through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is revealed that the view of self is a distorted and inverted view, and not a correct view. Next...

First, by refuting the object of cognition through formal reasoning (*pramāṇa*), it is revealed that the real self is not an object of valid cognition and is not an objective reality (*svabhāva-viṣaya*).

Therefore, it is now concluded that [the self] is a transformation of consciousness; outside of consciousness, there is definitively no real self. Second, the establishment of the formal reasoning to demonstrate *vijñaptimātra* is complete.

△ Third, the conclusion and judgment regarding the two types of grasping: innate (*sahaja*) and conceptual (*vikalpita*). First, the conclusion regarding their respective categories. Second, the judgment of their...
Existence and non-existence. The first fetter belongs to both types.
Furthermore, there are briefly two kinds of self-grasping: first, innate; second, conceptual. Innate self-grasping...
Due to the power of internal causes consisting of false habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from beginningless time, it is always coexistent with the body;

it functions spontaneously without depending on false teachings or false conceptualization, and is therefore called "innate" (*sahaja*). This is further of two kinds: first, that which is constantly continuous.

In the seventh consciousness, taking the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its objective essence (*ālambana-svabhāva*), it immediately transforms and gives rise to a reflection within its own mind as its image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), and thus falsely clings to it as a real internal self. This [seventh consciousness] is intermittent.

In the sixth consciousness, taking either collectively or individually the images of the five appropriated aggregates (*pañcopādānaskandha*) transformed by the [eighth] consciousness as its objective essence, it immediately transforms and gives rise to its own mind.

[The shadow within] is taken as a [distinct] characteristic; thus, one falsely clings to it as a real self. These two types of self-clinging are subtle and difficult to sever, remaining until the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Only during the subsequent stage of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), by repeatedly practicing the superior contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), can they be eliminated.

Although the clinging to a conceptual self possesses the cause of beginningless internal perfuming, it must also depend on the power of present external conditions; it does not arise simultaneously with the body.
It arises only after waiting for false teachings (as external conditions) and the arising of false discrimination within oneself; therefore, it is called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*).
It exists only within the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This is also of two kinds:

first, taking as its object the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha-lakṣaṇa*) as taught by false teachings (namely, those that are distinct, simultaneous, or neither, etc.), it relies upon these as its objective essence (*ālambana-svabhāva*), which immediately transforms; it then gives rise to the shadows within its own mind as its objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), and through conceptualization and deliberation, clings to them as the basis for a self.

Second, taking as its object the characteristics of a self (*ātma-lakṣaṇa*) as taught by false teachings (such as being large or small, indefinite, etc.), it relies upon these as its objective essence, which immediately transforms.
The sixth consciousness arises, taking the shadows within its own mind as its objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), and through conceptualization and deliberation, clings to them as a real self.

These two forms of self-clinging are coarse and thus easy to sever; at the moment of the initial path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), by contemplating the suchness (*tathatā*) revealed by the emptiness of sentient beings within all phenomena, one is able to eliminate them.
The characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) as taught by heterodox teachings are precisely those taught by non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).

The characteristics of the self (*ātman*) as taught by heterodox teachings are those taught by the six masters of the non-Buddhists. The rest may be understood accordingly. II. Judging their Existence or Non-existence. This section has three parts:
first, judging existence or non-existence by means of their characteristics; second, judging existence or non-existence by means of their basis and pervasiveness; third, citing scriptural evidence.

First: Regarding all such instances of self-grasping described above, while the aggregates external to one's own mind may either exist or not exist, the aggregates internal to one's own mind exist entirely.
Therefore, all instances of self-grasping take as their object the characteristics of the impermanent five appropriated aggregates, falsely grasping them as a self.

The aggregates external to one's own mind refer to the *ālambana* (the objective essence); the aggregates internal to one's own mind refer to the *nimitta-bhāga* (the image-aspect). The rest may be understood accordingly.
△ Second, a judgment on existence or non-existence based on the locus of dependence.

However, because the characteristics of the aggregates arise from conditions, they exist like an illusion; whereas the self that is falsely grasped exists absolutely not, as it is merely a product of arbitrary conceptual construction.
(Arising from conditions refers to the *paratantra-svabhāva*; arbitrary conceptual construction refers to the *parikalpita-svabhāva*.)
△ Third, citing scriptural authority:
Therefore, a sutra says: "Bhikṣus, you should know that all views of a self held by śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others in the world arise entirely in dependence upon the five aggregates of clinging.
(2. The correct refutation of the mark of a self is concluded.)

△ Second, the explanation of objections through questions and answers, in two parts: first, the direct explanation of the objections; second, the establishment of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). In the first part, there are three sections:
first, the explanation by way of memory, cognition, and recitation; second, the explanation by way of the creation of karma and the experiencing of its fruit;
third, the explanation by way of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. Now, the first section.
If a real self (*ātman*) does not exist, how can there be such things as recollection, cognition, study, and the recording of enmity or favor?

(Answer: Since the real self you maintain is permanent and unchanging, it should be as it was later, just as it was before; thus, those [subsequent] events would not exist. Or, it should be as it is later, just as it was before; thus, those [prior] events would not be non-existent.

This is because the essence of the later state is no different from that of the earlier. If you claim that it is the functions (*vṛtti*) of the self that change over time, and not the essence of the self itself—

This reasoning is also incorrect. If activity were not separate from substance, it would follow that [substance] must be eternal; if substance were not separate from activity, it would follow that [substance] must be non-eternal.

First the objection is posed, and then the refutation follows. Within the response, the refutation first proceeds by examining existence and non-existence in terms of priority and posteriority, stating: "Since the self..."
If it were eternal and unchanging, then the former would necessarily be like the latter, and the latter would necessarily be like the former.

If the latter were like the former, then the former would originally have had no such things as memory, consciousness, recitation, learning, or the accumulation of enmity and favor; these should not exist in the latter.

If the former were like the latter, then since the latter already possesses memory, consciousness, recitation, learning, enmity, and favor, the former should not be devoid of them. This is because the latter [is compared] with the former.
Because their essence is not distinct. Next, the passage beginning with "If one were to say... refutes the shifting position by examining the permanence or impermanence of essence and function.

Fearing that the opponent might shift their position by claiming, "The function of the self may undergo change over time without contradiction, while the essence of the self remains permanent and unchanging," he refutes this, saying:
"This reasoning is also incorrect, because essence and function are certainly inseparable. Since function is not separate from essence, then the essence..."
If the essence were not separate from its function, then since the function is impermanent, the essence would likewise have to be impermanent.
However, each sentient being possesses a fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) that is of a single continuous nature, which sustains the seeds and serves as the basis for all phenomena.
Because they act as mutual causes through the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*), such phenomena as memory and cognition are possible;
therefore, the objection you have raised constitutes a fault for your own position, not for our school.

Since this [passage] refutes the grasping at a self by means of the relationship between preceding and succeeding entities and functions, it thereby clarifies the principle by which such phenomena as recollection and cognition are possible.
"Root consciousness" refers to the eighth consciousness. "Of a single type" means that it is exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta).
"Continuity" means evolving without interruption. "Sustaining seeds" means being able to maintain the seeds of both mundane and supramundane phenomena.
"All phenomena" refers to the preceding seven evolving consciousnesses along with their mental factors, as well as form and other dharmas; these act as causes for one another.

This means that the active manifestation of all phenomena (*dharmas*) perfumes the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), such that these very phenomena become the cause of the fundamental consciousness.
Furthermore, the seeds stored within the fundamental consciousness give rise to active manifestations, such that the fundamental consciousness becomes the cause of those phenomena.
By virtue of this power of perfuming (*vāsanā*), functions such as memory and cognition are possible; what need is there for a real self (*ātman*)? Therefore...

"Setting forth the objection that you have a flaw" concludes the refutation of the two preceding sections. "It is not [a flaw] in my own school" concludes the subsequent restatement of the correct principle.
△ Second, the explanation by way of the creation of karma and the experiencing of its fruit.
If there is no real self (*ātman*), who is it that performs karma and who receives its fruit? (Answer:
Since the real self you postulate is devoid of change, just like space, how could it possibly perform karma or receive its fruit? If it were subject to change, it would necessarily be impermanent.
This also first presents an objection and subsequently provides a refutation. If there were no transformation, then there would be neither agent nor experiencer, just like empty space;
how could empty space be a real self? If there were an agent and an experiencer, then there would be transformation, and thus it would necessarily be impermanent;
and how could that which is impermanent be a real self?

Nevertheless, because the power of causes and conditions acts upon the mind and mental factors of all sentient beings, their continuity remains uninterrupted; thus, there is no logical contradiction in their performing karma and experiencing its fruits.
Furthermore, since this [argument] refutes the grasping at a self by means of both the unchanging and the changing, it thereby clarifies that [the self] does indeed exist.

This is the principle by which karma is created and its fruit is experienced. The eight consciousnesses and their associated mental factors (*citta-caitta*)—both in their active manifestation (*pravṛtti*) and as seeds (*bīja*)—act as mutual causes and conditions, arising in continuous succession without ever being interrupted. In this way, the principles of creating karma and experiencing its fruit are fully established.
Why, then, must one separately cling to the notion of a substantial self (*ātman*)? △ Third, the explanation in terms of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
"If there were truly no self, who would transmigrate through the various realms of birth and death? And who, moreover, would grow weary of suffering and seek to proceed toward Nirvana? (Answer:
Since the "real self" you grasp at lacks both arising and ceasing, how can one speak of the transmigration of birth and death?

Being eternally like space, it is not afflicted by suffering; why then would it grow weary of it, renounce it, or seek to proceed toward Nirvana? Therefore, what that person says is always for their own [sake].
This also first presents the objection and subsequently provides the refutation; both the text and its meaning are clearly evident.
However, within the continuity of body and mind of sentient beings, various afflictions arise, and [they] perform various karmas through the power of these afflictions and karmas.
(The reason is that) because they suffer while wandering through the various realms of saṃsāra, and because they feel weary of the suffering of those realms, they seek to proceed toward nirvāṇa.
This also refutes their attachment and restates the correct principle. The initial section, which correctly explains and resolves objections, is concluded. II.
Concluding the Proof of Consciousness-Only (*Vijñaptimātra*).

Therefore, it is known that there is certainly no real self (*ātman*), but only various consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) which, from beginningless time, have arisen in succession, the preceding perishing as the succeeding is born.
The continuity of cause and effect, through the熏習 (*vāsanā*) of delusion, manifests as the semblance of a self. The ignorant falsely grasp at this and cling to it as a self.
This concludes the initial refutation of the grasping at a self. Furthermore, this false grasping at a self is the very root of the birth-and-death of segmented existence (*paricchinna-saṃsāra*).
As long as even a hair’s breadth of the great obstacle to *nirvāṇa* without remainder has not been exhausted, one is still termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Though one may currently achieve the nine successive meditative absorptions, one cannot attain the exhaustion of outflows and become an Arhat;

Speaking in terms of the arising of the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*): as for these indeterminate and fluctuating conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*), as well as erroneous discourses on "neither [identity nor difference] nor both," these arise from discrimination and are termed "afflictions of view" (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). If these afflictions are not eliminated, one will ultimately remain a worldling or a non-Buddhist.
Therefore, those who wish to be disciples of the Buddha must first direct themselves toward this treatise to investigate its meaning according to its principles.
Only when my grasping at a self has been utterly cleared away and does not sprout again can I truly have a share in the cultivation and realization of the Buddha-dharma.

If this is not so, then even if one upholds the precepts, practices seated meditation, and is extensively learned and widely informed, as long as the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) has not been subdued, one merely becomes an externalist who is attached to the Buddha-dharma.
Is this not something to be feared? △ Second, the refutation of the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), in two parts. First, the general inquiry.

their position is irrational. Why is this? Because dharmas such as the "great elements" (mahābhūta) are composed of multiple entities, like an army or a forest.
They must be provisional and not real. How, then, can it be said that they are apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: **Thesis:** The twenty-three factors, such as the great elements (*mahābhūta*), which arise from subsequent conceptual grasping, are provisional and not real.

**Reason:** Because they are composed of many constituent parts (*sattva*, etc.). **Example:** Like an army or a forest. 2. [The refutation] by means of the subject (*grāhaka*) and the object (*grāhya*).
[They] mutually contradict one another.

Furthermore, if the twenty-three dharmas such as the "great elements" (*mahābhūta*) were substantially real, they would have to be like the three entities such as *sattva* [i.e., *puruṣa*, *prakṛti*, and *manas*];

that is, they would not be composites dependent upon [the combination of] three entities. Moreover, since the three—*sattva* and so forth—are themselves the great elements and so on, the great elements and so forth should likewise be composites dependent upon three entities.
"Establishment" (*siddhi*) and "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) are not eternal; the same applies to their examples.
This is because they falsely imagine that these three things—the "established" and so forth, namely the twenty-three dharmas—can be established.

Therefore, the "establisher" and the "established" mutually refute one another. As for the statement that "transformation is not eternal; the same applies to its examples," [it refers to] the three...

The primary substance (*prakṛti*) is the agent of accomplishment; therefore, they maintain that it is capable of transformation. The great elements (*mahābhūta*), etc., are the objects of accomplishment;

therefore, they maintain that they are impermanent. However, if they claim that the agent of accomplishment is itself the object of accomplishment, then since the primary substance is already capable of transformation, the great elements, etc., should likewise be capable of transformation.
Since the great elements, etc., are already impermanent, the primary substance should likewise be impermanent.
[End of section]. △ Third, the mutual refutation by means of essence and function.

Regarding the statement that the three fundamental entities each possess multiple functions: this refers to their capacity to produce twenty-three dharmas.

Because they are distinct. If it is argued that the substance (*svabhāva*) of the three [causes] pervades the twenty-three phenomena, and therefore they are not manifold, then since the three substances already pervade [them], the three capacities (*śakti*) must also pervade them.

Because there is nothing else apart from these [elements] in this location. △ Fourth, the refutation of the three combining to form one:

If you admit that the substance and characteristics of these three things are each distinct, how could they combine to collectively form a single characteristic (such as "greatness" and so forth)? It is not possible for them to be uncombined when they are the three;

nor can they transform into a single characteristic at the time of combination, because the substance at the time of combination is no different from the substance when they were uncombined. If you say:
If the three entities differ in substance but are identical in characteristic, this would contradict your own tenet that substance and characteristic are one.
[In that case,] the substance [of the three entities] should be like their characteristic [and thus also] indistinctly one, just as the [great elements such as] earth and so forth are;

The three [elements] such as earth are particulars (*viśeṣa*), while the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth are common to all three; this is your position. Since both the general and the particular are real entities (*dravyadharma*), they belong to the same category.
It should not be either one or three.

they maintain that the characteristic of *sattva* is identical to the essence of *sattva*, and so on, up to the point that the characteristic of *tamas* is identical to the essence of *tamas*. Furthermore, the three are distinct.

When these three undergo transformation, if they do not combine to form a single characteristic (such as color), they should remain as they were before the transformation;

First, the non-union is refuted. Next, if there are three [parts] below, the union is refuted.

He refutes this, saying: It cannot be said that each of the three possesses both a general and a specific characteristic.

Even if each of the three dharmas were to possess two characteristics, the general characteristic of *sattva* would not be the general characteristic of *rajas*, nor would the general characteristic of *rajas* be the general characteristic of *tamas*, and so on, up to the general characteristic of *tamas* not being the general characteristic of *sattva* or *rajas*. Because they are distinct, the aggregate must also consist of three [aspects]. How then is it that we perceive them as a single entity, such as "form" (*rūpa*)? 6. Refuting the view that each possesses its own three aspects:

If it is argued that the substance of each of the three [factors] possesses its own three aspects (such as *sattva* and so forth), yet these are difficult to discern because they are blended and intermingled through conjunction; therefore—

Moreover, since the twenty-three dharmas—such as the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth—are all composed of the three [factors], they would have no mutual distinction when compared to one another.

Consequently, the causes (the three factors), the effects (the twenty-three dharmas), and the mere measures (*pramāṇa*), as well as the various great elements and sense organs, would be undifferentiated.

Otherwise, each [of these functions] would fail to be established. If that were the case, then a single sense organ would have to apprehend all objects, or a single object would have to be apprehended by all sense organs.

Consequently, the distinctions between sentient and insentient things, pure and impure objects, as well as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), which are clearly observed in the world, would all become indistinguishable; this would constitute a great error.
The *tanmātras* are the five subtle elements (*pañcatanmātra*). The "great elements" (*mahābhūta*) are the five gross elements. The "senses" (*indriya*) are the eleven sense organs.
As for the claim that a single sense organ should perceive all objects: this is because each sense organ is composed of the three constituents (*triguṇa*) without distinction.
Alternatively, it follows that a single object should be perceived by all sense organs, because each object is likewise composed of the three constituents without distinction.

Because they are distinct. The initial direct refutation is concluded. Question: In the subsequent passage, it states that each of the Tathāgata’s five faculties operates upon the objects of the five sense-fields;

They maintain that there are six categories of ultimate reality: (1) substance, (2) quality, (3) activity, (4) great existence, (5) sameness-and-difference, and (6) inherence.
Regarding the category of substance, they maintain nine types: (1) earth, (2) water, (3) fire, (4) wind... [and so forth].

Since those imputed impermanent, real dharmas consist of both those possessing material resistance (*sapratigha*) and those lacking material resistance (*apratigha*), the first refutation concerns those possessing material resistance. The external real dharmas apart from the mind—which is characterized by resistance and impermanence—are existent phenomena. This is not a school that asserts they possess a truly existent nature.

The reason (*hetu*) is: because they have spatial dimensions and because they are analyzable. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like an army or a forest. Second, the refutation of those without resistance: the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:
Those external real dharmas apart from the mind—which you assert to be without resistance and impermanent—are existent phenomena; [they] should not be...
The school that asserts that there exists a real intrinsic nature apart from consciousness argues: "Because it lacks material obstruction, it is like the mind and mental factors.
2. Refutation by means of two phrases concerning real qualities.

Furthermore, those [elements] which they maintain— earth, water, fire, and wind (the subject)— should not be subsumed under the category of "substantial entities" (*dravya-padārtha*) that possess resistance (the thesis),

because they are objects of touch for the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) (the reason), just like solidity, moisture, heat, and motion (the example). Likewise, those very things they maintain— solidity, moisture, heat, and so forth (the subject)—

should not be subsumed under the category of "qualities" (*guṇa-padārtha*) that lack resistance (the thesis), because they are objects of touch for the body-faculty (the reason), just like earth, water, fire, and wind (the example).
The three elements of earth, water, and fire, when contrasted with blue and other colors, are all equally objects seen by the eye; one should apply this same critique accordingly.

Therefore, it is known that there are no real earth, water, fire, or wind possessing distinct intrinsic natures such as solidity or moisture, nor are there any real earth, water, fire, or wind perceived by the eye.
They maintain that earth, water, fire, and wind are subsumed under the category of "substance" (*dravya-pada*) because they possess resistance;
and solidity, moisture, heat, and motion are subsumed under the category of "quality" (*guṇa-pada*) because they lack resistance.

Now, first using the quality-category’s lack of resistance as a homologous example (*sapakṣa*), we shall refute the error of their attachment to the substance-category possessing resistance. Next, using the substance-category’s possession of resistance...
This serves as a homologous example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) to refute their attachment to the category of qualities (*guṇa-pada*) as being non-obstructive (*apratigha*).
This is because they share the same cause—being touched by the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*)—and there is no distinct cause [for them to differ].

Since there is no distinct cause, how can you falsely imagine that while some qualities are substantially obstructive, others are non-obstructive, and that these qualities must each exist as real entities? Regarding earth, water, fire, and so forth, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
Furthermore, those [entities] they maintain—earth, water, and fire (the subject)—should not be subsumed under the category of "substance" (*dravya*) because they possess resistance (the reason);

for example, like blue and other colors (the example). Likewise, those very [entities] they maintain—blue, red, and other colors (the subject)—should not be subsumed under the category of "quality" (*guṇa*) because they lack resistance (the reason);
for example, like earth, water, and fire (the example). They are seen by the visual faculty (the reason). Therefore, [the categories of substance and quality as maintained by them] are untenable.
Therefore, it is known from below. This concludes by demonstrating the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

That is to say, since those [entities] they grasp—the categories of substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*)—are all unestablished, one knows that earth, water, fire, and wind, as well as solidity, moisture, heat, and motion, are all devoid of real dharmas.
Furthermore, when people falsely claim to see earth, water, fire, and wind with their eyes, how could there truly be earth, water, fire, or wind existing apart from consciousness? It is merely...
Earth, water, fire, and wind are merely the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) manifested by the eighth consciousness;
they are non-dual in nature with solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion. None of them are real dharmas external to the mind.

Yet, when the eye sees them, it again takes that *nimitta-bhāga* of the eighth consciousness as its substantial basis (*pratibimba*), while the eye-consciousness itself manifests its own *nimitta-bhāga* as the object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Nor do they truly perceive the essential nature of the object. If the eye were to truly see real fire, why would it not be hot?
If it were to truly see real water, why would it not be moist? △ Third, the refutation of the category of "real," "obstructive," and "permanent."
Furthermore, regarding those "real categories" (padārtha) that they maintain to be resistant and permanent (the subject):
because they all possess resistance (the reason), like coarse earth and so forth (the example), they must be impermanent (the thesis).
△ Fourth, regarding the unimpeded nature among all categories:
Among the meanings of all categories, those things apprehended by the physical sense organs (the subject) must all be impeded (the thesis),
because they are admitted to be apprehended by the physical sense organs (the reason), just like earth, water, fire, and wind (the example).
△ Fifth: Regarding the two categories of the real (*vastu*), there are two propositions that mutually refute all other propositions.

Furthermore, those things they grasp as non-real—such as qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, which are subsumed under the category of "non-real"—should not possess a distinct intrinsic nature apart from consciousness (the thesis).

This is because they are subsumed under the category of "non-real" (the reason). It is like the son of a barren woman (the example). [The same applies to] the five propositions beginning with "real" (*sat*) which are subsumed under the category of "existent" (*mahā-sat*).
[Thesis: These existent phenomena must not have a distinct intrinsic nature apart from consciousness. [Reason: Because they are included within [the category of] non-existence.
[Example: Like flowers in the sky and so forth.
△ 6. Refuting the nature of "Great Existence" (mahāsattā).
That which they grasp as the "Great Existence" (the subject, *dharmin*) must lack a distinct intrinsic nature apart from [the categories of] substance (*dravya*) and so forth (the thesis, *pakṣa*).

This is because it is admitted that the Great Existence is not non-existent (the reason, *hetu*). It is like substance, quality (*guṇa*), and so forth (the example, *dṛṣṭānta*). If the Great Existence were separate from substance and so forth (the subject), it would not be "Existence."

Because they (the opponents) admit that existence (*sattā*) is distinct from substance (*dravya*) and so forth (the reason), it is like absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and the like (the example).
Just as there is no separate existence for non-existence, how could there be a separate existence for substance and so forth?

If there were a separate existence apart from existent things (*bhāva*), there would likewise have to be a separate non-existence apart from non-existent things (*abhāva*). Since that is not the case, how could this be so? Therefore, their [notion of] existence is merely a delusion.
Investigation:

First, two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are established to refute the existence of "wholeness" (*avayavin*). If it is admitted that it exists, then it ought not to be separate from substance, quality, and action.

If it is admitted that it is separate from substance, quality, and action, then it must be non-existent. This is easily understood; for example, as with [the concept of] "non-existence," which is not non-existent.

[The author] replies: Furthermore, he refutes [the opponent's view] by means of reasoning. The opponent claims that because this "Great Existence" (mahāsattā) exists, it is able to possess real qualities and activities;

thus, Great Existence is the "possessor" (śaktimat), while real qualities and activities are the "possessed" (śakya). Since the possessor is not the possessed, they must necessarily be distinct from one another.

Now, we raise this objection: If real entities and their activities must necessarily be possessed by a distinct "Great Existence" (mahāsattā), then this Great Existence itself must further possess an "existence-nature" (sattātva) in order to exist.
For if Great Existence were not non-existent, [it would require another existence].
Yet there is no separate entity called "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*) by which [substances, qualities, and actions] exist.
How is it that substances, qualities, and actions are not non-existent, while you must necessarily posit this separate Great Existence for them to exist?

Furthermore, if one were to allow a separate Great Existence as a distinct entity apart from substances and so forth, then one should likewise allow a separate non-existence apart from non-substances and so forth.
This is the "natureless" (*niḥsvabhāva*). Since there is no separate "natureless" apart from those "non-existent dharmas," how could there be a separate "nature" apart from these "existent dharmas"?
Therefore, that which they grasp as a "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*) possessing a nature, distinct from substance, quality, and action, is nothing but a false conceptualization.
7. Refuting the Nature of Identity and Difference (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*).

Furthermore, it is logically impossible that the nature of "reality" (sāmānya), as conceived by them— which exists as something distinct from and separate from the substance, quality, and action— is anything other than [identical to] those substances, qualities, and actions themselves.
This first section provides a general refutation; the following establishes formal arguments (*pramāṇa*) to dismantle [the opponent's position].
Let it not be that this [commonality and difference] is also not a real entity, quality, or action (i.e., the commonality and difference residing upon them).

This is because [if it were], it would be distinct from the substance and so forth [as its own separate essence], just as qualities and actions [are distinct from their substrates and thus not real entities themselves].

They maintain that the category of substance (*dravya*) is not the category of quality (*guṇa*), and the category of quality is not the category of action (*karman*). Furthermore, they hold that the category of generality-and-particularity (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) is not the categories of substance, quality, or action;

yet, they still discuss the nature of identity and difference (*tulyatva-anyathātva*) with respect to substance, quality, and action. Therefore, the present refutation states: The generality-and-particularity as it is apprehended by them is the subject (*dharmin*);
it follows that it is not the generality-and-particularity of substance, quality, and action—this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). This is the reason (*hetu*).
It is said: Because it differs from substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and activity (*karman*), it is like the categories of quality and activity, which are not the category of substance.

Furthermore, since [substance and so forth] would then be subsumed under non-substance and so on—because they differ from the nature of substance and so on—it is like the cases of quality, activity, and substance, where there is no mutual identity or difference between them.

The former inference refuted that the nature of generality and particularity (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) is unrelated to substance, quality, and action (*dravyaguṇakarma*). This present inference refutes that substance, quality, and action are unrelated to the nature of generality and particularity.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Substance, quality, and action are the subject (*dharmin*); they are not subsumed under substance, quality, and action themselves—this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is:

because they are distinct from the nature of generality and particularity that belongs to substance, quality, and action. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is, for instance, [the nature of generality and particularity itself].
Virtue and activity are indeed equal; this is because the nature of identity and difference does not transcend being provisionally established based upon all phenomena (*dharma*).
Since they falsely cling to the existence of a separate intrinsic essence that is not identical to the phenomena themselves, then the phenomena likewise are not identical to identity and difference.
If identity and difference are not identical to the phenomena, then by what would one establish identity, and by what would one establish difference? If [it is claimed that] the phenomena...
Since they are neither identical nor different, then from the perspective of one reality toward another reality, they cannot be called identical;

and from the perspective of reality toward qualities (guṇa) or activities (karman), they cannot be called different. Since there is neither identity nor difference, one should not sometimes call it "reality," sometimes "quality," or sometimes "activity."

The nature of identity and difference (sāmānya-viśeṣa) regarding earth and the other elements, when examined in relation to the substance of earth and so forth, should be understood by analogy with this.
The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that the nature of identity and difference is a real entity (*dharmin*), and not a nature of identity and difference residing upon earth and the others;

the reason (*hetu*) is that there exists a nature of identity and difference distinct from earth and the others; the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like water, fire, wind, and so forth. Furthermore, earth and the others should be the real entities.
This is precisely the thesis that [earth] and so forth do not exist. The reason (*hetu*) is stated: "Because they possess a nature of identity and difference distinct from earth and so forth.

The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is water, fire, wind, earth, and so forth. Since the nature of identity and difference is already devoid of earth, water, fire, and wind, then earth, water, fire, and wind must also necessarily be devoid of the nature of identity and difference.
If identity and difference were to be separated from earth, then earth would be like water, fire, and wind; if earth were to be separated...
Regarding identity and difference: in relation to earth, it cannot be called identical; in relation to water, fire, and wind, it cannot be called different.
Thus, through successive relations, there is neither identity nor difference. Furthermore, how could it then be called earth, water, fire, or wind?
If there were no reality-nature (tattva-tā) distinct from reality itself, then reality and so forth would likewise have no reality-nature distinct from them.
If reality-nature existed apart from reality and so forth, then non-reality-nature would likewise have to exist apart from non-reality and so forth; yet this is not the case.
How is this so? Therefore, the nature of identity and difference is merely a conceptual designation (*prajñapti*).

This is further refuted by means of reasoning. According to their view, it is by virtue of the nature of identity and difference that substances, qualities, and activities become identical or different;

yet that which effects this identity or difference is not itself the object of identity or difference. Therefore, they claim it exists as something distinct. If this were the case, then it should follow that...

Furthermore, there would be another "commonality-and-difference-nature" (sāmānyaviśeṣatva) that causes this commonality-and-difference to function as such, which would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress.

Now, just as with the commonality-and-difference-natures of real entities, qualities, and activities, there is no separate commonality-and-difference-nature of real entities, qualities, and activities that causes them to function as such;
therefore, outside of real entities, qualities, and activities, there should likewise be nothing else.
It is by means of the commonality and difference of substance, quality, and action that substance, quality, and action themselves are established as common and different.

Furthermore, if one were to admit that there exists a distinct commonality and difference of substance, quality, and action apart from substance, quality, and action, then there should likewise exist a distinct non-commonality and non-difference of non-substance, non-quality, and non-action apart from non-substance, non-quality, and non-action. As for that non-substance, non-quality, and non-action...

Externally, since there is nothing distinct that is not itself of the nature of generality and particularity, how could there be a separate "nature of generality and particularity" apart from these [real] substances, qualities, and actions?
Therefore, the nature of generality and particularity is merely a conventional designation; one must not falsely cling to it as being substantially existent.
△ Eight: Refutation of the Category of Combination (saṃghāta).

Furthermore, the referent of the category of combination as maintained by them (the subject, *dharmin*) is certainly not substantially existent (the thesis, *pakṣa*), because it is not subsumed under categories such as "substance" (*dravya*) and so forth (the reason, *hetu*), just like that which is absolutely non-existent (the example, *dṛṣṭānta*).
[Objection: They maintain that substance and so forth are obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); [Response: This shall now be examined through reasoning.

[It is] argued: Since [the whole] is not even substantially existent, how much less so can that which they themselves admit—the category of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*)—be substantially existent, given that it is not apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?
Even if they were to further maintain that conjunction is an object of direct perception, for the reasons stated above, it is still not substantially existent.

The first section, clarifying that the entities of the various categories (*padārtha*) are not substantially real, is concluded. △ Second, demonstrating that the various categories are not apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

[Thesis: Those [entities] such as "substantiality" (*dravyatva*), which are the subjects (*dharmin*) under discussion, are not directly perceived as having a self-nature (*svabhāva*) that exists independently of consciousness.
[Reason: Because they are admitted [by the opponent] to be objects of cognition (*jñeya*). [Example: Like the hair of a tortoise and so forth (which are objects of non-valid mental consciousness).
This first clarifies that the various categories (*pada*) are not objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, [the thesis is: the cognition (*jñāna*) which takes this real category as its object (the subject, *dharmin*) is not subsumed under a cognition that is a direct perception of the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of a real category apart from consciousness (the predicate, *sādhya*).
The reason (*hetu*) is: because it arises through a combination with a provisional (*prajñaptika*) dharma. It is like [the cognition] taking a quality (*guṇa*) as its object.

[Thesis: The cognition [that arises] when conditions are assembled—up to and including that which is extensively explained—is not subsumed under the cognition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of a self-nature (*svabhāva*) that is separated from the assembly of consciousnesses.
[Reason: Because it is produced through conventional conjunction (*saṃvṛti-saṃyoga*). [Example: Just like the cognition of reality (*tattvajñāna*), etc. (the example).
This further clarifies that the cognizing subject is not a cognition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Since the objects of the six categories lack substantial reality, the cognitions of those six categories are likewise all non-valid cognitions (*apramāṇa*). The initial formal refutation is concluded.
△ Second, the conclusion of their invalidity.
Therefore, the categories such as "substance" (*dravya*) posited by the Vaiśeṣikas are likewise merely conceptual constructs based on deluded sentiments.
The word "likewise" refers back to the Sāṃkhya school mentioned above, clarifying that both are equally false attachments without any distinction of superiority or inferiority.
△ Third, the refutation of the eight theories beginning with Maheśvara has two parts: first, the refutation of Maheśvara; second, the refutation of the remaining seven by analogy.
This consists of two parts: first, the statement; second, the refutation. Now, for the first:
there are those who maintain that there exists a single Great Īśvara whose essence is real, all-pervasive, and eternal, capable of producing all phenomena.
They reckon that this deity possesses four attributes: first, substantiality; second, omnipresence; third, permanence; and fourth, the capacity to produce all phenomena. Second, the refutation:

Their adherence to these views is irrational. Why is this so? If a phenomenon has the capacity to produce [other things], it must necessarily be impermanent. All [phenomena] that are not... [are impermanent].
That which is eternal necessarily lacks omnipresence; that which is not omnipresent is not real.
(If it were the case that) its essence is both eternal and omnipresent and possesses all functional capacities, then all phenomena should arise simultaneously in all places and at all times.

(If you argue that they) must depend on the desires of sentient beings or various auxiliary conditions before they can arise (thereby involving three causes), this contradicts your own doctrine that [the Great Lord Maheśvara] alone is the single cause.

Furthermore, either desire and its objects should also arise simultaneously, because the cause—namely, Maheśvara—is eternally present. First, the capacity to produce [effects] is refuted by showing that [the cause] is eternal, omnipresent, and real.
Next, the capacity to produce is refuted by showing that [the cause] is eternal, omnipresent, and endowed with all functional capacities.
If it were omnipresent, effects would have to arise in all places; if it were eternal, they would have to arise at all times. Being endowed with all functional capacities...
If [the Lord] were capable [of independent action], then all phenomena should arise simultaneously. If he must depend upon desire and conditions, then he is not the sole cause.
If one grants that he is the sole cause, then desire and conditions should also arise simultaneously, because desire and conditions would likewise have Maheśvara as their cause.
2. Applying this logic to refute the other seven [causes].

Other [schools] maintain that there exists a Great Brahmā, Time, Space, the Primordial Limit, Nature, the Self, or the Permanent Void, which are substantially real, possess all functional capacities, and give rise to all phenomena;
all such views are refuted in the same manner as this.
First, they calculate that Mahābrahmā is eternally abiding and substantially existent, possessing all functional capacities and giving rise to all phenomena.

Second, they calculate time. Third, they calculate space. Fourth, they calculate the primal limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), which is the primordial chaos. Fifth, they calculate spontaneity (*svabhāva*). Sixth, they calculate empty space (*ākāśa*).
Seventh, the proponents of the *puruṣa* (Self) all claim that it truly exists, possesses all functional capacities, and gives rise to all phenomena;
these are likewise refuted in the same manner as the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*). This concludes the third section, the refutation of the eight theories including the Great Lord.
△ Fourth, the refutation of the two types of theories concerning sound. This has two parts: first, the introduction; second, the refutation. Now, the first part.

There are others who hold a biased attachment to the *śabda-vidyā* (the science of grammar) among the five sciences, asserting that sound is eternal because it serves as a definitive and unchanging authority (*pramāṇa*) for expressing all phenomena.
Some maintain that the nature of all sounds is eternally abiding, not produced from conditions, but rather exists only through manifestation dependent upon conditions in order to convey meaning.
△ Second, the refutation.
Both [positions] are irrational. Why is this so? First, regarding the sound of the *Abhidharma* (the subject):

since it is admitted to be expressive (the reason), it must be impermanent (the thesis), just like other sounds (the example; for other sounds are also expressive). [Furthermore,] all other sounds (the subject)...

Furthermore, it should follow that the essence of sound is not (truly existent and) permanent (the thesis), just like jars, garments, and so forth (the example), because it depends upon various conditions (the reason).
The refutation of the two types of theories on sound is concluded. △ Fifth, the refutation of the Lokāyatika (Worldly Teacher) doctrine, in two parts: first, the introduction; second, the refutation.
Now, the first:
There are non-Buddhists who cling to the notion that the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of earth, water, fire, and wind are real, permanent, and capable of producing coarse [objects].
Regarding "form" (*rūpa*): the coarse form that is produced does not exceed the dimensions of its causes; thus, although it is impermanent, its substance is substantially existent.
Regarding the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), there are three positions: first, that it is real; second, that it is eternal; and third, that it is capable of producing coarse form.

Regarding the coarse form that is produced, they merely maintain that it is substantially existent. Coarse form is also called the "progeny-atom" (*putra-paramāṇu*), which is precisely that which is produced.
The effect and its causal dimension are also called the "parent atom" (*paramāṇu*), which is the ultimate atom (*aṇu*). This is the cause capable of producing [the effect];
that is to say, the coarse matter produced has the ultimate atom as its very substance, and therefore does not exceed the dimension of the cause.

Since it does not exceed the dimension of the cause, although it is impermanent, its substance is substantially existent. △ Second, the refutation of the two [theories]. First, the refutation of the productive ultimate atom.
Second, the refutation of the coarse matter produced [from atoms]. First:
That too is irrational. Why? Because the subject (dharmin) under discussion—the atom as it is conceived—possesses spatial parts (hetu), like a line of ants (example);
therefore, its substance must be unreal (thesis).
This first refutes [the notion of] substantiality. If atoms possessed spatial dimensions, they would aggregate to form objects, just like an ant trail;
this is because they would necessarily possess the characteristics of coming and going.
If [the atom] lacks spatial parts (reason), then, like the mind and mental factors (example), it should not combine to produce coarse resultant matter (thesis).
This next section refutes the producer: since the mind and mental factors lack physical form, they cannot aggregate to constitute coarse matter.
Since it can produce an effect (the cause), just like that which is produced [by it] (the analogy), how can you say that the atom is permanent (the thesis)?
A father must necessarily resemble his son; since the son is impermanent, how could the father be permanent? II. Refuting the gross matter that is produced has two parts:
first, refuting that it does not exceed the dimension of its cause; second, refuting that cause and effect occupy the same location. The first part also has two sub-sections. First:
First, the refutation of the [opponent's] position. Second, the refutation of their defense. Now, for the first:
Furthermore, since the produced effect does not exceed the magnitude of its cause, it should—like an atom—not be designated as coarse matter (*audārika-rūpa*).

In that case, this resultant matter (the effect-form), being identical to the atoms, would not be apprehended by the material sense organs such as the eye; this would contradict your own tenet. [Your position is:
"The produced effect is a real entity (dharma) and is not called coarse matter; it should not be apprehended by the material sense organs such as the eye. This is your thesis.
The reason given is that it does not exceed the measure of its cause, just as, for example, an atom (*paramāṇu*).

To say this contradicts their own tenets is because they maintain that while the producing atoms are invisible, inaudible, undetectable by smell, and imperceptible by touch, the resulting fruit is necessarily visible, audible, detectable by smell, and perceptible by touch.
II. Refuting the Defense, which has three parts: 1. Refuting the conjunction of dimension and quality; 2. Refuting the pervasiveness of the self-cause.
Third, the refutation of the majority view regarding conjunction (*saṃyoga*). First:

If it is argued that the resultant form (the effect) is perceived by the sense organs because it conjoins with magnitude (*parimāṇa*) and grossness (*sthūlatva*), and thus, though not gross in itself, appears gross; therefore, it is what can be apprehended by the sense organs.
This first section sets forth the salvific argument. [Thesis: It is not coarse because it does not exceed the magnitude of its causes;

[Reason: because it is conjoined with coarse qualities; [Example: like the gross resultant form (the *dharmin*). Since the resultant form which is grasped as an object (the *dharmin*) is identical in magnitude to its causes (the *hetu*), it should be like an atom (*paramāṇu*, the *dṛṣṭānta*);

[Thesis: it lacks conjunction with coarse qualities. Alternatively, [Thesis: even an atom (the *dharmin*) should be conjoined with coarse qualities; [Reason: because there is no distinction in location; [Example: like gross resultant form.

Since the color of the effect is identical to the magnitude of the cause, if the effect were identical to the cause, it should not be coarse; if the cause were identical to the effect, it too should be coarse.
△ Second, refuting the pervasiveness of its own cause.

If it is argued that the resultant form (*phalarūpa*) is omnipresent within its own constituent causes (*hetu*), and because those causes are not unitary, the resultant may be designated as "gross," then this resultant form would necessarily consist of multiple entities, just as the locations of its constituent causes are distinct.
If this were the case, this resultant form would fail to be gross; consequently, it would also not be perceivable by the sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*).
First, the opponent’s position is stated: "If the resultant form (*phala-rūpa*) pervades its own causes," this means that the produced effect pervades the producing atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Because there are many producing atoms, the resultant form becomes gross. Next, the refutation consists of two parts. First, a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is presented:
"That which is asserted by them—the produced resultant form—is the subject (*dharmin*); its essence must not [be singular]."
First school: They claim that because their locations are distinct, they are like the causes for a location; that is to say, each individual atom abides in its own position.

To this, [the author] refutes them by stating, "If that were so," and so forth, arguing that by abiding in their respective positions, they still do not constitute a coarse object and thus cannot be seen by the eye.
△ Third, the refutation of many parts combined.

If the effect is coarse because it is composed of many parts, then the many causes—the atoms—should likewise not be subtle; they would suffice as sense objects on their own, so what need is there for an effect?
Since it is composed of many parts, it cannot be substantially real. Thus, your own position is internally contradictory from beginning to end.
The opponent counters: "Gross form does not arise from the dimensions of the atoms themselves;
rather, it is because the resulting effect is a conglomeration of many parts that it constitutes gross form and is thus apprehended by the sense organs. Refutation:
If this were so, then even when many atoms are combined according to their causal dimensions, they should likewise not be subtle, and would suffice to be apprehended by the five sense organs.
Since it is already within the scope of the cause, what further use is there for the produced resultant form? Moreover, since resultant form is composed of many parts, it can be analyzed;
thus, it should not be substantially existent. Why did you previously claim that it does not exceed the measure of the cause and yet exists as a substantial entity?
Is this not a contradiction between your earlier and later statements? This concludes the first section: Refuting [the claim] that it does not exceed the measure of the cause. △ Second [section].
