Refuting the two [positions] that cause and effect occupy the same location: first, the direct refutation of cause and effect occupying the same location; second, the refutation of the defense that the essence of the effect is one.
Now, the first:

Furthermore, since both the effect and the cause are substantially existent, they must both possess spatial obstruction and therefore cannot occupy the same location, just as two atoms (*paramāṇu*) cannot.
The subject (*dharmin*) is the causal dimension of the resultant form (*rūpa*) as you conceive it; the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it does not occupy the same location;
the reason (*hetu*) is "because it possesses simultaneous material obstruction" (*sapratighatva*); the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like two atoms (*paramāṇu*).

If it is claimed that the essence and characteristics of cause and effect mutually accommodate one another—just as sand receives water or medicine enters molten copper—this describes a shifting argument.
It means that when the cause enters the color of the effect, the effect then receives the cause; when the effect enters the subtle atoms of the cause, the cause then receives the effect.
Since they are distinct entities yet coexist, how could this not be like sand receiving water or medicine entering copper? How could it not be so?
[Objection: They occupy the same location.
Who allows that the substance of sand and copper receives the water and the medicine? Or else, they must be separate and undergo transformation; they cannot be one, nor can they be permanent.
[Response: First, the refutation states: Although sand and copper occupy the same location as the water and the medicine, the sand remains sand and the water remains water.

Copper is copper; medicinal herbs are medicinal herbs. Who permits that their substance should receive water and medicine? Next, he refutes this by concession: "If it were permissible for them to receive [the substances], then they could be separated;

it would not hinder the pouring out of the water while leaving the sand behind. But upon entering [the mixture], they must undergo transformation, and one thus perceives the copper having altered its very substance."
If it can be separated, it is not one; if its essence undergoes change, it is not permanent. If it is not one, how can it be called "not exceeding the measure of its cause"?
If it is not permanent, how can you say its essence is substantially real? △ Second, refuting the rescue that the essence of the fruit is one.

Furthermore, if the substance of the coarse form-fruit were a single entity, then when one part is perceived, one should perceive the whole, because that part and this part are identical in substance.
That part would have to be exactly like this part. If you do not admit that the whole is perceived, it contradicts the principle of [substantial] unity;
if you do admit that the whole is perceived, it contradicts worldly reality. Therefore, what they maintain fails whether one advances or retreats; it is merely a matter of following [convention].

This is a false conceptualization based on emotional attachment. Fearing that they might offer the defense: "Although the causal characteristics are many, the essence of the fruit is one," [the author] refutes this. To advance [this argument] is to grant it;
to retreat from it is to deny it. The rest may be understood accordingly. This concludes the second section: the specific refutation of the thirteen schools. △ Third, the general refutation.
Section Four: Two Parts. First, the general heading; second, the specific refutation. Now, for the first:
although the various classes of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are numerous, the existent phenomena they cling to do not exceed four types.

△ Second, the specific refutation is divided into four parts: first, the refutation that the phenomenon and its nature are identical; second, the refutation that the phenomenon and its nature are different;
third, the refutation that they are both identical and different; and fourth, the refutation that they are neither identical nor different. Now, the first [part].
First, there is the position held by the Sāṃkhyas and others that the existent thing (*bhāva*) and its nature of existence (*sattā*) are identical in essence. This position is irrational.
Why? Because it would follow that all phenomena are themselves the nature of existence; thus, like the nature of existence itself, they would all be indistinguishable in essence.

This would contradict [the doctrine that] the three qualities (*guṇas*), such as *sattva*, and their derivatives—the twenty-three principles (*tattvas*)—possess distinct essential natures and characteristics. It would also contradict the differentiation of phenomena as perceived in the world.
Furthermore, if form and so forth were identical to the nature of form and so forth, then form and so forth should not possess distinctions such as blue or yellow.

There is the "existent phenomenon" (*dharma*), which refers to the twenty-three phenomena produced, such as the Great Elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth. There is the "existent nature" (*sattva*), which refers to the productive primordial nature (*prakṛti*), namely the three qualities (*guṇa*):
*sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The twenty-three phenomena asserted [by the opponent] are existent phenomena;

their essence must not differ from the [proponent's] thesis, because they are of the same nature as the existent nature (*sattva*). The example is like the existent nature itself. The rest may be understood accordingly.
△ Second, [the view] that phenomena (dharma) and their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) are distinct.

Second, [the view] that there exist phenomena and an existence-nature (astitva-svabhāva), etc., whose essences are definitively different, such as in the Vaiśeṣika school and others. Their adherence is irrational.
Why is this? It is because it must not be the case that all phenomena lack an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

If they were non-existent like that which has already ceased and is no longer perceived, it would contradict [your own tenet] that the substantiality (*dravya*) and other such natures are not non-existent, and it would also contradict what is directly perceived by the world as existing entities.
Furthermore, if form (*rūpa*) and so forth did not have the nature of form and so forth, then, like sound and the like, they would not be objects of the eye and the other sense faculties.

There are categories of existence (*dharma*), namely substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*). There is the nature of existence (*sattā*), namely the nature of Great Existence (*mahāsattā*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Those [categories] you maintain—substance, quality, and action—are the subject (*dharmin*).

Their essence is unapprehendable; this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because they lack the nature of existence (*sattā*). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like that which has already ceased to exist.
Furthermore, regarding the form (*rūpa*) you maintain, it is the subject. It should not be an object of the eye; this is the thesis. The reason is: because it is not [the category of] form.

Because it is of the nature [of sound]. It is illustrated by sound and so forth. That which they maintain—sound—is the subject (*dharmin*). The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it should not be an object of the ear.

The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is not of the nature of sound. The illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like visible form (*rūpa*) and so forth. △ Third, the refutation of being both identical and different.
Third, they maintain that the existent entity (*dharma*) and its existence-nature (*sattā*) are both identical and different, as in the case of shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and so forth.

This position is irrational. Why? Because the faults regarding identity and difference are the same as those previously mentioned; because identity and difference are mutually contradictory, their substrates (*svabhāva*) must necessarily be distinct;
and because if one were to hold that identity and difference share the same substrate, it would certainly not be established. Let it not be that all phenomena are identical.

Regarding "identity and difference": the faults of identity and difference are the same as those previously mentioned. That is to say, if they were identical, the fault would be the same as that of the Sāṃkhya school;

if they were different, the fault would be the same as that of the Vaiśeṣika school. Even if identity and difference were contradictory yet could coexist in the same substance, it would not follow that all phenomena could likewise do so.

Because they are of one and the same substance, or because oneness and difference would be merely conventional and not real, yet you cling to them as real; thus, your reasoning is certainly untenable.
If one realizes that oneness and difference are merely conventional and not real—like the reflections of water and fire appearing together in a mirror—then even if one were to speak of them...
If they were both identical and different, what would be the harm? Yet, because they falsely cling to these as being real, such a principle is certainly impossible.
△ Fourth, refuting that they are neither identical nor different.
The four [positions] that maintain that an existent entity and its existence (sattā) are neither identical nor different, such as those held by the Ājīvikas and others, are irrational. Why is this?
Because the grasping at identity and difference is identical to the grasping at sameness and difference.
That is to say, if it were not "one," it would be the same as "different"; if it were not "different," it would be the same as "one. Regarding the expression "neither one nor different":

does it function as a negation (*paryudāsa*) or as an affirmation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*)? If it were solely an affirmation, there should be no double negation. If it were merely a negation, [it would be a simple denial].
One should not hold any attachment. If it were both negation (*pratiṣedha*) and affirmation (*vidhi*), they would be mutually contradictory.
If it were neither affirmation nor negation, it would result in mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Regarding your statement that [the self] is "neither one nor different":
does this consist solely of negation, or is it solely an affirmation? If it were solely an affirmation, then either "not one" would affirm "different," or "not different" would affirm "one."
It must not be a case of neither negation nor affirmation. If it were merely a negation, then there would be nothing further to be grasped;

how then could one still maintain that both the "existent dharma" and the "nature of existence" are real? If one says it is both a negation and an affirmation, then they would be mutually contradictory.
If one says it is neither an affirmation nor a negation, then ultimately no real meaning is established, resulting in mere frivolous discourse (*prapañca*).

Furthermore, [to claim that things are] neither identical nor different contradicts what is commonly known in the world—that there exist entities that are either identical or different—and it also contradicts one's own tenet that phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) are definitively and substantially existent.
Therefore, those words are merely a forced attempt to evade fault;
let no wise person mistakenly accept them.

The Buddha-dharma frequently states that the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—are neither identical nor separate, and that phenomena (*dharma*) and their true nature (*dharmatā*) are neither one nor different.

This is because these are merely negations (*paryudāsa-pratiṣedha*), fundamentally devoid of any conceptual attachment. Thus, one realizes that all phenomena arise through conditions and lack intrinsic nature.

Because all things are like illusions and lack substantial reality, one can correctly manifest the Middle Way, remaining far removed from the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of nihilism and eternalism, or emptiness and existence.

Since those [opponents] falsely cling to the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena as being definitively and substantially existent, they merely claim "neither existence nor non-existence" as a pretext to evade refutation.
However, because this is not a negation based on the absence of such clinging, it is merely subsumed under the four types of false attribution (*catur-viparyāsa*). How could this possibly be...?
How could one take their speech as being identical [to the truth] and erroneously grant it the status of the True Dharma?

However, because non-Buddhists falsely cling to the notion that there are real dharmas external to the mind, all four propositions are termed "slanderous. If one can thoroughly realize that there are no dharmas external to the mind, [then these propositions lose their basis].

Without any attachment, the four propositions then become four gateways. That is to say: it may be that phenomena (*dharma*) and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) are identical, because a wave is nothing other than water;
it may be that phenomena and the nature of phenomena are distinct, because water is not itself the wave;

it may be that phenomena and the nature of phenomena are both identical and distinct, because they are without differentiation from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), yet possess differentiation from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).

Because they are distinct. That is to say, it is also possible for phenomena (*dharma*) and their true nature (*dharmatā*) to be neither identical nor different, because while the nature remains unchanging yet constantly follows conditions, the phenomena constantly remain unchanging while following conditions.
The first section, refuting the non-Buddhists, is concluded. △ Second, refuting the other vehicles [consists of two parts]: first, a general refutation by means of hypothetical questions;
second, a specific refutation according to their attachments. Now, the first part.
How is it that the various dharmas such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which other vehicles (yānas) maintain to exist substantially apart from consciousness, do not exist? (Answer:
Because those [dharmas] they maintain—form, the formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*)—are logically non-existent.
Not upholding the true teachings of the Mahāyāna, they cling only to the provisional explanations of skillful means; therefore, they are called followers of other vehicles (śeṣayāna).

They postulate fifty-seven dharmas across five categories: one mental dharma, forty-six mental concomitants (caitta), eleven material dharmas (rūpa), fourteen non-associated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra), and three unconditioned dharmas (asaṃskṛta).
They falsely claim that matter, the non-associated formations, and the unconditioned [do not exist].

Regarding the category of "dharmas": [the opponent] maintains that there exists a real nature distinct from mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). Therefore, we shall now refute their tenets. II. Refuting [their views] individually according to their attachments (three parts):

1. Refuting material dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*); 2. Refuting non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*); 3. Refuting unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). In the first [section], there are two parts: 1.

Refuting the opposition between the resistant (*sapratigha*) and the non-resistant (*apratigha*); 2. Refuting the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*). In the first [of these], there are again two parts: 1. First...
The outline lists two parts: the general refutation and the specific refutations. Now, for the first:
furthermore, the form that is clung to is generally of two kinds. First is the resistant, which is composed of atoms; second is the non-resistant.
It is not composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*).

"Resistant form" (*sapratigha-rūpa*) refers to the five sense organs and the five sense objects; "non-resistant form" (*apratigha-rūpa*) refers to the form included within the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
In the Mahāyāna, it is clarified that all these are the objective images (*nimitta-bhāga*) of consciousness. Other vehicles erroneously cling to the notion that resistant form is composed of atoms.
That which is non-obstructive (*apratigha*) is not composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*). Nevertheless, all such things are asserted to be real matter external to the mind.

II. Specific Refutation [of Non-Obstructive Matter]. This has two parts: first, the refutation of obstructive matter; second, the refutation of non-obstructive matter. In the first part, there are two sections: first, clarifying that obstructive matter is not real;

second, clarifying that it is merely a transformation of consciousness. In the first of these, there are again two sections: first, a brief clarification; second, an extensive exposition. Now, the first.
That resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) is certainly not substantially real, because the atoms (*paramāṇu*) that constitute it are not substantially real.

II. A detailed exposition of these two [points]: first, clarifying that the constitutive atoms are unreal; second, concluding that the constituted resistant form is unreal. The first [section] has two parts:
first, refutation based on the presence or absence of material obstruction; second, refutation based on the presence or absence of spatial dimensions.

First: If atoms possessed material resistance (*sapratigha*), they would be like jars and so forth—conventional (*prajñapti*) rather than real (*dravya*). If they lacked material resistance, they would be like non-form (*arūpa*);
how then could they aggregate to form jars, robes, and the like?

The thesis that the atom (*paramāṇu*) as you conceive it is a functional entity (*dharmin*) is a mere designation and not a reality. The reason (*hetu*) is that it possesses material obstruction (*sapratigha*).

The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like a jar or similar objects. Furthermore, the thesis that the atom as a functional entity cannot be integrated into a composite of resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) is because it lacks material obstruction.
The example is like non-form (*arūpa*). △ Second, refutation by means of the presence or absence of spatial parts (*digbhāga*).
Furthermore, if atoms possessed spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*), they would necessarily be divisible and thus could not be substantially real.
If they lacked spatial dimensions, they would be like non-material phenomena (*arūpa*); how then could they aggregate to receive light and cast shadows? (Consider this:

when the sun rises and illuminates a pillar or similar object, light and shadow appear on its eastern and western sides respectively—the east receiving the light and the west casting the shadow. Since these locations are distinct, [the atom must have parts].

The atoms (paramāṇu) that are grasped must necessarily possess spatial dimensions (digbhāga). Furthermore, when one sees or touches objects such as walls with the eye or the body, one perceives only this side and does not perceive the other part.
Since the composite object is nothing other than the collection of these atoms, these atoms must necessarily possess spatial dimensions.
Moreover, wherever atoms reside, there must necessarily be distinctions between above, below, and the four cardinal directions; otherwise, [they could not occupy space].
In that case, just as non-form (arūpa) lacks resistance and obstruction, there would be no principle for the collective aggregation of [atoms] to constitute gross form.

Alternatively, if one grants that atoms interpenetrate one another without resistance and obstruction, then they too should constitute gross form. Since you now grant that their aggregation constitutes gross form, it follows that atoms must certainly possess spatial dimensions (digbhāga).

Furthermore, since you maintain that the resistant resultant form which is produced is nothing other than the atoms themselves, if the atoms lacked spatial dimensions, then [the resistant form] should likewise [lack them].
There would be no obstruction. If you accept this, then it would not be an obstructive resistance (*pratighāta*).
Therefore, the atoms (*paramāṇu*) you maintain must possess spatial dimensions; because they possess spatial dimensions, they can be analyzed, and thus they are certainly not substantially real.

First, the refutation of atoms possessing spatial parts (*sapradeśa*) is stated as follows: "The subject (*dharmin*) is the atom; the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it is certainly not substantially real (*dravyasat*);

the reason (*hetu*) is that it possesses spatial parts and is thus analyzable; the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is such things as jars and garments. Next, the refutation of atoms lacking spatial parts (*apradeśa*) is stated as follows:
"The subject is the atom; the thesis is that it cannot aggregate to receive light and cast a shadow; the reason is that it lacks spatial parts; the example is..."
As with non-form (*arūpa*), one next further investigates in various ways to clarify that it must possess spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*); this may be understood from the text.

This concludes the first section, clarifying that the atom (*paramāṇu*) which constitutes [matter] is not real. △ Second, the conclusion that the resistant (*sapratigha*) matter which is constituted is not real.
Therefore, the existence of resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) as a substantial reality is not established.
Since it is not substantially real, it is clear that it is merely a transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*). This concludes the first section: clarifying that resistant form is not real.

△ Second, clarifying that [all things] are transformations of consciousness, in three parts: 1. A general inquiry and explanation; 2. An individual explanation based on conditions; 3. A summary conclusion.
[The argument] is established. Now, first [of all]:
"Do the five consciousnesses not have a basis and an objective support consisting of form (*rūpa*)?
This is a general inquiry. The "basis" (*āśraya*) refers to the five sense faculties; the "objective support" (*ālambana*) refers to the five sensory objects.

Although they are not formless, they are transformations of consciousness. That is to say, when consciousness arises, by the power of internal causes and conditions, it transforms and manifests as appearances resembling the eye and so forth, or visible forms and so forth;
these very appearances then serve as its basis and object-condition.
This is a general explanation. Although these ten kinds of form are not without a basis or an object of cognition, they are nonetheless the manifestations of consciousness itself.

That is to say, when the five consciousnesses arise, through the power of the internal eighth consciousness’s grasping of the seeds of the objective part (*nimittabhāga*) as causal conditions and the force of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), they manifest as the semblance of the five sense organs—such as the eye—and the five sense objects—such as visible form.

And they appear. By means of these five consciousnesses, it is precisely these manifestations of the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) produced by this eighth consciousness that serve as their direct support (*āśraya*) and indirect object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). They do not exist externally to consciousness as something composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*). II. Separate Explanations of the Support and the Object-Condition.

This has two parts: first, clarifying the support; second, clarifying the object-condition. Now, the first part: The *ālayavijñāna* is the support for the six consciousnesses. It is called the "support" because it acts as the basis for their arising. Furthermore, it is the support for the five consciousnesses in two ways: first, as the "direct support" (*samanantara-āśraya*), which refers to the immediately preceding moment of consciousness; second, as the "supporting faculty" (*indriya-āśraya*), which refers to the physical sense organs. Here, it is explained that the five consciousnesses take the manifestations of the faculties and objects produced by the eighth consciousness as their direct support and indirect object-condition, rather than being established by external atoms.
However, the sense organs such as the eye are not apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); they are known to exist through inference based on their capacity to produce consciousness.

These are merely functional capacities and are not produced by external [matter]. Since the principle of external, resistant form (*rūpa*) is already untenable, it follows that these must be merely manifestations of internal consciousness.
That which gives rise to the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth is called the "eye-faculty" and so forth. This serves as the basis for the arising of the eye-consciousness and the others;

that is to say, the five faculties beginning with the eye. Unlike the five sense objects, which can be apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), these are known to exist only through inference (*anumāna*) because they are capable of giving rise to the five consciousnesses.
Although these five faculties belong to the category of form-dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*), they are nevertheless merely...
The functional capacities upon the eight consciousnesses do not exist externally to the consciousness as atoms produced by other causes.

Since the existence of external, resistant matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*) as they are grasped has already been refuted through the aforementioned analysis, it is logically untenable; therefore, these must be merely manifestations of internal consciousness.
Because they can give rise to the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, they are designated as the "five sense organs," such as the eye-organ. This is because...
This serves as the predominant support for the arising of the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness. △ Second, the clarification of the objects of perception has two parts:
first, a general indication of their existence or non-existence; second, a detailed explanation of their existence or non-existence. Now, the first part.

Since the principle of external objects serving as objective conditions for these consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, does not exist, one must certainly admit that what is transformed by one's own consciousness constitutes the objective condition.

△ Second, the specific explanation of existence and non-existence has two parts: first, explaining that external objective conditions do not exist; second, revealing the internal [objective conditions].
Conditions are not non-existent; there are two parts: first, the refutation of attachment, and second, the conclusion by way of analogy. The first part has four sections:
first, the refutation of the view that the producer is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); second, the refutation of the view that the combination is the object-condition;

third, the refutation of the counter-argument that the atoms (*paramāṇu*) at the time of combination are the object-condition; fourth, the refutation of the counter-argument that the state of the accumulated atoms is the [object-condition].
Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). First:
that which is capable of inducing a consciousness resembling itself—this you maintain to be the object-condition for this [consciousness]. It is not merely that which can produce it;
otherwise, even causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and so forth would also be termed the object-condition for this consciousness.
This refutation of the grasping [to such a view] differs from the *Ālambanaparīkṣā*. That treatise first refutes that atoms are not the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), stating:

"Regarding the five consciousnesses, even if atoms were the condition, they would not be the objective condition, because their image is absent in the consciousness, just like the eye-faculty and so forth.
Here, however, it is the five faculties themselves that are reckoned as the objective condition; therefore, it says: "Namely..."
Regarding that which can induce a consciousness resembling itself: you maintain that these are the objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for this [consciousness].

That is to say, the eye-faculty induces the visual consciousness, and the visual consciousness resembles the eye in its capacity to see; the ear-faculty induces the auditory consciousness, and the auditory consciousness resembles the ear in its capacity to hear, and so forth.
You thus maintain that those five faculties are the objective conditions for these five consciousnesses. However, as for the objective condition...
As for the condition (*pratyaya*), it must possess both the meanings of "being able to produce" and "carrying an image"; it is not merely the single meaning of "being able to produce.

If that which is merely able to produce could be called an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), then since both the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) also possess the single meaning of being able to produce, would they not also be called object-conditions?
△ Second, refuting the calculation that the conjunction (*saṃnipāta*) is the object-condition.

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): (or it may be argued that) when the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, cognize forms and so forth, they merely take a collection as their object because they appear similar to those [objects].

This too is irrational, because the appearance of the collection does not possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) distinct from the individual atoms (*paramāṇu*). For when one analyzes that [composite] object, it appears as those [atoms].
Because consciousness does not arise with respect to the characteristic of a composite object, that characteristic of a composite is not substantially existent;
therefore, it cannot be said to be the objective condition (*ālambana*) for the five sensory consciousnesses, lest things such as a second moon also give rise to the five sensory consciousnesses.
This is identical to what is refuted in the *Ālambanaparīkṣā*, though the method of refutation differs slightly.

That treatise concedes the existence of an object (*ālambana*) but denies its status as a causal condition (*pratyaya*), stating: "In relation to the five consciousnesses, even if there is an object, it is not a condition, because its substance is non-existent, just like a second moon.
Here, there is no such concession; rather, it merely establishes a formal argument (*prayoga*): "The [object] associated with..."

This is an existent phenomenon (*dharma*). It is our thesis that it is not the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the five consciousnesses. The reason (*hetu*) is that it is not substantially existent (*dravyasat*). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like a second moon.
△ Third, refuting the counter-argument that at the time of aggregation, the atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitute the object-condition.

It is not the case that atoms in a state of mutual conjunction can each serve as the objective support (*ālambana*) for the five consciousnesses, because the aspect of an atom does not exist within these [consciousnesses].

Nor is it the case that atoms individually possess a single aspect of conjunction (which could serve as the objective support for the five consciousnesses), because when they are not in conjunction, this aspect of conjunction does not exist.
It cannot be said that the state of conjunction is [identical to] the state of non-conjunction.
At that time, because these atoms possess distinct essential characteristics and forms, it is known that in the state of aggregation,
the atoms of form and so forth— just as when they are not aggregated— are certainly not the objects of the five consciousnesses.

If it is claimed that even during the state of aggregation, the five consciousnesses still take individual atoms as their objects, then it is certainly untenable that these consciousnesses do not bear the aspect of atoms.
If it is claimed that each individual atom possesses its own distinct aspect of aggregation, then it would follow that its essence differs from when it is not aggregated;
this, too, is untenable. If the essence and aspect of the atom [do not...]* *Note: The source text appears to be truncated at this point.*
If they were different, then at the time of their aggregation, the atoms would still remain individual atoms; how then could they constitute the objective domain of the five consciousnesses?
△ Fourth, refuting the counter-argument that the state of aggregated atoms constitutes the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
There are those who maintain that when individual atoms (*paramāṇu*) such as form (*rūpa*) do not aggregate, they are not the objects of the five consciousnesses;

however, when they are in a state of mutual aggregation, a coarse characteristic (*sthūla-lakṣaṇa*) arises through their reciprocal support, and this becomes the object of those consciousnesses. They hold that this characteristic is substantially real and constitutes the objective referent (*ālambana*).
This describes a shift in argument. The coarse aspect constitutes the object-field (*ālambana*) of this consciousness; this is the sense of being "endowed with an aspect" (*sākāra*).
That aspect is not separate from the atoms (*paramāṇu*), and its substance is substantially existent; this is the sense of being "endowed with the capacity to produce.
Since these two factors are complete, it serves as the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for this consciousness.
That position is untenable because, at the stage when atoms are gathered together in a mass, their essential nature is identical to that when they are not yet gathered.

(If it were claimed that the five consciousnesses take those gathered atoms as their object, then, just as with objects such as jars and bowls—where the size is the same—the atoms that constitute them would also be identical.

Consequently, the consciousnesses perceiving the characteristics of those [jars and bowls] should have no distinction between them. (If there were a distinction between the jar and the bowl, then, at the stage when they are gathered together, each individual atom...)

Each [consciousness] must abandon the subtle and circular characteristics [of atoms]; for if they were not abandoned, the consciousness that takes coarse characteristics—such as those of jars or bowls—as its object would be unable to take the subtle characteristics of infinitesimal atoms as its object.

If one were to allow that a consciousness of coarse characteristics could take a realm of subtle characteristics as its object, then other consciousnesses taking other realms as their objects would likewise [be able to do so], leading to mutual confusion among all objects.
Because a single consciousness would then have to take all objects as its cognitive domain.
For example, suppose there is one jar composed of ten thousand atoms, and another small bowl also composed of ten thousand atoms;
since both consist of an equal number of ten thousand atoms, what difference could there be between them? You maintain that the five consciousnesses take those atoms as their objects...

If atoms were to aggregate in subtle harmony, one should not perceive the distinction between jars and bowls. If such distinctions are perceived, then the atoms must have abandoned their original characteristics.
If the atoms do not abandon their original characteristics, then [the aggregates] would be incapable of being apprehended by the five consciousnesses.

If you grant that the five consciousnesses with coarse characteristics can take extremely subtle characteristics as their objects, then you must also grant that visual consciousness can take sound, odor, taste, and tangibles as its objects.
How could this possibly be acceptable? This concludes the first part: the refutation of the attachment. II. Conclusion by way of analogy.
If even granting the existence of atoms leads to such faults, how much more so when there are no truly existent atoms external to consciousness?
All the various refutations presented above were made even while conceding that atoms are real; yet they still incur such errors.
How much less could there be any truly existent atoms distinct from consciousness? How, then, can one maintain that there are external objects of perception?

This is indeed the condition (*pratyaya*). Having first clarified that external objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) do not exist, [it follows that] one definitively knows that the semblances of form and so forth transformed by one's own consciousness serve as the objective conditions for the five consciousnesses. Part Two: Revealing that internal objective conditions are not non-existent.
By this, it is known with certainty that the semblances of form and so forth transformed by one’s own consciousness (as the basis) function as the objective conditions for the [five] consciousnesses.
The seeing-portion arises based on that [object] (appearing as if it were form) and undergoes transformation; because it bears its image (its aspect), it takes that as its object of cognition.
"Carrying that image" is the meaning of the two characters "object-condition" (*ālambana*). "Arising in dependence upon it" is the meaning of the single character "condition" (*pratyaya*).
This correctly explains the object-condition: it is exclusively the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) transformed by one's own consciousness, and not a phenomenon external to the mind.
However, when consciousness transforms [into an object], it manifests instantaneously as a single image according to the magnitude of that objective essence;
it does not transform separately into a multitude of atoms (paramāṇus) that then combine to form a single entity.

In the Āgamas and other sūtras, the Buddha spoke of atoms merely to enable those who cling to coarse matter as having substantial reality to analyze it away [so they may know its lack of reality]; it was not said that all forms actually possess atoms. Furthermore, [this is the case].
The masters of yoga, through their conceptual wisdom (*parikalpita-prajñā*), gradually analyze and deconstruct coarse material forms until they reach that which cannot be further analyzed;

this is conventionally designated as the "ultimate atom" (*paramāṇu*). Although these ultimate atoms still possess spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*) and thus remain analyzable, if one were to further deconstruct them, they would appear as mere emptiness and would no longer be called "form. Therefore, it is said that the ultimate atom is the limit of form.
This clarifies that the images transformed by consciousness are like those in a mirror, which change instantaneously according to their dimensions;

it is not the case that atoms are first transformed and subsequently combined to form objects. Next, further doubts are addressed: the "atoms" mentioned in the teachings do no more than indicate that coarse matter is provisional;
they do not imply a separate admission that atoms are substantially real. Furthermore, regarding what is seen in meditative observation:
An atom (*paramāṇu*) is merely a provisional designation for the limit of form based on conceptualizing wisdom; how could there ever be a real atom existing outside of the mind?
*Yoga*—here translated as "correspondence"—refers to one who practices meditative concentration on conceptualized objects according to the Mahāyāna principle;
because object and principle correspond, such a person is called a *yogācāra*. The two explanations based on the [two types of] conditions are complete. △ Third, the summary.
Established.
From this, one should know that all resistant forms (*sapratigha-rūpa*) are manifestations of consciousness and are not composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
This concludes the first section: Refuting Resistant Forms. II. Refuting Non-Resistant Forms (*apratigha*).
The remaining non-resistant forms (*apratigha-rūpa*), being of the same category as these resistant ones, are likewise not substantially real.

Alternatively, because they are non-resistant—just like the mind and mental factors—they certainly cannot be real matter. While all resistant forms possess manifest characteristics of matter, even when investigated through reasoning, they do not exist apart from consciousness;
how much less so for non-resistant forms, which lack manifest characteristics of matter? How could they possibly be said to be truly real matter?

Dharma. The shadows cast by the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) after they have ceased are called "non-resistant form" (*apratigha-rūpa*); this is precisely the object-field of dharma (*dharma-āyatana*). The first section, refuting resistant and non-resistant [form], is concluded. II.

Refuting Manifested and Unmanifested Form (*vijñapti-avijñapti-rūpa*), in three parts: 1. A general inquiry and explanation; 2. A specific refutation of attachments; 3. A conclusion establishing [the position of] "only" [consciousness].
Consciousness. Now, first:
[The opponent asks,] "Are not informative and non-informative form (*vijñapti-avijñapti-rūpa*) truly existent? [The answer is: These are not truly existent. Why is this so?

△ Second, the specific refutation of the two attachments: First, the specific refutation of informative and non-informative form; second, the general clarification of the three paths of action (*karmapatha*). First:

Furthermore, there are three [parts]: first, the refutation of bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*); second, the refutation of vocal intimation (*vāg-vijñapti*); and third, the refutation of non-intimation (*avijñapti*). Now, for the first:

if bodily intimation were substantially existent, what would its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) be? If one says it is shape (*saṃsthāna*), then it is not substantially existent, because it is analyzable.
This is because when shapes such as long and short are analyzed down to their ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), they can no longer be perceived. If one says it is...
Motion (*gati*) is also not substantially existent, because it perishes as soon as it arises (without reaching another location). This is because there is no sense of movement or transition;

furthermore, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) perish without depending on a cause. If their destruction were to depend on a cause, it would follow that they are not yet destroyed [at that time], since they would then be established as effect-phenomena (*phaladharma*).

If one were to claim that there exists a distinct kind of form (*rūpadharma*)—neither manifest color (*varṇarūpa*, such as blue or yellow) nor shape-color (*saṃsthānarūpa*, such as long or short)—which is produced by the power of the mind, [it is refuted as follows:]...

To claim that this [kind of matter] can move the hands and so forth, and thus name it "bodily informative action" (*kāyavijñapti-karman*), is also logically untenable. If this single type of matter were itself movement, [it would follow that matter is impermanent].

The refutation of this argument is as previously stated. If it were a cause of motion, it would be identical to the wind element; yet the wind element lacks a substantial essence (*svabhāva*) and cannot be manifested, so it should not be termed "informative" (*vijñapti*).
Furthermore, since wind consists of the subtle element of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*), and tangibility is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it cannot correspond to the nature of good or evil.

It should be understood that the same applies to manifesting odor and taste, which are likewise exclusively indeterminate. Therefore, bodily informative action (*kāyavijñaptikarma*) is certainly not substantially real.

Among the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), visible form (*rūpa*) is of two kinds: first, manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*), such as blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth; this is also called "substantial color" (*dravya-rūpa*).
Second, shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*), such as long, short, square, round, and so forth; this is also called "conceptual color" (*prajñapti-rūpa*).
As for sound, odor, taste, and tangibility, although they are termed substantial colors, none of them are manifest colors nor are they shape-colors; they are merely resistant (*sapratigha*).

That is all. Furthermore, among the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), only the two of visible form (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*) pertain to all three natures—wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

The other three—odor, taste, and touch—belong exclusively to the indeterminate. Since bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*) now pertains to actions of all three natures, one should not take touch, odor, or taste as bodily intimation. The rest may be understood accordingly.

However, with the mind as the cause, the material forms such as hands manifested by the fundamental consciousness arise and perish in a continuous succession, moving toward other locations (though there is no actual motion).
Because it represents the mind, it is conventionally designated as "bodily intimation."
Previously, the physical manifest (*kāya-vijñapti*) was refuted as being non-substantial. This clarifies that conventional designations (*prajñapti*) are not destroyed;

yet these conventional designations depend solely upon the transformations of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*), thereby manifesting back toward the mind. Ultimately, there are no real dharmas external to the mind. △ Second, the refutation of the vocal manifest (*vāk-vijñapti*).
Vocal intimation (*vāg-vijñapti*) is likewise not substantially existent as the nature of sound. A single momentary sound—even if granted to be substantial—lacks the capacity for signification.

While a multi-momentary continuum possesses the capacity for signification, it is not substantial. Furthermore, external resistant form (*bāhya-pratigha-rūpa*) has already been refuted previously; thus, one must not continue to maintain that it is substantially existent.

However, due to the sixth consciousness, the consciousness (in the above passage) transforms into what resembles sound; arising and ceasing in continuous succession, it appears as if there were representation.
It is not contradictory in principle to describe these as "provisional names" (*prajñapti*) and "vocal intimation" (*vāgvijñapti*).

This is because one first refutes the attachment to substantiality and subsequently establishes the provisional name, as can be understood from the text. △ Third, the refutation of non-intimation (*avijñapti*).

Since the manifest (*vijñapti*) is in fact non-existent, how could the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) be real? Nevertheless, it is established as a designation based on the limits set by the wholesome or unwholesome intentions and vows;

thus, there is no logical contradiction. That is to say, this unmanifest is either designated based on the stage when the seeds—perfumed by the wholesome or unwholesome intentions that give rise to superior bodily and vocal actions—increase;
or it is designated based on the cessation of the two evils of body and speech within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Because they are established based on volition (*cetanā*), these two kinds of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) are both conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*).

Non-informative matter is precisely that which is unconditioned and formless. This, in turn, is twofold: first, the discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*); second, the discipline co-existent with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*).

Discipline can be either wholesome (*kuśala*) or unwholesome (*akuśala*), whereas that which is co-existent with concentration is exclusively wholesome. The reason for not mentioning the discipline co-existent with the Path (*mārga-sahaja*) is as follows:

The Path (*mārga*) can also give rise to non-informative action (*avijñapti*). However, since it is produced by the power of the Path, one certainly does not conceive of it as a real entity external to the mind;

therefore, it is not analyzed here. Regarding the production of superior bodily and vocal unwholesome volitions: this refers to the mental resolve to engage in unwholesome disciplinary acts (*asaṃvara-karman*) for a certain duration.
This mind perfumes the foundational consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), thereby giving rise to non-informative unwholesome discipline (*asaṃvara-avijñapti*) for that same duration.
This is the ritual procedure. One generates a superior resolve through body, speech, and wholesome intention—namely, the mental aspiration to receive a particular virtuous precept.

This mind perfumes the foundational consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), thereby giving rise to a corresponding non-informative (*avijñapti*) precept. Within meditative concentration, one cultivates the intention to cease unwholesome conduct;

this is the precept concomitant with concentration (*samādhisamvara*), which likewise gives rise to the non-informative. Because it consists merely in the non-performance of evil, it is termed "non-manifest" (*avijñapti*). First, the specific refutation [of the opponent's view].
The discussion of manifest and non-manifest [action] is concluded. △ Second, a general explanation of the three paths of action.

In the sūtras, the World-Honored One taught that there are three types of karma; yet, by now speaking only of the volition of mind (*cetanā*) while negating (the existence of) bodily and vocal karma, does this not contradict the sūtras?

[Answer: It does not negate [bodily and vocal karma] as being non-existent; it merely states that they are not the "substantial" form (*rūpa*) as you [opponents] conceive them to be. Rather, it refers to the volition that can move the body.
That which is associated with the body is called bodily action (*kāyakarman*). The volition (*cetanā*) that initiates speech and is associated with speech is called vocal action (*vākkarman*).
Because both types of volition—deliberation (*vitarka*) and determination (*vicāra*)—are associated with the mind and cause movement within the mind, they are called mental action (*manaskarman*).
The volition that initiates body and speech, when it performs an action, is called "karma" (this refers to the karma of body and speech).

Because this [volition] is that which is traversed by the two types of deliberative volition (*niścaya-cetanā*), and because it universally produces the two kinds of ripened fruits (*vipāka-phala*)—either suffering or happiness—it is also called a "path.
Therefore, the seven preceding paths of action (of body and speech) also have volition as their intrinsic nature; alternatively, they are [the paths] of body and speech.

Although the manifest [action] (vijñapti) is not itself volition (cetanā), because it is set in motion by the intermediate volition, it is metaphorically designated as "action" (karma). Furthermore, because it is that which is traversed by volition, it is called a "path of action" (karmapatha).
Volition (*cetanā*) is of three kinds: first, volition that initiates action; second, volition that deliberates; and third, volition that determines.

"Path" (*mārga*) means a road or a way through which one passes; the rest is self-evident. This concludes the second section: the specific refutation of attachments. △ Third, the summary of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).
From this, one should know that there is truly no external form; there is only internal consciousness, which transforms and appears as if it were form.

This concludes the first section, the refutation of material phenomena (rūpa-dharma). △ Second, the refutation of non-associated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra) in three parts: first, a general demonstration that they lack substantial reality or function;
second, a specific refutation of acquisition (prāpti), non-acquisition (aprāpti), and so forth; third, a collateral refutation of the attachment to latent dispositions (anuśaya). Now, the first part:
The dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are likewise not substantially existent. Why is this?

Because acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), and so forth do not possess a substantial nature or characteristic that can be apprehended like that of matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), or mental factors (*caitta*); nor is a function distinct from matter, mind, or mental factors that can be apprehended.
From this it is known that [this entity] is certainly not substantially real; rather, it is a provisional designation based upon the states of form and so forth. (Thesis:
This existent phenomenon is certainly not a separate substance or function distinct from form, mind, and mental factors, just like form, mind, and so forth. (Reason:

Because it is admitted to be included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), or because it is not included among mind, mental factors, form, or the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). (Example: Just like absolute non-existence. It is certain.
[Thesis: It is not substantially existent; [Reason: because it is not subsumed under any other real dharma; [Example: like other conventional dharmas. [Conclusion:
It does not have a substantial essence.

"Associated" (*saṃprayukta*) means "harmonious. Because [factors] such as acquisition (*prāpti*) are not capable of being cognitive objects (*ālambana*), they do not associate with the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).

Because they lack material resistance (*sapratigha*), they do not associate with material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*). Because they possess arising and ceasing (*utpāda-vyaya*), they do not associate with unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

Since they are distinguished from these four categories of phenomena, they are termed "dissociated formations" (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). In the Mahāyāna, these are considered provisional (*prajñapti*).

Twenty-four types [of atoms] are established, none of which exist as real entities external to consciousness. The Hīnayāna establishes fourteen types, all of which they grasp as being substantially real;
therefore, they are now refuted. Generally, when presenting the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this term is used as the subject (*dharmin*) of the proposition.
This refers to the fourteen types of positions held by others. One says: "The thesis is that there is certainly no real entity or function distinct from matter, mind, and mental factors;

the reason is that they are admitted to be subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); the example is like matter, mind, and so forth. Another says: "The thesis is that they are certainly not substantially existent;
the reason is that they are either not subsumed under mind, mental factors, matter, or the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); the example is..."
Just as [something] is ultimately non-existent. Third, [the argument]: The thesis is that [acquisition and non-acquisition] do not possess a real substantial entity (*dravya-svabhāva*).

The reason (*hetu*) is: "Because they are not subsumed under other real dharmas (*dharma*). The example (*udāharaṇa*) is: "Like other conventional dharmas (*prajñapti-dharma*). Here, "other real dharmas" refers to form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and mental factors (*caitta*);

"other conventional dharmas" refers to things such as reflections in a mirror, flowers in the sky, or the moon in water. II. A detailed refutation of acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), and so forth, in six parts. First, the refutation of acquisition (*prāpti*).

It is not attained. There are six [points]: first, the destruction of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*); second, the destruction of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); third, the destruction of mindless meditative absorptions (*acittaka-samādhi*, etc.);

fourth, the destruction of the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*); fifth, the destruction of the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*). Regarding the first two: first, the interrogation, response, and refutation;
second, the conclusion and presentation of the correct principle. Now, the first [of these].
Furthermore, how is it known that acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) possess a real entity and function distinct from form, mind, and so forth? Because it is stated in the Sūtra:
"Such a person is endowed with wholesome and unwholesome [dharmas]; the noble one is endowed with the ten dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)."
Furthermore, it is said that ordinary beings do not possess the noble dharmas, while all Arhats do not possess the afflictions.
The terms "possessing" and "not possessing" correctly indicate acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).
Furthermore, "That [is] below" refers to the Mahāyāna inquiry. "The Sūtra [is] below" refers to the response from the other vehicles. The ten dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are:
right speech, right action, right livelihood, right mindfulness, right concentration, right view, right intention, right effort, right liberation, and right knowledge.
The Sūtras do not state that these [attainments] possess a real substance or function distinct from matter, mind, and so forth; thus, they fail to establish [your] proof.

Furthermore, it is said that a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) accomplishes the seven jewels. Could it be that he actually accomplishes the bodies of others—such as female attendants, elephants, and horses—or the insentient objects such as the jewel and the wheel?

If you argue that "accomplishment" is a metaphorical designation for having mastery over the jewels (rather than a separate, substantially existent dharma called "attainment"), then [the same would apply to] all sentient beings regarding their wholesome...
Regarding unwholesome dharmas, why do you not allow that they are likewise established through conventional designation? Why must you insist that there is a "possession" (*prāpti*) as a real entity?

If you argue that because the seven treasures exist in the present, they can be conventionally designated [as such], how do you know that the wholesome and unwholesome dharmas being established [in this way] exist independently of the present?

If they were independent of the present, then it would follow logically that these real dharmas—both wholesome and unwholesome—would not exist at all; therefore, there must necessarily be wholesome seeds in the present.
Because they are equal.
The following sections all constitute Mahāyāna refutations. The term "equal" refers to the seeds of evil and the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*).
Previously, it was clarified that acquisition has no essence; subsequently, it is further clarified that acquisition has no function.

Furthermore, regarding this "acquisition" (*prāpti*) of dharmas, what superior function does it possess? If one says that it is the cause capable of producing [dharmas], then all sentient beings should produce unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) noble dharmas by means of this acquisition.
Moreover, insentient things such as grass and trees do not possess this acquisition; they should therefore never arise.

Yet, why is it that insentient things are currently seen to arise? Furthermore, those who have not yet acquired wholesome dharmas, or those who have acquired them but have already lost them, would likewise lack this acquisition and thus should never [attain] them.

[Regarding] the arising [of wholesome dharmas]: Why is it that wholesome dharmas which have not yet been attained are now attained, and there are also those wholesome dharmas which were previously lost and are later regained?

If you claim that although they are not currently being attained because they were either unattained or already lost, they can nevertheless arise by virtue of having "simultaneously-arisen" acquisition (*sahaja-prāpti*) as their cause, then the two types of "arising" (*jāti*) and "arising-of-arising" (*jāti-jāti*) that you maintain would be useless.
Furthermore, if [the cause] possesses the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—as simultaneously-arisen acquisitions, then at one and the same time, the wholesome...

Evil and neutral [dharmas] should likewise manifest all at once. If it is argued that they do not manifest all at once because they await other causes, then this "acquisition" (prāpti) would be useless.

If one further maintains that acquisition is the cause of non-loss for dharmas—since sentient beings accomplish those [wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth] dharmas by means of this cause of acquisition—then all dharmas that can be accomplished are never separate from sentient beings. If they were separate from sentient beings...
Sentiment is truly unobtainable; therefore, with respect to dharmas, both [attainment and non-attainment] are useless. Since attainment is truly non-existent, non-attainment is likewise non-existent.
This concludes the first section: the interrogation, response, and refutation. △ Second, the conclusion and presentation of the correct principle.

However, based on the various states (*avasthā*) of phenomena that can be established in relation to sentient beings, three kinds of "attainment" (*samanvāgama*) are provisionally designated: first, attainment as seeds (*bīja-samanvāgama*);

second, attainment through mastery (*vaśitā-samanvāgama*); and third, attainment as manifest activity (*samudācāra-samanvāgama*). The term "non-attainment" (*asamanvāgama*) is likewise provisionally designated as the opposite of these.

Although there are many such categories, they are here provisionally designated in the state where the seeds of the false afflictions (*mithyā-kleśa*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) within the three realms have not yet been permanently destroyed.
Non-acquisition is termed "the nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*), because one has not yet attained the various noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).

Acquisition by way of seeds means that the untainted wholesome seeds have not been destroyed. Acquisition by way of mastery means that the roots of wholesome application (*prayoga-kuśalamūla*) have induced unimpeded [realization].
Acquisition by way of manifestation means that one has already entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and directly realizes the untainted noble [dharmas].
This is a dharma. Because it is established through this [attainment], its opposite is designated as "non-attainment" (*aprāpti*).

Although this non-attainment is not of a single type, for the time being, regarding those prior to seeing the Path who have not yet acquired the noble dharmas, it is termed "the nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*).

However, how could there be a real dharma of attainment or non-attainment existing separately outside the minds of sentient beings? △ Second, the refutation of the "homogeneous character" (*nikāyasabhāga*), in two parts.
First, the refutation through inquiry and response; second, the conclusion and presentation of the correct meaning. Now, for the first:
How is it known that there exists a real *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) distinct from form, mind, and so forth? Because it is taught in the Sūtra. As the Sūtra says:
"This is the homogeneity of those devas; this is the homogeneity of these humans," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, as below, the Mahāyāna poses the inquiry, and the Sūtra (or the remaining vehicle) provides the answer.
This sūtra does not state that there exists a real *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) distinct from form, mind, and so forth; therefore, it cannot serve as proof [for its existence].

If you claim that because similar cognition and similar speech arise based on this [entity], one knows that this *sabhāgatā* is substantially existent, then grasses, trees, and the like would also possess *sabhāgatā*, since they too can give rise to similar cognitions and similar speech regarding their own kind.
Would this not contradict the sūtra? Furthermore, if one were to conceive of "sameness" with respect to *sabhāgatā*...

If [it is argued that] this [homogeneity] arises because it has as its cause another homogeneity (of a different kind), yet that [other homogeneity] does not exist in such a way, how could this [present one] be so?

If you claim that [this homogeneity] is known to be substantially existent because it arises from that [prior homogeneity] as its cause to perform the same function and possess the same desire, [we reply:]...

This reasoning is also incorrect. Since the habitual tendencies of the past serve as the cause for the arising of a desire for common activity, what necessity is there to insist on the existence of a real, substantial "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā)?

This is the refutation according to the Mahāyāna. "Knowledge" (jñāna) means understanding; "speech" (vāk) means expression; "action" (kṛtya) means that which is performed; and "desire" (chanda) [means the wish].

This refers to what is intended by the vow; the rest may be understood accordingly. The interrogation, response, and refutation are now concluded. △ Second, the conclusion and presentation of the correct principle:
However, based on the distinctions among the similar states of the bodies and minds of sentient beings, "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) is provisionally established.
△ III. Refuting the Vitality Faculty (Jīvitendriya). 2. First, the interrogation and refutation; second, the conclusion and presentation of the correct meaning. Now, the first:
How is it known that there is a real vitality faculty distinct from form, mind, and so forth? Because it is taught in the Sūtra. As the Sūtra says:
Regarding the triad of vitality (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*): it should be understood that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is designated as "vitality.
This is also a question from the Mahāyāna, to which the other vehicles respond.

This sutra does not state that there exists a real entity of vitality distinct from form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth; thus, the proof is unestablished. Furthermore, this has already been established previously.

Since matter (*rūpa*) is not distinct from consciousness (*vijñāna*)—for warmth (*uṣman*), which is a material phenomenon, is never separate from consciousness—one may infer that there is no separate life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) apart from consciousness.
Furthermore, if the life-faculty were a real entity distinct from consciousness, it would have to be like feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth.

[Objection: If that is so, how does the Sūtra speak of three factors? [Reply: They are spoken of as three because their meanings are distinct, just as in the case of the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). [Objection: In the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), there is longevity (*āyus*) and warmth...

[Objection: It should not exist, because consciousness does not exist [there]. [Response: Does the Sūtra not state that "consciousness does not depart from the body"? [Objection: If that is so, how can it be called a "state without mind"? [Response:

That [cessation] refers to the cessation of the *pravṛtti-vijñānas* (active consciousnesses), not the *ālaya-vijñāna*. This consciousness possesses the causes for existence; this shall be explained in detail later.

This consciousness is sufficient to serve as the substance (*ātman*) of the three realms, the six destinies, and the four modes of birth, because it is a pervasive, constant, and continuous result of maturation (*vipāka*). There is no...
The claim that there exists a separate, substantially real life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is refuted by this Mahāyāna school.
First, they formally state the inference as follows: "Life-faculty" is the subject (*dharmin*); it does not exist as a separate, substantial entity, this is the thesis (*pakṣa*).

The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is not separate from consciousness (*vijñāna*). The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is like warmth. Next, they further state another inference: regarding that which is clung to [by the opponent]...

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is a functional phenomenon (*dharma*). It is not a substantial life-faculty; this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is substantially existent as something distinct from consciousness (*vijñāna*).

The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth. Regarding the three challenges and three responses that follow, their meaning is all readily understandable. As for the statement that they are explained separately according to their specific meanings:

There is only the single *ālaya-vijñāna*. In terms of its objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) as material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), that which is apprehended by the body-faculty (*kāya-indriya*) is called "warmth" (*uṣman*).

In terms of its seeds (*bīja*), which can sustain the root-body (*indriya-śarīra*), it is called "life-span" (*āyus*). In terms of its manifesting self-substance (*svabhāva*), it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). This is like the four right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*):

there is only a single vigor (*vīrya*), yet it is spoken of as four distinct categories based on the objects of cultivation—the abandonment of arisen and unarisen evil, and the cultivation of arisen and unarisen good. [This concludes] the interrogation and response.
The refutation is concluded. △ Second, the conclusion and presentation of the correct meaning:
However, based on the seeds that directly produce this eighth consciousness, the functional capacities (which sustain the body) induced by [past] karma possess specific differences;
these determine the duration of the persistence of form and mind, and it is upon this basis that "life-faculty" (*jīvitendriya*) is provisionally established.

△ Four: Refuting the Non-existence of the Two Mindless Absorptions, etc., in Two Parts. First, the interrogation, response, and refutation; second, the conclusion and presentation of the correct meaning.
Now, the first:
Furthermore, how is it known that the two mindless absorptions and the maturation of non-conception possess a real intrinsic nature distinct from matter, mind, and so forth?
If there were no real nature [of seeds], it would be impossible to prevent the mind and mental factors from arising.
Furthermore, as follows: "If there were no... is the inquiry of the Mahāyāna; "The other vehicles answer... is the response of the other vehicles.
The two mindless attainments refer to the non-Buddhist attainment of non-conception and the noble one’s attainment of cessation. The maturation of non-conception refers to the fourth dhyāna.
One conceives of the fruit of the formless realm (*ārūpya*).

If, in the state of being without mind, there were a distinct, real dharma—different from matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*)—that could obstruct the mind, it would be called the "mindless absorption" (*acittaka-samāpatti*).
Similarly, when matter is absent, if there were a distinct, real dharma—different from matter and mind—that could obstruct matter, it would be called the "formless absorption" (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).

Since that is not the case, how could this be so? Furthermore, why must there be real entities to obstruct the mind? Even conventional designations, such as embankments and dikes, are capable of obstruction.
This is the refutation according to the Mahāyāna. First, it establishes a parallel difficulty based on the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*);

next, it uses the metaphor of a dam to show that even the provisional (*prajñapti*) can serve as an obstruction. Both points may be understood from the text itself. The interrogation, response, and refutation are now concluded.
△ Second, the conclusion and restatement of the correct meaning.

This refers to the time when one cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*). During the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of concentration, because one feels aversion toward the coarse and restless mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), one generates a superior aspiration and restrains the mind and mental factors, causing them to become increasingly subtle and faint.
At the moment of the extremely subtle mind, this perfumes the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), establishing seeds of an intensely predominant state of aversion toward the mind and so forth.
Because these seeds of the mind and other factors have been impaired and suppressed by this process, the coarse and restless mind—

Because these [mental factors] do not temporarily manifest, the two meditative attainments are provisionally established based on this state. Since this seed is virtuous, the meditative attainment is also termed "virtuous.

Because one seeks the fruit of non-conception prior to the attainment of non-conceptualization, the seeds perfumed thereby attract the resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) of that [heavenly] realm.
Based on this, coarse and agitated perceptions and so forth do not function; in this state, "non-conceptualization" (asaṃjñika) is provisionally established.
Because it is established based on the maturation-consciousness (vipākavijñāna), it receives the name "maturation. Therefore, these three dharmas are also not substantially existent.
The seeds of the mind of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā-citta*) and so forth refer to the seeds of the primary minds (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) associated with revulsion.
The seeds of the mind and so forth refer to the seeds of the six preceding evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and their associated mental factors.

This indicates that while the coarse and active minds and mental factors temporarily do not manifest, the subtle minds and mental factors of the eighth and seventh consciousnesses continue to manifest.

Furthermore, if one merely suppresses and extinguishes the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) along with their associated mental factors (*caitta*), it is termed the "attainment of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).

If, in addition, one simultaneously suppresses and extinguishes the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the innate self-clinging (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*) within the seventh consciousness, it is termed the "attainment of cessation" (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

In both of these states, they do not correspond with the specific object-oriented mental factor of concentration (*samādhi-caitta*); rather, the name "attainment" is applied to them only as a conventional designation. However...
Since their seeds are wholesome dharmas, their meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) are also designated as "wholesome.

Because the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) brings about the retributive fruit of rebirth in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), it is called the "retribution of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*). Thus, it is clear that these three phenomena do not exist as real entities apart from consciousness.

Scroll Two Composed by the Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu
△ Five: Refuting the Characteristics of Conditioned Phenomena (2). First, the interrogation, response, and refutation; second, the summary and presentation of the correct meaning.
Now, the first:
How is it further known that the characteristics of conditioned phenomena possess a real intrinsic nature distinct from form, mind, and so forth? Because it is taught in the *Sūtra*.
As the Sūtra says: "There are three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned," and so forth, at length.
This too is a question posed from the perspective of the Mahāyāna, to which the other vehicles provide the answer. Regarding the "three conditioned [phenomena]," this refers to what is stated below:

"In brief, there are three kinds of phenomena that definitely exist: first, phenomena known through direct perception, such as form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth; second, phenomena currently being experienced..."
Dharmas are such as jars, garments, and the like; these two types of dharmas are known by common worldly consensus to exist.

Third are dharmas that possess functional activity, such as the eyes, ears, and so forth, whose existence is established through their respective functions. These three categories encompass all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) dharmas.

The characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) are the four marks: arising, abiding, change, and cessation; this applies to both matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), as well as to jars, garments, and the like.

Furthermore, since the eye, ear, and so forth, each possess the characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, this sūtra does not state that [these] characteristics—arising, abiding, and so on—are distinct from matter and mind and possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Thus, it fails as proof [for your position].

It is not the case that the sixth grammatical case (*ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti*) necessarily expresses a separate entity; for the essence of matter and mind is precisely the characteristics of matter and mind’s arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.

Therefore, [characteristics such as] arising and ceasing cannot be the substance (*ātman*) of that which possesses them (*lakṣya*). [Furthermore, they] must necessarily be distinct from the substances [such as] matter and mind (*rūpa-citta*), lest characteristics such as solidity also be distinct from their respective substances.

Moreover, if characteristics such as arising and ceasing were to be the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) while being distinct from the substance of that which possesses them, then [the substance] would be devoid of arising, ceasing, and so forth.

Likewise, the substance of the characteristics of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) would also have to be distinct from the substances [such as] True Suchness (*tathatā*) and space (*ākāśa*). Furthermore, regarding the four characteristics such as arising...
If their essences were both substantially existent, then they should all simultaneously exercise their functions at all times—namely, arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.
If [the four characteristics] do not arise simultaneously because they are mutually contradictory, then their four substances would likewise be contradictory;
how could they possibly coexist?
The following sections all constitute the Mahāyāna refutation [of the opponent's position]. Regarding the eight inflections (*vibhakti*): first, the substance; second, the action;
third, the instrument; fourth, the purpose; fifth, the source; sixth, the possession; seventh, the location; eighth, the vocative.

Now, as for the word "of" (*-asya*) in the sūtra’s description of the three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned, this single character "one" (*eka*) signifies the sense of possession; it is precisely the sixth inflection, the possessive case. This clarifies [the point].
