The "beginningless time" refers to the realm (*dhātu*) that serves as the universal basis for all phenomena. "Realm" has the meaning of "cause.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* also states that while the substance of the various seeds exists by nature from beginningless time, they are newly perfumed and activated by defiled and pure factors.
Among sentient beings, those who possess the dharma of being capable of attaining parinirvāṇa possess all seeds—both contaminated and uncontaminated—from beginningless time.
Those who possess [the nature of] being incapable of attaining parinirvāṇa lack the seeds of the three types of enlightenment.

There are many such scriptural passages that serve as authentic proof. Furthermore, since it is taught that sentient beings inherently possess five distinct natures from the beginning, there must certainly exist innate seeds (*dharmatā-bīja*) that do not arise through perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Moreover, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that those in hell possess the three non-conditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

The faculty of outflows (*āsrava-indriya*) is the seed (*bīja*), not the active manifestation (*samudācāra*). Furthermore, it is the nature of seeds abiding in the fundamental character (*prakṛtistha-bīja-svabhāva*), which has been transmitted through successive generations from beginningless time by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-pratilabdha*).
"Parinirvāṇa" means entry. There are three kinds of bodhi: namely, śrāvaka-bodhi, pratyekabuddha-bodhi, and anuttara-bodhi.
There are five kinds of gotra: namely, the icchantika-gotra, the śrāvaka-gotra, and the pratyekabuddha-gotra.

The indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*) is the Tathāgata lineage (*tathāgata-gotra*). The three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) are as previously explained. △ Third, the summary conclusion:

By these proofs, the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) exist inherently by their very nature (*dharmatā*) and are not produced through perfuming (*vāsanā*). The same should apply to the tainted [seeds].

It is the nature of things (*dharmatā*) that seeds exist; they increase through perfuming (*vāsanā*) rather than being produced by a separate perfuming. Such is the establishment [of the system] whereby cause and effect do not become confused.

First, masters such as Viśuddhasoma and others establish only the "original existence" (*mūla-siddha*). △ Second, masters such as Nanda and others establish only "newly perfumed" (*nava-vāsanā*) existence, which also has three parts:
first, the explanation of the meaning; second, the citation of proofs; third, the reconciliation of contradictions. Now, the first [part].

There is another interpretation: all seeds arise through perfuming (vāsanā). However, because both the perfumed (bhāvya) and the perfumer (bhāvaka) have existed since beginningless time, it is said that all seeds are established from the beginningless past.

Since seeds are merely another name for habitual tendencies (vāsanā), and habitual tendencies necessarily exist by virtue of perfuming—just as the fragrance in sesame seeds arises because they have been perfumed by flowers.
△ Second, citing scriptural authority:
As stated in the Sūtras, "Because the minds of all sentient beings are perfumed by various defiled and pure dharmas, they possess an accumulation of immeasurable seeds.
The Treatise states that internal seeds necessarily involve perfuming, whereas external seeds may or may not involve perfuming.
No. Furthermore, the three types of perfuming—namely, name-and-word (*nāma-pada*), etc.—comprehensively encompass all seeds of contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena.

Since these three exist by virtue of perfuming, the seeds of the contaminated must necessarily arise dependent upon perfuming. The arising of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) seeds likewise occurs through perfuming;

thus, the various sacred teachings speak of "perfuming through hearing" (*śruta-vāsanā*), meaning that it arises through being perfumed by the sublime Dharma (*saddharma*) which flows forth from the pure *dharmadhātu*.
This is because it possesses the nature of the seed for supramundane mind.
As for the three types of perfuming: first, the habit-energy of linguistic expression; second, the habit-energy of self-clinging; and third, the habit-energy of the links of existence.
These are explained in detail as presented in the eighth fascicle. Regarding the true Dharma that flows equally from the pure dharma-realm, this refers to all...

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, having realized the wondrous principle of the pure *dharmadhātu* through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), subsequently employ subsequent wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) to accord with sentient beings, issuing forth language and script to explain and manifest the principle of the pure *dharmadhātu*, enabling all sentient beings to seek awakening by following these names.
This emanated True Dharma corresponds with the pure *dharmadhātu*; therefore, it is called "equal" (*sama*).
[This concludes the] flow. △ Third, resolving contradictions:

Sentient beings are originally distinguished by their spiritual lineages (*gotra*) not based on the presence or absence of untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*), but rather established according to whether there are obstructions or no obstructions.

As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: "If, regarding the object of True Suchness (*tathatā*), there are those who possess the seeds of the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) that are ultimately [incurable]," and so forth.

They are established as having the nature of not attaining parinirvāṇa. If there are those who possess seeds of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that are ultimately [present] but lack those of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one portion is established as the śrāvaka lineage and another portion as the pratyekabuddha lineage.

If there are none who possess seeds of either of the two obscurations ultimately, they are established as the tathāgata lineage. Thus, it is known that the distinctions among lineages exist from the very beginning.
[This is] established based on [the presence of] obstructions or the absence thereof; it is not spoken of in terms of the actual existence of untainted seeds (anāsrava-bīja).
The statement regarding the accomplishment of the three untainted seeds in hell refers to the sense that they are capable of arising in the future, not that their substance already exists.
The nature of those who do not attain parinirvāṇa is precisely the lineage of the icchantikas; the rest may be understood accordingly.

Second, the masters such as Nanda and others establish only the theory of new perfuming (*navavāsanā*). △ Third, the correct principle of Dharmapāla’s doctrine, which integrates both the original and the new, has three parts:
first, the formal explanation; second, the refutation of the preceding views; third, the conclusion. Now, the first part.

There is an interpretation that seeds each consist of two categories: first, those that are innate (*sahaja*), which means they exist naturally within the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) from beginningless time as functional distinctions among the four aggregates, five constituents, twelve bases, and eighteen elements. It is based on these that the Blessed One [taught].
It is taught that all sentient beings have, from beginningless time, possessed various *dhātus* (elements/potentials), which exist by their very nature (*dharmatā*) like a cluster of *akṣa* fruits.

Other proofs cited are explained at length as in the beginning; this is called the "seed abiding in its original nature" (*prakṛtistha-bīja*). Second is the "arising at the beginning" (*ābhisamskārika*).
This means that from time immemorial, it has existed through repeated manifestation and habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Based on this, the Blessed One taught that the mind of sentient beings is perfumed by all defiled and pure phenomena, such that it is an accumulation of immeasurable seeds.

The various treatises also state that the seeds of defilement and purity arise due to the perfuming of defiled and pure phenomena; these are precisely what are called "seeds produced by habituation" (*abhyāsa-saṃskṛta-bīja*).

△ Second, the refutation of the preceding [position] has two parts: first, the refutation of the view that [the seeds] exist only as original; second, the refutation of the view that they are produced only through new perfuming. Now, the first:
If they existed only as original, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) should not serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the ālayavijñāna. As it is said in the Sūtra:

"All dharmas reside within the storehouse-consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*); the consciousness likewise resides within dharmas. They are mutually the nature of effect and also constantly the nature of cause. The *Zongjing* commentary explains:
"All dharmas reside within the storehouse-consciousness" means that it is able to contain and store them; that is to say, it acts as two kinds of conditions for all dharmas:
first, it serves as their seeds; second, it serves as their substratum (*āśraya*). "The consciousness likewise resides within dharmas" means it is what is contained [by them].
It is also a "storehouse" (ālaya), meaning that the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the *ālaya-vijñāna* also function as two conditions for one another:
first, they nourish those seeds in the present life; second, they project and plant those seeds for future lives. This is because they arise from one another.
The meaning of this verse is that the ālayavijñāna and the various evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñānas) mutually produce one another at all times, serving as cause and effect for each other.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that the ālayavijñāna and the defiled phenomena (saṃkleśadharma) serve as mutual causes and conditions (hetupratyaya).
It is like the wick and the flame, which mutually produce and burn one another; or like a bundle of reeds, which stand supporting one another.

It is solely by relying on these two factors—the seed and the manifestation—that the principle of mutual production is established as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), for no other causal condition can be found.

If seeds were not produced through perfuming (*vāsanā*), how could there be a relationship of causal condition between the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the ālayavijñāna? [For it would mean] that they do not perfume one another to cause growth.

Even though it may be called a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), let it not be [concluded] that wholesome and unwholesome karma can produce a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*), because [karma] also serves as a causal condition for the ripened fruit.

Furthermore, various sacred teachings state that seeds arise through perfuming (*vāsanā*); all such [positions] contradict that [doctrine of] yours. Therefore, [seeds] exist only as innate (*prakṛtistha*).
Thus, [your position] contradicts both reason and scripture.

Perfuming and growth can only be termed *adhipati-pratyaya* (dominant condition), whereas perfuming and production are termed *hetu-pratyaya* (causal condition). The rest may be understood accordingly. △

Second, the refutation that [the outflow-free nature] is produced solely through new perfuming (*navābhyāsa*) has three parts: first, the direct refutation; second, the response to the teaching; and third, the concluding reproach. The first part [the direct refutation] has two sub-sections:

first, the refutation of the incorrect view; second, the revelation of the correct view. The first of these [the refutation of the incorrect view] has two further divisions: first, a direct refutation by means of the cause of the conditioned outflow-free state;
second, a refutation of the counter-argument that the nature of the mind (*cittaprakṛti*) serves as the cause of the outflow-free state. This is the first.
If [dharmas] were produced solely through initial arising, then conditioned uncontaminated (anāsrava) phenomena would not be able to arise, as they would lack inherent causes and conditions.
Furthermore, contaminated wholesome [dharmas] should not serve as seeds for the uncontaminated, lest uncontaminated seeds could also produce the contaminated.

If this were admitted, it would follow that contaminated [phenomena] could arise again even in Buddhas, and that wholesome [dharmas] and so forth could serve as seeds for unwholesome [dharmas] and so forth.

"Conditioned and untainted" refers to the bodhi of the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna-bodhi*). Regarding this bodhi of the four wisdoms, there must logically exist primordial, abiding seeds (*pūrvasthita-bīja*).
Prior to ascending the [bodhisattva] stages (*bhūmi*), all wisdom derived from hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) belongs exclusively to the tainted (*sāsrava*).
These can only serve as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) to assist those untainted seeds in gradually increasing; they cannot function as causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, if it were granted that contaminated phenomena could serve as seeds for uncontaminated phenomena, then conversely, uncontaminated phenomena would also have to serve as seeds for contaminated phenomena.

Yet, since Buddhas have already realized the uncontaminated, they would still be able to give rise to contaminated states—how could this possibly be logical? Moreover, contaminated and uncontaminated states are diametrically opposed in nature;
if these two could mutually serve as seeds for one another, then by the same logic, the two natures of good and evil, which are likewise diametrically opposed, would also [be able to do so].
Can they serve as seeds for one another? △ Second, the refutation of the further claim that the nature of the mind is the cause of outflow-free [dharmas], which has three parts:
first, presenting what they rely upon; second, refuting their erroneous understanding; third, stating the correct meaning of the sutra. Now, the first part.
Although the Vibhajyavādins maintain this position—that the sūtra states, "The nature of the mind is originally pure;

because it is defiled by adventitious afflictions, it is called 'impure'; when separated from afflictions, it transforms into the untainted (anāsrava)"—and take this as proof, they thus claim that untainted phenomena do not arise without a cause.
△ Second, refuting their erroneous interpretation.

Regarding the term "mind-nature" (cittatva), what meaning does that [sūtra] intend? If you claim that the sūtra teaches the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as being primordially pure (*prakṛtiviśuddha*), then emptiness is not the cause of the mind (the four wisdoms).
Furthermore, since the principle of emptiness is an eternal dharma (*nityadharma*), it certainly cannot be the seed of all phenomena. This is because its essence is... [prior].

Because there is no subsequent transformation [of its nature]. If you claim that the sutra teaches the mind itself to be primordially pure (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*), then it would follow—just as the Sāṃkhya school maintains—that although the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) undergo transformation, the essence (*svabhāva*) remains eternally one.
Furthermore, an unwholesome (*akuśala*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*) mind would also have to be wholesome (*kuśala*).

If you accept this [position], then even an unwholesome or neutral mind would have to be associated with faith (*śraddhā*) and other such wholesome mental factors (*caitasika*). If you do not accept this, then [your position] must be abandoned.
[An unwholesome or neutral mind] is not the essence of a wholesome mind; thus, it is not even called "wholesome," let alone being "untainted" (*anāsrava*).

Furthermore, although a tainted wholesome mind differs from the unwholesome and the neutral, since it is designated as "defiled" (*saṃkliṣṭa*), its nature—just like that of unwholesome minds—is certainly not untainted.
Therefore, no tainted wholesome mind should serve as the direct cause for what is untainted. [If one were to allow that the tainted serves as the cause for the untainted...]
[This would be] the cause of outflows. Furthermore, do not think that wholesome and unwholesome states, etc., may likewise serve as mutual causes for one another.

Moreover, if you claim that a mind with outflows (sāsrava-citta) is by nature untainted (anāsrava), then a mind that is untainted must [by parity of reasoning] be by nature tainted, because both are equally mental phenomena (citta-dharma).

Since no distinct causal conditions can be found [to differentiate them], and furthermore, if the nature of the mind of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana-citta) were untainted, then the state of being an ordinary person would be untainted.

If [you argue that] one currently manifesting [such a mind] should be called a noble one (*ārya*), yet [you maintain that] although the nature of the mind of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is untainted (*anāsrava*),

it is not designated as "untainted" because its characteristics are defiled— thereby avoiding the fault [of over-applying the term "noble"]— then since the mind is not untainted when manifesting, [it cannot be a noble mind].

The seeds of the mind are likewise not untainted (*anāsrava*). Why? Because your own treatise states that there are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who possess only the accomplishment of untainted seeds;
for seeds and their manifestation are identical in nature and characteristic.
△ Third, the presentation of the correct meaning of the sūtra.
Now, when the sūtras speak of the "purity of the nature of the mind" (*cittaprakṛti-viśuddhi*), they are referring to the *tathatā* (suchness) revealed by the principle that the mind is empty.

This is because *tathatā* is the true nature of the mind; alternatively, it is because the essence of the mind is not itself an afflictive dharma—possessing these two meanings—it is called "pure by nature."
It is not that the nature of the tainted mind is itself untainted; therefore, it is called "fundamentally pure."
The first section, the refutation of incorrect views, is concluded.

△ Second, the revelation of the correct view: From this, one should believe that all sentient beings have possessed untainted seeds since beginningless time, which do not arise through the process of perfuming.

It is established by the nature of things (*dharmatā*) that in the subsequent stage of superior progress, [the seeds] are perfumed and increased so that uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) arise.

Taking these [inherently existing seeds] as the cause, when uncontaminated phenomena arise, they in turn perfume and form new seeds, which increase and become more excellent until the perfection of Bodhi is attained.
One should understand that the seeds of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are likewise inherently existing and function in this same manner.

Second, the refutation of the position that seeds are solely newly perfumed (*navavāsanā*). This concludes the first part: the direct refutation. Second, the general explanation of the three [points], which has three sections: 1. Generally establishing that internal seeds necessarily involve perfuming; 2. Establishing that the untainted (*anāsrava*) arises through the perfuming of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*); 3. Establishing the spiritual lineages (*gotra*) based on the obstructions. Now, the first section: The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, fascicle 1, states: "The seeds of all phenomena are of two kinds: those that are innate (*prakṛtistha*) and those that are produced by perfuming (*paribhāvita*). This means that the seeds of all phenomena are established as being of two types. First, the innate seeds: these are the seeds that have been transmitted from beginningless time within the continuum of sentient beings, existing as the very nature of the mind. Second, the seeds produced by perfuming: these are the seeds that arise from the repeated perfuming of the mind by various conditions. Regarding this, some claim that there are only seeds produced by perfuming and no innate seeds at all. This is not so. Why? Because if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the Mahāyāna teachings, the seeds for the arising of the Mahāyāna path would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Mahāyāna path would never arise. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the Śrāvaka teachings, the seeds for the arising of the Śrāvaka path would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Śrāvaka path would never arise. Moreover, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the Pratyekabuddha teachings, the seeds for the arising of the Pratyekabuddha path would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Pratyekabuddha path would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Three Vehicles, the seeds for the arising of the Three Vehicles would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Three Vehicles would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Two Vehicles, the seeds for the arising of the Two Vehicles would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Two Vehicles would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the One Vehicle, the seeds for the arising of the One Vehicle would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the One Vehicle would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Four Noble Truths, the seeds for the arising of the Four Noble Truths would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Four Noble Truths would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of Dependent Origination, the seeds for the arising of the realization of Dependent Origination would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the realization of Dependent Origination would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Six Perfections, the seeds for the arising of the Six Perfections would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Six Perfections would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Ten Stages, the seeds for the arising of the Ten Stages would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Ten Stages would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Three Bodies, the seeds for the arising of the Three Bodies would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Three Bodies would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Five Eyes, the seeds for the arising of the Five Eyes would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Five Eyes would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Six Supernormal Powers, the seeds for the arising of the Six Supernormal Powers would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Six Supernormal Powers would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Ten Powers, the seeds for the arising of the Ten Powers would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Ten Powers would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Four Fearlessnesses, the seeds for the arising of the Four Fearlessnesses would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Four Fearlessnesses would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Eighteen Unique Qualities, the seeds for the arising of the Eighteen Unique Qualities would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Eighteen Unique Qualities would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Great Compassion, the seeds for the arising of Great Compassion would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, Great Compassion would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Buddha-nature, the seeds for the arising of the realization of Buddha-nature would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the realization of Buddha-nature would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Tathāgata’s Wisdom, the seeds for the arising of the Tathāgata’s Wisdom would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Tathāgata’s Wisdom would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Dharma-body, the seeds for the arising of the Dharma-body would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Dharma-body would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Sambhogakāya, the seeds for the arising of the Sambhogakāya would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Sambhogakāya would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Nirmāṇakāya, the seeds for the arising of the Nirmāṇakāya would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Nirmāṇakāya would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Three Jewels, the seeds for the arising of faith in the Three Jewels would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, faith in the Three Jewels would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Three Learnings, the seeds for the arising of the Three Learnings would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Three Learnings would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Four Foundations of Mindfulness, the seeds for the arising of the Four Foundations of Mindfulness would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Four Foundations of Mindfulness would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Four Right Efforts, the seeds for the arising of the Four Right Efforts would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Four Right Efforts would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Four Bases of Psychic Power, the seeds for the arising of the Four Bases of Psychic Power would be absent. Since they lack such seeds, the Four Bases of Psychic Power would never arise. Therefore, it is known that there must be innate seeds. Furthermore, if there were no innate seeds, then even when one hears the teachings of the Five Faculties, the seeds
Although the various holy teachings state that internal seeds definitely involve perfuming (*vāsanā*), they do not definitively state that all seeds arise solely through perfuming.
How could one then completely deny the existence of innate seeds? Nevertheless, even innate seeds must be made to flourish through perfuming before they can produce their fruit;
therefore, it is said that internal seeds definitely involve perfuming.
△ Second, both [the mundane and supramundane] are permeated by the uncontaminated through the perfuming of hearing.

This perfuming of hearing is not merely the perfuming of new contaminated seeds; rather, when one hears the true Dharma, it also perfumes the originally existing uncontaminated seeds, causing them to gradually increase and flourish until they successively give rise to the supramundane mind. Therefore, this [perfuming] is also called [the cause of the supramundane].

Regarding the nature of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) seeds newly perfumed within the perfuming of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*): these are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and are capable of producing superior maturation (*vipāka*) results;

they serve as the supreme dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for supramundane phenomena (*lokottaradharma*). Regarding the nature of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) seeds [perfumed within the perfuming of hearing]:
these are not comprised within what is to be abandoned; they serve as the direct causal condition (*hetupratyaya*) for supramundane phenomena.

However, because these primary causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya) are subtle, hidden, and difficult to comprehend, [the teachings] provisionally designate the dominant conditions (adhipati-pratyaya) of the three types of wisdom—
which are coarse and manifest— as the seeds of supramundane mind through skillful means.
△ Third, establishing the spiritual lineages (*gotra*) based on obstacles is twofold: first, the primary meaning of the nature;
second, an ancillary refutation of future births. Now, for the first:
the intent in establishing the universal and particular lineages based on obstacles is primarily to reveal whether or not the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) exist.
There are none. That is to say, if one were entirely devoid of untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*), then the seeds of those two obstacles could never be destroyed;

such a person is established as one who lacks the nature for *nirvāṇa*. If one possesses only the untainted seeds of the two vehicles (and lacks the Mahāyāna seeds), then the seeds of the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) can never be destroyed;
such a person is established as belonging to the lineage of the Śrāvaka, while another portion is established as [the lineage of the Pratyekabuddha].

Regarding the lineage of the Pratyekabuddhas: if they also possess the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) of a Buddha, then the seeds of both obstructions can be permanently eliminated, and they are accordingly established as having the lineage of a Tathāgata.
Thus, it is precisely due to the presence or absence of these untainted seeds that there is the distinction between obstructions that can be severed and those that cannot.
However, because untainted seeds are subtle, hidden, and difficult to perceive, [the classification] is made in relation to them.

If it is by means of the obstructions (which may or may not be severed) that the distinctions of the nature [of the seeds] are manifested, otherwise, what further cause would there be for those two types of obstructions such that one is capable of being destroyed while the other is incapable?

If it is argued that this distinction between the two obstructions—those that can be destroyed and those that cannot—is due to the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), then why not likewise admit the same for the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*)? If they were originally entirely non-existent...
If the seeds of the outflows (*āsrava*) were [inherently] present, then the various noble paths (*āryamārga*) could never arise. Who, then, would be able to destroy the seeds of the two obstacles?
Yet, it is said that the distinct natures of the seeds are established based on the obstacles.
△ Second, refuting [the claim] that they will arise incidentally:

Since it is certain that those noble paths have no possibility of arising, to say that the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) possess the sense of being "to be produced" in the future is also certainly unreasonable.
The second section on the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna) is concluded. △ Third, the summary and reprimand:
However, throughout various sacred teachings, it is stated everywhere that there are innate seeds (*prakṛtistha-bīja*); [your position] contradicts all such meanings.
Therefore, [the view that seeds] arise only at the beginning contradicts both principle and scripture.
2. The refutation of the preceding [view] is concluded. △ 3. Conclusion.
From this it should be known that the seeds of all phenomena each have two categories: those that are innate (*sahaja*) and those that are newly arisen (*ārambhika*).

The *Zongjing* says: "The aggregate of the eighth consciousness, as well as the objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the five matured faculties (*vipāka-indriya*) transformed by it, and furthermore..."

The matured *pariṇāma-vipākaja* sense organs (*indriya*) and the first six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) that are results of maturation (*vipāka*) possess no new seeds, because they are extremely weak and thus incapable of perfuming (*vāsana*).
They arise solely from pre-existing, original seeds.

As for the nourished (*aupacayika*) five sense organs, these matured sense organs, and the objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the five sense objects—which are outflows (*niṣyanda*) and transformations of the first six consciousnesses—all [arise from original seeds].

There may be two versions for each, namely the original and the new. The above concludes the explanation of the meanings of the "original" and "new. △ Third, the meaning of seeds (bīja) has four parts: first, explaining internal seeds; second, explaining external seeds; third, explaining how internal and external seeds possess the meaning of having two causes;

and fourth, explaining the presence or absence of perfuming (vāsanā) in internal and external seeds. Now, the first part: Internal seeds refer to the seeds of the various dharmas that exist within the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna). They are called "internal" because they are contained within the ālayavijñāna. They are called "seeds" because they are capable of producing their respective fruits. These seeds are of two kinds: those that are innate (upapattilābhika) and those that are acquired through cultivation (prāyogika). Innate seeds are those that have been transmitted through beginningless time and are present naturally within the ālayavijñāna. Acquired seeds are those produced by the perfuming of wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate dharmas. These seeds are further categorized as being either determinate (niyata) or indeterminate (aniyata). Determinate seeds will inevitably produce their fruit when the conditions are met. Indeterminate seeds may or may not produce their fruit depending on whether the necessary conditions are present. Furthermore, these seeds can be categorized as being either defiled (sāsrava) or undefiled (anāsrava), and as being either mundane (laukika) or supramundane (lokottara). This concludes the explanation of internal seeds.

However, the meaning of "seed" (*bīja*) briefly comprises six aspects. First, momentary destruction (*kṣaṇika-nirodha*): this means that as soon as its substance arises, it must necessarily perish in the immediate subsequent moment;

only when possessing superior functional power does it constitute a seed. This excludes permanent phenomena (*nitya-dharma*), for since the permanent lacks transformation, one cannot say that it possesses the capacity for productive activity.
That which is unchanging cannot be subject to immediate cessation; nor can it be said to possess the capacity for production.
Thus, it lacks superior causal efficacy. Therefore, all unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) eternal phenomena, as well as the eternal self (*ātman*) postulated by non-Buddhists, cannot be described as seeds.
Second, they must exist simultaneously. That is to say, it constitutes a seed only when it exists in a state of simultaneous conjunction with the manifest resultant dharmas that it produces.
This excludes cases where they occur sequentially or are necessarily separated. Although the manifest and the seed belong to different categories, they do not contradict one another.

Within a single continuum, there is simultaneously the capacity for production; this is not like the case where seeds produce their own kind (where the preceding seed relates to the subsequent seed), which are mutually exclusive and necessarily do not coexist.
Therefore, when a seed produces a manifest state, cause and effect are necessarily simultaneous; however, when a seed induces another seed, cause and effect are not simultaneous.
Although the cause and fruit of a seed possess both the sense of being simultaneous and the sense of being non-simultaneous, we now take only that which exists at the same time in the present.
The causal function that is capable of producing a fruit is alone designated as a "seed" (with respect to the future).

Since that which has not yet arisen [the future] and that which has already ceased [the past] lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the designation "seed" is established solely in dependence upon the production of a present active fruit (*pravṛtti-phala*). It is not on the basis of projecting its own kind [into the future] that it is called a "seed.
Therefore, one should simply say that it coexists with its fruit.

The objection states: If momentary cessation (*kṣaṇabhanga*) can serve as a seed, then since this applies to all things when viewed in relation to what precedes or follows them, or in relation to themselves or others, everything possessing the nature of momentary cessation should be able to serve as a seed. Now, let us examine this by means of the second criterion:
that which is prior and subsequent does not coexist; that which is definitively separated cannot be conjoined. Within a single body, there is conjunction, yet it is certainly not [the case that]...
They must be dissociated; only when they exist simultaneously in the present, without preceding or succeeding one another, can they be called seeds.
Therefore, phenomena belonging to another's continuum, as well as phenomena from one's own continuum that occur sequentially, cannot be said to be seeds.
Third, it must persist continuously: that is to say, only that which continues as a homogeneous stream over a long period until reaching the ultimate stage constitutes a seed.
This excludes the [first] seven evolving consciousnesses, as they are subject to change and interruption, and thus do not accord with the nature of a seed.
This demonstrates that seeds arise from their own kind.
The objection states: "If the seeds perfumed by manifest activity were also simultaneous with their fruit, they too should be called 'seeds. Now, we distinguish them by means of the third criterion:

the seventh consciousness is either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), and thus undergoes transformation; the first six consciousnesses are sometimes active and sometimes inactive, and thus have interruptions.
Only the eighth consciousness is of a single type—neutral (*avyākṛta*)—and continues uninterruptedly for a long duration."
Only after reaching the stage of the Vajra Path, within the ultimate state (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*), can it be termed untainted (*anāsrava*).
Prior to this, it constantly functions in conjunction with tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) and serves as the support for the seeds of those taints.
Therefore, the seeds of those various phenomena depend upon it to mutually induce their own kind and eventually reach maturation.

Fourth, the determination of nature (*svabhāva-niyama*). This means that only when the capacity to produce wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth is determined according to the power of its cause does it constitute a seed.
This excludes the false attachments of other schools who maintain that a cause of one nature can produce an effect of a different nature; [for us], there is the sense of having causes and conditions.
The objection states: If that which constantly evolves together is what is called a seed, then seeds such as the wholesome should produce manifest phenomena such as the defiled.
This [point] is now excluded by means of the fourth definition.
Fifth, [the seed] depends upon various conditions. This means that it must depend on the superior efficacy of the convergence of the various conditions for its own fruit;

only then does it become a seed. This refutes the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) adherence to a spontaneous cause (*svabhāva-hetu*) that, independent of various conditions, constantly and simultaneously produces fruits.

Alternatively, it refutes other schools who hold that conditions are never non-existent; here, it clarifies that the conditions upon which the seed depends do not possess a permanent nature. Therefore, regarding the seed...
[The] fruit does not arise constantly or simultaneously.
An objection is raised: If the nature [of the seeds] is determined, they are then called "seeds.

Since the seeds of the three natures are thus eternally present and co-existent, they should, at all times, give rise to the simultaneous manifestation of the three natures. Now, by means of the fifth...

The meaning is distinguished as follows: although seeds serve as the cause, they must still depend upon the harmony of various conditions (*pratyaya*) before they can produce a fruit, such as the case where visual consciousness arises from nine conditions.

Furthermore, mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) additionally depend on three conditions—namely, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Since material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) further depend on the dominant condition, they require a multitude of conditions; thus, [the notion of a single cause] is refuted.

The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) cling to the notion of spontaneity (*svabhāva*); [the seed] must have a condition (*sāpekṣa*) in order to exclude that attachment. Furthermore, it excludes the attachment of other schools that the condition is eternally non-existent.

Sixth, it "draws forth its own fruit," meaning that with respect to various distinct fruits such as form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), each [seed] draws them forth individually; only then does it become a seed.

This refutes the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) tenet that a single cause produces all effects, or the tenet of other schools that matter (rūpa) and mind (citta), etc., serve as mutual causes and conditions. It is objected:
If a nature is determined and depends upon various conditions to be called a "seed," then how can a single virtuous cause [produce] various...
When conditions converge, all wholesome fruits arise; the same applies to unwholesome and neutral [fruits].

Furthermore, when the seeds of a wholesome mind converge with various conditions, they can produce wholesome form; when the seeds of wholesome form converge with various conditions, they can likewise produce a wholesome mind.
Now, distinguishing this by means of the sixth principle, the respective and corresponding fruits each induce their own results.
When [a dharma] arises, it is not produced from a single cause as all effects; nor do form and mind serve as mutual causes and conditions for one another.
Only the specific functional capacities (śakti-viśeṣa) within the fundamental consciousness (the eighth consciousness), which possess these six characteristics, constitute seeds;
they do not belong to any other [consciousness].
The first section, clarifying internal seeds, is concluded. △ Second, clarifying external seeds.

External grains such as rice and wheat (the eighth category) are so designated because they are manifestations transformed by consciousness (subsumed under the aspect of the object, *nimitta-bhāga*); thus, the name "seed" is established metaphorically, for they are not actual seeds.
△ Regarding the meaning of the two causes possessed by the internal and external seeds of the three knowledges (*traividyā*):
the power of these internal and external seeds is able to produce all proximate and primary fruits; this is called the "producing cause" (*janana-hetu*).
Furthermore, it draws forth distant and residual fruits so that they do not suddenly cease; this is called the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
Regarding internal seeds: consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and name-and-form conditions the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and so forth.

These are called the immediate, direct fruits produced by the producing cause (*janakahetu*). After death, the remains of the corpse do not perish; these are called the distant, residual fruits drawn forth by the drawing cause (*ākṣepahetu*).

Regarding external seeds: from the seed the sprout arises, and from the sprout the stalk and so forth arise. These are called the immediate, direct fruits. After the grain and so forth have withered, they do not perish; these are called the distant [fruits].
This is a remnant fruit. However, since external seeds are said not to be actual seeds, they can only be borrowed as a metaphor for internal seeds.
△ Fourth, clarifying the existence or non-existence of the perfuming of internal and external seeds.
The seeds (of all phenomena within the eighth consciousness) necessarily arise and are nurtured through perfuming (*vāsanā*). These seeds can directly produce their fruits;
this is the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). External seeds may or may not undergo perfuming (they merely serve as) dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

If one wishes to distinguish the fruits that are produced, one must take internal seeds as the direct causal conditions for those various things (for external grains, wheat, and so forth, are all...). This is [the case].
Because it is a manifest fruit produced from the seeds of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-bīja*) within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).
External seeds are of two kinds: those with perfuming (*vāsana*), such as sesame seeds and flowers; and those without perfuming, such as seeds producing sprouts, stalks, and so forth.
Regarding what is called "the fruit produced from seeds of common characteristics," this refers to external grains such as rice and wheat, all of which—

This is because it is subsumed within the realm of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). This concludes the explanation of the meaning of seeds. △ Fourth, the explanation of the meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*) has three parts:
first, the general heading; second, the detailed explanation; third, the concluding judgment. Now, the first:

Based on what meaning is the term "perfuming" (vāsanā) established? Both the perfumable and the perfumer each possess four characteristics that cause seeds to grow and develop within the fundamental consciousness;
therefore, it is called "perfuming."
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the two [parts]. First, the explanation of the perfumable (bhāvyatā); second, the explanation of the perfumer (bhāvaka). Now, the first:
what are the four characteristics that define the perfumable? First, the quality of stable endurance (*sthira-svabhāvatā*): if a dharma continues as a homogeneous stream from beginning to end.

That which is capable of maintaining habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) is that which is perfumed (*bhāvya*). This excludes the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), as well as sound, wind, and so forth, because their nature is not stable and persistent;

therefore, they are not what is perfumed. "Of one kind" (*ekajātīya*) means stability; "continuous" (*prabandha*) means persistence. One should formulate the formal argument (*prayoga*) as follows: The evolving consciousnesses are the subject (*dharmin*).
The [proponent of] the doctrine that [the ālayavijñāna] is not perfumable states: "Because its nature does not abide firmly, like sound, wind, and so forth.
Second, regarding the neutral (avyākṛta) nature: if a dharma is impartial and non-opposing, and is capable of containing habitual tendencies (vāsanā), it is then that which is perfumable.
This excludes those whose wholesome or defiled potencies are so powerful that they leave no room for anything else; therefore, they are not objects of perfuming (*bhāvanīya*).

Consequently, the Tathāgata’s eighth pure consciousness—being exclusively and supremely wholesome—carries only the seeds previously perfumed during the causal stage (the untainted wholesome seeds), and does not receive new perfuming.

Question: If that which is of a stable nature were to serve as the perfumed, then the pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*) of the Tathāgata would also be of a stable nature and should likewise be the perfumed.
This can be understood by distinguishing it through the second definition.

Third, the quality of being susceptible to perfuming (*bhāvanīyatva*). If a phenomenon is sovereign and its nature is not rigid or dense, such that it can receive habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it is what is perfumed.
This excludes the five mental factors associated with the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
Because the mental factors depend on others (and are not sovereign), and because unconditioned phenomena are rigid and dense (and do not receive habitual tendencies), they are not what is perfumed.

Question: If that which is stable and indeterminate (avyākṛta) constitutes the perfumable (bhāvyam), then the five mental factors associated with the eighth consciousness are likewise stable and indeterminate;
furthermore, unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) are also stable by nature.
Why are they not perfumable? Now, this is distinguished by means of the third criterion.

Fourth, it must possess the nature of being in mutual conjunction with the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*). If it is simultaneous and co-spatial with the perfuming agent—neither identical nor separate—it is then the perfumable (*vāsyatva*).
This excludes other bodies and moments preceding or following [the perfuming agent], as they lack the sense of mutual conjunction; therefore, they are not perfumable.

Question: If that which is firmly established as indeterminate (avyākṛta) and lacks stable continuity cannot be the perfumed object (bhāvyatva), then the eighth consciousness of another person could also be the perfumed object;
furthermore, even within one's own eighth consciousness, preceding and succeeding moments could stand in relation to one another as objects of perfuming.
Now, let us examine this by means of the fourth criterion. Other [types of] consciousnesses do not occupy the same location; preceding and succeeding moments do not exist simultaneously.
Only the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) possesses these four criteria and can thus be the object of perfuming (*bhāvyatva*), whereas mental factors (*caitta*) and the like cannot.
The first section, explaining the four characteristics of the perfumable (*bhāvyamāna*), is concluded. △ Second, the explanation of the perfuming agent (*bhāvakatva*).

What are the four characteristics of the perfuming agent? First, it must possess arising and ceasing. If a phenomenon is impermanent and possesses the functional capacity to produce and grow habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it is a perfuming agent.
This excludes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), which do not change before or after and thus lack the function of producing and growing [tendencies].

Therefore, they are not perfumers (*bhāvakatva*). Second, there must be a superior function. If there is arising and ceasing, and furthermore, if the power is intensified such that it can induce habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), then it is a perfumer.
This excludes the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of maturation (*vipāka*), as their power is weak and inferior;
therefore, they are not perfumers.

The first meaning is understandable. Next, one should ask: if that which possesses arising and ceasing is capable of perfuming, then the resultant (*vipāka*) mind and mental factors also possess arising and ceasing and should therefore be capable of perfuming. Now, this is distinguished by the second meaning:
it must be either wholesome, unwholesome, or obscured-neutral, and its power must be particularly strong to be designated as "capable of perfuming."

The three realms of existence (*tribhava*) undergo increase and decrease. If there is a superior function (and it must be repeatedly cultivated), it can be increased; if [defilements] are suppressed and eliminated, they can be decreased.

That which gathers, preserves, and plants the latencies (*vāsanā*) so that they are not lost or destroyed is the perfuming agent (*bhāvakatva*). This excludes the perfected wholesome dharmas of the Buddha-fruit from being subject to increase or decrease; therefore, they are not perfuming agents.
If those were to act as perfuming agents, they would not be perfected, and the Buddha-fruits before and after would necessarily have degrees of superiority.
"Inferior.

He asks: "If that which possesses arising and ceasing, as well as superior functional capacity, is what can act as a perfuming agent (*vāsaka*), then the first seven consciousnesses in the state of Buddhahood (*buddhatva*) should be able to act as perfuming agents.
Now, let us exclude them by means of the third criterion. In the state of Buddhahood, [the cultivation...]"
It is perfectly fulfilled; there is nothing further to be increased. Evil has been cultivated until it is completely exhausted; there is nothing further to be diminished.
Even if one were to undergo perfuming, then since the former Buddha would have acquired a greater quantity of untainted seeds through perfuming, he ought to be superior to a later Buddha.

Fourth, it evolves in conjunction with that which is perfumed (*bhāvyamāna*). If it is simultaneous and co-spatial with the perfumed, being neither identical nor separate, it is indeed a perfumer (*bhāvaka*).
This excludes the possibility of conjunction with another person’s body or with preceding and succeeding moments; therefore, these are not perfumers.

Question: If that which possesses arising and ceasing, possesses superior efficacy, and possesses increase and decrease were the perfuming agent, then the seven [consciousnesses] of another person should also be perfuming agents.
Furthermore, the seven [consciousnesses] of one's own continuum, when viewed in relation to one another across preceding and succeeding moments, should likewise be perfuming agents.
Now, let us exclude this by means of the fourth criterion: the bodies of others do not occupy the same location, and successive moments are not identical.
It is at that time.
Only the seven evolving consciousnesses and their associated mental factors possess a dominant functional efficacy and undergo increase and decrease;
being endowed with these four characteristics, they are capable of perfuming.

The two-part explanation of the four meanings of the perfuming agent (the first seven consciousnesses and their mental factors) is complete. The two-part detailed explanation is complete. △ Third, the summary and judgment, in two parts:
first, the summary; second, the judgment. Now, the first:

Thus, the perfuming agent (the aforementioned seven consciousnesses and their mental factors) and the perfumed consciousness (the eighth consciousness) arise and perish together, thereby performing perfuming.
The meaning [of "perfuming"] is thus established. It causes all dharmas within the seeds of the eighth consciousness that are being perfumed to arise, grow, and be nourished.
Just as one perfumes sesame seeds, it is therefore called "perfuming" (*vāsanā*).
This establishes the name for "perfuming" (*vāsanā*). *Kusumbha* (苣蕂) refers to sesame seeds; in the Western lands [of India], they are used to make fragrant oil for anointing the body.
First, the fragrant flowers and sesame seeds are pounded together until crushed, and then the oil is pressed out; thus, the oil becomes fragrant and delicious.

Here, the sesame seed is used as a metaphor for the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), while the fragrant flowers are used as a metaphor for the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of the preceding seven evolving consciousnesses.

When the perfuming consciousnesses and so forth arise from their seeds, they immediately act as causes and further perfume to form new seeds. These three factors revolve in a cycle where cause and effect are simultaneous.

(In terms of the arising of characteristics, it is) like a wick producing a flame and the flame consuming the wick; (in terms of mutual dependence, it is) like bundles of reeds leaning against one another.
Thus, cause and effect exist at the same time, and this principle remains unshakable.
This section demonstrates the characteristics of perfuming (*vāsanā*). Its principle is thoroughly established and cannot be subverted; therefore, it is unshakable.
△ Second, the judgment:

the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) that act as perfumers produce seeds, and from seeds arise active manifestations. Like simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), they obtain the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Seeds produce their own kind successively; like the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), they project an outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).

These two causes alone possess the nature of a direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) with respect to their fruits. Apart from these two types of causes, all other phenomena are merely dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and the like, not direct causal conditions.
Even where they are designated as "causal conditions," it should be understood that this is merely a figurative expression.

The co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) refers to the fact that the effect and the cause exist simultaneously. The virile fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*) refers to the fruit accomplished through the activity of a person.
The similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) refers to the fact that the cause and the effect are similar. The outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).
This refers to the similarity between the fruit and its cause. The ten causes and five fruits are explained in the eighth fascicle [of this work].
This concludes the first section, which provides two clarifications regarding the characteristics of causes: first, the heading, and second, the explanation. △ Third, the conclusion.
This is called the brief explanation of all aspects (*sarvākāra*).

The first section, the explanation of the three gates beginning with "self-characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*), is concluded. △ Second, the explanation of the three gates beginning with "unknowable" (*ajñeya*).
This has two parts: first, the general statement; second, the detailed explanation. Now, the first [part].

What are the modes of activity (*ākāra*) and the objects (*ālambana*) of this consciousness? They are: the appropriation (*upādāna*), the locus (*sthāna*), and the cognition (*vijñapti*), which are unknowable.

Part Two: Detailed Explanation [of the Modes of Activity and Objects] has two sections: first, the explanation of the gates of modes of activity and objects; second, the explanation of the gate of the unknowable. Within the first section, there are two parts:
first, a brief explanation; second, an extensive explanation. Within the first part, there are again two sections: first, clarifying the modes of activity; second, clarifying the objects.
First, "apprehension" (vijñapti) means discernment (vijñāna). This is precisely the aspect of activity (ākāra), because consciousness has discernment as its active mode of manifestation.
△ Second, the explanation of the objects of focus (*ālambana*).

"Locus" (*sthāna*) refers to the location, namely the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), because it is the basis upon which all sentient beings depend. There are two types of appropriation (*upādāna*).

This refers to the various seeds and the body endowed with sense organs (*sendriya-kāya*). Regarding the "various seeds," this refers to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of signs, names, and conceptualization.
Regarding the "body endowed with sense organs," this refers to the [five] material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) and their bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Both of these are grasped and maintained by consciousness as its own substance, because they share the same security and peril. Thus, both the grasping and maintaining and the bases are [the objects of appropriation].

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of the eighth consciousness: by the power of causal conditions, at the very moment the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the ālayavijñāna arises, it internally transforms itself into seeds and the body with its sense organs, and externally transforms itself into the receptacle world.

It then takes these three types of transformed objects—which are objective spheres (*viṣayaviṣaya*)—as its own object-condition for the seeing aspect (*darśanabhāga*), because the latter arises in dependence upon them as its mode of activity (*ākāra*).

Grasping (*upādāna*) has two meanings: first, to take [something] as its own essence; second, to maintain it so that it does not disperse. Feeling (*vedanā*) has two meanings: first, to experience [something] as an object;
second, to give rise to sensation and awareness. The eighth consciousness takes seeds as its object and fully maintains them so that they do not disperse.

Regarding the two meanings of "appropriating as its object," when it takes the sense organs and the body as its object, it possesses four meanings: first, it appropriates them as its own substance because they share the same indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*);

second, it maintains them so that they do not disperse, for they remain intact throughout the duration of a single lifetime; third, it takes them as its object through direct perception, as they are its immediate objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*);
and fourth, it causes sensation and awareness to arise, because their security and peril are shared in common. If it takes the physical world (*bhājana-loka*) as its object, it only...

"To possess" means to take [the object] as its objective domain; this is one sense [of the term]. The initial brief explanation is concluded. Part Two: The Detailed Explanation has two sections: first, the detailed explanation of the aspect (*ākāra*);

second, the detailed explanation of the object-condition (*ālambana*). Within the first section, there are three parts: first, a brief indication of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*); second, a general discussion of all the parts;
third, the conclusion that returns to the seeing-part. Now, the first part.
Among these, "that which cognizes" refers to the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*). It possesses the function of cognition with respect to its own objects of perception;
this function of cognition is subsumed under the "seeing portion" (*darśanabhāga*).
II. General Discussion of the Various Portions has three parts: first, Nanda’s establishment of two portions; second, Dignāga’s establishment of three portions.

The third section, "Protecting the Dharma," establishes four divisions. The first of these has three parts: first, the formal establishment of two divisions; second, the refutation [of others] and the establishment of the *svasaṃvittibhāga* (self-cognizing division) alone by Sthiramati;
and third, the conclusion clarifying the cited proofs. Now, the first part.
However, when the substance of a contaminated consciousness arises, it always manifests in the likeness of both the object and the subject;

one should know that its associated mental factors are likewise so. That which appears in the likeness of the object is called the *nimittabhāga* (image-part), and that which appears in the likeness of the subject is called the *darśanabhāga* (seeing-part).
△ Second, the refutation of Sthiramati’s position that only the self-cognizing portion (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) exists.
If the mind and mental factors lacked the aspect (nimitta-bhāga) of an object of cognition, they would be unable to cognize their own respective objects;
or else, each one would be able to cognize all things, because its own object would be like other objects, and other objects would be like its own.
Visual consciousness takes form as its object; auditory consciousness takes sound and so forth as its objects; these are called their respective objective spheres (*ālambana-viṣaya*).

If visual consciousness lacked the aspect of form (*nimitta-bhāga*), it would be unable to take form as its object. If auditory consciousness lacked the aspect of sound, it would be unable to take sound as its object.
Furthermore, if visual consciousness were able to take form as its object even without the aspect of form, then it might likewise be able to take sound as its object without the aspect of sound.

Just as [a consciousness] can take fragrance and so forth as its object while taking sound, fragrance, and so forth as its objective referent (*ālambana*), so too other consciousnesses, although they do not take form as their objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), may nonetheless take form as their object.
Just as with one's own object, so it is with another's object; just as one's own object may be non-existent yet cognizable, so too another's object may be non-existent yet cognizable.

Just as with one's own consciousness, so it is with other consciousnesses: if one's own consciousness can take another's object as its object, then other consciousnesses can likewise take [one's own] object.
Because it is its own object.
If the mind and mental factors lacked the aspect (of the seeing-portion) that serves as the objective condition, they would be unable to perceive, like space and so forth;
or else, space and so forth would also be capable of perceiving.
If the mind were able to take an object without having a subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), then empty space, which lacks a subjective aspect, should likewise be able to take an object.
△ Third, the conclusion and citation of proof:

Therefore, the mind and mental factors must necessarily possess two aspects. As it is said in the Sūtra: "All things are nothing but cognition; there is no objective referent apart from that which is cognized."

In all cases, there are neither the subject that perceives nor the object that is perceived; each [aspect] evolves spontaneously from the seeds of its own respective division (the two divisions of appearance and seeing) to manifest as active functioning.
The *Sūtra* refers to the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra*. "All objects of cognition are non-existent" means that external objects do not truly exist.

"The division between the cognizer and the cognized" refers to the two parts: the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*). This concludes the first section, where Nanda establishes the two-part theory. **II.

Dignāga’s Establishment of the Three-Part Theory.** This section has two parts: first, distinguishing it from the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna); second, the formal establishment of the three parts. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections. First: [text continues].
This departs from the partial meaning of the Hīnayāna. Second is the presentation of the correct teaching of the Mahāyāna.

First, regarding those who maintain that there exists an object of cognition distinct from consciousness: they assert that the external object is the *ālambana* (the objective support), while the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) is called the *ākāra* (mental aspect), and the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part) is called the *vastu* (substantive entity).
This is because [the latter] is the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). Mind and mental factors share the same basis (*āśraya*).

Although the mental factors (*caitta*) share the same sense-faculties (*indriya*), the same objects (*ālambana*), and similar modes of activity (*ākāra*) as the primary mind (*citta*), their characteristics are distinct;
for while the primary mind is consciousness (*vijñāna*), the mental factors consist of sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth, each having its own specific characteristic.
"Phenomena" (vastu) refers to the self-substance and the mental concomitants—that is, the caittas.

Although these phenomena are numerous and so forth, it means that the substance of the mind-king (citta-rāja) is the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga), and the substances of the mental concomitants are likewise the seeing-part; therefore, they are equal in their characteristics. △ Second, the presentation of the correct teaching of the Mahāyāna.

For one who has realized that there is no objective referent apart from consciousness, it is taught that the *nimittabhāga* (image-part) is the object (*ālambana*), the *darśanabhāga* (seeing-part) is called the mode of apprehension (*ākāra*), and the self-substance upon which both the image and seeing depend is called the "entity" (*vastu*), namely the *svasaṃvittibhāga* (self-verifying part). If this [self-verifying part] were non-existent, [the others could not exist].

One should not be able to recollect the mind and its mental factors (the analogy), because—just as [the *darśana-bhāga*] cannot necessarily recollect an object it has never previously experienced—one would likewise be unable to recollect them;

for while the mind and its mental factors share the same supporting faculty (*āśraya*) and have similar objects of cognition (*ālambana*), their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are each distinct, since their functions, such as discerning and experiencing, differ from one another. (This refers to the self-cognizing portion of the mind-king.)
Although the objects are likewise equal in number to the mental factors, their characteristics differ because there are distinctions in the essential natures of consciousness, sensation,
and so forth.
"Recollection means knowing. If the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) were not experienced by the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*), it certainly could not be known;
by this analogy, one can understand that if the seeing-part were not experienced by the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvedanabhāga*), how could it possibly know itself?"

Therefore, the ancients used a bolt of silk as a metaphor for the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect), a measuring rod for the *darśanabhāga* (perceiving aspect), and wisdom for the *svasaṃvedanabhāga* (self-verifying aspect).

Regarding the statement that "the objects of perception are similar," it means that both the mind-king (*citta*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) each take their own transformed objective aspect as their object of perception.
Regarding the statement that "the modes of activity (*ākāra*) are distinct," consciousness (*vijñāna*) takes discernment as its mode of activity, while sensation (*vedanā*) takes experiencing...
Appropriation (*ādāna*) has the aspect of activity (*kriyā-lakṣaṇa*), and so on, up to volition (*cetanā*), which has the aspect of formation (*abhisamskāra-lakṣa��a*).

Regarding the statement "although the entities are equal in number," it means that the substance of the primary mind (*citta-rāja*) is the self-witnessing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), and the substance of the mental factors (*caitta*) is likewise the self-witnessing portion.
This concludes the initial analysis distinguishing [the Mahāyāna] from the Hīnayāna. △ Second, the formal establishment of the three portions (*tri-bhāga*).

However, when each mind and mental factor arises, if one investigates them through reasoning, each possesses three parts, because there is a distinction between the object of cognition (*prameya*), the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the result of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).

Furthermore, the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) must necessarily have a substratum as their essence. As it is said in a verse of the *Saṃtānāntarasiddhi* (or *Pramāṇasamuccaya*): [citation].

The aspect resembling the object (the *nimittabhāga*) is the "object of cognition" (*prameya*). The aspect of the grasper (the *darśanabhāga*) and the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) are designated as the "means of cognition" (*pramāṇa*) and the "result of cognition" (*pramāṇaphala*), respectively.
These three are not distinct in their essence.

Each has three parts; that is to say, each individual mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and each individual mental factor (*caitta*) possesses these three parts. It is not that there are only three parts shared among them collectively.
That which is measured is the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part); that which measures is the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part); and the fruit of measurement is the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-verifying part).

"Fruit" here carries the meaning of the essential substance upon which [the other parts] depend. When it is said that the substances of those three are not distinct, it is because they are of one and the same consciousness.
It can be seen that there is no object apart from the mind. Second, Dignāga’s establishment of the three-fold division is complete.
△ Third, Dharmapāla’s establishment of the four-fold division has two parts: first, the formal explanation of the four divisions; second, their subsumption into the single mind. Now, the first part.
Furthermore, if one analyzes the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) in detail, they should consist of four parts. Three parts are as previously described;

there is additionally a fourth, the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*). If this were absent, what would cognize the third part? Since the nature of the mental divisions is the same, they would all necessarily be self-cognized.
Furthermore, if there were no self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*), the self-cognizing portion would be without a fruit, for all means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) must necessarily have a fruit.

One should not falsely imagine that the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*) is the third fruit [of the self-cognizing portion], because the seeing portion is sometimes subsumed under non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
For this reason, the seeing portion does not cognize the third [portion]; that which cognizes its own essence must necessarily be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Regarding the statement "Since the mental divisions are identical, they should all be self-cognized":

this means that just as the *darśana-bhāga* (the seeing division) must be cognized by the *svasaṃvedana-bhāga* (the self-cognizing division), so too the *svasaṃvedana-bhāga* must be cognized by a *svasaṃvedana-svasaṃvedana-bhāga* (the self-cognizing-of-the-self-cognizing division).

Regarding the statement "All that is a means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) must have a result (*phala*)": this means that since the *darśana-bhāga* is the means of cognition, the *svasaṃvedana-bhāga* serves as its cognitive result (*pramāṇaphala*).

Now, the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) is also the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and it must likewise take the self-cognition-of-self-cognition aspect (*svasaṃvitti-svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) as its result of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).

Therefore, the ancients compared the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) to a bolt of silk, the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) to a measuring scale, the self-cognizing aspect to the act of knowing, and the self-cognition-of-self-cognition aspect to the person.
Furthermore, they compared the object-aspect to a reflection in a mirror, the seeing-aspect to the luster of the mirror, and the self-cognizing aspect—

The mirror surface is used as a metaphor for the *svasaṃvittibhāga* (self-cognizing division), and the back of the mirror is used as a metaphor for the *svasaṃvittisaṃvittibhāga* (cognition of self-cognition). Alternatively, the *svasaṃvittibhāga* may be metaphorized as the mirror, and the *svasaṃvittisaṃvittibhāga* as the copper [of which it is made].

The *Zongjing lu* states: "There are four types of *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect): first, the *nimitta* called 'true reality' (*dharmatā*), whose essence is *tathatā* (suchness); this is the true..."

1. The characteristic of ultimate reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*): because it is the true nature. 2. The characteristic of the objective sphere (*viṣaya-lakṣaṇa*): that which is called the "characteristic of the name" (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), meaning it serves as the object for the sense faculties and the mind.

3. The characteristic of formal appearance (*ākāra-lakṣaṇa*): this exists only in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) because they possess formal characteristics; it includes both reflections and substantial objects, and is exclusively what is transformed by consciousness (*vijñāna*).

4. The characteristic of the referent (*artha-lakṣaṇa*): this refers to the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the signified meaning (*abhidheya-artha*) that is expressed by the signifier (*vācaka*). Regarding these...
Among the four aforementioned types of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), only the latter three are taken as the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*). Furthermore, there are two kinds of objective aspects:

first, that which is suddenly transformed by consciousness, which is the primary object (*maulika-artha*); second, that which consciousness and its associates perceive as an object by transforming only a reflected image (*pratibimba*), without apprehending the primary object.
The subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) consists of five categories: first, "seeing" as realization, which refers to the three fundamental wisdoms (*mūla-jñāna*).
1. The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is [called "seeing"]. Second, illumination is called "seeing"; this applies to both the sense faculties and the mind, as both possess the quality of illuminating.

Third, that which is capable of cognizing is called "seeing"; this applies to all three internal parts [of consciousness], as they are all capable of cognizing. Fourth, recollective understanding is called "seeing," because it is that which explains the meaning of what is recollected and understood.
Fifth, inferential deliberation is called "seeing," which refers to the mind of inference (*anumāna*) that deliberates upon all things.

Regarding the object-field: among these five aspects of consciousness, with the exception of the five material sense-faculties and the two internal [aspects], all others are subsumed under the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*).

The self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) refers to that which can directly realize its own seeing-portion; because it takes the image-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its object without error and is capable of acting as the realization itself.
