The portion that realizes the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvittisaṃvitti-bhāga*) refers to that which can directly realize the third [aspect], the self-cognizing portion.
[It is so named] because it does not err in its perception of the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*). It receives its name from that which is realized.
If one does not penetrate these four divisions and yet claims to possess a mind, this is merely recollecting names and phrases; one knows nothing of the true meaning of the mind’s formation.

Since both essence and function are lost, the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) is entirely absent. In the end, one remains bound by the conditions of mind and objects, with no way to attain liberation.

Among these four divisions, the first two (the *nimitta-bhāga* and the *darśana-bhāga*) are the external (function); the latter two (the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* and the *svasaṃvitti-svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) are the internal (essence).

The first (the *nimitta-bhāga*) is exclusively the object (*ālambana*). The latter three (divisions) pertain to both (the subject and the object): namely, the second (the *darśana-bhāga*) takes only the first (the *nimitta-bhāga*) as its object;

it may be either valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), and either direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*). The third (the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) is able to take the second (the *darśana-bhāga*) as its object.

And as for the fourth, the *svasaṃvittisaṃvedana-bhāga* (the self-cognizing consciousness of self-cognition): the fourth, the *svasaṃvittisaṃvedana-bhāga*, takes only the third (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) as its object, and not the second (*darśana-bhāga*), because there would be no purpose [in doing so].
Both the third and the fourth are subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

It was previously explained that there must be four divisions; here, these are further analyzed according to their internal essence and external function, the subject and object of cognition, and the distinctions among the three types of valid cognition—direct perception, inference, and non-cognition—which are not identical. "Useless" means, as the term implies, that they are of no benefit.
Therefore, each and every mind and mental factor is composed of four parts; thus, while they possess both the capacity and the object of cognition, there is no fault of infinite regress.
Neither identical nor separate, the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is established.

For if the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) and the aspect that cognizes the self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti-saṃvitti-bhāga*) did not mutually perceive one another, then one would have to posit yet another cognition to cognize the latter, resulting in the fallacy of infinite regress.
Now, because they function as mutual subject and object—just like a mirror—[the system is coherent].
The mirror’s surface and its back are like a person and their wisdom; therefore, there is no fault of infinite regress. Because they are fourfold distinctions, they are not identical;
because they are solely this one mind, they are not separate. This was first established as a conclusion, and subsequently supported by scriptural evidence.
Therefore, it is said in a verse of the Sūtra: "The minds of sentient beings possess two natures;
throughout all internal and external divisions, they are entangled by the grasped and the grasper, appearing in various distinctions."
Regarding the two natures of the minds of sentient beings: the two internal parts constitute one, and the two external parts constitute one.

Regarding all internal and external divisions: the internal also has two parts, and the external also has two parts. "The entanglement of the grasped" refers to the bondage of the characteristics of the object;
"the entanglement of the grasper" refers to the bondage of the perception of the subject. "Seeing various distinctions" refers to seeing...
This is because it is categorized within the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The meaning of this verse is that the nature of sentient beings' minds is composed of two parts—namely, the internal and the external.

(Because all sentient beings) are bound by the grasped object (*grāhya*) and the grasping subject (*grāhaka*), they perceive various things as either valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), or as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or...
This refers mostly to the distinctions [between the various aspects]. In this verse, that which is called "seeing" (darśana) refers solely to the seeing-portion (darśana-bhāga).
First, the verse was cited; this is its further explanation. Having first correctly elucidated the four divisions, [the text proceeds to] (2) subsume them within the single mind.
These four divisions may be subsumed into three, because the fourth is included within the self-cognizing division (*svasaṃvittibhāga*). Alternatively, they may be subsumed into two.

Because the latter three are all of the nature of being cognitive subjects (*ālambaka*), they are all subsumed under the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*). This term "seeing" does not refer exclusively to the seeing-portion;
rather, it signifies the sense of being a cognitive subject. Alternatively, they may be subsumed as one, because their essence is not distinct, as stated in a verse of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*:
"Due to the attachment of one's own mind, the mind evolves appearing as external objects. That which is seen does not exist; therefore, it is said to be 'representation-only' (*vijñaptimātra*)."

Regarding the mind (*citta*): it must be understood that in various places it is taught that there is only a single mind. Furthermore, this term "single mind" necessarily includes mental factors (*caitta*), as they are invariably associated with it.

Thus far, in order to reveal the distinctions within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one part was used to refute the unity, three parts were used to refute the duality, and four parts were used to refute the triad.
Now, in order to reveal the perfect fusion of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the fourth part may be subsumed within the third, such that one may speak of only three parts.
Furthermore, the internal three may be subsumed within the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*).
Furthermore, while one may speak of two divisions, the mutual manifestation [of subject and object] is fundamentally without two distinct entities, such that one may speak of "one mind" alone.
The verses of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* serve as proof for this principle of one mind.

However, what is called "one mind" does not mean negating the eight mind-kings (*citta-rāja*) and fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*), nor does it refer to a separate, singular True Suchness Mind (*tathatā-citta*).
This is considered the Great Universal Dharma-gate. Because the substance of the four divisions is without distinction, it is termed "One Mind.
Thus, one should know that among the eight mind-kings and fifty-one mental factors, whichever king or factor one may select, [it is all this One Mind].
All possess four parts. According to whatever four parts exist, their substance is without distinction; it is solely the one mind.

Thus, we know that in each and every royal palace, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Furthermore, since the substance of the four parts is without distinction, the function is also without distinction through the fusion of substance and function.
Therefore, it can be said that a single form and a single fragrance are none other than the Middle Way, and are merely...
Form consists solely of odor and so forth. This concludes the general discussion of the various parts [of consciousness]. △ Third, returning to the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga):
therefore, the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of consciousness is precisely discernment (*vijñapti*); this discernment is the seeing-part of consciousness.

The detailed explanation of the aspects (*ākāra*) is concluded. △ Second, the detailed explanation of the objects of cognition (*ālambana*), which has two parts: first, the explicit clarification of what is transformed;

second, the summary of the objects of cognition. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, clarifying that only the locations and so forth are transformed; second, clarifying that the mind and so forth are not transformed.

The first section also has two parts: first, the formal explanation; second, the concluding demonstration. The first part also has two sections: first, clarifying that what is transformed by the power of karma is determinate; second, clarifying that what is transformed by the power of meditative concentration is indeterminate. The first of these [three] also has three parts: first, the receptacle world; second, seeds; third, the sense-faculties and the body. Now, the first: The receptacle world is determined by the collective karma of sentient beings. It is not determined by the individual karma of a single person. Why? Furthermore, since the receptacle world is vast and expansive, it cannot be established by the karma of a single person alone. Therefore, it is known that the receptacle world is determined by the collective karma of all sentient beings. What is called the "locus" refers to the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).

By the power of the ripening of its common seeds, it transforms into the appearance of the container-world (*bhājanaloka*), such as form and so forth—namely, the external primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) of the world-receptacle.

Although the transformations produced by each sentient being are distinct, their appearances are similar and their locations are not different, just as the light of many lamps appears as one and pervades everywhere.
This first provides a general explanation that the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) is transformed by consciousness.
It is called "external" because it is not grasped and does not produce sensations; it does not mean that it actually exists outside of consciousness. This must be understood.
(Question: Of whom is this maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) that transforms into this appearance? One interpretation holds that it belongs to all [sentient beings].
Why? As stated in the sūtras, it arises through the collective dominant power of the karma of all sentient beings.

Another interpretation holds that if this were so, then Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would actually transform this into a defiled land (*saṃkliṣṭa-kṣetra*), and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) would actually transform it into another [land].

Furthermore, regarding these various pure and wondrous lands within this realm, as well as those noble ones (anāgāmins) who, weary of the realm of form, are born into the formless realm and will certainly not descend again—since they do not transform [the world] into this land, what would be the use [of such a transformation]?

Therefore, it is the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) of those currently residing here and those destined to be born here that transforms into this realm. The Sūtra speaks of "all" based merely on a partial aspect.
As for the statement "only those," since all those with identical karma transform together, the first interpretation is too broad.
The second interpretation—that those with identical karma transform together—is acceptable; however, it is too narrow when considered in terms of their current dwelling.
Furthermore, [the claim that it refers to] those about to be born is also not pertinent; therefore, it is refuted by the third school.

According to another interpretation: if that were so, then at the time when the receptacle world (bhājanaloka) is about to be destroyed, since there would be neither those currently dwelling there nor those about to be born, whose ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) would transform into this [impending] realm?
Moreover, there are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who, weary of the realm of form, are born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): although one will eventually be born there later, at present no physical body exists [there], as the number of kalpas is exceedingly remote. Why, then, would one pre-emptively transform into the lower lands of the desire and form realms?
Furthermore, if the sentient beings of the desire and form realms possessed physical bodies, they would differ in coarseness and subtlety from the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) of a different stage.
The upper and lower realms are vastly separated; they do not support one another. Thus, what benefit would there be for this consciousness to transform into that [different realm]?
This first refutes the second previous position.

However, the transformed land is fundamentally intended to serve as the support and object of enjoyment for the material body (*rūpakāya*). Therefore, if it can provide support and utility for the body, it is transformed into that [land].
Consequently, even if one is born in the respective native land of another direction, that consciousness can likewise transform this [present] land into its own respective native land.
Thus, at the time when the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) is about to be destroyed or is first being formed, although there are no sentient beings, [the land is still transformed].
It also appears as the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*). This refers to that which is commonly experienced by all;
if it is experienced individually, it should be understood accordingly, because what is seen differs among ghosts, humans, gods, and so forth.

This explanation establishes the correct meaning. "Common enjoyment" refers to that which is common within the category of the common. "Individual enjoyment" refers to that which is uncommon within the category of the common.
Regarding the statement that what is seen by ghosts, humans, and devas differs, the *Zongjing* says:
"Devas see it as a ground adorned with jewels; fish see it as their cave-dwelling; humans see it as clear, cool water; and ghosts see it as a river of pus and fierce [waves]."
Fire is merely the distinct objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) transformed by the consciousness of the karmic actions of those four classes of sentient beings;

there is no separate external object of the four types apart from the mind. The old claim that "a single object corresponds to four minds" is incorrect. If one were to say it is a single object, [it would be untenable].

It has not yet been determined what kind of object this is. If there were a separate object existing apart from the appearances transformed by the four classes of sentient beings, that would mean there is a phenomenon external to the mind.
This concludes the first section on the receptacle world. II. Seeds.
Regarding "all seeds": this refers to all the seeds of contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena maintained by the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).

Since this [eighth] consciousness is comprised within the nature of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), these [seeds of contaminated phenomena] are its objects of perception (*ālambana*). As for the seeds of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena, although they likewise rely upon this consciousness, they are not comprised within this [indeterminate] nature;
therefore, they are not its objects of perception. Nevertheless, even though they are not its objects of perception, they [also coexist with this fundamental...]
Consciousness has never been separate [from it], just as true suchness (tathatā) is the very nature of consciousness; thus, it does not contradict the principle of consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra).
△ III. The Body with Sense Organs.

Regarding the "body with sense organs": this refers to the transformation of the maturation consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*)—by the power of the ripening of its specific seeds—into what appear as the sense organs (*indriya*) of pure ultimate reality, as well as the bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of those organs (the six coarse physical locations). These consist of the internal primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
Because it is appropriated (*upātta*), it is termed "internal. This first clarifies that which is uncommon among the uncommon.

Due to the power of the maturation of seeds possessing common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-bīja*), [the basis] also transforms into something resembling those [objects] in the locations of other bodies;

otherwise, there would be no sense of experiencing other [bodies]. Regarding this, there is an interpretation that [it does not only transform the bases of others] but can also transform the five sense organs (*indriya*) of others into something resembling matter (*rūpa*).
The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states that [the body] appears as the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*) of oneself and others. Regarding this, there is one interpretation:
it is only able to transform [itself] into what resembles the locus upon which the sense faculties depend; for the sense faculties (which resemble matter) of another are not utilized by oneself.

Nevertheless, when the treatise says "appearing as the five sense faculties of oneself and others," it merely explains the meaning that one's own consciousness and the consciousnesses of others each undergo their own transformation. Therefore, [it does not mean that one actually] produces the other...
Whether [the practitioner] attains parinirvāṇa on this earth or elsewhere, their remaining physical remains continue to be perceived as a continuity.
This clarifies the "commonality within the uncommon. The first interpretation is incorrect; the second is correct, as both can be understood accordingly.

Thus, regarding those who are born in other realms and so forth: because consciousness is able to transform the basis of others, the physical remains continue to be perceived as a continuity. This is because...
Because the five sense faculties of others are transformed, the corpse can no longer be seen or heard.
Nevertheless, this continuity of the corpse is due, on one hand, to the power of its own projecting cause and, on the other, to what is transformed by the common perception of others;

thus, it is still termed "that which is common within the uncommon. This concludes the first section clarifying that what is transformed by the power of karma is determinate. △ Second, the clarification of meditative concentration (samādhi).
That which is transformed by power is not fixed.
Thus far, we have merely discussed the distinctions of the external vessel-world and the internal bodies as transformed by the power of karma (as they are).

However, regarding the vessel-world and bodies transformed by the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and so forth—whether belonging to Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or other noble ones—their realm-levels (*dhātu-bhūmi*) and their status as self or other are not [fixed].

It is certain that the bodies and environments that are transformed are for the most part continuous and constant, whereas the transformations of sound, light, and so forth are for the most part temporary,
because they are produced by the striking force of manifesting conditions.
As for the environment (*bhājana*), it manifests as pure or impure; as for the body (*deha*), it manifests as noble or ordinary. Therefore, they are not fixed.

To benefit sentient beings during a single lifetime, these are provided as the "enjoyment for others" (*parasaṃbhoga*); thus, the bodies and environments generally persist in a continuous succession. Nevertheless, there are also those that are temporary.
Because they arise and strike forth in accordance with those specific capacities and conditions, sound and light are for the most part temporary;
yet there are also those that are continuous. The initial formal explanation is now concluded. △ Second, the concluding demonstration.

To state briefly the objects transformed by this eighth consciousness: they consist of the impure seeds, the ten bases of form, and the manifest forms included within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
"Defiled seeds" refers to all the seeds within the appropriated [basis]. "The ten bases of form" refers to the five faculties and the five objects.
"Forms that appear as real within the sphere of mental objects" means that when the mental consciousness perceives an object, there are both real and provisional [forms];

here, it specifically designates the forms that are results. This concludes the first section, clarifying that only the spheres and so forth are transformations. △ Second, clarifying that the mind and so forth are not transformations.
Why is it that this eighth consciousness cannot transform into something resembling mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) as its object? (The answer is:

There are, briefly, two types of transformation of contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*): first, that which transforms into an object by the power of causes and conditions—namely, the eighth, the first five, and a portion of the sixth;

second, that which transforms into an object by the power of conceptualization (*vikalpa*)—namely, the seventh and a portion of the sixth. Of these, the first (transformation by causes and conditions) must necessarily [exist].
[The objects] have practical utility. Later [in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, it will be explained that] they are merely objects for the *nimittabhāga* (image-part) and do not possess practical utility.

Now, regarding the transformations of the *vipākavijñāna* (maturation-consciousness), the forms (*rūpa*) and so forth that are transformed in accordance with causes and conditions must necessarily possess practical utility.

If, however, it were to transform [into] mind (*citta*) and so forth, there would be no practical utility, because the minds and mental factors (*caitta*) within the *nimittabhāga* (image-part) are incapable of cognitive apprehension (*ālambana*). Therefore, those [transformed entities] must exist.

[Only] that which has practical utility [can arise from the transformations of this eighth consciousness]. Even if it were to transform into unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and so forth, they would likewise lack practical utility;
therefore, the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) does not take as its objects the mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitta*), or unconditioned phenomena. (This refers to the stage of outflows;

however,) upon reaching the stage of no-outflows at the fruit of Buddhahood, since it is associated with the supreme wisdom of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), although there is no conceptual discrimination, the mirror-substance remains limpid and pure.
Therefore, even if [the mind and mental factors] have no practical utility, they still manifest their images. Otherwise, the Buddhas would not be omniscient. The *Zongjing lu* states:
"First, transformation through conditions and causes (*pratyaya-pariṇāma*) rather than transformation through conceptualization (*vikalpa-pariṇāma*);

this refers to the five consciousnesses, their associated mental factors, and the eighth mind-king (*citta-rāja*), because their objective-referent image-parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) arise from their own seeds. Second, transformation through conceptualization alone."
Those that are not transformations of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) are the seventh and eighth consciousnesses with outflows (*sāsrava*), along with their five mental associates (*caitta*).
This is because the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) that they transform arises solely from the mind of discrimination (*vikalpa-citta*).

The third category—those that are both—is the sixth consciousness with outflows and all eight consciousnesses without outflows (*anāsrava*), because they are able to universally perceive both provisional (*prajñapti*) and substantial (*dravya*) phenomena. The fourth category—neither—is the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

This is the functioning [of consciousness]. Because it lacks substantial reality and because it does not arise as the same species as the perceiving subject, the initial correct explanation of the transformed object is concluded.
△ Second, the summary of the objects of cognition.

Therefore, during the state of being with outflows (sāsrava), this maturation-consciousness (vipākavijñāna) takes as its objects only the receptacle world, the sense organs, the body, and the seeds of outflows—collectively termed the "threefold nature of the objective sphere" (trividhālambana).

In the realms of desire and form, [the mind] possesses all three types of objects. In the formless realm, it takes only contaminated seeds as its object, because of the aversion to and departure from form.

Since there is no form resulting from karma (such as the physical body or the vessel-world), it does not take these as objects; however, there is still form resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*).
Thus, it is not contradictory in principle for that consciousness (of the eighth heaven of the four formless states) to also take this *samādhi-phala-rūpa* as its objective domain.
The first section, explaining the two gates of the aspects (*ākāra*) and the objects (*ālambana*), is completed. △ Second, the explanation of the gate of the "unknowable.
It is called "unknowable" because the aspects of this [eighth consciousness’s] cognitive capacity (*pramāṇa*) are extremely subtle and thus difficult to discern;
or because its internal objects of grasping (*upādāna*) are also subtle; and because the magnitude of the external receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) is difficult to fathom. Thus it is named.
[Question: It is unknowable. [Question: Why is it difficult to know the mode of activity (*ākāra*) by which consciousness apprehends its object? [Answer:

Just as in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), where all constantly active minds and mental factors have ceased, one must believe that the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) which does not depart from the body exists.
However, one must necessarily admit that the attainment of cessation possesses the eighth consciousness, because it is comprised within the category of sentient beings;
as it is when there is a mind, so it should be understood to be in states such as the non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñika*).
First, the cognizing subject is unknowable, because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is extremely subtle.

Second, the object of cognition is unknowable, because the three types of objects—the five pure material sense-faculties (*rūpa-indriya*) which are internal appropriated [bases], their seeds, and the external receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) extending throughout the ten directions—are all difficult to measure due to their subtlety.
Next, the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established as follows:

To demonstrate that the eighth consciousness exists, the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: **Thesis:** The state of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is a functional entity (*dharmin*) in which the eighth consciousness exists.

**Reason:** Because it is comprised within the category of sentient beings (*sattva*). **Example:** Just as it is when one possesses a mind; the same applies to the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) and the heaven of non-conception (*asaṃjñideva*).

Since the eighth consciousness still exists even in the attainment of cessation and the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), how could its modes of activity (*ākāra*) not be difficult to know?
This concludes the two explanations regarding the three gates beginning with "the unknowable."

Essentials of Contemplating the Mind According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* Scroll Two Essentials of Contemplating the Mind According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* Scroll Three Composed by the Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu

△ Third, the explanation of the gate of association (*saṃprayoga*) has three parts: first, a general clarification through question and answer; second, a detailed explanation of the essence and function;
third, the conclusion establishing the association. Now, the first:

With how many mental factors (*caitta*) is this consciousness associated? It is always associated with contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*). The *ālaya*...

The ālayavijñāna, from beginningless time until it has not yet undergone transformation, is at all times— whether in states involving noble ones or ordinary beings, elevation or decline, concentration or distraction—
constantly associated with these five mental factors. This is because these five are subsumed under the category of universal (sarvatraga) mental factors, which are present in every state of mind.

Below this [section on] consciousness, a question is posed. From "Constantly with... onwards, a verse is cited as the answer. From "Ālaya... onwards, there is a general explanation. "Not yet transformed" refers to the period prior to the Vajra Path.
The remainder is explained as follows in the sub-commentary. △ Second, the detailed explanation of essence and function has five parts:

first, the explanation of contact; second, the explanation of mental attention; third, the explanation of sensation; fourth, the explanation of perception; fifth, the explanation of volition. Now, the first [part].

Contact (*sparśa*). This refers to the differentiation of the transformation [of the object] at the moment of the conjunction of the three—the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness. Its essential nature consists in the contact of the mind and mental factors with their respective objects;
its functional activity consists in serving as the basis for sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth.

Discrimination (*vikalpa*) means the sense of apprehending what resembles [the object]; this is the function of contact (*sparśa*). Transformation (*vipariṇāma*) is the function of the triad [of faculty, object, and consciousness].

That is to say, at the time when the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness comes together, it causes the various mental factors (*caitta*) to arise in succession; this is termed "transformation."
This mental factor of contact (*sparśa*) is able to experience that which resembles [the object]. This first provides the direct explanation; below, it is further explained.

That is to say, because the sense faculty (*indriya*), the object (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) accord with one another, they are called the "threefold conjunction" (*trikasamnipāta*). Contact arises depending upon them (the threefold conjunction) and causes them to attain harmony;

therefore, this mental factor of contact is said to be the state of the conjunction of those three. [In this process], the sense faculty can serve as the basis (*āśraya*), the object can serve as the objective support (*ālambana*), and consciousness depends upon the sense faculty to apprehend [the object].

Regarding the object (the third of these three): all three possess the functional capacity (activity) to accord with all mental factors (*citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*). Therefore, they are called "transformations" (*vikāra*).

Contact (*sparśa*) arises resembling that [transformation]—namely, the functional capacity to accord with the arising of all mental factors—and is thus termed "discrimination" (*pariccheda*). However, among the three harmonies (*saṃnipāta*), it is only contact that is induced to arise by the power of the transformation of the sense organ;
because it excels the consciousness and its object, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises speak of it alone as "discrimination."
"The variation of the sense-faculties (*indriya-vikāra*).

This explains in turn the variation of the discrimination of the threefold conjunction (*trikasamnipāta*). Below the section on "the variation of the sense-faculties," there is an explanation of a doubt. Namely, a doubt arises as follows:

"If contact (*sparśa*) is already the discrimination of the variation of the threefold conjunction, why do the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises speak only of the discrimination of the sense-faculties?"

Regarding this transformation, the commentary states: "When the power of the transformation of the faculties induces the arising of contact, it is because the faculty is superior to the object of consciousness.

According to the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) interpretation, the faculty possesses four meanings that make it uniquely superior: first, by virtue of being primary; second, by virtue of being proximate to the production of mind and mental factors.
Third, because it is universal (*vyāpin*): it is not only a mental factor (*caitta*), but can also produce the mind (*citta*). Fourth, because it is constantly continuous (*nitya-santati*):

although consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the primary [condition], it produces mental factors immediately; however, it does not produce the mind itself, and thus is not universal. Because it is interrupted, it is not continuous.
Since the object (*viṣaya*) is not the primary [condition] and is also not immediate, although it is universal and can produce both the mind and its mental factors, it... [is not constant].
They do not arise in succession, because when consciousness arises, the object arises, and when consciousness ceases, the object ceases.
Contact has as its intrinsic nature the bringing together of all minds and mental factors so that they equally touch the object.
This further explains how the mind and mental factors take contact with objects as their nature regarding form. That is to say, each of the eight primary minds has its own associated mental factors;
this mental factor of contact enables each to bring about harmony so that they may contact the object.

Since this mental factor of contact (*sparśa*) possesses the functional capacity to facilitate the arising of other mental factors similar to the [threefold] conjunction, its function is to serve as the basis for feeling (*vedanā*) and the rest.
This is because the *Udayavyaya Sūtra* states that the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations all have contact as their condition.

For this reason, it is said that consciousness, contact, feeling, and so forth, arise from the conjunction of two, three, or four factors. The *Yogācārabhūmi* mentions only [contact] together with feeling and perception.

Regarding "volition as the basis": because volition is the primary and most eminent factor within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), it is cited here to include the remaining forty-seven mental factors.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises describe it simply as the basis for feeling (*vedanā*) because contact (*sparśa*) is proximate and predominant in the production of feeling.

That is to say, the aspects of the desirable and so forth apprehended by contact are extremely close to the aspects of the beneficial and so forth apprehended by feeling. Furthermore, [it is said that]...

Because it is superior in its capacity to trigger [the arising of sensation] compared to others, this passage explains that the function [of contact] is to serve as the basis for sensation, perception, volition, and so forth. The word "etc.

(ādi) collectively subsumes all other mental factors belonging to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), and does not refer solely to the single mental factor of volition (*cetanā*). The *Yogācārabhūmi* mentions only sensation and perception.

Regarding "volition" (*cetanā*): this is a case of subsuming the secondary by means of the primary. As for the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* speaking only of "feeling" (*vedanā*), this is a case of subsuming the remote by means of the proximate, and furthermore, subsuming the inferior by means of the superior.
As for the statement that consciousness, contact, feeling, and so forth arise from the conjunction of two, three, or four factors:
consciousness arises from the conjunction of the two factors of sense faculty and object; contact arises from the conjunction of the three factors of sense faculty, object, and consciousness.
Feeling, perception, volition, and so forth, all arise from the fourfold conjunction of faculty, object, consciousness, and contact.
Contact grasps an agreeable aspect, which is extremely proximate to the beneficial aspect grasped by feeling; therefore, it is the predominant factor that induces [feeling].
Contact grasps a disagreeable aspect, which is the adverse and harmful aspect grasped by feeling. Contact grasps a neutral aspect...

It is not a characteristic of being disagreeable. Likewise, its being a characteristic that is neither conducive to benefit nor conducive to harm, as it is taken up by feeling (*vedanā*), is also thus.
Furthermore, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of contact (*sparśa*) is real and not nominal, because it is a mental factor (*caitta*) among the six groups of six dharmas. (4)

Furthermore, because it is subsumed under "nutriment" (āhāra) and because it can function as a condition (pratyaya) among the twelve links [of dependent origination], it must possess a real intrinsic nature (svabhāva), just like sensation (vedanā) and the other [links]; it is not merely the conjunction of the three [factors].

This is the refutation of that position. Some maintain that contact (*sparśa*) arises from the conjunction of the three [sense organ, object, and consciousness], and that contact is simply this conjunction itself, having no separate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, we now establish the thesis that it possesses an intrinsic nature by means of three reasons, using feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth as analogies:

first, because it is a mental factor (*caitta*) among the six groups of six; as for the "six groups of six," these are the six consciousnesses, the six contacts, the six feelings, and the six perceptions.

The six volitions (*cetana*) are the same as the six cravings (*trṣṇā*). These two are subsumed under the four nutriments (*āhāra*); the four nutriments are: edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), contact-food (*sparśa-āhāra*), volition-food (*manahsaṃcetanā-āhāra*), and consciousness-food (*vijñāna-āhāra*).
The third [category] consists of those that act as conditions; that is to say, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) condition contact (*sparśa*), and contact conditions feeling (*vedanā*).
The initial explanation of *sparśa* (contact) is concluded. △ Second, the explanation of *manasikāra* (attention).
*Manasikāra* has the nature of being able to arouse the mind; its function is to direct the mind toward its objective support (*ālambana*).

That is to say, this [attention] can awaken the seeds of the mind that are about to arise (causing them to arise), and it can also direct [the mind that has already arisen] so that it moves toward the object. Therefore, it is called *manasikāra*.
Although this [attention] can also induce mental factors, because the mind is the primary factor, it is said only to "induce the mind.

Some say that this attention causes the mind—which is currently correctly perceiving this object—to turn toward a different object; therefore, it is said that this attention maintains the mind upon a single object, causing it to abide there.

Therefore, it is called *manasikāra* (attention). Both of those [two] positions are irrational: if it causes the mind to turn toward a different object, it would not be a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*);
if it holds the mind to abide upon a single object, it would not differ from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

First, the correct explanation of the essence and function. The phrase "Some say" below introduces alternative interpretations; the phrase "They both" below refutes them. All of these can be understood accordingly.
△ Third, the explanation of sensation (*vedanā*).

Feeling (*vedanā*) has the nature of experiencing the aspects of objects that are favorable, unfavorable, or neutral. Its function is to give rise to craving, because it can produce the desire for union with, separation from, or neither of these two [regarding such objects].
This is the correct explanation of its essence and function. Toward a favorable object, one desires union; toward an unfavorable object, one desires separation. Regarding...

It is neither conformable nor contrary to the object; though one does not hope for union with it, nor does one hope for separation from it—hope is precisely desire, and desire is termed craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

Some state that there are two kinds of feeling (*vedanā*): first, objective feeling (*viṣaya-vedanā*), which refers to the experiencing of the objects of perception (the three types of objects, such as the agreeable and so forth); second, self-feeling...

Feeling by nature (*svabhāva-vedanā*). This refers to that which takes the simultaneously arising contact (*sahaja-sparśa*) as its object-condition (*ālambana*). Herein, feeling by its own nature alone is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of feeling;
for feeling by way of an object (*viṣaya-vedanā*) shares common characteristics with other phenomena.

This presents an alternative interpretation. As for the statement that [feeling] shares its characteristics with others, it means that it possesses the common characteristic of being the object of the "king" (the primary consciousness).
That explanation is irrational, because feeling certainly does not take the simultaneously arising contact as its object.

If one were to claim that this feeling arises resembling contact and is thus called "experiencing contact," then every effect that resembles its cause would have to possess the sense of "experiencing the cause," and all such effects would consequently be of the nature of feeling (*vedanā*). Furthermore, [contact...]

Since it is the cause of feeling, and thus receives this cause, it should be called "feeling of the cause" (hetu-vedanā); [contact] would not be the intrinsic nature of feeling. What, then, is its intrinsic nature?
The following sections all constitute refutations. First, the primary refutation:

if it is held that feeling definitely does not take simultaneously-arisen contact as its object, then since feeling is produced by contact yet does not take contact as its object, it would be like a father giving birth to a son, but the son not acknowledging the father. The rest may be understood accordingly.

If it is argued that, just as a king enjoys various kingdoms and districts, feeling (vedanā) is called "feeling by its own nature" (svabhāva-vedanā) because it is the entity that experiences the sensation produced by contact (sparśa), this reasoning is also incorrect.
It contradicts your own tenet [that feeling has the nature of experiencing the contact that arises simultaneously with it]. Furthermore, feeling cannot be self-cognizing (svasaṃvedana).

If it is argued that although feeling experiences contact, it does not relinquish the nature of feeling and is thus called "feeling by its own nature," then it would follow that all phenomena (dharmas) are likewise [feelings].
This is because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of feeling [is non-existent], for all phenomena do not abandon their own nature. Therefore, what he has said merely deceives infants.
Next, the counter-argument is refuted. His counter-argument states: "Contact is like a kingdom or a city, and feeling is like a king.
Contact can produce feeling, just as one is called a 'king' only by virtue of having a kingdom or city. Feeling can experience contact, just as a king can [experience his realm]."

It consumes various kingdoms and cities, yet it avoids the fault of being named after its cause; therefore, it is said that "feeling" (vedanā) is that which can experience the essence of feeling produced by contact.
This is like saying that a king can experience the royal essence produced by his kingdom.

However, since it is stated that it experiences the essence of feeling produced by contact, it cannot be experiencing the contact that arises simultaneously with it, which contradicts the previously held position. Furthermore...
That which is produced by contact is itself the essence of sensation (*vedanā*). How, then, could it be further apprehended by means of sensation?

If you further argue that it is called "sensation by its own nature" (*svabhāva-vedanā*) because it does not abandon its own nature, then since all phenomena do not abandon their own natures, could they all be called sensation?
Therefore, the following section concludes with a refutation.
However, as for objective feeling (*viṣayavedanā*), it is not a feeling shared with other [mental factors].

That which experiences the three aspects—favorable and so forth—and is strictly restricted to oneself is called objective feeling, because it is not shared with the other mental states and their modes of activity.

Because those [opponents] falsely conceive that the feeling of an object (*viṣaya-vedanā*) is a characteristic shared with others, they separately establish "feeling as self-nature" (*svabhāva-vedanā*).

Now, having first refuted the notion of feeling as self-nature, I shall clarify that the feeling of an object is not a characteristic shared with others. Feeling has the characteristic of experiencing (*anubhava*) an object;
consciousness has the characteristic of discerning (*vijñapti*) an object; and perception has the characteristic of grasping the image (*nimitta-grahaṇa*) of an object.
They take aspiration for their characteristic; up to and including wisdom, which takes the discernment of the observed object as its characteristic.
Therefore, they are all unique. The third explanation of sensation is concluded. △ Fourth, the explanation of perception.
Perception (*saṃjñā*) has the nature of grasping the image of an object and the function of establishing various conventional designations (*nāma-pada*).

That is to say, one must first establish the specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the object—such as its dimensions, height, beauty, or ugliness—before being able to subsequently give rise to various conventional designations accordingly.
△ Fifth, the explanation of *cetanā* (volition).
*Cetanā* has the nature of causing the mind to engage in activity. Its function is to employ the mind toward wholesome categories and so forth.
That is to say, it can apprehend the objective conditions, such as the characteristics of correct causes, and drive one's own mind to perform wholesome actions and the like.

Grasping the characteristics of objects that are correct causes leads the mind to produce wholesome categories; grasping the characteristics of objects that are false causes leads the mind to produce unwholesome categories;
grasping the characteristics of objects that are neither correct nor false leads the mind to produce neutral categories. All of these are due to the power of the mental factor of volition (*cetanā*).
This concludes the second section: the detailed explanation of its essence and function. △ Third, the conclusion establishing its association.
Since these five are subsumed under the category of universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), they are necessarily associated with the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Their characteristics as universal factors shall be explained in detail later. Although these five—contact and the others—differ from the storehouse consciousness in their subjective aspects (*ākāra*), they are termed "associated" because they share the same time of arising, the same basis (the sense organ), and the same objective referent (the entity).
This will be explained in detail later; this refers to the fifth fascicle. Regarding their distinct modes of activity (*ākāra*): consciousness has discernment as its mode of activity;
contact has the act of touching as its mode of activity; attention has the alerting of the mind as its mode of activity; feeling has the experiencing of reception as its mode of activity;
perception has the grasping of images as its mode of activity; and volition has the performance of action as its mode of activity.
Furthermore, the *Zongjing lu* states: "It is called 'correspondence' (*samyoga*) because of four kinds of equality:

first, equality of entity; second, equality of locus; third, equality of time; and fourth, equality of basis. 'Equality' here has the meaning of similarity. Because their substance is each only one, they are called equal in entity.
Because the characteristics of the objects are similar, they are called equal in objective referent. This concludes the third section, the Explanation of the Door of Correspondence. △ Four.
Section Two: The Gate of Association with Feeling. First, the explicit clarification of association with equanimity; second, the exclusion of association with other feelings.
Now, the first:
the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of this consciousness is extremely indistinct; it cannot discriminate between the characteristics of disagreeable or agreeable objects, being subtle and uniform.
It proceeds in continuous succession; therefore, it is associated exclusively with the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

Furthermore, the sensation associated with this consciousness is solely a true maturation (*vipāka*), because it proceeds in accordance with previously projected karma and does not depend on present conditions, proceeding solely by the force of virtuous or non-virtuous karma.
For this reason, it is exclusively the sensation of equanimity. As for the two sensations of suffering and pleasure, they are born of maturation (*vipākaja*) [and belong to the preceding category].
The six consciousnesses are not the true maturation (*vipāka*), because they arise only in dependence upon present conditions. Furthermore, they are not associated with this [eighth consciousness].

Moreover, because this consciousness is eternally unchanging, sentient beings constantly grasp it as their internal self (*ātman*). If it were associated with the two feelings of pleasure and pain, it would undergo change;
how then could it be grasped as the self? Therefore, it is associated only with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). [Question: If...
[Question: How can this consciousness also be a maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) summoned by unwholesome karma? [Answer:

Since it is admitted that wholesome karma can summon the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), this [unwholesome karma] should likewise be so; for the feeling of equanimity does not contradict the categories of suffering or pleasure (just as in the case of the analogy).
Just as neutral (*avyākṛta*) dharmas can likewise [produce results], both wholesome and unwholesome [dharmas] bring about their respective fruits.

If these were feelings of suffering or pleasure, they would necessarily be clearly manifest; however, the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the eighth consciousness is extremely obscure—this is one point.
Furthermore, if it were any other type of feeling, it would necessarily grasp the objective characteristics (*nimitta*) of either disagreeable or agreeable objects; yet, the eighth consciousness...

It cannot discern the characteristics of favorable or unfavorable objects; this is the second point. If it were the sensation of suffering or pleasure, its mode of activity (*ākāra*) would necessarily be coarse;
however, the eighth consciousness now has a subtle mode of activity; this is the third point. If it were any other type of sensation, there would necessarily be fluctuation and detachment;
however, the eighth consciousness is exclusively of one kind—an unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*); this is the fourth point. If...
Other feelings necessarily involve interruption. Now, the eighth consciousness evolves as a continuous stream; these are the five meanings.

Because it possesses these five meanings, it is associated exclusively with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*); the rest can be understood accordingly. △ Second, distinguishing that it is not associated with others.

(Question: How is it that this consciousness is not associated with mental factors such as those of the "particular object" category? (Answer: Because they are mutually contradictory; namely, [it is because] desire...

Aspiration (*chanda*) functions by turning toward desired objects; this consciousness (*vijñāna*), however, is subject to karma and lacks aspiration. Resolve (*adhimokṣa*) functions by determining and maintaining an object with certainty;
this consciousness is dull and lacks such determination. Mindfulness (*smṛti*) functions by clearly remembering previously experienced objects;

this consciousness is obscure and inferior, unable to maintain clear recollection. Concentration (*samādhi*) is able to cause the mind to focus one-pointedly on a single object; this consciousness is spontaneous and momentary.
Regarding the distinct objects: wisdom (*prajñā*) functions only by discerning matters such as attainment (*prāpti*). This consciousness is subtle and indistinct, and thus cannot perform discernment;

therefore, it does not associate with the distinct-object mental factors. Furthermore, because this consciousness is exclusively of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*), it does not associate with wholesome (*kuśala*) mental factors, nor with those that are defiled (*kliṣṭa*)—including the root and secondary afflictions.
Although the four factors such as regret (*kaukṛtya*) can pertain to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature, they are nonetheless interrupted.
Because it is abandoned, it is certainly not associated with the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).

First, the non-association with the specifically objective mental states (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*) was examined in detail; next, the non-association with the wholesome, the defiled, and the indeterminate was briefly examined. Both may be understood according to the text.
The fourth section, the gate of the association with feeling (*vedanā-samprayoga*), is concluded.

△ Fifth, the gate of the three natures (*tri-lakṣaṇa*). (Question: There are four kinds of phenomena (*dharma*): namely, the wholesome (*kuśala*), the unwholesome (*akuśala*), the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), and the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Under which of these categories is the *ālayavijñāna* subsumed? (Answer: This consciousness is exclusively unobscured-unspecified, because it is of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*). It is...
If this [ālaya-vijñāna] were itself wholesome or defiled, then the processes of saṃsāra and its cessation would be impossible to establish.

Furthermore, since this consciousness is the basis for what is wholesome and what is defiled, if its own nature were wholesome or defiled, it would contradict itself and thus could not serve as the support for both types of phenomena simultaneously.
Moreover, because this consciousness is by nature that which is perfumed (bhāvyatva), if it were wholesome or defiled, it would be like an extremely fragrant [substance].
It is odorous; it should not be susceptible to perfuming (if it were). Because there would be no perfuming, both the causes and effects of defilement and purity would fail to be established.

Therefore, this consciousness is exclusively unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). "Obscured" (*nivṛta*) refers to defiled phenomena, because they obstruct the Noble Path and can veil the mind, preventing it from being pure.

This consciousness is not defiled, hence it is called "unobscured. "Neutral" (*avyākṛta*) refers to that which is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, characterized by being neither desirable nor undesirable.
Because its fruits and its own specific nature (as a cause) can be definitively described, it is neither wholesome nor unwholesome;

therefore, it is called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*). It is exclusively "unobscured-indeterminate" for three reasons: first, because it is of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*); second, because it is the basis for both the wholesome and the defiled;
and third, because it is the nature of that which is perfumed (*bhāvya*). The rest may be understood accordingly. 6. Explaining the Mental Factors (*caitta*) by Way of Analogizing Them to the King.
Second: First, the formal explanation; second, the refutation of divergent views. Now, for the first:
"Contact and so forth are also like this" means that, just as the ālayavijñāna is comprised solely within the category of the unobscured-neutral (anivṛta-avyākṛta) nature.
The same applies to contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*).

Since all associated mental factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*) must necessarily share the same nature, these five—contact and the others—are, like the *ālayavijñāna*, also results of maturation (*vipāka*). Their objects (*ālambana*) and modes of activity (*ākāra*) are both unknowable;

they take as their objects the three types of realms (the seeds, the sense-faculties and the body, and the external world), are associated with the five factors, and are non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Therefore, it is said that contact and the others are likewise.
The five factors are associated, namely the single mind-king and the other four mental concomitants (*caitta*). The rest may be understood. △ Second, the refutation of divergent views:

There is an interpretation which holds that contact (*sparśa*) and the others, like the *ālayavijñāna*, are also both maturation (*vipāka*) and possess all seeds (*sarvabījaka*). This is explained at length, and so forth...
The statement that "the unobscured-neutral [factors] are also like this" (as mentioned in the verse) is made because there is no specific distinction [stated]. That explanation is irrational.

Why? Because contact (*sparśa*) and the other [mental factors] depend upon consciousness and lack autonomy—just as greed (*rāga*), faith (*śraddhā*), and so forth [depend on the mind-king and cannot be perfumed]—they cannot receive perfuming (*vāsanā*).

How, then, could they be identical to consciousness in their ability to maintain seeds (*bīja*)? Furthermore, if contact and the others were also able to receive perfuming, then [consciousness] would have to be manifold.
The nature of the seeds consists of six types. If this is so, from which seed does the fruit arise?

Logically, it cannot be said that it arises from all six, for we have never seen multiple seeds produce a single sprout. If one were to say that the fruit arises from only one seed, then the remaining five seeds would be rendered useless.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that they produce the fruit sequentially, because the perfuming (vāsanā) occurs simultaneously.

Because their power must also be equal. Furthermore, it cannot be said that the six results arise simultaneously, lest six eye-consciousnesses and so forth arise at once within a single sentient being in a single moment.
The section beginning with "There is an interpretation" first presents the opponent's position. The section beginning with "He says" follows by refuting it.

[The opponent argues that] the five mental factors, such as contact (*sparśa*), cannot be called "all-seeds" (*sarvabījaka*), because the term "all-seeds" is necessarily applied only to that which has been perfumed (*vāsita*).

Therefore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated as follows: "The five mental factors, such as contact, are the subject (*dharmin*); they cannot receive perfuming, this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). This is the reason (*hetu*).

It is said that consciousness lacks self-mastery, just as craving, faith, and so forth do. Furthermore, [the text] refutes the counter-argument that contact and other factors may also receive perfuming (*vāsanā*).

Even if one were to grant that they receive perfuming, then since there is one mind-king and five mental associates (*caitta*), each would individually receive the perfuming of various dharmas, resulting in six distinct seeds of dharmas. When the fruit arises, it would then have to arise from these six...
[To say that they] arise—whether arising from one [cause], arising sequentially, or arising all at once—is in every case contrary to reason.

[The opponent] defends [the position], saying: "Who says that contact (*sparśa*) and the other [mental factors] can also be perfumed (*vāsita*) and hold the various seeds? [The proponent] refutes: "That is not so. How then could contact and the others be called 'all-seeded' (*sarvabījaka*) in the same way as consciousness (*vijñāna*)?

[The opponent] offers a false interpretation, saying: "It is because each of the five [factors beginning with] contact possesses a semblance of the characteristic of a seed; this is what is meant by [the term]."
Because all types [of mental factors], such as contact (*sparśa*) and so forth, have objects of cognition (*ālambana*) that are necessarily identical to those of consciousness;
because in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), contact and the other five mental factors necessarily possess objects of cognition (which are the *nimittabhāga* resembling seeds);

and because the direct object-condition (*sākṣād-ālambanapratyaya*) must certainly exist for each of these five mental factors—nevertheless, this *nimittabhāga* resembling seeds within contact and the others does not serve as a causal condition (*hetupratyaya*) for the arising of manifest consciousness and so forth. This is illustrated by the analogy [of the reflection].

Just as that which appears like the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) upon [the transformation of] touch and so forth is not the support (*āśraya*) for consciousness, it is also like the appearance of fire, which lacks the function of burning.
[The opponent] offers this defense, but it is unreasonable.

For the objects of perception (*ālambana*), such as the appearance of seeds and so forth upon touch and so forth, must first await the subsequent mention of "appropriation" (*upādāna*) before they can be compared to consciousness. Therefore, [the verse] previously stated "all seeds" (as the basis for the argument).

It is said: "The term 'fixed' (niyata) refers to the sense of being able to receive perfuming and maintain seeds (referring to the ālayavijñāna itself, not to the contaminated seeds within its objects).
Otherwise, there would be the fault of redundant phrasing in the root verse."
This refutes the attempt to falsely rescue [the position] by claiming that the *bhāga* (aspect) constitutes all seeds (*sarvabīja*).

Since the *bhāga* consists of contaminated seeds and is subsumed under the fifth category of the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it can be analogously applied to the "king" (*rāja*)—namely, the primary consciousness—as in the case of contact (*sparśa*) and other mental factors. Now, regarding "all seeds":
This refers to the third section on the characteristics of causes. How could it be analogous to [the case of] contact and so forth?

If one were to take "all seeds" (*sarvabīja*) as the objective support (*ālambana*), then within the appropriated basis (*upātta-āśraya*) there would yet again be seeds as objective supports; would this not be a case of redundant expression?
Furthermore, what they have stated—that because the statement lacks qualification, all cases may be analogized—does not constitute valid proof.

Otherwise, it would follow that the five [factors] such as contact (*sparśa*) would also possess the capacity for discernment (*vijñapti*) like consciousness, and that contact and the others would also be associated with contact and the others like consciousness.
For this reason, it should be understood that the same applies [to other factors] as well; they are explained according to what is appropriate, not in a universal sense.
Contact (*sparśa*) and the others do not take discernment (*vijñapti*) as their mode of activity (*ākāra*).

Contact does not associate with contact, and so on, up to volition (*cetanā*) not associating with volition, because there are no two contacts within a single moment, and so on, up to no two volitions. (6)

The section on the analogy of the King and his Ministers regarding the mental factors is concluded. △ Seven: Explaining the Section on the Analogy of Cause and Effect. Part Two: First, elucidating the correct doctrine;

second, refuting divergent views. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the direct explanation of the verse; second, resolving objections to reveal the underlying principle. Now, the first section.
(Question: Is the ālayavijñāna discontinuous or permanent? (Answer: It is neither discontinuous nor permanent, because it is perpetually evolving.
"Perpetual" means that from beginningless time, this consciousness has been a single, continuous stream, always uninterrupted;

for it is the fundamental basis for the designation of the three realms, the six destinies, and the four modes of birth, and its nature is firm and stable, maintaining the seeds so that they are not lost. "Evolving" [means...]

This means that from time immemorial, this consciousness arises and perishes moment by moment, undergoing transformation from prior to subsequent states; as the cause ceases and the fruit arises, it is neither permanent nor unitary.

Because it can be perfumed by the [first] seven evolving consciousnesses to form seeds, the term "constant" (*nitya*) excludes interruption, while "evolving" (*pravṛtti*) indicates its non-permanence.
Like a violent torrent, the law of cause and effect is such that it is neither interrupted nor permanent, but continues in succession.

For a long time, there is drifting and drowning; this consciousness is likewise. From beginningless time, it continues in a succession of arising and ceasing, being neither permanent nor annihilated, causing sentient beings to drift and drown so that they do not attain liberation.

Furthermore, just as a violent torrent, though struck by winds and other factors, gives rise to various waves yet its flow does not cease, so too this consciousness, though encountering various conditions to give rise to visual consciousness and the rest, remains constant.
It is a continuity. Furthermore, it is like a violent torrent, where water, fish, grass, and other objects are carried along, moving up and down with the current without being abandoned.
This consciousness is likewise; it constantly evolves in conjunction with internal habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and external factors such as contact.

Through these teachings and analogies, the meaning is revealed that this consciousness is neither interrupted nor eternal in its beginningless cause-and-effect relationship. That is to say, the nature of this consciousness has, from time immemorial, been momentary.
In each moment, as the fruit arises, the cause ceases. Because the fruit arises, there is no annihilation; because the cause ceases, there is no permanence.
This absence of annihilation and permanence is the principle of dependent origination. Therefore, it is said that this consciousness perpetually revolves like a flowing stream.

"Cause and effect" excludes the grasping at a self; "arising and ceasing" excludes the grasping at permanence. Because there is arising and ceasing, it is not permanent; because there is cause and effect, it is not a single entity.

It is like a torrential stream that flows in continuous succession: within this flow, viewed from the perspective of what precedes, it is called the "effect," and viewed from the perspective of what follows, it is called the "cause.
Therefore, it is neither annihilated nor eternal, and can thus be used as a metaphor for this consciousness. Furthermore, there are three points of similarity: first, its capacity to...
First, because it is like being adrift and drowning. Second, because while the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are intermittent, this [storehouse consciousness] is uninterrupted;

it is like waves that arise and subside, yet the current does not cease. Third, because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) constantly follow and evolve along with it;

the internal habitual tendencies grasped by the consciousness are likened to fish within the water, and the five [factors] such as contact (*sparśa*) associated with the consciousness are likewise present.

The Dharma is like grass upon the surface of water; the rest may be understood accordingly. △ Second, resolving objections to reveal the principle. There are two rounds of question and answer. (The objection states:
"If the past and future are not substantially existent, it would be reasonable that they are not eternal; however, how could they not be annihilated? How could annihilation be possible?"
Establishing the Correct Principle of Dependent Origination (The Response): If the past and future were substantially existent, one could grant that there is no annihilation;

however, how could they not be permanent? Yet even permanence does not establish the correct principle of dependent origination. (Nevertheless,) how can one merely refute the errors of others and thereby have one’s own position established?
If one does not demolish the false tenets [of others], it is difficult to clarify the correct principle. At the stage when the preceding cause ceases...
The subsequent fruit arises immediately, just as the two ends of a scale rise and fall simultaneously. In this way, cause and effect continue like a flowing stream;
what need is there for their coming and going (to exist substantially) in order for them not to be discontinuous?
The weighing at both ends serves as a metaphor for cause and effect. The rising and falling of the scale serves as a metaphor for arising and ceasing.
That the rising and falling are simultaneous serves as a metaphor for arising and ceasing being of the same single kṣaṇa, such that there is no sequence of before and after.

(Furthermore, it is difficult [to maintain your position]). Since the cause exists at the present time, and the subsequent effect has not yet arisen, of what would that cause be the cause? At the time when the effect is present...

If the prior cause has already ceased and passed away, whose fruit would the result be? Since there is neither cause nor fruit, who could avoid the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism? [The answer is: ...
If one claims that at the very time the cause exists, the subsequent effect already exists, then since the effect is already inherently present, why would it need to depend on the preceding cause?

Since the meaning of "cause" is thus nullified, how could the meaning of "effect" possibly exist? With neither cause nor effect, how could one avoid the extremes of nihilism and eternalism (as in our Mahāyāna)?

The principle of cause and effect is established solely by means of the functional activity (*kāritra*) of phenomena existing in the present; thus, it avoids the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism and accords with the logic of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Therefore, your objection does not apply to our Mahāyāna orthodoxy. If the essence of the fruit were already inherently existent, then its function would likewise have to be so, because the causes and conditions upon which it depends would also be inherently existent.
(In that case, both essence and function would be primordially existent; why then would there be a need for further...)

Since there is no meaning of a cause, there is also no meaning of an effect. Consequently, according to your position, cause and effect definitively do not exist. You should therefore have faith in the correct principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in the Mahāyāna.

That is to say, this correct principle—the intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena—is profound and subtle, transcending words; it cannot be reached by conceptual cognition or its verbal expressions.

All current discourse regarding cause, effect, and so forth, is merely a conventional designation based on superimposition and similarity. One provisionally establishes [these terms] by observing that present phenomena possess the capacity to project subsequent states.

Regarding the future fruit, one speaks in contrast to the present cause; observing that present phenomena possess characteristics that repay what preceded them, one provisionally establishes a "past cause.

Regarding the present fruit, one speaks in contrast to this [past cause]. "Provisional" means that within present consciousness, there appears an aspect resembling that [future fruit which was the past cause].

In this way, cause and effect (in their entirety) do not depart from the single moment of the present phenomenon; this principle is manifest, remaining far removed from the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, and accords with the Middle Way. All...
The wise should practice and study accordingly.
It is simply this single momentary dharma of the present: viewed in relation to what precedes it, it is called the "fruit"; viewed in relation to what follows it, it is called the "cause.
When speaking of past causes in reference to the present fruit, then eons as numerous as the atoms of dust prior to this moment are just like today. Thus...
In the transformation of present consciousness, there appears an aspect resembling past causes, yet it does not actually take past events as its object.

This is because the past has already ceased and is therefore unobjectifiable. By means of present causes, one predicts future fruits; thus, even after immeasurable eons, they are as clear as looking at the palm of one's hand.
This occurs through the transformation of present consciousness into an aspect resembling future fruits, yet it does not actually take them as its object.
This concerns future phenomena. Because the future has not yet arisen and thus lacks anything that can serve as an object of perception (*ālambana*), it is said:
"Throughout the ten periods of time and across all ages, beginning and end do not depart from the present moment. Furthermore, the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) states:

"The past and future have no substantiality; the perfuming of moments belongs solely to the present. At the very moment when a deluded thought arises in the present, that deluded thought deviates from the Truth; this is called..."
This refers to the "first consciousness. It does not mean that a consciousness previously non-existent suddenly arises for the first time;

rather, it is called the "first consciousness" because it is known to span horizontally across all places and penetrate vertically through immeasurable times—all of which is precisely this present single mind, with no other principle whatsoever.
This concludes the initial clarification of the correct doctrine. △ Second, the refutation of divergent views has two parts: first, the actual refutation; second, the concluding exhortation.
This section has two parts: first, the refutation of other schools; second, the refutation of the Sautrāntika school. The first part also has two sections: first, the statement of their tenet;
second, the refutation thereof. Now, for the first:
another school asserts that although past and future do not exist, there is the principle of cause and effect in constant succession, namely, the present dharma.

Even that which is most rapid still possesses two moments: the time of arising and the time of ceasing. At the time of arising, it responds to the cause (which is termed the characteristic of the fruit);

at the time of ceasing, it draws forth the fruit (which is termed the characteristic of the cause). Although there are these two moments, their substance is one. As the preceding cause is precisely ceasing, the subsequent fruit is precisely arising.

Although their essential natures and characteristics differ, both are equally existent. Such cause and effect are not mere conceptual constructs; yet they are free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, and thus avoid the objection:
"From where does the prior cause come? To what does the subsequent effect belong? What wise person would abandon this and believe in anything else?
△ Second, the refutation: Those [arguments] are mere empty words and lack any real meaning. How could a single moment contain two times? Arising and ceasing are mutually contradictory;

how could they be identical to the present? If cessation were present, arising would have to be future. It is called "arising" because it exists, and since it is already present, [it cannot be future].

It is called "cessation" because it is non-existent; how could it not be past? If cessation were not non-existent, then arising would not be existent. Since arising is presently existent, cessation must be presently non-existent.
Furthermore, these two are contradictory; how could they be one in essence? This is not like the case of suffering and pleasure, for we observe that such a thing [a contradiction] does exist.

If arising and ceasing were identical, there would be no distinction between their two temporal phases (the beginning and the end). If arising and ceasing were distinct [in time], how could one say that their substance is the same?
Therefore, the claim that arising and ceasing both exist simultaneously in the present and share a single underlying substance is logically untenable.

How can this be tolerated? First, it refutes the two moments within a single thought-moment. Furthermore, "the two" below refers to the subsequent refutation of the identity of the essence of arising and ceasing.
For those who do not see such a thing as suffering and pleasure, the two phenomena of arising and ceasing are analogous to the two sensations of suffering and pleasure.
This is a definitive contradiction. How could there be a single essence? The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: Arising and ceasing are the subject (*dharmin*);

their essence is definitely not one, this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because they are contradictory. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: like suffering and pleasure. This concludes the refutation of the other schools.
△ Second, the refutation of the Sautrāntika school.
The principle of the causal continuity (saṃtati) as conceived by the Sautrāntikas and others is also untenable,
because they do not admit the existence of the ālayavijñāna capable of maintaining the seeds (bīja).

Although the first six evolving consciousnesses may also possess the relationship of cause and effect when viewed in relation to one another, they are frequently interrupted and cannot continue in an uninterrupted stream.

If there were no fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) to receive perfuming and maintain the seeds, by what principle could the dependent origination of the continuous succession of cause and effect be established?
The initial direct refutation is concluded. II. Conclusion and Exhortation.
Based on this, one should have faith in the correct principle of the causal continuity of dependent origination as taught in the Mahāyāna.
This concludes the seventh section: the Gate of Explaining the Dharma through Analogies of Cause and Effect. △ Eighth: The Gate of Explaining the Stages of Subduing and Severing. It has two parts:
