first, the formal explanation of the meaning of relinquishing the *ālayavijñāna*; second, a general clarification of the various names for the eighth consciousness. Within the first part, there are two sections; the first is the formal clarification of the capacity [to relinquish].
The Section on Abandoning. Second, distinguishing and indicating that what is abandoned is merely a name. This first part has two sections: first, clarifying the correct meaning;
second, refuting divergent interpretations. The first of these also has two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, resolving objections. Now, the first [the direct explanation].
This consciousness has been revolving continuously like a stream since beginningless time. Until what stage is it finally abandoned? It is finally abandoned at the stage of an Arhat.
That is to say, when the noble ones have completely severed the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and reached their ultimate exhaustion, they are called Arhats.
At that time, because this consciousness is forever separated from the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) of the afflictions, it is said to be "abandoned. In this context...
Regarding the term "Arhat" (Worthy One): it comprehensively encompasses the stage of the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) in all three vehicles.

This is because they have forever destroyed the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*; this is the meaning of "slayer of thieves"). Because they are worthy of receiving the sublime offerings of the world (this is the meaning of "Worthy of Offerings"). Because they will never again undergo birth within the realm of segmented existence (*bhavāgra*;
this is the meaning of "no-birth"). How is this known? The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states: "All Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas..."
Because the *ālayavijñāna* has not yet been fully accomplished. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"When Bodhisattvas attain enlightenment, they simultaneously sever the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), thereby becoming Arhats and Tathāgatas."
"Dauṣṭhulya" (coarseness) is another name for seeds. An *arhat* is the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) in the Hīnayāna;
a *pratyekabuddha* is the stage of no-more-learning in the Madhyamāyāna; and a *tathāgata* is the stage of no-more-learning in the Mahāyāna.

Next, citing the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it is shown that a *tathāgata* is also called an *arhat*, because he has abandoned the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and thus attained [the state of] an *arhat*.
The Arhat becomes a Tathāgata by severing the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). △ Second, resolving objections, which has two parts:
first, the question; second, the answer. Now, the first.

If that were so, then since Bodhisattvas (after entering the stages) continue to manifest afflictions even as they gradually subside, and their seeds of affliction have not yet been permanently and completely severed—
thus being non-Arhat— they should all possess the ālayavijñāna. Why, then, does that very *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* state that "all non-regressive Bodhisattvas do not possess the ālayavijñāna"?
If one relies on the previous meaning, then it would be only upon attaining Buddhahood that a Bodhisattva could be named an Arhat and only then abandon this consciousness.
Since it is now stated that even non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas do not yet achieve [this], he asks about it.
This is because from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, Bodhisattvas are already termed "non-retrogressive. II. The Response, which has two parts: 1. First, an explanation based on the Two Vehicles.
"Returning the mind" (*huíxīn*) is called "non-retrogression. Second, regarding those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, it is termed non-retrogression. Now, for the first [case]:

it is taught that those of the Two Vehicles who, at the stage of the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣaphala*), turn their minds toward great enlightenment (even if they have not yet ascended to the stages), will certainly not retrogress into the arising of afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Because they are proceeding toward enlightenment, they are subsequently renamed "non-retrogressive bodhisattvas. They do not...
One who has realized the *ālayavijñāna* (though still designated as a bodhisattva) is included within this category of arhats;
therefore, that treatise does not contradict this meaning.
Because they do not give rise to afflictions, they are called "non-retrogressive. Because they advance toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), they are called "Bodhisattvas.
That treatise refers to such a person as a non-retrogressive Bodhisattva; it does not refer to one who directly cultivates the Mahāyāna and has ascended to the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Therefore, there is no contradiction. 2. Second, defining "non-retrogression" with respect to those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward.
Furthermore, because all afflictions never again arise for Bodhisattvas from the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*) upward,

because they proceed spontaneously within the swift current of the Dharma, because they initiate various conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) amidst all formations, and because they advance and increase moment by moment,

it is only at this stage that they are called "Bodhisattvas who have truly attained non-retrogression. Nevertheless, although these Bodhisattvas have not yet completely severed [the remaining] heterodox...

Having thoroughly familiarized themselves with the seeds of afflictions within this consciousness, the four types of afflictions—namely, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), self-love (*ātma-sneha*), and so forth—no longer grasp and store it as their internal self.
Consequently, they permanently relinquish the name "ālaya" (storehouse);
therefore, it is said that [at this stage] the ālayavijñāna is no longer established. Furthermore, in this verse, those [at the Immovable Ground and above] are also called "Arhats."
This clarifies that those who practice the Mahāyāna directly must reach the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) or above before their afflictions (*kleśa*) can be permanently suppressed;

they may then also be called *arhats*. Sentient beings who are adrift and drowning due to their cognitive attachment to phenomena (*jñeya-dharma-abhiniveśa*) undergo inconceivable transformational birth-and-death (*nirmāṇa-cyuti*), which is termed the "swift current of phenomena" (*dharma-vega*).
Having attained mastery, this is termed "spontaneous revolution," wherein every moment of mind flows [in liberation].
One enters the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge); therefore, one progresses and increases further with every passing moment. This concludes the first section: Clarifying the Correct Meaning.

△ Second, Refuting Divergent Interpretations, in two parts: First, the Direct Refutation; Second, Refuting the Defense. Within the first part, there are two sections: First, Narrating the Calculations;
Second, Refuting and Criticizing. Now, the first [section].

There is an interpretation that from the first bhūmi upward, Bodhisattvas—because they have already realized the principle of True Suchness (tathatā) as manifested by the two emptinesses of self and phenomena;

because they have already attained the two kinds of superior wisdom, both fundamental and subsequently acquired; and because they have already severed the two layers of obstacles, both afflictive and cognitive—are able to give rise to all modes of conduct within a single mode of conduct.
Thus, although they may give rise to the active manifestation of various afflictions for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, those [afflictions] do not constitute [actual defilement].
Because of these faults of affliction, this [bodhisattva] is also called a non-retrogressive bodhisattva.

However, although this bodhisattva has not yet completely severed the innate afflictions, they no longer grasp at the conceptualized views of self, craving, and so forth associated with this consciousness as their own internal self.
By virtue of this, they also relinquish the name "ālaya"; therefore, it is said that they do not constitute an ālayavijñāna.
Consciousness. Within this verse, it is also stated that those from the first bhūmi upward are called *arhats*. Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states as follows:
"Although Bodhisattvas of the ten stages have not yet permanently severed all afflictions (*kleśa*), these afflictions are like poisons suppressed by mantras or medicines;
they do not give rise to any faults of the afflictions. In all stages, they are like *arhats*."
Since the Han [practitioners] have already severed the afflictions (*kleśa*), they are also called *arhats*.
△ Second, the refutation:

Their explanation is irrational because from the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) onward, there still exist innate self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), self-love (*ātmasneha*), and so forth, which grasp and store this [ālayavijñāna].
If consciousness is taken as the internal self, how can it have already abandoned the name "ālayavijñāna"?

If its abandonment is defined as the fact that the conceptualization of a self, self-view, self-love, and so forth no longer grasp and store [it], then those in the stages of training, such as the stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), would also have already abandoned the name "ālayavijñāna.
To accept this would contradict what is taught in all the treatises.
△ Second, the refutation of the defense, which is further divided into two parts. First, the statement of the defense; second, the refutation. Now, the first part.
The afflictions that arise in Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) are all due to correct knowledge (*saṃprajanya*) and do not constitute a fault.
This is not the case for those such as Stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*); how then can the latter (the fruits of Stream-entry, etc. be used as an analogy for these Bodhisattvas on the stages?
△ Second, the refutation:

Although the afflictions arising within those six consciousnesses do not constitute a fault when one possesses correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), the seventh consciousness—while in the state of a tainted mind (*sāsrava-citta*)—spontaneously manifests as it clings to and stores this [eighth] consciousness.
How could it not be the same as that of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and others?
For this reason, it is known that their explanation is irrational.

This concludes the first section, which correctly clarifies the stage of being able to relinquish [the storehouse consciousness]. Second, distinguishing and indicating that what is relinquished is merely a designation:
However, because the Arhat has completely and utterly exhausted the afflictive latencies (*dausthulya*) within this consciousness, they no longer grasp and store [it as a self].
The ālayavijñāna is taken as one's own internal self; because of this, it permanently loses its name "ālaya" (storehouse), which is what is meant by "abandoning" it.
This does not mean abandoning the entire substance of the eighth consciousness, lest an arhat be without a consciousness to maintain the seeds and thereby immediately enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
An Arhat has severed all afflictions and is said to have realized *nirvāṇa* with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

Because the substance of the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) still persists, it is able to maintain the previously existing seeds of outflows (*āsrava*), thereby ensuring that the physical body with its sense organs and the life-span do not cease.

Only when the remaining residual karmic retribution is exhausted does one enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*). If this consciousness did not exist to maintain the seeds, then the body—
One’s life-force would then immediately be extinguished and one would enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
How then can there currently exist those who have realized arhatship yet still abide in the world? This concludes the initial correct explanation of the meaning of relinquishing the *ālayavijñāna*.

△ Second, a comprehensive clarification of the various alternative names for the eighth consciousness, in two parts: first, the correct explanation of the various names; second, the conclusion that returns to the two states. Now, the first part.
However, although the eighth consciousness is fully possessed by all sentient beings, it is established under various names according to its different functions.
That is to say, it is called "citta" (mind) because it is the accumulation of seeds perfumed by various dharmas;

it is called "ādāna" (appropriation) because it grasps and maintains the seeds and the material sense organs so that they do not perish; and it is called the "basis of the knowable" because it can provide...

Because it serves as the basis for all phenomena known through defilement and purification, it is called the "seed-consciousness" (*bīja-vijñāna*), as it is able to universally sustain all seeds of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
These various names apply throughout all stages; alternatively, it is called the *ālaya*.
Because it gathers and stores all factors belonging to the category of affliction so that they are not lost;

and because it is grasped as an internal self by means of the view of self, craving for self, and so forth—this name applies only to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*), and not to those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) or non-regressive Bodhisattvas, because [for them] there is no longer the sense of being grasped by afflicted factors.
Alternatively, it is called the "maturation-consciousness" (*vipākavijñāna*), because it is capable of drawing forth birth and death.

Because it is the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) of wholesome and unwholesome karma, this name applies only to the stages of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and the various bodhisattvas;

it does not apply to the stage of the Tathāgata, as there still exist dharmas that are maturation-born and neutral (*avyākṛta*). Alternatively, it is called the "stainless consciousness" (*amala-vijñāna*), because it is the support for all most extremely pure, untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas.
This name exists only in the stage of the Tathāgata (or, if [it is said otherwise], in the stage of the Bodhisattva).

In the stages of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they possess contaminated seeds that are susceptible to perfuming (*vāsanā*), because they have not yet attained the thoroughly pure eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
As stated in the Sūtra: "The Tathāgata’s stainless consciousness is the pure, uncontaminated realm;
it is liberated from all obstacles and is associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom."
The *Sūtra* refers to the *Tathāgataguṇavyūha-sūtra*. "Stainless consciousness" (*amala-vijñāna*) indicates its name.
"Pure outflow-free realm" (*anāsrava-dhātu*) demonstrates its meaning. "Liberated from all hindrances" clarifies that liberation from hindrances has reached its ultimate consummation.
"Associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom" clarifies the mental factor of wisdom associated [with it], which is termed the "Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom."
Because the name *ālaya* carries a heavy fault and is the first to be abandoned, it is mentioned specifically (and first) in this verse.

As for the substance of the *vipākavijñāna*, it is abandoned by a bodhisattva when about to attain enlightenment, and it is also abandoned by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas upon entering the nirvāṇa without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*).
However, as for the substance of the *amala-vijñāna*, there is no time of its abandonment, for its benefit and happiness for sentient beings are inexhaustible.
Because they exist at all times; because they pervade all states [of mind]; and because they correspond to their respective meanings [of defilement or purity], they should be explained accordingly.
Within the stage of sentient beings, it is called the defiled mind; within the state of Buddhahood, it is called the pure mind.

Within the stage of sentient beings, it maintains and upholds impure seeds and impure material faculties; within the state of Buddhahood, it maintains and upholds untainted seeds and untainted material faculties.

Within the stage of sentient beings, it is termed the support for the objects of knowledge that is defiled; within the state of Buddhahood, [it is termed the support for the objects of knowledge that is pure].
It is called the "basis for the purification of the objects of knowledge. Within the category of sentient beings, it is termed the "worldly seed-consciousness";
within the stage of Buddhahood, it is termed the "supramundane seed-consciousness. Therefore, it is said that one should explain according to the meaning.

However, the statement herein that those of the two vehicles abandon [this consciousness] upon entering the nirvana without remainder is still spoken according to the provisional teachings of the Shared Vehicle (Tongjiao). If one relies on the Great [Vehicle],...
According to the ultimate meaning, there exists a pure land outside the triple world where Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are born and receive the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*).
Yet, they have not yet abandoned the substance of the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*). Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"Although these people conceive the thought of extinction and enter into nirvāṇa, they seek the Buddha’s wisdom in that land and hear this [Dharma]."
Sūtra: "Only by means of the Buddha-vehicle does one attain extinction; there is no other vehicle. △ Second, the conclusion returning to the two stages:

Now, the eighth consciousness generally has two stages. First, the stage with outflows (*sāsrava*), which is subsumed under the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) and is associated only with the five factors beginning with contact (*sparśa*).
It takes as its object only the previously mentioned spheres of appropriation and environment. Second, the stage without outflows (*anāsrava*), which is exclusively of a wholesome nature.

[It is] subsumed [under the category of mental factors]. It is associated with twenty-one mental concomitants (*caitta*), namely: the five universal (*sarvatraga*) and the five object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*) [mental factors], and the eleven wholesome (*kuśala*) ones.
(Because the five universal mental factors are always associated with all minds, [this consciousness] is also associated with the untainted (*anāsrava*) eighth [consciousness]).

Because it constantly delights in realizing and knowing the objects under observation, (it can be associated with wholesome desire). Because it constantly maintains a firm conviction regarding the objects under observation, (it is associated with wholesome resolve). Regarding what has been previously experienced...

Because its objects are always clearly remembered, it is associated with wholesome mindfulness (*smṛti*). Because the Blessed One has no unconcentrated mind, it is associated with wholesome concentration (*samādhi*).

Because he constantly discriminates all phenomena, it is associated with wholesome wisdom (*prajñā*). Because it is constantly associated with extreme purity, faith, and so forth, it is associated with the eleven wholesome mental factors (*caitasika*).

Because it is undefiled, it is not associated with the roots of unwholesomeness or the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Because it is free from distraction, it is not associated with the four indeterminate states (*aniyata*). This also...
It is associated exclusively with the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), because it functions spontaneously and perpetually in a state of equilibrium.
It takes all phenomena as its objective sphere (*ālambana*), for the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) universally perceives all phenomena.

It is also exclusively the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). This means that within the state of outflow-free (*anāsrava*) cognition, it is identical to the outflowing (*sāsrava*) state in being exclusively the feeling of equanimity.
However, it takes all phenomena as its objective referent (*ālambana*), which differs from the outflowing state that takes only the three categories of objects as its referents.

This concludes the initial formal explanation of the verse. II. Proving the Existence of the Fundamental Consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*). This section has three parts: first, the inquiry and response providing a general outline.
Second, the specific exposition of the scriptural authority and reasoning; third, the summary conclusion and exhortation to believe.
Regarding the first [of these]: (Question: How should one understand that this eighth consciousness has a distinct self-substance apart from the visual and other consciousnesses? (Answer:
Because the sacred teachings and correct reasoning serve as the definitive criteria of measurement.

△ Second, the specific exposition of the scriptural authority and reasoning, in two parts: first, citing the sacred teachings; second, revealing the correct principles. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, citing Mahāyāna scriptures; second, citing other schools. Regarding the first, there are two sub-sections: first, directly citing the sūtras to prove the existence of the eighth consciousness;

second, demonstrating that Mahāyāna is the word of the Buddha (*āptavāda*). The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) states that seven fundamental sūtras are cited, namely the three Mahāyāna and four Hīnayāna texts.

Within the first of these, there are again two parts: first, the direct citation of the sūtras to prove the existence of the eighth [consciousness]; second, the demonstration that Mahāyāna is the sacred word.
Regarding the measure [of authority]: first, I shall properly cite three sūtras and four verses.
As it is said in the Mahāyāna Abhidharma Sūtra: "The element (dhātu) existing from beginningless time is the common support for all phenomena;
because of this, there are the various realms of existence as well as the attainment of nirvāṇa."
*Abhidharma*. This is translated as "Incomparable Dharma. This refers to the first verse cited above.
The subsequent text provides three successive explanations of its meaning.
Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this eighth consciousness is subtle, it is revealed through its functions (*kāritra*). This constitutes the first half of the verse.

The first half [of the verse] reveals the eighth consciousness as functioning as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); the latter half reveals its function as the support (*āśraya*) for both the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*) and its cessation (*nivṛtti*).
This constitutes the first round of explaining the meaning, following the initial division of the sections.

The "realm" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of "cause. It refers to the seed-consciousness; because this seed-consciousness has been transmitted and continued in succession from beginningless time, it can maintain the seeds of all phenomena—both tainted and untainted, including form and mind—and directly gives rise to these phenomena, it is therefore called the "cause. The "basis" (*āśraya*) has the meaning of "condition.

It refers to the appropriating consciousness (*ādāna-vijñāna*); because from beginningless time it serves as the equal support for all phenomena (whether manifesting as tainted or untainted), it is called the "basis."

Therefore, it is called the "condition" (*pratyaya*). That is to say, because the seed-consciousness (*bīja-vijñāna*) is able to maintain all seeds (it is the "maintaining consciousness"), and because it serves as the basis for manifest phenomena (*pravṛtti-dharma*), it transforms into those [manifest phenomena] by virtue of its seeds, and acts as their support by virtue of its maintenance.
"Transforming into that" means transforming into the receptacle world (bhājana-loka) and the body with sense organs (sendriya-kāya) by means of seeds.

"Serving as the support for that" means acting as the basis for the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna). Because the [appropriating] consciousness (ādāna-vijñāna) is able to appropriate the five material sense organs, the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, evolve in dependence upon it.
Furthermore, because it serves as the support for the manas, the sixth mental consciousness (manovijñāna) depends upon it.

Furthermore, because the *manas* and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are both subsumed under the category of "transformative consciousnesses" (*pravṛttivijñāna*), they must rely upon simultaneous bases (*sahabhū-āśraya*), just as the visual and other sensory consciousnesses do.
Since the eighth consciousness is logically of the nature of consciousness, it likewise takes the seventh consciousness as its simultaneous basis.
This is what is meant by the functioning of this [seventh] consciousness as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
This explains the meaning of the first half-verse.

"Because of this existence" means because of the existence of this [eighth] consciousness. "The existence of the various destinies" means the existence of the [six] destinies, such as the wholesome and unwholesome;
that is to say, because of the existence of this eighth consciousness, it maintains all phenomena conducive to the process of transmigration, causing them...

Sentient beings transmigrate through birth and death; although both afflictions and karma give rise to this transmigration, it is the *gati* (destinies) that are the primary result, and thus they are specifically mentioned.
Alternatively, the term "various destinies" (*gati*) refers generally to both the agents who go and the places to which they go, as well as the requisites for those destinies.

It also receives the name "destiny" (*gati*). All afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and birth depend upon this consciousness; thus, it functions as the support for the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*).
This explains the third phrase of the latter half of the verse. All phenomena that conform to transmigration—namely, the contaminated seeds of afflictions, karma, and birth—are as follows:

"afflictions" refers to the two types of afflictions, namely those of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and those of thought (*vitarka*); "karma" refers to the three types: wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable (*āniñjya*).
"Karma" refers to birth—namely, the four modes of birth: womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born. "Destinations" (gati) refer to the retributions of the six realms;
"those who go" (the goers) refer to afflictions and karma, which are also termed the "requisites for the various destinations."
Regarding the attainment of nirvāṇa: it is because this consciousness exists that the attainment of nirvāṇa occurs.
That is to say, because this eighth consciousness exists, it maintains all factors conducive to cessation, thereby enabling the practitioner to realize nirvāṇa.
In this context, only that which can realize the path is mentioned, because nirvāṇa does not exist in dependence upon this consciousness;
or, this refers only to the nirvāṇa to be realized, as it is the primary object sought by the practitioner;

or, this mentions both nirvāṇa and the path together, since both are definitively subsumed within the category of the "class of cessation" (nirodha-pakṣya). That is to say, the word "nirvāṇa" in the verse indicates the cessation that is realized.

The phrase "subsequently realized" indicates the path by which realization is attained. Through the path that is capable of severing, one severs the afflictions to be severed until reaching the state of ultimate exhaustion, thereby realizing nirvana.
Both the subject that severs and the object that is severed depend upon this consciousness;
thus, it functions as the support for the process of cessation.
This explains the fourth line of the latter half of the verse. All phenomena conducive to cessation (*nirodha*) consist of the two types of untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*):

those that are original (*prakṛtistha*) and those that are newly perfumed (*navasaṃskṛta*). "Returning" (*pratyāgama*) has the meaning of "reverting toward"; it refers to the path capable of realization.

"Cessation" (*nirodha*) has the meaning of "quiescent stillness"; it is precisely the *nirvāṇa* that is realized. Furthermore, both the path that can bring about cessation and the act of returning to cessation are the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
That which is returned to and that which is ceased are both the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*), which is *nirvāṇa*. This concludes the first explanation of the meaning of the verse.
Furthermore, in this verse, the first line demonstrates that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this eighth consciousness exists eternally from beginningless time.
The subsequent three lines demonstrate that it serves as the general and specific basis (*āśraya*) for both defiled (*saṃkleśa*) and purified (*vyavadāna*) phenomena.

Defiled phenomena refer to the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and its origin (*samudaya-satya*), namely, birth—which is the destination—and the afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma which are the means of reaching it. Purified phenomena refer to the truths of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and the path (*mārga-satya*).
That is to say, both the nirvāṇa that is realized and the path by which it is realized both exist in dependence upon this consciousness;
for it is logically untenable that they depend upon the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and so forth.
This is the second interpretation of the meaning of the verse. The second phrase, "the basis for all phenomena," generally reveals the substratum of both defilement and purification.
The third phrase, "by which there are the various realms of existence," specifically reveals the substratum of defilement.
The fourth phrase, "and the attainment of nirvāṇa," specifically reveals the substratum of purification. The births to which one goes are suffering.
The truths are as follows: the delusions and karma that lead toward [suffering] are the truth of origin (*samudaya-satya*); the nirvāṇa that is realized is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*);

and the path that realizes it is the truth of the way (*mārga-satya*). Since the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) cannot be perfumed or maintain seeds, they are not the basis for either defiled or pure phenomena.

Alternatively, the first phrase reveals that the substance of this eighth consciousness has been in continuous succession since beginningless time; the latter three phrases reveal that it serves as the basis for the three natures—
namely, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)— which should be understood respectively.
This is the third explanation of the meaning of the verse. The phrase "the basis of all phenomena" reveals that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is not separate from this consciousness.
The phrase "by which there are the various realms of existence" reveals that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is not separate from this consciousness.
And the phrase "attainment of nirvana" reveals that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is not separate from this consciousness.
Now, the various meanings explained in these verses could not exist apart from the eighth consciousness.
To summarize the three preceding explanations of the meaning, all must be understood in relation to the eighth consciousness. This concludes the first verse.
Furthermore, that same sutra states: "Because it contains and stores all phenomena, this consciousness of all seeds is therefore called the ālaya;
I have revealed this to the superior ones."
This is the second verse cited above, which is explained in the following text:

"Because this fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) possesses all seeds, it is able to store and conceal all defiled phenomena (saṃkleśa-dharma). Based on this, the name 'ālayavijñāna' is established.
It is not like [the Sāṃkhya doctrine of] the Primal Nature (prakṛti) transforming into the Great One (mahat) and so forth; [here], the seed and the fruit are not [identical in substance]."
Because they are one; because the supported and the support arise and perish together.
This first explains how the seed-consciousness contains and stores all phenomena, which is not the same as the Sāṃkhya doctrine of the *pradhāna* (primordial nature) or *avyakta* (the unmanifest).
The *pradhāna* is also called the *sattva* (excellent nature). They [the Sāṃkhyas] reckon that although cause and effect are distinct, their essence is one. Now, this clarifies...
First, they differ because the seed and the essence of the fruit are not identical; thus, they are not the same.

Second, they differ because [the opponent] maintains that although the fruit undergoes arising and ceasing, the cause is eternal, whereas here it is clarified that both the dependent (the fruit) and the basis (the cause) arise and cease together. Thus, they are not the same.
Because it mutually contains and conceals the defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), and because sentient beings grasp it as their self (*ātman*), this consciousness is called the *ālaya*.
This correctly explains the meaning of the third term, "ālaya. The eighth [consciousness] contains and conceals the defiled phenomena.
The seeds give rise to active manifestations; this is the sense of "storing [them]. Active defilements permeate and form seeds within the eighth consciousness;
this is the sense of "being stored [within them]. Sentient beings grasp it as their internal self; this is the sense of "being grasped [as a self]."
Because it possesses these three meanings, it is called the *ālayavijñāna*.
Those bodhisattvas who have entered the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and attained true realization (*abhisamaya*) are termed "victors" (*jināḥ*);

they are able to realize and understand the *ālayavijñāna*, and therefore our World-Honored One has correctly revealed it for their sake. Alternatively, [the term] may also apply generally to all bodhisattvas, including those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*). All are so named.

O Victorious One, although those prior to the Path of Seeing have not yet realized or understood the *ālayavijñāna*, they are able to believe in and understand the principle of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) and seek its fruit, which is the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*);
therefore, it is taught to them as well. This is not the case for the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
This explains the fourth phrase, "The Victorious One has revealed me," and simultaneously concludes [the section]. The second verse ends.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* also states: "The ādānavijñāna is profound and subtle;
containing all seeds like a violent torrent, I do not reveal it to the foolish and ignorant, fearing they would conceptually grasp it as a self."
This is the third verse cited above, which is explained in the following text:

Because it is able to maintain the seeds of all phenomena (*dharma*), and because it is able to grasp the [five pure] material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) along with their bases, and furthermore because it is able to grasp the continuity of birth (*upapatti-saṃtati*) through the bonds of affliction (*saṃyojana*), this consciousness is called *ādāna*. [This applies even to] sentient beings who lack the nature [for liberation].

Because its bottom cannot be fathomed, it is said to be "profound" (*gambhīra*). Because those of the lineage who seek quiescence (*śamaikāyana-gotra*) cannot penetrate it, it is called "extremely subtle" (*sūkṣma*).

It is the true seed of all phenomena; when struck by conditions, the waves of the evolving consciousnesses arise. (And this nature of the seed-consciousness arises and ceases from moment to moment,) yet it is constantly uninterrupted, like a violent torrent.
"Ordinary" (*bāla*) refers to those lacking the [Mahāyāna] nature; "foolish" (*mūḍha*) refers to those who seek quiescence. Fearing that they might—

Being unable to realize or understand this profound and subtle principle, they further give rise to conceptual discrimination and falsely cling to it as a self; thus they fall into the various evil destinies and are obstructed from giving birth to the Noble Path.
Therefore, our World-Honored One did not expound [this] for them. Only the eighth consciousness possesses such characteristics.
As for those sentient beings without nature—namely, the icchantikas—they are tossed about by this eighth consciousness, which prevents them from attaining liberation;
thus it is said that they "cannot fathom its bottom. As for those of the lineage inclined toward tranquility—namely, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas of fixed nature—for them, this...
Because one is submerged and drowned by the eighth consciousness without realizing it, it is said that one cannot penetrate [to its truth].

Since it directly produces the manifest activities (*pravṛtti*), it is called the "true seed. Even those with *icchantika* tendencies who do not give rise to false attachments are still able to temporarily roam among humans and devas;

however, if they give rise to conceptual discrimination, they will inevitably fall into the evil destinies. Likewise, even for those of the Two Vehicles who do not give rise to false attachments, they are still able to...
One realizes supramundane fruits. If one gives rise to conceptual discrimination, it will inevitably obstruct the Noble Path;
therefore, the Buddha did not teach the eighth consciousness to such ordinary and ignorant people. The third verse concludes.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* also states this: "Just as when the ocean encounters wind and waves, various billows arise and their manifest activities proceed without interruption;

so too is it with the ocean of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Struck by the winds of objects and the like, the waves of the various consciousnesses constantly arise, and their manifest activities proceed."
This is the fourth verse cited. The first four lines explain solely by means of the analogy, while the latter four lines clarify through the union of the dharma and the analogy;
both may be understood. The conclusion is indicated in the following text.
The various consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and others, lack the quality of the great ocean that constantly flows in succession, giving rise to the waves of all consciousnesses;
therefore, we know that there exists a distinct eighth consciousness-nature.
The above concludes the direct citation of three sutras and four verses; below this is the summary of the brief and the indication of the extensive.
Within these immeasurable Mahāyāna sūtras, it is each specifically stated that this eighth consciousness exists.
The first section, correctly citing sutras to prove the existence of the eighth [consciousness], is concluded. II. Demonstrating that the Mahāyāna is authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*).
All Mahāyāna sūtras accord with selflessness (*anātman*), contradict the notion of a "person" (*pudgala*), and turn away from saṃsāra while tending toward nirvāṇa.
[These Mahāyāna sūtras] praise the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; they disparage the various non-Buddhist paths; they set forth phenomena such as the aggregates (skandhas);

and they negate [theories] such as the *pradhāna* (primordial matter). Therefore, all who delight in the Mahāyāna accept that these Mahāyāna sūtras are indeed able to reveal the non-erroneous principle.
Because they are subsumed under the category of *sūtra*, they are like the *Ekottarika Āgama* and others, which are likewise included within the authority of the "words of the Buddha" (*āptāgama*).

Because these followers of the Hīnayāna do not believe in the existence of the eighth consciousness, they consequently slander and repudiate the three sūtras and four verses cited above, falsely claiming that they are not the sublime teachings spoken by the Buddha.
Therefore, we now establish a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to demonstrate that they are indeed sublime teachings.
The inference states: "The Mahāyāna sūtras are the subject (*dharmin*); they are able to reveal the non-erroneous principle... [to be continued].

The thesis is that which is subsumed under the authority of the Buddha’s teaching (*āgama*). The reason (*hetu*) is: "Because it is included within the sūtras, such as those stating that all [phenomena] conform to selflessness (*anātman*), contradict the notion of a person (*pudgala*), and even negate a supreme nature (*jāti*), etc.
The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is, for instance, the *Ekottarika-āgama* and others.
Furthermore, the noble Maitreya establishes that the Mahāyāna sūtras are truly the word of the Buddha by means of seven reasons. First, because they were not predicted beforehand:

if these Mahāyāna sūtras were [merely] composed by others after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa for the purpose of destroying the True Dharma, why did the World-Honored One—not [as he did regarding] those terrifying events that would arise in the future—fail to predict them in advance within the Sūtras and Vinaya?

1. Because there are predictions (*vyākaraṇa*). Since the two vehicles have both been practiced [since after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa], the teachings of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna have always coexisted from the beginning;
how then can one know that the Mahāyāna alone is not the word of the Buddha? 2. Because it is not the domain of others. That which is taught in the Mahāyāna is vast and profoundly deep;
it is not within the sphere of deliberation for non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and the like. It has never been taught in their sūtras or śāstras, even if they were to [attempt to] compose them.

Furthermore, they do not believe in or accept this Mahāyāna teaching; therefore, the Mahāyāna sūtras are not the word of the Buddha. Fourth, because [the status of] it as such would be universally established (*prasiddha*).

If one were to claim that the Mahāyāna was spoken by another Buddha (either of the past or from another direction) and is not the word of the present Buddha [Śākyamuni], then—since the path of all Buddhas is identical—it is logically established that the Mahāyāna teaching is indeed the word of the Buddha. Fifth, because of existence and non-existence. If...
If you admit that there is a Mahāyāna Dharma, you must then believe that these various Mahāyāna teachings were spoken by the Buddha;
for apart from these sūtras, no sublime Mahāyāna Dharma can be found. If you claim that there is no Mahāyāna Dharma, then the Śrāvaka-yāna teachings would likewise not exist;
because apart from the Mahāyāna, it is certain that there is no possibility of attaining Buddhahood. Who, then, has appeared in the world to teach [the Mahāyāna]?

Regarding the Śrāvakayāna: since you admit that the teachings of the Śrāvakayāna were spoken by the Buddha, yet you alone do not accept the Mahāyāna scriptures and instead disparage them, this is unreasonable.
Sixth, because it serves as an antidote: those who rely on the Mahāyāna sūtras and diligently practice them [overcome these faults].
All [of these] are capable of inducing non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and are able to correctly counteract all afflictions (*kleśa*).

Therefore, one should believe that this was spoken by the Buddha. Because the seven meanings differ from the literal text, the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) expressed in the Mahāyāna is extremely profound;

one must not grasp its meaning merely according to the literal words, nor give rise to slander by claiming it is not the word of the Buddha. For this reason, the Mahāyāna is truly the word of the Buddha.

It is said: As the verse of the *Vyūharatna-śāstra* expresses this meaning: "Because it was not previously predicted as co-arising, because it is not the objective domain of others, because its existence and non-existence are fully established, and because its antidote is expressed in different words."
The first section, citing the Mahāyāna sūtras, is concluded. △ Second, citing other schools. There are four sūtras in total.
Within the sūtras of other schools, it is also taught with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) that the ālayavijñāna possesses a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding the teaching with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*): fearing that those foolish Śrāvakas might give rise to false discrimination and grasp it as a self, [the Buddha] did not yet dare to reveal and explain it explicitly.
That is to say, within the Āgamas of the Mahāsāṃghika school, this [eighth consciousness] is spoken of with intentional meaning as the "root-consciousness" (*mūlavijñāna*),

because it is the support for the visual and other consciousnesses, just as a tree root is the basis for the trunk and so forth. The visual consciousness and the others do not possess such a characteristic.
This is the first sūtra cited above.
In the Āgama—here translated as "Sūtra"—both the Sthavira school and their commentators on the Vibhāṣā explain that this [eighth consciousness] is cryptically termed the *bhavāṅga-vijñāna*.

It exists; that is to say, it is the cause of the three realms of existence (*tribhava*). This [eighth consciousness] alone is constant and pervasive, serving as the cause for the three realms of existence.
This is the second sūtra cited here.
Within the Mahīśāsaka school (it is also implicitly stated that this eighth consciousness is called) the "aggregate that exhausts birth-and-death" (*ātyantika-saṃsāra-skandha*).

Apart from the eighth consciousness, there is no other aggregate-dharma capable of exhausting the limits of birth-and-death while remaining perpetually uninterrupted. This refers to [the case of] the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), where all...
Form is interrupted [in states such as] the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), where other minds and mental factors cease. Furthermore,

since it has already been fully established (in the preceding refutation of the clinging to dharmas) that non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) have no distinct intrinsic nature apart from form, mind, and so forth, only this [eighth] consciousness can be called the "aggregate that exhausts birth and death" (*paryantajanmamaraṇaskandha*).
This refers to the third sutra cited above. Regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), they mean the five aggregates.

Among these five aggregates—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and the first six consciousnesses—none can exhaustively reach the limit of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), because they are subject to interruption or because they lack a distinct, independent essence.
In the *Ekottarika-āgama* of the Sarvāstivāda school, this [eighth consciousness] is also taught through intentional terminology (*saṃdhyābhāṣa*) as the *ālaya*. That is to say:
"They love the *ālaya*, they delight in the *ālaya*, they rejoice in the *ālaya*, and they find joy in the *ālaya*. This refers to the *ālayavijñāna*.
These four names are established because it is the object of craving, both collectively and individually, throughout the three periods of time. Sentient beings grasp it as their true self.
As long as this internal self-clinging has not been severed, there is constant attachment; therefore, the ālayavijñāna is the true locus of attachment.
One should not cling to the other five appropriated aggregates (*pañcopādānaskandha*) as the true locus of attachment.

Those born in a realm of exclusively painful sensation do not give rise to attachment toward the other appropriated aggregates, for they constantly feel aversion toward them, thinking, "What am I? [referring to the self].
At that time, one thinks: "I shall abandon this life, this commonality of existence (*nikāya-sabhāga*), and this suffering body and mind, so that I may enjoy happiness according to my own will.

Thus, the five objects of desire (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) are not the true locus of attachment; for even those who have abandoned desire do not crave the five exquisite desires, yet they still love the self.
Furthermore, pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) is not the true locus of attachment; for those who have abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna [do not crave it].
Although such a person may weary of pleasant feelings, because they still cherish the self, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is not the true locus of attachment.

This means that even one who is not yet an Arhat (a non-learner) but has faith in the principle of non-self does not give rise to greedy attachment toward the view of a self; nevertheless, they still give rise to love for the internal self.

Furthermore, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and so forth are also not the true loci of attachment. This means that even one who is not yet an Arhat but seeks the cessation of the mind [does not find it there].

Even though those who have become weary of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and so forth may do so, because they still cherish the "self," the physical body (*rūpa-kāya*) is likewise not the true object of their attachment.

Even for those who are free from the defilement of form (*rūpa-rāga*) and thus weary of the physical body, because they still cherish the "self," the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*)—which lack a distinct intrinsic nature apart from form and mind—are also not the true objects of attachment.
(This is visible to all. Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) as well as those in training (*śaikṣa*) give rise to self-love (*ātma-sneha*).
At that time, although there may be attachment to or aversion toward the other aggregates, attachment to the self (*ātma-sneha*) necessarily arises toward this eighth consciousness;
therefore, this [eighth consciousness] alone is the true locus of attachment. By this, one understands the name *ālaya* mentioned in that [Ekottarika Āgama].
This concentration reveals exclusively this (eighth) ālayavijñāna; this is precisely the fourth sūtra cited.
The character "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) refers generally to the three periods of time; the character "pleasure" (*sukha*) refers specifically to the present;

the character "delight" (*abhinandana*) refers specifically to the past; and the character "joy" (*prīti*) refers specifically to the future. Therefore, it is said that these are the general and specific aspects of craving.
This refers to the objects of the three periods of time. It is exclusively a realm of painful sensation, namely the Avīci Hell and a portion of the animals and hungry ghosts.

"The remaining appropriated aggregates" refers to all phenomena comprised of the five aggregates, excluding the eighth consciousness. "Those who have abandoned desire" refers to those who are free from craving.
This refers to those above the first dhyāna. "One who is free from the defilements of the third dhyāna" refers to those above the fourth dhyāna.

"The view of a self-body" (satkāyadṛṣṭi) refers to the view that clings to a self based upon the body. "One who seeks the cessation of the mind" refers to one who practices the ninth meditative attainment, the cessation of perception and feeling (nirodhasamāpatti).
"One who is free from the defilements of form" refers to those above the sphere of infinite space. The rest may be understood accordingly. This first citation is from the authoritative scripture.
[End of section]. △ Second, revealing the correct principle, in three parts: first, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent; second, citing sūtras to reveal the principle;
third, concluding the summary and pointing to the extensive [text]. Now, the first part.
Having already cited the authoritative scriptures (*āgama*), one should now demonstrate the correct reasoning (*yukti*).
△ Second, citing sūtras to reveal the principles, in ten parts: 1. The mind that holds the seeds; 2. The ripening mind (*vipākacitta*); 3. The substance of the realms of existence and birth;

4. That which is appropriated (*upātta*); 5. Vitality, warmth, and consciousness; 6. The mind at the time of birth and death; 7. The basis of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); 8. [The eighth...]

The essence of the consciousness-nutriment (*vijñānāhāra*). Ninth, there is consciousness in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*); tenth, defiled and pure minds. Regarding the first three [sections]:
first, citing sutras to provide proof and explanation; second, refuting divergent interpretations; third, summarizing to establish the conclusion. Now, the first [section].
It is said in the Sūtras that it is called "mind" (*citta*) because it is the locus where the seeds of all defiled and purified phenomena accumulate and arise.
If this eighth consciousness did not exist, then that "mind which holds the seeds" described in the Sūtra would be impossible.

This is because the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are interrupted during the five states lacking mental activity, such as the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); whereas [in states with mental activity], the conditions such as the sense faculties, objects, and attention are present.
The classification of the [three] natures is likewise [as follows]: because they arise and pass away easily, like lightning and so forth, their nature is not firmly established.

Because they do not abide firmly, they cannot be perfumed; because they are interrupted, they cannot maintain seeds. Therefore, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are not the mind in which the seeds of defilement and purity are accumulated.
This [eighth] consciousness, however, is of a single type (indeterminate), constant, and uninterrupted, like a mustard seed or a lamp wick; it is firm.
Abiding as that which is perfumable (the correct view), this accords with the meaning of the "mind that holds seeds" as taught in that sūtra.

If one does not admit the existence of a mind capable of holding seeds, it would not only contradict the sūtra but also violate correct reasoning; for regarding all phenomena of the defiled and pure classes that arise, [although they are themselves perfumers, if...]

Because [the eighth consciousness] would not serve as the object of perfuming (*bhāvanīya*), it could not be perfumed to form seeds. Consequently, the defiled and pure phenomena that arise [from them] would all lack subsequent results, and their efforts would be in vain.
Furthermore, since there would be no causal seeds when the defiled and pure arise, this would be equivalent to the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) adherence to spontaneous generation (*svabhāva*).

Since matter (*rūpa*) and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are not of the nature of mind, they are—like sound, light, and so forth—not stable by nature; thus, [the claim that they can serve as seeds] is logically untenable.

How could defiled or pure internal dharmas, being themselves perfumed [by other states], be able to maintain seeds? Furthermore, since those two dharmas (form and formations) are transformations of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*) and lack a real intrinsic nature apart from consciousness, how can they be maintained as the basis for internal seeds?
As for the various mental factors (*caitta*) associated with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), like that consciousness itself, they are intermittent and easily abandoned or arise;
moreover, since they are called "mental factors," they depend upon the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and lack autonomy, and thus are not of the nature of mind (*citta*).

Therefore, [the storehouse consciousness] cannot maintain seeds nor undergo perfuming; thus, it stands to reason that there must be a distinct mind which maintains the seeds (namely, the eighth consciousness).

This "mind that maintains the seeds" is spoken of in terms of its causal characteristics (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*). The text is easy to understand. △ Second, the refutation of divergent interpretations has five parts:

first, the refutation of the view that the various consciousnesses receive perfuming and maintain seeds; second, the refutation of the view that the six consciousnesses function simultaneously to receive perfuming and maintain seeds;

third, the refutation of the view that matter and mind act as seeds for their own respective categories; fourth, the refutation of the view that the past and future are substantially existent; fifth, the refutation of [erroneous] attachments.

The Emptiness of the Dispelling of Characteristics consists of two parts: first, the initial [section], and second, the middle [section]. The first part contains two sub-sections: first, the narration of the attachment; second, the refutation. Now, for the first:

some say that since beginningless time, the six consciousnesses have relied upon the faculties, objects, and so forth across successive states (hence there are the various distinctions of the three natures).

However), although phenomena undergo transformation, their category (namely, this category of the six consciousnesses) remains without distinction; it is that which is perfumed and capable of maintaining seeds.
Through this, both the causes and effects of defilement and purity are established. Why, then, insist on the existence of an eighth consciousness-nature?
△ Second, the refutation.
His statement is devoid of meaning. Why is this so? (If) one clings to the category of consciousness as being real, then one is identical to the non-Buddhist Tīrthikas (such as the Vaiśeṣika).

If it is granted that this category of consciousness (*vijñāna-jāti*) is merely nominal (*prajñapti*), then it would lack superior efficacy and could not maintain the real seeds (*bīja*) of internal phenomena.

This first refutation is based on the distinction between the nominal and the real. For instance, visual consciousness is the category of visual consciousness, auditory consciousness is the category of auditory consciousness, and so forth.
If one were to hold that these are real entities, it would be equivalent to the Vaiśeṣika position that the category of "sameness" (*sāmānya*) is a real entity.
If you admit that it is merely conventional (prajñapti), how could it possibly receive perfuming or maintain seeds?

Furthermore, as for the category of consciousness (vijñāna-jāti) that you uphold, by what nature is it subsumed? If that category of consciousness were either wholesome or unwholesome, it would not be able to receive perfuming.
Because it is admitted that [the *vijñapti*] is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), just like the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

If this category of consciousness were of an indeterminate nature, then at the time when wholesome or unwholesome minds arise, there would necessarily be no indeterminate mind present. How could such a category [of consciousness] be severed [if it were not perfumed]?

Nor can it be said that while the substance (*dravya*) may be wholesome or unwholesome, the category (*jāti*) is exclusively indeterminate; for a distinct category must necessarily share the same nature as its distinct substance.

This section is approximately a refutation based on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). First, if [the mind] were of a virtuous or non-virtuous nature, it would follow as a thesis that it could not be perfumed.

The reason is that it is admitted to be determinate (*vyākṛta*). The example is like cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Second, if [the mind] were of an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature, it would follow as a thesis that it would be interrupted and unable to receive perfuming.
The reason is that there is no indeterminate state at the time of a virtuous or non-virtuous mind. It is like [the alternation of] suffering and pleasure.

Furthermore, at the time of feeling, there is no neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Moreover, since its substance is already either wholesome or unwholesome, it should not be described as being merely indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
This refutes their alternative calculation.

Furthermore, in the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), since the six consciousnesses are absent, this [eighth] consciousness must likewise be absent. Since it is thus subject to interruption, its nature is not stable.
How can it be maintained that [the mind] abiding [in such a state] is capable of sustaining seeds or receiving perfuming? Furthermore, since the minds of Arhats or ordinary beings (pṛthagjana)—

even if their six types of consciousness are identical in being neutral (avyākṛta)— would [otherwise] be subject to perfuming by defiled dharmas (in the case of the Arhat), or by uncontaminated dharmas (in the case of the ordinary being),
to admit this would entail logical fallacies.

This further refutes [the theory] by showing that there are interruptions within the categories of the six consciousnesses. Furthermore, it refutes [the theory] by considering the perfuming of ordinary beings and noble ones.

Moreover, the sense organs such as the eye, or other dharmas, share the same category as the visual consciousness and so forth—both the category of the organ (the basis) and the category of the dharma (the object) being neutral (*avyākṛta*).

Consequently, they should each be able to mutually perfume one another. However, since you do not admit that the categories of the organs or the categories of the dharmas undergo perfuming, [your position] is untenable.
The claim that "the category of consciousness receives perfuming" is further refuted by analogy with the categories of the sense organs (*indriya*) and phenomena (*dharma*).

If it is asserted that the category of consciousness receives perfuming, then why is it not likewise admitted that the categories of the sense organs and phenomena receive perfuming? If it is not admitted that the categories of the sense organs and phenomena receive perfuming, then...
How could the various types of consciousness alone receive perfuming?
Furthermore, as for the six groups of consciousness, whether in terms of their substance or their categories, two moments—preceding and succeeding—are not simultaneous.
Just as moments separated by an interval do not mutually perfume one another, so it must be that the perfumer and the perfumed necessarily exist at the same time.
This further refutes [the opponent's position] by means of the inability of preceding and succeeding moments to act as perfumers (*vāsanā*).

For if there were only a single moment, it could not be designated as a "category" (*jāti*); furthermore, there is no principle for two moments to arise simultaneously. It must be in relation to preceding and succeeding moments that something is called a category.

For instance, take the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) of the present moment: whether it is compared to a preceding moment of visual consciousness or to a succeeding moment of visual consciousness...

Because it is consciousness, it is called a "category" (*jāti*). If one considers it in relation to the ear-consciousness and other consciousnesses of the subsequent moment, it is not called a category.
This is true for each of the remaining five consciousnesses. Thus, since the category of consciousness exists in both the preceding and succeeding moments, it does not occupy a single location;

it is like the separation between oneself and another. How, then, could they mutually perfuse one another? This concludes the first refutation: that the category of consciousness cannot receive perfuming.
The section on the maintenance of seeds is concluded. △ Second, the refutation of the simultaneous transformation and perfuming by the six consciousnesses.

For those who maintain that only the six consciousnesses transform simultaneously, since—by the reasoning presented above—they cannot be the objects of perfuming, they likewise lack the capacity to maintain seeds.
Some say that the six consciousnesses arise simultaneously; the first five are the perfumers (*vāsaka*), and the sixth is the perfumed (*vāsyamāna*).
Because they are simultaneous, the meaning of perfuming is established, and it can maintain the seeds. Now, the following refutation is made based on the aforementioned reasoning:
This means that because the sixth consciousness is intermittent and because it encompasses all three natures (trividha-svabhāva).

△ Third, the refutation of the view that matter and mind serve as seeds for their own respective classes, in two parts: first, the presentation of the tenet; second, the refutation. Now, the first part.

There are those who maintain that within the respective categories of matter and mind, the preceding moment serves as the seed for the succeeding one, thereby establishing the relationship of cause and effect;
thus, the previously stated argument—that "mind" (citta) is designated as the seed of both defilement and purity, referring to the eighth consciousness—is not proven.
That is to say, the matter (*rūpa*) of the preceding moment can serve as the seed to project the matter of the immediately succeeding moment.

The preceding matter is called the cause, and the subsequent matter is called the effect. The same applies to the mind (*citta*) and other phenomena; therefore, there is no need for an eighth consciousness that maintains the seeds (*bīja*).
△ Second, the refutation.

That position is irrational because there is no perfuming (*vāsanā*). This means that since there is no mutual perfuming between those of the same class (the preceding and the succeeding), how can one maintain that the former serves as the seed for the latter?
Furthermore, if there were interruptions within that same class, it would follow that they could not arise again. [This applies even to] the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) who have attained realization.
At the time of death, since the seeds of both matter and mind have already been severed, there should be no remaining subsequent aggregates;

for they maintain that at the moment of death, matter and mind serve as the seeds for future existence, while they do not admit the existence of a fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) that sustains the seeds.

Furthermore, one should not maintain that matter and mind mutually serve as seeds for one another’s arising, because it has already been stated previously that the evolving consciousnesses and material phenomena are not susceptible to being perfumed (vāsya).
First, the refutation based on the impossibility of forming seeds without perfuming can be understood. Next, the refutation based on the presence of interruptions is as follows:

regarding the statement that "if there were interruptions, [the seed] should not arise again," since they falsely maintain that preceding matter and mind serve as the seeds for subsequent ones, then just as in the case of those born in the formless heavens—where the preceding matter has been severed for many eons—it should follow that matter would not arise again.

Furthermore, regarding the realms (*dhātu*): for example, one who is born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) has already severed their prior mental states for many eons; it would be illogical for the mind of perception (*saṃjñā-citta*) to arise again.

Moreover, when those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) realize the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), they understand that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are without self;

thus, the seeds of form and mind have been severed. If there were no eighth consciousness as the substrate of maturation (*vipākavijñāna*), there would be nothing to maintain the remnants of that former form and mind.
If that were so, there would be no remaining five aggregates after the fruit [of Arhatship] has been attained.

Why is it, then, that those who have personally realized the state of an Arhat but have not yet entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* still possess the bonds of the fruit that have not yet been completely extinguished?

Nor should one say that they descend [to a lower realm], for we fear that such a person might instead calculate that by returning to a lower realm from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the mind itself serves as the seed of form; thus, there would be no [need for] non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*).
When the thought-mind arises again, it takes form (*rūpa*) as its seed; therefore, it is said that the evolving consciousnesses and form are not objects of perfuming (*vāsanā*).

This has already been explained previously. Since they are not objects of perfuming, how could they possibly serve as seeds? This concludes the third section: Refuting that form and mind act as seeds for their own respective classes.
△ Fourth, Refuting the Real Existence of the Past and Future, in two parts: First, the statement of the tenet; second, the refutation.

First: Some say that all phenomena of the three periods of time exist; since cause and effect arise and respond such that nothing fails to be established, why labor to insist on the existence of an eighth consciousness capable of maintaining seeds?
However, the Sūtras state that the mind is the seed [capable] of giving rise to defiled and pure manifest phenomena.
Because the functional force of the mind is powerful, it is said that the past is the cause and the present is the effect; the present is the cause and the future is the effect.

Thus, the mutual response between cause and effect is entirely established. However, the following section of the sutra addresses potential objections, stating that since all phenomena of the three periods of time...
Each [factor] constitutes its own seed. Why, then, does the Sūtra speak only of the mind as the seed? The answer is:
because the power and function of the mind are predominant, it is mentioned specifically. △ Second, the refutation.
That explanation is irrational. The past and future are neither permanent nor present; like flowers in the sky and the like, they are not substantially existent.
Furthermore, because they lack functional activity, they cannot be maintained as having the nature of causes and conditions.
If there were no eighth consciousness capable of sustaining the seeds of defilement and purity, then all cause and effect would fail to be established.

The past and future are existent dharmas. This is the thesis of those who do not maintain that they are substantially real (*dravyasat*). The reason is: because they are neither permanent nor manifest.

The example is: like flowers in the sky and so forth. Furthermore, the past and future are existent dharmas; this is the thesis of those who cannot maintain that they possess the nature of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

The reason is: because they lack functional activity (*kāritra*). The example is: like flowers in the sky and so forth. The rest may be understood. (4) Refuting the substantial existence of the past and future.
[End. △ Five: Refuting Attachment and Dispelling the Notion of Emptiness.
There are those who cling to the principle of the Mahāyāna’s emptiness that dispels characteristics as being ultimate;

[they are unable to provide a correct understanding according to the truth, but] rely on fallacious inference (*sādṛśya-anumāna*) to deny the existence of this [eighth] consciousness and to deny all phenomena. They specifically contradict and harm the scriptures cited previously, and consequently...

[The arising of] wisdom, the abandonment [of delusions], the realization [of cessation], and the cultivation [of the path], as well as the causes and effects of defilement and purity—all such dharmas—are grasped as being unreal;

thus, one falls into great false views. This is because even those non-Buddhists who disparage the causes and effects of defilement and purity do not claim they are entirely non-existent, but merely grasp them as being unreal.
If all dharmas were indeed not truly existent, then Bodhisattvas would not need to strive to abandon [unreal things].
Within the cycle of birth and death, who among the wise would diligently cultivate the unreal provisions for enlightenment,
seeking out the son of a barren woman to serve as an army in order to eliminate the enemy that is illusion?
The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) do not claim that [causality] is entirely non-existent;
they merely maintain that it is not real, meaning that defiled causes do not necessarily bring about evil results, and pure causes do not necessarily induce good results.

Now, this class of Mahāyāna followers, who maintain that the causes and effects of both defilement and purity—namely, wisdom and abandonment, as well as realization and cultivation—are all unreal, how does this differ from the false views of the non-Buddhists? Indeed...
By interpreting the meaning solely according to the literal text, one fails to grasp the underlying intent (*sandhi*) of the Tathāgata’s words; how can one not fear such a calamity?

The "illusory enemy" is a metaphor for the unreal cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), while the "army of the son of a barren woman" is a metaphor for the unreal provisions for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*).
Question: The *Prajñāpāramitā* states that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, and even *nirvāṇa* is likewise [illusory]. How is this so?

"Is it not like an illusion or a transformation? Would one not thereby fall into false views? He replied: "A difference as slight as a hair's breadth results in a separation as vast as heaven and earth.

Prajñā deeply clarifies that all phenomena are empty and entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are able to constitute dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Within this dependent origination, the causes and effects of defilement and purity—comprising wisdom, abandonment, realization, and cultivation—are distinguished down to the finest detail without the slightest confusion. Although...

They are not indiscriminate; each lacks intrinsic nature. Therefore, they are neither a real self nor real dharmas. Now, since you negate conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), how could you possibly establish ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)?
Furthermore, the preceding text of this treatise states: "All minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) arise dependently (*paratantra*);
thus, like magical illusions, they do not truly exist. This was said in order to eliminate the false attachment [to the existence of] minds and mental factors apart from [their causal conditions].

Because objects truly exist, it is said that "there is only consciousness. If one were to grasp this "consciousness-only" as being truly existent, that would likewise be a form of clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), just like grasping at external objects.
Furthermore, the later text states: "The various characteristics of consciousness as previously described are based on conventional reasoning;
they are not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). In the true ultimate, mind and speech are transcended. Thus, [this teaching] is in accord with the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

What is the distinction? One should know that to grasp [phenomena] as truly existent constitutes the superimposition of existence (*samāropa*), while to grasp them as non-existent constitutes the denial of existence (*apavāda*).
Although both are forms of denial, they differ in being wholesome or unwholesome. Those who give rise to the view of existence do not repudiate cause and effect;

they still remain among humans and devas, yet they are unable to transcend the two kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Those who give rise to the view of emptiness, however, repudiate cause and effect as being non-existent.
They fall into great peril and hardship, destined forever to sink into the suffering of the three evil realms. Therefore it is said: "If one attains it, the Dragon Girl immediately becomes a Buddha;
if one loses it, even Sunakṣatra falls into hell. To let it slip from the hand like a mouse or vanish into the void like a bird is called slandering the true Prajñāpāramitā."

Therefore, that which resembles inference is called "poisonous knowledge" (*viṣajñāna*). However, the *Zhengjingshi* (Mirror of the Source) states: "Bhavaviveka refutes existence in order to establish existence;
Dharmapāla refutes emptiness in order to establish emptiness. When Bodhisattvas compose treatises, it is like using medicine primarily to eliminate disease;
yet when sentient beings cling to the medicine itself, it becomes a disease. What can the Bodhisattvas do about this? Thus [it is said].
There are two gates: emptiness and existence. If one does not cling to them, they are distinct yet unified; when unified, both are perfected.
If one clings to them, they are joined yet increasingly separated; when separated, both are harmed. Students must therefore reflect with care and discern clearly.
This concludes the second section, the Refutation of Divergent Interpretations. △ Third, the Summary and Conclusion.
Therefore, one should believe that there exists a mind capable of maintaining the seeds (*bīja*), upon which the causes and effects of defilement and purity are established.

That mind is precisely this eighth consciousness (*aṣṭamavijñāna*). This concludes the section on the initial mind that maintains the seeds. 2. The Maturation Mind (*vipākacitta*): This is spoken of in terms of its resultant characteristics.

Furthermore, a sūtra states: "There is a maturation-consciousness (vipākacitta) which is the fruit induced by wholesome and unwholesome karma. If this eighth consciousness did not exist, [this would be impossible].
Furthermore, because the so-called "maturation consciousness" (*vipākacitta*) mentioned in the Sūtra would otherwise be untenable;

that is to say, because visual and other sensory consciousnesses are intermittent and do not constitute the fruit of karma at all times, like flashes of lightning and the like, they are not maturation consciousness.

This first establishes two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to demonstrate that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are not the retributive mind (*vipāka-citta*). One states: "The eye-consciousness and so forth are the subject (*dharmin*);
they are not the retributive mind, this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because they are intermittent. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like flashes of lightning and so forth."
The second [position] states: The subject is the visual consciousness and so forth; the thesis is that they are not *vipāka*-minds. The reason is:
because they are not at all times the fruit of karma. The example is like lightning and so forth.

This is because a portion of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) visual consciousness and so forth is the fruit induced by completing karma (*pūrṇa-karman*), and is thus termed "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*). However, when wholesome or unwholesome visual consciousness and so forth arise, they are not [of this nature].
This is because of the nature of karmic fruit (*karmaphala*).
It is not possible for a ripened maturation (*vipāka*) to be interrupted and then resume; such a phenomenon does not occur in the case of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth.
