This is a further explanation of the reason why that which is subject to interruption cannot be considered a ripened maturation. That is to say, if...
Regarding the calculation that the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) is the maturation (*vipāka*): since it is a maturation, it should not be something that, once severed, continues again.

This is because life-force (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*) have never been observed to continue after being severed. Life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is precisely life-force; "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes warmth.
For warmth is the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of consciousness, and the life-faculty is conventionally established (*prajñapti*) based upon consciousness; they are both alike in this regard.
It is comprised within maturation (*vipāka*). Even the maturation of life-span and warmth cannot be severed and then resumed;

how much less could the substance of the maturation-consciousness (*vipākacitta*) be severed and then resumed? It is clear, therefore, that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are certainly not the maturation-consciousness spoken of in that sutra.

Among the six consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, although there is a portion that is neutral (avyākṛta) and constitutes retribution (vipāka), it is induced by karma that has reached fulfillment through wholesome or unwholesome [actions].
Nevertheless, like sound and other such phenomena, because it does not continue in a constant stream, it is merely "born of maturation" (vipākaja) rather than being true maturation (vipāka).
This is a further explanation of the reason why [these states] are not the fruit of karma at all times; therefore, they are not called true *vipāka*. To explain:
suppose someone asks, "It may be granted that the six wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses are not *vipāka* minds.

But why can the six neutral (*avyākṛta*) consciousnesses produced by karma not be considered *vipāka* minds? Now, the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established as follows: Regarding the [neutral consciousness] produced by karma...

The six consciousnesses that are "feeling-neutral" (vedanā-avyākṛta) are phenomena that exist; they do not belong to the school [that asserts] true maturation (vipāka). The reason is that they are not continuous;

the analogy is like sound and so forth. As for the statement that they are "born of maturation," this refers to the fact that based upon the true maturation—the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) as the collective retribution—there arises the distinct retribution induced by completing karma (pūrṇakarma); all of these are termed "maturation-neutral."

One must certainly admit the existence of a true ripening consciousness (*vipākacitta*) which, as the fruit of the projecting karma, is pervasive and uninterrupted, capable of transforming itself into the body and the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*), and acting as the support for sentient beings.
This is because it is logically impossible for the body and the vessel-world to exist apart from this true ripening consciousness;

furthermore, non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) lack substantial reality, and the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are not constantly present. If [this ripening consciousness] did not exist...

As for this eighth consciousness (the true resultant maturation), what transforms the body and the environment? Furthermore, by depending on what dharma is it established as the constant basis for sentient beings?

This [passage] relies upon the two aforementioned means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are not the resultant maturation consciousness;

it thereby clarifies that the "true resultant maturation consciousness" must refer to the eighth consciousness. Since non-associated dharmas (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) fundamentally lack substantial reality, one should not speak of them [in this context].
The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is a resultant mind (*vipākacitta*); the rest may be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, whether one is in meditative absorption (*samāhita*) or not (if not in absorption), there is distinct volition; when in meditative absorption, however, there is no such volition.
In principle, there arise many bodily sensations (*kāyika-vedanā*).

If these [bodily sensations] were non-existent, then at a later time, due to the absence of volition (*manasikāra*), the body would not experience ease, or conversely, due to other forms of volition, it would not experience weariness or injury.
If a truly resultant consciousness (*vipākacitta*) did not constantly maintain (*upādāna*) this body, how could such bodily sensations—whether of ease or weariness—in exist at that subsequent stage?

(Therefore, one should know that unless one is a Buddha, [it is already established]. If) in the nine realms other than the Buddha, when other wholesome states of mind and so forth arise, there must necessarily arise at the same time as those wholesome or unwholesome [states] a truly ripening (*vipāka*) mind.
[Question: Why is it that only the Buddha lacks a ripening mind? [Answer: When it is admitted that such a ripening mind arises, at that very moment—

It is not the Buddha (but rather the nine realms), because they are sentient beings. Consequently, these nine realms of sentient beings always possess a truly resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*);
that consciousness is precisely this eighth consciousness.
This further demonstrates, by way of the distinctions in mental activity at a prior time, how it can cause the body to experience different sensations at a later time;
thus one may verify the functional power of the truly heterogeneous ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*).

For instance, when a person enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*) without any discursive thought, their body becomes tranquil and comfortable. Yet, at the very moment of entering absorption, they have already forgotten their body and are unaware of its comfort.

It is appropriate [to hold this]. If there were no true *vipāka*-consciousness arising simultaneously with that meditative consciousness to maintain this body, then after emerging from meditation—once the meditative state has ceased—the body should no longer experience a sense of well-being.
Because a true *vipāka*-consciousness arises concurrently with the meditative state and is perfumed by it, the body continues to experience such well-being even after one has emerged from meditation.
It remains merely pleasant and comfortable. Furthermore, it is like a person who is unsettled and engages in much discursive thought;
their body then becomes exhausted and damaged. Yet, while they are engaged in correct reflection, they forget their own body and are unaware of its exhaustion and damage.
If there were no true ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) arising simultaneously with that reflection to grasp and sustain this body, then, regarding that reflection—
[The thought] has ceased. Since there is no further deliberation, the body should no longer suffer exhaustion;

yet, because the true resultant consciousness (*vipāka-citta*) continues to evolve in tandem with that deliberation and is perfumed by it, the body remains exhausted even after the deliberation has ceased.
The rest may be understood accordingly. This concludes the second section on the resultant consciousness. △ The essence of the realms, destinies, and modes of birth.
This refers to the substance of the three realms, the five destinies, and the four modes of birth. The preceding section clarified the mutual retribution of cause and effect;
this section speaks of the substance of the destinies and modes of birth, because where there is cause and effect, there must necessarily be a substance.
Furthermore, a sūtra states that sentient beings transmigrate through the five destinies (*gati*) and the four modes of birth (*yoni*).

If this eighth consciousness did not exist, the substance (*ātman*) of those five destinies and four modes of birth would not be possible; for it must be a real entity that is constant, pervasive, and unmixed—only such a dharma possessing these four characteristics can be established as the true substance of the five destinies and four modes of birth.
The five destinies (*gati*) are those of devas, humans, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.

Asuras are not mentioned because they are either subsumed within the four destinies or included within the destiny of hungry ghosts. The four modes of birth (*yoni*) are womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born.

Devas are transformation-born; humans possess all four modes of birth, though for the most part they are womb-born; hell-beings are exclusively transformation-born; and hungry ghosts and animals each possess all four modes of birth.

"Substantially existent" means it is not merely a provisional designation; this excludes the formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). "Constant" means it functions without interruption; this excludes the neutral states born of maturation (*vipākaja-avyākṛta*).
"Pervasive" means it extends throughout the three realms; this excludes form (*rūpa*) and the first five consciousnesses. "Unmixed" means it is exclusively of a neutral nature (*avyākṛta*);
this excludes the six consciousnesses that are either wholesome or unwholesome.

It is not a non-maturation phenomenon (*avipāka-dharma*). This is because the destinies and births would become confused, as one would be abiding in one destiny while giving rise to the phenomena of other destinies and births.
This first excludes the six consciousnesses—whether wholesome or unwholesome—from being the substance of the destinies and births.

While actually in the human destiny, one may give rise to wholesome phenomena of the heavenly destiny, or give rise to the three kinds of unwholesome phenomena; the same applies when in other destinies. If [one were to] establish...
If it were the very essence of the destinies and births, would it not be confused?
Although the various resultant forms and that portion of the five consciousnesses produced by karma are not confused, they do not pervade all destinies and births.

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), those two types [of formations] are entirely absent. Furthermore, although the various wholesome states acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*) and that portion of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) produced by karma proceed toward all realms of rebirth without confusion, they do not exist constantly.
Moreover, the dissociated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) lack a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
For these reasons, none of them can be established as the substantial entity of the actual realms of rebirth.

This excludes other indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), as they do not constitute the substance of the destinies (*gati*) or births (*upapatti*).

Regarding the various resultant forms (*vipāka-rūpa*)—namely, the five sense faculties, the three objects of odor, taste, and touch, and a portion of the object of visible form—that which is produced by the karma of the five consciousnesses is indeterminate by way of being born of maturation (*vipākaja-avyākṛta*).
The two consciousnesses of nose and tongue are restricted solely to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); [as for] eye and ear...
Body-consciousness is restricted to the first dhyāna. Heterogeneous resultant (vipāka) matter is restricted to the two realms of desire and form; therefore, both are not universal.
Wholesome states acquired at birth are those obtained through retribution. Those mental consciousnesses produced by karma are likewise born of maturation (vipākaja) and are neutral (avyākṛta).
The rest may be understood accordingly.

Only the eighth [consciousness], the truly resultant (*vipāka*) mind, together with its five associated mental factors (*caitta*), is truly constant, pervasive, and unmixed; it is the actual basis for the courses of existence (*gati*).

If this truly resultant mind did not exist, then when one is born in the formless realm—where there is no form or the five sensory consciousnesses, and only the sixth consciousness arises at times in states such as the wholesome—the state [of that consciousness] would lack the "appropriation" (*upādāna*) [of the body] and thus should not be included within the courses of existence.
Even if one were to allow that the courses of existence include all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena, [this mind is still necessary].

The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is that which is comprised within the destinies (*gati*). However, when noble ones who are non-returners (*anāgāmin*) are born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and give rise to untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*), they would not be comprised within the destinies;

this would contradict correct reasoning, because although non-returners reside in the formless realm, according to principle they must still be comprised within the destiny of gods (*devagati*) by way of apparitional birth (*upapāduka*).

This is intended to avoid the fault mentioned in the preceding text—that wholesome states and so forth would not be comprised within the destinies—and to avoid the error that these non-returners would likewise not be comprised within the destinies. Therefore, it is established that only true maturation (*vipāka-dharma*) is truly real.

The essence of the destinies and births is such that only the Tathāgata is not subsumed under the five destinies or four modes of birth, because the Buddha possesses no further dharmas that are resultant (*vipāka*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*).
Nor is he subsumed under the three realms, because he is free from the three outflows (*āsrava*) and has already abandoned the truths of suffering and its origin.
Since all seeds of conceptual proliferation have been eternally severed, the reality of the destinies and births is, in truth, exclusively...

Regarding the resultant consciousness (*vipākacitta*) and its mental factors (*caittas*), it is logically impossible for those consciousnesses and mental factors to exist apart from the eighth consciousness;
therefore, one knows that this distinct eighth consciousness exists.
This correctly clarifies that the substance of the destinies and births is solely the eighth consciousness. The Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) is the fruit of the three realms;

the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*) is the cause of the three realms. Regarding "the seeds of conceptual proliferation" (*prapañcabīja*): "seed" has the meaning of "cause," and "cause" has the meaning of "realm. The rest is understandable.

This concludes the section on the substance of the destinies and births within the three realms. 4. Possession (*upātta*). This refers to the fact that the destinies and births are not intermingled, because...
There is that which is appropriated (*upātta*). Appropriation is the function of the very substance itself.

Furthermore, a sutra states: "The body possessing material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) is appropriated. If this eighth consciousness did not exist, that which performs the appropriation (as described in the sutra) would not exist;
namely, the five material sense-faculties and their bases (which, in the past, have already ceased, and in the future, have not yet arisen).
Only the present world is possessed of appropriation (*upātta*). That [appropriation] must necessarily be by means of a mind capable of appropriating;
however, it is exclusively this eighth *vipāka*-mind (the storehouse consciousness). It is projected by prior karma and is not [of the nature of] wholesome, defiled, or other [moral qualities].

Being of a single class (*ekajātīya*) and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is universally capable of serving as the basis for the sense-faculties and maintaining the continuity of the embodied form through the appropriation of the material organs. The evolving consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, do not possess such a characteristic.

This passage correctly clarifies that the *vipākavijñāna* (maturation-consciousness) is capable of appropriating (*upādāna*) the physical body composed of the sense organs. The text is easy to understand.

The intent of this statement is to demonstrate that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), such as the visual consciousness and so forth, lack any single category [of mind] capable of continuously and universally appropriating one's own internal physical body with its sense organs.

It does not, however, intend to show that only the maturation-consciousness is capable of appropriation; for if it did, one would have to conclude that the physical bodies of the Buddhas are without appropriation.

Because it is that which undergoes sensation (*vedanā*). However, it is only the *vipāka*-consciousness that can maintain and appropriate (*upādāna*) the contaminated physical body (*rūpakāya*); therefore, this statement is made.
This explains away an anticipated objection. The objection states:

"If only the *vipāka*-consciousness can maintain and appropriate the sense-faculties and the body, then since a Buddha lacks a *vipāka*-consciousness, would his physical body not lack appropriation? Therefore, the present explanation says: "This is only the *vipāka*..."
The phrase "capable of appropriating" merely indicates that the evolving consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, are incapable of appropriation;

it does not indicate that only the ripening consciousness (*vipākacitta*) is capable of appropriation. This is because the stainless pure consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*) is also capable of appropriating the untainted form-body (*anāsrava-rūpakāya*).
However, as for the tainted form-body (*sāsrava-rūpakāya*), only the ripening consciousness is capable of appropriating it.
This refers to the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). Because they arise from present conditions, they are like sound, wind, and so forth.

As for their being wholesome, defiled, and so on, this is because they are not projected by karma, and thus are like non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). As for their being born of maturation (*vipākaja*), this is because they are not true maturation, because they do not depend on [the body] universally, and because they are not continuous, like flashes of lightning and so forth;
they cannot grasp and maintain the contaminated physical body (*sāsrava-rūpa-kāya*).

In this context, three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are established. First: the thesis is that the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), as the subject (*dharmin*), cannot grasp and maintain the contaminated physical body (*sāsrava-rūpa-kāya*).
The reason (*hetu*) is: because they arise from present conditions. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: like sound, wind, and so forth. Second:

the thesis is that those [consciousnesses] which are wholesome, defiled, and so on, as the subject, cannot grasp and maintain the contaminated physical body. The reason is: because they are not projected by karma (*karma-ākṣepa*).

Therefore, it is like non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Third, as for the claim that "that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is a phenomenon (*dharmin*) that cannot grasp and maintain a contaminated physical body (*sāsrava-rūpa-kāya*)," this is the thesis (*pakṣa*).
The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is not a true maturation; because it does not serve as a universal basis;
and because it is not continuous. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like flashes of lightning and so forth.

The mention of "all mind-consciousnesses" (citta-vijñāna) also includes the mental factors (caitta), because they are necessarily associated with them— just as the term "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra) also includes the mental factors.
This clarifies that since the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna) cannot grasp or maintain [the body], their associated mental factors likewise certainly cannot grasp or maintain it either.

Neither the material sense-faculties nor the formations dissociated from mind can appropriate a body possessing material sense-faculties, because they lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*), just like space and so forth.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
The material sense-faculties and the formations dissociated from mind are the subject of the thesis (*dharmin*); they cannot appropriate a body possessing material sense-faculties.
Regarding the body and its basis, the reason provided is that there is no object of perception (*ālambana*), with space and the like serving as the analogy.
Therefore, there must exist a distinct mind capable of appropriation; that mind is precisely this eighth consciousness.

Having already established the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to exclude other minds, mental factors (*caitta*), matter (*rūpa*), and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) from being capable of appropriation (*upādāna*), it is now concluded that only the eighth consciousness is able to appropriate.
This concludes the fourth section: "That Which Is Appropriated. △ Fifth: Life-force (*āyus*), Warmth (*uṣman*), and Consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Since this consciousness maintains the sense-faculties and the body, it also maintains life-force and warmth.
Furthermore, a sūtra states that life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—these three—mutually support one another so as to abide in a continuous succession.
If this eighth consciousness did not exist, then the consciousness described in that sūtra as being able to sustain life-force and warmth so that they endure for a long time would be impossible.

This is because the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are intermittent and subject to change, like sound or wind; they lack the constant sustaining function required to be established as that which maintains life-force and warmth.

As for consciousness, it refers exclusively to the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*). It is uninterrupted and unchanging, like vitality (*āyuṣ*) and heat (*uṣman*), and possesses the constant function of sustaining [the body];
therefore, it can be established as the consciousness that sustains vitality and heat. The Sūtra states that these three factors—vitality, heat, and consciousness—mutually support one another.
Since vitality and heat are of a single continuous stream (if they were so), how could consciousness alone not be likewise? Would this not accord with correct reasoning?
This correctly clarifies that the support for vitality (*āyuṣ*) and warmth (*uṣman*) must necessarily be the eighth consciousness, and not the other evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
[Objection: Although it is taught that these three factors mutually depend upon and support one another, you admit that warmth alone does not pervade the three realms (*tridhātu*);
why, then, do you not admit that consciousness alone could exist intermittently?

This uses the fact that "warmth" (*uṣman*) is not omnipresent as an analogy to clarify that "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) can arise intermittently. The meaning is that what sustains life and warmth does not require an eighth consciousness.
To say that warmth is not omnipresent throughout the three realms is because there is no warmth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
[The answer is: This does not constitute a fault or a difficulty with respect to the preceding principle.
That is to say, if a place possesses all three factors in uninterrupted succession, they may maintain one another constantly; otherwise, there would be no function of constant mutual maintenance.

It was previously by means of this principle that the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) mentioned among the three factors was shown to be definitive [as the ālayavijñāna], and not as referring to the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*). Now, even if warmth is cited as being non-pervasive, how could it undermine [the argument]?

The preceding reasoning (that at the time of relinquishing warmth, life-force and consciousness are not relinquished; if life-force and consciousness were relinquished, they would necessarily be relinquished along with warmth) is therefore established.

Furthermore, among these three factors, since both life-force and warmth are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), it is known that the consciousness which sustains life-force and warmth is like life-force and warmth themselves.

It is certainly not the case that this [consciousness] is untainted (*anāsrava*). (If one were to refer only to the six consciousnesses rather than to the maturation-consciousness as the consciousness that sustains life-force and warmth, then when an Anāgāmin) is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and gives rise to an untainted mind—at that time, which consciousness could sustain his life-force?
(An untainted consciousness cannot sustain a tainted life-force.

For this reason, it is known that there exists a maturation-consciousness, uniform and ever-present, which is capable of sustaining life-force and warmth; that consciousness is precisely this eighth consciousness.

This explains the previous objection; it may be understood according to the text. Section Five concludes the discussion on life-span (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Section Six: The Mind at the Time of Birth and Death.
Having already clarified the capacity of the present mind to maintain the sense organs, the body, life-span, and warmth, this section next clarifies the master that precedes death and follows birth.

The text is divided into four parts: first, citing scriptures to provide proof and explanation; second, refuting divergent interpretations; third, reconciling with other schools; and fourth, a specific explanation.
First, regarding the mind at the time of death:
Furthermore, a sutra states that when sentient beings are taking birth or at the time of their passing away, they necessarily abide in a state of either a distracted mind or a conscious mind.

It is not a state of no-mind, nor is it a concentrated mind. If this eighth consciousness did not exist, then as that sūtra states, the distracted mind at the time of birth and death would be impossible;
for at the time of birth and death, the body and mind are昏昧 (obscured), like being asleep without dreaming or in a state of extreme fainting.

At such times, the manifest evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) certainly do not arise. Furthermore, in this state [of birth and death], the modes of activity (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*) of the six kinds of evolving consciousnesses do not exist.
Because it is cognizable, as in the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), the six types of evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) necessarily do not manifest;
their modes of activity (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*) are necessarily cognizable, just as they are at other times (i.e., times other than the state of birth and death).

However, because the true maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is extremely subtle, both its mode of activity and its object are imperceptible. This is the fruit of the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) [from birth until death]. One.

It is that which continues in succession, being eternally without transformation; it is this very state of scattered consciousness (not a mindless absorption), termed the "mind at the time of birth and death."
This does not contradict correct reasoning.
The first formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: **Thesis:** At the time of birth and death, the manifesting consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) certainly do not arise.

**Reason:** Because the body and mind are in a state of profound stupor and confusion. **Example:** Just as during sleep without dreams or at the time of extreme fainting. The second formal argument is as follows:

It is said: In the state of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are the subject (*dharmin*). It is the thesis (*pakṣa*) that they necessarily do not manifest. The reason (*hetu*) is:

because their mental aspects (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*) cannot be known. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like the state without mind (*acittaka*). The third measure (*pramāṇa*) states: The six kinds of evolving consciousnesses are the subject.
It is the thesis that they are not the mind at the time of birth and death. The reason is: because their mental aspects and objects must necessarily be knowable.

Because it is known [to be so]. It is analogous to other times when there is only the true resultant consciousness (*vipāka-citta*), which is subtle and imperceptible yet exists as a state of distraction;
this alone can be called the "mind at the time of birth and death. △ Second, the refutation of divergent interpretations, which has two parts.
First, the statement of the opponent's position; second, its refutation. Now, for the first:
some say that at this stage of taking birth, the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are certainly absent;

rather, it is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that apprehends the object, either by depending on the five consciousnesses, or by depending on the instruction of others, or with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as its cause (and only then arises). At this stage of birth, these [consciousnesses]...

Since the cause cannot be apprehended, the mental consciousness at the stage of rebirth is likewise absent (this is directly termed the "state without mind," and does not refer to a state of scattered mind with existence).

This does not mean that the seeds within the eighth consciousness are not taken as the cause of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), but rather that the three [consciousnesses] beginning with the five sensory consciousnesses are separately taken as its causes.
At the stage of taking birth, there is likewise no mental consciousness; this is fundamentally identical to the correct teaching.

To falsely claim that the mental consciousness is absent because its various causes cannot be found would imply that it must also be absent in the formless heavens (*ārūpyadhātu*), where those causes do not exist.
Could it be that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) never arises at all? △ Second, the refutation:
If that were so, then for sentient beings born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the mental consciousness associated with the formless meditative absorption would never arise thereafter;

for the concentrated mind must necessarily be induced by means of the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) of the distracted mental consciousness. You [claim] that this distracted mental consciousness must arise either from the five sensory consciousnesses or through the instruction of another.

It can be produced. Now, as for the five consciousnesses, they depend on instruction from others; since such [instruction] is necessarily absent within that formless realm, there is no basis for the arising of a distracted mind induced by meditative concentration.
(Since there is neither a distracted mind nor a concentrated mind, and since there is neither [the former] nor concentration as a cause, how could the six consciousnesses exist?)
Whosoever is born in the heavens—whether in the realm of desire, form, or formlessness—at the very first moment of birth, they are necessarily devoid of conscious awareness.

Once born, they must first give rise to a scattered consciousness that first cognizes the place of birth, second cognizes the place from which they came, and third cognizes the cause of their rebirth;
thereafter, according to their respective birthplace, they either experience various pleasures or enter [meditative states].

Regarding the various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), even those born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) must wait until half a kalpa has passed before their perceptions (*saṃjñā*) can entirely cease to function.
Therefore, it is said that the concentrated mind must necessarily be induced by the distracted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). The rest may be understood accordingly.

If it is argued that those meditative attainments (of the formless realm) manifest suddenly at a later time due to the power of habitual practice, then why do they not manifest at the very moment of initial birth (and instead necessarily wait for a later time)?
Furthermore, at the time of initial rebirth in the desire or form realms, the consciousness resulting from habitual practice should also manifest;
why does it likewise not manifest immediately? If [the opponent claims] it is because of dullness, then [it must be asked] why it is not so at the beginning...

[It] manifests before one. This is precisely the cause [mentioned in the preceding text] for the mental and physical states being obscured and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) not appearing—that is, this very obscuration is the mind of a distracted existence.
As for its subsequent ability to manifest through the power of habitual practice, it arises from seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*). Why labor to state three separate causes?

There are three causes: namely, their own reckoning of the five consciousnesses as one; second, the teachings of others; and third, meditative concentration. This concludes the refutation of divergent interpretations.
Next, extending [the analysis] to other schools.

There are other schools that maintain that during states such as birth and death, there exists a distinct category of subtle mental consciousness whose aspects and objects of perception are both imperceptible;

one should know that this is precisely this eighth consciousness. This is because the well-established [sixth] mental consciousness is not like this (in being a single category of subtle and imperceptible entity).
△ Fourth, a specific explanation of the mind at the time of death.
Furthermore, at the time of death, due to wholesome or unwholesome karma, the sensation of cold gradually arises from either the lower or upper parts of the body.

If this eighth consciousness did not exist, that phenomenon (the gradual arising of cold) would not be possible; for the [first] seven evolving consciousnesses cannot maintain the body (that is to say, the eye-consciousness...).

The five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, are distinct because they each rely individually upon [the five faculties, such as] the eye and so forth; furthermore, because they do not manifest at times when conditions are lacking, [they are distinguished from] the sixth [consciousness].

Because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does not abide in the physical body—since its objects of perception (*ālambana*) are not fixed—it dwells pervasively within the body [among the sense faculties], following after the various sensory objects without ever abandoning them for even a moment.
Because it is constantly continuous, cold contact should not arise gradually from that sixth mental consciousness.

Rather, it is only the *vipāka*-mind (the resultant consciousness), which, by the power of prior karma, is constantly and pervasively continuous, that maintains the appropriation (*upādāna*) of the bodily parts; when it abandons the locus of appropriation, cold contact then arises.
Birth [is defined] by the fact that life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are inseparable from one another.

Wherever the sensation of cold arises, it is identical to the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*); thus, although it is also a transformation of this consciousness, it is nonetheless taken as an object (*ālambana*) without being appropriated (*anupātta*).
Therefore, one knows that this eighth consciousness definitely exists.
By the power of wholesome karma, the consciousness ascends to be born among humans and devas; therefore, the sensation of cold gradually arises from below.
By the power of unwholesome karma, the consciousness sinks to be born in the various evil realms; therefore, the sensation of cold gradually arises from above.
The remainder may be understood. This concludes the sixth section on the mind at the time of birth and death. △ Seventh, the basis of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Having already treated the times of birth and death, this further treats the characteristics of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the entry into the womb.
Furthermore, a sūtra states: "Consciousness is conditioned by name-and-form (nāmarūpa), and name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness.

These two dharmas depend upon one another in mutual succession, like a bundle of reeds, arising simultaneously. If this eighth consciousness did not exist, then the very essence of that consciousness (referred to in the sūtra as being conditioned by name-and-form) would not be possible.
For that same sūtra provides its own explanation: "Name" refers to that which is non-material (arūpin), namely feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and mental formations (saṃskāra).

The four aggregates [of feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness] and form—namely, the *kalala* and so forth—these two exist in mutual dependence upon consciousness; consciousness is one, and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) together constitute one.
Like two bundles of reeds, they serve as conditions for one another, functioning simultaneously at all times, never being separated.

The evolving consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and others, are subsumed within "name. If this eighth consciousness did not exist, what could be designated as "consciousness"? Nor can it be said that [consciousness] is included within "name."

The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) refers only to the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), which take name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as their object; "consciousness" [in this context] refers to the sixth [mental consciousness].

Because the five sensory consciousnesses do not exist at the stage of the *kalala*, and because the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) arise intermittently, they lack the power to constantly sustain name-and-form.
How, then, could it be said that they always serve as the condition for name-and-form? Therefore, the term "consciousness" in that sutra correctly and exclusively reveals the eighth consciousness.

*Kalala*—this is translated as "impure mixture" (*zāwèi*) and also as "thin curd" (*bóluò*). It refers to the initial stage of conception, wherein the essence of the father and mother is taken as the body.
The term "and so forth" (*děng*) includes the remaining four stages. The second week is called *arbuda*.
This is called *kalala* (the embryo). On the twenty-first day, it is called *arbuda* (the closed mass), which means "soft flesh.
On the twenty-eighth day, it is called *peśī* (the lump), which means "firm flesh. On the thirty-fifth day, it is called *praśākhā*, which means "limbs and joints.

Up to this point, it is subsumed under the stage of *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form). After the sixth week, the six sense faculties gradually form; this is then subsumed under the stage of *ṣaḍāyatana* (the six sense bases). The rest...
To be known.

Composed by the Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu. △ Regarding the substance of the eight consciousnesses as food:
previously, this was discussed in terms of the stages of arising and ceasing; now, it is discussed in terms of the stage of abiding. The text is divided into two parts:

first, citing the sūtras to provide a general explanation of the four kinds of food; second, specifically revealing that the consciousness-food (*vijñānāhāra*) is exclusively the true retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).

First: Furthermore, a sūtra states that all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment (*āhāra*). If this eighth consciousness did not exist, the substance of the "consciousness-nutriment" mentioned in that sūtra would not be possible.
That is to say, the sūtra states that there are four kinds of nutriment: first, edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).

Transformation and decay constitute its characteristic. This refers to the three [objects]—odor, flavor, and the tangible—which are bound to the desire realm and serve as the food that nourishes the sense faculties and benefits the body and life during the process of transformation and decay.

For this reason, the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) is not included within the category of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), because visible form has no utility at the time of transformation and decay.

"Segment" (*kavaḍa*) means form; it means division. It is also written as *piṇḍa*, meaning that there is a physical portion that can be grasped and taken up. Regarding "having transformation and decay as its characteristic":
it is only when food has been transformed and decayed within the belly that it becomes the functional characteristic of providing nourishment.

Because at the initial moment of entering the mouth, no benefit or harm is yet perceived, it is not termed "nutritive food. "Bound to the desire realm" refers to [the realms of] form and formlessness... [omitted].
In all realms, neither [of these two] subsists on edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).

Second is the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*), which has the mind as its basis and the contact with objects as its characteristic. This means that when tainted contact (*sāsrava-sparśa*) first apprehends an object, it grasps [objects such as] joy and pleasure, thereby causing the sense faculties to be refreshed and satisfied;
thus, it functions as a form of nutriment. Although this mental factor of contact is universally associated with all consciousnesses, it [functions as nutriment] only [in specific instances].
Regarding those [nutriments] belonging to the six consciousnesses, the meaning of "food" is predominant [in their case].
This is because contact is a coarse and manifest object, and it excels in nourishing [the body] by grasping at joy and pleasure, as well as the equanimity that is conducive to benefit.

Contact (*sparśa*) is one of the five universal mental factors (*citta-sādhāraṇa-dharma*). "Defiled contact" (*sāsrava-sparśa*) distinguishes it from contact associated with untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*).
When people today watch performances or listen to music, they may forget to eat yet remain tireless;
this is precisely taking contact as nutriment (*sparśāhāra*).

Third (the sixth): Among the mental factors associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), volition (*cetanā*) has the characteristic of aspiration. This refers to contaminated volition that operates in conjunction with the mental factor of desire (*chanda*).
By aspiring toward desirable objects, it is able to perform the function of nutriment for the sake of sustaining the body and life.

Although this mental factor of volition is also universally associated with all [six] consciousnesses, its status as nutriment is particularly predominant when it belongs to the mental consciousness; for the mental consciousness aspires toward its objects.

Because one aspires for excellence, volition (*cetanā*) is also one of the five universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-caitta*). "With outflows" (*sāsrava*) distinguishes this from volition associated with uncontaminated consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna-saṃprayukta*).
It is like the story of a man of old who was fleeing from danger; his child was too young to follow him, so he hung a bag of ashes [from the child's neck].
From within the beam, he said to the boy, "If you are hungry, there is food in the bag between the beams.
The young child looked toward the beam and thought of the food; though many days passed, he did not die. Later, another person arrived, and the boy told him to take it down.

Once he saw that it was only ashes, the boy’s life immediately ended. This is the manifestation of thinking about food. Furthermore, the case of hoping for a plum to quench one's thirst is likewise [a matter of] thinking.

Food. Fourth is the food of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*), which has the characteristic of maintaining (*dhāraṇa*) the sense faculties so that they do not disintegrate; this refers to contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*).

Through the power of nourishment from edible food, contact, and volition, it increases and is able to perform the function of food. Although this consciousness pervades the nature of all [six] consciousnesses, it is primarily...
Among the eight consciousnesses, the meaning of "nutriment" (*āhāra*) is predominant, because they possess the excellence of continuous succession and the capacity for sustaining [the body].
Furthermore, this refers specifically to contaminated consciousnesses (*sāsrava-vijñāna*), thereby excluding uncontaminated pure consciousnesses (*anāsrava-śuddha-vijñāna*).

Although the eighth consciousness, being stainless (*vimala*), also sustains the uncontaminated form-body (*anāsrava-rūpakāya*) and may thus be called a supramundane, uncontaminated nutriment, here we are considering it from a single perspective.
All sentient beings abide by means of nutriment; thus, that which maintains the contaminated body must be the contaminated eighth consciousness.
"Of one kind" refers to its being indeterminate in nature. "Continuous" refers to its uninterrupted transformation.
Accordingly, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that these four nutriments are subsumed within three aggregates (*skandha*), five bases (*āyatana*), and eleven elements (*dhātu*).

These four are called "nutriments" because they are able to sustain the bodies and lives of sentient beings so that they do not perish or cease. Edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is functional only within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Although the nutriment of contact (and the nutriment of mental volition), which are subsumed under the universal mental factors, pervade all three realms, they nevertheless function in dependence upon the six [corresponding] consciousnesses.
[They] exist or do not exist according to consciousness.

Regarding the three aggregates (*skandha*): among the five aggregates, edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); contact-food (*sparśa-āhāra*) and volition-food (*manahsaṃcetanā-āhāra*) are subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*);
and consciousness-food (*vijñāna-āhāra*) is subsumed under the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Regarding the five bases (*āyatana*): among the twelve bases, edible food...

These are subsumed within the three bases (āyatana) of odor, flavor, and tangibility. The food of contact (sparśāhāra) and the food of volition (manosaṃcetanāhāra) are subsumed within the base of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana).

The food of consciousness (vijñānāhāra) is subsumed within the base of mind (manāyatana). Regarding the eleven elements (dhātu): among the eighteen elements, the food of morsels (kavalīkārāhāra) is subsumed within the three elements of odor, flavor, and tangibility;

the food of contact and the food of volition are subsumed within the element of mental phenomena (dharmadhātu); and the food of consciousness is subsumed within the element of mind (manodhātu) and the six elements of consciousness.
This is a summary. Regarding the presence or absence [of these] according to the consciousnesses:

as in the first dhyāna, where the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue are absent, there is no contact (*sparśa*) or volition (*cetanā*) associated with the nose-consciousness or tongue-consciousness; there is only contact and volition associated with the eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mental-consciousness.
From the second dhyāna upward, the first five consciousnesses are absent, and thus the first five [types of contact and volition] are absent.
The two nutriments of contact and volition associated with consciousness exist only as those associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
If explained from the perspective of their predominance, they are referred to simply as the nutriment of volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*).

In the Heaven of Non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*), since the sixth consciousness is absent, there are no two nutriments of contact and volition associated with that sixth consciousness; however, there do exist those associated with the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses].
Regarding the two types of mental factors (*caitta*), the meaning of "food" is not predominant; there is only the food of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*).

Having first cited the sutras to comprehensively clarify the four foods, [the text now proceeds to] △ secondly, specifically demonstrate that the food of consciousness is exclusively the true maturation (*vipāka*).

The evolving consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth, are intermittent and subject to transformation; they are not capable of sustaining the body and life-force at all times and in all circumstances.
This is because they are interrupted during the mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), deep sleep, fainting, and within the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*).

Furthermore, even when they are present, they undergo change according to their respective bases (the sense organs), their respective objects, and across the three natures, the three realms, and the nine stages. Therefore, regarding the sustenance [of the body and life-force]...

The body and life are neither pervasive nor permanent. For those who maintain that there is no eighth consciousness, on what basis could they claim that all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment (*āhāra*)?

It cannot be said that in the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), although consciousness is currently absent, past or future consciousnesses serve as nutriment; for such [past and future consciousnesses] are not present and are not permanent, being like space.

Flowers and the like lack both substance and function. Even if one were to claim that consciousness possesses substance and function with respect to the past and future, since it is not subsumed under the present, it is like space and other such things;

therefore, it does not have the nature of nutriment. Furthermore, it cannot be said that the mind in meditative absorption and so forth can serve as nutriment for sentient beings in a state of non-consciousness (*acittaka*), because at the time of abiding in that non-conscious state, those [preparatory] minds and mental factors have already ceased and thus belong to the past.
This is because it is not established that [the non-associated formations] have already been consumed as food.

Furthermore, it cannot be said that non-associated formations such as the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) constitute that food, because they are not included among the four types of food, such as edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), and because non-associated dharmas (which are distinct from matter, mind, etc.
lack substantial existence.

This precisely clarifies that the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñānas) lack the capacity to sustain the body and life, and thus cannot be established as the substance of the nutriment of consciousness (vijñānāhāra).
If the evolving consciousnesses were taken as nutriment, then during states devoid of mind (acittaka), there would necessarily be no nutriment.
If one were to take past or future consciousness as nutriment, since the past and future are neither present nor permanent, lacking both substance and function, they would be like empty space.

[The opponent] says: "How can a flower in the sky serve as food? [The proponent] replies: "Past and future consciousnesses are existent dharmas; this is not a school that maintains that consciousness is non-existent. The reason (*hetu*) is:
"Because they are not present, are not eternal, and lack both essence (*svabhāva*) and function (*kāritra*). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: "Like a flower in the sky.

Fearing that there might be a rebuttal stating, "Consciousness possesses its own essence and function in each instance throughout the past and future; how then could it lack essence and function? [the author] now refutes this.
It is said: Although the essence and function of the past and future exist within consciousness, the essence and function of the past belong to the past and are not subsumed under the present;
likewise, the essence and function of the future belong to the future and are not subsumed under the present.
For example, when there is currently not a single thing before one, it is called "empty space. Can empty space possibly be eaten? The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) states: [The past...]

The entity and function that have not yet been cognized are a subject of proof (*dharmin*). It is not the thesis (*pakṣa*) that they are of the nature of nutriment (*āhāra-svabhāva*). The reason (*hetu*) is: "because they are not included within the present.

The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like space. Regarding the phrase "the mind and so forth that enter meditative absorption," this refers to the minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) prior to absorption.
The rest may be understood accordingly.

There are those who maintain that even in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and other such states, the sixth consciousness still exists and can function as nutriment for those sentient beings;
this describes a further refinement of their position. The term "and others" (*ādi*) includes the remaining four states devoid of mind (*acittaka*).

That position is irrational; it shall be refuted extensively later. Furthermore, if they claim that the sixth consciousness can serve as nutriment, then one must explain what serves as nutriment when an uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) sixth consciousness arises while born in the two higher realms.
This is because uncontaminated consciousness and so forth destroy existence (*bhava*).

In that case, the body and life-force cannot serve as food for one another. Furthermore, it is not possible to maintain that there are contaminated seeds (*sāsrava-bīja*) within the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) sixth consciousness that can act as such food;
this is because uncontaminated consciousness and its associates, like *nirvāṇa*, are determinedly incapable of sustaining contaminated seeds.
Moreover, it cannot be said that the body and life-force of sentient beings in the higher realms sustain one another by acting as mutual food.

Furthermore, because the four types of nutriment do not sustain the body and life-force therein (in the formless realm), and because there is no body in the formless realm such that life-force would have nothing to support it;

and if one were to claim that the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous character) sustains life-force in the formless realm, then since the *nikāya-sabhāga* and so forth are merely conventional designations lacking substantial reality, how could they possibly sustain life-force?

From this, it is definitively known that there exists a distinct, truly ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) which is different from the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), and which is of a single nature, constant, and pervasive, and which grasps [the body].
The maintenance of the body and the non-cessation of its functions depend on this. It was with reference to this that the Blessed One said:
"All sentient beings subsist upon food.
This refutes the opposing view, which will be extensively refuted later in the ninth chapter, "The Chapter on the Presence of Consciousness in the Cessation Attainment" (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
The untainted mind refers to the mind associated with the wisdom of the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). The rest may be understood accordingly.

Sentient beings are established solely based on the appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*). Since the Buddha lacks tainted [aggregates], he is not subsumed under the category of sentient beings (or, at times, because he does not abide by means of nutriment).

When it is said that the Buddha is the unsurpassed among sentient beings and that he dwells by means of nutriment, one should know that all such statements are spoken based on skillful manifestations.

This explains away an anticipated objection. The objection states: "Since all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment, when the Buddha transforms the eighth consciousness into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), what serves as his nutriment?
Therefore, the present explanation says: "Sentient beings are established solely based upon the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*);
the Buddha is not a sentient being, so why would he need to subsist by means of nutriment? Furthermore, the objection continues: "If the Buddha..."
He is not included among sentient beings. Why, then, does another sutra state that "the Buddha is the supreme among sentient beings"?
Furthermore, while the Buddha was in the world, he also consumed solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*). How are these points to be reconciled? Therefore, the present commentary explains:
all such statements were spoken based on skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and manifestations.
Since the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is of the nature of the supreme nutriment, that consciousness is precisely this eighth consciousness;

thus the point is established. This concludes the section on the essential substance of the eight consciousnesses as nutriment. 9. There is Consciousness in the Attainment of Cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

The preceding [section] was revealed by way of the gate of *pravṛtti* (evolution); now it is revealed by way of the gate of *nivṛtti* (reversion). The text is divided into two parts. First: Refuting the absence of the eighth consciousness.
Second, refuting the existence of a sixth consciousness. First:

Furthermore, a sūtra states that for one abiding in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the activities of body, speech, and mind are all extinguished without exception, yet life-force (*āyus*) is not extinguished.
Nor is it separated from warmth; the faculties do not undergo transformation or decay, and consciousness does not depart from the body.

If this eighth consciousness did not exist, then the consciousness that "does not depart from the body" for one who abides in the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), as stated in the Sūtra, would be impossible. This is because the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth have coarse and active modes of activity (ākāra).
Regarding the objects of perception, because one inevitably experiences mental fatigue and develops weariness toward those [evolving consciousnesses], one seeks their temporary cessation;
by gradually subduing and eliminating them until they reach the stage of total exhaustion, one establishes the person who dwells in the meditative attainment of cessation based on this state.

Therefore, within this meditative attainment, those [various evolving] consciousnesses are all extinguished, provided that one does not admit the existence of a subtle, uniform, and ever-present consciousness that maintains life-force and other functions.

On what basis is it said that consciousness does not depart from the body? If you claim that because those six types of consciousness arise again at a later time—like a tertian malaria—the consciousness is said not to have departed from the body, then one should not say that mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) have ceased.
Since consciousness and perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth must arise and cease simultaneously [with the mind], one would likewise have to say that mental formations do not depart from the body.
Furthermore, life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and the sense-faculties (*indriya*) should also be like the six consciousnesses [in that they could re-arise after having ceased].

This would constitute a great error. Therefore, one must admit that there exists an eighth consciousness which, like vitality (*āyuṣ*), warmth (*uṣman*), and so forth, is truly not separated from the body.
Furthermore, if during this state there were no consciousness at all, it would—like a clod of earth or a stone—not be reckoned among sentient beings;

how then could one say that such a person is "an noble one abiding in the meditative attainment of cessation"? Moreover, if the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) were absent in this state, who would be able to maintain the sense faculties, vitality, and warmth?
Because there is no appropriation (*upādāna*), all [the aggregates] would perish and be destroyed, like a corpse; thus, life-force (*jīvita*) and the other [factors] would not exist.
This being so, subsequent consciousness would certainly not arise again. To say that [consciousness] does not depart from the body implies that it must belong to something.

Since the various ripening consciousnesses (*vipākavijñāna*), once they have abandoned this body, do not depart to rely upon another body and then arise again, [this is impossible]. Furthermore, even if one were to grant that subsequent consciousness arises again, if this state [of the intermediate existence] did not exist...
If the seed-holding consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) did not exist, how could subsequent consciousnesses arise without seeds?

This is because, as established in the preceding text, past and future phenomena, as well as non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*), do not possess real substantial entities; furthermore, it has already been refuted that material phenomena (*rūpa*) and other such dharmas exist apart from consciousness, nor that they can receive perfuming or hold seeds.
Nevertheless, in mindless states such as the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), [the continuity of consciousness] remains just as it does in states with a mind.
It is established that the eighth consciousness truly exists, because it possesses the faculties, life-force, and warmth, and is comprised within the category of sentient beings.

By this reasoning, those who abide in the meditative attainments of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) must certainly possess the eighth consciousness; it truly does not depart from the body (this "not departing from the body" does not refer to the subsequent arising of the evolving consciousnesses).

The state of mindlessness, such as the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), is a functional entity (*dharmin*). This is the thesis (*pakṣa*) that the eighth consciousness truly exists. The reason (*hetu*) is:

"because it possesses the faculties (*indriya*), life-force (*āyus*), and warmth (*uṣman*), and is comprised within the category of sentient beings (*sattva*). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: "just like a state with mind. 2. Refuting the existence of the sixth consciousness.
If it is argued that in this state [of the meditative attainment of cessation] there exists a sixth consciousness, and thus it is called "not separated from the body," this too is unreasonable;

for this [attainment of cessation] is also termed the "mindless attainment" (*acittaka-samāpatti*). If one were to further argue that it is called "mindless" because the [first] five consciousnesses are absent, then all meditative attainments would have to be termed "mindless," since in all such attainments the five bodies of consciousness are absent.
Furthermore, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is inherently included [within the category of mind].

Among the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), as with the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), [consciousness] does not exist in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Alternatively, because the mental aspects (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*) of consciousness in this state cannot be known, it is like vitality (*āyuḥ*) or heat (*uṣman*), and thus is not the sixth consciousness.

If there were a consciousness in this state whose aspects and objects could be known, it would—like other states involving mind—not be included within this state of cessation, for its primary purpose is the cessation of mental activity.

Because one enters this meditative attainment (nirodhasamāpatti) by means of a consciousness that can cognize its objects through their characteristics, this [argument] correctly refutes the attachment to the existence of a sixth consciousness during the state of nirodhasamāpatti.
The formal syllogism (*prayoga*) is as follows: "The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is the subject;
it does not exist during the state of nirodhasamāpatti is the thesis (*pakṣa*); because it is included within the six evolving consciousnesses is the reason (*hetu*); for example, like..."

Regarding the first five consciousnesses: next, one may formulate a syllogism as follows. "The consciousness in this state of cessation is the subject (dharmin); it is not the sixth consciousness, the thesis (sādhya). The reason (hetu) is:

because its mode of activity (ākāra) and object of cognition (ālambana) cannot be known. The example (dṛṣṭānta) is like vitality (āyus), warmth (ūṣman), and so forth. Next, one states the counter-syllogism:
"If there were a consciousness in this state that possessed a knowable mode of activity and object of cognition, it would be the subject; [it would not be the sixth consciousness]."

The thesis is that [the state of] the attainment of cessation is included within the category of the "cessation" stage. The reason is that one enters the attainment of cessation by means of a consciousness that is capable of discerning the object and the aspect of quiescence.
The analogy is like other states of mind that possess consciousness.
Furthermore, if the sixth consciousness exists in this state, do the mental factors associated with that [sixth consciousness] exist or not?
Below, this will be refuted further by examining the existence or non-existence of mental factors. Now, both are questioned; first, the position that mental factors exist will be refuted.
If there were mental factors (*caitasika*) present, the Sūtra should not have stated that for one abiding in this meditative absorption, all mental activities (*cittacāra*) are extinguished;

nor should it be called the "absorption of the cessation of sensation and perception" (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti*). [The opponent] replies: In the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of this absorption, one merely feels aversion toward sensation and perception; therefore, within this absorption, only sensation and perception are extinguished. [Thus, only these two—] sensation and perception...

The Dharma [states]: "Among all mental factors (*caitta*), those that assist the mind most strongly are uniquely termed 'mental formations' (*citta-saṃskāra*). When it is said that 'mental formations cease,' what contradiction is there? [Refutation:

If it were as you say, then in the state of the "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), only perception (*saṃjñā*) would cease. This is because, during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), one merely feels aversion toward perception.
Yet, you do not admit this [that only perception ceases]. Since both feeling (*vedanā*) and perception alone assist the mind so strongly, when these two cease, the mind should likewise [cease].
[Question: "How can the sixth consciousness still exist [if it has been extinguished]?

[Response: The intent of the defense is that only feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are extinguished, while the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and the remaining mental factors (*caitta*) are not.

To refute this, the argument first challenges the position by using the example of the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñi-sattva*). It then clarifies that since feeling and perception are powerful supports for the mind, once feeling and perception have been extinguished...
Since the mind has no support, how could it not perish along with them? [The opponent] says:

"Just as when bodily formations (kāya-saṃskāra) such as inhalation and exhalation cease, the body still remains; why then must one demand that the mind perish in the same way as the formations of sensation and perception (vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra)?
[The author] refutes this: "If that were so, then when vocal formations (vāk-saṃskāra)—namely vitarka and vicāra—cease, speech should not cease; yet this is not what you yourself accept."

However, regarding the application [of mental factors] to the substance of phenomena (*dharma*), there are those that are universal (*sarvatraga*) and those that are not. When a universal factor ceases, the phenomenon necessarily ceases along with it;
when a non-universal factor ceases, the phenomenon may still persist. Non-universal factors include, for example, inhalation and exhalation;
for when these cease, the body still remains. Vitarka and vicāra are subsumed under the category of universals; if they were to cease, speech would certainly no longer exist.

Feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are also included among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), just as volition (*cetanā*) and the others are, because they are admitted to be universal mental factors.

Therefore, when feeling and perception cease, the mind (the six consciousnesses) must necessarily cease along with them. How, then, can it be said that while feeling and perception have ceased, the mind still remains?
Furthermore, since volition and the others are admitted to be universal mental factors, when feeling and perception cease, those [volitions and so forth] should likewise cease.
[They] cease accordingly. Since this is so, other mental factors such as faith (*śraddhā*) and the rest are likewise absent in this state [of the meditative attainment of cessation].
It cannot be claimed that while the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) have ceased, other mental factors could still remain. How then can it be said that there are remaining mental factors?

Since it is admitted that volition (*cetanā*) and the others are not absent in this state, feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) must also be the same, for they are likewise universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*). Furthermore, this...

If there were volition (*cetanā*) and so forth within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there would necessarily also be contact (*sparśa*), because all other mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) arise without exception through the power of contact.
If one admits that contact exists, one must also admit that feeling (*vedanā*) exists, because feeling has contact as its condition.
Since one admits that feeling exists, perception (*saṃjñā*) must also arise, for they are inseparable.

The "saving" interpretation holds that while inhalation and exhalation cease, the body does not cease; by analogy, one knows that while feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) cease, the mind (*citta*) does not cease.

The "refuting" interpretation holds that when applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) cease, speech necessarily ceases; by analogy, one knows that when feeling and perception cease, the mind necessarily ceases.
This is because feeling and perception are universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), whereas inhalation and exhalation are not.

Therefore, regarding what are called the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma): feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), desire (chanda), wisdom (prajñā), mindfulness (smṛti), attention (manaskāra), and resolve (adhimokṣa).
Concentration (*samādhi*) is present throughout all states of mind; these are called the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).
Since this is commonly accepted by other vehicles, one may use it as an analogy to refute [the opponent's position]. The rest can be understood accordingly.

(The opponent) offers this defense: "Just as feeling conditions craving, it is not the case that all feelings can give rise to craving. Therefore, although contact conditions feeling, it is not the case that all contacts can give rise to feeling.
For this reason, the logic of the objection is not established. (The critic) refutes this: That defense is incorrect, because there is a distinction.

That is to say, the Buddha himself specified that only those feelings produced by contact associated with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśaja-vedanā*) serve as the condition for the arising of craving; he never [stated otherwise].

In some places, it is specified that feeling arises from contact; therefore, if there is contact, feeling must necessarily arise. It is a settled principle that feeling is concomitant with perception (*saṃjñā*).

Alternatively, as in other states, feeling and perception would not cease either, because one maintains that volition (*cetanā*) and other factors exist within this state [of the attainment of cessation].

To assert this would contradict the statement regarding the cessation of mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra-nirodha*), and it would also fail to establish what is called the "attainment of the cessation of feeling and perception" (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha-samāpatti*).

The opponent’s intention is that since it is not necessary for all sensations (*vedanā*) to give rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), one may infer by analogy that it is likewise not necessary for all contacts (*sparśa*) to give rise to sensation.

The refuter’s intention is that while the Buddha himself specifically distinguished and indicated cases where sensation does not give rise to craving, he never made such a distinction regarding contact not giving rise to sensation.
Since there is this difference, how can it be used as an analogy? Alternatively, one should further establish a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to refute it as follows: "That..."

The subject (*dharmin*) asserted here is "this state. The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that "feeling and perception are not extinguished. The reason (*hetu*) is: "because there is volition (*cetanā*) and so forth.
The example (*udāharaṇa*) is: "just as in other states possessing mind (*sacittaka*). This concludes the refutation of the position that mental factors (*caitasika*) exist.

If there were no mental factors (*caitta*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) would certainly not exist either; for we do not observe other [consciousnesses], such as visual consciousness, existing independently apart from their associated mental factors.
Furthermore, if the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga-caitta*) associated with the other [five] consciousnesses were to cease, the mind would necessarily cease along with them.

(If one were to claim that the mental king [the primary consciousness] exists while sensation and so forth do not, then) sensation and the rest would not be included among the "great ground" factors (*mahābhūmika*), because they would not be present in all states of mind. Moreover, this consciousness would not be...

Because [mental factors] are associated [with consciousness], if one were to admit that this consciousness lacks associated mental factors, then— since the triad of contact (the mental factor), the sense faculty, and the object would not be in conjunction—
it would follow that there is no support (the faculty) and no objective referent (the object), etc., and thus it would, like form and other such phenomena, not be able to be called "mind."

This refutes the counter-argument that within the state of the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), there exists only the sixth consciousness as the mental king (*cittarāja*) and no mental factors (*caitta*).

Furthermore, a sūtra states: "With the mind (*manas*) and phenomena (*dharma*) as conditions, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises; from the conjunction of these three comes contact (*sparśa*);

arising together with contact are sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*). If it were admitted that the mental consciousness exists within this attainment of cessation, then because of the conjunction of these three, [the aforementioned mental factors would necessarily arise].

There must necessarily be contact (*sparśa*). Since contact is established as being concomitant with feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*), how could there be consciousness (*vijñāna*) without mental factors (*caitta*)?

If it is argued that at other times the triad [of sense organ, object, and consciousness] possesses the power to constitute contact, and that the arising of contact produces mental factors such as feeling, then [in this case] because one has previously cultivated aversion toward mental factors during the preparatory stage for this meditative attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the three factors (organ, object, and consciousness) lack the capacity while in this state; thus, contact is not established.

[When] contact no longer arises, mental factors (*caitta*) do not arise either, nor do sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth. If that is so, it should be called a "concentration in which mental factors are extinguished" (*nirodha-caitta-samādhi*).
Why then is it described only as the "extinction of sensation and perception" (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha*)?

If you argue that at the time of aversion one only feels aversion toward sensation and perception, and because these two are extinguished, all mental factors are extinguished, and the name of the concentration is established based on what was previously averse to—then, in this [attainment of cessation], the mind (*citta*, i.e., the sixth consciousness) would also [be extinguished].
It should be extinguished by the sixth consciousness, because it necessarily co-arises with the feeling and perception that are to be suppressed, just like other mental factors (*caitta*).
Otherwise, how could this meditative absorption also be called the "mindless absorption" (*acittaka-samāpatti*)?
This also further refutes the attachment to the existence of a mind-king (citta-rāja) without mental factors (caitta). "Intention" (manas) is the faculty; "phenomena" (dharma) are the objects.

Consciousness arises from these two conditions; contact arises from the conjunction of the three. Where there is contact, there must necessarily be sensation (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and volition (cetanā).
How can there be only the mind-king (citta-rāja) without mental factors (caitta)? "If it is argued... below provides a further defense; "If that were so... below provides a further refutation.
Next, "If it is argued... provides yet another defense; next, "Since that is so... provides yet another refutation.
Since both sensation (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā) have ceased, all other mental factors must likewise cease; how then could one claim that the mind-king alone persists?

Furthermore, even if one were to grant that the mental consciousness exists during this state of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), what would its nature be? It cannot be defiled, nor can it be indeterminate (avyākṛta).

This is because such states—defilement or indetermination—do not exist within wholesome meditative attainments. Moreover, any other defiled or indeterminate sixth consciousness must necessarily be associated with mental factors (caitta);
