Furthermore, when the five consciousnesses arise, there must necessarily be a simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that is capable of inducing the subsequent moment of mental consciousness to arise. Why, then, would one rely upon the five consciousnesses as their "opening-and-guiding support" (*kai-tao-i*)?
All of the above refutations of the first school are correct. However, what follows—whether in terms of refutation or establishment—is not consistent with reason.

In states such as mindless sleep or fainting, when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has ceased and subsequently arises again, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the manas are both constantly continuous;
they too should serve as the "opening and guiding support" (*kai-dao-yi*) for that mental consciousness. If [you claim] that it [the mental consciousness] only uses the preceding...

If [it is argued that] those of the same class provide guidance [for one another], why is it not likewise accepted for the five consciousnesses? Since this is not accepted for them, [the objection does not apply].
How can that (the mental consciousness) alone be so?
How could the ālayavijñāna and manas serve as the *āvedhaka-āśraya* (opening-and-guiding support) for the mental consciousness? This is the first error.

To employ the preceding [moment] of its own kind as the basis for opening and guiding, and then to refute it—this is the second error. Furthermore, they do not allow for the five sensory consciousnesses to have their own kind as [their opening-and-guiding support].
The Guide [the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*] originally states that it is not so, yet you instead seal it as such; this is the third error.
When the manas associated with the wisdom of equality first arises, it must necessarily do so by means of the sixth consciousness entering the contemplation of the two emptinesses;

therefore, one should likewise apply that (sixth consciousness) as its leading support (*āśraya*). As for the pure eighth consciousness co-arising with the mirror-like wisdom, at its initial [arising], it must necessarily...

Furthermore, the maturation-consciousness (*vipākacitta*) arises induced by the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses; moreover, it relies upon either the defiled manas (*kliṣṭamanas*) or a wholesome mind associated with compassion and vows (*karuṇā-praṇidhāna*).
Since this is so, one must necessarily admit that the eighth consciousness also takes the sixth and seventh consciousnesses as its "opening and guiding" support (*āśraya*).
Therefore, the statement of that [first proponent] fails to investigate the principle at all.
The defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) is the seventh consciousness, while the wholesome mind associated with compassion and vows is the sixth consciousness.

It is said that because a Bodhisattva, by means of these compassion and vows, benefits sentient beings throughout long kalpas and does not grasp at nirvāṇa, the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) also takes this [sixth consciousness] as its "opening and guiding" support (*āśraya*).
This interpretation is entirely erroneous.
One should explain the five consciousnesses as follows: among the first six consciousnesses, whichever consciousness is employed serves as the *āśraya-pravartaka* (conducive support).
For the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), its own preceding moment of the same class, or the seventh or eighth consciousnesses, serve as the conducive support.

For the seventh manas-consciousness, its own preceding moment of the same class, or the sixth consciousness, serves as the conducive support. For the *ādānavijñāna*, its own preceding moments of the same class, and...
The sixth and seventh [consciousnesses] serve as the *āśraya-pravartaka* (guiding bases); all of this is consistent with reason, as previously explained.
However, there are many points of error, which will become clear later on. This concludes the second school’s interpretation. △ Now follows the third school’s correct interpretation.

This interpretation—that which is the "enabling condition" (*āśraya*)—is also unreasonable. An enabling condition is defined by four characteristics: (1) it must exist; (2) it is the object of cognition (*ālambana-dharma*); (3) it is sovereign;

and (4) it functions as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Because these four qualities enable and guide the subsequent arising of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), it is called an "enabling condition.
This applies exclusively to the mind (*citta*) and not to mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth.

This is the correct explanation of the meaning of the "opening and guiding support" (*āśraya*). The term "existent" (*sat*) excludes the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), because they are not substantially real.
The term "conditioning phenomena" (*dharma*) excludes matter (*rūpa*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because they lack the capacity for cognitive apprehension (*ālambana*).

The term "predominant" (*pradhāna*) excludes mental factors (*caitta*), as they depend on others and lack sovereignty. The term "immediately preceding" (*samanantara*) excludes those of a different category and those that arise simultaneously with the acquisition (*prāpti*).

If this [preceding thought] and that [subsequent thought] do not arise simultaneously, it is said that this [preceding thought] possesses the power of opening and guiding for that [subsequent thought].

Since it is admitted that the eight consciousnesses of a single body can arise simultaneously, how can those of different categories serve as the *āśraya* (supporting condition) for one another by way of opening and leading (*kai-dao*)?

If it were granted that they could serve as such a support, then the eight types of consciousness would not arise simultaneously; this would then be identical to the position held by certain Hīnayāna schools that minds do not arise concurrently.

Furthermore, within a single body, various consciousnesses arise together—sometimes two, sometimes three, and so on up to seven or eight—their number being indefinite. If [you argue that] this support merely excludes [the possibility of] more or fewer [than a specific number], and does not...

To distinguish it from other categories: all [dharmas] are permitted to mutually function as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*). If that were so, then material faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and the like—which arise simultaneously with the mind but belong to a different category—would likewise have to be so;

they too would be able to mutually function as equal-and-immediate conditions. This would contradict the sacred teaching that equal-and-immediate conditions apply only to minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

However, the statement in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* that matter (*rūpa*) may also possess equal-and-immediate conditions is a form of concessive-refutative discourse (*anujñā-pratiṣedha-vākya*). That is to say, it provisionally concedes the position of the Hīnayāna.

This is because [the principle of] the equal and immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) between preceding and succeeding moments of form and mind subverts [the attachment to their mutual functioning as] causal conditions (hetupratyaya). Otherwise, it would not be so.
The word "etc. (ādi) would then be rendered useless. If you claim that the word "etc.

does not exclude [the presence of] greater or lesser functional power, but merely indicates similarity of kind—[implying that] even those of the same kind as form possess the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)—then this contradicts your own prior tenet that consciousnesses of different kinds act as equal-and-immediate conditions.

This refutes the previous erroneous view that [the mind and mental factors] mutually serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). However, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* below provides a further explanation to address an underlying objection.

The objection states: "If the equal-and-immediate condition applies only to the mind and its mental factors, why does the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* state that matter (*rūpa*) may also possess an equal-and-immediate condition?
Now, it is explained: the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* [makes this statement] in order to refute...
The followers of the Hīnayāna falsely cling to the notion that the sequential continuity of matter and mind constitutes the nature of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Therefore, even if one were to concede that matter and mind arise sequentially from one another, this would only allow for the existence of the *samanantara-pratyaya* (immediately preceding condition), but it would lack the meaning of a *hetu-pratyaya* (causal condition).
Were it not so, the character "equal" (*sam*) in the term *samanantara* would be rendered useless; for "equal" implies equality.
This definition has two aspects: first, it excludes a disparity in magnitude; second, it indicates homogeneity. Regarding the exclusion of a disparity in magnitude:

this means that the activity of mind is extensive, whereas the activity of matter is limited. Therefore, mind serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for mind alone, but does not serve as an equal-and-immediate condition for matter.
Since the activity of matter is limited, it lacks the status of being an equal-and-immediate condition. Second, regarding the indication of homogeneity:

Just as with the preceding visual consciousness, it is called "homogeneous" (sabhāga) in relation to the subsequent visual consciousness; however, in relation to auditory, olfactory, or other types of consciousness, it is not homogeneous.
The rest may be understood accordingly.
Therefore, regarding the eight consciousnesses, each takes only its own kind as its "opening-and-guiding" support (*āśraya*).

This is in deep accord with both scripture and principle, for it is impossible for the same kind [of consciousness] to arise simultaneously. As for the "immediately preceding" support (*samanantarāśraya*) of mental factors (*caitta*), it should be explained according to the consciousness with which they are associated.

Although mind and mental factors arise together as different types, they are mutually associated and harmonized such that they appear as one; they necessarily arise and perish together, and their activities are identical.

They must necessarily be identical. When one [consciousness] acts as an opening and guiding condition (*ābhimukhī-karaṇa*), the others also act as opening and guiding conditions; therefore, they function as one another’s equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

This is not necessarily the case when various consciousnesses are compared with one another, so it should not be taken as an analogy. Furthermore, mental factors (*caitta*) are not "opening and guiding supports" (*ābhimukhī-karaṇa-āśraya*), because they lack the principle of predominance (*prādhānya*) regarding what is produced and induced.

First, having refuted previous errors, the correct principle is established. Next, regarding the "opening and guiding" support (*āśraya*) of the mental factors (*caitta*), one should raise this objection:

"If the word 'equal' (*sama*) necessarily signifies being of the same class (*sajātīya*), then since the various mental factors arise simultaneously with their associated mind-king (*cittarāja*) as distinct classes, how can it be said that they follow the consciousness? To this, we now offer the following explanation: "However, they are mutually..."
Because they must be equal. "Entity" refers to the substantial basis; "function" refers to the activity performed.

For example, the mental factors associated with visual consciousness necessarily share the same eye-faculty as their basis with the visual consciousness, and necessarily share the same visible object as their objective condition with the visual consciousness.
The rest may be understood by analogy. As for the statement that when one [mental factor] acts as an opening and guiding condition (*ābhāsana-pratyaya*), the others also act as such:

this refers to the time when visual consciousness arises simultaneously with contact (*sparśa*); at that moment, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth—even whether they are wholesome or defiled—all arise in accordance with it.
Regarding their acting as successive conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for one another: this refers to the way in which the various mental factors mutually induce each other’s arising. All...
Regarding the mutual relationship between consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), there is no sense of association, conjunction, fixed co-arising and ceasing, or identity of activity.
Therefore, one should not use mental factors (*caitta*) as an analogy to falsely assert that they serve as one another’s equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

However, below the section on mental factors, the scope of their dependence and objects (*ālambana*) is distinguished as being either broad or narrow; if one speaks of the equal-and-immediate condition, then—
It is broad; therefore, mental factors (*caitta*) may mutually serve as bases for one another. If one says that the "basis" (*āśraya*) refers only to the leading [factor], then it is narrow;
thus, the mind-king (*cittarāja*) is called the basis, while mental factors are not, because they cannot function as the sovereign.

If it is claimed that the mental factors associated with the mind (citta-samprayukta-caitta), as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*), likewise arise only from their own respective categories— and not induced by the mind-king (*citta*) or other heterogeneous mental factors—
then at the time of the initial transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses,

the equal-and-immediate condition for the associated faith (*śraddhā*) and other factors would be lacking (because faith and so forth do not exist when the seventh and eighth consciousnesses have not yet undergone transformation). This would contradict the noble teaching that all minds and mental factors arise from four conditions.
Regarding "arising":

since the preceding text contains expressions indicating that things of the same category [are produced], it is not permitted that mental factors (caitta) of a different category could induce production;
therefore, this is explained.

In states such as mindless sleep or fainting, although the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has been interrupted, when it arises again, its "opening and guiding" support (*āśraya*) is simply its own preceding class [of consciousness].

It should be understood that the same applies to the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), which have been interrupted. [Question: Since they have been interrupted for a long duration, why are they called "uninterrupted" (*anantara*)?

[Answer: Because there is no intervening mind of a different class, they are termed "uninterrupted. [Question: At the moment the preceding thought-moment ceases, the succeeding thought-moment does not yet exist. What, then, performs the opening and guiding?

"Now, at the time when consciousness arises, the preceding momentary thought no longer exists; how then can it act as a guide? [The answer is: "Because at the time of its prior cessation, it has already acted as a guide for the present consciousness.

Why then trouble to posit a guide-support (*āśraya*) of a different category? However, within the Noble Teachings, it is sometimes said that the first six consciousnesses mutually induce one another."

As for those who claim that the seventh and eighth consciousnesses arise based on the sixth and seventh, this is all said in reference to their being distinguished as superior dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and not as immediate antecedent conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*);
therefore, there is no contradiction. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "If these consciousnesses are immediately followed by various consciousnesses, they necessarily arise."
This is stated to be their immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, when these six consciousnesses serve as the immediate conditions for those [subsequent] six consciousnesses, they are designated by the name "mental faculty" (*manas-indriya*); thus, there is no contradiction between this general statement and the specific application.
Therefore, the reliance upon one's own kind is in profound accord with both scripture and reasoning.
First, the meaning of "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) is clarified; second, the explanations found in the sacred teachings are harmonized—both can be understood.
Finally, the intent of the term *yoga* is specifically identified. Regarding the words "this" and "that," they appear to apply generally to both self and other;

however, their actual meaning refers only to preceding and succeeding moments within one's own continuum. Thus, it is said that while the expression is general, the intended meaning is specific. Second, [the discussion of] various collateral arguments.
The discussion on the supports of consciousness is concluded. △ Third, the summary that returns to the root verse regarding the supports.

The ancillary treatise is finished; one should now analyze the primary treatise. Although this (second) transforming consciousness possesses three supports, the phrase "depending on that and evolving" in the verse only reveals the first two.
This is to demonstrate that the support and the object-condition of this consciousness are identical [to those of the eighth consciousness].

Therefore, furthermore, because the first two [bases] possess superior functional utility (the verse speaks of them specifically), or because the "opening and guiding" basis is easily understood (the verse does not mention it).

Regarding the first two [types of dependence]: the first is the causal dependence (*hetu-pratyaya-āśraya*), which is the seed-consciousness; the second is the simultaneous dependence (*sahabhū-āśraya*), which is the eighth manifest consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

This concludes the section on the gate of explaining the bases (*āśraya*). △ Third, the gate of explaining the objects of cognition (*ālambana*) has two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the resolution of objections.

Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the brief explanation; second, the detailed explanation. Now, the first: [The text continues with the brief explanation of the objects of cognition.]
Thus, the support of this consciousness has already been explained. What is its object? It is that very [consciousness] itself.
"That" refers to the aforementioned consciousness which serves as its support, for the Noble Ones have taught that this consciousness takes the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) as its object.

△ Second, the detailed explanation has two parts: first, the explanation of those who have not yet transformed their basis (*āśraya*); second, the explanation of those who have already transformed their basis.
Regarding the first, there are four schools of interpretation; the fourth school is correct. Now, the first school’s interpretation is presented.
There is an interpretation that this manas takes as its object both the substance of that eighth consciousness and the five associated mental factors; so it is stated in the treatise regarding manas.

Because it is constantly associated with the grasping at "I" and "mine," it takes that [object] as its substance and its associated mental factors (*caitta*) as its objects, respectively grasping them as "I" and "mine.

However, since all mental factors are not separate from consciousness, just as the expression "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) also includes the mental factors, the verse says simply "takes that as its object";
thus, there is no contradiction with the scriptures.
△ Second School’s Explanation.
There is an interpretation: that [previous] explanation is logically untenable, for there is nowhere it is stated that [the manas] takes contact (*sparśa*) and so forth as its objects.

It should be said that this manas takes only the "seeing" (*darśana-bhāga*) and the "image" (*nimitta-bhāga*) of that consciousness as its objects, respectively grasping them as "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to the self" (*ātmīya*). [This refers to] the image and the seeing [parts].
Because both take consciousness as their substance, they do not contradict the teachings of the Sage.
△ Third school’s interpretation:

There is an opinion that this explanation is also unreasonable, because within the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect), the five material sense organs and their objects are not the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Furthermore, within the *nimitta-bhāga*...

The receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) is an external object. If the manas were to take this as its object, it would follow that—just like the five consciousnesses—it also takes an external object; and it would follow that—just like the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in relation to the five consciousnesses—it takes a common object.

Furthermore, since it would give rise to the grasping of "mine" (*mamakāra*) based on the sense organs and their objects, those born in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) would not grasp at "mine," because they have become weary of form and are born in those heavens where form does not transform into the nature of sense organs and objects.
Therefore, it must be said that this manas takes only the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and its [seeds] as its object.

The seeds are respectively grasped as "self" and "what belongs to the self. Since these seeds are merely the functional capacities of that eighth consciousness and are not substantially existent entities, this does not contradict the holy teachings.
△ The fourth school provides the correct interpretation.
There is an opinion that the previous explanations are all unreasonable because the seeds of form and so forth do not belong to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Furthermore, the treatise states that seeds are substantially existent (*dravya-sat*); if one were to claim they are merely nominal (*prajñapti-sat*), they would be like non-existence, for [nominal things] cannot serve as the immediate causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for all phenomena. Moreover...
This view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) associated with this seventh consciousness arises spontaneously as a single class in constant succession.

How could it possibly involve separate attachments to "self" and "mine" (as occurs, for example, in the sixth mental consciousness)? This is because it is impossible for two distinct objects—such as annihilationism and eternalism—to be grasped simultaneously within a single moment of mind.
Furthermore, one should not say that the two attachments to "self" and "mine" of this seventh consciousness arise sequentially, for [this seventh consciousness...]
Because consciousness has, from time immemorial, transformed as a single flavor (without distinctions of prior or subsequent stages), it is called *satkāya*.
This translates as "accumulation. *Satkāyadṛṣṭi* is precisely the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). At the very moment of grasping at a self—
When one cannot separately grasp at "mine" while simultaneously grasping at "mine" as primary, one likewise cannot separately grasp at a "self.
Therefore, these two graspings—like the two graspings of annihilationism and eternalism—can never arise together.
Since this view of self associated with the seventh consciousness arises spontaneously, as a single class, and continues in a constant succession, it therefore possesses only...
It is the grasping at a self; there is no further grasping at "mine.

One should understand this intention: it takes only the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) as its object, and not other [parts such as the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), seeds, or mental factors].

Because that [seeing-part of the eighth consciousness] has been subtle from beginningless time, continuing as a single homogeneous stream without interruption, it appears to be permanent and unitary; thus, it is always associated with all phenomena.

Because it serves as the basis [for the notion of "mine"], this seventh consciousness merely grasps the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving portion) of that eighth consciousness as its internal self (*ātman*).

Although the treatises state only this much, the expression "mine" (*mamakāra*) is used here by virtue of the force of the discourse. Alternatively, this seventh consciousness grasps that [eighth consciousness] as "the self of my self," thereby taking the grasper itself to be the self.
Because that which is grasped is taken as "mine," the two terms "self" and "mine" are explained in terms of meaning with reference to the single view of self. If one were to speak in this way:

This is well in accord with the principles of the teachings, for in many places it is stated that the seventh consciousness possesses only the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); furthermore, the two types of grasping—the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) and the grasping at what belongs to a self (*ātmīya-grāha*)—never arise simultaneously.

Because it is continuous, it appears as if permanent; because it is of a single class and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it appears as if unitary. This concludes the first explanation regarding the basis of the non-transformed state.
△ Second, the explanation of the transformed basis:

(However, the seventh consciousness) in the stage prior to transformation takes only the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) of the *ālaya-vijñāna* as its object. Once the transformation of the basis has occurred, it also takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its object.

Because the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) realizes ten kinds of equality, it knows the differences in the inclinations (*adhimukti*) of sentient beings and manifests various images of the Buddha.
This verse refers, for the time being, to the period before the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*);

therefore, it speaks only of this [wisdom] taking that storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its object. This is because the principle governing the commonality and particularity of awakening and delusion ought to be thus.
There is neither self nor the object of a self, because they are either pervasive or non-pervasive.
As for the ten kinds of equality: first, the equality of supreme delight in all marks; second, the equality of all experiences and dependent origination;
third, the equality of being free from distinct marks and the absence of marks; fourth, the great compassion that extensively rescues and aids others.
1. Equality. 2. Equality of great compassion that does not depend on others. 3. Equality in manifesting according to the inclinations of all sentient beings.
4. Equality in being revered and loved by all sentient beings in their speech. 5. Equality in which both the mundane and the tranquil are of one single flavor. 6.
Equality in which all mundane phenomena—suffering and pleasure—are of one single flavor. 7. Equality in cultivating and planting [roots of merit] without...
The measure of merit is ultimately equal. Within this, one realizes ten types of equality, which explains the meaning of taking *tathatā* (suchness) as the object.
Knowing the differences in the inclinations (*adhimukti*) of all sentient beings explains the meaning of taking other phenomena as objects.
Because the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) is awakening, its objects of focus are universal; because the afflicted manas is delusion, its objects of focus—

This is restricted. Because the Wisdom of Equality takes the realm of selflessness as its object, its object is all-pervasive, universally encompassing both *tathatā* (suchness) and all other phenomena.

Because the defiled *manas* takes the realms of self and phenomena as its objects, its object is not pervasive; it is exclusively the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness and nothing else.
The initial formal explanation is concluded. △ Second, the resolution of objections.
(Question: How is it that this seventh consciousness takes its own support—the eighth consciousness—as its object? (Answer: It is like a subsequent moment of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Since it is already fully established that the preceding moment of mind—which has already ceased—is the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the subsequent consciousness and thus serves as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), what fault could there be in asserting that this [storehouse consciousness], which is the supporting basis (*āśraya*), likewise functions as an object-condition? Furthermore, what objection can be raised?
The third section, explaining the gate of the object-condition (*ālambana*), is concluded. △ Fourth, the explanation of the two gates of nature (*svabhāva*) and aspect (*ākāra*).
The verse states that "reflection (*manana*) is its nature and aspect. This simultaneously reveals the self-nature and the mental aspect of this consciousness.
This is because reflection is taken as its self-nature, and it further employs that very reflection as its mental aspect. By means of this, the designation "manas" is also explained concurrently.

It is given this distinct name because it is able to engage in precise deliberation; thus, it is called *manas*. In the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), it is able to precisely deliberate upon the characteristics of the grasped self;
in the stage after the transformation of the basis, it likewise precisely deliberates upon the characteristic of non-self.
△ Fifth, the section explaining the concomitance with defilements.
This [manas] is associated with how many mental factors? Briefly stated, it is always concomitant with four types of afflictions.

Herein, the term "concomitant" (sahita/samprayukta) signifies the meaning of association. That is to say, from beginningless time until the transformation of the basis has not yet occurred, this manas functions spontaneously and constantly.
It is based on the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and is associated with four root afflictions. What are these four?
They are self-delusion, self-view, self-pride, and self-love; these are called the four kinds.
Furthermore, before revealing the rest, we first clarify the faults of this [notion of] self.

"My delusion" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*); it denotes being deluded regarding the mark of a self (which is a transformation of one's own mind) and being confused about the principle of selflessness (*anātman*, which is *tathatā*).

Therefore, it is called self-delusion (*ātma-moha*). Regarding self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*): this refers to the grasping at a self; it is the false conceptualization of a self upon that which is not a self or a dharma—namely, the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness.
Therefore, it is called self-view. Regarding self-pride (*ātma-māna*): this refers to arrogance; relying on the self one has grasped, it causes the mind to become haughty.

Therefore, it is called "self-pride" (*asmimāna*). "Self-love" (*ātmasneha*) refers to self-greed (*ātmatṛṣṇā*); because one develops a deep attachment toward the grasped self, it is called self-love (as stated in the verse).

The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that pride and love can coexist with views; it also shows that pride can coexist with love. This excludes the position held by other schools—that views, love, and pride lack the quality of association (*samprayoga*).
These four [afflictions] constantly arise to disturb and cloud the internal mind, causing the external evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) to function [in a defiled manner].

[The afflictions] such as giving and so forth are always associated with defilement. Sentient beings revolve in the cycle of birth and death because of these, and are unable to escape; therefore, they are called "afflictions" (*kleśa*).
This correctly explains the characteristics of the four afflictions and reveals their faults. "Inner mind" refers specifically to the seventh [consciousness].
Consciousness (*vijñāna*). "External evolving consciousness" refers to the first six consciousnesses.

Because the seventh consciousness falsely gives rise to self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), self-pride (*ātma-māna*), and self-love (*ātma-tṛṣṇā*), it causes the various practices of the five perfections to be unable to forget signs (*nimitta*), thereby resulting entirely in outflows (*sāsrava*).
For this reason, it is called "defiled" (*saṃkleśa*). If one wishes to transcend saṃsāra, one must first diligently contemplate non-self (*anātman*). However, as for this seventh consciousness—

The innate self-grasping (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*) is subtle and difficult to sever; it must first employ the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*) together with its associated primary mental factor of correct wisdom (*samyag-prajñā-citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*).

By relying on the teachings and principles of the Mahāyāna, one must observe reality as it is (*yathābhūta-pratyavekṣā*), so that the seeds of the correct understanding of non-self (*anātma-samyag-dṛṣṭi-bīja*) gradually permeate and become firmly established.
Only when these reach the stage of maturation will untainted, actual wisdom (*anāsrava-bhūtajñāna*) manifest before one. Furthermore,
One must repeatedly and diligently cultivate this very untainted, true wisdom; only then can the four seeds of affliction be permanently severed.
Nowadays, people speak at once of the six perfections and myriad practices, yet they never apply their minds to the gateways for destroying the grasping at phenomena.
Is it not difficult, then, to seek liberation from saṃsāra? Question: Since it is by means of the seventh [consciousness] that the first six consciousnesses are brought about...
It is constantly accompanied by affliction (*saṃkleśa*). Logically, one must directly employ the seventh consciousness to cultivate the contemplation of non-self (*anātman-vipaśyanā*);

only then will it be like cauterizing a disease at its correct point or felling a tree at its root. Why, then, is the sixth consciousness employed first? The answer is: because of the ego-grasping (*ātma-grāha*) of the seventh consciousness.
Since the former is fundamentally conditioned and perfumed by the sixth consciousness, the sixth consciousness remains the locus of the disease and the root of the tree.

This is even more so for the seventh consciousness; from beginningless time until the stage of non-transformation, it is consistently comprised within the nature of obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta), and does not associate with wholesome mental factors such as faith. Furthermore, it lacks desire, resolve, mindfulness, and meditative concentration.

How could one be able to personally cultivate the contemplation of non-self? Therefore, when we resolve upon the Mahāyāna mind, we must first develop deep faith and understanding regarding the characteristics and nature of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
Only then, by cultivating the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*), can it be called the "factor conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
Otherwise, even if one cultivates various practices, they will merely be the causes for the out-flowing karma of humans and devas.
[End. (Question:
Those [fundamental afflictions] are of ten kinds; why are there only four [associated with this consciousness]? (Answer:

Because of the presence of the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the other four views—the two types of grasping, the extreme view, and the false view—do not arise, for two cognitions cannot coexist within a single moment of mind.
The following section consists of questions and answers that resolve doubts. Since all views (*dṛṣṭi*) have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence, they do not arise simultaneously. [Question:

Why does this consciousness necessarily possess the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) rather than other types of views? [Answer: The two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) and false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) arise solely from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*);

they belong exclusively to what is abandoned by the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*). The afflictions associated with this [seventh consciousness] are exclusively innate (*sahaja*) and are necessarily present.

Because it is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there is no [clinging to] a self or what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*), nor is there the false view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) consisting of the two views of annihilationism and eternalism;

these all arise based on the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). The view of a self associated with this seventh consciousness does not arise based on those [views of] a self, what belongs to a self, or the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism;

therefore, there is no clinging to a self or what belongs to a self, nor the view of extremes. Because it constantly grasps at an internal self, the view of a self must necessarily exist. Since the view of a self is thoroughly determined, there is no room for doubt.
Because one gives rise to attachment to a self, hatred cannot arise. Therefore, the afflictions associated with this consciousness are only four.

[Question: How can the three—view, pride, and attachment—arise together? [Answer: There is no contradiction in their modes of activity (*ākāra*); what fault is there in their arising together? [Question again:

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that greed causes the mind to sink, while pride causes the mind to uplift; how can these not be contradictory? [Answer: This refers to the distinction between conceptualized (*vikalpita*) and innate (*sahaja*) [afflictions].
Regarding external objects and internal objects, those that are overcome and those that are relied upon, there is a distinction between the coarse and the subtle;

therefore, the texts concerning these two do not contradict one another in meaning. That is to say, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* refers to the afflictions of discrimination associated with the sixth consciousness that crave external objects and overpower external persons;
because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are coarse, they cannot arise simultaneously. This verse from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, however, refers to...
The innate afflictions associated with the seventh consciousness crave internal objects and rely upon the internal self;
because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are subtle, they do not contradict one another. The fifth section, the explanation of the gate of association with defilement, is concluded.

△ Sixth, the explanation of the gate of other associations, in two parts: first, those prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); second, those after the transformation of the basis. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the direct explanation of the meaning of the verse; second...

Next, the meaning of "reception" (*vedanā*) is discussed. This section also has two parts: first, the question-and-answer presentation of the verse; second, the detailed explanation of the verse’s meaning. Now, the first part. (Question:

Are there only these four mental factors (*caitta*) associated with this mind? (Answer: No. (The verse says: "And because it is accompanied by other [factors] such as contact (*sparśa*) and so forth."

△ Second, the detailed explanation of the meaning of the verses has two parts: first, one school [asserts] that there are no mental factors (*caitta*) other than these; second, four schools [assert] that there are other mental factors. Now, for the first:

according to one interpretation, these mental factors of the *manas* are only nine: the four previously mentioned, plus the remaining five dharmas, namely contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), and so forth. That is to say, contact and attention.
Feeling, perception, and volition—because the mind and the universal mental factors are necessarily associated [with them].

Since the previous verse stated that contact and so forth coexist with the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), there is a concern that these [factors] might likewise be considered "unobscured-neutral" (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) as before. To distinguish these [mental factors associated with the seventh consciousness] from those associated with the eighth, the word "the rest" (*śeṣa*) is placed [in the verse].
Furthermore, the particle "and" (*ca*) carries the sense of "aggregation. Thus, the four preceding and the five succeeding factors together constitute the mental factors associated with the manas.

[Question: Because it is always associated [with mental factors]. [Question: For what reason does this manas lack other mental factors? [Answer: It is because desire (*chanda*) is the aspiration for an object not yet attained;
this seventh consciousness spontaneously takes as its object an already attained state and has no such aspiration. Therefore, it lacks desire.

Resolve (*adhimokṣa*, a mental factor): This consists of the firm grasping of an object not previously determined. Since this seventh consciousness has, from beginningless time, constantly taken a fixed object as its range and is perpetually sustained by that [grasping], it lacks resolve.

Mindfulness (*smṛti*, a mental factor): This consists solely of the recollection of things previously experienced. Since this seventh consciousness constantly takes as its range objects currently being experienced and has nothing to recollect, it lacks mindfulness.

Concentration (*samādhi*, a mental factor): This consists solely of binding the mind to focus one-pointedly on a single object. [Since this consciousness does not so bind itself, it lacks concentration.]
Regarding the object: this seventh consciousness spontaneously and momentarily perceives distinct objects. Since it does not focus on a single [object], it lacks fixity.

That is to say, when this seventh consciousness takes that eighth [consciousness] as its object, both the perceiving subject and the perceived object are entirely subject to momentary arising and ceasing;
what precedes does not resemble what follows, and what follows does not resemble what precedes.

Wisdom (a mental factor) is itself the view of self; therefore, it is not mentioned separately. Because the wholesome [eleven mental factors] are pure, they do not coexist with this defiled consciousness.
The arising of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) necessarily depends on the temporal distinctions of the states of the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).

Since this consciousness is always associated with the four root afflictions, which remain of one kind before and after without distinction in their state, there are no secondary afflictions coexisting with this consciousness.

Afflictions (*kleśa*). Remorse (*kaukṛtya*, a mental factor) is the regret for actions previously committed. This seventh consciousness spontaneously and constantly takes the present object as its domain.

It does not repent of prior karma; therefore, there is no *kaukṛtya* (remorse). Sleep (*middha*) necessarily depends upon the heaviness and dullness of body and mind, and arises only temporarily through the power of external conditions.
This seventh consciousness has, from beginningless time, been a single type of internal grasping that does not rely on external conditions; therefore, sleep does not exist in this consciousness.
Vitarka and vicāra (the two mental factors of applied and sustained thought) both function by way of the external gates, involving shallow or deep investigation and coarse or subtle discernment.
It is said: this (seventh) consciousness functions solely by way of the internal door; because it is of a single type that clings to a self, it is not associated with those (vitarka and vicāra).

Taking the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) and other such spheres as its object is called the "external gate" (*bāhyamukha*). Taking the seeing-division (*darśanabhāga*) of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its object is called the "internal gate" (*adhyātmamukha*).
Superficial investigation and coarse verbal expression is termed "vitarka" (*vitarka*). Profound investigation and subtle verbal expression is termed "vicāra" (*vicāra*).
Next, among the four schools, there are two remaining mental factors (*caitasika*). First, the refutation of the preceding [view] and the general presentation; second, the four schools.
An alternative interpretation. First, regarding the initial point:

there is a view that his explanation of the remaining [syllables] is irrational. This is because the verse separately states that this [seventh category] is subsumed under the "obscured-unspecified" (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) nature.
Furthermore, it would lack the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) concomitant with the mind; for primary afflictions must necessarily be accompanied by secondary afflictions.
Therefore, the other [single] word in this verse (is precisely correct), as it reveals the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
△ Second, the distinct interpretations of the four schools; the fourth school is the correct one. Now, first, the interpretation of the initial school.
Regarding this, there is an interpretation that five secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are universally associated with all defiled minds. As stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*:
torpor (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), and heedlessness (*pramāda*) are always associated with all categories of defilement;
for it would be impossible for something to be defiled if it were devoid of these five factors, such as unserviceability (*akarmanyatā*). [End of] Afflictions.
At the time of arising, since the mind is already defiled, in the state of a defiled mind there must necessarily be those five [factors].
If an affliction arises, it must do so by virtue of lack of pliancy (*akarmaṇyatā*), agitation (*auddhatya*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), and heedlessness (*pramāda*).

Although agitation (*auddhatya*) pervades all defiled minds, it is particularly intense in the state of greed (*lobha*); therefore, in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it is described as being a derivative of greed. This is similar to how sleep (*middha*) and regret (*kaukṛtya*), although...
Although these [factors] pervade the minds of all three natures (*trisvabhāva*), because they are predominant in the state of delusion (*moha*), they are described as being divisions of delusion.
Lack of functional capacity is *styāna* (sloth); agitation is *auddhatya* (restlessness). The rest may be understood accordingly.

Although other passages in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* state that there are either six or ten secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) that pervade all defiled minds, those [passages] describe them as pervasive based on specific meanings;
it is not the case that these [six or ten] actually pervade all defiled minds.

That is to say, among the twenty secondary afflictions, [the six] are understood to apply to both the coarse [afflictions arising from] conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) and the subtle [afflictions arising] simultaneously with birth (*sahaja*), while [the ten] apply to both the obscured (*nivṛta*) and the neutral (*avyākṛta*).
The unwholesome [factors] (akuśala) can also universally obstruct concentration and wisdom; because their characteristics are thus manifest, six [types] are taught.

Furthermore, among the twenty-two secondary afflictions (upakleśa), they are explained as being pervasive across both the coarse [conceptual] and subtle [innate] [afflictions], and because they encompass both the two natures of the unwholesome and the obscured-unneutral (nivṛtāvyākṛta).

It is said that [these ten] "pervade all defiled minds. Therefore, these five secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) mentioned here [are distinct from] those two categories—the six universal [mental factors] and the ten pervasive ones—each being explained according to different meanings;

they are not mutually contradictory. However, there are fifteen mental factors associated with this [defiled] mind: namely, the nine aforementioned dharmas, the five secondary afflictions, and the wisdom (*prajñā*) of the object-specific category.
Although the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is subsumed under the wisdom of the object-specific category, within the fifty-one mental factors, its specific meaning [is as follows]:
Because they are differentiated, they are divided into two:
the twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), which consist of the two from among the "ten minor" and the eight from among the "great" [afflictions], as will be explained in detail below.
"Understanding" refers to the mode of activity (*ākāra*). Regarding the "twenty-two," this includes the addition of wrong desire and wrong resolve. As for the distinction in meaning:
the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is exclusively defiled, whereas wisdom (*prajñā*) encompasses both the defiled and the pure. The rest may be understood accordingly.

(Question: For what reason does this mind lack other mental factors? (Answer: It is because the ten types of minor derivative [afflictions], such as anger and so forth, have coarse and agitated modes of activity.

This seventh consciousness is subtle and refined; therefore, it does not coexist with those [minor derivative afflictions]. Among the two types of "lack of shame" (*āhrīkya*) and "lack of dread" (*anapatrāpya*), these are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*), whereas this [seventh consciousness] is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
It is not associated with those [major derivative afflictions], such as "distraction" (*vikṣepa*), which causes the mind to wander toward external objects;

rather, this [seventh consciousness] constantly arises by internally grasping the single category of the object that is the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, and thus does not wander externally.

Therefore, that [state of distraction] does not exist in this consciousness. Regarding "lack of clear comprehension" (*asaṃprajanya*), it refers to the arising of physical, verbal, and mental activities directed toward external objects that transgress established norms;
since this [seventh consciousness] is exclusively an internal grasping, it does not coexist with that [lack of clear comprehension]. There are no other mental factors [associated with it].
The meaning is as previously explained.
△ Second school’s interpretation:
There is an interpretation that one should state there are six secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) that are universally associated with all defiled minds. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
Lack of faith, laziness, heedlessness, forgetfulness, distraction, and faulty wisdom are associated with all defiled states of mind.
If forgetfulness, distraction, and faulty wisdom were absent, the mind would necessarily be unable to give rise to the various afflictions;

for it is only by taking as an object a category of previously experienced phenomena that one gives rise to forgetfulness and erroneous discernment, which in turn give rise to the afflictions such as craving.
When afflictions arise, the mind necessarily wanders, all because of the occurrence of distraction (*vikṣepa*) toward objects.

This [distraction] consists of three mental factors: forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), and unwholesome wisdom (*dausprajñā*). Erroneous discernment is, in fact, unwholesome wisdom.
Lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) are mutually contradictory in their modes of activity; thus, they cannot arise universally in all defiled minds.

When the treatises state that five factors are universal to defiled minds, this refers to [the fact that] their functions extend to both coarse and subtle levels, and they oppose only wholesome factors.

Furthermore, because these pure secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) pertain to both the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) natures, the *Yogācārabhūmi* speaks of ten universals. The meaning is as previously explained.

This generally clarifies that restlessness (*auddhatya*) and lethargy (*styāna*) are mutually exclusive. The subsequent discussion in the treatise, beginning with "The treatise says," allows for the resolution of potential objections.

However, these nineteen mental factors associated with the mind consist of the nine previously mentioned dharmas, the six secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), along with mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and [the factor] similar to lethargy.
This separate mention of mindfulness follows the previous explanation of wisdom; and as for the inclusion of concentration, it refers to the one-pointed focus upon a single category.
Because the object of the grasped self has never been abandoned, and because it is accompanied by torpor (*styāna*), this consciousness is associated with particularly heavy ignorance;
since the mind is torpid, there is no restlessness (*auddhatya*), as that is directly contrary to this [torpor], nor are there any other mental factors (*caitta*).
It should be understood as above.
Here, mindfulness (*smṛti*) and concentration (*samādhi*) are added, which excludes restlessness (*auddhatya*).

Regarding this separate explanation of mindfulness—following the previous explanation of wisdom—it means that although forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*) has mindfulness itself as its substance, there is a distinction in their meanings. △ Third.
Commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa*.
There is an interpretation that further states there are ten secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) that are universally associated with all defiled minds. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

heedlessness (*pramāda*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), lethargy (*styāna*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), wrong desire (*mithyā-chanda*), wrong resolve (*mithyā-adhimokṣa*), wrong mindfulness (*mithyā-smṛti*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), and [wrong concentration].
These ten are present in all defiled minds, as they pervade all locations and are bound to the three realms.
If there were no wrong desire (*mithyā-chanda*) or wrong resolve (*mithyā-adhimokṣa*), the mind could not give rise to the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
This is because one must first find pleasure in union with or separation from an object, and apprehend its characteristics, before greed and other afflictions can arise.
"Wrong thought" (*vitarka*) is, in this context, forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*). "Improper awareness" (*asamprajanya*) is, in this context, unwholesome wisdom (*daurprajña*).

Regarding the phrase "toward the objects experienced," etc.: this refers to desirable objects. Toward such [objects], wrong desire is the longing for union; toward undesirable objects, wrong desire is the longing for separation.

Furthermore, one determines and confirms the characteristics of a desirable thing through wrong view, and only then does greed arise. One confirms the characteristics of an undesirable thing... [and so forth].
When one perceives an object as attractive, it is precisely at that moment that aversion arises.

Those who harbor doubts regarding principles have no hesitation whatsoever concerning objective phenomena such as form; therefore, a mind associated with doubt must also possess (a form of) distorted resolve (*mithyādhimokṣa*).
Furthermore, that which involves hesitation even toward an objective referent is not the "doubt" (*vicikitsā*) among the afflictions, just like [ordinary] uncertainty.

The "human stump" (a person who is like a tree stump) is not designated as an affliction (*kleśa*). Other sources do not state that these two mental factors—*mithyā-chanda* (wrong desire) and *mithyā-adhimokṣa* (wrong resolve)—are universal (*sarvatraga*) to all defiled minds.

This is because *mithyā-chanda* directed toward unpleasant objects and the *mithyā-adhimokṣa* associated with doubt are both subtle; they are not coarse afflictions and are therefore omitted [from the list of universals], though they are not entirely absent.

Regarding other sources which state that there are either five or six secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), their mutual presence or absence is to be understood according to the principle explained above.
This explains the objection that false resolve (*mithyādhimokṣa*) does not pervade all defiled minds. The objection states:
"Resolve has the nature of maintaining a conviction regarding a determined object, whereas doubt has the nature of hesitation; these two are contradictory.

How, then, can false resolve pervade all defiled minds? The answer states: "Those who doubt the principles, although they harbor uncertainty regarding the principles of the Truths (*satya*), [nevertheless...]"
Regarding objects such as form (*rūpa*), there is necessarily no doubt; therefore, they can still be associated with resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).

Even if one has doubt regarding an object, it is not termed an affliction (*kleśa*); thus, when there is doubt about an object, although there is no resolute conviction, erroneous resolute conviction (*mithyā-adhimokṣa*) does not preclude its association with the affliction of doubting the principle. The rest may be understood accordingly.

These mental factors associated with the manas are twenty-four. That is to say, the nine aforementioned dharmas, the ten secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the five object-specific factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa*).
All should be explained according to the principles established in the preceding text. It should be understood that there are no other mental factors [associated with the manas], as stated above.
△ The Fourth School’s Correct Interpretation.

There is an interpretation stating that all previous explanations have failed to exhaust the principle. Furthermore, when one doubts whether a future life exists or not, what characteristic of desire or resolve could there be therein?
(Therefore, perverse desire and resolve are not pervasive throughout all defiled minds. When afflictions arise, if there were no *styāna* (sloth), they would necessarily be indeterminate.
There is the faculty of lack of pliancy (*akarmaṇyatā*). If restlessness (*auddhatya*) were absent, there would be no agitation, and it would be like a virtuous state or other non-defiled states.
If there were no distraction (*vikṣepa*) within a defiled mind, it would not be a wandering mind; thus, it would not be a defiled state of mind.

Furthermore, if there were neither loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*) nor lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*), how could afflictions arise and manifest? Therefore, in all defiled minds, these [factors] are necessarily present.

It arises in association with eight kinds of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*): namely, torpor (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), heedlessness (*pramāda*), forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), and lack of correct awareness (*asamprajanya*).
Regarding forgetfulness and lack of correct awareness—if these two are considered to have mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as their intrinsic nature—they do not pervade all defiled minds.
Why is this? Because it is not the case that all defiled minds involve the discernment (*vivecana*) of what has been previously experienced.
If [forgetfulness and lack of clear comprehension] have ignorance as their intrinsic nature, they must arise as universal defilements of the mind;
for it was previously stated that if there were no loss of mindfulness and lack of clear comprehension, how could afflictions arise?
Not all defiled minds take previously experienced objects as their cognitive object; therefore, forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), which has mindfulness as its intrinsic nature, is not universal.

Not all defiled minds possess discernment; therefore, incorrect awareness (*asamprajanya*), which has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its intrinsic nature, is not universal. The rest may be understood accordingly.

However, these eighteen mental factors associated with this [manas] consist of the nine previously mentioned dharmas, the eight secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the wisdom (*prajñā*) of the object-specific category (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa*).

There are no other mental factors; this should be explained in accordance with the three passages from the treatise (*śāstra*) cited earlier. If one explains it in this way, it does not contradict either reason or scripture.

The treatise cites three passages: namely, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* explains five pervasive [factors] in defiled minds, while the *Yogācārabhūmi* explains six pervasive factors and ten pervasive factors in defiled minds.
These should be interpreted according to the preceding [analysis], which is precisely the explanation for the passage concerning their pervasion of the coarse and the subtle.

This concludes the initial formal explanation of the meaning of the verse regarding the second transformative consciousness, within the section on the gate of association (*saṃprayoga*) prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

△ Second, the analogy for the meaning of feeling (*vedanā*).
With which feelings is this afflicted manas associated?

Since the second transformation has already been explained through the sixth section on its association with other mental factors, [the text] further provides an analogy based on the first transformation.

This section discusses the gate of association with feeling (*vedanā*). First, a provisional question is raised to introduce the topic; below follow three interpretations, of which the third is considered correct.

One interpretation holds that this [seventh consciousness] is associated only with the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*), because it constantly grasps the *sākṣin-bhāga* (perceiving portion) of the eighth consciousness as "self," thereby giving rise to a sense of joy and attachment. Another interpretation maintains that this is not so;
for if it were as stated, one would have to admit that the feeling of joy exists even up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), which contradicts the teachings of the Noble Ones (*ārya*).
Regarding this statement, the following meaning should be explained: [The first dhyāna] is associated with four types of feeling.

That is to say, when born in the evil destinies, it is associated with the feeling of sorrow (*daurmanasya*), because it is the result of maturation (*vipāka*) induced by unwholesome karma. When born in the human realm or the desire heavens (*kāmadhātu*), as well as in the first and second dhyānas, it is associated with the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*), because it is the result of maturation induced by wholesome karma belonging to stages where joy exists. In the third dhyāna, it is associated with the feeling of pleasure (*sukha*).
It is associated with pleasure because it is the result of maturation (vipāka-phala) induced by wholesome karma directed toward stages possessing pleasure.

From the fourth dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), it is associated with equanimity because it is the result of maturation induced by wholesome karma directed exclusively toward stages of equanimity.

The Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) refers to the summit of the three realms of existence; it is the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). The rest may be understood accordingly.

There is another interpretation which holds that this [explanation] is also illogical. This seventh consciousness, from beginningless time, spontaneously and uniformly takes the internal as its object and clings to it as "self.
It is eternally without fluctuation, and because it is dissociated from changing sensations (*vipariṇāma-vedanā*), this *manas* is merely...

Regarding the distinctions in the meaning of the *ālayavijñāna* mentioned previously (in the verses), these have all been explained separately. If there were four types of feeling (*vedanā*) associated with it, they too would have been explained separately (in the present verse).

Since they are not explained separately, it is certain that [this seventh consciousness] is identical to that (*ālayavijñāna*). Therefore, its association (*samprayoga*) is likewise [only of one kind].

There is only the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), which is the sensation of transformation—meaning the sensations of grief, joy, suffering, and pleasure that change and differ from one another. The rest may be understood.
This concludes the section on "not yet having transformed the basis" (*apravṛttāśraya*). 2. "Having already transformed the basis" (*parāvṛttāśraya*):
In the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), it is associated with the eighteen mental factors previously mentioned.

In the stage where the basis has already been transformed, it arises simultaneously with only twenty-one mental factors—namely, the five universal (*sarvatraga*) factors, the five object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*) factors, and the eleven wholesome (*kuśala*) factors.

This is because, like the eighth consciousness in its state of transformed basis, it is associated exclusively with the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*); it functions spontaneously and always operates with impartiality toward its objects.
The "Equal Transformation" refers to the Wisdom of Equality, which realizes the ten kinds of equality; it is also exclusively associated with the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
This concludes the sixth section, the Explanation of the Remaining Correspondence Gates. △ Seventh, the Explanation of the Three Natures Gate.

(Question: By what nature are the mental factors (*caitta*) of the *manas* subsumed? (Answer: They are subsumed under the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), and not by others [such as the wholesome, the unwholesome, or the non-obscured-unspecified].
This is because the four afflictions and so forth associated with this mind are defiled phenomena; they obstruct the Noble Path and conceal one's own mind, and are therefore termed "obscured.
Since they are neither wholesome nor unwholesome, they are called "unspecified" (*avyākṛta*). (Question: If these are afflictions, why are they not unwholesome?

Answer: As stated above, the seeds of the various afflictions and so forth belonging to the two realms are gathered and stored by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), such that they do not manifest as active states (*pravṛtti*).

These are subsumed under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). This is because the consciousness upon which these concomitant afflicted dharmas rely is extremely subtle, lacks strong conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and functions spontaneously (*svarasa-vāhin*).
It is also subsumed under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). If the basis has been transformed (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), it is exclusively of a wholesome nature (*kuśala*).
8. Explanation of the Section on Realm-Binding (*dhātu-bandhana*):
(Question: To which realm is the mental factor (*caitta*) of the manas bound? (Answer: It is bound to whichever realm that [storehouse consciousness] from which it arises belongs.
This means that for one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the mental factors associated with the manifest *manas* are bound to the desire realm.

This should be understood to apply likewise up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Spontaneously and constantly taking the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) of its own level as its object, it clings to it as an internal self;

this is because it does not take other levels as its object. If the matured storehouse consciousness (*vipākālayavijñāna*) of another level manifests before one, one is said to be "born" in that level. [The *manas*] is defiled.
The manas, even as it takes that [ālayavijñāna] as its object, clings to it as the "self. Thus, it is bound to that [ālayavijñāna], and is therefore called "bound to it."

Alternatively, being bound by the afflictions and so forth of that stage is called "being bound to that [stage]. If one has already undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), then one is no longer bound.
"That stage" refers to any one of the nine stages within the three realms. Alternatively, it refers to being [bound] by the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) of that stage.

"Bound" (*baddha*) is explained in terms of the sense of being an object-condition (*ālambana*). Alternatively, "bound by the afflictions of that stage" is explained in terms of the sense of association (*samprayoga*).
△ Ninth, the explanation of the gate of subduing and severing has two parts: first, the formal elucidation of the undefiled *manas*;
second, the further clarification of the pure *manas*. Now, the first part.
(Question: This afflicted manas (*kliṣṭamanas*) has continued in succession since beginningless time. In what state is it permanently severed, or is it only temporarily severed? (Answer:

It does not exist in the Arhat, in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), or on the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*). "Arhat" here generally indicates the stage of the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣaphala*) for all three vehicles.

In this stage, both the seeds and the active manifestations of the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) are permanently severed and extinguished; therefore, it is said that [the afflicted mind] does not exist.

(If it were to exist,) in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), when entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and during supramundane paths (*lokottara-mārga*) involving untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-bhāvanā*), both are temporarily suppressed and extinguished; for this reason as well, it may be said that [the afflicted mind] does not exist.
This refers to the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭa-manas*). Since beginningless time, it has functioned as a subtle, uniform, and spontaneous stream.

Although the various mundane paths with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*), even when virtuous, cannot suppress or extinguish the grasping at a self associated with this consciousness, the supramundane path of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna-anāsrava-mārga*) possesses the capacity to suppress and extinguish it.

This is because the fundamental understanding of true selflessness (*bhūta-nairātmya-adhigama*) can contradict that grasping at a self; thus, the supramundane subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) manifests.

At that time, it is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of that [fundamental realization of true selflessness], and it also contradicts this afflicted manas, because both the realization of true selflessness and the subsequently attained wisdom are untainted (*anāsrava*) paths; thus, they are both termed "supramundane paths" (*lokottaramārga*).

Furthermore, since the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is the outflow of the noble path and is characterized by extreme tranquility, this afflicted manas is likewise temporarily non-existent [during its occurrence]. However, upon emerging...

Because the seeds of this [defiled mind] have not yet been permanently severed, once one has emerged from the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) or the supramundane noble path, this [defiled manas] manifests again.
It continues to function in a constant succession throughout the stage until it is extinguished.

Furthermore, because the afflictions associated with this defiled manas are innate (*sahaja*), they are not abandoned by the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*); and because they are defiled, they are not [abandoned by the Path of Meditation].

Because these afflictions associated with the defiled *manas* are extremely subtle, all their seeds are abandoned instantaneously at one time along with the lowest-of-the-low (*mṛdumṛdu*) afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), since their potencies are equal; this occurs precisely when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) manifests.
By suddenly severing these seeds, one becomes an Arhat; thus, this is attained only at the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). [Regarding those] who never again give rise [to such afflictions]:

as for those of the two vehicles who have reached the stage of no-more-learning and turn toward the Mahāyāna, although they are in fact Bodhisattvas from the moment they first resolve [for enlightenment] until they attain Buddhahood, [they are not yet called so].
It is also called *arhat* because its meaning—such as "worthy of offerings" (*arhat*) and so forth—is equivalent [to that of other stages]; thus, it is not mentioned separately.
Regarding the lowest-of-the-low afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), these refer to the extremely subtle innate greed, delusion, and pride within the sixth consciousness.
When categorized by the nine grades across the nine stages of the three realms, this constitutes the eighty-first. This is due to...
Because it is extremely subtle, its power of affliction is equal to that of the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*).
Its seeds cannot be severed except by the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).

However, since the innate afflictions within the sixth consciousness are divided into eighty-one grades, they are severed gradually grade by grade; such is not the case for the afflictions associated with this seventh consciousness.
It is because this subtle class [of consciousness] does not differentiate between the three realms or the nine stages that it is said to be "abandoned all at once" (*tunduan*).

Regarding this, there is one interpretation: the manas is associated exclusively with the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

There is another interpretation: that [previous] explanation contradicts both scripture and reasoning. This is because the sūtras state that the supramundane *manas* exists;
furthermore, when the *manovijñāna* is undefiled, it must necessarily have a co-arising, non-common support (*sahaja-asādhāraṇa-āśraya*), just as it does when it is defiled.
This is a general refutation of the preceding [position]. The Sūtras state that there is a supramundane manas, yet they deny its existence;
does this not contradict the scriptures? Furthermore, a defiled mental consciousness must necessarily have a supporting faculty (manas-indriya), yet they deny its existence;
does this not contradict reason? What is called "undefiled mental consciousness" refers precisely to the sixth pure consciousness associated with the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga).

Regarding the phrase "simultaneously arising and non-common support," this refers to the seventh mental faculty (manas). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The pure mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is the subject (*dharmin*).

It is necessarily accompanied by a pure *manas* as its simultaneously arising and non-common support; this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is subsumed under the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: like the mental consciousness when it is defiled.
The treatises state that the ālayavijñāna is invariably and always active in conjunction with one consciousness, namely the manas.
When the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) arises, it is active in conjunction with two: the mental consciousness and the manas.

If any one of the five sensory consciousnesses arises, it is active in conjunction with three. This continues until, at times, all five sensory consciousnesses arise simultaneously, in which case it is active in conjunction with seven.

The simultaneous transformation [of consciousnesses] is as clear as this. If you maintain that the seventh consciousness does not exist when one abides in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), then at that time the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) would have no accompanying consciousness;

thus, it would not be the case that consciousnesses always necessarily transform simultaneously with one another. Furthermore, when the sixth consciousness enters uncontaminated contemplation (*anāsrava-dhyāna*) and abides in the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), if the seventh consciousness were absent, then at that time the storehouse consciousness would be accompanied by only the sixth consciousness.
How, then, could it be said that "if the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises..."?

At that time, the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) necessarily functions together with these two. The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "Manas is always associated with the four afflictions; this is its defiled state.
Alternatively, when it reverses those associations and takes prideful elevation as its mode of activity, it becomes an equanimous mode of activity; this is its non-defiled state.

Thus, one should know that this manas is common to both the defiled and non-defiled states. If, based on the statement in the root treatise (*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*) that the state of an Arhat lacks the defiled manas, one were to conclude...

The seventh consciousness does not exist; for according to the treatise, one should abandon the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) at the stage of Arhatship, and [if that were so], the eighth would likewise not exist.

Since that [eighth] is not the case, how could this [seventh] be? Furthermore, various treatises state that by transforming the seventh consciousness, one attains the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).
Like the other wisdoms [such as the great perfect mirror and the wondrous observation], that [wisdom of equality] must certainly have a basis and associated mental factors.
If this [seventh] consciousness—the pure consciousness—did not exist, that [wisdom of equality] would likewise not exist;

for it is impossible for the dependent mental factor (the pure, untainted wisdom) to exist apart from its support (the mind-king). Furthermore, it cannot be said that this [wisdom of equality] depends upon the six evolving consciousnesses.
This is because it is permitted that the Buddhas constantly exercise the Wisdom of Equality (samatā-jñāna), which is like the Mirror-like Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) in its uninterrupted continuity.
This extensively clarifies the contradiction with the teachings.
Furthermore, if the seventh consciousness did not exist in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), that eighth consciousness would lack a simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*).

However, it must necessarily have such a support, because its nature is like that of other [sensory] consciousnesses (such as the visual consciousness, etc.), and also because it is like [the case of] one who has not yet realized the person (*pudgala*).
For one who has not yet realized selflessness (*pudgala-nairātmya*), the clinging to a self (*ātma-grāha*) persists constantly;

likewise, for one who has not yet realized the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), the clinging to a self in phenomena (*dharma-ātma-grāha*) must also persist constantly.
