If this seventh consciousness did not exist during these three states, upon what consciousness would that clinging to a self in phenomena depend?

It cannot be said that it depends on the eighth [consciousness], because that [eighth consciousness] lacks the mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā*) with which it is associated, and [the clinging to a self in phenomena] is itself a form of wisdom.

From this, one should believe that the noble path of the two vehicles and the meditative absorption of cessation [exist] within the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), and that this seventh consciousness functions constantly therein.
This is because they have not yet realized the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

Furthermore, in various treatises, the first five consciousnesses are used as homologous examples (*sādharmya*) to prove the existence of the seventh [mental faculty], which serves as the simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) for the sixth consciousness. If, at the time the noble path arises and during the stage of no-more-learning, the [pure] seventh...
The seventh [consciousness] would then serve as the support for the sixth; thus, both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*) established would be fallacious.

Alternatively, if it were argued that the five consciousnesses likewise lack a support (i.e., the five sense organs), then since the five consciousnesses must always have a support, the same should apply to the sixth as well.

This extensively clarifies the contradiction with reason. One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows: The eighth consciousness of the stage of no-more-learning is the subject (*dharmin*). It necessarily possesses a pure seventh consciousness as its co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*);
this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is of the nature of consciousness (*vijñānatva*). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: like the visual consciousness and so forth.

The selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) is the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). The selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Regarding the principle [stated] as "by means of the five common characteristics," it refers to the formal syllogism (pramāṇa) as follows: The subject (*dharmin*) is the sixth consciousness; the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it necessarily possesses the seventh mental faculty (*manas*) as its co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*).

The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is subsumed under the category of evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: just as the first five consciousnesses must take the five sense organs as their co-existent supports.
Now, if one were to claim that this applies to the noble paths of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), [the following would apply].

In that position, there would be the fault of the non-establishment of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇā-siddha*) regarding the thesis, because the seventh pure consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*) does not exist as the co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) for the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) associated with the sixth consciousness;

this is because a co-existent support is not necessarily present. Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) commits the fallacy of being "inconclusive due to commonality" (*sādhāraṇa-anaikāntika*), since the first six consciousnesses are all... [common].

Regarding the reason that [the sixth consciousness] is subsumed under the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), while the five consciousnesses necessarily have a support (*āśraya*), the sixth consciousness does not necessarily have a support in the untainted state (*anāsrava*).
Thus, the opponent raises the fault of indeterminacy (*aniyata-doṣa*), asking: "Is the sixth [consciousness] like the preceding five?"

Is there necessarily a basis at all times? Or, as in the case of the first five [consciousnesses] during the untainted state (*anāsrava*), is it not necessary for the sixth [consciousness] to have a basis as well?
This concludes the first section, which refutes the preceding errors. △ Second, the presentation of the correct principle.

Therefore, it is certain that there exists an undefiled mind (*anāsrava-manas*) which is constantly present during the three states mentioned above—the state of the cessation-attainment of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa-nirodhasamāpatti*) and the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*).

When the verse states that these [three states] do not exist, it is said with reference to the defiled mind (*kliṣṭamanas*); it is just as when it is said that the four states lack the *ālayavijñāna*, yet this does not mean the eighth consciousness is non-existent.
This case should be understood in the same way.

Those who lack the *ālayavijñāna* consist of four categories: the Arhats of the three vehicles and the Buddhas. This concludes the initial section, which correctly clarifies that while there is no defilement, there is purity.
△ Second, a general explanation of the distinctions between defilement and purity.
This differentiation of the manas consists briefly of three types: first, the manas associated with the view of a personal self (pudgala-ātman);
second, the manas associated with the view of a phenomenal self (dharma-ātman); and third, the manas associated with the wisdom of equality (samatā-jñāna).
The view of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*) is the innate grasping at a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*); the view of phenomena (*dharma-dṛṣṭi*) is the innate grasping at phenomena (*sahaja-dharma-grāha*).

The first (the [view] associated with the grasping at a self) pervades all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) throughout their continuum at all times, as well as those in training (*śaikṣa*) of the two vehicles up to the seventh stage.

Previously (with the exception of those who have turned their minds toward the stage of no-more-learning), a certain class of *śaikṣa* bodhisattvas (in the uncontaminated state do not manifest [the view of self];
however, in the state of a contaminated mind, that [mental consciousness] still takes the *ālayavijñāna* as its object and gives rise to the view of a personal self (*pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi*).

Next, regarding the mental consciousness associated with the grasping of phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), it is constant and continuous for all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas alike. As for all bodhisattvas, when the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena manifests before them—

At that time, it does not manifest. However, during the stage when the fruit of the wisdom of dharma-emptiness (*dharmanairātmya-jñāna-phala*) is not present before one, that [mental consciousness] still takes the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) as its object and gives rise to the view of a self in phenomena (*dharmātmadṛṣṭi*).

Later, [in the case of] the mental consciousness associated with the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*), which is common to all Tathāgatas and continues at all times, or for a Bodhisattva—during the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the first stage (*bhūmi*) and the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) following the first stage—when the fruit of the wisdom of dharma-emptiness is not manifesting, it likewise does not arise. Yet, regarding the fruit of the wisdom of dharma-emptiness...

In the stage of being present before one, that [mind] takes as its object either the stainless (pure consciousness), or the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), and so forth, giving rise to the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).

The Tathāgata’s wisdom of equality takes the immaculate consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*) as its object; the Bodhisattva’s wisdom of equality takes the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) as its object.
The rest may be understood accordingly.

At the stage when the view of a personal self (*pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) arises, the view of a self in phenomena (*dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) must also necessarily manifest; the grasping at a self must necessarily depend [upon it].
They arise from the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), just as at night one might mistake a tree stump for a person.

Therefore, although the functions of the two views—the view of a self (*ātman*) and the view of phenomena (*dharma*)—are distinct, they do not contradict one another, as they both rely upon the same wisdom (a mental factor), much like visual consciousness and other such cognitions.
Although their essence is one, they possess multiple functions, such as the discernment of blue, yellow, red, and so forth, without contradiction; this case should be understood in the same way.
The metaphors of the "deluded stump" and so forth illustrate the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). The metaphors of "persons" and so forth illustrate the clinging to a person (*pudgala-grāha*).

Regarding the section on "self and phenomena," this explains a potential objection. That is to say, an objection might be raised: "It was stated above that the clinging to 'I' and 'mine' (*ātma-ātmīya-grāha*) certainly do not arise simultaneously;
how, then, can the two views of self and phenomena (*ātma-dṛṣṭi* and *dharma-dṛṣṭi*) arise together here? Now, it is explained: although their functions differ, they do not [contradict one another].

This is not contradictory, because both [graspings] rely upon the same single wisdom (*jñāna*), and it is impossible for two distinct wisdoms to exist within a single moment of consciousness. Furthermore, an objection is raised:

"If there is only a single wisdom, how can there be two graspings? We now explain this: Just as a single visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) simultaneously discriminates blue and yellow, or as a single auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) hears a bell and a drum at once—how could this be contradictory?
One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows: The two graspings—the grasping of self (*ātman*) and the grasping of phenomena (*dharma*)—... [are simultaneous].

This is a formal argument (*dharmasādhana*). The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that [the two] are not contradictory. The reason (*hetu*) is: "because they both depend upon a single cognition (*buddhi*). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is:
"just as the substance of visual consciousness is one, yet it discerns many forms (*rūpa*)."

When the noble path or the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) manifests for those in training (*śaikṣa*) of the two vehicles; when the fruit of the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons manifests for bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment during the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*);

and for bodhisattvas of gradual enlightenment who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] when the fruit of the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons manifests—for these three types of individuals, there arises only the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), because their grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*) has already been suppressed by the noble path, the meditative absorption of cessation, and the fruit of the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons. This is not the case for those of the two vehicles who are beyond training...

In the case of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those who have turned their minds [from the Hīnayāna] toward this state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), when the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*) does not manifest, they likewise give rise only to the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), because their grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) has already been severed.
For all Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward—whether sudden or gradual—their grasping at a self never functions again;

it is either permanently severed (in the case of those who have turned their minds from the state of no-more-learning) or permanently suppressed (in the case of those who are sudden-awakened or those in training who have turned their minds).

Therefore, when the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*) has not yet manifested (even though one may be on the eighth bhūmi or above), one still gives rise to attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

This is because the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*) is not incompatible with attachment to phenomena. As a sūtra states: "From the eighth bhūmi upward, all afflictions (*kleśa*) no longer manifest;

there remains only the cognitive obstruction (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) which is the basis for the [attachment to] self. It should be understood that this cognitive obstruction is [the latent] seed, not the active manifestation (*pravṛtti*).
If it were not so, the seeds of affliction would not yet have been permanently severed, and [the storehouse consciousness] would also have to be called "present.

However, this [storehouse consciousness], which is associated with the mental faculty (*manas*) that clings to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), is termed "non-defiled" for the followers of the two vehicles and the like; yet for Bodhisattvas, it is also termed "defiled," because it correctly constitutes an obstruction to their wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
For this reason, it is also termed "obscured-unspecified" (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*); this is what is taught for the followers of the two vehicles and the like.

It is called "unobscured" (anivṛta) because it is associated with this dharma-grasping (*dharmanairātmya-saṃprayukta*) and does not obstruct that wisdom [of the emptiness of persons]. Furthermore, although this seventh consciousness is produced from and bound by the eighth, it is not the true *vipāka-vijñāna* itself;
rather, it is subsumed under what is "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*), because it arises at all times from the true *vipāka-vijñāna*.
It is called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*). [Question: One part of the first six consciousnesses that is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is called "born of maturation.
Why is this seventh consciousness also called "born of maturation"? [Answer: Because this name can be applied universally to include it;

for example, although the term "dominant condition" (*adhipatipratyaya*) properly refers to the six sense faculties, everything else not subsumed under the other three conditions is included within this category of the dominant condition. (The same applies here.)

The initial formal explanation of the verse text is concluded. △ Second, proving the existence of the seventh [consciousness] has three parts: first, a general introduction through question and answer;
second, a detailed exposition of the teachings and principles; third, a summary that resolves objections. Now, the first part.
(Question: How should one understand that this seventh consciousness has a distinct self-substance apart from the eye-consciousness and the others? (Answer:
Because the authoritative scriptures and correct reasoning serve as the definitive criteria.

△ Second, the specific explanation of the teachings and principles has two parts: first, the explanation of the sacred teachings; second, the revelation of correct reasoning. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, the direct explanation;
second, the reference to the extensive [commentaries]. Now, the first.
That is to say, the Bhagavat has explained the three distinct meanings of *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna* in various sūtras: that which accumulates and gives rise [to phenomena] is called *citta*;
that which cogitates is called *manas*; and that which discriminates is called *vijñāna*. These are the three distinct meanings.
"Bhagavān" refers to the World-Honored One (Bhagavat), which encompasses six meanings. The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* states:

Because all Tathāgatas are forever unbound by any afflictions, they possess the meaning of sovereignty (*vaśitva*). Because they have been refined and tempered by the fiercely blazing fire of wisdom, they possess the meaning of intensity (*tejas*).
Because they are adorned with the thirty-two excellent marks of a Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa*), they possess... [the meaning of beauty].
The meaning of being dignified and majestic: because there is nothing he does not know regarding the perfection of all supreme qualities.
The meaning of possessing renown: because he is approached and honored by all the world, who all praise him. The meaning of possessing auspiciousness:

because he possesses all virtues and constantly applies skillful means to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings without ever becoming weary or negligent. He is possessed of honor.
It values the ultimate meaning (*artha*). Because it is able to destroy the four Māra-enemies, it is called Bhagavat. According to the Hīnayāna, they do not understand these three distinct meanings;
they falsely reckon that the past is called *manas*, the present is called *vijñāna*, and the future is called *citta*.
Now, this is explained by means of the true meaning of the Mahāyāna.

Although these three meanings apply generally to all eight consciousnesses, they are manifested according to their predominant characteristics. The eighth is called *citta* (mind), because it gathers the seeds of all phenomena and gives rise to the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of all phenomena.

The seventh is called *manas* (intellect), because it takes the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and so forth as its object, constantly and thoroughly deliberating upon them as being "self" and "mine.
The remaining six are called *vijñānas* (consciousnesses), because they discern their respective objects within the six spheres of sensory experience, being coarse, active, and intermittent.

Because it evolves, as stated in the verses of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*: "The storehouse consciousness is called 'mind' (*citta*); that which has the nature of reflection is called 'intellect' (*manas*);
that which can cognize the characteristics of various objects is called 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*)."

Regarding the three meanings that apply to all eight consciousnesses: all eight are called *citta* (mind), because there are eight mind-kings (*cittarāja*), and each possesses the meaning of "accumulating and arising" (*saṃcita-utpāda*).

All eight are called *manas* (intellect), because each of the eight consciousnesses possesses the immediately preceding, extinguished consciousness as its *samanantara-manas*, and they all possess the meaning of "deliberation" (*manana*).
All eight are called *vijñāna* (consciousness), being termed the "eight consciousnesses," for each and every one possesses the function of "discernment" (*vijñapti*).

Therefore, regarding the manifestation according to what is predominant: the meaning of "accumulation" (*saṃcita*) is predominant in the eighth [consciousness]; the meaning of "reflection" (*manana*) is predominant in the seventh;
and the meaning of "cognizing objects" (*vijñapti*) is predominant in the first six.

As for those who take the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and so forth as a self through reflection, this includes all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), those on the paths of training (*śaikṣa*) among the two vehicles, and Bodhisattvas prior to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), with respect to the contaminated (*sāsrava*).
Regarding the state of mind: this seventh consciousness takes the ālayavijñāna as its object and constantly and thoroughly deliberates upon the *pudgala* as a self.

For those of the two vehicles and bodhisattvas, during the state of meditative absorption (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and when the fruit of the knowledge of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*) is present, this seventh consciousness takes the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) as its object and constantly and thoroughly deliberates upon the self of phenomena (*dharma-ātman*). For bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*), regarding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)...

At the stage when the fruits of wisdom are present before one, this seventh consciousness takes the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) as its object and constantly and thoroughly deliberates upon the two kinds of selflessness.
In the state of a Tathāgata, this seventh consciousness takes the stainless consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*) as its object and constantly and thoroughly deliberates upon the two kinds of selflessness.
Furthermore, Mahāyāna sūtras state in various places that there is a seventh consciousness; therefore, this seventh consciousness definitely exists as a distinct entity.
It has already been explained extensively previously (in the section on the first transformation), so it need not be established here again.
Moreover, the *Vimokṣa-sūtra* also separately mentions this seventh consciousness, as its verse says: "The defiled mind (*kliṣṭamanas*)."
At all times, the various afflictions arise and cease together [with it]. Once liberated from these afflictions, it neither existed in the past nor will it exist in the future.

That sutra itself explains the meaning of this verse as follows: there is a defiled mind that, from beginningless time, has always arisen and ceased simultaneously with four afflictions—namely, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), attachment to self (*ātma-sneha*), pride of self (*ātma-māna*), and ignorance of self (*ātma-moha*). When the path of antidote arises and the afflictions have been severed, this...
The mind then attains liberation from them. At that time, the afflictions associated with this mind do not merely cease to exist in the present;
they also do not exist in the present, past, or future, because all afflictions lack an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

If we consider this from the perspective of deluded consciousness, the single thought-moment of the present accumulates the seeds of immeasurable afflictions, karma, and suffering from the past, and is capable of giving rise to immeasurable affairs of afflictions, karma, and suffering in the future. However, the past has already ceased and the future has not yet arisen;
thus, only this single moment of mind can be said to possess substantiality. Yet, the substance of this mind shifts and flows from moment to moment, ever-new.
The new does not abide; how could it ever possess a substantial reality? It is based on this deluded mind that one falsely perceives the distinctions of the three periods of time.
If one is able to seek the mind and find it utterly unobtainable, then since the present itself is non-existent, how could the three periods of time exist?
Only by severing the three periods of time in a single sitting can one universally penetrate them. Furthermore, since the mind cannot be found...

It is attained. How could it have form, characteristics, directions, or boundaries? Only by its vanishing throughout the ten directions can it universally illuminate the ten directions. Therefore it is said:

"The lands of the dust motes and the realms of self and others are not separated by even a hair’s breadth; the ten ages of past and present, from beginning to end, do not depart from the present moment of thought.
This is what is meant by "neither past nor future existence. For this reason, that which is called "confrontation" [is as follows]:
The path of cultivation that eradicates afflictions is not like the mutual slaughter of worldly armies arrayed in opposing ranks to confront one another.
Rather, it is simply through the wisdom of the two emptinesses to deeply contemplate that afflictions fundamentally lack intrinsic nature;
since they do not arise from themselves, nor from others, nor from both together, nor without cause, they are merely the result of the harmony of causes and conditions.

[The interlocutor] says: "It is so. Though there is birth through delusion, at the very moment of this delusive birth, it does not exist within, nor does it exist without, nor does it exist in between.
It does not exist in the past, nor in the present, nor in the future. Birth is itself non-birth; ultimately, it has no self-nature (*svabhāva*).
Since self-nature is absent, how can there be other-nature (*parabhāva*)? Since both self and other are absent, how could there be common nature (*sabhāga*)?"

If even that which exists is difficult to obtain, how much more so that which arises without cause? Contemplate in this manner without ceasing. By understanding the perfuming of the seeds, the seeds of delusion will naturally vanish.
Thus, it is said in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* section of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: "Question: At the time of severing the afflictions..."

Is it for the sake of abandoning the *paryavasthāna* (active outbursts), or for abandoning the *anuśaya* (latent tendencies)? (*Paryavasthāna* refers to active manifestation; *anuśaya* refers to the seeds. Answer: One abandons only the *anuśaya*;
the *paryavasthāna* then ceases to arise. Question: Is it for the sake of severing the past, the future, or the present? Answer: It is not a severance of the past, future, or present;
yet it is said that there is severance across the three times. Why is this? Because if there were a mind with latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) in the past...
Because it ceases spontaneously, its nature is already severed; what further remains to be severed?
If there were a mind with latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) in the future, its nature would not yet have arisen; since its substance is non-existent, what could possibly be severed?

If there were a mind with latent dispositions in the present, its nature would necessarily not persist beyond that moment; what further need would there be for severance? Furthermore, regarding the presence of latent dispositions... [text ends]
The mind associated with latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and the [mind] that is not in conjunction are two distinct states; therefore, even in the present, the former is not what is to be abandoned.
Nevertheless, due to the two conditions of another’s intention and internal right attention (*manasikāra*), a mind associated with right view arises as the antidote to the afflictions it opposes.
When this [antidotal] mind arises and that [afflicted] mind ceases, they are equal.
It is impartial. One should understand that this principle serves as the antidote to arising and ceasing. A mind associated with right view can act as an antidote;
it possesses no latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) in the present life, nor does it possess latent tendencies in the past.
This momentary mind, free from latent tendencies, likewise possesses no latent tendencies in the future. From this point onward, it proceeds by itself.

Within the personal continuum (*saṃtāna*) in which the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have already been abandoned, all subsequent mundane states—whether virtuous or neutral—that are comprised within the world are free from latent dispositions across the positions of the past, future, and present. Therefore, it can be said that [the dispositions] are abandoned throughout the three times.
This concludes the initial formal explanation. △ Second, the reference to the extensive [treatise].
Such teachings as these exist in all the various schools; fearing that the text would become too prolix, I shall not describe them at length.

This concludes the first section, which clarifies the sacred teachings. △ Second, revealing the correct principle, in three parts: first, concluding the preceding and introducing what follows; second, revealing the correct principle;
third, referring to the extensive texts and exhorting belief. Now, the first part.
Having already cited the authoritative scriptures (*āgama*), one should now demonstrate the correct reasoning (*yukti*).
△ Second, the demonstration of correct reasoning has six parts: first, pervasive ignorance; second, being the condition for the arising of consciousness;

third, that which is called "mind" (*manas*) due to its cogitation; fourth, the distinction from the mindless attainments; fifth, the defilement in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*); sixth, the defilement during the three natures and at all times. First:
This section has two parts: first, the formal demonstration of its constant activity; second, a further explanation of its exclusivity (*āveṇika*). Now, for the first:
as the sūtras state, "exclusive ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) is subtle, constantly active, and obscures reality.
If this [seventh] consciousness did not exist, then that [exclusive ignorance] would not exist. This means that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) constantly give rise to delusion in all states.
The non-associated ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) obscures the true meaning and obstructs the noble eye of wisdom. As a verse in the *Gāthā* says:
"The mind that is directed toward the true meaning, This [ignorance] always acts as its obstacle; It accompanies all mental states— This is called non-associated ignorance."
This refers to the fact that at the very moment the wisdom-mind capable of illuminating true reality is about to arise, there is a certain factor that constantly acts as an obstacle to it.
This obstructive factor accompanies all ordinary beings throughout their states of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral mental natures;
it is what is known as "unshared ignorance" (*āveṇikī avidyā*).

Therefore, the sūtras state that those of the class of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) dwell perpetually in the long night, blinded by ignorance (*avidyā*), their minds shrouded in stupor and intoxication, never having awakened.

If, while in the state of an ordinary being, there were even a moment when this ignorance did not arise, it would contradict the meaning of what is taught in the sūtras regarding "dwelling perpetually in the long night" and so forth.

[This is because] both [the state of an ordinary being and the arising of ignorance] coexist within the state of an ordinary being; yet, there exists the ignorance that deludes one regarding the principles of reality.

This is not tenable, for it is illogical. This [unshared] ignorance cannot be established as depending upon the six consciousnesses, because this ignorance would either be intermittent—like the six consciousnesses—or else those six consciousnesses would be perpetually defiled by it. If the existence of the *manas* is admitted, this fault does not occur.
The first section, the full exposition of the ever-active [manas], is concluded. △ Second, the alternative explanation of the "unshared" (āveṇika).
The defiled manas is always associated with the four afflictions. Why is the ignorance (avidyā) that co-exists with these alone termed "unshared"?
This poses a question to introduce the following discussion. There are three interpretations of the subsequent text, of which the third is correct. One interpretation holds:

"What fault is there in calling this [affliction] 'unshared' (*āveṇika*), even though it consists of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) associated with it, rather than being a root affliction (*mūla-kleśa*)?"
This means that the ignorance (avidyā) which co-exists with this [manas] is a root affliction (*mūlakleśa*).

However, the self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), the conceit of self (*ātma-māna*), and self-love (*ātma-sneha*) that co-exist with it are not subsumed under the category of root afflictions; rather, they are merely secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

Therefore, although these four delusions arise together, three of them are not of the same class (*asabhāga*); thus, this ignorance alone is termed "unshared" (*āveṇika*). Furthermore, why is this so?
[This is] an error. This first interpretation is entirely incorrect.

There is another view which holds that his explanation contradicts both reason and scripture, because these three—view (*dṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and craving (*tṛṣṇā*)—are not mentioned among the purely secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

Because these three are subsumed within the ten fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), it is stated in various places that the defiled manas (*kliṣṭamanas*) is always associated with four afflictions.
Among those four, it should be said that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the primary one, even though it arises simultaneously with the other three—view (*dṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

It is also called "unshared" (*āveṇika*) because, from beginningless time, it has been perpetually inwardly deluded (failing to comprehend the principle of emptiness), never having engaged in introspection (merely falsely clinging to a self without ever turning back toward the truth).

This is due to the predominance of ignorance (*moha*). [Question: Should these three afflictions—view and so forth—which coexist with this [ignorance], not be termed "associated" (*saṃprayukta*)? [Answer:
If each of these three factors manifests as a primary factor (*pradhāna*), they should also be termed "unshared," just as in the case of ignorance itself. To accept this is without fault.
If one were to designate what predominates at these times, they would be called "unshared": namely, in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra-pravṛtti*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*) predominates;

when obstructing the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), views (*dṛṣṭi*) and pride (*māna*) predominate. As for views, they involve a biased attachment to a single principle and a refusal to maintain an open mind.

Because pride leads to arrogance and self-reliance, one is unwilling to seek [knowledge] from others; thus, this second school’s explanation is indeed correct, yet it does not fully capture the underlying intent.

According to another interpretation, this ignorance is called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*)—just as the eighteen unshared Buddha-qualities (which belong exclusively to the Tathāgata)—for this ignorance is likewise unique.
[Objection: Since this seventh consciousness exists, if that were the case, then the afflictions associated with the other six consciousnesses would also not exist within this seventh consciousness;
should they not, therefore, also be designated as "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*)? [Response: The designation "unshared" is established solely on the basis of its preeminent significance.
"Not common" (asādhāraṇa) does not mean that whatever is mutually absent is called "not common.

Rather, it refers to the ignorance associated with the seventh consciousness (*manas*), which has functioned constantly since beginningless time, obstructing the true meaning [of reality] and untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). Such a superior functional activity is absent in other consciousnesses and exists only in this consciousness;
therefore, it is called "not common. [Objection: If that is so, then the three [factors] that coexist with it—view, pride, and attachment—would also possess [this same superior function].
[Question: It should be called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*). [Answer: Because ignorance (*avidyā*) is the primary factor, it alone receives this name of "unshared.

Alternatively, even when the other three [defilements] act as the primary factors, they may also be called "unshared"; however, here we speak of ignorance as "unshared" only in contrast to the delusion (*moha*) associated with other consciousnesses.
Furthermore, there are two types of unshared ignorance: first, the ever-active unshared [ignorance], which does not exist in other consciousnesses; second, [the occasional unshared ignorance].
"Acting alone and not shared" means that this consciousness does not exist [independently].
For now, the section from "ignorance" (*avidyā*) upward is explained in the same manner as the second school’s interpretation.

From "unshared ignorance" (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) downward, one must distinguish that while it bears the single name "unshared," it possesses two meanings; only then will its full significance be thoroughly exhausted. First, "constantly active" (*nitya-pravṛtta*)...
The "common" [ignorance] refers to that which constantly arises in active manifestation during the state of being with outflows (*sāsrava*), without interruption;
this exists only in the seventh consciousness and is absent in the other six consciousnesses. It is precisely this that is now designated as "unshared ignorance" (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*).

Second, the "independently occurring unshared" [ignorance] does not arise simultaneously with the other nine root afflictions, but is uniquely deluded regarding the objects of the Truths (*satya-viṣaya*).
It exists only in the sixth consciousness; therefore, it does not exist within this seventh consciousness. Thus, it is not this [seventh consciousness] that is designated as "unshared" (asādhāraṇa).

Accordingly, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that there are two types of ignorance (*avidyā*): if it is concomitant with craving and so forth, it is called "associated ignorance" (*saṃprayuktāvidyā*). It is not...

That which is concomitant with greed and so forth is called "solitary ignorance" (*āveṇikī avidyā*). Regarding this solitary ignorance, it is further divided into two senses: that which is primary and that which is non-primary.

If it is primary solitary ignorance—that is, when it does not coexist with the ten minor defilements such as anger—it is capable of initiating karma. It is abandoned solely by the path of vision (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*), as stated in the Sūtra:

"Because the noble learners (*śaikṣa*) have eternally severed their uncommon ignorance (*asādhāraṇāvidyā*), they do not create new karma. This refers specifically to primary solitary ignorance as being "uncommon."

Ignorance (*avidyā*) does not refer to that which functions as a constant mental concomitant (*anuvartaka*) within the seventh consciousness as its unique [affliction]. Furthermore, it is not the case that it acts as a primary independent factor (as the ten minor derivative afflictions such as anger each act as their own primary).

This category of ignorance also extends to those abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because it—along with the ten minor derivative afflictions such as anger—is common to both what is abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation.
If one discusses the ignorance of the seventh consciousness, it likewise co-exists with greed and the other afflictions;

it is also subsumed under "associated ignorance" (*samprayukta-avidyā*), but because it takes "constant activity" (*nitya-pravṛtti*) as its primary characteristic, it is specifically designated by the term "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*). Furthermore, regarding this unshared [ignorance], there is a further distinction between two meanings:
that which is "primary" and that which is "non-primary. That which is primary is abandoned solely through the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*).
Being non-principal, they are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation, yet all of them are associated only with the sixth consciousness;
they are not like the seventh consciousness, which is ever-present and unique. Therefore, they are specifically analyzed in detail.

The "ever-active" (*nitya-pravṛtta*) unique [afflictions] (are exclusively abandoned by cultivation; therefore, they are so designated). They are absent in other schools. The "independently active" (*kevala-pravṛtta*) unique [afflictions] (since they exist in both primary and non-primary forms, and pertain to both abandonment by seeing and cultivation, they obtain this designation).
Both of these [types] exist across all five categories.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, the afflictions (*kleśa*) are divided into five categories (*pakṣa*): first, the category abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering;

second, the category abandoned through the vision of the truth of origination; third, the category abandoned through the vision of the truth of cessation; fourth, the category abandoned through the vision of the truth of the path; and fifth, the category abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
"Category" (*pakṣa*) means a division or a class. Each of the ten root afflictions [is thus classified].
Because they arise from delusion regarding the principles of the truths (*satya*), each has its own category. Under each individual truth, many afflictions arise; thus, their categories differ.
The "ever-active" (*nitya-pravṛtti*) non-common [afflictions] exist only in the seventh consciousness and belong exclusively to the category of those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*);
therefore, it is said that they are absent in other categories. As for the "independently active" (*pṛthak-cara*) non-common [afflictions], if they are not primary, they are pervasive.

Regarding the five categories (*pañca-varga*), it is therefore said that they exist both here and there; however, this [ignorance] is the primary independent one and is abandoned only by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
One should also say that it does not exist within these [five] categories, but it is omitted from mention because it is not the central meaning here.
This concludes the section on the ever-active ignorance (*nitya-pravṛtti-avidyā*). 2. Ignorance as the Condition for the Arising of Consciousness.
Furthermore, a sūtra states: "With the eye and visible forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises; and so on, in detail, until:

with the mind and mental phenomena as conditions, mental consciousness arises. If this seventh consciousness did not exist, then that [mind] which serves as the condition for mental phenomena would not exist.

This is because, just as the five [sensory] consciousnesses must necessarily have the five faculties—such as the eye—as their dominant, non-common, simultaneous supports, mental consciousness likewise [requires such a support]. Since it is the sixth...

It is logically necessary to admit that this [seventh] consciousness likewise possesses such a basis (*āśraya*). If this [seventh] consciousness were non-existent, how could that [sixth consciousness’s predominant, unique, and simultaneous] basis exist?
Furthermore, it cannot be said that the physical heart-mass (*rūpa*) is its basis, for it is designated as such [only in the sense of being the support for the mental faculty].

[Objection: Since the mind (*manas*) is not form (*rūpa*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—by depending on the mind—is able to possess all three types of discrimination: intrinsic, recollective, and conceptual. If it were to depend on form, it would be identical to the five [sensory] consciousnesses, which possess only intrinsic discrimination.

Therefore, it would follow that [the mental consciousness] lacks the two types of discrimination, namely recollection and conception. [Response: Furthermore, one cannot say that the five consciousnesses lack a simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*).
For they arise simultaneously with their respective sense organs, just as a sprout arises together with its seed, or a shadow with its object.
Furthermore, since consciousness and its sense organ necessarily share the same object—just as the mind and its mental factors—they are invariably simultaneous.
The five sense organs serve as the supports for the five consciousnesses by virtue of three common characteristics: first, they are predominant, because consciousness arises from the sense organs.
Second, they are not shared: visual consciousness relies exclusively upon the eye-faculty and is not shared with auditory consciousness or the others.
Third, they are co-existent: when the eye sees, consciousness simultaneously cognizes; they occur in the same moment without temporal sequence. This is likewise for the other five [senses].
The five faculties are like seeds; the five consciousnesses are like sprouts. The five faculties are like forms; the five consciousnesses are like shadows.
The five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) are like the mind-king (*citta-rāja*); the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are like mental factors (*caitta*).

It should be understood that the same applies to the mental faculty (*manas*) and the sixth [consciousness]. By this principle, it is fully established that the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*)—just like the five [sensory] consciousnesses such as the visual—must have a specific basis (*asādhāraṇa-adhiṣṭhāna*) for manifesting its own name [as "mental consciousness"], which is not subsumed under the immediately preceding [moment of] mind (*samanantara-pratyaya*), but is rather the support (*āśraya*) produced by the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Because it is universally established that the six consciousnesses are each subsumed under one [of the sense organs]. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

The subject (*dharmin*) is the universally established mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). It must have a dominant basis (*adhipatipratyaya*) for its arising that is not subsumed by either the uncommon [organ] which manifests its own name, nor by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
This is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is universally established as being subsumed under one of the six consciousnesses.

It is analogous to the visual consciousness and so forth. Regarding the statement that they are not included among the "immediately preceding conditions" (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"If these six consciousnesses serve as the immediately preceding condition for those [subsequent] six consciousnesses, then this [preceding consciousness] is designated by the name 'mental faculty' (*manas-indriya*).

This refers to the preceding, extinguished consciousness acting as the "opening and guiding support" (*avakāśa-āśraya*) for the subsequent one; it is for this reason that the provisional designation "mental faculty" is established. Now, this case is the same.

At that time, the predominant basis is not subsumed under the immediately preceding mind (*manas*) of those [preceding moments]. This concludes the section on how consciousness arises with the two as conditions.
△ Third, that which is called "mind" (*manas*) is the faculty of reflection.
Furthermore, a sūtra states: "That which cogitates is called the manas. If this [seventh] consciousness did not exist, that [cogitating manas] would necessarily not exist.
That is to say, when the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is present, the immediately preceding manas has already ceased and no longer exists;

since it is logically impossible for the past or future to exist [in a substantial sense], the function of cogitation of that [past immediately preceding manas] could certainly not be established. This being so, how [is it explained in the sūtra]?
To say that "cogitation" (*manana*) is what constitutes the mind (*manas*) is [merely] a figurative designation (*prajñapti*). This reasoning is also incorrect;

for if there were no actual cogitation, upon what basis could the figurative designation "mind" be established? If it is argued that when the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) was previously present, there was indeed cogitation (which, though now ceased, remains as a past event), [that too is insufficient].

It is given the name "manas" (mind), yet it is not realized that this refers to the sixth consciousness. At that time [when the sixth consciousness is active], although there is deliberation (*manana*), it is merely termed "vijñāna" (consciousness);
how could it be called "manas"? Therefore, one knows that there exists a separate seventh manas which constantly and thoroughly deliberates; this is precisely what is named "manas.
As for the "equal-and-immediate manas" (*samanantara-manas*) that has already ceased, it is only by depending upon this seventh [manas] that the name "manas" is metaphorically applied to it.

Question: In the second fascicle, the refutation of external objections states that it is also illogical for the provisional to necessarily depend upon the real. Now, however, you say there is no correct deliberation;
upon what, then, could the provisional be established? Is this not a contradiction of your own words? Answer: It is merely a worldly designation.
There are cases where the conventional is explained based on the ultimate, and there are also cases where the conventional is explained without relying on the ultimate;

they are not uniform. Examples of explaining the conventional based on the ultimate include: explaining the "conceptual path of vision" (sākṣātkriyā-mārga) based on the "true path of vision" (darśana-mārga);
explaining "external seeds" based on "internal seeds"; and explaining the "immediately preceding mind" (samanantara-manas) based on the "reflective mind" (manana-manas), and so forth. Not...

Based on the real, one speaks of the provisional. For example, while a rabbit has no horns, one provisionally speaks of "rabbit horns"; while a tortoise has no hair, one provisionally speaks of "tortoise hair.

Furthermore, just as there are not two moons, yet one provisionally speaks of "two moons," and while space has no flowers, one provisionally speaks of "flowers in the sky," even so, although the two aspects—the perceived and the perceiving—are neither self nor dharmas, they are provisionally spoken of as "self" and "dharmas," and so forth. Therefore, it is said that the provisional must depend [on the real].
This is also unreasonable. Furthermore, if one were to insist that the conventional does not necessarily depend upon real entities, would that not likewise be unreasonable?

Moreover, if "the real" is defined in terms of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena, then mental cognition (*manovijñāna*), which functions through deliberation, operates only with respect to the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena;
how could it ever directly apprehend their specific characteristics? It is merely within the context of these general characteristics...
This is merely a distinction between the real and the conventional. △ Fourth, the distinction between the two mindless absorptions.

Furthermore, the Sūtra states that there are two different types of absorption: the non-conceptual (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and the cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). If the seventh defiled manas did not exist, those two absorptions would have no distinction.
This is because both of these absorptions equally cease the six consciousnesses along with their associated mental factors; in terms of their substance and number, they are identical.

If the seventh defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) did not exist within these two meditative attainments—one (the attainment of non-conception) being present and the other (the attainment of cessation) being absent—then what would distinguish those two attainments?
If it is argued that they differ due to distinctions in their preparatory application, realm, level, support, and so forth, this is logically untenable;
for the cause of such distinction exists precisely because of this [seventh consciousness]. If this [seventh consciousness] were absent...
Furthermore, there would be no cause for that distinction. Therefore, it must certainly be the case that there is a distinct entity here:

"substance" refers to the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), and "number" refers to the mental factors (*caitta*). It is said that within these two types of cessation, the mind-kings that are extinguished are all alike—the six consciousnesses—and the mental factors that are extinguished are all alike—the fifty-one.
This remains so even if one does not distinguish between the two types of intentionality: the defiled and the undefiled.

As for their distinctions, there would then be no difference between the two concentrations. "Preparatory application" refers to mental attention (*manasikāra*); "basis" refers to the teaching (*deśanā*).
The phrase "and so forth" includes their essential nature and their provisional designation. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* clarifies that these two concentrations differ in five respects:
first, their basis; second, their essential nature; third, their provisional designation; fourth, their mental attention; and fifth, their realm and stage. First, the basis:
As for their differences: the attainment of non-conception is cultivated by followers of non-Buddhist paths based on the false teachings expounded by those non-Buddhists;
the attainment of cessation is cultivated by disciples of the World-Honored One based on the correct teachings expounded by the World-Honored One.

Regarding their essential natures: the essence of the attainment of non-conception is contaminated (*sāsrava*), while the essence of the attainment of cessation is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). Thirdly, regarding their provisional designation:
The [state of] non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is conventionally established based on the afflicted mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-manas*) taking the ālayavijñāna as its object.

The attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is conventionally established based on the unafflicted mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-manas*) taking the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) as its object. Regarding the four types of mental attention (*manaskāra*):

the non-conceptual absorption is preceded by the preparatory application of the mental attention of definitive renunciation (*atyantaniḥsaraṇa-manaskāra*); the attainment of cessation is preceded by the mental attention of temporary cessation (*tatkāla-vyupaśama-manaskāra*).

Regarding the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) and the five realms and levels: the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is bound to the level of the purity of equanimity and mindfulness within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

The attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) enters by relying on the level of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), yet it is not bound to that level.
△ Fifth, the defilement of the Heaven of No-Conception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).
Furthermore, a sūtra states: "In the realm of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñisattva), the mind and mental factors are extinguished throughout the duration of one lifetime.

If this [seventh] consciousness did not exist, those [beings in the realm of non-conceptualization] would have no defilement; that is to say, for a long period they lack the six evolving consciousnesses.

If this manas were absent, then the co-emergent grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) would likewise be absent. Yet, there is no one anywhere who remains bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) throughout the entirety of a single lifetime. [Otherwise, such a state would be impossible.]

There is no grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) there at all. If that [Heaven of Non-conception] were devoid of grasping at a self, it would be like *nirvāṇa*, and thus it would not be something censured and loathed by the noble ones (*ārya*).
[The opponent] defends: "Grasping at a self exists in that Heaven of Non-conception; it ceases only after the first half-aeon, and arises again during the second half-aeon.

Therefore, because it exists, there is no such fault as being like *nirvāṇa*. [The refuter] rebuts: Because there is no grasping at a self for a long duration—the four hundred and ninety-nine intervening aeons—there is the flaw of being like *nirvāṇa*. [The opponent] defends: "..."

[Objection: Because there is [the grasping of a self] in the past and future, such a fault [as being like *nirvāṇa*] does not arise. [Refutation: That [past and future] is not present and is not eternal;

since it does not exist, the fault [of being like *nirvāṇa*] remains. Furthermore, because that which is obtained—the maturation of non-conception—is absent, the obtainer [the sentient being who possesses the retribution of non-conception] is also absent.

This maturation of non-conception is a dissociated dharma (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), which is merely a provisional designation based on the states of matter and mind. This has already been refuted previously.

[This refutes the view that it is not substantially real: If the manas did not exist, the ālayavijñāna would also not exist. Since the ālayavijñāna does not exist, there would likewise be no perfuming (*vāsanā*). It has already been demonstrated that the notion of other dharmas receiving perfuming is irrational;
therefore, there must be a distinct defiled manas that constantly gives rise to the grasping of a self in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*).
For this reason, both the noble ones (*ārya*) and the ordinary sages alike revile and loathe it.

Regarding the statement "that which is obtained is non-existent": this refers to those sentient beings who, prior to the attainment of the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), seek the fruit of non-conceptuality.

Consequently, seeds perfumed by that seeking bring about its maturation (*vipāka*). The defiled *manas* takes that [maturation] as its object and clings to it as a self; based upon it, coarse and mobile ideation and so forth do not function.
Within this state, the "retribution of non-conceptuality" (*asaṃjñi-vedanīya*) is provisionally established. If this [state] did not exist... [the second... would not exist.
Regarding the seven consciousnesses: the retribution of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) would then not exist. △ Sixth, [the proof regarding] the defilement of the three natures at all times.
Furthermore, a sūtra states that when ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) possess wholesome, defiled, or neutral minds, they are always accompanied by the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*).

If this [seventh] consciousness did not exist, that [grasping of a self] would not be possible; for even when ordinary beings possess minds of the three natures (the six evolving consciousnesses), although they externally manifest [wholesome or unwholesome states], [they remain internally defiled].

Although one performs various karmas, internally one constantly clings to a self. Because of this clinging to a self, the wholesome karmas—such as giving, morality, and meditation—that arise within the six consciousnesses cannot eliminate their objective signs (*nimitta*).
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that the defiled manas serves as the support for the [six] consciousnesses.

As long as it has not been extinguished, one is not liberated from the bondage of the apprehension of signs (*nimittabandhana*) [which is defiled]. Once the manas has been extinguished, one is liberated from the bondage of signs. Thus it is said.

The "bondage of signs" (nimitta-bandhana) refers to the fact that because the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) constantly clings to a self, it causes the first six consciousnesses to be unable to realize that their objects are like illusions and so forth.
Consequently, they are constrained by the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) and the sign-division (*nimitta-bhāga*), and thus lack autonomy; hence it is called the bondage of signs.
Based on this meaning, there is a verse that says: "In this way, the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) is the support of consciousness.

As long as this mind has not been extinguished, consciousness will never be liberated from its bonds. Furthermore, during moments of wholesome or non-obscured neutral states of mind, if there were no self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*), those states would not be *sāsrava* (tainted).
This is because the afflictions belonging to the six consciousnesses within one's own continuum would [otherwise] not be associated with it.

Because wholesome states and so forth do not arise simultaneously [with their opposites] (if one objects), and because past and future afflictions bound by conditions do not exist as real entities according to principle.
This is because they do not become tainted (*sāsrava*) due to the afflictions of others, nor should it be that they become untainted (*anāsrava*) due to the liberations of others.
"Afflictions of others" refers to past and future afflictions; "liberations of others" refers to the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) in past and future lives.
When the six present consciousnesses give rise to wholesome or non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena, they are already not associated with afflictions.

They arise together. If it is claimed that they are "with outflows" (sāsrava) because past and future afflictions exist, then the outflow-free (anāsrava) thoughts arising after emerging from meditative absorption by those such as Srotāpannas would necessarily become with outflows, since those [past thoughts] were previously realized as outflow-free.
Furthermore, the wholesome and indeterminate minds of those practicing the seven stages of preparation (saptaprayoga) would also become outflow-free.
Because it will necessarily realize the untainted (*anāsrava*) in the future.

Furthermore, it cannot be said that there exists a separate latent disposition (*anuśaya*) apart from the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). It is not comprised within the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*), nor does it arise manifestly in the continuum during states such as the wholesome (*kuśala*).

By means of this, the wholesome and other states become tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*). That [dissociated entity] is not substantially real (*dravyasat*); this has already been [stated] in the preceding text.
Because it is universally established, one cannot say that those wholesome states and so forth arise from contaminated seeds;

thus, they are established as contaminated [only] by means of a contaminated cause—namely, solely through the seventh [consciousness] which clings to a self. If there were no seventh consciousness clinging to a self, then those seeds would previously lack a cause that could render them contaminated.

Nor is it by virtue of contaminated seeds that those [wholesome states in their active manifestation] become contaminated dharmas; otherwise, [the wholesome states within] the stages of training (śaikṣa-bhūmi) would not [be established as such].
Because an untainted (*anāsrava*) mind (in its active manifestation) could also become tainted (*sāsrava*), since it still possesses the seeds of the tainted;
and because although karma such as generosity may be induced by afflictions (*kleśa*), once the afflictions have departed, [the karma] does not arise simultaneously with them.

Therefore, [afflictions] are not the direct cause of being tainted, for the term "tainted" signifies that which arises simultaneously with the outflows (*āsrava*). Furthermore, neutral (*avyākṛta*) karma is not induced by afflictions. That...

Furthermore, how can they become *sāsrava* (contaminated)? All things that are *sāsrava* become so only by arising and ceasing simultaneously with the manifest afflictions (*kleśa*) within one's own continuum, thereby mutually augmenting one another;

it is through this that the seeds of *sāsrava* phenomena are perfumed, and when these subsequently manifest from those seeds, the meaning of being *sāsrava* is established. Just as this is the case for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), so it is for those in training (*śaikṣa*).
"Arising from oneself" clarifies that it is not the afflictions of another. "Manifestly active afflictions" clarifies that they are not latent seeds (*anuśaya*).

"Arising and ceasing simultaneously" clarifies that they do not arise at non-simultaneous times. "Mutually augmenting" means that the giving and so forth initiated by the six consciousnesses mutually increase and benefit the seventh consciousness’s grasping at a self.

The outflow-tainted states of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), although not coexistent with the outflows (*āsrava*), arise from seeds of outflow-tainted states from a previous time; therefore, they are established as being outflow-tainted.
This explanation does not contradict reason.
This is the resolution of an objection. The objection states: "If the term 'outflow-tainted' necessarily signifies coexistence with the outflows, then in the stage of one beyond training..."

Since one has already attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) within the intermediate stage [of the path of cultivation], why are the five faculties and the five consciousnesses still termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*)? We now explain this:

although the five faculties and the five consciousnesses—which are phenomena with outflows—within the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) do not coexist with the seventh consciousness that possesses outflows, they nevertheless arise from outflow-tainted seeds previously perfumed, as their maturation (*vipāka*) has not yet been emptied.
Therefore, they become tainted (*sāsrava*). This does not contradict reason;

for it is because the manas constantly gives rise to the grasping at a self that wholesome and other dharmas acquire the status of being tainted. If this manas did not exist, [this would not be the case].
That [meaning of being with outflows] is certainly not present [in that state]. Therefore, one knows that there exists this separate seventh consciousness.
This concludes the second section: Demonstrating the Correct Principle. △ Second: Pointing to Extensive Exhortations for Faith.
There are many logical arguments proving the existence of this consciousness. Following the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, six types will be briefly described here.
Those who possess wisdom should study them with faith.
The detailed explanation of the teachings and principles is concluded. △ Third, the summary resolving objections:
However, regarding those sūtras that speak of six consciousnesses, one should know that they employ a provisional method of exposition (*anuvartana-yukti-mukha*).
Alternatively, they speak of six by following the six bases (*āśraya*), the sense organs; yet, as for the categories of consciousness, there are actually eight kinds.
This is because within the mental faculty (*manas*), both the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are subsumed.

The second explanation of the second transformation is complete. △ Third, the explanation of the third transformation has two parts: first, clarifying the six gates such as "differentiation" (*viśeṣa*);

second, clarifying the three subsequent gates such as "common support" (*sādhāraṇāśraya*). Within the first part, there are two sections: first, explaining the four gates beginning with "differentiation"; second, [explaining...].

The mental objects experienced by the mind involve both gates. The first [section] further has two parts: first, the formulation of the question and the presentation of the verse; second, the explanation and establishment thereof by means of the treatise. Now, for the first:
Having thus explained the second transformation, what are the characteristics of the third transformation? The verse says: "In succession..."

The three transformative consciousnesses have six types of distinctions: (1) the gate of differentiation; (2) the gate of essential nature, which takes the apprehension of objects as its characteristic; (3) the gate of mental aspects;
(4) the gate of the three natures, consisting of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and that which is neither.
Below this, nine sections are used collectively to explain the characteristics of the third transformation. First, four sections are presented. 1.

The Section on Association with Mental Factors (*caitta*): This refers to the three phrases concerning "these mental factors are universal" and the initial twenty phrases beginning with "the universal [factors] such as contact" found in the text below.
2. The Section on Coexistence with Feeling (*vedanā*): This refers to the passage in the text below stating that "it is associated with the three feelings."
One phrase constitutes the seventh, the gate of common reliance; that is, the phrase "relying on the fundamental consciousness. Eight is the gate of simultaneous operation;
that is, the three phrases beginning with "the five consciousnesses manifest according to conditions. Nine is the gate of the stages of arising and ceasing;

that is, the four phrases beginning with "the mental consciousness is constantly manifesting. II. Explaining and establishing [the meaning] through the treatise has three parts: first, explaining the gate of differentiation; second...
This concludes the two gates of nature (*lakṣaṇa*) and characteristics (*svabhāva*). Third is the gate of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Now, for the first [of these]: The Treatise says:

Following the transformation of consciousness as the capacity for mental construction (*vikalpa*), one should next analyze the characteristics of the transformation of consciousness as the capacity for cognizing objects (*viṣaya-vijñapti*).

There are, in total, six varieties of this consciousness, corresponding to the distinct categories of the six sense organs (*indriya*) and their six respective objects (*viṣaya*). That is to say, they are named eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), and so forth.

The mental consciousness (manovijñāna) derives its name from following the six sense faculties (indriya), because it possesses five meanings. These five are: basis (āśraya), origination (samutthāna), belonging (parigraha), and so forth.
"Assistance. As with the faculties (*indriya*), this correctly clarifies that the names of the six consciousnesses are established based upon the faculties. Regarding the five meanings:

first, they abide in dependence on the six co-existent faculties, such as the eye; second, they are produced by the six faculties; third, each is individually bound to its respective faculty; fourth... [text truncated]
They assist the faculties in discerning their objects; each of the five [sensory consciousnesses] has as its object the domain corresponding to its respective faculty.

Although all six groups of consciousness arise in dependence upon the mind (*manas*), they are designated by the name "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*) according to their unique [respective] basis, just as with the five groups of sensory consciousness.

There is no fault of over-extension. Or rather, it is named "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*) because it relies solely upon the mind (*manas*). This explains that while the names of the consciousnesses are established based on their specific supports, the mind (*citta*) and mental faculty (*manas*) do not follow this same rule;
this is the resolution of the anticipated objection. The objection states:

"If the five consciousnesses also rely upon the seventh [consciousness] as their basis for defilement and purification, why is the sixth alone named 'mental consciousness'? The response to this is: Although all six consciousnesses rely upon the mind, the first five...
Consciousnesses [in general] take the *manas* (mind) as their common support; however, only the sixth consciousness takes the *manas* as its uncommon support.

Therefore, the name "mental consciousness" (*mano-vijñāna*) is established according to this uncommon support. This is just as the five groups of sensory consciousness each rely on a single sense organ and are each named according to their respective uncommon supports, thereby avoiding the fault of mutual confusion.
Furthermore, while the first five may also rely on material organs (*rūpīndriya*), the sixth relies solely on [the *manas*].
"In your view, it is therefore merely called 'mental consciousness' (*manovijñāna*). Furthermore, an objection is raised:

if the sixth [consciousness] is named 'mental consciousness' solely because it depends upon the mind (*manas*), then the eighth [consciousness] also depends solely upon the mind and should likewise be named 'mental consciousness. Moreover, the seventh [consciousness] depends solely upon the eighth;
should it not then be named 'mind-consciousness' (*cittavijñāna*)? Now, we explain this: here, we are merely distinguishing the six [consciousnesses]."

The name "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is derived from its specific function. If the eighth [consciousness] is called "mind" (*citta*), and the seventh is called "intellect" (*manas*), these names are established based on their predominant meanings of "accumulation" and "cogitation" respectively.
Although they are mutually dependent, this does not fall under the category of being named after the sense-faculty upon which it relies.

Alternatively, they may be named according to their objects—ranging from consciousness of form (*rūpa-vijñāna*) up to consciousness of mental phenomena (*dharma-vijñāna*). This is because such names are established in accordance with the objects and conform to the meaning of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
That is to say, the discernment (*vijñapti*) of the six objects—form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena—is what is called "consciousness.

Among these, the five consciousnesses of form and so forth discern only their respective single objects, such as form. The consciousness of mental phenomena, however, is capable of discerning all phenomena; alternatively, it is that which is capable of discerning [their] distinctions.

The Dharma [consciousness] alone receives the name "Dharma-consciousness" (whereas the first five [consciousnesses] can only cognize their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as objective realms and cannot cognize differentiated dharmas; thus they are not called Dharma-consciousness).
Therefore, the names of the six consciousnesses are likewise free from the fault of confusion.

This further clarifies that the names of the six consciousnesses are established based on their respective objects. The passage beginning with "Form and so forth" (*rūpādi*) explains away an anticipated objection. The objection states:

"The five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are also all termed 'dharmas,' and these dharmas are likewise nothing but the five sense-objects themselves and the shadows (impressions) left behind by those five sense-objects."
Why is the sixth consciousness alone named "Dharma"? There are two meanings for this explanation:
first, while the first five consciousnesses each restrict themselves to a single sense object (*viṣaya*), the sixth consciousness comprehends all six sense objects;

second, while the first five consciousnesses only cognize uniform, essential natures (*svabhāva-viṣaya*), the sixth consciousness can cognize various differentiated phenomena (*dharma*). Therefore, they do not overlap or confuse one another.

Subsequently, the names of the six consciousnesses established according to their respective objects are spoken of based on the state in which the five material sense-faculties have not yet attained mastery.

If one attains mastery such that the various sense faculties function interchangeably, and a single faculty gives rise to consciousness perceiving all objects, it may be designated according to whichever faculty is predominant;
thus, there will be no error of confusion.
These six consciousnesses have two types of names. The former, from "eye-consciousness" up to "mind-consciousness," are names established according to the sense faculties (*indriya*).
The latter, from "form-consciousness" up to "dharma-consciousness," are names established according to the objects (*viṣaya*).
However, these latter names established according to the objects apply only to the state of non-mastery; once [the practitioner] reaches the stage of mastery over the faculties...
If they were used interchangeably— such that a single sense organ could give rise to consciousness capable of universally perceiving all objects—

then even the designations "consciousness of form" up to "consciousness of phenomena" would inevitably suffer from mutual confusion. Only by establishing these names according to their respective supporting organs can the error of such confusion be avoided.

The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* (Madhyamaka section) states that each of the Tathāgata’s five faculties operates with respect to all five objects. This is said provisionally based on coarse, manifest, and homogeneous objects.

However, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states that the wisdom of accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) discerns the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings and initiates transformations through the three types of action, such as providing the four kinds of answers. If it did not universally perceive all six sensory objects, it would lack this capacity.

This is the explanation of the objection. The objection states: "If it is claimed that the sense faculties function interchangeably, such that a single faculty gives rise to consciousness and perceives all objects, why does the *Vyūha-śāstra* state only that each of the Tathāgata’s five faculties operates with respect to the five types of sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), rather than stating that they operate universally across all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*)?
The explanation states: "For now, this is based on coarse, manifest, and homogeneous [perceptions]."

This refers only to the objects [of perception]; it does not mean that [the mind] does not universally take all objects as its conditions. Therefore, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* is further cited to prove universal conditioning.
Regarding the phrase "coarse and manifest objects of the same class," this refers to the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).

This is because their characteristics are coarse and manifest, and furthermore, they belong to the same category of objective phenomena. These coarse and manifest objects of the same class [are perceived] when one has not yet attained the stage of mastery.
Regarding those things that are definitively incompatible: even in the state of sovereign mastery (*vaśitā*), they can still serve as mutual objects of cognition;

how much more so in the case of mental objects (*dharmālambana*), which are by nature subtle and do not obstruct one another. How could it be that in the state of sovereign mastery, one would instead be unable to universally cognize them?

As for the "four types of answers" (*catuḥ-pratipatti*): "answer" (*pratipatti*) here means "response. The first is the categorical answer (*ekāṃśa-vyākaraṇa*); the second is the analytical answer (*vibhajya-vyākaraṇa*); the third is the counter-question...
Regarding the four types of responses: the fourth is the response by setting aside (*sthāpanīya*).

However, because the bases (*āśraya*) and objects (*ālambana*) of the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are coarse, manifest, and universally established, they are not mentioned here in this verse.
The bases were already explained previously as the occasion required; as for these objects (*ālambana-viṣaya*), we shall wait until the occasion arises to explain them.

This is an explanation of a doubt. The doubt is as follows: In the previous verse concerning the seventh consciousness, there were two sections regarding its support (*āśraya*) and its object (*ālambana*).

Why, then, are these not mentioned for the six consciousnesses here? The answer is: These six evolving consciousnesses rely upon the six sense organs (*indriya*) and take the six sense objects (*viṣaya*) as their objects;
because they are coarse, manifest, and universally established, the verse does not mention them. However, in the preceding treatise, they were discussed because it was convenient for the context.

Having already provided this digression on the supports (*āśraya*) of the various consciousnesses, we shall now—taking advantage of the present context—expound upon the distinctions among the objective spheres (*ālambana-viṣaya*) of these six consciousnesses.
