The first section, the "Explanation of the Gate of Distinctions," is concluded. △ Second, the explanation of the two gates of nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Next, regarding the statement that "cognizing objects constitutes its nature and aspect," this simultaneously reveals both the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the cognitive aspect (*ākāra*) of the six consciousnesses.
Since consciousness has the cognizing of objects as its intrinsic nature, it likewise employs that very [cognizing of objects] as its cognitive aspect.

By means of this, the specific designation "consciousness" (defined as "that which cognizes") is also explained: because that which is able to discern and differentiate objects is termed "consciousness. As stated in the Sūtra: "The eye..."
What is consciousness (*vijñāna*)? It refers to the discernment of various forms (*rūpa*) based on the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). This is explained in detail up to:
what is mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*)? It refers to the discernment of all phenomena (*dharma*) based on the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*).

That sutra speaks, for the time being, of that which is discerned by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) in the state where the basis has not yet been transformed (*aśraya-parāvṛtti*), as well as [the discernment] based on the other [shared] bases [and that which is discerned] in the state where the basis has been transformed, as previously explained.

The common support (*sādhāraṇa-āśraya*). This means that the five consciousnesses further require a supporting consciousness (*vijñapti-āśraya*), a defiled and pure support (*kliṣṭa-śubha-āśraya*), and a fundamental support (*mūla-āśraya*).
The sixth consciousness likewise further requires a fundamental support. The rest may be understood. △ Third, the section explaining the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

(Question: To what nature do these six evolving consciousnesses belong? (Answer: They are comprised within the natures of the wholesome (*kuśala*), the unwholesome (*akuśala*), and that which is neither (*avyākṛta*).

"Neither" refers to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); because it is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, it is called "neither. That which can bring about benefit and advantage in this life and future lives is called "wholesome.
Although the pleasant fruits of human and celestial realms can bring about benefit in this life, they do not do so in future lives.
Therefore, it is not called "wholesome. Because it can cause harm and detriment in both this life and future lives, it is called "unwholesome.
Although the bitter fruits of the miserable realms (apāya) cause harm in this life, they do not do so in future lives; therefore, they are not unwholesome.
Because it cannot be definitively categorized within the context of the beneficial or harmful meanings of wholesome and unwholesome, it is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).

This first explains the meaning of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). However, regarding the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is further divided into the obscured (*nivṛta*) and the unobscured (*anivṛta*);
since these were already explained previously, they are not repeated here.

These six evolving consciousnesses, when associated with the eleven [mental factors] such as faith, are subsumed under the nature of the wholesome; when associated with the ten dharmas such as lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), they are subsumed under the nature of the unwholesome;
and when associated with neither, they are subsumed under the nature of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

This demonstrates the characteristics of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) within the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Regarding the ten dharmas such as lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and so forth: first is lack of shame;

second is lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), which are two among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*); third is anger (*krodha*); fourth is resentment (*upanāha*); fifth is concealment (*mrakṣa*); sixth is vexation (*pradāśa*).

Seven: envy (*īrṣyā*). Eight: avarice (*mātsarya*). Nine: harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*). These are seven of the ten secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Ten: anger (*krodha*). This is one of the six root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).

These ten are comprised exclusively within the category of unwholesome (*akuśala*) nature. As for the eight major secondary afflictions (*mahābhūmika-upakleśa*), the remaining three minor secondary afflictions, and the remaining five root afflictions, these all pertain to both the unwholesome and the obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) natures; therefore, they are not [included here].
I shall explain this. For instance, suppose there is a person who gives rise to greed, delusion, pride, doubt, and various views and attachments;

yet, if these do not arise together with a lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and a lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*), they are merely termed "obscured-unspecified" (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). The same applies to the arising of restlessness (*auddhatya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and so forth.
It is likewise for the arising of deception (*śāṭhya*), guile (*māyā*), and arrogance (*mada*); however, [these become defiled] only when associated with a lack of shame and a lack of dread of blame.

Only when associated [with these] are they called unwholesome (*akuśala*). When they do not arise together with shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), they are all termed obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).

If they are not associated with wholesome mental factors (*kuśalacaitta*), nor associated with any of the afflictive mental factors (*kleśacaitta*), but are associated with any one of the universal (*sarvatraga*), object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*), or four indeterminate (*aniyata*) factors, then they are all termed [unobscured-]unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

[The nature of] concealment (*nivṛta*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). There is one interpretation [which holds]: the six consciousnesses of the three natures do not necessarily arise simultaneously (because these six consciousnesses), as they turn toward external objects (*bahir-mukha-pravṛtti*) and their respective natures—wholesome and so forth—are mutually contradictory.

That is to say, the first five consciousnesses necessarily arise being guided by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as their basis for discernment (*vikalpa-āśraya*); only when they arise together and share the same object-field (*ālambana-viṣaya*) [do they function].

Because [the five consciousnesses] would then become either wholesome or defiled. If one were to admit that the five consciousnesses operate simultaneously with all three natures (tri-niṣyanda), then the mental consciousness at that time would also have to be associated with all three natures;
this would contradict correct reasoning. Therefore, they certainly do not coexist [in this manner].

As for the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts stating that the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) arises simultaneously with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and is associated with all three natures, that statement of "simultaneity" is made in reference to multiple moments (*kṣaṇa*). As it is said:

Since [the mind] is single-minded—meaning it is not restricted to a single arising-and-ceasing (here, based on a single thought-moment, which definitely does not admit simultaneity)—there is no fault of contradiction.
This clarifies the meaning of whether the three natures (trisvabhāva) coexist or do not coexist. There are two schools of interpretation. Herein, the first school clarifies that they do not coexist.

First is the formal explanation; next, from "Yogācāra... onwards, is the resolution of objections—both can be understood accordingly. However, as this does not accord with the principle, the following interpretation is taken as correct.
There is another interpretation: the six consciousnesses may arise simultaneously with respect to the three natures (i.e., at their initial occurrence).

This includes the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) that are *taṭastha* (indeterminate), as well as those of the *nisyanda* (outflowing) category—whether wholesome or defiled—which may arise in large numbers (five types or four types) or in small numbers (three types or two types), as it is possible for them to arise together.

Furthermore, although the five sensory consciousnesses and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) necessarily arise together, they do not necessarily share the same nature, such as being wholesome and so forth; this was the point established previously regarding the mental consciousness.
At that time, the objection that [the auditory consciousness] must pertain to all three natures (trividha-svabhāva) would be rendered futile here; therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"If a person has entered into samādhi and arises from that concentration upon encountering the condition of a sound, this is the arising of a residual auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) that functions simultaneously with a wholesome mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) associated with that samādhi.

It is not the case that the mental consciousness alone, associated with that samādhi, can perceive this sound. If it were otherwise, [since there would be no auditory consciousness], [there would be no perception of sound]."
Because one does not perceive this sound, one should not emerge from meditative absorption (samādhi). Nor does one emerge from absorption at the very moment of perceiving the sound;

rather, having first perceived the sound, if there is a subsequent desire, only then does one emerge. This is because the ear-consciousness (śrotra-vijñāna) that suddenly hears a sound while in absorption is, by its nature, not wholesome.
For one who has not yet transformed the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), the mind that suddenly falls [into the object]—the five sensory consciousnesses—is necessarily in a state of meditative absorption.

Because [all such cases] belong to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), this provides clear proof that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) co-arising with the five [sensory] consciousnesses is not necessarily identical in nature—whether wholesome and so forth—to those five consciousnesses.

In all instances, it is merely stated that the mental consciousness co-arising with the five [senses] also takes as its object the spheres [the five sense-objects] apprehended by those five consciousnesses.
It is not said that [the mental consciousness] is necessarily of the same nature (wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral) as the five [sensory] consciousnesses. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"The absence of the five consciousnesses during the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*) is spoken of in terms of the majority of cases."
This second school correctly clarifies that the six consciousnesses and the three natures can coexist.

For instance, when a wholesome eye-consciousness of the outflowing type (*niṣyanda*) is correctly observing a Buddha or correctly reading a scripture, if the ear suddenly hears a sound, the nose suddenly smells an odor, or the body suddenly perceives a tactile sensation, then the corresponding *sātaka* (sudden) or *āvega* (impulsive) mental states must belong to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Furthermore, this applies to defiled [consciousness] of the outflowing type as well.

When visual consciousness correctly perceives beautiful forms while watching a theatrical performance, and the ear suddenly hears sounds and so forth, the mind falls into a state of "sudden engagement" (*ābhoga*), which likewise belongs to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
This is one proof that these three natures can arise simultaneously.

As for their claim that even if the five consciousnesses proceed with all three natures, the mental consciousness at that time must also correspond to all three natures—they fail to realize that the simultaneous mental consciousness [is not necessarily so].

Consciousnesses necessarily share the same object, yet they do not necessarily share the same nature. For instance, the mental consciousness that has entered meditative absorption is categorized as wholesome;

however, the ear-consciousness that suddenly hears a sound while one is precisely in that state of absorption is merely an incidental indeterminate (avyākṛta) consciousness. Why must they necessarily be of the same nature?

Furthermore, fearing that one might raise the objection: "How can there be auditory consciousness within meditative absorption? we now provide this explanation: The mental consciousness within meditative absorption cannot apprehend sound;
if there were no sudden auditory consciousness (*ābhoga-śrotra-vijñāna*), then one would be unable to perceive the sound. Furthermore, fearing that one might raise the objection:
"How do you know that there must necessarily be a sudden auditory consciousness within meditative absorption to perceive this sound? we now provide this explanation.
It is said: "If one does not perceive the sound, one should not emerge from meditative absorption.

Fearing that this might lead to further difficulty—namely, that at the moment of perceiving the sound and emerging from absorption, since the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) has already arisen, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) would no longer be wholesome within absorption—the present text therefore explains:

It is not at the time of perceiving the sound that one emerges from absorption; rather, while the ear-consciousness, which is a spontaneous indeterminate state (*aurasāvyākṛta*), is precisely perceiving the sound, the mental consciousness is still [in a state of]...

While in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one awaits a specific object of expectation before emerging from that absorption. Thus, it is known that although the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) during absorption is of a virtuous nature (*kuśala*), this does not preclude the simultaneous arising of the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*), which is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).
Fearing that one might further ask, "How do we know that the auditory consciousness within meditative absorption is not of a virtuous nature?

I shall now explain: for one who has not yet undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), the mind falls into a state of sudden, spontaneous occurrence (*ābhoga-citta*) even while in absorption.
Because it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). From "By this, below... the conclusion and proof may be understood. In the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*, further objections are addressed.

Regarding "equipoise" (*samāhita*): the Sanskrit term is *samāhita*. This refers to the cultivation of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), which are balanced and non-biased, drawing forth (*āhita*) meritorious qualities;
thus it is translated as "equipoise. Within the state of equipoise, wholesome concentration and wholesome wisdom are associated with the sixth consciousness.

Because one abides in a state that is pliant and upright, the five consciousnesses generally do not arise. Thus, in this *Miśrakābhidharmahṛdaya*, it is stated that they are absent based on their general non-occurrence;
it does not mean that the five consciousnesses of sudden encounter (*sūter*) absolutely never arise within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

If the three natures arise simultaneously within the five sensory consciousnesses, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) follows whichever one it predominantly attends to, thereby sharing that same nature.
If there is no such predominant attention, it is then of an indeterminate nature. Thus, it is possible for the six evolving consciousnesses to possess all three natures simultaneously.

Furthermore, for instance, at the time of prostrating to the Buddha and performing repentance and vows, if the visual consciousness takes the physical form of the Buddha as its object, it is of a wholesome nature.
If it takes objects such as flowers or banners and spontaneously gives rise to greed, it is of a defiled nature. If it is neither wholesome nor defiled, it is of an indeterminate nature.
If the auditory consciousness takes the sound of the Dharma as its object, it is of a wholesome nature; however, if it takes sounds that are either beautiful or foul as its object...
Spontaneous attachment or aversion constitutes a defiled nature. If it is neither wholesome nor defiled, it is of an indeterminate nature.

When the nose-consciousness smells an odor without grasping or attachment, it is of a wholesome nature. If, upon encountering a pleasant fragrance, one spontaneously becomes attached, or upon encountering another scent, one spontaneously feels aversion, this constitutes a defiled nature.
If it is neither wholesome nor defiled, it is of an indeterminate nature. [The same applies to] the body...
If consciousness is alert, diligent, careful, and solemn without laxity, it is of a virtuous nature (*kuśala-dharmatā*).

If it is characterized by much negligence and does not accord with dignified decorum (*īryāpatha*), it is of a defiled nature (*kliṣṭa-dharmatā*). If it is neither virtuous nor defiled, it is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta-dharmatā*).

Furthermore, when the gustatory consciousness (*jihvā-vijñāna*) is experiencing food, if no craving or attachment arises toward the taste, it is of a virtuous nature. If one spontaneously [responds] to good or bad tastes...
Greed and hatred are of a defiled nature; if they are neither wholesome nor defiled, they are of an indeterminate nature.

Therefore, when the five consciousnesses arise simultaneously, it may be that the eye-consciousness is wholesome while the ear-consciousness is defiled and the nose-consciousness and others are indeterminate; or the ear-consciousness may be wholesome.

Visual consciousness is defiled; the remaining consciousnesses are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Alternatively, the wholesome may be predominant and the defiled few; or the defiled may be predominant and the wholesome few;
or the wholesome and defiled may be predominant and the indeterminate few; or the indeterminate may be predominant and the wholesome and defiled few;

or it may possess only one nature, or only two natures, or all three natures. The phenomena are not uniform. As for the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), if it follows the five [sensory] consciousnesses...

When there is a specific focus, the [first five] consciousnesses share the same nature—wholesome or defiled—as that focus. If there is no specific focus, they are subsumed under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature.

Furthermore, for example, at the very moment of prostrating or practicing seated meditation, while the body-consciousness is wholesome, the mental consciousness may arise as indeterminate or as a defiled mind;
thus, it is not uniform. Therefore, the first five consciousnesses do not pose any hindrance.
The three natures arise simultaneously; yet, there is no fault of the sixth consciousness being associated with all three natures at a single moment.
The above explanation, concerning the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), is concluded.

Having attained the state of mastery, it is comprised solely of the wholesome nature. This is because the Buddha’s physical and mental aggregates are subsumed under the Truth of the Path (and thus contain nothing unwholesome);
furthermore, because the seeds of conceptual proliferation have been eternally extinguished, they are also devoid of the indeterminate.
Attaining mastery means that within the state of Buddhahood, the *vipākavijñāna* (maturation-consciousness) is transformed into the *amala-vijñāna* (stainless consciousness).
At that time, because the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*) become untainted (*anāsrava*), the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) they produce also become untainted.

Furthermore, because the mental faculty (*manas*) is purely untainted, the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) it produces is also purely untainted. These five faculties are termed the "untainted form" (*rūpa*) of the Buddha. [The eight consciousnesses...]
All are termed the Buddha’s untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*). As for form (*rūpa*), it is adorned by the merits of the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
As for mind, it consists of the mental states associated with the four wisdoms of enlightenment (*catur-jñāna-bodhi*). Therefore, they are all subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

Since the seeds of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca-bīja*) have been eternally extinguished, this mental state associated with the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) and the Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*)...

[These] categories are all comprised exclusively within the nature of the wholesome (*kuśala*). This concludes the first section: the explanation of the four gates, beginning with "differentiation" (*prabheda*).

△ Second, the explanation of the two gates: "mental factors" (*caitta*) and "concomitance with sensation" (*vedanā-sahabhū*). This has two parts: 1. A brief presentation of mental factors followed by a detailed explanation of their concomitance with sensation;

2. A detailed explanation of the specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the six classes of mental factors. In the first part, there are two sub-sections: 1. Positing the question and citing the verse (*kārikā*); 2. Explaining and establishing it through the commentary (*bhāṣya*). Now...
First:

With how many mental factors (*caitta*) are the six consciousnesses associated? The verse says: These mental factors are the universal, the object-specific, the wholesome, the afflictions, the secondary afflictions, and the indeterminate;
they are all associated with the three feelings.

△ Second, the explanation through the treatise is divided into two parts. First, a brief explanation of the mental factors (*caitta*) across the six stages. Second, a detailed explanation of their association with the three types of feeling (*vedanā*).
Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the general heading; second, the specific explanation. This is the first [the general heading].
The Treatise says: These six evolving consciousnesses are, in general, associated with six categories of mental factors (*caitta*), namely the universal (*sarvatraga*) and so forth.

Part Two: A Detailed Explanation, which has two sections. First, the explanation of the names and meanings of the mental factors; second, the explanation of the classification of the six categories. Now, the first section.
They always arise in dependence upon the mind, are associated with the mind, and are bound to the mind; therefore, they are called "mental factors" (*caitta*).
This is just as things belonging to a self are designated by the term "mine" (*ātmīya*); one must understand this.

While the mind apprehends only the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of its objects, the mental factors also apprehend their specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), thereby assisting in the accomplishment of the mind's activity; thus they receive the name "mental factors. It is, for example, like... [the analogy].

Just as a master painter provides the model and an apprentice fills in the colors, so too the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that consciousness (*vijñāna*) can discern the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of an object, while attention (*manasikāra*) discerns the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) not yet discerned by consciousness. This explains the meaning of how the various mental factors (*caitta*) discern their respective objects.
Therefore, contact (*sparśa*) is able to discern whether the object of this [consciousness] is agreeable or otherwise, and feeling (*vedanā*) is able to discern this [object].

The characteristics such as apprehension (*saṃgraha*) and so forth: perception (*saṃjñā*) is able to comprehend this characteristic of the cause for verbal expression (the object-condition of consciousness);

volition (*cetanā*) is able to comprehend these characteristics of the primary cause and so forth (the object-condition of consciousness). Therefore, attention (*manaskāra*) and the others are called mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).

(In the phrase "is able to comprehend this," the word "this" [此] correctly indicates that mental factors do not only take particular characteristics as their objects, but also take general characteristics as their objects.)

These are the phrases concerning the specific characteristics grasped by the various mental factors (*caitta*). The first [phrase] explains the preceding phrase, while the second simultaneously clarifies the meaning of the following four phrases.
Regarding "agreeable characteristics" (*manāpa-lakṣaṇa*) and so forth: "and so forth" includes disagreeable characteristics (*amanāpa-lakṣaṇa*) and neutral characteristics (*madhya-lakṣaṇa*).
"Appropriating" (*parigraha*) means that which is favorable and beneficial. "And so forth" includes that which is adverse and harmful, as well as that which is neither favorable nor adverse.
Furthermore, "the cause of verbal expression" refers to the specific characteristics (*pramāṇa*) of the objective domain. Regarding "the correct cause," etc., the term "etc.
includes the false cause as well as causes that are neither correct nor false.

In another place it is further stated: Desire (*chanda*) also discerns the aspect of the object of consciousness that is desirable; resolve (*adhimokṣa*) also discerns the aspect of the object of consciousness that is determined;

mindfulness (*smṛti*) also discerns the aspect of the object of consciousness that has been habitually practiced; concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) also discern the aspects of gain and loss, etc., regarding the object of consciousness.

It is by means of these [mental factors] that one can give rise to wholesome, defiled, and other such mental concomitants (*caitasika-dharma*) toward the objective sphere. This is also [the case for all of them].
Regarding the object of focus (*ālambana*), it also grasps its specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
This further explains that all mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), such as those with distinct objects, possess the functional capacity to assist and accomplish the activities of the mind.

"Shuāng" (串) is synonymous with "guàn" (慣). As for concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) also discerning characteristics such as gain and loss: they discern the characteristic of gain, and [from this] arise...
Wholesome mental factors (citta-saṃprayukta-dharma) are termed right concentration (samyak-samādhi) and right wisdom (samyak-prajñā); they discern the characteristics of what is lost.
Defiled mental factors are termed wrong concentration (mithyā-samādhi) and wrong wisdom (mithyā-prajñā); they discern the characteristics of what is neither attained nor lost.

As for other indeterminate (avyākṛta) mental factors, their concentration and wisdom likewise belong to the indeterminate category. This concludes the first explanation: the definition and meaning of mental factors. △ Second, the explanation of the six stages.
Distinctions:
Although all mental factors (*caitta*) are identical in name and meaning, there are six categories of distinctions among them. Namely: five universal factors (*sarvatraga*);
five object-specific factors (*viniyata*); eleven wholesome factors (*kuśala*); six afflictions (*kleśa*); twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*); and [the indeterminate factors].

There are four types of *niyata* (fixed) mental factors. Thus, across these six categories, there are fifty-one [mental factors] in total. 1. The first are called the "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*) because they are invariably present in all states of mind. 2.

The second are called the "object-specific" (*viniyata*) because they arise by taking specific objects as their respective conditions. 3. The third are called the "wholesome" (*kuśala*) because they can only arise within a wholesome state of mind.

4. The fourth are called the "afflictions" (*kleśa*) because their nature is subsumed under the root afflictions. 5. The fifth are called the "secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*) because they are exclusively afflictive...

Because they are of the nature of being outflows (*niṣyanda*) of affliction (*kleśa*), these six are called "indeterminate" (*aniyata*), as they are not fixed with respect to being either wholesome or defiled.
However, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* combines these six into five by treating the root afflictions and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) together, since both are defiled.

Furthermore, it distinguishes these five states by means of four "all-inclusives" (*sarvatraga*): namely, all natures (*sarvabhāva*), all stages (*sarvabhūmi*), all times (*sarvakāla*), and all [mental] concomitants (*sarvasahagata*).

Among the five categories [of mental factors]: the universal factors possess all four types of "all-encompassing" (sarvatraga). The specific-objective factors possess only the first two types of "all-encompassing" (i.e., all three natures and nine stages).
The wholesome factors possess only one type, namely "all stages. Defiled factors lack all four types. The indeterminate factors possess only one type, namely "all natures."
By means of these distinctions among the five categories:
"all natures" refers to the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral;

"all stages" refers to the nine stages within the three realms, namely, the stage of mixed habitation of the five destinies, up to the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; "all times" refers to [existence]...
This is the occasion for the distinctions between the states of the mind being without outflows (*anāsrava*) or with outflows (*sāsrava*).

"All are associated" means that they arise simultaneously, universally corresponding with the eight consciousnesses as the sovereign minds (*citta-rāja*). This concludes the brief explanation of the six categories of mental factors (*caitta).

II. Extensive Explanation of Association with the Three Feelings (*vedanā*). This has two parts: 1. Explaining the meaning of the three feelings. 2. Clarifying what is associated and what is not. Now...
First:
These six evolving consciousnesses are easily detached and indeterminate; therefore, all of them can be associated with the three types of feeling (*vedanā*).

This is because they all experience the three aspects of objects: the agreeable, the disagreeable, and that which is neither. When experiencing the aspect of an agreeable object, which brings gratification to body and mind, it is termed pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
The experience of an object that is disagreeable, which oppresses both body and mind, is called the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhā vedanā*).
The experience of a neutral object, which is neither oppressive nor pleasing to either body or mind, is called the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant (*aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā*).

This is a general explanation of the meaning of the three types of sensation (*vedanā*). "Change" (*vipariṇāma*) refers to transformation; "liberation" (*vimukti*) refers to turning away from and liberation from [that transformation].

The rest is understandable. These three sensations are each further divided into two. Those associated with the five sensory consciousnesses are called "bodily sensation" (*kāyikī vedanā*), because they depend specifically on the body.
That which is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is called mental feeling (*caitasikī vedanā*), because it relies solely upon the mind.
Bodily feeling (*kāyikī vedanā*) is also termed external feeling, while mental feeling is termed internal feeling. There are three types of bodily feeling and three types of mental feeling;
these constitute the six feelings. Furthermore, when distinguished according to the six consciousnesses, they constitute the eighteen feelings.

Furthermore, all three [types of sensation] are common to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), because painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*) also arises from the uncontaminated.
This is because those who cultivate the uncontaminated must necessarily undergo hardships and afflict their mental resolve.

Alternatively, each may be divided into three: namely, those to be abandoned by seeing (the three feelings), those to be abandoned by cultivation (the three feelings), and those not to be abandoned (the three feelings).
Those to be abandoned by seeing refer to the three types of sensation associated with conceptual afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*).

Those to be abandoned by cultivation refer to the three types of sensation associated with innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*). Those not to be abandoned refer to the three types of sensation associated with the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, there are three categories: those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those who are neither.
The three types of feeling of one in training are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). The three types of feeling of one beyond training are not to be abandoned (*aheya*).

"Neither" refers to those who are neither in training nor beyond training; this denotes all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). The three types of feeling of those who are neither are abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).
[The first] is abandoned. Furthermore, the two or three feelings are not [exclusively] abandoned by both [the path of seeing and the path of cultivation], nor are they non-abandonable.

For those in training (śaikṣa), the three feelings are abandoned only by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) or are non-abandonable. For those beyond training (aśaikṣa), the three feelings are exclusively non-abandonable.

Alternatively, they may be divided into four categories in total: namely, (1) pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), which is wholesome (*kuśala*); (2) painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*), which is unwholesome (*akuśala*); (3) neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*), which is [either] obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) or unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*);
and (4) feeling that is of both types of unspecified nature. According to another interpretation, each of the three feelings may be further divided into four natures.

This is because [in the case of pleasant feeling], there is the spontaneous greed and delusion arising simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), as well as the spontaneous afflictions in the realms of pure suffering (*ekānta-duḥkha-gati*) which do not give rise to unwholesome karma.
Because it is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), that [affliction] is capable of being associated with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"If all afflictions arise spontaneously (*svarasena*), they are found to manifest in association with all three feelings (*vedanā*).

If [the affliction] extends to all bodies of consciousness (i.e., the first six consciousnesses), it is universally associated with all three faculties of feeling within those consciousnesses; if it does not extend to all bodies of consciousness, it is not so.
[This] is associated with all [three types of] feeling (vedanā) on the mental level (manobhūmi). The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:

"If afflictions (kleśa) bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) that arise spontaneously (svarasa) incite unwholesome conduct, they are also unwholesome (akuśala); the remainder [which do not incite such conduct] are all obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta)."
Thus, one should know that each of the three types of sensation (vedanā) has four categories.

First, the three sensations are allocated to the three natures (tridhātu); since the indeterminate (avyākṛta) has two sub-types, they are collectively divided into four. This interpretation is too restrictive;

only when the three sensations are each shown to encompass the four categories of wholesome (kuśala), unwholesome (akuśala), obscured-indeterminate (nivṛtāvyākṛta), and unobscured-indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta) does the full significance of this principle become exhausted.
Alternatively, they are divided into five in total: suffering (*duḥkha*), pleasure (*sukha*), grief (*daurmanasya*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Within the [remaining] three [feeling-aggregates], suffering and pleasure are each divided into two because their characteristics differ in terms of whether they afflict or gratify the body and mind, and because they differ in being non-conceptual versus conceptual, and in being more intense or slight.
Non-suffering-and-non-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha*) is not divided into two because its characteristic differs neither from afflicting nor from gratifying the body and mind.

Because they are non-conceptual and because they function with equality, this explains how the three feelings are also called the five feelings. Since suffering gives rise to grief and pleasure gives rise to joy, it is said that each is divided into two.
There are generally three meanings: first, that which oppresses the body is called suffering (*duḥkha*), and that which oppresses the mind is called grief (*daurmanasya*).

Physical gratification is called pleasure (*sukha*); mental gratification is called joy (*prīti*). In the second case, that which is without conceptual differentiation (*avikalpa*) is called suffering (*duḥkha*) or pleasure;

that which is with conceptual differentiation is called sorrow (*daurmanasya*) or joy. In the third case, that which is most intense is called suffering or pleasure; that which is slight is called sorrow or joy.

Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is designated simply as "equanimity" (*upekṣā-vedanā*) because it cannot be divided into two. First, it lacks the characteristics of either physical or mental oppression or gratification;
second, it is of a single flavor and non-discriminative in nature; third, it functions with equanimity, without being weighted toward either side.
Therefore, it is indivisible.

All pleasant feelings associated with the five sensory consciousnesses are always termed "pleasure" (*sukha*), because they merely gladden the body and lack conceptual discrimination; they cannot be termed "joy" (*prīti*).
Pleasant feelings associated with the mental consciousness, if occurring within the desire realm or the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the first two dhyānas, are termed "joy."

It is simply because it gladdens the mind. If it occurs in the fundamental stages of the first or second dhyānas, it is called pleasure (*sukha*) and joy (*prīti*), because it gladdens both body and mind.

If it occurs in the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) or the fundamental stage of the third dhyāna, it is called pleasure alone, because it is exceptionally profound in its tranquility and free from conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*).
This is a detailed explanation of the two feelings of joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*). "Preparatory stage" (*sāmantaka*) refers to the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*);
"fundamental" (*maula*) refers to being properly established in the concentration itself. The rest is understandable.
All painful sensations associated with the five sensory consciousnesses (because they oppress the body and are non-conceptual) are always termed "suffering" (and cannot be termed "grief").

Regarding that which is concomitant with mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), there is one interpretation: it is exclusively sorrow (*daurmanasya*). This is because it oppresses the mind; furthermore, various holy teachings state that the dejected feeling on the level of the mental ground is termed the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*).

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that for sentient beings born in the hells, immediately following the maturation (*vipāka*) [of their birth], there is a continuous succession of suffering and sorrow produced by maturation (*vipākaja-vipāka*).
It further states that the discursive thought and investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*) in the hells are concomitant with sorrow (and moreover, that a portion [of hell-beings] experiences pure sensation).

The same applies to the realms of hungry ghosts and animals. Thus, we know that mental states involve particularly heavy and distressing sensations, which are still designated as "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*);
how much more so for other lighter ones?

This section below provides a detailed explanation of the meanings of the two sensations of sorrow and suffering (*duḥkha*). Those associated with the five sensory consciousnesses are always termed "suffering. This...
This is easy to understand. Since the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is characterized by oppression, it should apply to both the terms "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*) and "suffering" (*duḥkha*).

Now, according to the first school’s interpretation, they allow it to be called only "sorrow" and do not allow it to be called "suffering," because they have not yet reached the point of understanding that what is particularly grave and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) is precisely what is termed "suffering.
This can be known from the cited evidence; the following text will refute this itself.

According to one interpretation, [the mental consciousness] is associated with both [mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and physical pain (*duḥkha*)]. Among humans and devas, it is always termed "distress," because it is not particularly intense.
In the realms of animals and hungry ghosts, it is termed either "distress" or "pain," depending on whether the experience is mixed or pure: if it is mixed, it is called distress;

if it is pure, it is called pain, because there are degrees of intensity (where mild is called distress and severe is called pain). In the hells, it is termed only "pain," because the experience is purely intense.
Because they are non-conceptual.
This is the correct interpretation of the second school. *Naraka*—translated here as "vessel of suffering"—refers to the hells.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that if all afflictions arise spontaneously, they are found to manifest in relation to all three types of sensation (*vedanā*).
The detailed explanation is as before. Furthermore, it is taught that the innate *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity) is comprised solely of the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) nature;

one should know that the *antagrāhadṛṣṭi* (view of extremes) is likewise so comprised. The painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*) associated with these two views must certainly belong to the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), and is not comprised within the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Why? Because the treatises state that the faculty of grief is not unspecified. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states regarding the various [beings] in hell...

Regarding the faculties: the other three are certainly not accomplished as active manifestations (*samudācāra*). The same applies to the purely suffering realms of hungry ghosts and animals (as stated in that treatise).

The "other three" refer necessarily to the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and sorrow (*daurmanasya*). This is because in those [purely suffering destinies], the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is necessarily accomplished as an active manifestation.
This citation from the treatise serves as proof that the mental sensation experienced in the hells is designated solely as "suffering" (*duḥkha*) and cannot be called "grief" (*daurmanasya*).

The detailed explanation is as previously stated: namely, that which does not pervade all groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) is associated only with the three faculties of sensation belonging to the mental level (*manobhūmi*).
This is one proof for why the mental level receives the designation of "suffering. Furthermore, the faculty of grief is never indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). And...
Within the sixth consciousness, the co-emergent view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) belong exclusively to the indeterminate (avyākṛta).
They can be associated with painful sensation (duḥkhavedanā); this constitutes the second proof that this mental ground (manobhūmi) should be designated as "suffering.

Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that among the eleven faculties (indriya), only eight are present in hell; the manifestation of the remaining three faculties is certainly not established there.

As for that passage, although it does not explicitly state what the "other three" are, by inferring from the meaning, the other three must refer to the faculties of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*).
This is because the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) necessarily manifests in the hells;

this constitutes the third proof that the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) there should be called "suffering. Regarding the statement that beings in hell possess eight faculties: first, the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*); second, the ear-faculty (*śrotrendriya*).

The faculties are: (1) the eye faculty, (2) the ear faculty, (3) the nose faculty, (4) the tongue faculty, (5) the body faculty, (6) the life faculty, (7) the faculty of suffering, and (8) the faculty of equanimity.
Now, among the twenty-two faculties, the two faculties of male and female are not mentioned because they are of no use in the hells.
The mental faculty as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-manas*) is not mentioned because the six consciousnesses do not always function. It is not...
Regarding the statement that the five faculties beginning with faith, as well as the three untainted faculties, may exist as seeds but certainly do not manifest:
this is because they are easy to understand. Regarding the definite existence of the five material faculties: this is because the suffering retribution they attract must necessarily involve a body.

Even if the five faculties were absent, one would not experience suffering. As for the existence of the life faculty: it is due to the fruit of suffering projected by karmic maturation (*vipāka-karman*).
Because there is an uninterrupted continuity throughout the duration of a single lifetime, those who possess the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) experience exclusively suffering;
those who possess the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya) do so because, within the hells, the seventh and eighth consciousnesses remain constantly associated with the feeling of equanimity.

[Objection: Is it not the case that [the roots] are abandoned? That [in the hells] they are definitely not accomplished [is established]. How do we know that the [Yogācāra] text speaks only of their being contained [within existence]?
This does not allow for the existence of the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) in hell; rather, it should be the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

[Objection: It is admitted that this is the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). [Response: One should not state that those [in hell] necessarily possess the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), because that treatise admits that the six consciousnesses are sometimes absent there.
The preceding text has already clarified that mental distress (*daurmanasya*) is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Therefore, [the opponent] merely refutes [this position], saying:
"If the eighth consciousness were not the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), how could the *Yogācārabhūmi* take the immediately preceding mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) as the eighth?

However, since the six consciousnesses within the hells are admitted to be occasionally absent, how could one further establish an immediately preceding mental faculty? Since the mental faculty would be non-existent, [the eighth consciousness could not exist].
Thus, the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) need not even be refuted further.

(Furthermore, an objection is raised: It should not be that the aforementioned treatise speaks only of the "intermediate" (*upekṣā*) feeling, for it universally explains all faculties (*indriya*) without any specific reason to speak only of the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣāvedanā*).
Moreover, even if that treatise were to rely upon the intermediate feeling of equanimity to explain [the matter], how could it [possibly] say that...?
It is established that there are eight faculties.
Even granting that hell-beings lack the mental faculty (*manas*), they may possess the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

However, it is not necessarily the case that equanimity constitutes the eighth; alternatively, the seventh might be equanimity and the eighth sorrow (*daurmanasya*), which likewise cannot be determined. This is because of the [Yogācāra]...
This is because there is no explicit textual authority in the Abhidharma treatises to rely upon.

(The answer is: If one claims that because the five consciousnesses do not continue in succession, [only] the mind is afflicted, and therefore asserts that the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is definitively the eighth, then at the time of death, birth, or fainting, how could there possibly be the faculty of sorrow? Furthermore, some falsely maintain that the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is the eighth.

Eighth, this is likewise refuted by the same reasoning. Even if one were to maintain that either of the two sexual organs (male or female) constitutes the eighth [organ], this is logically untenable because, in the hells, the physical form is not fixed;
it is possible for those who have summoned such a state through their evil karma to lack either male or female form. This is due to their evil karma.

Because it causes the gates of the five sense faculties to constantly experience suffering, the five faculties—eye and so forth—are necessarily established; even if there must be one of the two sexual organs (male or female), [the five faculties are still required].
What use would there be for it even in those [other hells]? For in the Avīci Great Hell, there can be no seeking after sexual desire;

therefore, the eighth consciousness is necessarily associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), because both the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are constantly associated with equanimity.
This is precisely an investigation through reasoning that refutes the attachment to the existence of the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) in those hell-beings;

it simultaneously refutes the attachments to the faculties of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and the physical faculties (*rūpendriya*), demonstrating that they must necessarily possess the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

As in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, mental satisfaction is called "bliss" (*sukha*); because the faculty of joy (*saumanasya-indriya*) does not exist there, it is so designated. In the place of ultimate suffering, mental distress is called "suffering" (*duḥkha*);

because the faculty of grief (*daurmanasya-indriya*) does not exist there, it is so designated. Thus, the three remaining terms mentioned in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* definitively refer to grief, joy, and bliss.

This correctly concludes and clarifies that the mental experience in hell is suffering (*duḥkha*) and not grief (*daurmanasya*). Regarding the "Land of Ultimate Bliss," this refers to the Third Dhyāna.
Within the Third Dhyāna, the five sensory consciousnesses do not function; there is only mental joy (*saumanasya*).

Since it can be termed "bliss" (*sukha*) yet not "joy," by analogy with the extreme suffering in hell—where the five sensory consciousnesses do not function and there is only mental distress—it is likewise certainly termed [suffering].

If suffering (*duḥkha*) is not designated as sorrow (*daurmanasya*), and since the hell realms are established as being endowed with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*),
then what else could the Yogācāra statement— that the other three [faculties] definitely do not manifest— be referring to, if not sorrow, joy, and pleasure?

In other places, it is said that within those evil realms there is also "outflowing pleasure" (*niṣyanda-sukha*) similar to the aforementioned virtuous causes. This should be understood as being stated according to the principle of "concomitant occurrence" (*anuvartana*).

Alternatively, it is a general statement regarding other locations of mixed sensation; for only those places where there is necessarily no ripened pleasure (*vipāka-sukha*) are designated as "places of pure suffering.

Furthermore, when the various holy teachings refer to mental unpleasant sensation (*daurmanasya-vedanā*) as the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), this is said based on what is most prevalent, or in accordance with...

Regarding the "transformative perspective" (*paryāya-mukha*), there is no fault of contradiction. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that for those sentient beings born in the hells, immediately following the maturation (*vipāka*) [of their birth], there is a continuous succession of suffering and mental distress (*daurmanasya*) arising from maturation.
Furthermore, it states that the hell-beings possess vitarka and vicāra accompanied by mental distress, and that the same applies to one portion of the hungry ghosts and animals.
These statements are also based on the transformative perspective. Moreover, as for the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and the mind (*manas*) within those hells...

That which is associated with consciousness (*vijñāna-sahagata*) is of the same category as the other [realms’] mental faculty (*manas*) and the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasya*); it is metaphorically designated as "sorrow.

Alternatively, because that faculty of suffering (*duḥkha-indriya*) impairs both body and mind, although it is subsumed under the faculty of suffering, it is also called "sorrow" (by analogy). This is like the faculty of joy (*prīti-indriya*) in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the first and second dhyānas:
because it benefits both body and mind, although it is the faculty of joy, it is also called "pleasure" (*sukha*). The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and other treatises fully elucidate this meaning.

However, in the stage not yet reached (*anāgamya*), the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is certainly absent; for the treatises state that it possesses only eleven faculties: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, life, suffering, grief, joy, and equanimity.
From this, one should understand that even the mental feeling of distress (*daurmanasya*) in the stage of pure suffering is subsumed under the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
These various scriptural teachings have many different classifications; fearing that the text would become too voluminous, I shall not describe them in detail here.
This passage synthesizes various other treatises. Regarding "pleasure as a result of outflow" (*niṣyanda-sukha*):

as stated in the *Lokaprajñapti-abhidharma*, when humans raise six types of domestic animals and provide them with food and drink that are warm or cool, there are cooling intervals in the hot hells and warming intervals in the cold hells.
This warmth and coolness are results that resemble their preceding causes; they are also technically "ripened" (*vipāka*) fruits, though they are nominally designated as "outflow."
[From] the *Pravāhaṇī* [Sūtra]. Furthermore, as stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*: "In the Saṃjīva Hell, at times they are struck by cool winds and their flesh and blood are restored;
at other times they cry out the words 'Saṃjīva' (Revive), and those sentient beings suddenly come back to life."
When such flesh and blood arise, the brief experience of joy and pleasure is also termed "ripened pleasure" (*vipāka-sukha*).
This refers specifically to the hell realms with intervals (*sāntarāya-naraka*), and not to the Avīci Hell (*avīci-naraka*).

As for the "other places of mixed reception," this refers to the hells with intervals as well as the majority of hungry ghosts and animals. "Pure suffering" refers to the Avīci Hell and [the other hells without intervals].
A portion [of these] consists of ghosts and animals. Speaking according to the majority, this refers to the realms where humans, devas, ghosts, animals, and others possess discrimination;

therein, mental distress is designated solely as the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*). The rest may be understood accordingly. This concludes the initial explanation of the meaning of the three types of feeling.
△ Second, the explanation of simultaneous and non-simultaneous occurrence.

According to one interpretation, the six consciousnesses and the three feelings do not occur simultaneously, because they all function toward external objects and are mutually contradictory. As for the *pañcaka-sahaja-manovijñāna* (the mental consciousness co-arising with the five [sensory] consciousnesses):

The five [sensory consciousnesses] share the same five objects of cognition (*ālambana*). [If it were claimed that] these five are simultaneously accompanied by the three feelings (*vedanā*), then the mental consciousness (*manas*) would also have to be so; this would contradict correct reasoning, and therefore they certainly do not arise together.

As for the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts stating that the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) arises simultaneously with the three feelings associated with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), this refers to multiple moments (*kṣaṇa*), just as one speaks of "one mind" rather than a single moment of arising and ceasing. Thus, there is no fault of contradiction.

There are two interpretations of this. First, [the view] that they do not coexist is as can be understood from the meaning within the section on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) in the preceding text.

According to another interpretation, the six consciousnesses and the three types of feeling (*vedanā*) may coexist, because when encountering objects that are agreeable, disagreeable, or neutral, it is possible for them to coexist with all three feelings. This applies to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which is not fixed [in its nature].

Because the feelings (vedanā) of the five [sensory consciousnesses] are identical; because they give rise to a single feeling toward an object of exclusive attention; and because one who lacks such exclusive attention gives rise to equanimity (upekṣā).
For these reasons, the three feelings are compatible with the six consciousnesses simultaneously.
This is the second correct explanation. The meaning may be understood accordingly.

In the state of mastery, there are only pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), because the Buddhas have already severed all matters of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*).

Regarding the second section, the "Explanation of Mental Factors Accompanying Feeling," within the two gates: first, the brief presentation of mental factors and the detailed explanation of those accompanying feeling are concluded.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the specific characteristics of the six categories of mental factors has two parts: first, the formal explanation of their specific characteristics;

second, the reconciliation and demonstration of the Two Truths. Within the first part, there are five sections: first, the explanation of the universal and object-specific [mental factors]; second, the explanation of the wholesome; third, the explanation of the root afflictions...

[The section on] *upāyāsa* (affliction). Fourth, the explanation of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Fifth, the explanation of the indeterminate mental factors (*aniyata-citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*). Regarding the first [of these], there are two parts:
first, the presentation of the verse; second, the commentary. Now, the first [part].

The six categories of mental factors (*caitta*) were briefly indicated previously; now their specific characteristics should be explained in detail. First, regarding the nature of the initial two categories, the verse says:

"The first consists of the universal factors, such as contact (*sparśa*) and so forth. Next are the object-specific factors, namely: desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Their objects of focus differ."
△ Second, the commentary on the two [categories]. First, the explanation of the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).

Second, the explanation of the object-specific mental factors (*viniyata-viṣaya*). Now, the first. The treatise says: "Among the six stages, the first are the universal mental factors, namely the five beginning with contact (*sparśa*), as explained extensively before.

[Question: How should the characteristics of these universals be understood? [Answer: Because the scriptures (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*) serve as the definitive authorities (*pramāṇa*). Regarding this, the scripture is as follows:
As stated in the Sūtra: "With the eye and visible forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises. At the stage of the conjunction of these three, contact necessarily arises;

co-arising with contact, there are invariably feeling, perception, and volition," and so forth at length. By this, it is established that these four—contact and the others—are universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).
Furthermore, a sutra states: "If the sense faculties are unimpaired, the object is present before one, and attention (manasikāra) correctly arises, only then can consciousness be produced.
Another sutra further says: "If one directs attention toward a particular object, one cognizes that very object;
if one cognizes a particular object, one directs attention toward that very object. Therefore, these two factors—attention and cognition—are always in mutual association."

"Combined. And so on, as explained at length. For this reason, this mental attention (*manasikāra*) is also a universal (*sarvatraga*). There are numerous such scriptural authorities as authentic proofs.

Regarding the phrase "from the beginning... as explained at length," it refers to the passage ending with: "With the mind and phenomena as conditions, mental consciousness arises," and so forth. Next...
Regarding the phrase "and so forth, as explained at length": if one contacts this, one then discerns this, and so on, up to experiencing, grasping images, and performing volitional formations;
each of these is to be explained by means of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Principle: When consciousness arises, there must necessarily be a conjunction of the three—the sense organ, the object, and the consciousness. At that stage of the conjunction of the three, contact is invariably produced; furthermore, that conjunction of the three...
It must exist by means of contact (*sparśa*). If there were no contact, the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) would not be able to converge upon a single object.
Attention (*manasikāra*) draws the mind toward its own object; if this [attention] were absent, the mind itself would likewise be non-existent.
Feeling (*vedanā*) is able to experience an object—whether favorable, adverse, or neutral—and causes the mind to arise as joy, sorrow, or equanimity.
Alternatively, it is because when [a mind] arises that has abandoned its characteristics, there is no characteristic that accords with reason among these three [characteristics].

Perception (*saṃjñā*) is able to establish the boundaries and limits of its own object. If this perception were absent when the mind arises, it would be unable to grasp the characteristics of the object's boundaries.
Volition (*cetanā*) causes the mind to grasp the characteristics of correct causes and so forth, and to perform wholesome and other [unwholesome] actions.
Since there is no state in which the mind arises that lacks even one of these three factors, volition must necessarily exist. This serves as proof.

One should know that the five factors, such as contact (*sparśa*), are necessarily present whenever the mind arises; therefore, they are universal (*sarvatraga*). The others are not universal; their meaning will be explained when the occasion arises.
[If these were absent], the mind would be non-existent—meaning it would not engage with its own object, which is to say it would not manifest. *Cetanā* (volition) grasps the primary cause.

If one grasps the characteristic of the wholesome, one performs wholesome action; if one grasps the characteristic of a false cause, one performs unwholesome action; if one grasps a characteristic that is neither correct nor false, one performs indeterminate action.
The rest may be understood accordingly. This concludes the first explanation of the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).

II. Explanation of the Specific Mental Factors (*viniyata*). This has three parts: 1. Direct explanation of their essence and function; 2. Their manifestation in various states; 3. Analysis through various categories. In the first part, there are three sections.
First, the general name is explained; second, the specific meanings are explained; third, it is concluded that they are not universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*). Now, for the first [part]:

as for the "object-specific" (*viṣayapratiniyata*) factors, these refer to desire through wisdom (*chanda* to *prajñā*). Because their objects of perception (*ālambana-vastu*) are for the most part different, they are explained next after the six categories [of universal factors].

△ Second, the detailed explanation of the five [faculties] has five parts: first, the explanation of desire (*chanda*), up to fifth, the explanation of wisdom (*prajñā*). Within the first [section], there are two parts: first, the formal explanation;
second, the refutation of divergent interpretations. Now, the first.
What is desire (*chanda*)? Its essence consists in the longing for and the hope for an object that is desired. Its function is to give rise to diligence (*vīrya*) based upon this.
According to one interpretation, "the desired" refers to an object that is pleasing; because there is a hope to see, hear, or otherwise engage with such a pleasing thing, it is called desire.
[An objection is raised: In the case of an object that is loathsome, one hopes for its non-occurrence and desires its separation; would this not also constitute desire?

[Answer: This merely seeks that [object] which is loathsome; it does not coincide with the time [of seeking], or when one is separated from that loathsome object, there is something else. It is the nature of what is delightful (*abhipreta*) that coincides and is not separated [from the mind];
it is not that one gives rise to longing by seeking an object that is loathsome. Therefore, regarding objects that are loathsome or neutral, there is invariably no desire (*chanda*).
When one takes a delightful object as a cognitive object (*ālambana*), if there is no longing, then desire does not arise either. According to one interpretation, "that which is desired" means:
Regarding the object sought: because there is an aspiration toward objects that are to be rejoiced in or loathed, such as seeking union or separation, there is desire for them.

Regarding neutral objects, there is an absolute absence of desire. Even if one does not aspire toward objects that are the basis for rejoicing or loathing, desire will still arise [if there is another factor].

According to one interpretation, "that which is desired" refers to the object of observation; regardless of whether it is an object to be rejoiced in, loathed, or neutral, if it is something one wishes to observe, there is aspiration.

Because it is directed toward an object; if one does not wish to observe, and the mind spontaneously conditions an object according to the power of its causes and conditions, then there is no desire at all.
By this principle, desire is not a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*).
First, the essential nature and functional activity are correctly explained. Second, the object of aspiration is further explained, which generally involves three meanings.
The first meaning relies solely on what is desirable; this is too narrow. The second explains the sought-after object by combining both the desirable and the loathsome;
this also does not fully capture the principle. The third relies on the contemplation of desire; this alone is correct. △ Second, the refutation of divergent interpretations.
Some say that mental states and their concomitants (*citta-caitta*) apprehend an object only through the power of the desire for that object;

therefore, the Sūtra says that desire is the root of all phenomena (and thus must be a universal factor). That claim is incorrect. The apprehension of an object by the mind and its associates occurs by means of attention (*manasikāra*).
This is because the various sacred teachings state that when attention is present, consciousness arises. Nowhere is it ever said that desire can produce the mind and its concomitants.
For this reason, although it is said that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the root of all phenomena (*dharma*), does it follow that the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are all produced by craving?
Therefore, when it is said that desire (*chanda*) is the basis of all phenomena, it refers to all activities (*karma*) arising from desire;

or, it refers to how wholesome desire (*kuśala-chanda*) can incite right effort (*samyak-vīrya*), since that effort assists in accomplishing all virtuous deeds. Thus, the treatise states that this [desire] has effort as its support (*vīryāśraya*).
Karma.
Wholesome matters are necessarily accomplished through right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*), and right effort is further initiated by wholesome desire (*chanda*).

Therefore, it is said that wholesome desire is the root of all dharmas; this does not mean that mind and mental factors arise from desire. The rest may be understood accordingly. This concludes the first explanation.

The desire [to explain] is concluded. △ Second, the explanation of *adhimokṣa* (resolute conviction) has two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the refutation of divergent interpretations. Now, for the first: What is *adhimokṣa*?
Its nature (*svabhāva*) is the confirmation and sustaining of a determined object. Its function (*karman*) is that it cannot be led astray or moved by other conditions.
That is to say, through the power of the evidence provided by the principles of correct or erroneous teachings, one thoroughly determines and confirms the object of apprehension.

Because it cannot be diverted by other conditions, there is no resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) whatsoever regarding an object of doubt; nor is there resolute conviction in what is not a determined decision.
For this reason, resolute conviction is not included among the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).
"Decisive object" (*niścita-viṣaya*) means precisely that which is not an object of hesitation. The rest may be understood. 2. Refuting Alternative Explanations:
Some say that when the mind and its associates apprehend their respective objects, they are all characterized by *adhimokṣa* (resolute conviction), because there is no obstruction;

therefore, it is a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*). That explanation is irrational. Why? Because that which is capable of being unobstructed is precisely the various phenomena (*dharma*) that serve as the objects of cognition (*ālambana*). As for that which is not obstructed...

This refers to the mind and its associates (the subjective factors that take [an object] as their focal point), which thus function as the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). As for the superior conditions that initiate the mind and mental states, these are the sense faculties (*indriya*) and attention (*manasikāra*).

If one were to claim that it is by virtue of this [resolute conviction, *adhimukti*] that those superior conditions are initiated, then this resolute conviction itself would have to depend on yet another initiator, leading to the fallacy of infinite regress.

The meanings may be understood accordingly. This concludes the second [section], the explanation of *adhimokṣa* (resolute belief). △ Third, the explanation of *smṛti* (mindfulness), in two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the refutation of divergent interpretations. Now, the first: What is mindfulness?
Its nature consists in causing the mind to clearly and attentively remember (*smaraṇa*) and not forget objects previously experienced. It is concentration.
Its function is to serve as a basis. That is to say, it repeatedly recollects and maintains objects previously experienced so that they are not forgotten;

furthermore, because it is capable of inducing meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it does not give rise to mindfulness at all regarding objects of a nature never before experienced. Even regarding objects previously experienced, if one cannot clearly remember them, mindfulness likewise does not arise.
Therefore, mindfulness is certainly not included among the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).
△ Second, the refutation of divergent interpretations.

Some say that the arising of the mind must necessarily be accompanied by mindfulness (*smṛti*), because mindfulness serves as the cause for recollection at a later time; therefore, it [mindfulness] must be a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*).

That explanation is irrational. For if that were so, there would be no instances where delusion (*moha*), faith (*śraddhā*), and so forth exist at a later time, since they too would have existed previously. However, the preceding mind...

Mental factors (*caitta*). Or rather, it is the power of perception (*saṃjñā*)—which grasps the specific boundaries of an object—that is sufficient to serve as the cause for recollection at a later time.

If it is argued that recollection at a later time occurs because mindfulness (*smṛti*) exists as its cause at the moment the mind arises, then when delusion (*moha*) or other evils, or faith (*śraddhā*) and other virtues, arise at a later time, would these also [occur] simply because delusion, faith, and so forth exist at the moment the mind arises?
[Is it] the cause? How much more so for the power of the mind, mental factors, and perception, which are sufficient to serve as the cause of mindfulness (*smṛti*).

Why must one insist that mindfulness arises simultaneously with the mind? The third explanation of mindfulness is concluded. △ Fourth, the explanation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) has two parts:
first, the formal explanation; second, the refutation of divergent interpretations. Now, the first [part].

What is concentration (*samādhi*)? Its nature is to cause the mind to focus one-pointedly upon the object of observation without distraction. Its function is to serve as the basis for wisdom (*jñāna*).
That is to say, within the context of observing objects that are either beneficial, detrimental, or neither, concentration causes the mind to focus one-pointedly without distraction;

based upon this, there arises the wisdom of discernment (*viniścaya-jñāna*). (However,) the expression "one-pointedness of mind" merely indicates that whatever state one wishes to abide in, one is able to abide therein.

It is not necessarily the case that it [samādhi] exists only when the mind dwells on a single object. If it were otherwise, then during the stage of the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga), when one sequentially contemplates the various truths such as suffering across the upper and lower realms, the objects would differ from one moment to the next;

thus, there would be no meditative concentration (samādhi), as the mind would not be focused exclusively on a single object. If the mind were not bound in concentration upon an object, then meditative absorption (dhyāna) would not arise.
Therefore, [samādhi] is not a universal mental factor (sarvatraga).
That which accords with reason is called "attainment"; that which opposes reason is called "loss. That which is neither attainment nor loss is called the "object of neither.
If it is a discerning wisdom that is wholesome, one attains the former and abandons the latter; if it is a discerning wisdom that is defiled, one attains the latter and abandons the former.

If it is neutral (*avyākṛta*) decisive knowledge, it takes as its object the characteristics of that which is neither [wholesome nor unwholesome]. Therefore, concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) both pervade all three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Regarding the vision path (*darśanamārga*) that contemplates the various truths: one thoroughly observes the four truths of the desire realm and the four truths of the form and formless realms, thereby accomplishing the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and the eight knowledges (*jñāna*). As for "equipoise" (*samāhita*), it means to maintain with impartiality.
The meaning [of this term] is *samādhi* in Sanskrit. It is a mental factor of concentration (*samādhicaitasika*). In the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*, its original name is indeed *samādhi*.
△ Second, refuting divergent interpretations.

Some say that at that time, although the mind is not focused intently upon the object, concentration nevertheless arises; however, because its characteristics are subtle and hidden, it is subsumed under the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*). [This is refuted as follows:]

One should state the true words: if it is claimed that this [samādhi] necessarily causes the mind and its associates to harmonize and converge upon a single object, and is therefore a universal (sarvatraga) factor, this reasoning is also incorrect;
for such harmony is the function of contact (sparśa), not the function of samādhi.

Furthermore, if it is claimed that this [samādhi] is included among the universals because it prevents the mind from shifting its object for even a single moment, this too is unreasonable; for a single momentary mind, by itself, [does not shift].

Because it has the meaning of being unchanging (*avikāra*). If it is argued that it is included among the universal [mental factors] because the concentrated mind grasps its object, that too is irrational;
for it is attention (*manaskāra*) that causes the mind to grasp its object, not concentration.

Furthermore, some say that the essence of this concentration is the mind itself (it does not have a separate essence), since the Sūtra states that among the three trainings, concentration is the training of the mind, and it is also described as one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
That is not a valid proof. It is because [the sūtra] speaks of "one-pointedness of mind" and "training of the mind" by means of relying on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to collect the mind;

for concentration is subsumed under the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold path (*mārgāṅga*), just as mindfulness (*smṛti*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and so forth each have their own distinct intrinsic nature and are not identical to the mind itself.
