this is the first explanation of the mundane path, namely the four dhyānas and eight samāpattis which belong to the category of contaminated wholesome states. As for the supramundane path:
This refers precisely to the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*). The rest may be understood accordingly.

According to another interpretation, that [previous] explanation is not logically tenable; for if one has not yet reached a definitive mind through investigation into phenomena and principles, faith will not arise.
It would not be wholesome, like defiled minds and the like, because of the absence of pure faith.

Since the categories of shame (*hrī*) and dread (*apatrāpya*) have different bases (*āśraya*), although their objects (*ālambana*) are distinct, they both pervade all wholesome minds, as has already been stated.

If pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) were not produced in the supramundane path, then this factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) would not be untainted (*anāsrava*). If equanimity (*upekṣā*) and heedfulness (*apramāda*) were absent from the mundane path, then...
Because it is not [merely] the non-occurrence of tranquility, but rather the prevention of evil and the cultivation of good; furthermore, because one must subdue restlessness and heedlessness.
Since wholesome contaminated minds possess four factors—including diligence and the three roots—just like supramundane paths, they should likewise possess two [others]: equanimity and heedfulness.

When a wholesome mind arises, it does not harm things precisely because it opposes that which could cause harm; thus, it is given the name "non-harming" (*avihiṃsā*). Nevertheless, the treatise speaks of six [factors].
As for the eleven [factors] arising in each stage, these are merely stated according to whichever [factor] is predominant in each respective case.
Therefore, the claim made by the first interpretation—that the remaining seven are indeterminate—is certainly not reasonable.
This constitutes the second correct interpretation. First, it refutes the preceding errors; next, by stating "the treatise says below," it reconciles and explains the treatise cited therein.
Regarding the statement that "this or that is taught based on the predominance of this or that": this refers to the stage of determination (*niścaya*), wherein faith (*śraddhā*) predominates;

the stage of quiescence from defilement (*saṃkleśa*), wherein shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) predominate; and so on, up to the time of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgraha*), wherein non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) predominates.
It should be stated that among the eleven mental factors beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), ten are universal to wholesome minds, while pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is not.
Pliancy exists only in the state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*), for it is the thorough refinement of body and mind; it is absent in other states. As stated in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*:

"The ten wholesome mental factors are universal to wholesome minds, whether in the stage of concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*) or the non-concentrated stage (*asamāhitabhūmi*); however, within the mind of the concentrated stage, pliancy is added."

Therefore, this correctly explains that ten [mental factors] are universal while one is not. "Concentrated states" (*samāhita-bhūmi*) refers to the stage of meditative equipoise, namely, within the samādhis of the four dhyānas, the eight liberations, and so forth.
"Non-concentrated states" (*asamāhita-bhūmi*) refers to the stage of distracted mind within the desire realm.

There is an interpretation that the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of meditative concentration also receives the name "concentration" (*samādhi*), because it also possesses a slight degree of the sense of being harmonized and refined (*praśrabdhi*).

For this reason, pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) exists even in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Otherwise, it would contradict the *Maulī Bhūmi*, which states that the eleven factors beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) are common to all stages (*sarvabhūmika*).

This presents another divergent interpretation. "Preparatory application for meditative concentration" (*samādhi-prayoga*) refers to the preliminary means prior to concentration; it specifically points to the "not-yet-reached stage" (*anāgamya-samādhi*).

One view holds that pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) exists only within meditative concentration, because it is nourished by concentration and thus becomes harmonious and pervasive. The treatise states that [it exists] in the desire realm...
Regarding the various minds and mental factors within the realms, they are termed "non-concentrated stages" (*asamāhita-bhūmi*) due to the absence of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
As for the statement that there are eleven stages in total, this is because [the three stages] including those with vitarka and vicāra (*savitarkā savicārā bhūmiḥ*, etc. are all included therein.
This correctly clarifies that there is no *prasrabdhi* (serenity) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Next, I shall further explain the intended meaning of the treatise (*śāstra*) cited therein.

When the treatise states that all stages (*bhūmi*) comprise eleven types, it refers to the three levels of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) characterized by applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), and so forth;

it does not refer to the nine stages of the three realms (*tridhātu*). This is because the desire realm is designated as the "unstable stage" (*aniyata-bhūmi*), precisely due to its lack of *prasrabdhi*.
Regarding the "three stages": first, the fundamental first dhyāna is called the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra;

second, the preparatory stage of the second dhyāna is called the samādhi without vitarka but with vicāra; third, from the fundamental second dhyāna upward, all are called the samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra.
This concludes the section on the gate of the pervasive and non-pervasive. △ Third, the co-arising of the various consciousnesses.
The Section on Arising.

These eleven types have already been explained in detail; regarding their presence or absence according to the respective stages, within the seventh and eighth consciousnesses they exist [only] when present, while within the sixth consciousness they are definitely present in all states.
If it is not a state of meditative equipoise, there is the view that it lacks only pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). The five sensory consciousnesses possess only ten types.

There is natural distraction due to the absence of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). According to one interpretation, the five consciousnesses also possess pliancy; for those [five consciousnesses] that are wholesome and induced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) also possess a state of being harmonious and supple.
Furthermore, because they are conjoined with the Wisdom of Accomplishing What is to be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), they must necessarily possess pliancy.

In the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses], when they have not yet undergone transformation (*parāvṛtti*), there are no eleven wholesome factors; if they have already undergone transformation, they are all necessarily associated [with them].
As for the sixth consciousness, its outflowing (*sāsrava*) scattered wholesome states lack *praśrabdhi* (pliancy), whereas its outflowing meditative wholesome states possess all eleven.
It goes without saying that this does not apply to the untainted (*anāsrava*) state. Regarding the two interpretations of the five consciousnesses, the second interpretation is correct.
However, within the tainted (*sāsrava*) stage, the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses are bound exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and thus lack pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).

The visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses, which extend into the first dhyāna, possess a sense of composure and harmony as they are induced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*). If one reaches the untainted stage, [the situation changes].
The five consciousnesses associated with the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) necessarily all possess *praśrabdhi* (serenity).
△ Fourth, the section on association with the various feelings (*vedanā*).

(Question: With which feelings are these eleven wholesome [mental factors] associated? (Answer: Ten [wholesome mental factors] can be associated with the five feelings; [the eleventh,] *praśrabdhi*, is associated with one [feeling].
(Regarding the seeds: they exclude the two feelings of sorrow and suffering. This is because any feeling that involves oppression is necessarily devoid of tranquility.
△ Fifth, the section on association with specific objects.

These [mental factors] are all capable of being associated with the object-specific mental factors (*viṣaya-viniyata*), because they are not mutually contradictory with desire (*chanda*) and the others.
△ Sixth: The Section on the Mutual Inclusion of the Three Natures.
Eleven are exclusively wholesome.
△ Seventh, the gate of affiliation with the three realms:
pliancy is not affiliated with the desire realm; the remaining ten are all common to the three realms.
△ Section Eight: The Three Compendia of the Learners (*śaikṣa*) and Others. These all consist of the three categories of the learners and others.
The first fruit, second fruit, and third fruit, as well as the eleven virtues of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva, are all [the category of] those still in training (*śaikṣa*).
[The eleven wholesome factors] subsumed under the four fruits, the pratyekabuddhas, and the Tathāgatas are all subsumed under the category of "beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
All the eleven wholesome factors of ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) are subsumed under the category of "neither in training nor beyond training" (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa). △ Ninth:
The Section on the Mutual Subsumption of the Three Types of Abandonment.

They are not abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the six faculties, beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) and are not abandoned through seeing.

These six faculties are: the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), the faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*), the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

The first five faculties, beginning with faith, are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). If they are uncontaminated, they are subsumed within the three [uncontaminated] faculties.

Regarding the faculty of outflows (*āsrava-indriya*): here, the five faculties are first discussed in terms of being with-outflows (*sāsrava*). The nine untainted (*anāsrava*) faculties present during the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*) are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
The nine untainted faculties present during the stage of training (*śaikṣa-avasthā*) are called the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*).

The nine untainted faculties present during the stage of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa-avasthā*) are called the faculty of "one who has fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*). Although by means of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"...

The faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*). Having entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because there is nothing further to be known once the path has been seen, it is termed the faculty of "having fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Following the single moment of the path of seeing, one is then subsumed under the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Therefore, within the stage of cultivation, one abandons the faculty of "knowing the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) as well as the five contaminated faculties (*sāsravendriya*). These ten...
First, the wholesome (*kuśala*). Because it does not correspond with discriminative afflictions (*vibhāga-kleśa*), it is not abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*).

If it is contaminated wholesome (*sāsrava-kuśala*) or wholesome of preparatory application (*prayoga-kuśala*) that is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), it belongs to what is abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*).

If it is the truly uncontaminated wholesome, it is subsumed under what is not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*). (The nine faculties [are]: the five faculties beginning with faith, the mind faculty, the joy faculty, the pleasure faculty, and the equanimity faculty. △ Tenth: Conclusion of examples for remaining categories.
The distinctions regarding other categories should be contemplated according to reason;

their relationship with subsequent afflictions, such as the indeterminate ones, will be treated in the following section. This concludes the second part: the explanation of the wholesome mental factors.
△ Third, the explanation of the root afflictions has two parts: first, the presentation of the verse; second, the commentary. Now, the first.
Thus have the mental factors belonging to the wholesome state been explained. As for the mental factors that are afflictions (*kleśa*), what are their characteristics? The verse says:
Afflictions are said to be greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and wrong views.

△ Second, the commentary on the treatise has two parts: first, the direct explanation of the verses; second, the analysis by way of various categories. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, a brief explanation of the general name;
second, an extensive explanation of the specific names. This is the first [section].
The treatise states: Because these six natures—greed and the others—are subsumed within the category of root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), they receive the name "affliction.
Just as a tree possesses branches and leaves only when it has a root, all secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are produced by means of these six types of affliction;
therefore, these six are designated as the roots. All other secondary afflictions are merely derivatives of these.
Flow. Or because this is a particular state [of that], it is like branches and leaves. △ Second, the detailed explanation of the specific names has six parts:
first, the explanation of greed (*rāga*); sixth, the explanation of wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Now, the first.
What is greed (*lobha*)? Its nature is attachment to existence (*bhava*) and the requisites for existence (*bhavopakaraṇa*). Its function is to obstruct non-greed and to produce suffering;
that is to say, by the power of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) arise once again.

There is the "possession of existence" (*bhavopakarana*). Regarding the explanation of the wholesome in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*: the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are all that which is grasped and attached to by deluded cognition; therefore, they are called the "aggregates of grasping" (*upādānaskandha*).
Second, the explanation of hatred (*dveṣa*): What is hatred?
Its nature is that of malice and resentment toward suffering and the causes of suffering. It acts as an obstacle to non-hatred (*adveṣa*) and is characterized by a lack of peace.
Its function is to serve as the basis for misconduct; that is to say, hatred necessarily causes affliction and distress to body and mind, because it gives rise to various unwholesome karmas.

As previously explained, it is a source of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); because it causes affliction and distress to body and mind, it is called "the nature of insecurity. It gives rise to various...

Because it is an evil karma, it is said to be "the basis for evil conduct. Since this is exclusively evil and does not extend to the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta), it is said to be "of an unwholesome nature" (akuśala-svabhāva).
△ Third, the explanation of delusion (moha).
What is delusion (*moha*)? Its nature is confusion and darkness regarding all principles and phenomena. Its function is to obstruct non-delusion and to serve as the basis for all defilements.

This means that by the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), it gives rise to doubt, false views, and other root afflictions (*kleśa*)—such as attachment—as well as the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) such as anger, thereby performing actions that attract the defiled phenomena of future existence within the three realms of rebirth.

Isolated ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) is primarily deluded regarding the principle of the truths (*satya*), while associated ignorance (*saṃprayuktā avidyā*) is also deluded regarding phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, it is said that its nature consists of being obscured and ignorant regarding both principles and phenomena. "All defilements" refers specifically to the afflictions, karma, and birth within the three realms.
△ Fourth, the explanation of pride (*māna*).
What is pride (*māna*)? Its nature is the loftiness of mind toward others based on reliance upon one’s own excellence. Its function is to obstruct non-pride and to give rise to suffering.

That is to say, if one possesses pride, the mind does not become humble before the virtues of the Three Jewels—which are truly pure—and before those who possess virtue; instead, it competes by generating the notions of "self" and "other.
Because of this, one revolves endlessly in the cycle of birth and death and undergoes all manner of suffering. As for the distinctions of this pride, there are seven.

There are nine types, which arise with respect to the three categories of self, qualities, and objects. All of them are common to both those abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Within the state of an Ārya, since innate (*sahaja*) *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") is capable of manifesting, other varieties of pride (*māna*) may likewise arise from this [basis] within the state of an Ārya.
There is no error here.
Regarding the seven types of pride (*māna*): first, pride (*māna*), which refers to such things as a lack of respect for one's inferiors while looking down upon them.
Second, excessive pride (*atimāna*), which refers to falsely regarding equals as inferior, or falsely regarding superiors as one's equal. Third, pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*).
1. The pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*): regarding those who are superior as inferior. 2. The four types of pride of self (*asmimāna*):
falsely clinging to a self and thereby giving rise to arrogance. 3. The pride of superiority (*adhimāna*): having attained only a small measure of realization, claiming to be fully satisfied;

for example, mistakenly identifying the four *dhyānas* as the four fruits of the path. 4. The pride of inferiority (*hīnamāna*): while one is actually far inferior, falsely claiming to be only slightly inferior; or even though...

Knowing that the other is superior, one refuses to give rise to respect; this is the seventh type of false pride (*mithyāmāna*), which refers to falsely claiming to possess virtues when one actually lacks them.
Regarding the nine types of pride (*navavidhamāna*): with respect to the self (*ātman*), virtues (*guṇa*), and status (*sthāna*), each is divided into three grades—superior, equal, and inferior.

Here, "self" is the essence of a false, conventional designation that is grasped as real; "virtues" refers to the qualities one has cultivated; and "status" refers to the sphere of one's experience or position.
Whether it be "I am superior," "I am equal," or "I am inferior"; or whether it be "my qualities are superior," "my qualities are equal," or "my qualities are inferior";

or whether it be "my status is superior," "my status is equal," or "my status is inferior"—these are called the nine types. Based on these, one gives rise to either pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), or the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*);
this can be understood by reflection. Among these, the sevenfold and ninefold classifications are not discussed here; rather, they are categorized according to their constituent parts.

Regarding the arising of distinct afflictions: these are abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*). If they arise based on innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) by taking an object as their condition, they are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*). △ Fifth, resolving doubts.
What is doubt? Its nature is indecision and lack of resolution regarding whether the principles of the truths exist or do not exist.
Its function is to obstruct the absence of doubt and all wholesome qualities; for it is said that in one who is hesitant, the wholesome does not arise.

Question: It is true that if one hesitates, goodness will not arise; thus, the fault is indeed great. However, regarding greed, hatred, delusion, and pride, if one recognizes their faults, one can still apply the mind to eliminate them.
But as for the ultimate reality (*tattva*), which has not yet been clarified, how can one forcibly pretend to know what one does not know?
Answer: Forcibly pretending to know what one does not know is precisely the root of doubt. If...
To eliminate doubt, there is only one way: to maintain a humble mind and pursue extensive learning; to inquire with discernment and reflect with care;

to rely on the orthodox teachings as a compass and upon teachers and friends as one’s eyes. Furthermore, one must emulate Shun’s fondness for questioning and observation, and follow Confucius’s practice of taking both the good and the bad as teachers.
Only then can the root of doubt be severed forever, leading one directly to the ground of non-doubt.

There is another interpretation: this doubt has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence. This is because it is defined as doubt due to its function of hesitant discernment regarding the object under investigation;
furthermore, since *vicikitsā* (doubt) is a derivative of *mati* (intellection), and *mati* and *prajñā* are not different in meaning, [wisdom constitutes its essence].
This presents an alternative interpretation. "Vi" (毗) means "to assist" (助), which is synonymous with "to aid" (輔). Both *amati* and *prajñā* are translated as "wisdom" (*hui*).
To say that "vi- assists amati" constitutes a point of doubt is analogous to the saying: "Great doubt leads to great awakening;
small doubt leads to small awakening; no doubt leads to no awakening."

There is another interpretation: this doubt has a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of its own; because of this doubt, wisdom (*prajñā*) fails to reach a decision, yet it is not identical to wisdom itself.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that among the six afflictions, only the view (*dṛṣṭi*) is conventionally existent (*saṃvṛti-sat*), because it is a constituent part of wisdom.

The remaining five [afflictions] are substantially existent (*dravya-sat*) because each possesses a distinct nature. If you claim that doubt assists *mati* (wisdom), you would then be asserting that wisdom itself is [the agent].
If doubt (doubt as a substance; it may also assist consciousness) were to take wisdom as its essence, then wisdom would consequently become the essence of consciousness.
Since the meaning does not change through the assistance provided by another, this doubt does not have wisdom as its essence.

This is the correct interpretation. If [the term] is *nam*, it is translated here as "wisdom" (*jñāna*). Regarding wisdom (*jñāna*) and discernment (*prajñā*): both are the faculty of discernment (*prajñā*) among the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*).
Whether they are with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), whether wholesome (*kuśala*) or defiled (*kliṣṭa*), they may all be called discernment, and they may all be called wisdom.
However, within the state of being without outflows, that which is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) is termed discernment, while that which is conceptual (*savikalpa*) is termed wisdom. Nevertheless...
The fundamental [wisdom] and the subsequently attained wisdom are both termed "knowledge" (jñāna). The path-wisdom and the knowledge of the paths are both termed "insight" (prajñā).

Thus, one knows that names are established according to their functions; yet regarding their essence, they originally possess no dual nature. Consciousness (vijñāna) is the sovereign mind (citta-rāja).
Wisdom (*jñāna*) is a mental factor (*caitta*). If you claim that doubt has wisdom as its essence, then consciousness (*vijñāna*) should likewise have wisdom as its essence;
how could this be acceptable? First, I shall present a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) based on contradiction: Consciousness is the subject (*dharmin*);

it follows that it must have wisdom as its essence (*pakṣa*), because it assists wisdom (*hetu*), just as doubt assists wisdom (*dṛṣṭānta*). Next, I shall present the formal argument for my own position: Doubt, which assists wisdom...

This is an existent dharma. Its thesis is that it does not have wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence. The reason is that it possesses a distinct nature; it is not because its meaning undergoes transformation through the power of assistance.
An analogy is consciousness assisted by wisdom (*jñāna*). This concludes the fifth section, the resolution of doubts. △ Sixth, the explanation of evil views has two parts:
first, a general explanation of their characteristics and functions; second, a detailed demonstration of their distinctions. Now, the first part.
What is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)? It is the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with defilement that seeks after the principles of the truths in a distorted manner;
its function is to obstruct right vision and to bring about suffering, for those who hold wrong views undergo much suffering.
Because it involves investigation, its essence is wisdom (*prajñā*). Because it is inverted, it is termed "defiled. What is meant by inversion?

It is merely the false attachment to a real self and real dharmas. As for the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*), how have they ever failed to seek liberation from birth and death?
It is solely because they are entangled by the dual attachments to self and dharmas that they engage in various ascetic practices.
It would not be in vain; yet, in this life and in future lives, one will be unable to attain liberation.

Thus, if one wishes to transcend birth and death, can it not be considered an urgent task to destroy false views? Part Two: A Detailed Exposition of the Differences. This has two sections: first, the enumeration of the categories;
second, the explanation of their characteristics. Now, the first section.
These aspects of the [wrong] views differ in five ways.

△ Second, the explanation of their characteristics has four parts: first, the explanation of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) [up to...]; fourth, the explanation of the two graspings (*parāmarśa*). Now, the first.
First is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which consists of grasping at the five aggregates of clinging as "I" and "mine.

Its function is to serve as the basis for all types of speculative views. This [view] comprises both the conceptualized (*vikalpita*) and the innate (*sahaja*). As for the distinctions within this view, there are twenty positions, sixty-five, and so forth; these are all comprised within the category of conceptually arisen [views].

*Satkāya* (the view of a self-identity) is translated as "accumulation. This refers to the accumulation of the four great elements and the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), which is conventionally designated as a "body.
Based upon this body, one falsely gives rise to the grasping of "I" and "mine"; therefore, it is called the *satkāyadṛṣṭi*. Furthermore, this view serves as the root of all evil views;
for all views of extremes, heterodoxy, and the like, arise in dependence upon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Regarding this:

This fundamental view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), when the seventh consciousness takes the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its object and gives rise to a mental image within itself,
spontaneously grasping it as a self, is subsumed under innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*). Furthermore, when the sixth consciousness takes the five appropriated aggregates (*pañcopādānaskandha*)—
either collectively or individually— as its object and gives rise to a mental image within itself, spontaneously grasping them as "self" and "mine," this too is an innate affliction.

[They are] subsumed [under delusion]. If the sixth consciousness takes false teachings and false contemplation as its objects, giving rise to twenty phrases, sixty-five [phrases], and various other kinds of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), then these are subsumed solely under the delusions of discrimination. Regarding the "twenty phrases":
first, it is said that the self is large and form is small, and that form is within the self; second, it is said that form is large and the self is small, and that the self is within form.

The third [view] asserts that form (*rūpa*) itself is the self; the fourth asserts that the self is apart from form. The same fourfold application applies to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Thus, there are twenty propositions in total. Regarding the sixty-five propositions: for each of the five aggregates, one clings to it as the self and the remaining four aggregates as "mine" (*ātmīya*).
Within these four [categories], each possesses three factors: ornaments, servants, and dwellings. [Thus, for each aggregate: the self and...

The view of "mine" (*ātmīya*) consists of thirteen propositions. When these are discussed in relation to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) mutually, they total sixty-five. 2. Explanation of the View of Extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*).
The view of grasping at extremes refers to the adherence to either annihilationism or eternalism based upon that same view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).

Its function is to obstruct the middle way and the departure [from suffering]. This [view] comprises both the conceptualized (*vikalpita*) and the innate (*sahaja*) types. Among the various categories of views, there is that which clings to the past limit (*pūrvānta*).

The four theories of universal permanence, the theory of partial permanence, and the sixteen theories concerning the future— namely, those involving perception, non-perception, and neither— each consisting of eight views,
as well as the seven theories of annihilation and so forth, are all exclusively comprised within the category of views arising from discrimination.
To abide in the Middle Way is precisely the correct principle of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), which is neither annihilationism nor eternalism.

By realizing this correct principle of dependent origination, one is able to develop right faith in cause and effect, practice according to the teachings, and transcend birth and death; thus, the two attachments to annihilation and eternity are severed.
These directly obstruct this practice. Furthermore, there are two distinct types—innate (*sahaja*) and conceptual (*vikalpita*)—as explained in detail below.

As for the four views of permanence and so forth, they arise based on false teachings and false reflection; thus, they belong exclusively to the category of conceptual afflictions (*parikalpita-kleśa*).
Regarding the four views of permanence: first is the calculation of permanence for twenty eons; second is the calculation of permanence for forty eons.
The third [view] calculates eighty eons as permanent. The fourth reckons the wisdom of swift characteristics as falsely claiming permanence.

Regarding those who hold one part to be permanent: first, the Brahmā heaven is permanent while the self is impermanent; second, it is impermanent due to playful laughter; third, it is impermanent due to mutual observation of physical marks;
fourth, swift observation deems both the permanent and the impermanent. There are sixteen [views] regarding the existence of perception at the future limit (*paścimānta*).
Namely: first, the view that there is form; second, the view that there is no form; third, the view that there is both form and no form;
fourth, the view that there is neither form nor no form; fifth, the view of finitude; sixth, the view of infinitude;
seventh, the view of both finitude and infinitude; eighth, the view of neither finitude nor infinitude; ninth, the view of pleasure; tenth, the view of suffering; eleventh, the view of pleasure...

13. There is the view that there is suffering. 14. Twelve views of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure. 15. The single-perception [view]. 16. The diversified-perception [view]. 17. The limited-perception [view].
18. The infinite-perception [view]. Regarding the eight theorists on non-perception: 1. Those who possess form. 2. Those who are formless. 3.
Those who possess both form and formlessness. 4. Those who possess neither form nor formlessness. 5. Those who are finite. 6. Those who are infinite.

7. The theory of finitude and infinitude; 8. The theory of neither finitude nor infinitude. The eight theories of "neither" are identical in name and characteristic to the eight theories of non-perception.
The seven theories of annihilation are: 1. annihilation in this very body; 2. annihilation in the desire realm heavens; 3. annihilation in the form realm heavens; 4.

annihilation in the sphere of infinite space; 5. annihilation in the sphere of infinite consciousness; 6. annihilation in the sphere of nothingness; 7. annihilation in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
They cease at the sphere of non-perception (*asaṃjñāyatana*). These [views] all appear in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* of the Āgamas and are also known as the sixty-two views of the *Brahmajāla*.

This is the fundamental tenet of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) of the Western Regions. One should not cite the passage on the "demonic hindrances" (*māra-skandha*) from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* to explain them;
for the sixty-two views regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* refer to errors that arise during the cultivation of the mind.
This is not entirely the same as that. △ Third, the explanation of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). There are three types of wrong view:
namely, the denial of cause, effect, activity, and substantial reality; and all other erroneous attachments not subsumed under the four views (which are also included here).

This is because, like the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), its name and meaning are all-encompassing. These distinctions of this view [are found] among the various [evil] views and tendencies.

Among these, there are those who hold the two theories of causelessness regarding the past; those who hold the four views on whether the world is finite and so forth; those who engage in evasive equivocation (*amarā-vikkhepa*);
and those who conceive of five types of present nirvāṇa regarding the future. Or they conceive that Īśvara, Prajāpati, Brahmā, Śakra, or other such entities are eternal and unchanging;
or they conceive that Īśvara and others are the cause of all things; or they recklessly conceive various false forms of liberation. Or...
There are those who falsely cling to what is not the Path as being the Path; all such cases as these are subsumed under wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). These are:

first, the denial of the existence of causes, both wholesome and unwholesome; second, the denial of the existence of results, both suffering and happiness, which are summoned by wholesome and unwholesome causes;
third, the denial of the efficacy of wholesome and unwholesome actions; and fourth, the denial of the existence of the mundane and the supramundane.

Various conventional realities, such as father and son or the holy and the ordinary, which are not subsumed under the four views—namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth—are all subsumed under this wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
This is, for example, like how things not subsumed under the three conditions, such as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), are all subsumed under the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Regarding the two types of "causelessness" (*ahetuvāda*): the first is that which comes from the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), wherein one considers oneself to be primordial...
There is no present existence. First, one quickly observes and falsely claims that things exist without cause.

Regarding the four views on finitude: first, the perception of finitude; second, the perception of infinity; third, the view that the zenith is finite while the four cardinal directions are infinite; and fourth, the view that it is neither finite nor infinite.
Regarding the four types of evasive equivocation regarding death: first, one asks whether there is retribution for good and evil or not.
1. Whether there is another world or no other world; 2. Whether there is another world or no other world; 3. What is wholesome and what is unwholesome; 4.

Being ignorant, deluded, dull, and obtuse, answering according to the words of others; 5. Those who manifest nirvāṇa: first, some say that indulging in the five desires of the present life is itself nirvāṇa;
second, some say the first dhyāna is nirvāṇa; third, some say the second dhyāna is nirvāṇa.
[Some] claim that the third dhyāna is nirvāṇa; others claim that the fourth dhyāna is nirvāṇa.

Or they may reckon [it to be] Maheśvara and so forth—this is as refuted in the first fascicle regarding various false liberations. These are cases of taking what is not the fruit to be the fruit, and taking what is not the path to be the path;
that is, taking what is not the cause to be the cause. △ Fourth, the explanation of the two graspings (*dvaya-grāha*).

4. Adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). This refers to the grasping at any one view among all views, as well as the aggregates upon which it relies, as being the most excellent cause for attaining purification.
Its function is to serve as the basis for all conflict and contention. 5. Adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

This refers to the grasping at precepts and observances that accord with various views, as well as the aggregates upon which they rely, as being the most excellent cause for attaining purification. [Its function is] non-...
Its function is to serve as the basis for striving in vain and undergoing suffering;
this correctly explains the characteristics of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*).
Because of the adherence to views, mutual opposition arises and strife proliferates; because of the observance of false precepts, one undergoes wrongful toil and suffering that are empty of benefit.
However, there are passages that state: "Grasping [a non-result] as supreme is called the 'view of grasping at views' (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*);

grasping [that which is not a cause] as a means of purification is called the 'clinging to precepts and observances' (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). This is stated by way of mutual abbreviation. Alternatively, it is a door of reasoning for following along [with the context].

Otherwise, why would [the treatises] not describe the misapprehension of what is not cessation as cessation, or what is not the path as the path, as "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)? It is not [so described].
"Are they subsumed under the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*)?

This addresses the general objection. The meaning of the text is clear. The intent is to clarify that only when cause and effect are both conceptually constructed together is it termed "the two types of grasping";

if one constructs only cause or only effect individually, it merely belongs to false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). The initial correct explanation of the verse is concluded. △ Second, the classification by various categories.
Section Eleven: The Eleven Distinct Gates. First, the Gate of Simultaneous Arising and Discursive Origination (through to the eleventh gate, the Summary of Remaining Gates). Now, for the first:

Among these ten afflictions, both general and specific, six are capable of arising both simultaneously (*sahaja*) and through discursive origination (*vikalpita*), because they can arise both spontaneously and through deliberate reflection.
Doubt and the final three views arise only through discursive origination; they necessarily depend upon evil friends and false teachings.
Because they arise only after one has examined and reflected through the power of instruction, there are six in total;
yet, when distinguished in detail, they must be divided into ten. Thus it is said that there are ten afflictions in both their general and specific forms.

Among these six—greed, hatred, delusion, pride, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—those that arise spontaneously and naturally are called innate (*sahaja*) afflictions.

Those that arise from one part of discursive investigation are called "conceptual afflictions" (*vikalpa-kleśa*). These include doubt, wrong view, the grasping at views, and the grasping at precepts and rituals;

these four types arise solely through conceptualization. Innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) are those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); they are also called "afflictions of thought" (*citta-kleśa*).
Regarding the afflictions of discrimination (*vikalpita-kleśa*), these are the afflictions abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*). They are also called "afflictions of insight" (*darśana-kleśa*).

Among the views of extreme adherence (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), there is a position [held by some] that only [the view of permanence] is innate (*sahaja*). This is because the characteristic of the view of permanence is coarse;
it must necessarily be induced by the power of evil friends and the like. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts state: "Which view of extreme adherence is innate?"

Yes. This refers to those who have not yet entered the path of seeing (prior to the path of seeing) and are engaged in the realization of the learner (*śaikṣa-abhisamaya*). Having already suppressed the manifest afflictions arising from conceptual construction, they nevertheless give rise to such fear within their minds, thinking:
"Now, where is my 'I'? Thus, even birds and beasts, when encountering adverse conditions, all experience terror, fearing that their self will be annihilated.

The following section further analyzes the meaning of the innate nature (*sahaja*) of the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). The two attachments to annihilation and permanence are termed the "view of extremes.
Regarding this, there are two schools of interpretation. First, the initial school maintains that the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) is admitted to be innate in two cases:

first, those training in the realization of the truths (*abhisamaya*) who, having already suppressed the afflictions of the views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), still give rise to fear of annihilation; second, birds and beasts who lack [the capacity for] evil.

The *Shiyou jiao* (Treatise on the Instruction of Friends) states that while the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) do not arise [in animals], they do give rise to the fear of annihilation. Thus, we know that the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) extends to the innate (*sahaja*).

There is another interpretation: that treatise speaks according to coarse characteristics; in reality, the innate also commonly includes the speculative view (*parāmarśa-dṛṣṭi*), as seen in the case of birds, beasts, and the like.
Grasping at the self as eternally existing, one zealously accumulates provisions for a long duration;

therefore, treatises such as the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* all state that regarding the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), one grasps at them as either annihilated or eternal—whether this arises simultaneously with birth (*sahaja*) or through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpita*).

This is the second interpretation. It correctly allows that the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*) also extends to the innate (*sahaja*). The meaning of both [interpretations] may be understood accordingly.
The section on the gate of innate and discriminated [views] is concluded. △ Second, the gate of association within its own class (*sva-jātīya-samprayoga*).
(Question: Among these ten afflictions (*kleśa*), with how many are each associated? (Answer: Greed (*lobha*) and hatred (*dveṣa*), as well as doubt (*vicikitsā*), definitely do not arise together.

This is because the objects of love (*lobha*) and aversion (*dveṣa*) must necessarily differ; because doubt involves indecision regarding the object; and because greed lacks the quality of non-attachment. Greed may or may not be associated with pride (*māna*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*).

It is not certain, because that which is loved becomes the object of greed, while that which is despised becomes the object of pride; thus, their objects are not identical. Therefore, it is said [they are not necessarily concomitant].
They arise together. Since the objects of what is defiled (namely greed) and what is relied upon (namely pride) can be the same, it is said that they are associated.

Because the objects of the five views are all desirable, there is no fault in greed being associated with the five views. ○ Anger and pride, or anger and doubt, may or may not arise together (it is not necessarily fixed).

Since the object of what is reviled (namely anger) and the object of what is relied upon (namely pride) are not one and the same, it is said that they are not associated. [The object] of what is despised is pride.

Because the objects of hatred (which constitute *dveṣa*) can be the same, it is said that they may arise simultaneously. At the initial moment of hesitation (which constitutes *vicikitsā*), one has not yet hated the object; therefore, it is said they do not arise together.
However, when long deliberation fails to reach a decision (this is *vicikitsā*), one then becomes incensed (this is *dveṣa*); thus, it is said they can be associated.

This applies accordingly to both favorable and unfavorable objects (hesitation toward a favorable object does not produce hatred, whereas hesitation toward an unfavorable object produces incitement). Hatred (*dveṣa*) and the two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*: views and precepts) necessarily...

It is not associated [with them]. Because one clings to it as the supreme path and does not feel aversion toward those [objects], this [hatred] may or may not be associated with the three views—namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Since one gives rise to the view of permanence (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) regarding an aggregate that is pleasant and does not produce aversion toward it, it is said to be non-associated.

Regarding the aggregate of suffering, because one gives rise to the view of permanence and consequently produces hatred and resentment, it is said that [hatred] arises simultaneously with it. The view of annihilation is the opposite of this;
thus, it is said that hatred may be present or absent. As for wrong view, which denies both evil and good phenomena, it is said accordingly that hatred is either present or absent.
When one holds the view of annihilation regarding the aggregate of pleasure, aversion arises; when one holds the view of annihilation regarding the aggregate of suffering, aversion does not arise.

Therefore, it is said that by reversing this, one explains the presence or absence of aversion. When wrong view denies and slanders evil matters, aversion does not arise, because one falsely calculates that there are no evil fruits.
When wrong view denies and slanders good matters, aversion can arise, because one falsely calculates that there is no goodness.
Because pride is fixed toward its object, whereas doubt is not, there is no sense of association between pride and doubt.

Pride may arise simultaneously with all five views, as their modes of activity (*ākāra*) do not contradict one another; however, it necessarily does not co-arise with the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
When the grasping at a self is severed, because there is no longer any arrogance or reliance, it is the same as a portion of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Pride is fixed upon its object; that is, regarding both the self that is relied upon and the person who is looked down upon, there is absolute certainty and no doubt.
"It is the same as a portion of the view of a self-identity" means that one who grasps the inferior aggregates of suffering as a self does not [regard them as non-existent].
One who relies on their own [views] to despise others does so because they hold wrong views that deny or disparage wholesome things;

since such a person has nothing to rely upon when despising others, doubt—which lacks definitive resolution—is incompatible with view. Therefore, doubt and view certainly do not arise together. ○ Regarding the five views: they...
They must not be associated [simultaneously], because there cannot be multiple instances of wisdom (*prajñā*) within a single moment of mind.
Since all five views (*dṛṣṭi*) have defiled wisdom as their essence, they certainly do not arise concurrently within a single moment of mind.
Delusion (*moha*) is associated with all nine [types of mental factors]. All afflictions (*kleśa*) arise necessarily through delusion;
for it is impossible to sever the various afflictions without first destroying delusion. Delusion is none other than ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the root of all afflictions.
Furthermore, clear understanding regarding all principles and phenomena is termed "non-delusion" (*amoha*). Regarding these principles...

Delusion regarding phenomena is termed ignorance (*moha*). One should know that "principle" refers to the two principles of emptiness and the middle, while "phenomena" refers to the actual entities of conventional truth, including their various causes, conditions, effects, and functions. Delusion regarding the principle of the middle is called fundamental ignorance;
delusion regarding the principle of emptiness and delusion regarding phenomena are both called derivative ignorance. Understanding the principle of the middle is termed...

In the Madhyamaka, that which understands the principle of emptiness is called the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), and that which understands all phenomena is called the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*).

Therefore, these two names—principle and phenomenon—completely encompass the three truths. These two types of minds that understand delusion completely encompass the three delusions and the three contemplations.
If one does not realize that the single principle and phenomenon possess distinctions of division and synthesis, then there are seven kinds of two truths.
Regarding the differences among the five kinds of three truths, the four kinds of four truths, the four kinds of one truth, and the four kinds of no-truth:

how could one abandon delusion and attain liberation? It is by means of wisdom that one integrates and dissolves delusion. This concludes the second section, the Gate of Correspondence within One’s Own Category.
△ Section Three: The Gate of Association with the Various Consciousnesses. (Question:

With which consciousnesses are these ten afflictions associated? (Answer: They are entirely absent in the *ālaya-vijñāna*. In the *manas*, there are four (namely: delusion, view, pride, and craving). In the *mano-vijñāna*, all ten are present.
In the five sensory consciousnesses, there are only three—namely, greed, hatred, and delusion—because they lack conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). This is determined by weighing [the evidence].
...and so forth. Because they give rise to pride and the like, they are non-conceptual;
that is to say, the first five consciousnesses lack the two types of conceptualization—recollection and deliberation—and possess only innate conceptualization (*svabhāva-vikalpa*).
Pride arises from weighing and measuring; doubt and views arise from reflection and investigation. Now...
Since the five consciousnesses lack the two types of discrimination—recollection and conceptualization—they cannot engage in weighing or deliberative reflection.
Consequently, they are not associated with pride, doubt, or the five views. △ Fourth, the section on association with the various feelings.

(Question: With which sensations (*vedanā*) are these ten afflictions associated? (Answer: Regarding the three—greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*)—they are set aside [for the moment].

Both innate (*sahaja*) and conceptually constructed (*vikalpita*) [afflictions] may all be associated with the five sensations. This is because greed, when encountering adverse conditions, is associated with both sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*).

Hatred, when meeting favorable objects, is associated with joy (*saumanasya*) and pleasure (*sukha*). [Alternative Interpretation: According to one view, innate and conceptually constructed pride (*māna*) may be associated with that which is not suffering.
Fourth, it is associated with feeling (*vedanā*). Because [the mind] relies on the inferior aggregates of suffering, it is also associated with sorrow (*daurmanasya*).

According to one interpretation, co-emergent pride (*sahaja-māna*) also arises together with the feeling of suffering; for it has already been stated that the mental consciousness possesses the feeling of suffering.

However, pride through conceptualization (*vikalpita-māna*) and the like do not exist in the realms of pure suffering (*ekānta-duḥkha-gati*), because in those pure realms of suffering there are no false teachers, false teachings, and so forth. Nevertheless, they do not create karma that leads to rebirth in the evil destinies.

Karma must be incited by afflictions that arise from conceptual discrimination; [such karma leads to rebirth in the evil destinies]. Now, within those realms of pure suffering, there are no afflictions arising from conceptual discrimination. Therefore...

Doubt (and the last three wrong views) can be associated with four types of feeling (excluding only painful feeling). This is because doubt regarding the future absence of suffering and so forth is also associated with the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*).
As for the two graspings (*parāmarśa*), if they take as their object views associated with mental grief (*daurmanasya*) and so forth, at that time they may be conjoined with mental grief.
Fearing that someone might ask, "How can doubt be associated with joy? I now explain: there is no suffering in the desire for doubt, and it is also accompanied by the feeling of joy (*sukha-vedanā*).
Furthermore, fearing that someone might ask, "Since the two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*) hold [wrong views] to be supreme and pure, how could they involve sorrow? I now explain:
If one takes as an object views associated with grief, the precepts, or the aggregates that serve as their basis, it can also be associated with grief;
for instance, because there is also grief regarding various painful matters such as smearing oneself with ashes or plucking out one's hair.

According to one interpretation, the two innate views—view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—are associated only with the feelings of joy, pleasure, and equanimity;

because they do not coexist with the five sensory consciousnesses, there is no feeling of suffering, and because they are exclusively obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), there is no feeling of grief. As for the two conceptualized views (of self-identity and extremes), they may be associated with all four feelings, with the exception of suffering.

Grasping the aggregates associated with suffering as "self" or "belonging to self" and [viewing them as] permanent results in the experience of painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*). The view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) is the opposite of this (grasping the aggregates associated with pleasure as being annihilated), because it is associated with painful feeling.

According to one interpretation, if the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are innate (*sahaja*), they are also associated with painful feeling; for in places where one experiences exclusively suffering, they take the extremely painful aggregates as their object and are thus associated with suffering.
The treatise states that all innate afflictions manifest in connection with the three types of feeling.
The practice can be attained. The detailed explanation is as before. The remainder is as previously stated;
the detailed explanation is as before. This refers to the passage in the fifth fascicle explaining the three types of sensation (*vedanā*). The remainder is as previously stated;
that is, the analysis of the two views is the same as what was said regarding the first meaning, which allows for association with all four types of sensation.

This is explained according to the actual nature (a detailed exposition). If, however, one follows the coarse characteristics (to provide a general outline): greed, pride, and the four views are associated with the feelings of pleasure, joy, and equanimity;
hatred arises only in association with the feelings of sorrow, pain, and equanimity; ignorance can be associated with all five feelings;
and wrong view and doubt are associated with all four feelings, excluding pain.
The above analysis, whether subtle or coarse, concludes the definitive judgment regarding the association of the various feelings (*vedanā*).

The feeling of pleasure associated with both greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*) pervades the four lower stages (*bhūmi*). The feeling of pleasure associated with the remaining seven [mental factors]—excluding the desire realm—pervades the three dhyānas.

Doubt (*vicikitsā*) and independent delusion (*moha*) exist only within the desire realm; they are associated exclusively with the two feelings of mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*). Other feelings arise in conjunction with them.
This should be understood according to principle.
Furthermore, these are classified by way of their association with the various feelings (*vedanā*) belonging to each realm and stage (*dhātu-bhūmi*).

The four lower stages are: first, the mixed-dwelling [realm]; second, the first dhyāna; third, the second dhyāna; and fourth, the third dhyāna. From the fourth dhyāna upward, there is only equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Because they are associated with feeling (*vedanā*). As for the remaining seven [mental factors], excluding the three—greed, hatred, and delusion—as well as pride, doubt, and the five views, these are associated only with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Since there is no pleasure belonging to the mental ground in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), these are excluded from the desire realm and are restricted only to the three dhyānas.

Doubt and independent delusion (*moha*) are likewise associated only with the mental consciousness; therefore, within the desire realm, there is neither painful nor pleasant feeling, nor is there joy (*saumanasya*).
The former [explanation] was based on subtle characteristics; thus it was said that desire and doubt are without suffering and are associated with the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*).
Now, following coarse characteristics, since doubt has not yet reached a decision, how could there be joy? Furthermore, there are two types of independent delusion (*moha*):

first, the primary independent type, which alone is capable of initiating karma; second, the non-primary independent type, which arises only in conjunction with the secondary derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*). This...
These two types [of afflictions] exist within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). If one follows their coarse characteristics (*sthūla-lakṣaṇa*), they likewise lack the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*);

therefore, they are associated only with the feelings of mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*). The remaining realms and stages where afflictions arise in conjunction with the feelings of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*) and joy (*saumanasyavedanā*) may be inferred accordingly;

thus, they are not described in detail here. Section Four: The Gate of Correspondence with the Feelings is concluded. △ Section Five: The Gate of Correspondence with the Particular Objects (*viśeṣālambana*).

(Question: How many of these [afflictions] are mutually associated with the object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa*)? (Answer: Greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), and pride (*māna*) may arise together with five [of the object-specific mental factors].
This is because when greed, hatred, delusion, and pride are focused on a single object, concentration (*samādhi*) can also be present.

Doubt (*vicikitsā*) and the five views (*dṛṣṭi*) may each be associated with four [object-specific mental factors]. Doubt excludes resolve (*adhimokṣa*) because it is non-definitive. Views are not associated with wisdom (*prajñā*).
[Included] because they are not different from wisdom.
△ Sixth, the Section on the Mutual Inclusion of the Three Natures.
(Question: To which natures are these ten afflictions subsumed? (Answer: Hatred is exclusively unwholesome, because it harms oneself and others; the remaining nine...

[These] pervade both the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified natures. As for those belonging to the two higher realms, they are comprised solely of the unspecified [nature], because they are suppressed by meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
If those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) arise through discrimination (*vikalpita*), they are comprised solely within the unwholesome (*akuśala*), because they give rise to evil conduct.

If they are innate (*sahaja*) yet give rise to evil conduct, they are also comprised within the unwholesome, because they harm oneself and others. The remainder (those that are innate and do not give rise to evil conduct) are comprised within the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

The subtle [afflictions] do not obstruct the wholesome, because they do not constitute extreme harm or distress to oneself or others. It should be understood that the two innate views—the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—are comprised solely within the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);
for they do not incite unwholesome karma, and even though they frequently manifest, they do not obstruct the wholesome.
△ Section on the Ties of the Seven Realms and the Conditions of the Present, in three parts: first, clarifying the ties of the realms; second, clarifying their present manifestation;
third, clarifying their mutual conditioning. Now, the first part. (Question:
To which realm are these ten afflictions tied? (Answer: Hatred exists only in the desire realm; the others pervade all three realms.
△ Second, the explanation of their manifestation.
When one is born in a lower stage and has not yet abandoned the defilements of that lower stage, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the higher stages do not manifest.

Only when one attains the fundamental meditative absorption (*mauladhyāna*) of that higher stage can the afflictions of that higher stage potentially manifest; [this is because such is the case for those practicing as ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) or non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).]

Regarding the worldly-flavored dhyānas: although the various contaminated paths, by means of the wisdom of the contemplation of the two emptinesses, cannot suppress the afflictions arising from discrimination (*vikalpa-utpanna-kleśa*) nor the subtle innate afflictions within the seventh consciousness, they are nevertheless able to suppress and eliminate the coarse innate afflictions within the six consciousnesses.
By means of this, one gradually realizes the fundamental meditative concentrations (*mauladhyāna*) of the higher stages.

Those [coarse innate afflictions] arise solely from delusion regarding objective phenomena (*vastu-moha*), being triggered by the five external sensory objects; they function through the external gateways and are characterized by distraction.
[The coarse and active [afflictions] are precisely obstacles to meditative concentration; therefore, one subdues these coarse innate afflictions.

Once that [higher-level] concentration has been attained, the various afflictions—both conceptual and innate—of that [higher] level may all manifest. (As for those born in a higher level, the afflictions of the lower levels are not considered;
whether conceptual or innate, they may all arise. How is this known? Because [this occurs] within the state of the fourth dhyāna concentration.

Regarding those who possess [defilements]: because one who slanders liberation is reborn in hell, it is known that [a person] in a higher stage can give rise to the discriminative afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*) of a lower stage.

Furthermore, when one whose body is in a higher stage is about to be born [in a lower one], they give rise to the innate craving (*upapatti-sahaja-tṛṣṇā*) that moistens birth in a lower stage; thus, it is known that [a person] in a higher stage can give rise to the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) of a lower stage.

As for the statement in some places that "one born in a higher stage does not give rise to [afflictions of] a lower stage," this is said based on the majority of cases, or perhaps [it refers to a specific context].
The Gate of Conforming Transformation:

Regarding those who slander liberation, there was a monk of little learning who attained the four dhyānas and gave rise to overweening pride, falsely claiming to have realized the four fruits and that he would not undergo further existence.
Upon the end of his life, while in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), he beheld those four dhyānas.
While still subject to rebirth, they do not realize that they have not yet truly attained the four fruits of the path; instead, they claim, "I have now realized the four fruits.
Yet, they continue to undergo future births. If this were so, then the Buddha’s statement that an Arhat does not undergo further existence would surely be a falsehood.
This is because, within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), they give rise to this single thought, thereby slandering the liberation taught by the Buddha.
Mind. Thus, following the cessation of the existence in the four dhyānas, the subsequent existence in hell arises accordingly.

Regarding "craving that moistens existence," this refers to the spontaneous defiled attachment toward the state of future existence, such as the perverse craving directed toward one's parents at the time of entering the womb.
△ Third, the mutual conditioning of these factors.

The afflictions of the lower stages also take the higher stages as their objects; this is stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts. It is said that greed bound to the desire realm seeks rebirth in the higher stages because it relishes the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).

Since it is also stated that hatred can take the truths of Cessation and the Path as its objects through resentment and jealousy, it should likewise resent and envy the stages of detachment from desire.

Furthermore, those who grasp at "self" and "what belongs to self," or hold views of annihilationism, eternalism, and pride, taking all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as their general object, are able to take the higher stages as their objects. (Since this...)

The five afflictions—greed, hatred, pride, self-view, and doubt—are able to take the higher realms as their objects; it is established by reason that the remaining five—ignorance, views, and wrong views regarding precepts—are likewise able to take the higher realms as their objects.

However, where certain passages state that greed, hatred, pride, and so forth do not take the higher realms as their objects, this is said according to their coarse characteristics, or based on specific conditions (namely, from...).

Because one does not perceive the phenomena (*dharma*) of other stages (*bhūmi*) in the world as "self" (*ātman*) or "belonging to self" (*ātmīya*), it is said that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) does not take higher stages as its object.
Since the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) necessarily arises based upon the view of a self-identity, it is said that the view of extremes also does not take higher stages as its object.

Regarding "taking all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as the object": this refers to certain non-Buddhists who take all conditioned phenomena—both form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*)—of the three realms as their collective object, grasping at them as "I" and "mine," reckoning them as either annihilated or eternal, and exalting themselves above others.
Therefore, the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and pride (*māna*) can also take the higher [realms] as their objects.
However, if they rely on specific objects, this is not the case.

Defilements of the higher stages also take those of the lower stages as their objects. It is said that those born in the higher stages look down upon sentient beings of the lower stages, relying on their own superior qualities to disparage them.

Furthermore, because those who grasp at all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as "I" or "mine," and who cling to the views of annihilationism or eternalism, can take the lower stages as their objects, it should be understood accordingly that doubt and the latter three views also take the lower stages as their objects; yet it is taught that defilements of the higher stages do not take the lower stages as their objects.
This [is] also stated by way of the majority, or it is stated in reference to specific conditions.

The reason hatred (*dveṣa*) and delusion (*moha*) are not mentioned is that hatred does not exist in the higher realms, and delusion pervades all defiled minds. This concludes the section on the seven elements according to the door of present conditions.
△ Eighth: The Section on the Subsumption of the Three Categories, such as those in Training (*śaikṣa*).

(Question: By what [categories], such as those of training (*śaikṣa*), are these ten afflictions subsumed? (Answer: They are neither of training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), because those [of training and beyond training] are exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*).

Question: From the first fruit (srotāpanna) upward, the afflictions of the realm of thought (bhāvanā-heya-kleśa) still remain; why, then, are these not included within the category of those in training (śaikṣa)? Answer:

To investigate the truth and sever the afflictions is called "in training" (śaikṣa); when the truth is fully realized and the afflictions are exhausted, it is called "beyond training" (aśaikṣa). Although those from the first fruit upward still possess the afflictions of the realm of thought, [they are nonetheless classified as śaikṣas].
When one is correctly investigating reality, delusions do not manifest. However, upon emerging from contemplation, if mindfulness is lost, afflictions will then arise.

Thus it is said: "Only the sage who fails to maintain mindfulness becomes a madman; only the madman who is able to maintain mindfulness becomes a sage. Although those in the stages of the inner and outer ordinary beings have not yet realized the fruit, [they may still attain it].
If one is able to cultivate contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to suppress the afflictions (*kleśa*), one may say that "in a single thought-moment there is correspondence with the Buddha.

Thus, we know that although those in training (*śaikṣa*) of the Three Vehicles are already termed "sages," when they emerge from untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-vipaśyanā*), they may give rise to afflictions;

by analogy, this can be called "losing illumination in a single thought-moment" or "becoming deluded in a single thought-moment. △ Nine: The Section on What is Severed by Seeing, etc. (*darśana-heya*, etc.)
(Question: Of these ten afflictions, which are abandoned? (Answer: They are not non-abandonable, because they are not non-defiled dharmas.

Those that arise through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpaja*) are abandoned only by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), because they are coarse and easy to abandon. If they are innate (*sahaja*), they are abandoned only by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), because they are subtle and difficult to abandon.
The ten types of afflictions abandoned by the path of seeing are actually all abandoned simultaneously by means of the true path of seeing (*tattva-darśana-mārga*).

[This occurs] at that time. It is because they take the Four Noble Truths as their general object. However, regarding the delusion concerning the characteristics of the Truths, there is both a general and a specific sense. The general sense means that all ten [afflictions] are deluded with respect to the Four Truths;
for suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are the causes and bases for those ten afflictions, while cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are the objects of fear for them.

The specific sense means that the two views—the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—arise from being specifically deluded regarding the characteristics of the Truth of Suffering. They arise solely in delusion regarding the Truth of Suffering and do not arise based on the truths of Origin, Cessation, or Path. As for the remaining [eight afflictions], [they are deluded regarding all four truths].

The eight [afflictions] are universally deluded regarding the four truths. Because the two views—the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—arise specifically with respect to the fruit, which is the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), they are countered by the specific cultivation of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*).

Since these two belong exclusively to the object of the truth of suffering, their meaning is that they are solely delusions regarding suffering. That is to say, the three views—doubt (*vicikitsā*), the view of a self-identity, and the view of extremes—and the two graspings (*parāmarśa*) directly delude one regarding the principle of suffering;
the latter two grasp those three views, as well as ritual precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and the aggregates upon which they depend, as being [the path].

The "victorious purifiers" [the antidotes] function in relation to the views of self and others, as well as their associated retinues; according to their respective correspondences, they give rise to greed, hatred, and pride (thus, greed, hatred, and pride regarding the two types of grasping are distant from the delusion of suffering).
The associated ignorance shares the same [status] as these nine [afflictions]—its distance or proximity to the delusion [of suffering] being determined accordingly.

The non-associated ignorance is directly deluded regarding the principle of suffering (these ten all share the sense of being deluded regarding suffering). Doubt and false view are directly deluded regarding the origin [and the other two] truths (the three truths). Greed, hatred, and pride regarding the two types of grasping [are likewise related].

And so forth. One should understand this by analogy with suffering (that delusion regarding origin, cessation, and the path is likewise remote). However, hatred can also directly delude one regarding cessation and the path, because one gives rise to aversion and jealousy out of fear of them.
Such is the coarse characteristic of the direct and remote delusions regarding the truths.

This has already distinguished between what is abandoned through seeing and what is abandoned through cultivation; it further clarifies that delusion regarding the truths may be general or specific, and direct or indirect.
Regarding "one's own views and those of others": attachment is toward one's own views, aversion is toward the views of others, and pride is toward their retinue.

To explain in detail: (if) greed, hatred, and pride arise simultaneously with the five afflictions of discrimination, as well as views and doubt, they are abandoned accordingly [by the path of seeing].
As for the two innate views—the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes—and the craving, pride, and ignorance associated with those two views:
although these five are deluded regarding the truth of suffering, because they are subtle and difficult to sever, they are abandoned only by the path of cultivation. Furthermore, there is hatred...

Other [afflictions] such as craving, which arise in delusion regarding specific objects, do not contradict the contemplation of the truths; therefore, they too are abandoned through the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanā-heya*).

This further distinguishes two types of abandonment. First, those arising together with views and doubt; this refers to greed, hatred, and pride that arise in association with the five views and doubt.
Second, the two innate views; this refers to a portion of the innate views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
The section on the abandonment by means of the nine views is concluded. △ Section Ten: Establishing Names According to the Objects.
Although all afflictions possess an objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), the underlying substance (*svabhāva*) upon which they rely may either exist or not;

thus, afflictions are designated as "conditioned by an existent object" (*sālambana*) or "conditioned by a non-existent object. While the immediate objective aspect (*sākṣāt-ālambana*) of those afflictions is invariably contaminated (*sāsrava*).

As for the fundamental substance upon which they rely, it may also be untainted (*anāsrava*); these are termed afflictions that take tainted objects as their conditions or untainted objects as their conditions.

Those [afflictions] that arise taking an object within their own stage (*svabhūmi*) have a *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) that resembles the fundamental substance; these are termed afflictions arising from objects that are conceptualized phenomena.

Those [afflictions] that arise taking the Truths of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and the Path (*mārga-satya*), or objects of other stages, have a *nimitta-bhāga* that does not resemble that fundamental substance.

Because they are similar [to the object], they are called "objects arising from discrimination based on conditions" (this refers to having only names while lacking substantial substance or reflected images).

Regarding whether the substance relied upon exists or does not exist: when taking a present object as a condition, there is a fundamental substance to rely upon; when taking past or future objects as conditions, there is no fundamental substance to rely upon.
That which is the direct objective support (*sākṣātālambana*) is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*); this refers to the mind that undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*).
