Because these are afflictions (*kleśa*), the *nimitta-bhāga* (reflected image) that they transform must necessarily be contaminated (*sāsrava*).

As for the fact that the objective basis (*ālambana*) relied upon may be uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), it is because one gives rise to delusion, doubt, false views, anger, pride, and so forth, by taking as objects either the two truths of the Path (*mārga-satya*) and Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), or the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
Now, regarding this single thought-moment of the present, before the afflictions have arisen... [as previously stated].

Among the ten afflictions (*kleśa*), whichever single affliction arises possesses a *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect). Since there is a *nimittabhāga*, there must be a *darśanabhāga* (subjective aspect).
Once both the *nimitta* and *darśana* aspects exist, there are the *svasaṃvedana* (self-cognition) and *svasaṃvitsaṃvedana* (cognition of self-cognition);

thus, there are four parts. Among these four parts, the *nimittabhāga* belongs to form (*rūpa*), while the other three parts—the *darśana* and so forth—belong to name (*nāman*). These two, name and form (*nāmarūpa*)...

The term "all" (sarva) encompasses all phenomena without exception. Furthermore, regarding the aspects [of consciousness]: the seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) is common to the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);

the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvitti*) and the self-cognizing-of-self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvitti-svasaṃvitti*) are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Moreover, these four aspects may be subsumed into three, because the fourth is included within the self-cognizing aspect;
or they may be subsumed into two, because the latter three are all of the nature of the cognizing subject (*ālambaka*). Or they may be subsumed into...
1. Since their essence is not distinct, is the nature of these afflictions conceivable or inconceivable?
Furthermore, since these afflictions can take existent things as objects and can also take non-existent things as objects;
can take contaminated things as objects and can also take uncontaminated things as objects; and can take objective phenomena as objects and can also take names as objects—then what dharma [is it]?

It is not incomplete. What phenomena are not produced? Furthermore, when it can take as its object the contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas of its own stage or other stages, it encompasses the entirety of the six realms of ordinary beings (*ṣaḍ-gati*).
When it can take as its object the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas, it encompasses the entirety of the four realms of the noble ones (*ārya*).

When it can take as its object that which has a basis (*savastuka*), it encompasses the entirety of the ten realms in the present. When it can take as its object that which lacks a basis (*avastuka*), it encompasses the entirety of the ten realms in the past and future.
It may be said that within a single mote of dust lie infinite lands; self and other are not separated by the tip of a hair.
Ten ages of past and present, from beginning to end, do not depart from the present moment of thought. Who would say that the true nature of afflictions is not identical to Buddha-nature?
△ Eleven: Conclusion by analogy for the remaining gates.
The analysis of other categories should be contemplated according to reason.
One who wishes to correctly apply this principle by analogy should perceive the principle of the *dharmadhātu* within the afflictions themselves. This concludes the third section:
the explanation of the root afflictions. △ Fourth, the explanation of the secondary afflictions has two parts: first, the presentation of the verse; second, the commentary. Now...
First:
The characteristics of the six root afflictions have already been explained. What are the characteristics of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)? The verse says:
The secondary afflictions are said to be anger, resentment, concealment, vexation, envy, stinginess, deceit, guile, harmfulness, pride, lack of shame, lack of dread, and restlessness.
[These are] associated with torpor, lack of faith, as well as laziness, heedlessness, loss of mindfulness, distraction, and lack of correct awareness.

△ Second, the commentary has two parts: first, the direct explanation of the verse; second, the analysis by way of various categories. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, a brief explanation of the general name;
second, an extensive explanation of the specific characteristics; third, an explanation of the conjunctions "with," "and," and "as well as. Now, the first [section].
The treatise says: Because they are merely specific states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) and outflows (*niṣyanda*) of the root afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*), they are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
These twenty types are divided into three categories: first, the ten beginning with anger (*krodha*), which are called minor secondary afflictions because they arise individually;

second, the two beginning with lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), which are called medium secondary afflictions because they pervade all unwholesome states; third, the eight beginning with restlessness (*auddhatya*), which pervade...
Because they defile the mind, they are called "great secondary afflictions" (mahā-kleśa-mahābhūmika).
The term "distinctions of states" refers to those that lack an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The term "outflow-nature" (*niṣyanda*) refers to those that possess an intrinsic nature.
"Unwholesome" (*akuśala*) means evil. "Defiled mind" (*kliṣṭa-citta*) refers to both the unwholesome and the obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds.

△ Second, the detailed explanation of the specific characteristics has three parts: first, the explanation of the ten minor secondary afflictions; second, the explanation of the two medium secondary afflictions;

third, the explanation of the eight major secondary afflictions. Within the first part, there are ten sections, beginning with the explanation of *krodha* (anger) and continuing through the tenth, the explanation of *mada* (arrogance). Now, the first section.
What is anger (*krodha*)? Its nature is the outburst of indignation based on a presently manifest object that is disadvantageous.
Its function is to obstruct the absence of anger and to lead to the grasping of weapons. This is because one who harbors anger frequently manifests violent and evil bodily actions.
This has a portion of hatred (*dveṣa*) as its essence, for there is no distinct characteristic or activity of anger apart from hatred.
The bodily manifest karma of violence refers to the evil manifestations of brandishing weapons and engaging in mutual combat.
Forgetting one’s own life and that of one’s kin due to a momentary fit of rage, and thereby binding oneself to swift retribution—nothing is more extreme than this. Therefore, it is explained first.
△ Second, the explanation of resentment (*upanāha*).

What is resentment? Preceded by anger, it consists of harboring malice without relinquishing it; its essential nature is the binding of enmity. It functions as an obstacle to the absence of resentment.
Its function is to cause feverish distress; that is to say, one who harbors resentment is unable to endure [the offense] and is constantly tormented by heat.
This too has a portion of hatred (*pratigha*) as its essence, because apart from hatred there is no distinct characteristic or activity of resentment.
"Do not dwell on past wrongs; thus enmity will be rare. To harbor resentment without releasing it serves only to cause oneself needless distress and torment.
△ Third, the explanation of *mrakṣa* (concealment).
What is concealment? Its nature is to hide one's own committed transgressions out of fear of losing gain, livelihood, reputation, or fame; it is able to obstruct [the realization of] non-...
Its function is remorse and affliction; that is to say, because one who conceals a transgression will inevitably experience remorse and affliction, lacking peace and stability.

According to one interpretation, this concealment (*mrakṣa*) is subsumed under a portion of delusion (*moha*), because the treatise states only that it is a portion of delusion, and because one conceals one’s own faults out of a lack of fear regarding future karmic results.
According to another interpretation, this concealment should be subsumed under portions of both greed (*lobha*) and delusion, as one also fears the loss of benefit.
Yue (Nai) [states]: Because it conceals one's own faults, the treatise cites only the coarse and manifest aspect, speaking solely of the factor of delusion (*moha*).

This is like how restlessness (*auddhatya*) is said to be a factor of attachment (*rāga*); yet, since it is also said that restlessness pervades all defiled minds, one must not hold that it is exclusively a factor of attachment.
Sins, whether great or small, are extinguished through disclosure but increase through concealment. It is like a tree root:
if exposed, the tree withers; if buried, the tree flourishes. Therefore, those possessed of wisdom disclose and repent, being able to realize non-arising even through grave offenses.
Foolish people, however, greedily cherish their transgressions and conceal them, often [falling] due to minor faults.

This invites intense suffering. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śīla-sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva contemplates concealment as being like wearing a towering mountain upon one's head while treading upon a vast ocean.
How can those who cultivate the mind not be cautious! △ Fourth, the explanation of vexation.

What is malice (*pradāsa*)? It has resentment as its precursor; its nature is to be impetuous and fierce upon being provoked; it functions as an obstacle to non-malice; its activity is to sting like a gadfly.

This means that when one pursues past evils and encounters present adverse conditions, the mind becomes impetuous and fierce, frequently giving rise to clamorous, violent, wicked, base, and coarse speech because it stings others.
This, too, has a portion of hatred (*dveṣa*) as its essence; apart from hatred, there is nothing distinct.
Because their characteristic function is to cause vexation:

*qū* (pronounced with the initial *zhì*) and *shè* (pronounced with the initial *zhī*) are insects that move about and inflict poison upon people. Due to this vexation and delusion, one gives rise to the karma of harsh speech;
its venom exceeds that of snakes and vipers. Consequently, even after death, one receives the body of a poisonous insect, from which there is no escape.
One who cultivates the mind should strictly guard against these. Furthermore, anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), and vexation (*pradāsa*) all have hatred (*dveṣa*) as their essential nature.

Anger takes the present as its condition; resentment takes the past as its condition; vexation pursues the past while impinging upon the present. Anger gives rise to bodily action (*kāyakarman*); resentment resides primarily in the mind (*manas*);
vexation gives rise to vocal action (*vākkarman*). These are called the three distinct characteristics. △ Fifth, the explanation of envy (*īrṣyā*).

What is envy (*īrṣyā*)? Its nature is to be jealous and resentful, being devoted to one’s own fame and profit while being unable to endure the prosperity of others. Its function is to obstruct non-envy and to produce grief and distress;
that is to say, when one who is envious hears of or sees the prosperity of others, they harbor deep grief and distress because of their lack of peace.
This also has a portion of *dveṣa* (hatred) as its essence, for apart from hatred, there is no separate characteristic or function of envy (*īrṣyā*).
The *Mahāyāna-tattvārtha-sūtra* says: "That person’s wealth and nobility are all born of past merit;
how could my greed and envy possibly seize them? If one does not sever envy, one will constantly suffer poverty and lack further power. If one can [behave] toward others..."

When one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward wealth and honor, not relinquishing even a hair’s breadth [of merit], one obtains great merit. △ Sixth, the explanation of stinginess (*mātsarya*):

What is stinginess? It is the attachment to wealth and the Dharma, being unable to relinquish them wisely; its essential nature is secrecy and parsimony, and it functions as an obstacle to non-stinginess.

To have the practice of hoarding as one's occupation refers to the stingy person; their mind is characterized by much coarseness and rigidity because they cannot relinquish the accumulation of wealth and dharmas.
This has a portion of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as its essence, for apart from craving, there is no separate characteristic or function of stinginess (*mātsarya*).

Those who are stingy with wealth will be poor and destitute in every life; those who are stingy with the Dharma will be ignorant and dark-witted in every birth. One must not fail to exercise restraint in this regard.

△ Seventh, the explanation of *śāṭhya* (deceit). What is deceit? For the sake of profit and reputation, one feigns the possession of virtues. Its essential nature is guile and fraud. It functions as an obstacle to non-deceit.

Wrong livelihood is its activity; that is to say, it belongs to those who are deceitful and fraudulent, who harbor ulterior motives, and who frequently manifest unreal matters for the sake of wrong livelihood.
This has as its essence a portion of greed and delusion, because apart from these two, there is no distinct characteristic or function of deception.
For the clothing and food required for a single body, how much is truly needed? To practice such deception is to invite immeasurable sin.
One may also feel horror when considering the past causes of the four palanquin-bearers of Queen Mallikā (the account is found in the *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisāgara-sūtra*;
those who require it should seek it out). △ Eighth: Explanation of Sycophancy (*śāṭhya*).
What is guile (*śāṭhya*)? It is the nature of being crooked and devious for the purpose of deceiving others, manifesting through the feigning of artificial conduct.

Its function is to obstruct non-guile and [the receiving of] instruction. That is to say, one who is guileful and crooked, in order to deceive others, conforms to the requirements of the occasion and feigns expedient means.
In order to win over others' minds or to conceal one's own faults, one fails to submit to the correct instruction and admonition of teachers and friends;
this too has as its essence a portion of greed and delusion, for apart from these two, there is no distinct characteristic or function of guile (*śāṭhya*).
The straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). A mind of flattery and crookedness is contrary to the Way; therefore, it cannot be taught or instructed.
△ Ninth, the explanation of harm (*vihiṃsā*): What is harm?
It is the nature of causing injury and affliction toward all sentient beings with a mind devoid of compassion. It is able to obstruct non-harming (*avihiṃsā*).

Its function is universal affliction; that is to say, it afflicts others by harming them. This [harm] also has a portion of hatred (*dveṣa*) as its essence, because apart from hatred there is no distinct characteristic or activity of harm.
The distinct characteristics of hatred and harm should be explained in accordance with the wholesome [factors].
The absence of anger is called loving-kindness (*maitrī*); the absence of harm is called compassion (*karuṇā*). Therefore, the absence of loving-kindness is anger; the absence of compassion is harm.
These obstruct the path to enlightenment and invite the suffering of severe retribution. To oppress others is ultimately nothing but self-destruction. How lamentable!
△ Explanation of *mada* (intoxication/arrogance).
What is *mada*? It is the nature of being intoxicated and haughty due to deep attachment to one's own prosperity; it functions as an obstacle to non-intoxication (*amada*).
Its function is to serve as the basis for defilement; that is to say, because it causes all defiled phenomena to grow and increase in those who are intoxicated by self-conceit (*mada*).
This too has a portion of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as its essence, because apart from craving there is no distinct characteristic or function of self-conceit.

Prosperity must inevitably be followed by decline; how can one be intoxicated with pride? That which is relied upon as a flourishing event may not necessarily be preserved for long, yet the defilements that arise from it will follow one without ever departing.
Is this not truly tragic! The first section, the explanation of the ten minor secondary afflictions, is concluded.

△ Second, the explanation of the two medium secondary afflictions, in two parts: first, the individual explanation; second, the general clarification. Within the first part, there are two sections; the first explains *anapatrāpya* (lack of moral dread).
Second, the explanation of *anapatrāpya* (lack of moral dread). First:

What is *āhrīkya* (lack of shame)? Its nature is to disregard one’s own dharma and to treat the virtuous and good with contempt and rejection. Its function is to obstruct *hrī* (shame) and to cause the growth of unwholesome conduct.
That is to say, one who disregards their own dharma treats the virtuous and good with contempt and rejection, feeling no sense of shame regarding faults and evils.
It obstructs a sense of shame (*hrī*), because it causes various unwholesome actions to grow.
To revere one's own spiritual essence is called "regard for one's own dharma" (*svadharma-apekṣā*); to disregard one's own dharma is to be self-exposed and self-abandoned.
△ Second, the explanation of lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*).

What is lack of shame (*āhrīkya*)? It has the nature of disregarding the world and esteeming violence and evil; it functions as an obstacle to shame (*hrī*) and its activity is the growth of unwholesome conduct.
That is to say, one who has no regard for the world esteems violence and evil, feeling no sense of shame regarding faults and transgressions.
It obstructs shame and remorse, for it causes various unwholesome deeds to grow.
To guard against and cherish [the avoidance of] censure and reproach is called "regarding the world. Not regarding the world means being content to be beneath others.
△ Second, the general distinction.

Not feeling shame for one's faults and evils is the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of these two; therefore, the various holy teachings provisionally designate it as their essence (*tattva*).

If one were to insist that not feeling shame is the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of each, then there would be no distinction between the essences of these two, and consequently, these two dharmas should not arise simultaneously.

This is because such a meaning does not apply to sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth. If these two were established as distinct based on their dependence upon self and other, they would not be substantially existent, which would contradict the holy teachings.
If one were to allow that these two are substantially existent yet arise separately, this would further contradict the treatise’s statement that both pervade all unwholesome minds (*akuśalacitta*).

At the time of an unwholesome mind, regardless of the object it encounters, there is always the sense of slighting and rejecting the wholesome, as well as the sense of honoring and esteeming the unwholesome.
Therefore, these two factors both pervade the unwholesome mind; since their objects of perception do not differ, there is no fault in their arising separately.

However, when various sacred teachings speak of "disregarding oneself and others," "self" refers to one's own dharma and "others" refers to the world. Alternatively, within this very context, "self" refers to the wholesome and "others" refers to the unwholesome.

Because one's own benefit or loss is designated as "self" and "other," that which the treatise describes as being of the same category as greed and so forth is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of those [afflictions],
not their very nature (*svabhāva*).

To reject what is wholesome is to have no benefit for oneself; this is called being indifferent to oneself. To honor what is unwholesome is to suffer harm to oneself; this is called being indifferent to others.
The rest may be understood as explained in the section on *hrī* (shame) and *apatrāpya* (modesty). Regarding "greed and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes anger and delusion.
Through the absence of shame and modesty, greed, anger, and delusion are all allowed to grow and flourish; it assists in the formation of greed and the others, and is their outflow (*niṣyanda*).

Therefore, the absence of shame and remorse is called an unwholesome dharma; it is no different from that of birds and beasts. This concludes the second section of the two explanations on the secondary afflictions (upakleśa).

[Next] is the third section: the explanation of the eight great secondary afflictions. First is the explanation of *auddhatya* (restlessness), [continuing] up to the eighth, the explanation of *asamprajanya* (lack of clear comprehension).
Now, the first:
What is *auddhatya* (restlessness)? Its nature is that which causes the mind to be non-quiescent with respect to its objects; its function is to obstruct equanimity (*upekṣā*) and *śamatha*.

One interpretation holds that *auddhatya* is subsumed under a portion of *rāga* (attachment), because the treatise states only that it is a part of attachment, and because it arises from recollecting past pleasurable experiences.
Another interpretation holds that *auddhatya* is not subsumed under *rāga* alone, because the treatise states that *auddhatya* is pervasive (*sarvatraga*).

Because it is a defiled mind. Furthermore, the characteristic of *auddhatya* (restlessness) is non-quiescence; this is because it is said to be subsumed under the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*), and because *auddhatya* has no distinct characteristic apart from these common characteristics of the afflictions.
Although it is conventionally established based on all afflictions, it is designated as a part of greed (*rāga*) because it increases specifically during the state of greed.
According to another interpretation, *auddhatya* possesses its own distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that pervades all defiled minds, just like lack of faith (*āśraddhya*).

...and so forth. It is not that because it is designated as "belonging to another" (parabhāga) based on a conceptual construct, its essence (svabhāva) would therefore be unreal. Otherwise, [states such as] lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) and so on would also have to be considered merely conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*), since they too are designated in dependence upon others.

As for the treatise stating that this restlessness (*auddhatya*) is conventionally existent, it is an example similar to sleep (*middha*) and so forth: although these possess a real essence, they are described according to the characteristics of others [such as ignorance].
The specific characteristic of restlessness is agitation itself; it functions to cause the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) arising simultaneously with it to be non-quiescent.
Therefore, if this [restlessness] had no distinct characteristic apart from the various afflictions (*kleśa*), it should not be mentioned separately as an obstacle to *śamatha*.
Thus, lack of tranquility is not a distinct characteristic of this [restlessness].
*Śamatha*. This is translated as "cessation" (*zhi*). Its explanation has three meanings; the third is correct. △ Second, the explanation of *styāna* (sloth).
What is *styāna*?
Its nature is to render the mind incapable of functioning with respect to its object. It is able to obstruct *praśrabdhi* (pliancy) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).

That constitutes karma. Regarding this, there is one interpretation: torpor (*styāna*) is subsumed under a portion of delusion (*moha*). This is because the treatise states only that it is a portion of delusion, and because its characteristics—obscuration and heaviness—are those of delusion.
There is another interpretation: torpor is not subsumed under delusion alone; rather, it refers to a lack of functional capacity (*akarmanyatā*).
This is the characteristic of *styāna* (sloth). All afflictions (*kleśa*) are characterized by a lack of functional capacity;

since there is no characteristic of *styāna* distinct from this lack of capacity in the afflictions, although it is provisionally established based on all afflictions, its characteristic of delusion (*moha*) predominates, and thus it is described as a portion of delusion.

According to one interpretation, *styāna* has a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); although it is called a portion of delusion, it is actually a derivative flow (*niṣyanda*) of delusion, just like lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) and so forth.
It is not subsumed under delusion (*moha*) [in the treatise], as it is described according to its own specific characteristics; thus, it is conventionally existent (*saṃvṛti-sat*).

Like sleep and so forth, it is a real entity (*dravya-sat*). The specific characteristic of lethargy (*styāna*) is dullness and heaviness, which renders the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) arising simultaneously with it unfit for their function.
If lethargy were not distinct from the afflictions (*kleśa*), it would have no separate characteristic and should not be mentioned separately as an obstacle to insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Therefore, it lacks functional capacity; this is not the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of this [torpor]. The distinction between this [torpor] and delusion (*moha*) is as follows:

delusion has the characteristic of confusion and darkness regarding its object; it directly obstructs non-delusion (*amoha*), but it is not characterized by dullness and heaviness. Torpor has the characteristic of dullness and heaviness regarding its object;
it directly obstructs pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), but it is not characterized by confusion and darkness.
*Vipaśyanā* is translated here as "contemplation" (*guān*). Its explanation also has three meanings, of which the third is correct.

It is called "torpor" (*hūn*) because it is dull; it is called "sinking" (*chén*) because it is heavy. The distinction between these and "delusion" (*mōhē*) can be understood from the text. △ Third, the explanation of lack of faith (*aśraddhya*).
What is lack of faith (*aśraddhya*)? Its nature is a state of mental impurity characterized by an inability to endure, take pleasure in, or desire [the truth], virtue, and capability.

Its function is to obstruct pure faith and to serve as a basis for falling [into lower states]. This is because one who lacks faith is mostly indolent. One should understand that the three characteristics of lack of faith are the opposites of those of faith.
While all defiled phenomena each have their own distinct characteristics, this lack of faith alone has a turbid intrinsic nature and is further capable of causing turbidity in others.
Other minds and mental factors are like extremely filthy objects; they defile themselves and defile others. Therefore, this mind is said to have filthiness as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Due to lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), one does not tolerate, delight in, or desire [the truth], virtues, or capabilities. It is not that there is a separate intrinsic nature [for this lack of faith].
If one has wrong tolerance and desire regarding other matters, this is the cause and effect of that lack of faith, not its intrinsic nature.
If one harbors doubt, it is still possible for faith to arise; however, if one simply lacks faith, even the Buddha can do nothing about it.
Therefore, it is extremely defiled and turbid. △ Fourth, the explanation of indolence (*kausīdya*):

What is indolence? Its nature is laziness and sloth regarding the tasks of cultivation and abandonment within the categories of the wholesome and the unwholesome; it is able to obstruct diligence (*vīrya*).
Its function is to increase defilement; that is to say, because it causes the proliferation of defilements in those who are indolent.

Furthermore, even one who exerts effort toward various defiled matters is called indolent, because they regress from wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*). Likewise, one who exerts effort toward neutral matters (*avyākṛta*) is [indolent], because there is no progress or regression regarding the categories of the wholesome.
This [indolence] is subsumed under desire and resolve (*chanda-adhimokṣa*); it does not have a separate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). For example, as with [exertion] toward neutral matters...
To accept with patience and to desire [the Dharma] is neither pure nor defiled; it is neither faith nor lack of faith (one should know that it is likewise neither diligence nor indolence).
△ Fifth, relinquishing negligence.
What is heedlessness (*pramāda*)? It is characterized by a lack of restraint and cultivation regarding the categories of defilement and purification; its nature is one of unrestrained dissipation.

Its function is to obstruct non-heedlessness and to serve as the basis for the increase of evil and the diminution of good. That is to say, through laziness (*kausīdya*), greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*), one is unable to restrain or cultivate the dharmas of the defiled and purified categories;

this is collectively termed heedlessness. It does not possess a separate substantial entity. Although pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and so forth also possess this [characteristic], [they are not distinct from it].

It can. However, compared to those four factors—greed, hatred, delusion, and laziness—their power and function are weak and inferior; they merely obstruct the three roots of goodness and the factor of universal exertion (*sampragraha*).
When investigating the characteristics of this [heedlessness], there is no separate definition other than what may be inferred by analogy from the section on heedfulness (*apramāda*).
△ Sixth, the explanation of *muṣitasmṛtitā* (loss of mindfulness).

What is loss of mindfulness? Its nature is the inability to clearly remember various objects of focus (*ālambana*). Its function is to obstruct right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*) and to serve as the basis for distraction (*vikṣepa*).
This means that for one who has lost mindfulness, the mind is distracted. According to one interpretation, loss of mindfulness is a part of mindfulness itself.

[Included in the category of] defilements (*kleśa*). This is because it is taught as being associated with affliction. There is one interpretation: loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*) is subsumed under a portion of delusion (*moha*).

This is because the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that this [loss of mindfulness] is a derivative of delusion; since delusion causes mindfulness to be lost, it is termed "loss of mindfulness. There is another interpretation:

loss of mindfulness is subsumed under portions of both mindfulness and delusion. This is because the two preceding passages are merely abbreviated or elliptical expressions. Furthermore, the treatise states that this [loss of mindfulness] is pervasive.
Regarding the "defiled mind," there are three interpretations; the third is considered the correct one. △ Seventh, the explanation of distraction (*vikṣepa*): What is distraction?
Its nature is to cause the mind to wander and disperse among various objects of focus. It functions as an obstacle to right concentration and to wisdom.

Its function is to serve as a basis [for unwholesome states]. This is because those who are distracted give rise to wrong wisdom (*kuprajñā*). One interpretation holds that distraction is subsumed under a portion of delusion (*moha*), because the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that it is a part of delusion.

Another interpretation holds that distraction is subsumed under greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*), because the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises state that it consists of these three parts.
As for the statement in the *Yogācārabhūmi* that it is a part of delusion, this is because it pervades all defiled minds; that is to say, [it coexists with] greed, hatred, and delusion.

It causes the mind to flow and wander; because it excels other [afflictions], it is called distraction (*vikṣepa*). According to one interpretation, distraction has a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) (as stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*).

The statement that it consists of three parts [of the afflictions] refers to its being a derivative (*niṣyanda*) of those [greed, hatred, and delusion], just like lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and so forth.

It is not subsumed under those [three] themselves, but is designated as conventionally existent (*saṃvṛtisat*) by way of describing it according to the characteristics of others. Distraction has its own distinct characteristic, namely, agitation and turbulence, which causes...

Because the mental states and mental factors that arise simultaneously with them are all subject to wandering, if they were devoid of those three factors—greed, hatred, and delusion—they would have no distinct intrinsic nature of their own;
thus, it would be improper to speak of them separately as obstacles to samādhi.
The third meaning is also taken as the correct one. "Dull wisdom" refers to incorrect discernment (*mithyā-vicaya*). "Samādhi" is precisely right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). (Question:

What is the difference between the functions of agitation (*auddhatya*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*)? (Answer: The former (agitation) causes the mind to be easily diverted from its object; the latter (distraction) causes the mind to shift to other objects.
Although at a single moment there is no change in the understanding of the object or the conditions, because there is a sense of change within the continuum [of consciousness], [one might ask]:

"When the mind is defiled, due to the power of restlessness (*auddhatya*), it should always change its understanding and its objects from moment to moment. Why, then, is there sometimes concentration on a single object? [The answer is:

Because it may be restrained by the power of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and other factors, like a tethered monkey that remains still for a short time; therefore, both restlessness and distraction (*vikṣepa*) are universal [to all minds].

Regarding the defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*), this section further provides a detailed analysis and resolves doubts. The first question and answer addresses restlessness (*auddhatya*) through a specific analytical application.
"That which is easy to understand" refers to transforming the cognizing mind; "that which is easy to objectify" refers to changing the objective sphere (*ālambana*).

Furthermore, the subsequent question and answer clarify the resolution of doubts, as can be understood. △ Eighth, the explanation of *asaṃprajanya* (lack of clear comprehension). What is *asaṃprajanya*?

Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is erroneous understanding regarding the object of observation. Its function is to obstruct correct knowledge (*saṃprajanya*) and to lead to transgressions (*duṣkṛta*).
This is because one who lacks clear comprehension frequently commits transgressions. According to one interpretation, *asaṃprajanya* is a portion of wisdom (*prajñā*).

[It is] subsumed [under delusion]. This is because it is said to be wisdom associated with afflictions. One interpretation holds that non-apprehension (*asamprajanya*) is subsumed under a portion of delusion (*moha*), because the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that this is a part of delusion;
it is called "non-apprehension" because it causes one to know incorrectly.

Another interpretation holds that non-apprehension is subsumed under portions of both wisdom and delusion, because the two preceding passages speak of them by way of ellipsis. Furthermore, the treatise states that this pervades all defiled states.

Because of the mind, the third meaning is also correct. The detailed explanation of the individual characteristics is complete. △ Third, the explanation of the terms "with," "and," and "also" (in the verse):
The words "with," "and," and "also" indicate that the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are not merely twenty; for the *Vinayakṣudraka* and other texts state that there are further [afflictions].

Because it includes many types of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), one should know that the term "secondary affliction" also subsumes the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), as these are of the same nature as the outflows (*niṣyanda*) of those preceding root afflictions.
Furthermore, other defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*) that are of the same category as the afflictions [are also included].
They can only be called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), because they are not subsumed under the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).
They are other defiled phenomena of the same class as the root afflictions, such as remorse, torpor, vitarka, and vicāra that are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).

However, the reason only twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are taught here is that they are neither root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), nor are they merely coarse defilements—such as regret, sleep, and so forth—which extend to both the wholesome and the subtle.
Therefore, these other defiled phenomena are either specific states (*avasthā*) of these [root afflictions], or their outflows (*niṣyanda*).
All [of these] are subsumed within these twenty; they should be understood according to their respective categories as is appropriate.
The initial formal explanation of the verse is concluded. △ Second, the twelvefold classification by various gates.
First, the gate of the provisional and the real (up to) the twelfth, the gate of establishing names according to objects. Now, the first.
Among these twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), the ten minor ones and three major ones are definitely nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*).

Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), and laziness (*kausīdya*) are definitely substantially existent (*dravyasat*), as established by both scripture and reasoning. As for the three types—restlessness (*auddhatya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and distraction (*vikṣepa*)—[their status must be examined].
According to one interpretation, these are conventional; according to another, they are substantial. The principles and scriptural citations cited should be understood as previously explained.

Regarding the three great conventional existents: they are heedlessness, loss of mindfulness, and lack of clear comprehension. △ Second, the section on the distinction between innate and conceptual [afflictions].
All twenty are common to both innate (*sahaja*) and conceptual (*vikalpita*) [afflictions], because they arise through the power of these two types of fundamental afflictions.
△ Third, the section on mutual correspondence within their own class.

Among these twenty [mental factors], the ten minor ones do not arise simultaneously with one another, because they are mutually contradictory and their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are coarse and violent.
Because each acts as its own primary [defilement], there are two intermediate ones. All are associated with every unwholesome mind, corresponding to the unwholesome dharmas as appropriate.

Regarding the theory that the eight major [secondary defilements] arise universally with all defiled minds, it is held that they may arise in mutual association with both the minor and intermediate secondary defilements.
As for the statement in some places that six arise universally with defiled minds, this is because when torpor (*styāna*) or restlessness (*auddhatya*) are predominant, they do not coexist.
Because when torpor (styāna) is predominant, restlessness (auddhatya) is absent; and when restlessness is predominant, torpor is absent.
Therefore, it is said that these two do not pervade all defiled minds; only six factors are pervasive.
In some places, it is stated that only five [mental factors] are pervasive defilements (*sarvatraga-kleśa*).

This is because [factors such as] lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) contradict only the wholesome. These five factors—lethargy, restlessness, lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), and heedlessness (*pramāda*)—exist only in the absence of wholesome minds, yet they are present in both unwholesome (*akuśala*) and obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds; therefore, these five are said to be pervasive. As for their...
Regarding the two factors of forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*) and lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*): if their nature were a portion of delusion (*moha*), they would pervade all defiled minds;
if their nature were a portion of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), they would not pervade all defiled minds.

Although the single factor of distraction (*vikṣepa*) extends to both the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), it is nonetheless not [included] because it is sometimes suppressed.
This concludes the section on the universal [afflictions]. △ Fourth, the section on the simultaneous arising of the various consciousnesses.
Because these twenty afflictions are exclusively of a defiled nature, they do not arise simultaneously with the eighth consciousness. Within the seventh consciousness, there are only eight;

the distinctions regarding their inclusion or exclusion should be understood as explained above. Within the sixth consciousness, all may be present, including the ten minor and the coarse [afflictions].

Intensity (*tīvra*) is absent among the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). It is common to the intermediate [mental consciousness] and the eight great [wholesome mental factors]. It may be present in the five consciousnesses.
△ Fifth: The Section on Correspondence with the Various Feelings (*vedanā*).
Since these two [middling] and eight [great] mental factors are common [to all minds], they can be associated with the five feelings (*vedanā*).

According to one interpretation, among the ten minor [defilements], excluding the three—flattery (*śāṭhya*), deception (*māyā*), and pride (*mada*)—the remaining seven, such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth, are associated only with the three feelings of joy (*saumanasya*), sorrow (*daurmanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Regarding the three factors of flattery, deception, and pride, they are associated with four feelings, excluding only the feeling of suffering (*duḥkha*). According to another interpretation, the seven factors beginning with anger are associated with four feelings, excluding only [the feeling of] joy.

The three [mental factors] of *māyā* (deceit), *śāṭhya* (guile), and *mada* (pride) arise together with all five feelings (*vedanā*). As for the mental faculty, it possesses the feeling of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*), as has already been explained.

The characteristics of these feelings accompanying [these factors] are as described for the afflictions (*kleśa*); such is the actual meaning. If one follows the coarse classification (*sthūla-lakṣaṇa*):

*Krodha* (anger), *upanāha* (enmity), *pradāsa* (malice), *īrṣyā* (envy), and *vihiṃsā* (harmfulness) are associated only with the two feelings of mental grief (*daurmanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*). *Mrakṣa* (concealment) and *mātsarya* (avarice) are associated only with joy (*saumanasya*) and equanimity. As for the remaining three factors (*māyā*, *śāṭhya*, and *mada*), they further increase [the range of association].
Regarding pleasure (feeling), if it is intermediate (two) or great (eight), it corresponds to the five feelings according to the meaning of reality, following its coarse characteristics.
Regarding the twelve minor meanings, the latter meaning is correct. Such is the true meaning; this concludes the second correct interpretation.
Next, a brief judgment according to the coarse characteristics may be understood. △ Sixth, the Section on Correspondence with Specific Objects.
Thus, these twenty [mental factors] and the five object-specific factors (viṣayaviśeṣa) may all arise together, as they are not mutually contradictory.

Although defiled mindfulness and defiled discernment do not coexist with [pure] mindfulness and discernment, those portions of them that are subsumed under delusion (moha) can likewise be associated [with other mental factors].
Defiled mindfulness (*smṛti*) is precisely forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*); defiled wisdom (*prajñā*) is precisely lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*).

Mindfulness also takes as its object a present state or an object similar to what was previously practiced; since anger (*krodha*) can also take as its object a momentary past (not long gone), anger and mindfulness can also be associated (*saṃprayukta*).
When defiled concentration arises, the mind is also agitated; therefore, [anger] is also associated with distraction (*auddhatya*).
"Concentration (*samādhi*) and its associated [mental factors] are not contradictory;
this explains away the objection. The objection states: "Mindfulness takes an object previously experienced as its domain, whereas anger takes a present object as its domain;

how can they be associated? The answer and explanation are clear. Furthermore, the objection states: "How can concentration and distraction be associated? The explanation is likewise [to be understood].
This can be understood. △ Seventh, the Section on Correspondence with the Root [Defilements].
Among these, the two major and eight (or ten) minor [secondary defilements] are associated with the root afflictions.

The ten minor [defilements] definitely do not arise together with views (*dṛṣṭi*) or doubt (*vicikitsā*), because these [ten] are coarse and agitated, whereas those [views and doubt] are subtle and refined. As for the five dharmas beginning with anger (*krodha*), they may be associated with pride (*māna*) and delusion (*moha*), but not with...
Greed and hatred coexist; because they are divisions of hatred (*dveṣa*). Stinginess coexists with delusion (*moha*) and pride (*māna*), but does not coexist with greed or hatred;
because it is a division of greed. Arrogance (*mada*) coexists only with delusion; it differs from pride in its aspect (*ākāra*), as it is a division of greed.

Concealment (*mrakṣa*), deceit (*śāṭhya*), and guile (*māyā*) may coexist with greed, delusion, and pride; because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are not contradictory, they are merely divisions of greed and delusion.
The five factors beginning with anger (*krodha*)—namely, anger, enmity, resentment, jealousy, and harmfulness—are all subdivisions of hatred (*dveṣa*).

Since two instances of hatred cannot coexist within a single moment of consciousness, and since hatred and greed (*lobha*) certainly do not arise simultaneously, these five can only coexist with pride (*māna*) and delusion (*moha*).

Stinginess (*mātsarya*) is a subdivision of greed and does not arise concurrently with either greed or hatred. Arrogance (*mada*) is also a subdivision of greed and likewise does not arise with greed or hatred.
They arise simultaneously. As for the statement that attachment (*rāga*) and pride (*māna*) are distinct, it is because attachment causes the mind to sink, whereas pride causes the mind to uplift.
Question: In the *Fahua wenju*, pride is explained as being synonymous with arrogance (*mada*). How is this [distinction] to be reconciled? Answer:
The preceding text also states that because the objects stained by and those relied upon by them can be the same, attachment and pride may be associated. Furthermore...

*Stambha* (pride) has intoxication and arrogance as its essential nature; arrogance is itself *māna* (conceit). In common parlance, people often say "pride and arrogance" (*stambha-māna*) or simply "pride" (*stambha*).

Here, for the sake of brevity, we are considering the coarse characteristics of the minor derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*). At the very moment one is intoxicated with pride, it does not necessarily involve looking down upon others;

therefore, their distinct definitions are explained. Regarding the statement that "speech and conduct do not conflict," this refers to *mrakṣa* (concealment), *māyā* (deception), and *śāṭhya* (guile), which are subsumed under the category of craving.

They do not contradict delusion (*moha*). Furthermore, concealment (*mrakṣa*), deception (*māyā*), and guile (*śāṭhya*), which are comprised within the category of delusion, also do not contradict greed (*lobha*) or pride (*māna*).
△ Eight: The Section on the Mutual Inclusion of the Three Natures.

The seven minor [afflictions] and the two intermediate ones are subsumed exclusively under the unwholesome (*akuśala*). The three minor and eight major ones also pertain to the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).

The seven minor ones refer to anger (*krodha*), enmity (*upanāha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), resentment (*pradāsa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*). Since five of these are branches of hatred (*dveṣa*), they are exclusively unwholesome.

Concealment (*mrakṣa*), being accompanied by both greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*), nourishes sinful defilements; therefore, it is exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*). Stinginess (*mātsarya*), being characterized by parsimony and coarseness, forever blocks the path to merit;

therefore, it is exclusively unwholesome. As for the three—flattery (*śāṭhya*), deception (*māyā*), and arrogance (*mada*)—if they are associated with shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), they are termed "evil" (*pāpa*).
If it has not yet reached the stage of being indifferent to oneself and others, it is still termed "obscured-unspecified" (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
If the [great] eight [mental factors] arise together with any one of the ten unwholesome paths of action, they are termed "unwholesome" (*akuśala*).

If they correspond with other spontaneous afflictions (*kleśa*), they are likewise termed only "obscured-unspecified. △ Section Nine: The Gate of the Connection to Realms and Conditions; this also has three parts.
First, the realms of attachment (*dhātu-bandhana*) are clarified; second, their manifestation is clarified; third, their mutual conditioning is clarified. Now, for the first:

the seven minor [afflictions] and two middle [afflictions] are comprised solely within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); deceit (*māyā*) and guile (*śāṭhya*) pertain to both the desire and form realms (*rūpadhātu*); the remaining [pride (*mada*) and the eight great afflictions] pertain to all three realms.
△ Second, the explanation of their manifestation.

When born in a lower stage, one may manifest eleven [afflictions] of a higher stage (namely, the eight great ones, along with *mada*, *māyā*, and *śāṭhya*). This is because, by being attached to a higher meditative concentration, one gives rise to pride, deceit, and flattery toward others.

In the higher stages (*ūrdhvabhūmi*), the five [afflictions] such as anger (*krodha*) do not exist because of the absence of hatred (*dveṣa*). Furthermore, there is no concealed stinginess (*mrakṣamātsarya*), because these are unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Therefore, they are not mentioned.

If one is born in a higher stage, the latter ten [afflictions] of the lower stages may arise—namely, the two intermediate ones and the eight major ones—because wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) [which slanders liberation] and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) [which moistens rebirth] are capable of coexisting with them.

Because they arise from that [state]. As for the ten minor [defilements] arising in a higher realm, there is no basis for them to arise in a lower one, because they do not directly moisten rebirth nor do they involve the denial of cessation (*nirodha*).
△ Third, the mutual conditioning [of defilements].

The two intermediate [great] ones and the eight great [afflictions] take the higher [stages] as their objects; the lower [stages] likewise take the higher as their objects (and so do the upper ones), because they arise in association with craving and other such [defilements].

One interpretation holds that the ten minor [afflictions] of the lower [stages] do not take the higher as their objects, because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are coarse and proximate, and thus they do not grasp distant objects.

Another interpretation holds that envy (*īrṣyā*) and the others can also take the higher as their objects, because one gives rise to envy and so forth toward the dharmas of superior stages. The eight great [afflictions], as well as guile (*śāṭhya*) and deceit (*māyā*), also take the higher as their objects.

The [pride] associated with inferiority (ūnamāna) and so forth arises in conjunction with the pride that takes the lower as its object; furthermore, Brahmā practiced deceit and guile toward the Śākyaputras.
Arrogance (mada), however, does not take the lower as its object, because those lower levels are not objects of reliance for it.
Regarding the twelve minor meanings, the latter interpretation is superior; the rest may be understood accordingly. The section on the nine realms as present conditions is concluded.
△ Ten: The Section on the Mutual Inclusion of the Categories of Learners and Others.

The twenty [types of secondary afflictions] are all neither included within the category of those in training (*śaikṣa*) nor those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). These twenty are exclusively defiled (*kliṣṭa*), whereas those [in training and beyond training] are exclusively pure (*anāsrava*).
The meaning is as explained in the section on the root afflictions. △ Eleven: The Section on the Mutual Inclusion of the Three Cuts (*prahāṇa*).

The latter ten [afflictions] are exclusively abandoned through both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) (and are not non-abandonable), because they arise in association with both types of root afflictions—those that are conceptually constructed (*vikalpa*) and those that are innate (*sahaja*).

Those abandoned through the path of seeing arise simultaneously with root afflictions, either collectively or individually, according to the specific characteristics of the truths (*satya*) regarding which one is deluded.

Therefore, as appropriate, they all pertain to the four categories of the truths. Their relative proximity or distance from the delusion regarding the truths, and so forth, are all as explained for the root [afflictions].

Regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*) [discussed] herein, there are two interpretations concerning the first ten. One interpretation holds that they are abandoned exclusively through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because they take coarse objects as their domain and arise spontaneously (*svarasena*).
Another interpretation holds that they also pertain to both those abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned through cultivation.

This is because they arise through the power of the two types of fundamental afflictions—both conceptual (*vikalpita*) and innate (*sahaja*)—and because anger and other such states arise in relation to the views of others (as in the case of non-Buddhists). Thus, they also pertain to those abandoned through seeing. As for those abandoned through seeing, they follow...

The objects they take as conditions consist of the general and specific fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), all of which are comprised within the four categories (*catuṣkoṭi*). Regarding this, there is one interpretation:

anger (*krodha*) and the others arise only from taking as their object those afflictions that are deluded regarding the Truths (*satya*); they do not directly delude the Truths themselves, because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are coarse and superficial, and thus they do not grasp [the Truths] deeply.
There is another interpretation: envy (*īrṣyā*) and the others also directly delude the Truths, because envy and so forth arise toward Cessation (*nirodha*), the Path (*mārga*), and so on.
The latter ten are the two intermediate [unwholesome roots] and the eight great [unwholesome roots]. The former ten are the ten minor derivative [unwholesome mental factors].

Regarding this, there is a further interpretation below concerning the directness or indirectness of delusion with respect to the Truths (*satya*). There are two schools of explanation that may be consulted together; therefore, there is no need for selection or rejection.
△ Section Twelve: Establishing Names According to the Objects.

However, since the ten [afflictions] such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth take only existent things as their objects—necessarily depending upon a fundamental substance (*bhāva*) in order to arise—the ten minor [afflictions] take only existent things as their objects and do not take non-existent things as their objects.
From this, it is known that the two intermediate [categories] and the eight major [categories] take both existent and non-existent things as their objects;
for the eight major ones pervade all defilements (*kleśa*), and the two intermediate ones pervade all unwholesome states (*akuśala*).
Regarding the objects such as those with outflows (*sāsrava*), they should be understood according to the above principle.

That is to say, all twenty take both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as their objects; furthermore, they all take objective entities (*vastu*) as their cognitive domains (*viṣaya*).
Within these twenty dharmas, taking even a single one at random, it is likewise inconceivable in this manner. And yet, sentient beings—
Deluded and lacking self-awareness, they willingly endure the cycle of false and inverted saṃsāra.

It is like touching a treasure in the dark and injuring one's body, or like those with cataracts seeing empty flowers dancing in the air. How tragic this is! This concludes the fourth explanation of the secondary afflictions (upakleśa).

△ Fifth: Explanation of the Indeterminate Mental Factors (aniyata-caitta). Part Two. First, the citation of the verse; second, the commentary. Now, the first:
Having already explained the characteristics of the twenty secondary afflictions (upakleśa), there are four indeterminate factors. What are their characteristics? The verse says:
The indeterminate factors are said to be remorse (kaukṛtya), sleep (middha), vitarka, and vicāra. Each pair consists of two [types].

△ Second, the commentary on the treatise has two parts: first, the direct explanation of the verses; second, the analysis by way of various categories. Within the first part, there are three sections:
first, the explanation of the general name; second, the explanation of the specific names; third, the explanation of the two [categories] each having two [aspects]. Now, the first [section].

The treatise says: Remorse (*kaukṛtya*), sleep (*middha*), vitarka, and vicāra are designated as "indeterminate" (*aniyata*) because they are not fixed within the wholesome, the defiled, and so forth;

they do not necessarily pervade all minds like contact (*sparśa*) and the other [universal mental factors], nor do they necessarily pervade all stages (*bhūmi*) like desire (*chanda*) and the other [particular universal factors]. Therefore, they are given the name "indeterminate."
"Wholesome" refers to the nature of wholesomeness. "Defiled" refers to the natures of unwholesomeness and obscured-neutral. The term "and so forth" includes the unobscured-neutral nature.
Although the universal factors such as contact (*sparśa*) and the rest pertain to all three natures, they are not called "indeterminate" because they are necessarily universal to the mind.

Although the object-specific factors such as desire (*chanda*) and the rest pertain to all three natures, they are also not universal to the mind; because they are necessarily universal... [the universal factors are distinguished].

Because they do not pertain to all stages (*bhūmi*), they are also not called "indeterminate" (*aniyata*). Now, these [two] do not pervade all minds, nor do they pervade all stages; they merely pervade the three natures (*tridharmatā*).
Therefore, the name "indeterminate" is established for them. II. Explaining the specific names has two parts: first, explaining regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*);
second, explaining applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*). Herein is the first.

*Kaukṛtya* (remorse). This refers to the regret (*kaukṛtya*) regarding an action previously performed that was evil (or, conversely, regarding an action not previously performed that one now regrets not having done). Its intrinsic nature is remorse; its function is to obstruct *śamatha* (calm abiding).
This name "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*), which is applied to the cause, is established metaphorically upon the fruit—namely, the subsequent regret for an action previously performed that was evil.
Thus, regretting something not previously done is also subsumed under "remorse," as when one says in regret: "I previously did not perform such a task."
"I have committed an evil deed. This first explains *kaukṛtya* (remorse). In the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*, it is termed "evil deed" (*akuśala-kṛta*), which is a name established based on its cause.

Here, however, it is named according to its fruit; therefore, it is called "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*). Regarding its pervasion across the three natures: having previously committed an evil act, one now...
Regret: If one has not previously performed wholesome deeds and now feels regret, this is all called wholesome.
If one has already performed wholesome deeds and now feels regret, or if one has not previously committed unwholesome deeds and now instead feels regret, these are all called unwholesome.
If one has previously performed neutral deeds and now feels regret, or if one has not previously performed neutral deeds and now [feels regret]...
Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) still belongs to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). However, there is remorse for having previously committed evil and remorse for not having performed good;

although both are called "wholesome," if one loses the skillful means (*upāya*), one will be wounded by the arrow of sorrow and this is termed the "cover of remorse" (*kaukṛtyanīvaraṇa*). Thus, it is able to obstruct meditative stillness (*śamatha*).

Therefore, when a practitioner cultivates the five types of repentance (*pañca-pratikramaṇa*), what is truly valued is the permanent severing of their continuity and the diligent encouragement of all virtues; it is not [merely the feeling of regret].
It is merely a matter of subsequent recollection and regret.

*Middha* (sleep) refers to slumber; its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is to cause the body to lose its autonomy and the mind to become extremely dark and contracted (*saṃkṣepa*) regarding its objects. Its function (*karman*) is to obstruct insight (*vipaśyanā*).

This means that in the state of sleep, the body lacks autonomy and the mind is extremely dark and feeble, because it operates through a single sense-door (*ekamukha-pravṛtta*). The term "contracted" (*saṃkṣepa*) serves to distinguish it [from other states].

[This] is the clarity [of meditative concentration]. It is distinguished, in brief, from the thoroughness of the waking state. Taken together, this demonstrates that sleep is not without essence or function (even though it appears so).

Although it is provisionally designated by the name "extremely heavy sleep" within the five states of mindlessness (*acittaka*), it nevertheless possesses essence and function because, like other hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), it is associated with the mind (*citta-samprayukta*).
Thus, it certainly has both essence and function.

This also explains "sleep" (*middha*). It is called "obscuration" (*styāna*) because the mind is extremely dull and inferior; it is called "contraction" (*laya*) because it functions through only a single door.

While the [simultaneous] *manovijñāna* functions by turning toward all six sense-doors—both internal and external—the present "solitary" (*mukta*) *manovijñāna* turns toward only one internal door, lacking the other five external doors.
This state permeates all three moral natures (*tri-śīla*), because the mind is under the influence of sleep.
That which is associated with the sixth consciousness produces various dreams.

If one practices the ten wholesome paths of action, the six perfections, and so forth within a dream, it is termed "wholesome. If one commits acts such as killing, stealing, greed, or anger within a dream, it is termed "unwholesome.
Dreams that are neither wholesome nor unwholesome are termed "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*). However, sentient beings lack...
Since beginningless time, the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the unwholesome and the neutral have predominantly matured, while wholesome latencies have been produced only sporadically;

therefore, during sleep, they are able to obstruct right contemplation. Furthermore, committing evil in dreams is due to the force of spontaneous unwholesome habits and because it causes unreal harm and affliction to sentient beings.
Although it is termed "unwholesome," one does not incur a painful retribution on account of this. If, within a dream...

One performs good deeds. Because these roots of goodness have matured, and because they can further permeate and increase the roots of goodness, even if one does not actually benefit sentient beings, one nonetheless acquires merit thereby.
This is because although evil arises from one's nature, its power is weak due to its opposition to that nature;
whereas goodness also arises from one's nature, its power is strong due to its conformity with that nature.

It is strong. As for "other envelopments and fetters" (*paryavasthāna*): "envelopments" (*nīvaraṇa*) refers to the five envelopments: first, sensual desire; second, ill-will; third, sloth and torpor; fourth, restlessness and remorse; and fifth, doubt.

They are called "envelopments" because they cover and obstruct concentration and wisdom. Now, since sleep is already an envelopment, it should—like sensual desire and the others—possess its own intrinsic essence and function.
"Fetters" (*paryavasthāna*) refers to the ten fetters: first, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*); second, lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*)... [text continues].
3. Shamelessness (*āhrīkya*); 4. Lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*); 5. Sleep (*middha*); 6. Torpor (*styāna*); 7. Restlessness (*auddhatya*); 8. Remorse (*kaukṛtya*);

9. Envy (*īrṣyā*); 10. Avarice (*mātsarya*); 11. Anger (*krodha*); 12. Concealment (*mrakṣa*). Because they bind sentient beings and prevent their liberation, they are called "envelopments" (*paryavasthāna*).
Now, since sleep is an envelopment, it must, like shamelessness and the others, possess its own distinct substance and function.

One interpretation holds that these two have only delusion (*moha*) as their essence, because the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that they are subsumed under the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and the category of delusion.

Another interpretation holds that this is not so, because they also pertain to the wholesome. One should state that if these two are defiled, they have delusion as their essence; if they are pure, they have non-delusion (*amoha*) as their essence.
The treatise, relying on the defiled portion, states that they are subsumed under the secondary afflictions and the category of delusion. Yet another interpretation holds [the same].
This explanation is also unreasonable. (Although these two are also associated with the indeterminate, yet) the indeterminate is neither delusion nor non-delusion, because its nature is neither.

One should state that remorse has both volition (*cetanā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence: [it is] by way of wisdom because it clearly perceives, and by way of volition because it deliberates upon the action performed.

Sleep has both volition and perception (*saṃjñā*) as its essence: [it is] by way of volition because it functions in conjunction [with other states], and by way of perception because it perceives the various appearances of dream objects.

Since both treatises state that they exist as conventional realities (*saṃvṛti-sat*), those [states of] remorse and torpor that are defiled (*kliṣṭa*) are the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of delusion (*moha*).

Just as lack of faith and so forth are said to be subdivisions of delusion (*moha*), the following section generally distinguishes the essential characteristics (*svabhāva*) of remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*). There are four points in total; for now, regarding the first three points, it is incorrect to claim that they have no separate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of their own.

There is another interpretation: that explanation is also unreasonable. It is not the case that they have the conceptualization of wisdom (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) as their essence, because remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) repeatedly increase and intensify, enveloping both body and mind;

such is their nature. Therefore, it should be said that these two each possess a distinct substantial entity, because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) differ from those of other mental factors (*caitta*). (However, they...)
Because it is explained according to the characteristics of delusion (*moha*), it is called "conventionally existent" (though its essence is not non-existent).

This fourth interpretation is the correct one. The first explanation of regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) is concluded. △ Second, the explanation of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).

Vitarka (investigation) means searching; it causes the mind to be hurried and urgent, and its nature is to function coarsely with respect to the objects of mental discourse. Vicāra (analysis) means examining;
it causes the mind to be hurried and urgent, and its nature is to function subtly with respect to the objects of mental discourse.
Both of these have as their function the basis for the states of physical and mental composure or non-composure, and both employ a portion of volition (*cetanā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

They constitute its essence. Because their objects are respectively conceptualized speech (*manojalpa*)—without deep investigation (termed *vitarka*) and with deep investigation (termed *vicāra*)—their meanings are distinct.
If one were separated from the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), the distinct natures and categories of vitarka and vicāra could not be apprehended.
These two—vitarka and vicāra—refer to the states of physical and mental ease or unease, all of which arise in dependence upon vitarka and vicāra.
When there is no deep investigation, reflection is primary and wisdom assists; when there is deep investigation, wisdom is primary and reflection assists.

The rest may be understood accordingly. This concludes the second section, the explanation of the individual names. △ Third, the explanation of the two [categories], each having two [aspects], which contains three meanings.
The first two meanings are incorrect; the third meaning is correct.
Regarding the phrase "each has two": there is one interpretation that *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) each have two categories, namely the defiled and the pure.
There is another interpretation which holds that this explanation does not accord with correct principle, because mental torpor (*middha*) also possesses both defiled and pure aspects.

It should be stated [as follows]: like the previously mentioned defiled mental factors, some of these are primary afflictions (*kleśa*) while others are secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Within these two categories, each...

There are two categories: the unwholesome and the indeterminate; furthermore, each of these may consist of two further types: those currently active as entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) and those existing as latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The first interpretation erroneously assigns two sentences each exclusively to *vitarka* (initial inquiry) and *vicāra* (sustained examination).

The second interpretation, while recognizing that two sentences each apply to all four dharmas, wrongly asserts that they must be either the pair of the unwholesome and the indeterminate, or the pair of the active (*samudācāra*) and the seed (*bīja*).
Therefore, both are inconsistent with reason.

There is another interpretation: that previous explanation is also unreasonable because, following the four indeterminate states (*aniyata*), there is the statement [referring to] "these two [each having] two.
One should say that the single word "two" in the verse indicates two kinds of pairs: first, remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*); second, vitarka and vicāra.
These two pairs are distinct in their categories (remorse being different from sleep, and vitarka being different from vicāra). Therefore, [the word "two" in the verse refers only to the former].
The phrase "two of two" (*ge-er-zhi-wei-yany-bianji*) reveals these two pairs. Each of these two types further has two sub-types: namely, the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) and the non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*).
This is unlike the eleven wholesome mental factors (*cittasāṃprayuktadharma*) and the twenty-six afflicted mental factors, which each exist as single entities.

Alternatively, it is used to distinguish them from the purely afflicted [factors, i.e., the afflictions], whereas these [four] include both the non-afflicted and may also be subsumed under the wholesome. Thus, the statement that "each of these two has two" is based on various treatises; in some places, these four are also described as being "concomitant" (*anuvartin*).
Because of the afflictions (now specifically), in order to clarify the meaning of their non-fixity, it is said that "each of these two has two.
Therefore, the inclusion of this expression "each of these two has two" is profoundly useful.

The third section, "Correct Meaning," may be understood according to the text. This concludes the first part, the correct explanation of the verse. △ Second, the analysis by way of various categories consists of thirteen sections.
First, the category of the provisional and the real (up to). Thirteenth, the general conclusion regarding the remaining categories. Now, the first [section].

Among the four [mental factors], vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) are definitely nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*), as they are said by the Noble Ones to be a synthesis of volition (*cetanā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Regarding regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*), one interpretation holds that these two are also nominally existent, because the *Yogācārabhūmi* describes them as conventionally existent (*saṃvṛtisat*).

Another interpretation holds that these two are substantially existent (*dravyasat*), because it is only the latter two [of the four] that are described as nominally existent. However, within the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the term "conventionally existent" merely refers to that which exists in dependence upon other characteristics.

This statement does not indicate that the first two concentrations are merely nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*). Furthermore, although the substance of internal seeds is real, the treatise also describes them as conventionally existent (*saṃvṛtisat*).
△ Second, the section on correspondence within its own category.

Among these four, vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) are definitely not associated [with one another], as their essential natures are identical and differ only in degree of coarseness and subtlety.

The distinction between the three stages is established based on whether vitarka and vicāra are accompanied by defilement or free from defilement, rather than being based on the presence or absence of their seeds or their actual manifestation.
Therefore, there is no fault of confusion or overlap. Furthermore, both of these two factors (vitarka and vicāra) may be mutually associated with the two preceding states (kaukṛtya and middha).
The preceding [two types of] remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) also possess the sense of mutual association.
As for the distinction between the three stages: first, the stage with vitarka and vicāra; second, the stage without vitarka but with vicāra; and third, the stage without both vitarka and vicāra.
One might fear an objection being raised: since the two factors of vitarka and vicāra do not arise simultaneously, if [one were to ask] regarding the desire realm...

Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): even when one is in the first dhyāna, which is fundamentally a stage characterized by both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), if at the very moment vicāra arises, vitarka does not arise.
How is this different from a stage characterized by the absence of vitarka but the presence of vicāra? Therefore, the present explanation states:

the distinction between the three stages is established based on whether vitarka and vicāra are associated with defilement (*kliṣṭa*) or non-defilement (*akliṣṭa*). That is to say, if one has not yet abandoned defilement regarding both vitarka and vicāra, it is called [the stage] "with... [vitarka and vicāra].

Regarding the stages of *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought): if one is free from attachment to *vitarka* but not yet free from attachment to *vicāra*, it is called the stage of "without *vitarka* but with *vicāra*.

If one is free from attachment to both *vitarka* and *vicāra*, it is called the stage of "without *vitarka* and without *vicāra*. This is because these names do not depend on the presence or absence of the actual manifestation of those seeds;
therefore, there is no fault of confusion. During times of regret and during times of sleep, *vitarka* and *vicāra* may be present, even while one is actually asleep.
Even within sleep, regret can occur; therefore, both are associated [with the sixth consciousness]. △ Third, the section on the association of the various consciousnesses:
all four are not concomitant with the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, as explained previously.
Regret and sleep are associated only with the sixth consciousness, because they are not dharmas associated with the [first] five consciousnesses.

The meaning is as previously explained; this refers to what was distinguished and indicated in the section on the seventh consciousness among the two types of "transforming" consciousnesses (the first and second).
Because the first five consciousnesses spontaneously take present objects as their domain, they do not associate with remorse (*kaukṛtya*).
Since the five consciousnesses do not function during sleep, they do not associate with torpor (*middha*).

There is another interpretation: vitarka and vicāra also coexist with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). This is because the treatises state that the five sensory consciousnesses possess vitarka and vicāra;

furthermore, they state that vitarka and vicāra constitute the seven types of discrimination (*vikalpa*), namely those characterized by signs (*nimitta*) and so forth. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* further states that spontaneous discrimination refers to the five sensory consciousnesses.
