For this reason, the entry into the nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) is not mentioned; for once one has entered the nirvana without remainder, [the consciousnesses] no longer arise.

This is explained in two parts. The first interpretation is incorrect; the second is correct, as both can be understood. △ Third, the determination of whether these stages apply to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) or noble ones (*ārya*).
Within these five stages, ordinary beings possess four, excluding those in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Noble ones possess only the latter three.

Among them, for the Tathāgata and Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and above who have attained mastery, only one [stage] remains, because they lack [extremely heavy] sleep (*middha*) and fainting (*mūrchana*).

Ordinary beings and non-Buddhists are all termed "ordinary folk" (*pṛthagjana*), because they have not yet realized the noble Dharma and thus cannot enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

The noble ones of the three vehicles do not enter the absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) nor are they born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*); this applies from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward.
Having attained mastery over phenomena, they are free from the distress of extremely heavy sleep; they merely enter the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) at times.
This concludes the first section, from the middle of the second fascicle up to this point, which explains the characteristics of the three transformative consciousnesses.

△ Second, harmonizing the three transformative consciousnesses as they function simultaneously to demonstrate the two truths. This has three parts: 1. A general explanation of their simultaneous functioning. 2. A detailed analysis of their simultaneous functioning. 3. [The third part follows].
Regarding the meaning of "transformation," three points are presented to demonstrate the two truths. First:
for this reason, in all sentient beings, the eight consciousnesses consist of the mind (*citta*) and the manas, which always function together; if the sixth consciousness arises, [it also functions].
Thus, three [mental factors] arise together; the others, according to the convergence of conditions, arise from one up to five, thus ranging from four together up to eight together.
This is a brief explanation of the meaning of the simultaneous arising of consciousnesses.
"All sentient beings" refers collectively to the ten realms, encompassing both the noble and the ordinary; the rest may be understood accordingly.
△ Second, the analysis of the meaning of simultaneous transformation. There are six rounds of question and answer in total. This is the first round.
(Question: If a single sentient being possesses multiple consciousnesses arising simultaneously, how can it be said that he is one sentient being? (Answer:
If the status of being a sentient being were established based on the number of consciousnesses, then you would not be a sentient being during the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*).

Furthermore, when the mind of another continuum (*parasantāna*) is present before you, how could you be said to be a sentient being of your own continuum (*svasantāna*)? However, the establishment of a sentient being depends on [the continuity of the basis].
Whether [the life-faculty] is reckoned as being associated with the life-faculty itself or with the resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), both are consistent with reason;
for both of them are always present and exist as only one at any given time.
"Other part" (*parabhāga*) and "self-part" (*svabhāga*) are discussed by comparing them across the six realms of existence.
For instance, when one is currently a human being, humans constitute the self-part, while the other five realms are all termed the other part.

However, while actually being a human, one may suddenly give rise to the mind of a celestial being, or suddenly give rise to the mind of a hell-being, and so forth. If one relies solely upon the predominance of consciousness...

If sentient beings were established while young, then at the very moment they correctly give rise to the consciousness of the heavenly realm, they should be called "sentient beings of the heavenly realm.
Why, then, are they still called "sentient beings of the human realm"? Other cases may be understood by analogy.

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is a provisional designation based on the functional capacity of the physical and mental aggregates to maintain continuity without interruption. The ripening-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is the eighth [consciousness], the resultant retribution. It is non-...
This refers to the *vijñapti* (cognition). △ Second round of question and answer.
(Question: Since there is only one immediate antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for a single body, how can multiple cognitions arise simultaneously? (Answer:

Since you already admit that this single [immediate antecedent condition] can induce multiple mental factors (*caitta*) of subsequent moments, why do you not also admit that it can induce multiple minds (*cittas*)?

Furthermore, who has definitively stated that this condition (*pratyaya*) is singular? For those who assert that multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously admit that this condition is likewise multiple.
Moreover, when one desires to apprehend multiple objects at once and multiple objects are present before one, why would they not be apprehended instantaneously?
Since the power of the harmony between the sense faculties, their objects, and so forth, is equal [in all cases], it is unreasonable to claim that consciousness necessarily arises sequentially.

Therefore, furthermore, although the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of mental factors (*caitta*) is without distinction, since it is accepted that different categories—such as attachment and so forth—arise simultaneously, why would one not allow for the simultaneous arising of various types of consciousness?
Moreover, just as waves [in water] or reflections [in a mirror] arise as many based on a single [substratum], so too do multiple consciousnesses evolve simultaneously based on a single mind.
Furthermore, if one does not allow for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) to coexist with the five [sensory] consciousnesses, then [the mental consciousness] could not apprehend them.

The objects perceived by the five consciousnesses would not be clear, just as [an object] perceived by a solitary, distracted mental consciousness is not, because [in both cases] the object has long since ceased to exist.
Regarding the seventy-five dharmas maintained by the Hīnayāna, mental factors are singular.

Because a preceding extinguished mind induces the arising of a subsequent mind, it is said that within a single continuum there is only one equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). In the response, first a direct answer is given, followed by an indirect answer.
As for the direct answer: even if only a single equal-and-immediate condition were to induce the arising of multiple consciousnesses, there would still be no fault.

This is incorrect, because they also admit that a single equal-and-immediate antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) can induce the arising of multiple mental factors (*caitta*). To answer in reverse order:
since it is admitted that sentient beings each possess eight consciousnesses, it is also admitted that each of these eight consciousnesses possesses its own equal-and-immediate antecedent condition.

Furthermore, if you do not admit that many consciousnesses arise simultaneously, then when multiple objects—such as visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles—appear before one, how could they not be apprehended all at once within a single moment?
If you claim that although the sense organs and their objects are simultaneous, the consciousnesses occur sequentially, [this is untenable].

This would be unreasonable. Furthermore, since you already admit that multiple mental factors (*caitta*) arise simultaneously, why do you alone not admit that multiple mind-kings (*cittarāja*) may also function simultaneously?

Moreover, just as water and a mirror are singular while waves and reflections can be many, one knows that the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is singular while the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) can be many.
Furthermore, if one does not admit that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the five [sensory consciousnesses] exist at the same time...
If [the five consciousnesses] were simultaneous with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), then at the moment the mental consciousness arises, the preceding five would have already ceased.

This would be equivalent to the independent mental consciousness (*mukhyamano-vijñāna*) perceiving an object that has already ceased; how, then, could it be clear and distinct? △ Third Round of Question and Answer.
(Question: How is it that when associated with the five consciousnesses, there is only a single mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that can apprehend one or many objects such as visible forms?

(Answer: Just as each of the visual and other consciousnesses can also apprehend one or many within their respective domains, so too does this mental consciousness apprehend one or many among the five sensory objects.
What fault is there in this? For the two aspects—the objective image (*nimittabhāga*) and the subjective seeing (*darśanabhāga*)—of all six consciousnesses alike possess various characteristics.

Furthermore, there are those of the Lesser Vehicle who falsely calculate that there are five consciousnesses; therefore, they challenge the position that there is only a single consciousness, arguing that it should not be able to apprehend multiple objects simultaneously.

The answer and its explanation may be understood [from the context]. One should formulate the formal inference (*pramāṇa*) as follows: "The subject (*dharmin*) is a single consciousness occurring at one time."

The school that maintains that [consciousness] can apprehend multiple objects provides the reason: "Because both the aspect (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*) possess various characteristics. The analogy is:
"Just as a single visual consciousness can apprehend multiple colors and so forth. △ Fourth Round of Question and Answer.

(Question: For what reason do cognitions of the same class not arise simultaneously? (Answer: Regarding their respective objects, if [an object] cannot be discerned, then even many [cognitions] would be useless.
If it can be discerned, one [cognition] is already sufficient to discern it; therefore, others would be redundant.

"Similar [consciousnesses] do not coexist. This means that within a single moment, two visual consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously, and so on, up to two storehouse consciousnesses (*ālayavijñāna*) not arising simultaneously.
The meaning of the answer can be understood. The Fifth Question and Answer.

(Question: If that is so, since the five consciousnesses are already capable of cognizing their respective objects individually, what is the use of the simultaneously arising mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) to cognize them? (Answer:)

The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that arises simultaneously with the five [sensory] consciousnesses assists them in their arising; it does not merely function to cognize the objects of the five consciousnesses.

Furthermore, because this [mental consciousness] can clearly apprehend those objects of the five [sensory] consciousnesses in a manner distinct from the eye-consciousness and the other four, it is not without utility.
For this reason, the sacred teachings state that this mental consciousness is called "conceptual" (*savikalpa*), whereas the five consciousnesses are not.

The five consciousnesses are not like this; they possess only the discrimination of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), whereas the mental consciousness further possesses the two types of discrimination:
recollection (*anusmaraṇa*) and deliberation (*abhinirūpaṇa*). Question and Answer Number Six.

(Question: Since many consciousnesses arise simultaneously, why do they not associate with one another in the same way that the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) do? (Answer: Because they do not share the same object.

Even if they were to share the same object, their respective bases (*āśraya*) differ in substance and number; thus, they do not associate. For example, although the five sense organs and the five consciousnesses share the same objects, they do not associate with one another.
Regarding "not having the same object": visual consciousness takes visible form as its object, and so on, up to tactile consciousness taking tangibles as its object.

These two verses are cited to demonstrate that the three natures (trisvabhāva) are perfectly free from both existence and non-existence, thereby acceding to the Middle Way;
this is precisely the inconceivable Three Truths. The phrase "existence through false discrimination" clarifies that the defiled aspect of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) exists;

this is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). The phrase "the absolute absence of these two" clarifies that the imagined self and phenomena (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) are fundamentally empty; this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
In this context, there is only the phrase "emptiness," which clarifies that within the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) there exists the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).

Within that [perfected nature] as well, there is this same phrase, clarifying that the perfected nature is not separate from the dependent nature. This is precisely the non-duality of the ultimate and the conventional;
it reveals the essence of the Middle Way, the supreme truth (paramārtha-satya). Therefore, it is said that all phenomena are neither empty nor non-empty. Thus, they are one.
It is clear that all phenomena are none other than the Middle Way. The word "existence" (you) refers to the first phrase;
the word "non-existence" (wu) refers to the second phrase; and "because of existence" (ji you gu) refers to both the third and fourth phrases.
That "all phenomena exist" is the provisional (jia); that "all phenomena do not exist" is emptiness (kong); and that "all phenomena and because of existence" is the Middle (zhong). Therefore...

The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Phenomena produced through causes and conditions are emptiness, they are the provisional, and they are the middle. These terms—emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—are taught for the sake of easy understanding.
To speak of the ultimate reality, however, there is only the single Middle Way as the true essence.

This Middle Way is free from all marks; it is not that which is grasped by imaginary construction (*parikalpita*). It is precisely the meaning of emptiness in accordance with reality (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā*). The Middle Way is all things.
The Dharma is fully endowed with the dependent origination of others; that is, it is the meaning of being "not empty" according to reality.
Although there are two meanings—emptiness and non-emptiness—the essence is fundamentally neither empty nor non-empty.

Now, since it is said that all dharmas are neither empty nor non-empty, each of the eight consciousnesses is neither empty nor non-empty; this is precisely the Middle Way, naturally endowed [with these qualities].
The three truths are complete within each of the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*); each is neither empty nor non-empty, which is precisely the Middle Way.
By the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they are inherently complete with the three truths. The eleven material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are likewise each neither empty nor non-empty;

this is precisely the Middle Way. By the very nature of phenomena, they are inherently complete with the three truths. Furthermore, each of the twenty-four types of dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) is also...
Neither empty nor non-empty—this is the Middle Way. By the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is fully endowed with the three truths.
The six kinds of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas are likewise neither empty nor non-empty; they are the Middle Way. By the very nature of phenomena, they are fully endowed with the three truths.

This is the most prominent point where the lineages of the two schools, Nature (Xing) and Characteristics (Xiang), are interconnected. Yet people generally overlook and fail to perceive this. How can one bear such a state of affairs?
Why is this? This verse speaks provisionally based on the defiled portion of the *paratantra-svabhāva*. In reality, there is also a pure portion of the *paratantra-svabhāva*.

The defiled portion of the *paratantra* consists of the six categories of ordinary beings produced by causes and conditions; the pure portion of the *paratantra* is likewise produced by causes and conditions.

The four dharmas of the noble ones arise. Since each and every dharma of the six classes of ordinary beings is itself emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle Way, how could the dharmas of the four noble ones alone be otherwise?
Therefore it is said: "The ten realms of existence are none other than emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle Way.

The clear evidence for this lies herein; why then do you not believe it? The first section, "Difficulties Concerning the Causes of Consciousness-Only," is concluded. II. Explaining How Worldly Affairs Contradict the Fundamental Principle.
Objection:

If it is only internal consciousness that arises appearing as external objects, how is it that we perceive the world’s animate and inanimate things, with their fixed or unfixed locations, times, bodies, and functions?
Response: This doubt should be resolved by [the analogy of] dream-objects and the like.

Within this, there are four difficulties: first, the determination of place; second, the determination of time; third, the indeterminacy of the body; and fourth, the indeterminacy of the basis and function.
First, regarding the determination of place: for example, the Southern Mountains are situated in the south; one cannot use consciousness to cause them to be in the north.
Therefore, they are not merely consciousness. Second, regarding the determination of time: for example, when the consciousness that takes the mountain as its object arises...
Mountains certainly exist inherently. However, when the consciousness that perceives the mountain ceases, the mountain does not cease along with it;
therefore, they are not merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*). Regarding the uncertainty of the three bodies (*trikāya*):

for example, when many people look at a lamp’s light together, one who has a visual impairment sees five colors superimposed, which is false and may be called "mere consciousness. Those without such impairment all see only pure light.
This would then be a real object; therefore, it is not mere consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*). Fourth, regarding the instability of function, there are three further difficulties.
First, it is said: objects such as hairs or flies seen by one with cataracts have no function, whereas objects such as hairs or flies seen by one with healthy eyes do have function.
That which lacks function may be called "mere consciousness," but that which possesses function— [is it also mere consciousness?]

If these are substantial entities, how can they be called "consciousness-only"? The second [objection] says: Things obtained in a dream—such as food, drink, clothing, weapons, or poison—have no practical utility and may thus be called "consciousness-only.
However, things obtained during the waking state do possess practical utility;

why then are they called "consciousness-only"? The third [objection] says: For example, a *gandharva-nagara* (an illusory city) has no practical utility, whereas a city built of bricks and earth does.
[Objection: If [objects] were thus [merely consciousness], they would have practical utility; since the empty and the real are distinct, how can they be called "consciousness-only"? [Response:
To the statement "like dream-objects and so forth," one should cite the *Viṃśatikā-kārikā*: "Place and time are fixed as in a dream; bodies are not fixed as in the case of hungry ghosts;

many see the river of pus and so forth together; like a dream, it destroys utility. The first phrase answers the first [point], the fixity of place; the second phrase answers the second [point], the fixity of time.

[This addresses] the difficulty regarding the second and third phrases, which answer the objection that the third body is indeterminate. The fourth phrase answers the objection that its activity is indeterminate.
First, as for explaining the difficulty regarding the fixed location: suppose, for instance, one dreams of a mountain to the south;
when the mind within the dream further takes the north as its object, the mountain within the dream remains as it was to the south. How could this be?
Is there, then, a mountain that exists outside of the dreaming mind? To explain how this resolves the objection regarding the certainty [of the dream]:
suppose one sees a mountain in a dream. When the dreaming mind takes that mountain as its object, the mountain is indeed vividly present;
yet when the dreaming mind does not take the mountain as its object, the mountain remains nonetheless. How could it be that the mountain actually exists apart from the dreaming mind? (3)
Regarding the objection that the Buddha’s body is not fixed: for instance, there is a class of hungry ghosts who, at the site of the Ganges, all see a river of pus.
Although this is seen collectively by many such ghosts, could there truly be a river of pus?

If one understands that the river of pus seen by the hungry ghosts is summoned solely by their own karma and is a false vision of their own consciousness, then one will understand what people [of the present] see.
One sees the clear light of lamps and fires, up to the sun, moon, and stars, as well as mountains, rivers, and lands—exhausting all contaminated realms throughout the ten directions.
All these various environments and inhabitants are merely shared delusive visions; how could there be any real objects existing outside of consciousness?
Fourth, regarding the refutation of the objection that functions are not fixed: consider, for instance, obtaining food and drink in a dream.
Swords, weapons, and the like have no practical utility [in dreams], whereas seeing men and women engaging in sexual intercourse or losing seminal impurity does have practical utility.
Since both the real and the unreal are equally dream-objects, how can it be that the functions you cite are not uniform?
How could anything not be *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)? △ Third, resolving the objection regarding contradiction with the sacred teachings.

(Question: For what reason does the World-Honored One speak not only of the two bases of mind and mental objects (*manodharmāyatana*), but of twelve bases? (Answer: Those ten bases—the five faculties and the five objects—are also transformations of the fundamental consciousness;

they do not exist as separate, real entities. The World-Honored One merely spoke of these six pairs of phenomena in order to lead sentient beings into the contemplation of the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and to observe non-self.
This is like the provisional teaching of a "continuously existing sentient being" (*santāna-sattva*) for the purpose of refuting [the view of] permanence. Now, in the Mahāyāna teachings...

In order to lead sentient beings into the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), the teaching of "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*) is further expounded, so that they may understand that external phenomena likewise do not exist.

The twelve bases (*āyatana*) are taught to destroy the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*); [these] are fundamentally not real dharmas. For example, the term "continuum of sentient beings" is spoken merely to refute the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*);
how could one then further calculate [them] as permanent? △ Fourth, the explanation of the difficulty regarding consciousness-only establishing emptiness.
(Question: Is this nature of consciousness (*vijñapti-mātratā*) not also empty? (If one asks this: No, that is not the meaning. How so? (Answer: Because it is not an object of grasping.

That is to say, when one relies on the transformations of consciousness and falsely clings to them as real dharmas, through reasoning one thoroughly investigates and realizes they cannot be found; thus, they are said to be "empty of dharmas" (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

It is not [the case that it is empty] because the nature of consciousness-only (vijñaptimātratā), which is realized by non-conceptual wisdom beyond words, does not exist; rather, it is called the emptiness of phenomena (dharmaśūnyatā).

If this consciousness were non-existent, then conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) would be non-existent. Since conventional truth would be non-existent, ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) would also be non-existent, for the two truths are established in mutual dependence upon one another.
To negate these two truths is "badly grasped emptiness" (durgṛhītaśūnyatā), which the Buddhas declare to be incurable. One should...
One knows that all phenomena (*dharma*) are both empty and not empty. For this reason, the Compassionate Honored One (Maitreya) spoke the two preceding verses.

The intent of the objection here is as follows: since the twelve bases (*āyatana*) were taught by way of refuting a self (*ātman*), and those phenomena are already empty, then now, by way of refuting the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), he teaches Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Is consciousness itself not also empty? The meaning of the response can be understood [as follows].
One might fear that another will say: "Even if this consciousness did not exist, what would be wrong with that? Therefore, we now reply:

If this consciousness were absent, then conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) would be non-existent. For the eight consciousnesses and their associated mental factors (*caitta*) are all termed conventional truth.

The conventional is established in dependence upon the ultimate (*paramārtha*), and the ultimate is manifested in dependence upon the conventional. It is, for example, like form abiding in dependence upon space, and space being manifested in dependence upon form; it is also like waves and water.
It is established based on moisture; moisture is manifested through waves and water. Herein, once again, is seen the principle that the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual.
Who, then, would say that essence and appearance follow different tracks? △ Fifth, resolving the objection that the characteristics of form are not the mind.

(Question: If the various sense-bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) also have consciousness as their essence, for what reason do they appear as if they were the characteristics of form, and furthermore, why do they proceed as a single class, stable and continuous?

(Answer: Since beginningless time, through the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of false names and phrases, [the mind] falsely conceives of things outside the mind as being stable, continuous, and so forth.
Because it arises through the power of this [consciousness], no real entity can be found. Nevertheless, that which appears as external form serves as the basis for defiled and pure phenomena.
That is to say, if this [objective aspect] did not exist, there would be no inverted false attachment; consequently, there would be neither affliction nor pure phenomena.
Therefore, the various consciousnesses also appear as if they were forms. As a verse says: "The confused appearance and the confused substance must be admitted to be the consciousness of form."
As well as non-material consciousness: if there is no remainder, there is also nothing;
if there is no false attachment, then there is no defilement. Where there is no defilement, there is also no pure dharma.

For defilement and purity are relative phenomena, both established based upon conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Therefore, the defilement and purity of the ten realms are all termed "conventional."

Truth: if defilement and purity lack intrinsic nature, then the ten realms are all empty. If the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual, then it is clear that the ten realms are all the Middle Way.
"Disordered appearances" refers to the material forms produced by transformation; "the substance of disorder" refers to the mental substance that performs the transformation.
"Form-consciousness" refers to the disordered appearances produced by transformation; "non-form-consciousness" refers to the disordering mind that performs the transformation.
Regarding the essence (*tattva*): "If there is no 'other,' there is also nothing" means that if there is no transforming subject (*pariṇāman*), there is no transformed object (*pariṇāmya*);

and if there is no transformed object, there is also no transforming subject. The *Zhengjing* (Mirror of the Doctrine) states: "In Vasubandhu’s *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, there is only a single consciousness.

Furthermore, there is both conceptualizing consciousness (*vikalpaka-vijñāna*) and non-conceptualizing consciousness (*nirvikalpaka-vijñāna*). Conceptualizing consciousness is the consciousness of consciousness (*vijñapti-vijñāna*); non-conceptualizing consciousness..."
This refers to consciousness that resembles objects. All things within the entire dharma-realm, such as jars, clothing, and vehicles, are all non-conceptual consciousness.
By analogy, it can be said that there are further two types: conceptual form and non-conceptual form.
Conceptual form is, for example, as when one says that light is itself wisdom. Non-conceptual form is form composed of the four great elements. —Zhi Xu.

It is said: "Discriminating consciousness" refers to what the verse calls "non-material consciousness," while "non-discriminating consciousness" refers to what the verse calls "material consciousness.
Both material and non-material are termed "consciousness"; since there is no other phenomenon apart from consciousness, it is called "Consciousness-Only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
This is the primary tenet of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. From the following section, "By way of analogy," etc., it is...
That which has a disordered essence is called "discriminated form" (*savikalpa-rūpa*); that which has disordered characteristics is called "non-discriminated form" (*nirvikalpa-rūpa*).
Both the discriminated and the non-discriminated are termed "form. Since there is no other dharma apart from form, it is called "only form" (*rūpamātra*).

This is the basis for establishing the meaning of "only form, only fragrance," and so forth, in the Tiantai school. It truly arises because all dharmas lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), and [are merely] names.
It is also empty; therefore, one is able to deliver such a wondrous teaching. This is not something that can be conceived by those who merely seek out words and chase after phrases.
Furthermore, Master Linji established the four propositions based on this meaning: sometimes he "takes away the person but does not take away the environment."
That is to say, at times everything is merely form (*rūpa*), when the object is negated but the person is not; thus, everything is merely consciousness (*vijñapti*).
At times, both person and object are negated, whereby both form and consciousness perish. At times, neither person nor object is negated, whereby form and consciousness remain vividly present.
Furthermore, the Great Master Zhiyi established four modes of illumination based on this principle: the first is the illumination of the object by wisdom.
First is consciousness illuminating form: this is when conceptual consciousness illuminates non-conceptual form. Second is the object illuminating wisdom:
this is when conceptual form illuminates non-conceptual consciousness. Third is wisdom illuminating wisdom:
this is when conceptual consciousness illuminates non-conceptual consciousness. Fourth is the object illuminating the object: this is when conceptual form illuminates non-conceptual [form].
[This refers to] form (*rūpa*). [The opponent] asks: "If it is said that 'wisdom illuminates wisdom,' this would imply that the mind takes the mind as its object.

In that case, both the subject that perceives (*ālambaka*) and the object perceived (*ālambana*) would possess conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). How then can it be said that a discriminating consciousness illuminates a non-discriminating consciousness?

[The respondent] answers: "The subject that perceives is the *darśana-bhāga* (the seeing-part); therefore, it possesses the function of discrimination. The object perceived is the *nimitta-bhāga* (the image-part); it merely relies upon that mind..."
It takes this as its essence and manifests as an appearance of mind; it is like fire within a mirror, which lacks the function of burning.

Therefore, even if there were a truly substantial object (*saviṣaya*), it would still be called non-conceptual consciousness (*nirvikalpa-vijñāna*). △ Sixth: Explaining the objection that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) contradicts the tenet.
(Question: External objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth are clearly perceived; they are obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). How can you deny that they exist? (Answer:

When the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) and their simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) perceive the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) through direct perception, they do not grasp them as external. It is only later that the subsequent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), through its conceptualization (*vikalpa*), falsely gives rise to the notion of externality.

Therefore, the objects of direct perception are originally the self-aspect (*sva-nimitta-bhāga*) of consciousness; because they are transformations of consciousness, this is also taught in the Mahāyāna.
Because those external, real forms and so forth grasped by the mental consciousness are merely falsely imagined to exist, the Mahāyāna teaches that they are non-existent.
Furthermore, all objects such as form are not form yet appear as form; they are not external yet appear as external. Like the objects of a dream, they cannot be grasped as being truly external forms.
△ Seventh: Resolving the Objection Regarding the Contradiction between Dream and Waking States.

(The objection states: If all forms during the waking state are like dream-objects and do not exist apart from consciousness (the analogy), then just as when one awakens from a dream one knows that those [forms seen in the dream] are merely manifestations of mind, why is it that during the present waking state, one does not [know] the same regarding the forms that are one's own objects of perception?

[The questioner] says: [One] knows [that all is] merely consciousness (vijñaptimātra), just as when one has not yet awakened from a dream, one cannot know for oneself that what is seen is only mind; it is only upon reaching the time of awakening that [one realizes this].

One is able to retrospectively realize that there are no real objects external to the mind; one should know that the objective forms perceived at this very moment of awakening are likewise so (similar to a dream).

Until the stage of true awakening is reached, one cannot know for oneself that [these objects] are not truly existent. Upon reaching the state of true awakening, one is also able to retrospectively realize that, having not yet attained true awakening until now, one has been constantly dwelling in a dream.
Therefore, the Buddha taught that this is the long night of birth and death. It is because of this that [the nature of reality] remains uncomprehended.
The objective realm of form is consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

"Pursuing awakening" (*zhuí jué*) and "true awakening" (*zhēn jué*) are both pronounced with the entering tone (*rù shēng*). All other instances of the character *jué* (awakening) are pronounced with the departing tone (*qù shēng*).

There are two types of true awakening: first, partial true awakening, which refers to the stages from the first bhūmi upward; second, ultimate awakening, which refers to the supreme fruit of wondrous awakening (*mìào jué*).

Extending this principle further, there are also the awakening of similarity, the awakening of contemplative practice, the awakening of names and words, and the awakening that is the ultimate reality itself (*tathatā*).
One who possesses only the awakening that is the ultimate reality is like a person in a long dream while in deep sleep. △ Eighth: Explaining the difficulty of externally grasping another's mind.

[Objection: External forms do not truly exist; thus they may not be objects of internal consciousness. But since the minds of others truly exist, why should they not be the objects of one's own [consciousness]? [Response:]
Who says that the mind of another is not an object of one's own consciousness? It is simply said that it is not a direct objective condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana*).

That is to say, when the "image-part" (*nimitta-bhāga*) resembling the consciousness of another arises within one's own mind, this manifested image resembling the consciousness of another lacks any real causal activity.

It is not like the hand or other [limbs] which can directly grasp external objects, nor is it like the sun or other [luminaries] which can directly illuminate external realms; rather, it is merely like a mirror or similar [reflective surfaces].
The manifestation of external objects is called "knowing another's mind," yet this is not a direct cognition. That which is directly cognized is what one has transformed from within oneself;

therefore, a sūtra states: "There is not even the slightest dharma that can grasp another dharma. Rather, when consciousness arises, it manifests as resembling the appearance of that object, and this is called 'grasping' that thing.

Just as with the cognition of another's mind (since it necessarily cannot directly perceive its object), one should know that the same applies to the perception of form and the other five sense-objects (the five *viṣayas*): they likewise cannot directly perceive their original substance.
) If one realizes this meaning, then one will know that the mind of sentient beings within the minds of all Buddhas is called the "outflow-free (*anāsrava*) objective part" (*nimitta-bhāga*),
while the mind of the Buddhas within the minds of sentient beings is called the "outflow-possessing (*sāsrava*) objective part. However, the Buddhas do not...
It can cause the minds of those sentient beings to immediately realize the untainted (*anāsrava*). Sentient beings likewise cannot cause the minds of those Buddhas to revert to being tainted.
How could there be even the slightest phenomenon capable of grasping another phenomenon? It is nothing more than grasping its own perceived portion (*svabhāga*).
Since one cannot directly take another's mind as an object, but only takes the image manifested by oneself as the object, it is known that...
Furthermore, it is absolutely impossible for it to directly perceive the essential substance of the five sensory objects; it perceives only the images manifested by itself.
Since there is no external object to be perceived, one falsely gives rise to greed, hatred, and delusion within this state, and produces various views and conceits.
As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "The mind takes hold of the mind; through what is not illusion, illusory dharmas are formed. How lamentable! △ Nine.
Explanation: Resolving the objection that there are distinct objects which are not consciousness. [The Objection]:
Since there are indeed distinct objects, how can they be called "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*)? [The Response]: How extraordinary is this stubborn adherence! You raise doubts at every turn.
Does the teaching of "consciousness-only" merely speak of a single consciousness? [The Question]: If it is not so, what is its meaning? [The Response]: You should examine this with careful attention.
Listen. If there were only a single consciousness, how could there be the distinctions of the ten directions, ordinary beings and sages, the noble and the lowly, cause and effect, and so forth?
Who would speak for whom? What dharma would be sought? What would be sought for what purpose?
This first refutes the error of clinging to the notion of a single consciousness alone. The six realms are the mundane; the three vehicles and the Buddha are the noble.
Among the noble, the Buddha is the most honored; among the noble, the three vehicles are the lowest. Bodhisattvas are the cause; the stage of Buddhahood is the fruit.

Alternatively, one may discuss the relative honor and lowliness of the mundane and the noble separately; or one may discuss the cause and fruit of the honor and lowliness of the mundane and the noble separately. Suppose...
If there were no Buddhas, who would be able to teach? If there were no sentient beings, who would listen to what is taught?
If there were no teaching by the Buddha, what would constitute the Dharma? If there were no sentient beings, who would seek the Dharma?

Since there would be neither ordinary persons nor sages, nor high nor low, nor cause nor effect, and since there would be neither teacher nor teaching, nor seeker nor sought, it would then become ultimate emptiness.
If one were to negate [the existence of consciousness] and claim that even this single consciousness is non-existent, would this not be a great false view?

Therefore, one must know that the term "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra) possesses a profound underlying intent. The word "consciousness" (vijñāna) is used here to comprehensively indicate that every sentient being possesses eight consciousnesses, the mental factors (caitta) of six categories, the various distinctions between the perceived objects and the perceiving aspects (nimitta-bhāga and darśana-bhāga) that they transform, as well as their specific states and the principle of emptiness (śūnyatā-yukti) that underlies them.
It reveals suchness (tathatā). This is because: (1) it is the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of consciousness; (2) it is associated with consciousness (referring to the mind and mental factors);

(3) it is the transformation of the two (referring to the aforementioned objects); (4) it is the state (*avasthā*) of the [three types of] phenomena; and (5) it is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the [four types of] phenomena. Thus, all these phenomena do not exist apart from consciousness;

for this reason, they are collectively designated by the name "consciousness. As for the term "only" (*kevalam*), it merely excludes the attachment of deluded beings to the notion that [objects] exist as something definitively separate from consciousness.
"There truly exist form and so forth.

This is the correct explanation of the purport of the two characters *wei-shi* (consciousness-only). These very characters "consciousness" (*shi*) encompass all one hundred dharmas of the five categories:
first, the mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*), which are the eight consciousnesses; second, the mental concomitants (*caitta-dharma*), which are the six... [text truncated]

First are the mental factors (*caitta*), numbering fifty-one in total. Second are the mental states (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*), numbering twenty-four. Third are the material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), which are the objective images (*nimitta-bhāga*) perceived by the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*);
these number eleven in total. Fourth are the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-dharma*), which are the specific temporal states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of mind, mental factors, and matter;
these number twenty-four. Fifth are the unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), which are manifested through the emptiness of self and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*).

Regarding *tathatā* (suchness), there are six aspects explained according to their meanings. The eight consciousnesses are called "consciousness" because they are the self-characteristics of consciousness.

The mental factors (*caitta*) are also called "consciousness" because they are associated with consciousness. The objective and subjective poles (*nimitta* and *darśana*) are also called "consciousness" because they are transformations of these two.

The non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are three stages [of consciousness], and thus they are also called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) consists of four real natures, and thus it is also called "consciousness.

Mental factors (*caitta*) are called "consciousness"; this is in the sense of concealing the subordinate and manifesting the predominant. Aspect (*nimitta*) and vision (*darśana*) are called "consciousness";

this is in the sense of abandoning ambiguity to preserve purity, as well as the sense of subsuming the derivative back into the fundamental. Non-associated formations are called "consciousness"; this is in the sense of dispelling the false.
To preserve the ultimate meaning, that which is unconditioned is designated as "consciousness. This is the sense of eliminating appearances to realize the nature.

It merely negates the ignorant attachment to the existence of real form and so forth apart from consciousness; the phrase "and so forth" includes all attachments to both self and phenomena, as previously explained.

If one understands the intended meaning of the teaching on *vijñaptimātra* in this way, one will be able to proceed without error, properly prepare the accumulations (*saṃbhāra*), swiftly enter into the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), realize unsurpassed enlightenment, and rescue sentient beings from the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

One who completely negates [all things] as a result of misapprehending emptiness (*durgṛhītaśūnyatā*) contradicts both scripture and reasoning and cannot accomplish such great deeds for the benefit of self and others. Therefore, one must certainly believe that all things are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
This verse demonstrates that the teaching and reasoning of Vijñaptimātra possess great benefit.

By not clinging to the parikalpita (the imagined nature) as real, and by not repudiating the paratantra (dependent nature) and pariniṣpanna (perfected nature) as non-existent, one is able to remain free from error.

With non-erroneous wisdom as the eyes and the provisions for the myriad practices as the feet, when both eyes and feet function together, one enters safely into the great, cool land of dharmatā-śūnyatā, until even [ultimate] realization is attained.
Unsurpassed Enlightenment, which delivers sentient beings throughout the limits of the future—how could this be accomplished by one who wrongly grasps at emptiness?

The first section, the formal clarification of that which is transformed, is concluded. II. Extensive Explanation of External Objections (three parts): 1. Explanation of the objection concerning from what the discrimination arises;
2. Explanation of the objection concerning from what birth and death arise; 3. Explanation of the objection regarding the contradiction with the Sūtras on the three natures. Within the first [part]:
II. First, the objection is stated by citing the verse; second, it is established through the commentary. Now, the first part:
If there are only consciousnesses and no external objects at all, from what do the various forms of conceptual discrimination arise? The verse says:
"By means of the consciousness containing all seeds, such and such transformations occur; through the power of mutual interaction, this or that conceptual discrimination arises."

△ Second, establishing [the meaning] through the treatise has two parts: first, a brief explanation of the verses; second, an extensive explanation of the meaning of the verses. Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, explaining how defiled conceptualization arises from defiled seeds and manifestations; second, by analogy, explaining how pure conceptualization arises from pure seeds and manifestations.
This consists of five parts: first, the explanation of the first line; second, the explanation of the second line; third, the explanation of the third line;
fourth, the explanation of the fourth line; and fifth, a general elucidation of the meaning of the verse. Now, the first part.

The treatise says: "All-seed consciousness" refers to the specific functional capacities within the fundamental consciousness (the eighth consciousness) that can produce their own effects (i.e., all phenomena).
Because these specific functional capacities can produce four types of effects—homogeneous, retributive, human effort, and dominant—they are called "all-seeds.
(In this context,) the fruit of disconnection is excluded and not mentioned because it is not produced from seeds. Although that [fruit of disconnection] may...

[This] is a realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) and not a fruit of seeds; it must arise as actualized activity (*samudācāra*) within the true untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), for [the fetters of those afflictions] can only be severed [thereby].
Although this actualized path arises from untainted seeds, with respect to that fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*), there is a sense of indirect succession (*pāramparya*).

However, this is not what is intended by the primary meaning of this verse, because this verse speaks only of the seeds of the conceptualizing [consciousness] (*vikalpa*). These seeds of conceptualization are the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*); they are, in fact, the fundamental consciousness itself.

It is established as the name "consciousness" because it constitutes the substance. Since seeds lack a distinct nature apart from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the compound term "seed-consciousness" is used to distinguish them from that which is neither seed nor consciousness.
This is because there may be a manifest consciousness that is "consciousness" but not a "seed," and there may be external seeds that are "seeds" but not "consciousness.
Furthermore, the term "seed-consciousness" indicates the seeds held within the fundamental consciousness; it does not refer to that which holds the seeds.
The meaning of this distinction will be explained later.
△ Second, the explanation of the second phrase:

Within this consciousness, the seeds undergo such a transformation due to the assistance of other conditions, such as the manifesting consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). That is to say, from the state of arising—

When it reaches the stage of maturation, it manifests as many transformed seeds; this is stated repeatedly as "thus" (*evam*), meaning that all types of seeds—including those of the three kinds of perfuming, both common and uncommon—are fully subsumed within the seeds of consciousness.

Regarding the three types of perfuming (vāsanā): first, the perfuming of names and words; second, the perfuming of the grasping at a self (ātma-grāha); and third, the perfuming of the links of existence (bhavāṅga). These are fully explained in the text below.

The seeds of consciousness of common characteristics (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa-vijñāna-bīja*) are capable of bringing about the environmental retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*); the seeds of non-common characteristics (*asādhāraṇa-bīja*)...

It is capable of inducing the primary retribution (*vipāka*). Furthermore, there is that which is both common and uncommon, and that which is uncommon within the common; therefore, it is termed "equal" (*sama*).
This is explained in detail as presented in the *Mahāyāna-śamatha-vipaśyanā*. △ Third, the explanation of the third phrase.

The power of mutual reinforcement refers to the eight manifest consciousnesses, along with their associated mental factors (caitta), including their aspects of appearance (nimittabhāga) and seeing (darśanabhāga).
This is because they all mutually assist one another in relation to the seeds.

The term "and so forth" (ādi) includes the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Although these are provisionally established based on the states (*avasthā*) of matter and mind, they lack any substantial reality of their own;
nevertheless, they also possess the power of mutual assistance. △ Fourth, the explanation of the fourth phrase.
That is to say, the manifest consciousnesses (arising from seeds) and so forth are collectively termed "discrimination," because they all have false discrimination as their intrinsic nature.
Since there are many varieties of discrimination, the term "this and that" (*tattat*) is used.
The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes all mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), as they are all capable of conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

These various types of conceptualization further differ according to distinctions such as nature (*svabhāva*), feeling (*vedanā*), realm (*dhātu*), stage (*bhūmi*), and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—namely, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). Therefore, it is said that their "categories are many. △ Fifth:
General Explanation of the Meaning of the Verse.

The meaning of this verse is as follows: although there are no external conditions, various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) can still arise due to the specific transformation of all seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), as well as through the reciprocal influence of the eight manifesting consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
Why rely on external conditions for conceptual discrimination to arise?

First, having concluded the section on how defiled seeds and manifestations give rise to defiled discrimination, second, we shall apply this analogy to how pure seeds and manifestations give rise to pure discrimination.

One should know that the arising of all pure dharmas is likewise so: because they arise by depending on the fundamental consciousness, through the transformation of all pure seeds and their specific distinctions, as well as by taking the manifest pure dharmas as conditions to assist their production.
"All pure dharmas" refers to the fruits of the wisdom of the Three Vehicles. This concludes the brief explanation of the verse. II. Extensive Explanation of the Meaning of the Verse.
This has two parts: first, the inquiry; second, the explanation. Now, the first [the inquiry]:
Regarding the aforementioned analysis of the arising of seeds and manifestations through conditions, how should one understand the characteristics of this dependent origination?

Part Two: Explanation, which has two sections. First, the actual explanation of dependent origination; second, the concluding critique and referral to the extensive [treatise]. The first section has three parts. First, a preliminary clarification of the four conditions;

Explanation. First, there are four types of conditions (*pratyaya*).

The *Zongjing* states: "As for causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), they directly produce their own results within the gateway of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). As for immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*), they serve as..."

Regarding the meaning of "opening and guiding": all things are brought into existence. As for the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it is established only when there is a basis for mental deliberation; it is posited according to both direct and indirect relations.
As for the "dominant condition" (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it possesses a superior power that does not obstruct other conditions.

Part Two: Explaining [the four conditions] as fourfold. First, explaining the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Second, explaining the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Third, explaining the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Fourth, explaining the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
First, regarding the superior object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

First, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*): this refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) directly producing their own results. This essence is twofold: first, seeds (*bīja*); second, actual manifestations (*samudācāra*).

That which brings about the fruition is called the cause (*hetu*); that which assists in its arising is called the condition (*pratyaya*). "Conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) excludes non-conditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), referring instead to matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth.

That which directly accomplishes its own fruit is the cause; since it also possesses the sense of assisting in arising, the cause itself is the condition. Therefore, it is termed the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The distinction between seeds (*bīja*) and active manifestations (*samudācāra*) will be explained in the subsequent text.

"Seed" refers to the various distinctions in functional capacities within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) pertaining to wholesome, defiled, and neutral states across all realms and stages.
These [distinctions] are able to project subsequent functional capacities of their own kind and to give rise to simultaneous manifest results of their own kind.
This [distinction of functional capacity] is the nature of the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*) solely in relation to those [subsequent capacities of its own kind and simultaneous manifest results].
This first explains that the seed constitutes the essence of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

It can induce a subsequent capacity of its own kind—this is the meaning of "seed producing seed"—and it can give rise to a simultaneous manifest fruit of its own kind—this is the meaning of "seed producing the manifest.
Both of these are termed the nature of the causal condition.

The "active" [consciousnesses] refer to the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and their associated mental factors (*caitta*), as well as the perceived aspect (*nimittabhāga*), the seeing aspect (*darśanabhāga*), and the nature (*svabhāva*) of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the nine realms (*dhātu*), and the stages (*bhūmi*).

With the exception of the extremely superior wholesome states of the Buddha-fruit and the extremely inferior neutral (*avyākṛta*) states, all other phenomena perfume the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) to produce seeds of their own kind.
These [evolving consciousnesses, etc. are, in relation to those [seeds of their own kind], of the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). [Question: What is meant by this?

Question: Why is the eighth [consciousness] unable to act as a perfuming agent (*vāsaka*)? Answer: The nature of the eighth mental complex (*citta-varga*) is that which is perfumable (*bhāvya*). If it were also taken as a perfuming agent, there would then be nothing left to be perfumed. Question:

Why are the [factors of] nature, realm, stage, and so forth also unable to act as perfuming agents? Answer: It is not the case that the self-witnessing portion (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*), which serves as the basis, can act as a perfuming agent independently. Question: Why are the state of Buddhahood and inferior indeterminate states excluded? Answer: [Because they lack the necessary conditions for perfuming.]
[It is] indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Because atoms (*paramāṇu*) [and the fruit of Buddhahood] are spherical, these two do not perfuse to form seeds.
This passage explains that present activity serves as the substantial cause (*hetu-pratyaya*) for seeds. The *Zongjing* states:

"The first five evolving consciousnesses can perfume the seeds of the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the ālayavijñāna; the sixth mental consciousness can perfume the eighth [consciousness’s objective aspect]."
It is said that the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the seeds is twofold. The seventh manas-consciousness perfumes only the seeds of the seeing-division of the eighth consciousness.

Moreover, it is said that the seeing-division bestows power upon the image-division, enabling it to perfume seeds; furthermore, the seeing-division bestows power upon the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*).

Furthermore, it is said that when the first five consciousnesses perfuse the seeds of the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, they only perfume the seeds for the internal body and the external vessel-world—the actual five sense-objects—and do not perfume the others, because [the five consciousnesses] cannot take those as objects.

When the sixth consciousness takes the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its object, it perfuses two kinds of seeds: the seed of the seeing-aspect and the seed of the substance; both of these are seeds of the mind. Thus, it is consistent with...

The intermediate image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) is not perfumed. When the sixth [consciousness] takes the image-part of the eighth as its object, it may perfume three types of seeds:
namely, it perfumes the seeds of its own seeing-part that acts as the perceiver; and when it is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it also perfumes the five [seeds] of its own image-part.
The seeds of the objects (*viṣaya*). Furthermore, it perfumes the seeds of the essential natures (*svabhāva-bīja*) of the five sense organs and their objects derived from the eighth consciousness.

However, for the most part, it only perfumes the two types of seeds: those of the seeing-faculty (*darśana*) and the essential nature (*svabhāva*). When the sixth consciousness perceives the three objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, it only perfumes the seeds of the root-body (*indriya-kāya*) and the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
When it perceives the seeds as its object, it does not perfume seeds, for fear of falling into the error of infinite regress (*anavasthā-doṣa*). It is further stated that the eighth...

Furthermore, it is said that if the sixth [consciousness] takes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), or certain portions of the provisional (*prajñapti*) factors among the mental concomitants (*caitta*) as its objects, it does not perfume their essential natures (*bhāva*).

As for the seeds, they are indeed perfumed. When [the mind] takes a falsely constructed phenomenon as its object, because it is merely an "object of solitary projection" (*ekacchāyālambana*), it does not perfume the seeds of the *nimittabhāga* (image-part).

That half which arises from the substantial part (svabhāva-bhāga) is of an unobscured nature (anivṛta), while that half which arises from the perceiving aspect (darśana-bhāga) is of an obscured nature (nivṛta).
Manifest activities of the same class, when viewed in relation to one another, are not all *hetu-pratyaya* (causal conditions), because each arises from its own seed.
Furthermore, all manifest activities of different classes, when viewed in relation to one another, are also not *hetu-pratyaya*, because they do not produce [the result] directly.

As for those who say that manifest activities of different and similar classes are *hetu-pratyaya* when viewed in relation to one another, it should be understood that this is a metaphorical designation (*prajñapti*) or a provisional teaching (*anuvartana-mukha*). There are only...
To state that seeds are the nature of causal conditions (*pratyaya*) is merely an explanation emphasizing their predominant aspect; it is not a statement that exhausts the full principle.
For the Noble Ones have taught that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and the *ālayavijñāna* stand in a mutual relationship as causal conditions toward one another.

This passage briefly demonstrates the meaning of the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*). First, it distinguishes the mutual induction of similar active manifestations (*samprayukta-saṃtāna*), which constitutes the "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*) rather than the causal condition.
Even if seeds were absent, active manifestations would be unable to induce further active manifestations on their own.
For example, when the wick is exhausted, the preceding flame cannot induce the subsequent flame.

Next, to distinguish this from the assistance provided by the activity of heterogeneous factors, these are *adhipati-pratyaya* (dominant conditions), yet they are not *hetu-pratyaya* (causal conditions), because they do not produce [the effect] directly.

Next, it is shown that some say that actual manifestations (*samudācāra*) mutually serve as causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), while others say that only seeds (*bīja*) possess the nature of being causes and conditions.

One [position] is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*) for what follows along, and the other is merely based on highlighting what is predominant. Following the passage "Next, the Noble One says," the conclusion is reached that seeds and actual manifestations are definitively mutual causes and conditions.
This concludes the first part: the explanation of causes and conditions. △ Second, the explanation of "equality" (*samanantara*).

The immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the equal-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) refer to the eight manifest consciousnesses and their associated mental factors. The preceding group [of moments],
being equal in its own kind and acting as an uninterrupted opening and guidance for the subsequent [group], causes that subsequent group to arise with certainty within its own kind.
"Equal" (sama) refers to those of the same category. "Immediate" (anantara) means there is no interval between them. "Condition" (pratyaya) means that which assists in production.
The eight manifest consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) and their associated mental factors (*caitta*) constitute the actual substance of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).

This is to distinguish them from matter (*rūpa*), non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), as these lack the nature of being an equal-and-immediate condition. A mind-king (*cittarāja*) must necessarily be associated with mental factors.
The aggregation of those that appear as one is termed a "collection" (*rāśi*). "Successive" (*pūrvāpara*) indicates they do not exist simultaneously.
"Of the same kind" (*svajāti*) indicates they are not of a different kind. For example, a preceding visual consciousness in relation to a subsequent visual consciousness is termed "of the same kind";
however, in relation to auditory or olfactory consciousnesses and so forth, it is termed "of a different kind."
Because many seeds of the same kind arise simultaneously, they are not subsumed under this condition (ālambana-pratyaya), just as the dissociated factors (*viprayukta*) are not.
For this reason, the eight consciousnesses do not serve as conditions for one another.
This excludes seeds from being equivalent-to-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*), and it also excludes consciousnesses of different classes from being equivalent-to-immediate conditions.

This refers to the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). For instance, the eight consciousnesses and their various mental factors each possess seeds that evolve simultaneously with their respective manifest states (*pravṛtti*).

Insofar as the manifest arises from the seed, the seed may function as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). However, the manifest does not induce the seed, and thus it is not the immediate condition.
This is like a wick which can produce a flame but cannot induce a subsequent flame; for that which induces a subsequent flame must necessarily be the preceding [flame].

Because they are [respectively] seeds and manifest states. Therefore, seeds and manifest states are as incompatible as [two different types of consciousness]; they are not subsumed under this immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Since seeds and manifest states, though belonging to the same category, differ from one another, they do not constitute this condition;

thus, the eight consciousnesses in their active manifestation (*pravṛtti*) are each of a different category and are even more incompatible. How could it be permissible for them to act as immediate conditions for one another?

It is indeed due to this condition that the mind and mental factors, though constantly arising together, appear as a single unity because they are associated; since they cannot be established as distinct or separate,
they are able to serve as one another’s equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
This explains the anticipated objection. The objection states: "Since seeds and manifest activities are simultaneous, they do not function as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, since the manifest activities of the eight consciousnesses are of different categories, they also do not function as equal-and-immediate conditions.
If that is so, then since mind and mental factors are likewise simultaneous and of different categories yet arise together, how can they function as equal-and-immediate conditions?"

Is it by way of condition (*pratyaya*)? Now, this is explained: although they always arise together, their basis (*āśraya*) is not different, their objects (*ālambana*) are similar, and they must also be of the same nature (*sabhāga*).
Therefore, being associated and harmonized as if they were one, they can function as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
However, if we consider them merely as conditions (*pratyaya*), then the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) may serve as conditions for one another.
If, however, we consider them as supports (*āśraya*), then the term refers exclusively to the mind-king (*cittarāja*), as clarified in the fourth fascicle.
The mind that has entered into the state of nirvana without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa) is extremely subtle and weak;

it lacks the function of initiating [subsequent states], nor is there any dharma that arises as its immediate antecedent (samanantara). Therefore, it is not this condition. How is this known? The treatise provides a definitive statement:

"If, immediately following this [prior] consciousness, that [subsequent] consciousness necessarily arises, then this [prior consciousness] is said to be the immediate antecedent condition (samanantarapratyaya) for that [subsequent consciousness]. Thus it is understood.
This further excludes the final moment of consciousness upon entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, which is not termed an *samanantarapratyaya* (equal-and-immediate condition).
This is because, as there are no further dharmas to arise, it has no function to provide the opening and guidance [for subsequent moments]. This can be understood from the scriptural citations.
Question: If one relies on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, then there is not a single person who enters the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
As for those who have entered parinirvāṇa, how can this be reconciled? The answer is: that [teaching] reveals the ultimate reality, while this [teaching] provisionally employs skillful means;
thus, one should not raise an objection.
Based on this principle, it should be stated as follows: the ādāna-vijñāna may, within the three realms and nine stages, mutually function as any of them.

Regarding the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*): because there is an opening between the lower and upper realms in death and rebirth, it occurs that an outflow-free state (*anāsrava*) arises immediately after an outflowing state (*sāsrava*).
However, an outflow-free state never gives rise to an outflowing one; once the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) has arisen, it is necessarily uninterrupted (it is stainless).
The same applies when comparing the wholesome (*kuśala*) with the neutral (*avyākṛta*, specifically the maturation-consciousness).
Below this, the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is specifically determined by way of the eight consciousnesses. First, the eighth consciousness is now determined.
Regarding the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), it is considered in relation to its associated mental factors (*caitta*). There are twenty-one such associated mental factors;

yet, when speaking of "mirror-like wisdom" alone, it is because wisdom is the predominant factor. Whether virtuous or indeterminate, this is also the case when the eighth consciousness-king is compared with itself. That is to say:
Immediately following the maturation [consciousness], there arises the stainless [consciousness]; the stainless [consciousness] never gives rise to the maturation [consciousness].
(Question: From which realm does this eighth consciousness subsequently induce the outflow-free [consciousness]? (Answer: Either from the form realm or from the desire realm.

This refers to those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who, having directly resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*) and sought the fruit of Buddhahood, will certainly, after their final body in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), give rise to the untainted eighth consciousness (the pure consciousness).
Once their causal practices are fulfilled, they will necessarily be born in the Palace of Maheśvara within the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), where they will attain enlightenment.

As for those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) who turn back from their ultimate fruits to pursue Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), they will certainly, after their final body in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), give rise to the untainted [consciousness].
The eighth consciousness, as the "returning and proceeding" [consciousness], sustains the body of birth;

since this exists only within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), although he must necessarily proceed to the palace of Maheśvara before attaining Buddhahood, the body of birth sustained by the power of his original vow belongs to the Desire Realm. Thus, there is one interpretation.
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there are also śrāvakas who have turned toward the Mahāyāna and vow to maintain their physical bodies;
since this does not contradict either scripture or reasoning, the eighth untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) of a śrāvaka can likewise manifest after a mind of the realm of form.

This also discusses the eighth realm and stage that induces the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state. Within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are also *śrāvakas* who turn toward the Mahāyāna;

that is, an *anāgāmin* who, having been born into the form realm, realizes arhatship and, before entering final nirvāṇa, retains his body in the form realm to await the full completion of his merits. However, he is born into one of the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).

Therefore, those who have transcended the mundane dust can become Bodhisattvas. Although the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (the *Cheng weishi lun*) is also Mahāyāna, it is...
