The inferior exists only in Jambudvīpa, while the superior must be in the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpasaṃbhava*). To now rely on the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven is merely one of the thousand Śākyamunis within the Brahma-net. (From the *Qixin lun*)
The treatise likewise shares this intent. Although the principle is distinct and complete, the phenomena still retain a commonality. Expedient means and ultimate reality are mutually requisite;
their significance is not superficial. The Sage’s intention is difficult to fathom; one should simply believe in it with reverence.

The seventh evolving consciousness may also serve as an equal-and-immediate condition for one another across the three realms and nine stages, because it is bound to the place of birth where the eighth consciousness arises.
Whether tainted or untainted, they may produce one another, as they can mutually induce each other throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

The same mutual relationship holds between the wholesome and the indeterminate. Within the indeterminate, the defiled and the undefiled likewise mutually induce one another, because they can be drawn forth from each other during the preceding and succeeding stages of the fruit of the knowledge of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*).
This [mutual induction] occurs between the outflowing acquisitions (*sāsrava-prāpti*) of the desire and form realms and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) production;
it does not occur in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), because Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) are not reborn there.

This distinguishes the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) of the seventh consciousness. When associated with the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*), it is termed "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*);

when associated with the two types of grasping at self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*), it is termed "with-outflow" (*sāsrava*). Within the stages of the ten bhūmis, when one enters the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), it is termed outflow-free;
when one emerges from the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena, it is termed with-outflow. Therefore, they arise alternately as outflow-free and with-outflow.

This refers to the nature of the wholesome (*kuśala*). That which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature; thus it is said that they are likewise when compared to one another.
Furthermore, that which is associated with the two types of grasping—self and phenomena—is called "obscured" (*nivṛta*) and is also termed "defiled" (*kliṣṭa*).

When self-grasping has been suppressed or severed, that which remains associated only with the grasping of phenomena is called "unobscured" (*anivṛta*) and is also termed "non-defiled" (*akliṣṭa*). This applies to the noble ones (*ārya*) in the first, second, and third fruits who have entered [the path].
Within the stage of the contemplation of emptiness, it is termed "non-defiled"; prior to entering it and after having emerged from it, it is termed "defiled.
Thus, they also mutually induce one another. Those of dull faculties among the two vehicles attain birth in the formless realm because they are weary of form.
Bodhisattvas on the stages do not take birth in the formless realms because it is of no benefit;
however, if a Bodhisattva realizes the twenty-five kingly samādhis, they must also manifest in the formless realms. What is said now is merely a provisional teaching based on skillful means.

The sixth consciousness—whether it be the contaminated or uncontaminated, wholesome or unwholesome, belonging to the three realms and nine stages—is capable of acting as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for one another.
This is because they mutually induce one another during states such as the moistening of rebirth.

As for the initial arising of the uncontaminated [mind], it occurs only within the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), because the wholesome mind of the "decisive distinction" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) exists only within the Form Realm.

This defines the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) of the sixth consciousness. Both types of wisdom regarding the contemplation of the two emptinesses are termed "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).

That which is outflow-free is exclusively wholesome. That which is associated with the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*) is termed "with-outflow" (*sāsrava*). Outflowing states differ in that they may be wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, or unobscured-unspecified;

nevertheless, they all mutually induce one another. The wholesome states of the stage of "discrimination" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), namely the four [levels] beginning with "heat" (*uṣmagata*), are likewise included therein.
The roots of goodness cultivated during the stage of preparatory application must rely upon the four dhyānas before the outflow-free (anāsrava) state can arise;

therefore, it is said that this occurs "only after [rebirth in] the realm of form. This refers to what is known as "wisdom arising from meditative concentration" (*samādhi-jā-prajñā*). However, if one can accomplish the four dhyānas while among humans, this is termed "the mind subsequent to the four dhyānas";
it does not mean that one must necessarily be reborn in the heavens of the four dhyāna realms.

The visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses (in the desire and form realms) belong to two levels—the mixed-abode level and the level free from birth. The olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses belong solely to one level—the mixed-abode level of the single desire realm.

Each acts as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for its own kind. It should be understood that the same applies when they are compared with respect to their wholesome and other natures.

One interpretation holds that the five consciousnesses, whether contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), act as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*) for one another, because they may arise alternately before one has attained Buddhahood.

Another interpretation holds that uncontaminated [five consciousnesses] arise subsequent to contaminated [five consciousnesses], but contaminated [five consciousnesses] cannot arise subsequent to uncontaminated [five consciousnesses], because uncontaminated five consciousnesses do not exist except for a Buddha;
such [uncontaminated five consciousnesses] belong to the stage of a causal practitioner (*hetu-bhūmi*). Regarding the five [sensory] forms therein...

Because the sense faculties (*indriya*) are necessarily contaminated (*sāsrava*), and because they are subsumed under the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).

If it is argued that the five uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses can arise from the five sense faculties—which are contaminated, non-common (*asādhāraṇa*), necessarily co-existent (*sahabhū*), and share the same object (*samaviṣaya*)—this is logically inconsistent. This is because these two [the contaminated faculty and the uncontaminated consciousness] differ in their clarity or dimness regarding the object.

This passage judges the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) of the first five consciousnesses. They act as conditions for one another; that is, when the six destinies are viewed in relation to each other.

"Wholesome and so forth" refers to the distinctions among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Next, the explanation of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) has two interpretations; the first interpretation is incorrect.

Next, the meaning of "clarity versus obscurity" is explained: when the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) give rise to the five consciousnesses associated with the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), they are clear regarding their objects.

When tainted faculties (*sāsrava-indriya*) give rise to the tainted five consciousnesses—regardless of whether they are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—they are all obscure regarding their objects.
This concludes the second explanation of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). △ Third, the explanation of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Third is the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya). This refers to any phenomenon that, bearing its own characteristic, is that which is cognized or relied upon by the mind or its associated mental factors.
This essence is twofold: first, the direct; second, the indirect.

It is called the "object-condition" (*ālambana*) because it arises bearing the image of that [object]. It is further called a "condition" (*pratyaya*) because it assists in the production of consciousness.

That is to say, if a phenomenon exists, it can function as a productive condition; this excludes the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the imagined nature), which, being non-existent in essence, lacks the status of a condition even if it is taken as an object.
The phrase "bearing its own image" clarifies the meaning of being an object-condition, thereby excluding [the imagined nature].

The sense faculties (*indriya*) and the seed-consciousness (*bīja-vijñāna*) lack that specific characteristic; although they function as conditions (*pratyaya*), they are not the object-condition (*ālambana*).
Possessing these two meanings—existence (*sattva*) and bearing an aspect (*sākāra*)—it is termed the "object-condition.

As for the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its associated mental factors (*caitta*), when they are in association (*samprayukta*), they take this as their object of deliberation (*ālambana*) and take this as their basis of support (*niśraya*); because it is the object of deliberation, it is called the "object-condition."
It is called an "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*) because it serves as that which is relied upon. The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) states: 1.

That which has something to contemplate but is not that which is relied upon refers to the false attachments of pervasive conceptualization, such as the self and dharmas; this is because they lack any substantial essence. 2.

That which is relied upon but does not have something to contemplate refers to objects reflected in a mirror or water; this is because the mirror or water are not themselves capable of contemplation. 3. Both... [text truncated]
The fourth category, "neither," refers to those things other than what is reflected in mirrors, water,
and so forth, which are not objects of cognition.

If this objective aspect (nimittabhāga) is not separate in substance from the subjective aspect (darśanabhāga) with which it shares the same basis, and is that upon which the subjective aspect internally relies for its cognition,
one should know that it is the direct object-condition (sākṣādālambanapratyaya).
This first explains the direct objective condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*). Their substance is not separate; that is to say, the four divisions are of one single essence. The *Zongjing* states:

"First, there is a direct objective condition that arises from both the substrate (*bimba*) and the transformation of the mind; this refers to the five consciousnesses taking the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the five sense objects as their object.
Second, there is a direct objective condition that arises solely from the transformation of the mind, without depending on a substrate."
First, there are those that are the objective images (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the three objects of the eighth consciousness; these are immediate objective conditions (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*).

Second, there are those that are immediate objective conditions but do not arise from the transformation of the mind, nor do they arise from a substantial object (*bimba*); these are the suchness (*tathatā*) realized by fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Third, there are those that are immediate objective conditions but are not objective images; these are the two internal parts [of consciousness] which take each other as objects.

If this objective essence (ālambana-svabhāva) and the subjective aspect (darśana-bhāga) that perceives it are distinct in substance, yet by virtue of the former serving as an object, the latter can give rise to internal mental support,
one should know that the former is a remote object-condition (viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya).
This section explains the "indirect object-condition" (*parokṣālambanapratyaya*).
As for the "direct object-condition" (*sākṣātālambanapratyaya*), it is necessarily present in all cognizing minds, because a cognizing mind cannot arise without an internal basis of cognition.
Regarding the indirect object-condition, however, its presence in the cognizing mind is not fixed, as [a cognizing mind] may also arise even apart from an external basis of cognition.
Because it arises within the cognizing mind, this is what is meant in the second fascicle by the statement:
"All phenomena within one's own mind exist; phenomena outside one's own mind may exist or may not exist. The *Zongjing* says:
"First, there are those with a substantial essence (*svabhāva*) and objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*), which are real objects of cognition (*viṣaya*). That is to say:

1. The first five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), as well as the initial moment of the clearly manifest mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and a small portion of the independent mental consciousness (*svatantra-manovijñāna*)—these are [the first category].

2. Those with a substantial basis (*sanimitta*) wherein the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is provisional; these include those with a substantial basis that are purely reflected images (*kevala-nirbhāsa*) and those that carry a substantial basis (*sanimitta-nirbhāsa*).

3. Those without a substantial basis wherein the objective aspect is provisional; these are the purely reflected images without a substantial basis (*kevala-nirbhāsa-asanimitta*). 4. Those without a substantial basis wherein the objective aspect is real by nature (*tattva-svabhāva*).

Regarding the object (*ālambana*): it refers to the eighth consciousness-king taking three objects as its conditions, and fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) taking true suchness (*tathatā*) as its condition (for true suchness is the ultimate reality, and thus is termed "aspect";

yet fundamental wisdom does not possess an objective aspect). Furthermore, it is said that "carrying" (*dai*) has two meanings: first, "carrying along" (*jia-dai*), and second, "transforming and carrying" (*bian-dai*).
"Aspect" (*xiang*) also has two meanings: first, "essential aspect" (*ti-xiang*), and second, "phenomenal aspect" (*xiang-zhuang*). If fundamental wisdom takes...
Suchness is that which is perceived by way of carrying along both its essence and its aspect; it is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

This extends even to the perception of the internal two-fold aspect and the self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) perceiving the seeing part (*darśana-bhāga*), all of which are termed object-conditions because they carry along both essence and aspect.
When tainted (*sāsrava*) minds and mental factors, as well as the seeing part of untainted subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), perceive an object, they transform into an aspect.

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): regardless of whether it possesses substance or lacks substance, all instances where [the consciousness] undergoes transformation and carries along a phenomenal aspect (*nimitta*) are termed "object-conditions.

Furthermore, it is said that only those which are image-aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) are termed "transformative-carrying" (*pariṇāma-parigraha*). If there is no transformative image-aspect and [the cognition] directly adheres to the essence of the object, this is termed "directly-carrying" (*upādāna-parigraha*).

Regarding the eighth mental state (*citta-kṣaṇa*): there is one interpretation that it possesses only the directly perceived object-condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*), because it transforms spontaneously according to the power of karmic causes.

There is another interpretation that it must also definitely possess the indirectly perceived object-condition (*parokṣa-ālambana-pratyaya*), because it must rely on the transformation of another's consciousness into an objective form before it can transform itself. There is yet another interpretation.

Both of these explanations are untenable. It is reasonable that one’s own and another’s bodies and lands may be mutually enjoyed, because what is transformed by another can serve as the objective basis for oneself (thus, the first position—that there is only the direct object-condition—is unreasonable).

However, it is illogical for one’s own seeds to be enjoyed by another, and it is likewise unreasonable for what is transformed by another to serve as this [objective basis] for oneself (thus, the second position—that there must certainly be an indirect object-condition—is also unreasonable). Furthermore, all sentient beings naturally possess the distinctions of the five lineages (*pañca-gotra*). Not all...

Because the categories of sentient beings are all equal, one should state that for this category— the eighth consciousness— the remote object-condition (ālambanapratyaya) is indeterminate as to its existence or non-existence across all stages, whether it has not yet transformed or has already transformed.

Below this, the meaning of the presence, absence, and relative proximity or distance of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is specifically analyzed with respect to the eight consciousnesses. We shall first analyze the eighth consciousness.

There are three schools of interpretation, of which the third is correct. In the state prior to transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), the sense organs, the body, and the seeds definitely lack a distant object-condition;
however, the physical environment and the "dust-like" sense organs and bodies of others may possess a distant object-condition.

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): during the state of transformation, when the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) takes the ultimate truth as its object, there is certainly no remote object-condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*).

When the mirror-like wisdom takes the conventional truth as its object, there can be a remote object-condition. Furthermore, if it takes the present as its object, there is a substantial basis (*bhāva*); if it takes the past or future as its object, there is no substantial basis.
Therefore, it is said that the presence or absence [of a remote object-condition] is not fixed.

The seventh category of mind, in the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), is innate (*sahaja*)—referring to the dual grasping at self and phenomena—and therefore necessarily relies upon the objective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its external substantial basis;
thus, it invariably possesses a remote object-condition (*parokṣālambana-pratyaya*). In the stage after the transformation of the basis, this [remote object-condition] is not necessarily present:

if one takes pure consciousness as the object of non-self, there is still a remote object-condition; however, if one takes suchness (*tathatā*), the past, the future, or similar objects, there is no external substantial basis. Sixth.

Regarding the mental states (*citta-kalāpa*) characterized by sharp and intense modes of activity (*ākāra*), because they can operate with mastery throughout all stages (whether noble or ordinary), one should know that the external substance upon which they rely may or may not exist.
As for the remote object-condition (*parokṣālambana-pratyaya*), its existence or non-existence is indeterminate. This applies to the first five types of mental states.

In the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), because [the cognition] is coarse, dull, and inferior, it necessarily relies upon an external substantial reality (the objective sphere consisting of the five sensory objects);

therefore, a distant object-condition (*parokṣālambana-pratyaya*) is also invariably present. In the stage after the transformation of the basis, this is not invariably present; for instance, the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (all-accomplishing wisdom) can take dharmas of the past, future, and so forth as its objects, as there is no external substantial reality.
This passage explains the meaning of the proximity and remoteness, as well as the presence or absence, of the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the first seven evolving consciousnesses.

"Having an external object" refers to the simultaneous mental consciousness; "lacking an external object" refers to the independent mental consciousness (*manopavicāra*). The rest may be understood accordingly.
This concludes the third explanation: the objective condition. △ Fourth, the explanation of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

The fourth is the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*). This refers to any phenomenon that possesses a superior power or efficacy capable of acting as a condition for other phenomena, whether by favoring or opposing them;
therefore, it is called the dominant condition. Although the preceding three conditions are also dominant in nature, the present fourth condition is established separately to exclude those three.
It collects the remainder. This is for the purpose of revealing the distinct characteristics of the various conditions.
This dominant function of conformity and opposition operates in four locations, because there are four distinct matters: arising, abiding, accomplishment, and acquisition.

"Existing phenomena" (*saddharma*) refers to phenomena that possess substantial reality (*savastuka*). These may possess their own substantial reality, or they may be conventionally established based on the states (*avasthā*) of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), taking those very phenomena of form and mind as their substance.
All such phenomena are of the nature of dependence upon others (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and are not the same as the nature of universal conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
therefore, they are called "existing phenomena. Because of these phenomena, unarisen phenomena are either caused to arise or are made conducive to arising.
Furthermore, regarding already arisen phenomena, it may either comply with conditions to cause them to persist or oppose conditions to cause them not to persist;
regarding unformed phenomena, it may either comply with conditions to cause them to be formed or oppose conditions to cause them not to be formed; and regarding unattained phenomena...
Because it may either favorably cause [an effect] to be obtained or unfavorably cause it not to be obtained, it is called the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Although the functions of this dominant influence are numerous according to their specific objects, those that are preeminent and manifest are only twenty-two; one should know that these are precisely the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*).

1. The eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). 2. The ear faculty (*śrotra-indriya*). 3. The nose faculty (*ghrāṇa-indriya*). 4. The tongue faculty (*jihvā-indriya*). 5. The body faculty (*kāya-indriya*)—these five are called the five material faculties (*rūpa-indriya*).

6. The male faculty (*puruṣa-indriya*). 7. The female faculty (*strī-indriya*). 8. The life faculty (*jīvita-indriya*). 9. The mind faculty (*manas-indriya*). 10. The faculty of suffering (*duḥkha-indriya*). 11. The faculty of pleasure (*sukha-indriya*).

12. The faculty of grief (*daurmanasya-indriya*). 13. The faculty of joy (*saumanasya-indriya*). 14. The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣā-indriya*)—these five are called the five feeling faculties (*vedanā-indriya*). 15. The faculty of faith (*śraddhā-indriya*). 16. [The faculty of energy...]

Sixth, the faculty of exertion (*vīryendriya*). Seventh, the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*). Eighth, the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*). Ninth, the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*)—these five are called the five wholesome faculties (*pañca kuśalamūlāni*).

Tenth, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*). Eleventh, the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*). Twelfth, the faculty of "one who has fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*)—these three are called the three untainted faculties (*trīṇy anāsravendriyāṇi*).

The first five material faculties have as their nature the pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) of the eye and so forth, which are transformations of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) and its associates.
The term "consciousnesses and so forth" includes their respective seeds; "eye and so forth" includes the ear, nose, tongue, and body.

"Pure matter" refers to the purified four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which are the functional capacity for form within the eighth consciousness. They are not produced by external [elements] and are not the same as coarse [matter].
Visible form, odor, taste, and tangibles can be seen, smelled, tasted, and touched; however, they are known solely through inference (*anumāna*).
The two sexual organs are subsumed under the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*); therefore, they have as their nature a small portion of that [body-faculty]. As for the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*),...
It is merely a provisional designation based on the states of the seeds within the fundamental consciousness; it does not possess a separate nature [as an immediately antecedent condition].
The mental faculty (manas-indriya) has all eight consciousnesses as its nature.

If one considers the preceding moments of the eight consciousnesses and their associated mental states (citta-caitta-samūha) in relation to their subsequent moments within their own respective categories, they are subsumed under the condition of equal-immediate antecedent (samanantara-pratyaya).
However, here we do not distinguish between those of the same category and those of other categories;

rather, because they collectively possess the capacity—whether favorable or adverse—to bring about the arising, abiding, completion, and acquisition of all subsequent moments of mind and mental states, they are established as the dominant faculty (adhipati-indriya) acting as the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
The five faculties of feeling each have their respective feelings as their intrinsic nature.

The five faculties beginning with faith have faith and so forth (among the wholesome mental factors) and wholesome mindfulness and so forth (among the object-specific mental factors) as their intrinsic nature.
The five sensations—suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity—are the essential nature of the five faculties of sensation (*vedanendriya*).

Faith, diligence, and the wholesome factors among the specific mental objects (*viśeṣāyatana*)—namely, wholesome mindfulness, wholesome concentration, and wholesome wisdom—are the essential nature of the five spiritual faculties (*indriya*). These five wholesome faculties refer, for the time being, to contaminated (*sāsrava*) wholesome states.
The faculty of "knowing what is yet to be known" (*ājñātāvyājñendriya*) has three stages: 1. **The Fundamental Stage**:

This refers to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), specifically within the fifteen moments of mind, excluding the single final moment—the sixteenth moment—because in that sixteenth moment there is nothing further to be known that was previously unknown (it is therefore subsumed under the faculty of "having known," *ājñendriya*).

2. **The Preparatory Stage**: This refers to the levels of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), which are proximate to and capable of inducing the fundamental stage.

Regarding the stages: third is the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*). This refers to the period from when one generates a resolute and superior desire for the wholesome dharmas—because one seeks to attain the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the truths—until the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) that precede the attainment of the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

It is called the stage of equipment because it can provide distant support for the arising of the fundamental stage. Within these three stages, there are the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), as well as the mental faculty (*manas*).

The faculties of joy (*saumanasya*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) constitute the nature of this faculty of "the knowledge of what was not yet known" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*); however, they exist during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Because one feels distress while seeking to realize the superior dharmas at a later stage, there is also the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*); nevertheless, as it is not a fundamental wholesome faculty (*kuśalamūla*), it is generally not mentioned.

Among the fifteen moments of mind within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), all those factors of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, mental application, joy, equanimity, and pliancy belong exclusively to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because these constitute the supramundane path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), they are termed "not yet known" (*ajñāta*) because liberation has not yet been realized;

they are termed "to be known" (*ājñeya*) because liberation will necessarily be realized immediately thereafter. Therefore, these are established as the foundation for "the unknown-to-be-known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).

This refers to the state (*avasthā*). The preparatory stage (*prayoga*) is proximate in its ability to induce this state, while the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*) is remote in its ability to support the arising of this state.

Although that which is cultivated consists of the five roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and so forth, which are still with outflows (*sāsrava*), the wholesome states with outflows serve as the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
It assists in perfuming the originally existing seeds of untainted faith and so forth.

This refers to those naturally occurring (*dharmatā*) untainted seeds which, while in the stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*), are assisted and perfumed by tainted wholesome states;

thus, they gradually increase and mature, and will inevitably give rise to the actual manifestation of true untainted phenomena in the future. For this reason, it is called "that which is yet to be known" (*ājñātāvya*).
Regarding the knowledge of untainted roots of goodness:
those in the first three formless attainments possess these roots because they have acquired them through the superior path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) as a byproduct of cultivation;

or, for those of the two vehicles who turn toward the Great Vehicle, they also arise prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*) in order to realize the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasunyatā*). Furthermore, the untainted [knowledge] of the emptiness of persons (*pudgalasunyatā*) is subsumed within the nine stages.

Since all of those are subsumed within these faculties of a bodhisattva, the bodhisattva’s path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) also possesses these faculties; however, they are mentioned only in relation to the stages prior to the [ten] grounds (*bhūmi*), because that period is brief.

If one discusses the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), it exists properly within the four dhyānas, because the path of seeing of the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) necessarily...

Because they rely on the fourth dhyāna—though with the exception of the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception—those in the first three heavens of the formless realm can also possess this faculty.

This refers to a certain class of practitioners of the path of superior vision who, although relying on the fourth dhyāna to give rise to outflow-free (anāsrava) states, are also able to cultivate the higher three concentrations as collateral practice; thus, they [possess it] in the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, and nothingness.

There is also the faculty of "that which is yet to be known" (ājñāsyāmīndriya). Furthermore, although the outflows-free realization of the emptiness of persons within the nine stages of the three realms—attained by those of the Two Vehicles—is differentiated into the three faculties of "that which is yet to be known," "that which is already known" (ājñendriya), and "that which has been fully known" (ājñātāvīndriya), from the perspective of a Bodhisattva, all of these are subsumed under the faculty of "that which is yet to be known.
This is because they have not yet realized the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā). Therefore, when those of the Two Vehicles turn back...

Regarding those who are "heading toward the Great": although they have already fully realized the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) attained in the nine stages of the three realms through untainted wisdom (*anāsrava*), their attachment to phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*) has not yet been subdued;

thus, they still belong to the stage of accumulation (*sambhāra-avasthā*). Now, for the sake of realizing the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), even prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*), they give rise to this faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
Below the section on the Bodhisattva Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), there is an explanation that addresses a doubt. A doubt is raised as follows: "The Śrāvaka..."
The fifteen moments of mind during the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are still termed the fundamental stage of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
Only when the sixteenth moment is completed is it termed the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*).

Why, then, is the bodhisattva’s faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" said to exist only on the stages prior to the path of seeing? To explain this: while the bodhisattva is in the state of immediate succession (*ānantarya*).

Within the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it stands to reason that these faculties should also exist; however, they are mentioned only in relation to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) because the duration of a bodhisattva’s Path of Seeing is so brief.
This is because the Path of Seeing for a śrāvaka requires the contemplation of the four established truths (*vyavasthāpita-satya*): suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.

Ascending through the various realms, there are eight truths; thus, there are eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and eight knowledges (*jñāna*), totaling sixteen moments of mind, which are termed the "sixteen *kṣaṇas*.

As for their duration, it is relatively long. However, when a Bodhisattva perceives the Path, they contemplate only True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is not an established truth (*avyavasthāpita-satya*).
Although it involves many *kṣaṇas* until the matter is finally consummated, because these are equal in nature, they are collectively described as a single mind. Its...
At that time, it is abbreviated.

From the final moment of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) up to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), all nine untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*), such as faith and the rest, are of the nature of the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
For one who has not yet abandoned desire, there is sorrow and distress in seeking to realize the higher liberations.
There is also the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), which is not a primary wholesome root; therefore, it is generally not mentioned.

The sixteenth moment of mind of the two vehicles, upon realizing the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), and the Bodhisattva’s non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) upon ascending to the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), are both termed the final moment of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
This includes the final mind of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) and the final mind of the Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*).

All are termed the "diamond-like samādhi" (*vajropama-samādhi*). Since those of the two vehicles have already realized the true suchness of self-emptiness (*ātmaśūnyatā-tathatā*), and bodhisattvas have already realized the true suchness of dharma-emptiness (*dharmaśūnyatā-tathatā*), they are all termed those with the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātendriya*).
The meaning of the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is not discussed here; it may be understood from the text as it stands.
The nine untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) of all those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) are entirely of the nature of the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have fully realized the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), while the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have fully realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);

therefore, they are all termed "those who have already known. Those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward are also called "no-more-learners" (*aśaikṣa*); when compared with the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), they are termed "those who have already known."
It is known. Compared to the Tathāgata, even this is merely called "already known.
Although there is untainted (*anāsrava*) contemplation in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it is neither clear nor sharp; thus, it does not constitute the latter three faculties.

This is the resolution of a doubt. The doubt is as follows: "If it is the case that only those in the three lower formless realms can possess the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), then why is it that those in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)—who are not in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)—cannot also cultivate the untainted contemplations and enter the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)?
Why, then, do they lack the latter three of the twenty-two faculties? Therefore, the present explanation states: "Although they rely upon the Peak of Existence to cultivate the untainted..."
[They] enter the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). However, this absorption of cessation is preceded by the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of the perception of stillness;

it merely causes the exertion of discursive thought to cease, yet it is not clear or sharp. Indeed, to sever afflictions and realize the truth, one must necessarily possess the untainted direct realization (*anāsrava-abhisamaya*).

Now, for one who enters the absorption of cessation, the first six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) all cease to function simultaneously; therefore, [this state] cannot serve as a basis [for such realization].
Because they lack superior power and function in severing delusions and realizing principle, they are not the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*). As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"Though one may currently achieve the nine successive meditative attainments (*navānupūrva-samāpatti*), one cannot yet exhaust outflows and become an Arhat."

This is precisely the intended meaning. Therefore, if one wishes to exhaust the outflows (*āsrava*), one must cultivate the superior contemplation of the emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
Such is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*); the meanings of the other sections should be understood as they appear in the treatise.

This refers to the analysis through other categories, such as function, the provisional and the real, and even the realms of attachment (*dhātu-bandhana*), as extensively explained in the fifty-seventh fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
This concludes the initial clarification of the four conditions.
