△ Second, the ten causes of the collateral discussion, in three parts: first, explaining the establishment of causes based on the bases; second, explaining the inclusion of causes within the bases;
third, explaining the attainment of results through the causal bases. Regarding the first part, there are two sections: first, the heading and inquiry; second, the formal explanation. Now, the first.
These four conditions are established as ten causes based on the distinctions in meaning across fifteen bases.
How are these ten causes established based on the fifteen bases?
The *Zongjing* states: The ten causes are as follows. The cause of verbal designation (*anuvāda-hetu*) serves as the introductory gateway for all phenomena.

The cause of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*) brings about the understanding of manifest functional activities. The cause of projection (*ākṣepa-hetu*) brings about the formation of its own fruit. The cause of appropriation (*parigraha-hetu*) is able to encompass all conditions.
The cause of origination (*janana-hetu*) enables the various categories of things to arise. The cause of production (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*) causes all fruits to be accomplished.

[The section on] the causes is concluded. Regarding the cause of distinct determination (*pratiniyamahetu*), the categories are each separate. Regarding the cause of common function (*sahakārihetu*), the essence is collectively one and the same.

Regarding the cause of contradiction (*virodhahetu*), it can give rise to the gateway of obstruction. Regarding the cause of non-contradiction (*avirodhahetu*), it accords with the principle of dependent origination.

Part Two: The Proper Explanation has two sections. First, clarifying that the ten causes are established based upon fifteen locations. Second, subsuming the aforementioned ten causes under two causes.
There are ten [reasons] in the beginning and middle. First, the reason of conformity (*anuloma-hetu*) is established based on the basis of speech (*vāk-pratisthāna*). ... [omitted] ...
Tenth, the reason of non-contradiction (*avirodha-hetu*) is established based on the basis of non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa-pratisthāna*). Now, the first:

First is the basis of speech (*vāg-adhiṣṭhāna*). This refers to the nature of speech that arises from a phenomenon (*dharma*) which necessarily has a name (*nāman*), such as the perception (*saṃjñā*) that grasps the characteristics [of an object].

Based on this basis, the cause of conventional designation (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*) is established; that is, because one designates various meanings according to what is seen, heard, and so forth, based on this speech.
Thus, the speech that expresses is taken as the cause of the meanings expressed. Some treatises state that this "cause of conventional designation" is the name and the perception.

It is seen that because one grasps at signs according to names and adheres to them, speech subsequently arises. If one relies on what is stated in that treatise, it can be shown that this cause is the basis for speech.
There is a treatise; this refers to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*. The rest may be understood. △ Second, the causal condition of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*).

It is established based on the locus of experience. There are two loci of experience: namely, that which is depended upon (the object) and the nature of that which experiences (the subject). It is precisely based on these loci [that this condition is established].

The dependence cause (*apekṣā-hetu*) is established: that is to say, depending upon this [the experiencer] and those [the objects experienced], various things arise, persist, are accomplished, or are attained;
therefore, this [basis of experience] is the dependence cause for them.
Regarding the "grasper" (*grāhaka*) and the "grasped" (*grāhya*): for example, the hand is the grasper and the object held is the grasped, and so forth.
When undertaking a craft, the skill is the grasper and the degree of success (the *jiameng* rank) is the grasped, and so forth;
even up to pure karma being the grasper and the Pure Land being the grasped. It is in dependence upon the fruit that is grasped that the cause which grasps is established.

It causes those activities such as wholesome deeds (*kuśala-karman*) and pure deeds (*viśuddha-karman*) that have not yet arisen to arise; those already arisen to endure; those not yet perfected to be perfected;
and those not yet attained to be attained. △ Third, the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*): it is established based on the locus of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The third is the locus of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), which refers to the stage when internal and external seeds have not yet reached maturity.
It is precisely based on this locus that the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) is established, because it is capable of projecting its own distant fruit.

Internal seeds refer to non-common seeds; external seeds refer to common seeds. Through the continuous succession and mutual attraction of these habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they cause their own subsequent fruits to gradually mature.
This process, wherein seeds draw forth further seeds so that they are not severed, is called the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
Fourth, the "arising cause" (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*) is established based on the locus of moistened seeds.
Fourth (3), the basis for seeds that are moistened and ready to sprout (*sābhisyandana-janman-bīja-āśraya*). This refers to the stage when internal and external seeds have reached full maturity;
it is upon this very basis that the "cause of arising" (*utpatti-hetu*) is established, because it is capable of producing its immediate result.

This refers to the seeds of the three realms of existence (*tribhava*). Having already been moistened by craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), they are able to directly produce their own fruits;
thus, they are called the "cause of production" (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*). △ Fifth, the "appropriating cause" (*parigraha-hetu*) is established based on the six bases (*ṣad-āśraya*).
1. The basis of immediate cessation (*anantara-niruddha-āśraya*), namely the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) of mind and mental factors.

2. The basis of the object (*ālambana-āśraya*), namely the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of mind and mental factors. 3. The basis of the faculties (*indriya-āśraya*), namely the six faculties that serve as the support for mind and mental factors. 4.
The basis of functional activity (*kāritra-āśraya*), namely the functional activity of all instruments with respect to the action to be performed; this excludes [the agent].

All other auxiliary manifest conditions (besides the seed) are called the "instrument" (*karaṇa*). The ninth basis of human effort (*puruṣakāra-adhiṣṭhāna*) refers to the activity of all agents (*kartṛ*) with respect to the action to be performed;
that is, all other manifest conditions for the action (besides the seed) are called the "agent."
The ten bases for the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana-adhiṣṭhāna*) refer exclusively to untainted vision (*anāsravadarśana*).

Excluding that which merely draws forth its own seeds, all factors that can assist in drawing forth and realizing untainted phenomena are termed the "vision of reality. Based on these six bases in total, the cause of appropriation (*parigrahahetu*) is established.
That is to say, the capacity to appropriate the five [bases] brings about tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena, while the capacity to appropriate all six brings about untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena.
Therefore. △ Sixth, the inducing cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*). It is established based on the concordant bases (*anukūla-adhiṣṭhāna*).

There are eleven types of concordant bases, namely: the manifest activity (*samudācāra*) and the seeds (*bīja*) of all indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), defiled (*kliṣṭa*), and wholesome (*kuśala*) phenomena.

Regarding "action" (*caryā*): it refers to that which can accord with and conform to superior categories of dharmas of the same kind. It is precisely based on this point that the "inducing cause" (*ākṣepahetu*) is established;

that is, because it can induce the arising of superior categories of the same kind—whether they be the indeterminate, the defiled, or the wholesome—and because it can also induce the attainment of unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).

The indeterminate induces the indeterminate; the defiled induces the defiled; the wholesome induces the wholesome. Because each subsequent stage is twice as great as the preceding one, it is called a "superior grade" (*viśeṣa-bhāga*).
Furthermore, the wholesome is also capable of inducing the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); for although the nature of the unconditioned is inherently equal, [it is induced through this process].

This is because the indeterminate and defiled natures are extinguished through the power of wholesome factors, whereby [the latter] become manifest. △ Seventh, the cause of specific determination (*pratiniyama-hetu*):
It is established based on the locus of distinct functional capacities.

The twelfth is the basis for the function of differentiation. This refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), each of which possesses a specific capacity to produce and realize its own respective fruit (such that, with respect to the fruit it generates, there is no confusion).
It is precisely upon this basis that the cause of "determination" (*niyata-hetu*) is established;
that is, because each [cause] is able to produce its own fruit within its respective realm (*dhātu*) and so forth, and because each is able to obtain its own fruit within its respective realm.

The function of differentiation refers to the distinct seeds of form, mind, and so forth. To speak briefly in terms of the eighteen *dhātus*: the sense faculties (*indriya*) are definitely not the objects (*viṣaya*), and so on;
the objects are definitely not the consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and so on; and the consciousnesses are definitely not the sense faculties, and so on.

Furthermore, the eye is definitely not the ear, and so on; visible form is definitely not sound, and so on; and eye-consciousness is definitely not ear-consciousness, and so on. Each has its own seed, each [producing its own result].
Because it can produce, sustain, perfect, and cause the attainment of its own fruit, it is called the "cause of specific determination" (*pratiniyama-hetu*).

In the text, only production and attainment are mentioned; this is an elliptical abbreviation that implies sustenance and perfection as well. △ Eighth, the "cause of commonality" (*sahakāri-hetu*): it is established based on the locus of conjunction.

The thirteenth is the basis of conjunction (*sāmagrī-adhiṣṭhāna*). This refers to the bases ranging from the second, the basis of reception (*anubhava*), up to the twelfth, the basis of differentiated function (*viśeṣa-karma*).
Within the arising, abiding, accomplishment, and attainment of results, there is a power of conjunction; it is upon this very basis that the cause of common purpose (*ekārtha-hetu*) is established.

That is to say, the causes ranging from the second, the expectant cause (*apekṣā-hetu*), up to the seventh, the determinate cause (*pratiniyama-hetu*), all share the same single purpose, such as arising and so forth.
Because of their activity (*karma*), the aforementioned eleven bases (*āśraya*) are collectively termed the "basis of conjunction" (*saṃyoga-āśraya*).

The aforementioned six causes are collectively termed the "cause of common purpose" (*samāna-kārya-hetu*), because they share the same activity regarding the production, maintenance, completion, and attainment of the fruit. △
The nine contradictory causes (*viruddha-hetu*) are established based on the fourteen bases of obstruction (*āvaraṇa-adhiṣṭhāna*).
These fourteen bases of obstruction refer to those factors that can obstruct the arising, abiding, accomplishment, and attainment of a result.
It is precisely upon these bases that the contradictory causes are established, because they are able to oppose the processes of arising and so forth.

Just as defilement can obstruct purity, so too does purity obstruct defilement; likewise, the outflowing (*sāsrava*) can obstruct the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), and the outflow-free can also obstruct the outflowing.
All these are termed "contradictory causes" (*virodha-hetu*). △ Tenth, the non-contradictory cause (*avirodha-hetu*) is established based on the locus of non-obstruction.
The fifteenth is the basis of non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa-adhiṣṭhāna*). This refers to those factors that do not obstruct the processes of arising, abiding, accomplishment, and attainment;
it is upon this basis that the "non-contradictory cause" (*avirodha-hetu*) is established, because those factors do not contradict such events as arising and so forth.
It is not necessary for them to provide superior assistance; it is sufficient that they do not obstruct one another, and this is what is termed a "non-contradictory cause" (*avirodha-hetu*).
The first section, explaining how the ten causes are established based on fifteen locations, is concluded. △ Second, subsuming the aforementioned ten causes into two causes.
This has two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation. Now, the first part:
These ten causes are subsumed under two: first, the productive cause; second, the instrumental cause.

Second, the explanation of these as two [categories] has two parts: first, the general subsumption; second, the specific subsumption. Within the first part, there are two sections. First, citing the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
The two [sections] beginning with "The Stage Endowed with Vitarka" are all titles from among the seventeen stages of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. The first [section] further has two parts:
first, the citation of the text; second, the explanation of its meaning. This is the first [part].
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "The projecting seed (*ākṣepaka-bīja*) and the producing seed (*abhinirvartaka-bīja*) are called the productive cause (*janana-hetu*).
All remaining causes are subsumed under the instrumental cause (*upāya-hetu*)."
△ Second, the explanation of the meaning.

In this *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, among the six causes—namely, the projecting (*ākṣepaka*), the actualizing (*abhinirvartaka*), the producing (*āvāhaka*), the determining (*pratiniyama*), the co-operative (*sahakārin*), and the non-obstructive (*avirodhin*)—the seeds of the various causal conditions each have the distinction between being unripe and ripe.
If they are in the stage of being unripe, they are called "projecting seeds"; if they have reached the stage of being ripe...

The stage is called "arising" (*utpatti*). Among the six causes mentioned above, all causal seeds (*hetu-pratyaya-bīja*) are subsumed within these two stages [of "attraction" and "arising"] taught here in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.

Although those that manifest (*sammukhībhūta*) are also capable of producing, they are like the four causes—namely, the concomitant (*anuvartaka*), the contingent (*apekṣā*), the appropriating (*parigraha*), and the contradictory (*virodha*)—which, while possessing the capacity to produce their own seeds, are frequently interrupted. Therefore, [the arising stage is specifically designated].

This [Bodhisattvabhūmi] does not explain this in detail. Alternatively, among the four causes, those active manifestations that are capable of directly producing their respective fruits are also designated by the name "seed," even though they are actual occurrences (*samudācāra*).
This is because it is said that actual occurrences such as rice or barley are also called "seeds.

As for the remaining causes—namely, the first (the cause of designation), the second (the cause of dependence), the fifth (the cause of appropriation), the ninth (the cause of contradiction), and the six causes such as the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*)—those factors among them that are not *hetu-pratyaya* (causal conditions) are all... [as follows].

Because they are the remainder of the seeds of the productive conditions (*janana-pratyaya*) and the ripening conditions (*vipāka-pratyaya*), they are collectively said to be subsumed under the "expediency cause" (*upāya-hetu*).

This does not mean that these two types [of seeds] within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* belong exclusively to those two causes [the projecting and the actualizing causes] among the ten previously mentioned causes;
for among the remaining four causes—the inducing, the specific, the concurrent, and the non-contradictory—there also exist seeds of productive conditions. It is not only those [ten causes]...

The eighth [point] (is a general summary). It is called "the remaining causes" because, within those two previously mentioned causes (namely, the projecting cause and the producing cause), there are also seeds that are not *hetu-pratyaya* (causal conditions).

The "projecting seeds" (*ākṣepaka-bīja*) and "arising seeds" (*abhinirvartaka-bīja*) explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, although they share the same names as the third "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*) and fourth "arising cause" (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*) among the ten causes, differ in meaning; therefore, they are specifically explained here.
△ Second, citing the *Savitarkādi-bhūmi*, in two parts: first, citing the text; second, explaining the meaning. Now, the first:
The *Savitarkādi-bhūmi* states that the cause of arising (*utpatti-hetu*) alone is the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), while all others are subsumed under the instrumental cause (*upāya-hetu*).
△ Second, the explanation of the meaning.

The intent of this passage is as follows: among the six causes (such as the *ākṣepaka-hetu*), those that are either manifest activities (*pravṛtti*) or seeds (*bīja*) and are subsumed under the *hetu-pratyaya* (causal condition) are all termed "generative causes" (*janana-hetu*), because they are able to directly generate their own corresponding results. All remaining causes are [termed] "expedient" (*upāya*).
This [compendium] is not to be called the cause for arising as described in the *Savitarkādi-bhūmi*; it belongs exclusively to that [cause of arising] among the ten causes previously mentioned.

Because there are also causes among the other five causes that are not object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it is not only the nine [causes] remaining from those ten previously mentioned that are called "remaining causes" (*avaśeṣa-hetu*);
for there are also [causes] among those previously mentioned "arising causes" (*janaka-hetu*) that are not object-conditions.
The "causes of arising" (*utpādaka-hetu*) explained in the *Savitarkādi-bhūmi* are identical in name to the "cause of arising" among the ten causes, yet their meaning differs;
therefore, they are specifically explained here. The first section, the general inclusion, is concluded. △ Second, the specific inclusion.
The seeds of attraction and the seeds of actualization taught in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* are precisely those two causes (among the ten causes mentioned therein).
The remaining causes are the other eight [of those ten], even though they are included within the two [causes of] attraction and actualization.

There are causes that are not "causes of origination" (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*), yet because the seeds of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) are preeminent and manifest, they are specifically mentioned.
Although among the other causes there are also those that are not "causes of application" (*prayoga-hetu*), because the predominant ones are numerous and manifest, they are specifically mentioned.

In the *Savitarkādi-bhūmi*, it is stated that the cause of origination is the "cause of production" (*janana-hetu*), while the others are all "causes of application. This [which is explained here] is precisely what is meant by that [tenfold classification of causes].
Regarding the "causes of origination" (abhinirvṛtti-hetu) mentioned herein, one should understand that the remaining [nine] causes are all included therein.

Although there are seeds that are not *hetu-pratyaya* (causal conditions) among those that originate [phenomena], they are specifically mentioned because they are close and proximate to their results. Although there are necessarily seeds that are *hetu-pratyaya* among those that project [phenomena], they are not mentioned because they are distant and remote from their results and thus remain hidden.
The remaining nine [causes] are all subsumed under the category of *upāya* (expedient means). This should be understood by analogy.
The above should be understood.

It should be understood according to what precedes: that although among the nine causes there are those that are not causes by way of application (*upāya-hetu*), those that are predominant (*adhipati*) are numerous;

because they are thus manifested, they are explained specifically. The first section, clarifying the establishment of causes based on their bases, is concluded. △ Second, clarifying the subsumption of causes based on their bases.
Two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. Now, for the first:
upon what basis are the four conditions established as taught? Furthermore, how are they subsumed within the ten causes and the two causes?
The first question concerns the basis of the four conditions; the second question concerns the inclusion of the ten causes within the four conditions.

△ Second, the answer is twofold: first, answering how the four conditions rely upon fifteen bases; second, answering how the four conditions include the ten causes and two causes. Herein is the first.

The treatise explains the conditions (*pratyaya*): the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is established based on the basis of the seed; the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is established based on the basis of that which has ceased without interval;
the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is established based on the basis of the object; and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is established based on the remaining bases.
This is the formal response provided by the cited treatise. Below, it further clarifies the distinction between universal inclusion and restricted inclusion.
Herein, that which is termed "seeds" refers to the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) among the six bases:

namely, (3) the base of perfuming, (4) the base of moistened seeds, (11) the base of conformity, (12) the base of differentiated capacity, (13) the base of integration, and (15) the base of non-obstruction. It is within these six bases that the causal condition is found.

Regarding the categories of seeds: although these four bases—the initial basis for the arising of manifestation, the basis for experiencing [the result], the immediately preceding basis, and the basis of human effort—also possess causal conditions, they are frequently interrupted;

therefore, they are not mentioned here in brief. Alternatively, even those [manifested states] can directly produce their own seeds as results, and thus, like external grains such as barley, they are also designated by the name "seed."
This clarifies that the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is established based on seeds; this is stated in terms of a general inclusion.

Alternatively, the term "seed" here refers exclusively to the fourth [category] (the moistened seed). Regarding the distinctions between the immediate and the remote, the hidden and the manifest, and their respective inclusion or exclusion, it is as previously described.

This clarifies that causes and conditions are established based on seeds; it is a restricted categorization. This may be understood according to the principle of restricted categorization explained previously.

Regarding the terms "immediately preceding cessation" (*anantaraniruddha*) as the basis (*āśraya*) and "object" (*ālambana*) as the basis, one should know that these collectively manifest the bases for the two conditions—namely, the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).

It is not only the five [bases of immediately preceding cessation] and the six [bases of objects] that are definitively assigned to these two conditions, because the remaining thirteen types of bases [also function as such].
In the middle [of the three conditions], there is also the dual meaning of "immediate" (*samanantara*) and "object" (*ālambana*).
This clarifies that the condition of immediate succession is established based on what has ceased without interval, while the condition of the object is established based on the cognitive sphere;
it also possesses the sense of being universally inclusive.

Alternatively, what is here referred to as "immediately preceding" and "object" refers only to five or six [factors]. Although they exist in other places, they are omitted from mention here because they are relatively obscure.

This clarifies the immediately preceding cessation (*anantara-niruddha*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); it also carries the sense of being specifically delimited. Since the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is broad in scope, it need not be analyzed here.

This concludes the superior response regarding the four conditions based on fifteen points. △ Second, the response concerning the subsumption of the ten causes and two causes within the four conditions.

The treatise explains that among the [four] conditions (*pratyaya*), the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*)—which is subsumed under the "productive cause" (*janaka-hetu*) among the two types of causes—is the nature of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Among the four conditions, the intermediate two conditions (the immediately preceding condition and the object condition) are subsumed under the "appropriating cause" (*parigraha-hetu*) among the ten causes.

Although these latter three conditions are included within the "instrumental cause" (*prayoga-hetu*), because the dominant condition is predominant therein, it is mentioned specifically here; the others are not.

(9) Within the [category of] causes (*hetu*), there are likewise two intermediate conditions (*pratyaya*). However, because they are manifested specifically within the "appropriating cause" (*parigraha-hetu*), they are mentioned exclusively therein.
The initial "productive cause" (*janaka-hetu*) subsumes the meaning of the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*); the progression and regression are as previously explained.
Since one knows that the ten causes are subsumed within two causes, one then knows that the four conditions are likewise subsumed within those two causes.
Since one knows that the two causes can subsume the ten causes, one then knows that the four conditions also subsume the ten causes.

If one correlates the four conditions with the two causes, then the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), while the remaining three are all contributory causes (*upāya-hetu*). If, by means of the four conditions...

Regarding the ten causes: the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) subsumes those that produce; the immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) subsume those that sustain;

and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) subsumes the remaining eight. However, each of these also possesses both universal and specific applications, which may be considered through the analogy of advancing and retreating.
This concludes the second section: clarifying the inclusion of causes within the bases (*āśraya*). △ Third: Clarifying the attainment of results based on the bases of causal conditions.
II. First, the question; second, the answer. Now, for the first:
Regarding the causes and conditions that have been explained, there must necessarily be a fruit. How many such fruits are there, and by depending upon what location are they obtained?

First, the question regarding attaining the fruit through causes and conditions; second, the question regarding how many fruits there are; third, the question regarding the locus upon which the fruits depend.

△ Second, the answer in three parts: first, clarifying that the fruits are only five in number; second, answering regarding the locus from which the fruits are attained; third, answering regarding the attainment of the fruits through causes and conditions. Now, the first part.

There are five kinds of fruits. First is the ripening fruit (*vipāka*). This refers to the self-continuum’s actual ripening and the indeterminate states born of ripening (*vipākaja*), which are summoned by the impure wholesome and unwholesome dharmas (the two types of karma, the projective and the completing) performed by the first six consciousnesses. Collectively, these are termed the ripening fruit.
There are four meanings of "ripening" (vipāka): first, ripening at a different time, meaning that it is experienced at the time of receiving the fruit, not at the time of creating the cause;

second, ripening as a different nature, meaning that while the causes may be either wholesome or unwholesome, the fruit is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta); third, ripening as a different category.
This means that one creates karma in a single realm of existence (*gati*) and experiences its retribution in five realms of existence. It matures differently from the noble ones (*ārya*).

This is established based on the seeds of the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*). Regarding the term "outflowing" (*sāsrava*): it distinguishes [this] from untainted (*anāsrava*) wholesome states, which do not summon retributive results (*vipākaphala*).

Wholesome and unwholesome actions produced by the ignorance that initiates karma (*karmasamutthāna-avidyā*) are called "projecting karma" (*ākṣepaka-karman*), as they are capable of summoning the general retribution; this is termed "true" [karma].

Regarding maturation (*vipāka*): wholesome and unwholesome karma produced by the ignorance that moistens rebirth is called "fulfilling karma" (*pūrakakarma*). That which can bring about specific retribution is termed "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
True maturation is the very substance of the eighth consciousness, the fruit-of-retribution consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*). "Born of maturation" refers to [the other seven consciousnesses].
This refers to the various distinctions among the primary minds, mental factors, sense faculties, and the physical world that are obtained as immediate retribution (*vipāka*).

This true maturation (*vipāka*) and that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) are both subsumed under the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Based upon this, wholesome and unwholesome states subsequently arise; however, their essential nature is neither wholesome nor unwholesome.

The second is the result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*): it refers to that which is drawn forth by the cultivation of [the three natures, such as] the wholesome and so forth, being either of the same kind or resembling a prior action, such that the subsequent fruit follows accordingly.
Because they flow equally from their source, they are called "outflow" (*niṣyanda*). There are two kinds: first, the real; second, the semblance. Regarding the real outflow:

if one practiced virtue in a previous life, one will likewise be born with a fondness for virtue in this life; if one practiced evil in a previous life, one will likewise be born with a predilection for evil in this life.
This may manifest as either generosity or stinginess, purity or defilement, patience or anger, or diligence or indolence.
Whether concentrated or distracted, wise or foolish, faithful or faithless, greedy or non-greedy, ashamed or shameless, harmful or harmless—there are immeasurable such distinctions.
That the nature of birth is thus, without depending on cultivation, is entirely a true outflow (*nisyanda*).
Second, as for the similar outflow: having practiced a compassionate mind and non-harming in previous lives, one now experiences a long life as a result.
If one was free from illness in past lives, yet now experiences a short life and much sickness, it is because one harmed sentient beings in previous existences.

If one is now wealthy, prosperous, and at peace, it is because one was not stingy or greedy in past lives. If one is now poor, destitute, and deprived, it is because one was stingy, greedy, and a thief in past lives.

In past lives, one who refrained from sexual misconduct with others now experiences a loyal and virtuous retinue. In past lives, one who frequently committed adultery now experiences a wife and children who are perverse and immoral.
In past lives, one who spoke truthful words, meaningful words, gentle words, and words that promote harmony now experiences breath that is fragrant and pure;
their speech is verified by sincerity, their voice is clear and resonant, and their eloquence is uninterrupted. In past lives, one who engaged in false speech and frivolous chatter...
Regarding verbal misconduct such as harsh speech and divisive speech, one now experiences consequences such as stammering, muteness, and having one's words disbelieved by others;
these various future results all evolve in accordance with prior karma and are all similar to their respective outflows (*niṣyanda*).

Third is dissociation (*visamyoga*). This refers to the wholesome unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) realized through the abandonment of hindrances by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
The nature of these unconditioned phenomena is that they have no past, future, or present; yet, due to the two hindrances, they are not made manifest.

The two contemplations of the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena are called the untainted path. By abandoning the seeds of the two hindrances through this untainted path, one then realizes the two types of emptiness.

The *tathatā* (suchness) thus revealed is called the "fruit of dissociation" because it is free from entanglements. The two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) sever the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and become free from the bonds of the fragmented existence (*paricchinna-saṃsāra*).
The Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) severs the obstacle to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and becomes free from the bonds of the transformational existence (*pariṇāma-cyuti*).
Fourth is human effort (*puruṣakāra*). This refers to the work accomplished by various agents (*kartṛ*) employing various instruments (*karaṇa*).
The agent is termed "person" (*puruṣa*), such as those in the classes of farmers, artisans, merchants, and craftsmen.
The instrument is termed "effort" (*kāra*), such as writing implements, learning, tools, weapons, and technical skills. The work accomplished is termed the "result" (*phala*), namely—
These include fame, achievement, wealth, nobility, grain, crops, utensils, and so forth.
Fifth is "superior" (adhipati), which refers to all other fruits obtained apart from the aforementioned four.
For example, visual consciousness is the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) of the eye-faculty; auditory consciousness is the dominant fruit of the ear-faculty;
and so on, up to the fact that as long as the body has not disintegrated, it is the dominant fruit of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and so forth. The *Zongjing* states:

"In the case of maturation (*vipāka*), the cause gives rise to a fruit that ripens at a different time. In the case of outflow (*niṣyanda*), the nature of the cause and the fruit are identical, and their categories flow along without interruption."

Adhipati (sovereign) results are distinguished by their superior power and function, being able to assist other conditions. Puruṣakāra (human effort) results are those accomplished through one's own deeds, being able to acquire wealth and profit.
Visamyoga (disconnection) results consist of severing hindrances and realizing the truth, thereby transcending all taints and bonds.

This concludes the first section clarifying that there are only five types of fruits. II. Answering the question regarding the basis for attaining the fruits has three parts: First, citing the scriptural text; Second, providing a general explanation; Third, [the specific analysis].
Regarding the detailed explanation:

first, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts state that the "basis for the habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā-niśraya*) yields the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*), while the "concordant basis" (*anuvartaka-niśraya*) yields the flow-on fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).
The basis of true seeing attains the fruit of dissociation; the basis of human effort attains the fruit of human effort;
and the remaining bases attain the dominant fruit.
△ Second, the general explanation.

(One should know that herein) the term "locus of habitual tendencies" (vāsanā-sthāna) is used in a general sense; it indicates all functional capacities of the various bases that bring about retributive results (*vipāka-phala*), and does not refer exclusively to the locus of habitual tendencies.

The term "locus of conformity" (*anukūla-sthāna*) is also used in a general sense; it indicates all functional capacities of the various bases that induce results of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).

(The term "basis for true seeing" [satyadarśanāśraya] is used) not exclusively to refer to the basis that conforms [to the truth]. It is employed generally to manifest all the functional capacities of the various bases for realizing the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*).

(The term "basis for human effort" [puruṣakārāśraya] is used) not exclusively to refer to the basis for human effort. It is employed generally to manifest all the functional capacities of the various bases for bringing about the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).

(The term "the remaining bases" [avaśeṣāśraya] is used) not exclusively [for one specific case], but generally to manifest the attainment of the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) by all the various bases.

All functional capacities (do not exhaustively include the remaining eleven bases). Otherwise, the mention of the "remaining bases" would be too broad (as would be the mention of the "bases of the activity of a true seer in accordance with habitual tendencies").
This is too narrow.
△ Third, the explanation by way of restriction:

The "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) mentioned here belong exclusively to the third [basis], the basis of habitual tendencies; although they are also present elsewhere as maturation-causes (*vipāka-hetu*), they are not included here.
This [basis of habitual tendencies] also includes that which is not a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), yet it is a ripening cause whose fruit is distant in character;

habitual tendencies are likewise, and for this reason, this statement is made specifically regarding them. As for "conformity" (*anukūla*), it belongs exclusively to the eleventh basis (the basis of conformity).

Although the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) may also be obtained in other places, this [basis of conformity] obtains fruits that are not of outflow, and it is this [outflow] cause that brings about [such results].
The characteristics of superior conduct regarding good and evil are clearly manifested; the same applies to their conformity. Therefore, they are specifically mentioned here.

The term "locus of true vision" (*satyadarśana-sthāna*) refers exclusively to the tenth [basis] (the locus of reliance for true vision). Although other bases can also realize dissociation (*visamyoga*), this basis is also capable of attaining results that are not dissociation.

Nevertheless, because the characteristic of realizing dissociation is most prominent here, it is specifically mentioned. The term "locus of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-sthāna*) refers exclusively to...

[Commentary on the Ninth: The Basis of Human Effort (*puruṣakāra-adhiṣṭhāna*). Although the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) is also produced by other bases, this basis [of human effort] is also capable of producing fruits such as the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*) and so forth.
However, because its specific characteristics are manifest, it is mentioned specifically here. The phrase "the remaining [bases]" refers exclusively to the other eleven bases.
Although these eleven bases also obtain other fruits, they are capable of producing the sovereign fruit; yet, among those four remaining bases, this one...
Eleventh: [The fruit] is frequently summoned as predominant. Since the other four bases have already manifested the other four fruits, this is stated specifically here.

Both the text and its meaning are clear and may be understood. Second, the response regarding the attainment of the fruit based on the bases is concluded. △ Third, the response regarding the attainment of the fruit through causes and conditions.

Thus, among these five fruits, the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) is obtained through five causes—namely, the projecting, the actualizing, the determinative, the co-operative, and the non-obstructive—and one condition, the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).

The outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) is obtained through seven causes—namely, the projecting, the actualizing, the sustaining, the inducing, the determinative, the co-operative, and the non-obstructive—and two conditions: the first [the causal condition] and the last [the dominant condition].

[It] is obtained. As for the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*), it is [obtained] by means of the five causes: appropriation (*parigraha*), production (*ākṣepa*), determination (*anyathātva*), common operation (*ekakāryatva*), and non-contradiction (*avirodha*).

The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is obtained [through one condition]. Regarding the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), there is one interpretation that it is obtained through the dominant condition by means of the four causes—namely, dependence (*apekṣā*), appropriation (*parigraha*), commonality of purpose (*ekārthakriyā*), and non-contradiction (*avirodha*).

There is another interpretation that it is obtained solely through the eight causes—namely, dependence, attraction (*ākṣepa*), production (*abhinirvṛtti*), appropriation, inducement (*āvāhana*), determination (*pratiniyama*), commonality of purpose, and non-contradiction—but excluding the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
[The result] is obtained through three conditions. Regarding the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), all ten causes and four conditions may obtain it.
Within the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*), there are two interpretations; the second is correct. The rest may be understood. This concludes the secondary discussion on the ten causes.

△ Third, the correct demonstration of dependent origination has two parts. First, concluding the preceding and initiating the subsequent; second, explaining the characteristics of dependent origination.
Now, the first: the ancillary discussion is finished; one should now analyze the main argument.
△ Second, the explanation of the characteristics of dependent origination has two parts. First, clarifying the differentiation of the arising of seeds and manifestations;

second, clarifying the arising of seeds from manifestations. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, clarifying the differentiation of the arising of seeds according to the first half of the verse; second, clarifying the differentiation of the manifestation according to the latter half of the verse. This is the first [section].
The seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) can serve as three conditions to produce manifest discrimination, excluding the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).

That is to say, each of the eight consciousnesses has its own direct seeds; these are the direct causal conditions (*hetupratyaya*) for the active manifestations (*pravṛttivijñāna*) of those [eight consciousnesses] (since these seeds constitute the objective aspect [*nimittabhāga*] of the eighth consciousness).

As for the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for the subjective [consciousness], if the seeds of this [consciousness] provide auxiliary assistance to that [manifest consciousness], or do not obstruct it, they all constitute the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
The same should be understood for the arising of pure manifest activity through superior objects.

First, within the seeds deposited in the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the production of defiled discrimination is explained; subsequently, the production of pure manifest activity serves as an analogy to explain the production of pure discrimination.

Regarding the exclusion of the "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*), this refers solely to the mutual relation between prior and subsequent moments of the manifest consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*).

Establishing this basis, that which is called the "cognizing subject" (*ālambaka*) refers specifically to the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness and its five associated mental factors (*caitta*).
△ Second, explaining the manifestation of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) as indicated by the latter half of the verse, in two parts: first, explaining defiled conceptualization.
Second, the clarification of pure discrimination (*viśuddha-vikalpa*). This section has two parts: first, a general statement; second, a detailed explanation. Now, for the first:
when manifest discriminations are viewed in relation to one another, they can serve as three types of conditions, because there is no causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) [among them].
First, the seed induces the seed; second, the seed gives rise to the manifest; third, the manifest perfumes the seed. All of these possess the sense of cause and condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Now, however, when considering the manifest in relation to the manifest, there is no sense of cause and condition. △ Second, the detailed explanation has five parts:
first, regarding sentient beings in relation to themselves and others; second, regarding the eight consciousnesses in relation to one another; third, regarding their own kind...

Regarding the mutual observation of preceding and succeeding [moments]: (4) the fourth concerns the mutual observation of the mind and mental factors within the same aggregate; (5) the fifth concerns the mutual observation of the four parts within the same entity.
First, regarding the former:

it means that among the classes of sentient beings, self and others may mutually function as two conditions—namely, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)—with the exception of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
△ Second, regarding the mutual relationship among the eight consciousnesses themselves:
within the collection of the eight consciousnesses, when they are mutually related, there is invariably the presence of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

There is never the presence of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), while the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) may either exist or not exist. (First,) the eighth [consciousness] possesses the status of an object-condition for the [first] seven; that is to say, the seventh [consciousness] takes the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth as its object, and the first five [consciousnesses] take the eighth as their object.

Regarding the objective part (*nimittabhāga*): because the sixth consciousness universally takes both the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) and the objective-part of the eight [consciousnesses] as its objects, if the first seven [consciousnesses] were directed toward the eighth, they would lack the status of being an "object-condition" (*ālambanapratyaya*), because the other seven are not the substantial basis relied upon by the eighth.

Regarding the seventh [consciousness] and the first six: the five [sensory] consciousnesses lack the status of being an object-condition, because the five consciousnesses do not take the seventh consciousness as their object;

only the single sixth consciousness has the capacity to take the seventh as its object. Regarding those [six] and the seventh consciousness, all are entirely absent [of such a relationship], because the seventh does not... [take them as its object].

Because it takes the first six [consciousnesses] as its objects, the sixth [consciousness] lacks the status of being an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the [first] five consciousnesses; whereas the other five consciousnesses do possess the status of being object-conditions for that sixth consciousness.

This is because the five consciousnesses rely solely upon the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as their substantial basis, and therefore they do not take the sixth consciousness as an object.
△ Third, regarding the mutual relation of preceding and succeeding moments within their own category:
among the six types of consciousness within their own category, the succeeding moment can take three [of the preceding] as objects (excluding the *hetu-pratyaya*).

As for the others—the eighth, seventh, and the five preceding [moments]—they all further exclude the *ālambana-pratyaya* (objective condition), because they apprehend only present objects. If one were to allow that the subsequent "seeing" (*darśana-bhāga*) of the five [sensory] consciousnesses takes the "image" (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the preceding [moment] as its object, then the five [consciousnesses] with...

The seven [consciousnesses] (of their own kind) also have three conditions in relation to one another. Regarding the first seven (evolving consciousnesses) and the eighth (storehouse consciousness), the status of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) may also be applicable, because the active manifestations of the first seven can perfume and thereby produce the seeds of the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) within that eighth consciousness.

First, there is the formal explanation of how members of the same category relate to one another; second, there is the preceding discussion of the first seven [consciousnesses] in relation to the eighth, which further supplements the meaning that was not fully exhausted in the analysis of their mutual relations.
If one discusses the sense in which the other seven are not the objective supports (*ālambana*) for the eighth, then there is no remote object-condition (*parokṣa-ālambana-pratyaya*);
however, if one discusses the sense in which active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) infuse seeds (*bīja*), then it is possible for a remote object-condition to exist.

Condition: Because the seed undergoes perfuming and transformation by the active manifestation (*pravṛtti*), it arises as a transformation that is not distinct from its objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and relies upon the primary object (*ālambanavastu*).
△ Fourth, regarding the mutual relationship between the mind and mental factors within the same aggregate.

When factors of the same collection but different entities are viewed in relation to one another, they possess only the condition of predominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*). This is because associated mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) share the same objective basis (*ālambana-vastu*) and do not take one another as objects.

Alternatively, if one speaks from the perspective of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), it is said that they do not take one another as objects; however, if one speaks from the perspective of the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), it is also possible to say that there is the sense of taking one another as objects.

That is to say, various image-parts arise with each other as their objective basis. For example, the seeds within the eighth consciousness (which are image-parts) serve as the objective basis for contact (*sparśa*).

The objective counterparts (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the five mental factors (*caitta*), such as contact (*sparśa*), must have a substantial basis (*dravya*). Otherwise, they would not exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), where the physical body and the material world (*bhājana-loka*) are absent;

for if that were the case, those five mental factors would lack an object of perception (*ālambana*). Even if one were to concede that matter (*rūpa*) produced by meditative concentration exists in the formless realm, the five [mental factors] such as contact would still necessarily take seeds as their objects and manifest as resembling those seeds.

This is to avoid the conclusion that the objective counterparts of associated mental factors are not substantially identical to the objective counterparts of the primary mind (*citta*). Therefore, they must have a substantial basis.

The mind and its mental factors (citta-caitta) are conjoined and appear as one; therefore, they are called "assembled together" (*samprayukta*). However, because their characteristics and functions are each distinct, they are called "different entities" (*nānātva*).
The respective *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving portions) of each certainly do not take one another as objects.

Yet, their respective *nimitta-bhāga* (reflected-image portions) may mutually serve as the objective basis (*ālambana-pratibimba*) for one another, as in the case of the Formless Realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), where no physical body or external environment currently exists, and [the perception] relies solely upon the various [seeds] stored within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

The seeds of phenomena (*dharmas*) serve as the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the object-field. The five mental factors (*caitasika*), such as contact (*sparśa*) and its associates, rely upon these seeds—the objective aspect of this fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*)—as their substantial basis (*upādāna*).
They then manifest as an appearance resembling seeds, which serves as their cognitive object (*ālambana*).

If it were not admitted that they arise by mutually serving as each other's substantial basis, then contact and the other factors would be devoid of an objective field. This remains true even if one grants the existence of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding the matter of the form that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*): the mental concomitants (*caitta*) and the mind-king (*citta*) must necessarily share the same object of perception (*ālambana*).

There has never been a case where the mind-king, having already taken an object of threefold nature as its basis, while the mental concomitants do not take that same essential substance but instead manifest a distinct image-part (*nimittabhāga*).
△ Fifth, [an analysis] by way of comparing the four parts within the same entity.
The same-part (sabhāga-bhāga) functions as two conditions for the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga): as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

For the seeing-part in relation to that image-part, it possesses only the single sense of being a dominant condition. The same relationship holds between the seeing-part and the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).

It should be understood that the other two—the self-cognizing part and the self-cognizing-of-self-cognizing part—mutually function as both of these two conditions (dominant and object). Herein, this is not explained according to the seeds or the latent image-parts, but rather refers only to their manifest arising.
"Because they serve as mutual conditions;
the same applies to the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) and the self-cognition (svasaṃvitti) in relation to one another.

This means that the seeing-part can function as two types of conditions for the self-cognition, whereas the self-cognition serves the seeing-part only as a dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya), because the seeing-part cannot take the self-cognition as its object. This first clarifies the defiled portion.
The section on differentiation is concluded. △ Second, the clarification of pure differentiation:

The collection of the eight consciousnesses is purified; self and others mutually possess objects of cognition (by means of the mental states associated with the four wisdoms), because they are able to universally cognize them.

The exception is the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), which is not an object of the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), because logically the image-part lacks the functional capacity to act as a subject of cognition.

The Perfect Mirror Wisdom and the Wisdom of Equality both possess both the fundamental and the subsequently attained wisdoms. The Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done possesses only the subsequently attained wisdom;

its fundamental, ultimate wisdom takes only suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, whereas its subsequently attained, provisional wisdom universally takes both the provisional and the real aspects of form and mind as its objects.

All phenomena—whether with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned, past, present, or future—therefore allow for the meaning of the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*) to apply to both self and other in their mutual relation.
This is first explained by considering the four aspects (*catur-bhāga*) within the same substance (*sabhāva*).

There are twelve layers. First, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its object; because this is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is "transformation-carrying" (*pariṇāma-ādāna*).

Second, the seeing-part takes the seeing-part itself as its object. Third, the seeing-part takes the self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) as its object. Fourth, the seeing-part takes the verifying-the-self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvittisaṃvitti-bhāga*) as its object;
because there is no intervening delusion and because it is known with perfect clarity, these are all "clinging-carrying" (*upādāna*). Fifth, the self-verifying-part...

The *viṣayābhāsa-vibhāga* (the objective aspect) takes the *nimittabhāga* (the image aspect) as its object; because it manifests from its own substance, it is also a case of "transformation-carrying" (*pariṇāma-ādāna*).

According to the Nature School (*Xingzong*), this is fundamentally the wondrously pure and luminous essence of *bodhi*; how could there be "is" or "is not" within it? This is also a case of "co-inherence-carrying" (*sahaja-ādāna*).

Sixth, the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (the self-verifying aspect) takes the *darśanabhāga* (the seeing aspect) as its object; because it is no different from its original state when defiled, it is so. Seventh, the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga*.

1. The self-witnessing division (svasaṃvittibhāga) takes itself as its object; because its own essence is non-deluded, it is a case of "carrying along" (sākṣātkaraṇa). 2. The eighth, the self-witnessing division, takes the witnessing-of-self-witnessing division as its object;

because it is no different from the time of being defiled, it is entirely a case of "carrying along. 3. The ninth, the witnessing-of-self-witnessing division, takes the objective division (nimittabhāga) as its object; because it is the appearance of the mind itself, it is a case of "carrying along. 4.

The tenth, the witnessing-of-self-witnessing division, takes the subjective division (darśanabhāga) as its object; because it is the seeing of the mind itself, it is a case of "carrying along. 5. The eleventh...

The self-witnessing aspect (svasaṃvittibhāga) takes the witness-aspect as its object; because it is not different from the original [consciousness] at the time of defilement, the twelfth, the witness-of-the-witness aspect (svasaṃvittisaṃvittibhāga), takes the witness-aspect as its object, for its own essence is free from delusion.
The distinction between "transformative-carrying" (pariṇāmopādāna) and "concomitant-carrying" (anubandhopādāna) may be understood by analogy with the witness-aspect.

There is only the objective aspect (nimittabhāga), which ultimately cannot take the subjective aspect (darśanabhāga) as its object; for once it is designated as the "objective aspect," it is so defined.

These are therefore shadows transformed by the mind, which certainly lack the functional capacity to act as a perceiving subject (*ālambaka*). If one were to claim they possess such a capacity, it would be unreasonable.
Indeed, even at the stage of Buddhahood, the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) lacks the capacity to perceive; how much more so in the defiled state?

Now, regarding the two kinds of five sense organs—the *phu-ch'en* (tangible, physical) and the *sheng-yi* (ultimate, subtle)—and the four great elements and five objects of the sensory world (*bhājana-loka*):
Since both are equally the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the eighth consciousness, there is fundamentally no distinction between "intimate" and "distant.

Yet, through false discrimination, one is taken to be sentient and the other insentient; such delusion is profound indeed. Furthermore, the "reflected images conditioned by the six sense-objects" are merely the *nimitta-bhāga* of the independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
That Ānanda, in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, mistakenly identified these as his own mind was nothing short of delusion.
He mistakenly identifies the reflection as his own head. Therefore, the Tathāgata directly rebuked him, saying: "Tsk! Ānanda, this is not your mind;
it is a false conceptualization of the illusory appearances of external objects. This is precisely what commentators erroneously designate as the six consciousnesses; it is truly laughable.

Question: If it is maintained that the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) lacks the functional capacity to act as a cognizer (*ālambaka*), then how can the positions established by Tiantai—namely, "the object illuminates the object" (*jing zhao jing*) and "the object illuminates the wisdom" (*jing zhao zhi*)—be reconciled? Answer: Within this there are two meanings.

First, the names are fused while the meanings remain distinct; second, both names and meanings are fused. Regarding the phrase "names are fused while meanings are distinct": this refers to the perspective of having divisions (*yǒu fēn*).
A distinct form illuminates non-conceptual form as its object; it illuminates the object. With respect to conceptual form, it illuminates non-conceptual consciousness as its object;
it illuminates wisdom. Since both the conceptual and the non-conceptual are equally termed "consciousness," they are so designated.
They may also be designated by the same name, "form" (*rūpa*); thus, their names are fused. When there is conceptualization (*vikalpa*), it serves as the illuminator;

when there is no conceptualization, it is merely the illuminated. Thus, their meanings are distinct. This is consistent with the principle that the *nimitta-bhāga* (the objective aspect) lacks the functional capacity of being a subjective cognizer.
To say that both name and meaning are fused means that they are originally the wondrously luminous, unsurpassed Bodhi-purity.

The perfectly full true mind falsely manifests as the objective portion (nimittabhāga), such as the appearances of form and emptiness, and as the subjective portion (darśanabhāga), such as hearing and seeing.
It is like seeing two moons when there is but one moon: who can be said to be the moon, and who can be said not to be the moon? Thus, speaking according to ultimate principle:
There are sixteen layers. Of these, twelve have already been explained above; four more are now added: first, the aspect that takes the aspect as its object;

second, the aspect that takes the seeing as its object; third, the aspect that takes self-cognition as its object; and fourth, the aspect that takes the cognition of self-cognition as its object. Question:
Since it has been asked who is the moon and who is not the moon, this very seeing and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi.
How could there be "is" or "is not" within this? This [essence] cannot even be called "one";
how could there be "two"? Since it is not even two, how could there be "four"? Since it is not even four, how could there be...?
[Question: "Do you falsely claim that there are sixteen layers? [Answer: "It is not separate from your question that my answer is formed.

Since you have already stated that it cannot even be called 'one,' one knows that 'one' likewise lacks intrinsic nature. Therefore, it does not hinder the entire substance from manifesting as two, four, or sixteen.
If one does not allow for it to manifest as two, four, or sixteen, then it is fixedly 'one.'"
How can it be said that [the moon] is not even called "one"? For instance, if the moon were definitively two, why would those with clear vision still see it as one?
If the moon were definitively one, why would those who press their eyes see it as two?
Now, those who press their eyes see only its duality and do not know its unity; yet those with clear vision, having already known its unity, also know that it *can* be so.
To grasp at two while knowing two but not one is deluded sentiment; to know one and also know two is wondrous understanding.

If one claims that there are four divisions and twelve layers according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), yet no subject-object duality according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), this is a bifurcation of the true and the conventional.
If the true were fixed as one and [the conventional as many],...

[They are] different. How does this differ from the Sāṃkhya doctrine that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is determinately one? [In our view,] conventionally they are determinately different yet not fused.

How does this differ from the Vaiśeṣika doctrine that the nature of phenomena is determinately different? Furthermore, a verse (*gāthā*) says: "The eight types—mind, intellect, and consciousness—are distinct in appearance conventionally;

in reality, their appearances are not distinct. Because neither the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) nor the characterized (*lakṣya*) exists. This means that the conventional is the conventional of the ultimate.

It is like gold being fashioned into vessels: if the vessels are distinct, the gold is likewise distinct. It is not that conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) can establish its own distinctions apart from ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Ultimate truth is the truth within the realm of the conventional, just as a vessel is nothing other than gold. If there is no distinction in the gold, there is likewise no distinction in the vessel.
It is not that by negating conventional truth, ultimate truth dwells apart from the characteristics of phenomena. Therefore, the *Zongjing* [says]:
It is said: "In general, there are two types of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only): first, the complete (*sakala-bhāga*), and second, the incomplete (*vikala-bhāga*).

Because of the principle of lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it realizes the meaning of True Suchness (*tathatā*) following conditions; thus, the unarisen and undying merges with the arisen and dying, being neither identical nor different.
This is called the *ālayavijñāna*, which is the complete type. If one does not rely entirely upon the true mind, then phenomena do not [rely] upon..."

From the perspective of principle, to speak only in terms of arising and ceasing is not to speak of the complete portion (*sakala-bhāga*). Some say that when there is a substance outside the reflection, it constitutes the "half-portion" of *vijñapti-mātra*;
when both the substance and the reflection are reflections, it constitutes the "complete portion. This, however, is merely the "complete portion" within the *Vijñapti-mātra* school itself.

Furthermore, citing the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the commentary states: "The eight consciousnesses all possess arising and ceasing; they are all termed 'transformative characteristics' (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*). The eight...
All consciousnesses are in motion; they are all termed the "aspect of karma. The true nature of these eight [consciousnesses] is entirely termed the "true aspect. Alas! This can be contemplated.
The first section, clarifying how seeds and manifestations give rise to discrimination, is complete. II. Clarifying how manifestations and seeds give rise to seeds.
This has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. Now, the first part.
Since manifest discrimination arises by taking seeds and manifest phenomena as conditions, it stands to reason that seeds also arise by taking manifest phenomena and seeds as conditions.
How many conditions can manifest phenomena and seeds act as for seeds?
△ Second, the answer.

The seeds necessarily do not arise from the two conditions [of the immediately preceding condition and the object condition], because it is for the sake of establishing those two meanings—the immediately preceding condition and the object condition—that the mind and mental factors are said to arise (manifest).
When manifesting, they act as both conditions toward their own direct seeds, whereas toward seeds that are not their own, they serve only as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, with respect to their own direct seeds, the seeds themselves also possess both conditions; however, with respect to seeds that are not their own, they likewise serve only as the dominant condition.

The above constitutes the detailed explanation of the meaning of the verses, concluding the formal exposition on dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda). II. Conclusion, Refutation, and Reference to the Extensive Exposition:

Based on this principle that internal consciousnesses mutually arise as conditions, the logic and scriptural teachings regarding the differentiation of cause and effect are both established. As for the external conditions that are clung to [by others], [they are untenable].
Even if they were established, they would be useless; how much more so when they contradict both reason and scripture? Why then do you persist in such dogmatic adherence?
This first section concludes with a reprimand.
Although the term "discrimination" (vikalpa) is used, it generally indicates the mind and mental factors of the three realms; however, according to what is predominant, in various sacred teachings—
It is revealed through many gates; it is sometimes described as being twofold, threefold, fourfold, fivefold, and so on, as is fully and extensively analyzed in other treatises.

This [text] further refers to that extensive exposition. The two [aspects] refer to defiled discernment (*saṃkleśa-vikalpa*) and pure discernment (*vyavadāna-vikalpa*), or to the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*) and the manifesting consciousness (*khyāti-vijñāna*), or to that which does not fall into the mental faculty (*amanasikāra*) and that which falls into the mental faculty (*manasikāra*).

The three [aspects] refer to mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*). The four [aspects] refer to the wholesome (*kuśala*), the unwholesome (*akuśala*), the obscured (*nivṛta*), and [the unobscured-indeterminate].

The indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), the unobscured-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), and so forth—these are five. That is to say, cause and effect, suffering, pleasure, equanimity (*upekṣā*), and so on.
