Although there is internal consciousness but no external objects, by what means does the continuity of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) of sentient beings proceed? The verse says:

"By the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of various karmas, together with the habitual tendencies of the two-fold grasping (*dvaya-graha*), once the previous maturation (*vipāka*) has been exhausted, another maturation arises again."
△ Second, the explanation through the treatise consists of four parts. First, one school explains it in terms of the continuity of the grasping of karma (*karmopādāna*).

Second, another school explains it in terms of the continuity of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Third, yet another school explains it in terms of the continuity of the obstructive factors (*āvaraṇāṅga*).

Fourth, another school explains it in terms of the continuity of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). All four explanations possess valid principles, yet the fourth is particularly superior. Nevertheless, it is not...
This refutes the previous three interpretations. First:
The treatise states: "All karma" refers to meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable karma—namely, the volitional karma of contaminated wholesome and unwholesome types.
The attendants of karma are also designated by the name 'karma' because they are capable of collectively projecting and completing the two kinds of ripening fruits (*vipāka-phala*).

Although this [karma] perishes immediately upon arising and lacks the capacity to directly summon a future ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*), it nevertheless perfumes the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and gives rise to its own functional capacity.
This very capacity is termed "habitual energy" (*vāsanā*). It is formed by the perfuming of the residual force of karma;
it is called "habitual energy" to distinguish it from past and present karma. Such habitual energy continues in a successive stream until it reaches maturation.
At that time, it draws forth the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*). This demonstrates the superior dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the future fruit;
this explains the first line of the verse. Wholesome karma is called "meritorious karma" (*puṇya-karma*); unwholesome karma is called "non-meritorious karma" (*apuṇya-karma*);

and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), when contrasted with the distraction of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), is called "immovable karma" (*āniñjya-karma*). All three types of karma consist of volition (*cetanā*).

It constitutes the essential nature (*svabhāva*). The other mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) are called its retinue (*parivāra*). They likewise bring about maturation (*vipāka*) and are also termed "karma.

Regarding "past and present karma": this refers to manifest karma in the past. Once manifest karma has ceased, it is solely through the perfuming of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) that the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) is induced.

[Whether one takes] the perceived aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), or [takes] name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), or [takes] mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), or [takes] the root and the branches—the grasping subject and the grasped object are all subsumed under the two graspings (i.e., the two graspings in their active manifestation).

That which is perfumed and activated by those two graspings, and which directly produces a specific capacity upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), is called the "habitual energy of the two graspings" (*dvaya-grāha-vāsanā*).
This indicates the causes for the future maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*), namely, the mind and its associated mental factors.

The seeds of conditions and the seeds of karma coexist; that is, the seeds of karma coexist with the seeds of the two types of grasping (*upādāna*). This refers to the mutual relationship between distant and proximate conditions.
Although the seeds of karma are distant [conditions], their function of producing rebirth is manifest; therefore, the verse mentions them first.

This explains the second phrase of the verse. "Name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*): the first aggregate is "form" (*rūpa*), and the remaining four are "name" (*nāman*).

"Root" refers to the eighth consciousness; "branch" refers to the preceding seven consciousnesses. The seeds of karma are the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and thus they are called "remote assistance.

The seeds of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) are the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), and therefore they receive the designation of being "proximate. The rest may be understood from the text as it stands.
"Prior maturation" refers to the fruit of maturation produced by the power of karma from prior lives—up to as many as a hundred thousand prior lives.
"Subsequent maturation" refers to the fruit of maturation produced by the power of karma from subsequent lives—up to as many as a hundred thousand subsequent lives.

Although the seeds of the two appropriations (grasping at subject and object) arise wherever they are perfumed and are perfumed wherever they arise, leading to an inexhaustible experience of results, the karmic latencies have a limit to their yielding of results. Why is it said they have a limit? Because...

The ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) is by nature neutral (*avyākṛta*), because its nature differs from that of wholesome and unwholesome karma; it must ripen in a different lifetime and is thus difficult to bring about. What is meant by "inexhaustibility"?

It refers to the fact that the outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*) share the same nature [as their causes] and can therefore be produced simultaneously and easily.

Because the seeds of the karma that produces future lives ripen within this very body, when the previously acquired ripening fruit has been fully experienced, it is capable of producing yet another distinct ripening fruit.
Because of this, the cycle of birth and death revolves without end. Why depend upon external conditions for its continuity?

This explains the third and fourth lines of the verse. Regarding "the karmic latencies of action have an end when the fruit is experienced": for example, through the wholesome karma of observing the precepts, one receives the retribution of being born as a human or a deva;
if one does not cultivate further, then once that retribution is exhausted, one falls [into lower realms], and so forth.
The meaning of this verse is as follows: Saṃsāra is observable due to karma and the latencies of the two types of grasping;
it does not exist apart from consciousness, because the mind and mental factors constitute the very nature of those [karmas and latencies of the two graspings].

This is a general statement of the meaning of the verse. The explanation of the first school is complete. △ Second, the explanation according to the second school, which interprets it in terms of the continuity of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Furthermore, the continuity of birth and death arises from various habitual tendencies. Now, these habitual tendencies are generally of three kinds. The first is named...

Regarding "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*): this refers to the respective, direct seeds of conditioned phenomena (of the three natures). There are two types of "linguistic expression" (*nāma-vyavahāra*):

first, linguistic expression that denotes meaning, which refers to the specific distinctions of sound that can signify an object (excluding sounds that do not signify, as they are not names); second, linguistic expression that manifests objects.
The mind and mental factors that are able to cognize objects contain seeds perfumed by the two kinds of linguistic expression;
because they act as the specific causes and conditions for conditioned phenomena, they are called "linguistic expression habitual tendencies" (*nāma-kāya-vāsanā*).
Names are a form of mental distortion (*kuṭilībhāva*) applied to sounds; they are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) in nature and cannot, by themselves, perfuse seeds into matter or mind.

Nevertheless, because seeds arise based on names, they are termed "name-and-phrase seeds" (*nāma-pada-vāsanā-bīja*). The seeing parts (*darśana-bhāga*) and so forth of the first seven consciousnesses are not actually name-and-phrase in themselves.
For example, just as one reveals a referent meaning through spoken names, these minds and mental factors are able to reveal [their objects].
Regarding the objects of cognition: there are expressive designations (nāma-vikalpa) that accord with those objects; therefore, they are called "expressive designations that manifest objects.

Second, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*). This refers to the seeds of the false attachment to a self and what belongs to a self (*ātman-ātmīya*). There are two types of self-grasping:

first, innate self-grasping (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*), which is the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); this pertains to both the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. Second, conceptualized self-grasping (*vikalpita-ātma-grāha*).

Namely, the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self that is abandoned through seeing (which exists only within the sixth mental consciousness) perfumes seeds in accordance with those two types of self-grasping;

Furthermore, the continuity of birth and death proceeds by means of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering. The afflictions that initiate karma and moisten rebirth are called "afflictions.

A Detailed Explanation of the Limbs of Existence has three sections: first, the formal explanation of the nature of the limbs; second, an analytical examination of the meaning of the limbs; third, a classification according to various categories.
First: Now, the twelve links are briefly subsumed into four categories. First is the "projecting limb" (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*), which refers to ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*).

This is because they are able to project the seeds for the five effects, beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*). Within this, "ignorance" refers exclusively to that which can incite karma—whether wholesome or unwholesome—that directly brings about future rebirths.

That which is thus produced is what is called "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*). Consequently, all karma that is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), as well as auxiliary karma that is to be experienced in other lives, are not the member of "volitional formations."

"Consciousness and so forth" refers to name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling. "Auxiliary karma for specific [rebirths]" refers to the completing karma (*paripūraka-karman*) that can summon specific retributive results.

Second, the "projected factors" (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*) refer to the consciousness within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) that directly produces the consciousness subsumed under the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of the future.

These five [limbs] are the seeds [of the future existence], because they are induced by the preceding two limbs. Among these five, the seed of consciousness refers specifically to the direct cause of the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
With the exception of the three subsequent causes—the six sense bases, contact, and feeling—the remaining causal seeds are all subsumed under the category of the seed of name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
The latter three causes correspond to the sequence of their names; that is, they are the seeds of the three subsequent factors: the six sense bases, contact, and feeling.

Although the five types of seeds, including consciousness, are in reality simultaneous—having been perfumed and activated by karma—they are conventionally described as sequential in the various sacred teachings because they differ in terms of principal and attendant, general and specific, superior and inferior, and cause and effect.

Because the stages have a sequential order, it is said that there is a sequence of before and after. For this reason, the five members beginning with consciousness are also described as "active" (samudācāra).

Because they necessarily do not arise simultaneously.

The ignorance that initiates karma performs good and evil projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) and immediately perfumes the five types [of aggregates], such as consciousness and so forth, in the future;
there is certainly no sequence between them. For what reason are these five members established as distinct? There are two interpretations. First, regarding the member of consciousness (*vijñāna*):
This is the primary factor; the other four are its companions. Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is the general category, while the other three are the specific categories.

The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are superior, while contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are inferior. Contact is the cause, and feeling is the result. Because they differ in these characteristics, they are conventionally designated as preceding and succeeding.
Once the two [name-and-form and the six sense bases] have been perfumed and activated, when the time for maturation arrives, consciousness first manifests, followed by the arising of name.

The remainder may be understood accordingly.

The third is the "limb that produces," namely craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*). This is because they closely produce future birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

That is to say, conditioned by the delusion regarding internal matured results (*vipākaphala*)—that is, ignorance (*avidyā*) concerning the mark of self (being obscured regarding the principle of non-self and failing to know the suffering of future rebirth as it truly is)—one issues forth various karmas capable of directly summoning a future existence.
With these as conditions, one brings about the five results (consciousness and so forth) that directly produce the states of future birth and old age and death.

Having thus planted the seeds, furthermore, based on the delusion regarding external dominant fruits (*adhipati-phala*), one gives rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*) conditioned by the experience of objects (*viṣaya-vedanā*).

Conditioned by craving, the four types of grasping (*upādāna*)—namely, desire and so forth—arise again. Craving and grasping together moisten the seeds of projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) as well as the causes of the projected [five branches] (i.e., the seeds of the five branches).
These are then designated as the branch of "existence" (*bhava*), because they both enable the immediate proximity of the fruit of future existence (*punar-bhava*).

Therefore, delusion regarding the internal matured fruit (*vipāka-phala*) is precisely ignorance regarding the principle (*tattva-avidyā*). The karma that truly brings about future existence is the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

Delusion regarding the external dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) is precisely ignorance regarding phenomena (*vastu-avidyā*). These include the four types of grasping, such as sensual desire and so forth.
That is to say: first, clinging to sensual desire; second, clinging to views; third, clinging to precepts and observances; and fourth, clinging to the doctrine of self.
In some places, only the seeds of karma are called "existence" (*bhava*), because these alone can directly produce the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*).

The four members produced [thereby]—namely birth (*jāti*) and aging-and-death (*jarā-maraṇa*)—are so called because they are directly produced by craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*).

To manifest cyclic existence and to avoid the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, two sets [of links] are provisionally established; however, in reality, this is useless. Alternatively, one might exceed this number, which would lead to an infinite regress.
This is because the present fruits of birth, aging, and death arise from the ten causal links of the past, and the ten causal links of the present are determined [by the past].

II. Fifteen Classifications by Various Gates. First, the Gate of the Provisional and the Real. [End of section]. Fifteenth, the Gate of Subsumption under Afflictions, Karma, and Suffering. Now, the first.

Regarding the distinctions among the categories of these twelve links: nine are real and three are provisional (*prajñapti*). This is because the six links—namely, those such as formations that have already been moistened by craving—are combined to constitute the link of existence (*bhava*);

thus, the link of existence is provisional. Furthermore, the five links beginning with consciousness (which exist upon the fruit and consist of the three phases of birth, aging, and death) are distinguished according to their temporal stages;
since they are designated as "birth" and so forth, the two links of birth and aging-and-death are therefore provisional.
△ Section Two: The Gate of Being Either One Thing or Not One Thing.
Five [factors] are one thing, namely: ignorance, consciousness, contact, feeling, and craving. The remaining seven branches are not one thing.
△ Section Three: The Gate of the Defiled and the Non-defiled.

Three factors are exclusively defiled (namely, ignorance, craving, and grasping), because they are of the nature of affliction (*kleśa*). Seven factors are exclusively non-defiled (namely, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, birth, and aging-and-death).

Old age and death are both non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), because they are maturation fruits (*vipākaphala*). However, these seven factors, within their manifest states, can give rise to defilement;

therefore, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Chapter Ten), they are metaphorically described as comprising both the defiled and the non-defiled. The remaining two factors—the formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*)—comprise both types [the defiled and the non-defiled].
△ Section Four: The Distinct and Mixed Gates.

Ignorance, craving, and grasping are called "distinct characteristics" because they do not intermingle with the other members [of dependent origination]. The remaining members are "mixed characteristics."
"Solitary" (*du*) means "pure. As for the remaining nine being "mixed characteristics": this is because the six links already moistened [by craving] combine to constitute "existence" (*bhava*);
furthermore, the five beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) are designated by the names of "birth" (*jāti*) and so forth. △ Section on the Five Forms and Non-Forms.

Six [limbs] are exclusively mental factors (*citta-dharma*) and not material factors (*rūpa-dharma*): namely, ignorance (*avidyā*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*).
The remaining six limbs pertain to both categories of matter and mind.

△ The sixth [section] concerns the gates of the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) as the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This may also be divided into two gates:
both [the tainted] are exclusively subsumed under the conditioned because they are tainted; the untainted are unconditioned because they do not constitute factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
△ Section on the Three Natures (Svabhāva):

The three links of ignorance, craving, and grasping are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*) or obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). The link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) is exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*) or unwholesome.

The [existence] link (bhava-aṅga) is common to both the wholesome (kuśala) and the unwholesome (akuśala), as well as the non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta). The remaining seven links are exclusively non-obscured neutral;
however, within the stages (avasthā) of those seven links, both the wholesome and the defiled (kliṣṭa) also arise. Therefore, in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, they are provisionally said to be common to both.
△ Section on the Eight Elements and Bases (dhātu-bhūmi-mukha).
Although all are common to the three realms, they are either partial or complete.
"Partial" refers to one part of all [elements] in the two upper realms; "complete" refers to the desire realm. [This excludes] the Heaven of Non-conception (asaṃjñisattva-deva).
There is only the half-branch of form; the formless heavens possess only the half-branch of name;
and among the six sense bases, there is only one portion of the mind base.

The factors of the higher stages can suppress the afflictions of the lower stages; these consist of the six modes of activity, such as "suffering" and "coarse," because one generates them when seeking rebirth in those higher stages.

By means of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower stages, one initiates the practices (*caryā*) of the higher stages; by means of the practices of the higher stages, one suppresses the afflictions of the lower stages.

That is to say, one becomes weary of the suffering, coarseness, and obstruction of the lower [stages], and takes delight in the purity, excellence, and liberation of the higher [stages]. Once these practices of delight and weariness are established, one then initiates the karmic practices of the higher stages.

This may also be designated as the "Gate of the Counteractive and the Counteracted" (*pratipakṣa-pratipakṣya-mukha*). 9. The Gate of Subsumption under the Three [Categories] of Learners and Others (*śaikṣādi-traya-saṃgraha-mukha*).

All such [actions] are exclusively neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa). Because the contaminated wholesome karma (*sāsrava-kuśala-karma*) produced by noble ones (*ārya*) takes clear knowledge (*vidyā*) as its condition, it contradicts the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) and is therefore not subsumed under the links of existence.

From this, one should know that noble ones certainly do not create karma that brings about future existence (*punarbhava*), because they are no longer deluded in their pursuit of future suffering results.
Furthermore, through the mixed cultivation of dhyāna (*dhyāna-vyavakiraṇa*), they provide support for their previously accumulated inferior karma to arise.
There is no contradiction with principle regarding the Śuddhāvāsa heavens and so forth.
As for the point that it contradicts the "limbs of existence" (*bhavāṅga*): this means that a noble one (*ārya*) certainly does not create karma that brings about future existence (*punarbhava*).

Below, the text explains a difficulty. The objection states: "If that is so, then the karma cultivated through the mixed meditation (*vyavakīrṇabhāvanā*) for the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens should not be the limb of 'volitional formations' (*saṃskāra*); if it were [the limb of] formations..."
[The opponent] says: "If [the fourth dhyāna] were not a member of the path (*aṅga*), how could it induce birth in those heavens? Therefore, we now explain:

a person who has attained the fruit of non-return (*anāgāmin*) utilizes the previously cultivated fourth dhyāna—mixed with both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states—to nourish the prior karma of the three heavens of Puṇyaprasava, Vṛhatphala, and Avṛha, thereby being born in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*). It is not [the case that they are born there by means of the path-members]."
Since this karma is newly created, there is no contradiction with principle. △ Tenth, the section on what is abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) and so forth:

One interpretation holds that ignorance (*avidyā*) is abandoned solely by insight, because it must be deluded regarding the principles of the truths (*satya*) in order to be able to project [karma], and because noble ones (*ārya*) certainly do not create karma for future existence.
The two factors of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because they seek future existence and moisten rebirth.

The nine types of mind at the time of death are all associated with innate craving; as for the remaining nine factors, they are all subject to abandonment through both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
This section contains two interpretations, of which the second is the correct one; this is now the first interpretation. Regarding the nine types of death-minds:
for example, at the time of death in the desire realm, one may give rise to a mind of the desire realm, a mind of the form realm, or a mind of the formless realm.
It is the same for death in the form and formless realms. These three categories each have three, thus making nine.
There is an interpretation that all [factors] are common to both types of abandonment. This is because the treatise states regarding the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*):

"One has already abandoned one portion of all the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*)," for there is no link that is abandoned in its entirety. If the link of ignorance (*avidyā*) were abandoned only by the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*), how could it be said that the stream-enterer has not abandoned any [links] in their entirety?
If the links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) were abandoned only by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), how could it be said that they have already abandoned all links?
One part. Furthermore, that treatise states that all afflictions (*kleśa*) of an entire realm (*dhātu*) are capable of producing rebirth (*pratisandhi*).
It also states that the formations (*saṃskāra*) leading to the miserable destinies (*durgati*) are produced only by afflictions arising from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpaja*).

However, it does not say that the afflictions which moisten birth (*janma-sneha*) are exclusively abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), nor does it claim that all formations that induce future existence (*punarbhava*) are produced solely by afflictions abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*). For this reason...
It should be known that the three links of ignorance, craving, and grasping are each also subject to abandonment through both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation;
this is the second point, the correct doctrine. All afflictions of every realm are capable of linking one to rebirth:

namely, the afflictions of the desire realm link one to birth in the desire realm; the afflictions of the form realm link one to birth in the form realm; and the afflictions of the formless realm [link one to birth in the formless realm].
“Affliction” (*upāyāsa*) refers to the linking of birth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Since it is stated that the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the entire realm are capable of linking birth, and it is not said that only those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) moisten birth, we know that the two members of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) also pertain to those abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*).

Furthermore, since it is stated that only conceptual delusions (*vikalpa-kleśa*) can project action leading to the miserable destinies (*durgati*), it does not mean that all actions projecting future existence (*punarbhava*) are [only] seen [as such].
Since the afflictions to be abandoned give rise [to the formations], one knows that the single member of ignorance (*avidyā*) also extends to being abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

However, while the member of ignorance that directly gives rise to the formations leading to the miserable destinies (*durgati*) is abandoned only through seeing (*darśana-heya*), those that assist in giving rise to the formations leading to the various destinies are not fixed [as to their mode of abandonment].

The two factors of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), which directly moisten rebirth, are abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Those that assist [in moistening rebirth] are not fixed.
This clarifies that the afflictions (*kleśa*) that project karma and moisten rebirth all possess both primary and auxiliary aspects; therefore, their abandonment is likewise not fixed.
The evil destinies refer to the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and the Heaven of Non-conception, as well as other locations among the eight difficulties.

These must necessarily arise from the intensification of wholesome and unwholesome karmic actions through the discrimination of ignorance; only then can they perfume the seeds of the five fruits, such as the consciousness of the evil destinies.
Therefore, once a Srotāpanna has realized the Path, they permanently sever [rebirth in] the three miserable realms and the Heaven of Non-conception.

The seeds of the eight difficulties will never again cause one to fall into those states. Furthermore, innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*) can also assist in the production of karmic formations leading to the various realms of existence.

If it assists in producing evil karma that leads to the three miserable destinies, although it is innate, it is nonetheless abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*), because at the time of realizing the first fruit (*prathamaphala*), the gates to the three evil destinies are forever closed. [In contrast,] that which assists in producing [karma leading to] the human or celestial realms...
The "practitioner" [aspect] is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Even if one does not progress further, there are still seven more returns and goings;

therefore, it is said that the "auxiliary" [aspect] is indeterminate. The primary craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*) that nourish rebirth belong exclusively to innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*), and for this reason, they are abandoned only through cultivation.
However, the auxiliary craving and grasping that nourish rebirth are also associated with discriminative afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*).

If they belong to the category of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), they are abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*); if they belong to the category of innate [afflictions] (*sahaja*), they are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Therefore, it is also said that their "associates" (*sahāya*) are not fixed.

Furthermore, as for defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*), their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) should be abandoned; when the supramundane path (*lokottara-mārga*) which serves as their antidote (*pratipakṣa*) arises, those [defiled phenomena] are then permanently [eliminated].
Because they are abandoned: all contaminated (*sāsrava*) and non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*) phenomena are not by nature to be abandoned, because they do not contradict the [factors] of the Path.

[Question: Since it is said that they are "not by nature to be abandoned," how can it also be said that they "all pertain to both types of abandonment"? [Answer: Nevertheless, there are two senses in which they are said to be abandoned. First, because of being freed from bondage;

this means that the afflictions (*kleśa*) which take them as objects and are associated with them are abandoned (and thus they are said to be abandoned). Second, because they do not arise; this means that [the afflictions] based on conceptualization (*vikalpa*)...

Only when there is affliction (*kleśa*) does that phenomenon arise. Now, since its basis has been severed, it is rendered such that it will never arise again; therefore, it is said to be "severed. It is called "severance" in the sense of being free from bondage (*bandhana-vigama*).

It is taught that [among the twelve links], those that are contaminated but wholesome (sāsrava-kuśala)—namely, one portion of the *saṃskāra* and *bhava* links, as well as the five links beginning with *vijñāna*, and the two links of *jāti* and *jarāmaraṇa*—are non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Together, these constitute nine links.
They are abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because they are termed "abandoned" in the sense of non-arising.

It is said that among the members of the *saṃskāra* and *bhava* links, there is a portion consisting of karma that invites rebirth in the evil destinies, as well as the contaminated (*sāsrava*) meditative absorption of the *asaṃjñi-samāpatti* (which invites its fruit), and the five members beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) included within the *bhava* link. By including the cause within the effect, these are combined with birth (*jāti*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*), totaling nine members.
If, however, it is said that the twelve members are abandoned by both [vision and cultivation], this should be understood accordingly in relation to the aforementioned modes of abandonment.

This further distinguishes between what is to be abandoned by its own nature (*svabhāva-prahātavya*) and what is not to be abandoned by its own nature, thereby defining the meaning of abandonment through both insight (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*)—namely, the three links of ignorance, craving, and grasping, as well as one portion each of the formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) links—are termed "to be abandoned by their own nature" regardless of whether they are abandoned through insight or cultivation; this is because when the supramundane path first arises...

At that time, one suddenly severs the conceptual ignorance (*parikalpita-avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*), as well as unwholesome conduct (*duścarita*) and unwholesome existence (*abhava*).
When repeatedly cultivating the supramundane path, one gradually severs the innate ignorance, craving, and grasping.

Consequently, all contaminated (*sāsrava*) but non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*) factors—namely, certain portions of the wholesome within the members of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*), as well as the five members beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) and ending with birth (*jāti*) and old age (*jarā*)—are likewise severed.
The two factors of death have as their essence only the *vipāka* (maturation), being non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

They are not categorized as being abandoned by either the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*) or the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and are thus termed "not to be abandoned by nature. However, insofar as they are designated as "abandoned" based on liberation from bondage, they are subsumed under what is abandoned by cultivation.

This applies to the five factors such as wholesome conduct, wholesome existence, and the consciousness of humans and devas; specifically, it refers to the factors of birth, aging, and death for humans and devas. If, however, one considers...
Non-arising is called "cessation" (*prahāṇa*); this is comprised within what is abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*).

This includes, for example, unwholesome karma among the links of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*), as well as the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), and even the five links consisting of consciousness and so forth in the three miserable realms, the eight difficult conditions, and the heaven of non-perception, as well as the two links of birth and old age and death.
Regarding the various cessations mentioned previously, one should understand them accordingly: [these are] ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*).
Based on the explanation of the primary and auxiliary [factors], these pertain to both the abandonment through seeing (*darśana-prahāṇa*) and the abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahāṇa*).

As for the remaining factors, based on the two meanings of "separation from bondage" and "non-arising," they likewise pertain to both the abandonment through seeing and the abandonment through cultivation. This concludes the section on the ten doors of abandonment by seeing, etc. △ Eleven: The Door of Concomitance with Feeling (*vedanā-sahagata-mukha*).
Ten [factors] are associated with pleasure and equanimity (excluding the factor of sensation and the factors of old age and death).

This is because sensation does not associate with itself, and because in the state of old age and death, there is mostly an absence of pleasure and it is possible for equanimity to occur. Eleven [factors] may all be associated with painful sensation; however, they do not associate with the factor of sensation [itself].
△ Section Twelve: The Gateway of the Three Sufferings.

Eleven [links] are partially subsumed under the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*)—excluding the factors of death and old age. In the state of old age and death, pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*) is mostly absent;

since change-suffering is established based on the presence of pleasure, it is not mentioned here. Twelve [links] are partially subsumed under the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*); there is suffering within all the links.
Because of feeling (*vedanā*), the twelve [links] in their entirety are subsumed under the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

Since all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are the suffering of conditioned existence—if it is taught that they are called the suffering of conditioned existence based on the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*)—then eleven [links] in part are subsumed under the suffering of conditioned existence. This excludes the link of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), as there is no possibility of equanimity therein, as was explained above in the section on the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
The suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) has two meanings: a general sense and a specific sense.

If, with respect to all contaminated and conditioned phenomena that undergo momentary change, they are all termed the suffering of conditioned formations, then it generally encompasses the entirety of the twelve links.

However, if the suffering of conditioned formations is established solely upon the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), while the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) is established based on pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*) and the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) is established based on painful sensation (*duḥkha-vedanā*), then it specifically encompasses only a small portion of eleven links.
This is the division.
Such is the actual meaning; however, within the various holy teachings, what is taught is not fixed, as it follows the predominance of particular characteristics.
△ Thirteen: The Section on the Four Noble Truths.

All [factors] are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (these five: ignorance, craving, clinging, formations, and becoming), because they have the nature of the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*). Furthermore, five [factors] (formations and becoming) are also subsumed under the Truth of Origination.
[The members] consisting of karma (ignorance, craving, and grasping) are of the nature of affliction.
△ Fourteenth: The Gate of the Four Conditions.

When the various members are compared with one another, they definitely possess the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). As for the remaining three conditions, their presence or absence is indeterminate. [This is according to the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.]

In the Sūtras, based on the [distinction between] existence (*bhava*) and [its cause], it is said that there is only one [link]. This is because craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is viewed in relation to grasping (*upādāna*)—for craving is the seed of grasping and is capable of producing manifest grasping—and existence (*bhava*) is viewed in relation to birth (*jāti*)—for existence consists of the five factors such as consciousness (*vijñāna*), while birth refers to the actual manifestation of those same factors. Regarding the sense of being a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*):

if one asserts that the limb of consciousness is the seed of karma, then volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) also act as a causal condition for consciousness; however, if one asserts that the limb of consciousness is the seed of consciousness itself, then the limb of formations is not the direct cause of consciousness. The rest [is as previously explained].
Regarding the mutual relationship between the members [of dependent origination], there is no sense of being a causal condition (*pratyaya*).

However, when the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that ignorance (*avidyā*) has the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) as its causal condition, this is said based on the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the volitional action (*cetanā-karman*) that coexists with ignorance. Because it coexists with ignorance, the seeds of karma are metaphorically designated as "ignorance";

in reality, they are the seeds of the formative forces (it does not mean that ignorance itself is the causal condition for the formative forces). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains the mutual relationship of all the members [as follows]:...

Regarding the [conditioning] relationship (*pratyaya*), there may be three types. However, that which lacks the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is explained based on the currently active (*samudācāra*) members of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), as well as the member of existence (*bhava*) consisting solely of karmic seeds.

[The relationship of] ignorance (the currently active mental factor of delusion) to formations (the currently active mental factor of volition); craving (the currently active member) to grasping (the currently active member);

and the [mental states and factors] at the stage of birth to the [mental states and factors] at the stage of old age and death, possess the remaining two conditions—namely, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). [The relationship of] existence to birth is like that of feeling (*vedanā*) [to craving].

In relation to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), [existence] lacks the condition of immediate contiguity (*samanantara-pratyaya*) but possesses the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). As for the mutual relationship among the remaining members, they possess both the condition of immediate contiguity and the objective condition.

Neither of the two exists [as such] (there being only the predominant condition). Herein, for the time being, this is explained according to the actual dependent origination that is proximate, sequential, and non-confused;
otherwise, if these four meanings were viewed in relation to one another, their status as conditions would be indeterminate.
Those who are wise should reflect upon this in accordance with reason.
1. "Immediate" (*sāmantaka*) means not separated by an interval. 2. "In direct order" (*anuloma*) means not in reverse order. 3.
"Without confusion" means that one does not take formations (*saṃskāra*) as ignorance (*avidyā*), and so forth. 4. "Real" (*bhūta*) means not relying on a figurative or provisional explanation.
If they were viewed with an interval—as for example, viewing ignorance in relation to consciousness, or even up to aging-and-death—and if they were in reverse order...
[The relationship of] "expectation" (*āśaṃsā*), such as old age and death depending on birth, and so forth, down to formative forces (*saṃskāra*) depending on ignorance (*avidyā*).

If these were to be confused or intermingled, it would be explained by way of a provisional gate of sequential transition (*anuvartana-mukha*); the actual facts are not uniform. One may understand this by reflecting upon the principle of the four conditions (*pratyaya*) according to the preceding text.
△ Fifteen: The Gate of Subsumption under Affliction, Karma, and Suffering.

Regarding the inclusion of the twelve links within the three categories of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering: ignorance, craving, and grasping (the three branches) are subsumed under afflictions;

the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and a portion of existence (*bhava*) are subsumed under karma; and consciousness and the other [links], as well as birth, old age, and death, together with a portion of existence, are subsumed under suffering.

Where it is stated that karma fully encompasses [the members of] existence (*bhava*), one should know that this is said with reference to *karmabhava* (existence as karma), and not with reference to *janmabhava* (existence as birth).

Where it is stated that the member of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is subsumed under karma, that is because it refers to the seed of karma as the member of consciousness, and not because it refers to the seed of consciousness itself as the member of consciousness.

As for why the seven members beginning with consciousness—which are summoned by afflictions and karma—are designated solely as "suffering" (*duḥkha*), it is because they are subsumed exclusively under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) and do not extend to the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*). Furthermore, [this is so] in order to... [bring about] existence.
Because one gives rise to revulsion [and detachment] toward [the nature of] phenomena.
Second, the detailed explanation of the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*) is concluded. △ Third, the summary connecting [the exposition] to the meaning of the verse:
Since afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*) constitute the twelve members, these are able to cause the continuity of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The explanation of the third school is concluded. △ The fourth school explains through the continuity of causes and conditions in two parts:

first, the explicit clarification of the continuity of birth and death; second, the illustrative clarification of the continuity of pure dharmas. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, the heading and inquiry; second, the explanation;
third, the correlation with the verse. Now, the first section.
Furthermore, the continuity of birth and death arises from internal causes and conditions and does not depend on external conditions; therefore, there is only consciousness.

"Cause" refers to the two types of karma—outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*)—which directly induce the two kinds of birth and death (the *paricchinna* and the *pariṇāma*). Thus, they are called the cause.

"Condition" refers to the two obstacles—the afflictive (*kleśa*) and the cognitive (*jñeya*)—which assist in inducing the two kinds of birth and death. Thus, they are called the condition. Why is this so?
There are two types of birth and death.

Both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma are subsumed under the category of the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). However, because birth and death are manifested through the production [of effects] by karma, it is further termed the "cause" (*hetu*).
The rest may be understood accordingly. △ Second, the explanation has two parts. First, the explanation of *paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa* (segmented birth and death). Second...
This explains the death and rebirth of transformation.

First, regarding the death and rebirth of limited duration: this refers to the coarse maturational fruits of the three realms, which are produced by various contaminated wholesome and unwholesome karmas acting as causes, with the power of the afflictive obstacles serving as contributing conditions.
The length of one’s physical life is determined according to the force of these causes and conditions.
Because they have fixed limits, they are called "segmented" (*paricchinna*).
△ Second, the explanation of *parināma-śīti* (transformation-death) has three parts: first, the direct explanation; second, reconciling differences; third, analytical examination. Now, the first.

Second is the inconceivable death and rebirth through transformation (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*). This refers to the subtle and superior fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) produced by uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma involving conceptual differentiation, which is assisted by the power of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as its conditions.
Because life and body are transformed through the power of compassion and vows, they lack fixed limits;
thus it is called "transformation. It is that which is properly brought about and sustained by uncontaminated meditative concentration and vows, and its wondrous function is difficult to fathom.
[The commentary] states: It is named "inconceivable" (acintya).
It refers to untainted (anāsrava) karma with discernment, which is precisely conditioned untainted karma.
It transforms the body and life, meaning it changes the defiled into the pure and turns the short into the long. △ Second, reconciling differences.

Alternatively, it is called the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*), because it is produced in accordance with the intentions and vows [of great compassion]. As stated in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* by way of analogy:
"Just as, taking grasping as a condition and having tainted karma (*sāsrava-karman*) as the cause, one who continues into a future existence is born into the three realms of being;

likewise, taking the ground of the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā-bhūmi*) as a condition and having untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) as the cause, there are Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and..."
Bodhisattvas who have already attained mastery produce the three kinds of "mind-made bodies" (*manomaya-kāya*).
These are the very "mind-made bodies" mentioned in the Śrīmālā-sūtra; they are precisely what we now call the inconceivable body of transformation and change (*pariṇāmi-cyuti-bhava*).

It is also called the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body). Because the power of untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) transforms [the body] so that it differs from the original body—just as a transformation is not newly produced—it is as stated in a treatise:
(Question: "If a Śrāvaka who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) has eternally exhausted future existence (*punarbhava*), how can they realize unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*)?
(Answer: "They realize unsurpassed awakening by relying on the *nirmāṇakāya*, not the body resulting from karmic retribution (*vipākakāya*); therefore, there is no contradiction with reason."

This explains the inconceivable transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which is also called the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). This can be understood by consulting the citations from the lower part of the treatise.
The second section, "Resolving Differences," is concluded. △ Third, "Brief Analysis."

Although the continuity of birth and death is also brought about by active manifestations (*samudācāra*), it is because the seeds (*bīja*) are necessarily present that the verse speaks of them exclusively [whereas active manifestations are not necessarily present].

△ Second, the continuity of pure phenomena (*viśuddha-dharma*) is explained by analogy.

The cycle of birth and death throughout the past, present, and future does not depend on external conditions; since it arises from internal consciousness, one should know that the continuity of pure phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) is likewise so.
That is to say, since beginningless time, there have been untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) dependent upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

Through repeated perfuming (*vāsanā*) by the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and other factors, these seeds gradually increase in strength until, at the ultimate stage of attaining Buddhahood, they completely transform and abandon their original state.

The seeds of the defiled consciousness (*saṃkleśa-vijñāna*) are transformed to give rise to the pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*) of the seeds of purity. It sustains the seeds of all meritorious qualities;
by the power of its original vows, it manifests various sublime functions throughout the limits of the future, continuing without end.
From this, one should know that there is only internal consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).

Regarding the first point, "that which can universally conceptualize": what is its intrinsic nature?
This is posed as a hypothetical question to investigate its arising. There are two interpretations; the first is incorrect, while the second is correct.

According to one view, all eight consciousnesses and their associated mental factors that are subsumed under the outflows (*āsrava*) are capable of universal conceptualization, being false discrimination (*abhūtaparikalpa*).
Because it is their intrinsic nature, and because they all manifest as if they were the grasped object and the grasping subject (as stated in the Holy Teachings),
the ālayavijñāna is said to have as its object-cause (*ālambana*) the seeds of the false attachment to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The "apprehended" (*grāhya*) and the "apprehender" (*grāhaka*) are precisely the "object of cognition" (*ālambana*) and the "subject of cognition" (*ālambaka*).

This demonstrates that all eight consciousnesses are capable of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*). Following the explanation of the *ālayavijñāna*, further scriptural evidence is cited to show that the eighth consciousness is also capable of pervasive conceptualization.
Since the object of cognition is itself the seed of false attachment, the subject of cognition must necessarily also be false attachment.

There is another interpretation: regarding those mental states of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses that grasp at a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*), these are capable of universal conceptualization (*parikalpa*).

This is because the Sūtras state that only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is capable of universal conceptualization; furthermore, since "mind" (*manas*) and "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*) are designated as "mind-and-consciousness" (*mano-vijñāna*), they constitute both deliberation (*vitarka*) and discrimination (*vikalpa*), and thus are capable of universal conceptualization.

Therefore, the first five consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness are not capable of universal conceptualization. As for the grasping at a self and phenomena, it must necessarily be wisdom (*prajñā*).

Because [it is] a mental factor (*caitta*); because the two types of grasping must necessarily be accompanied by the mental factor of ignorance (*avidyā*) (the eighth consciousness is associated with the two mental factors of lack of wisdom and delusion, but it is not the universal conceptualizer);

because it is not taught that ignorance possesses a virtuous nature; and because delusion (*moha*) and non-delusion (*amoha*) are mutually incompatible (the various virtuous mental factors are not the universal conceptualizers).

Because it is not observed that there is an adherence [to a self] which guides the wisdom realizing emptiness (as in the analogy); because adherence to existence and adherence to non-existence do not arise simultaneously (thus the mental factor of *sādhu-mati* is also not the universal imputing agent);

and because there has never been an adherence that is not an impregnating cause (*vāsanā*) (the eighth consciousness is merely the object of impregnation; it certainly does not possess the two types of adherence to self and phenomena).

Furthermore, because all contaminated (*sāsrava*) minds and mental factors do not realize the true principle, they are all termed "false conceptualization" (*abhūta-parikalpa*), yet not all of them are termed the "active imputing agent."

"Not pervasive" and "not conceptualizing" refers to the first five contaminated consciousnesses and the eighth contaminated consciousness;
