The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that it is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because it serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the mind and mental factors of pervasive conceptualization. (Question: Why then is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) not the object of that [pervasive conceptualization]? (Answer: [It is not, because it is not an object of conceptualization.]

Because the real is not an object of apprehension for false conceptual attachment, even if it is spoken of in terms of a successive sequence, it may still be considered an object of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).

Although that which is thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita*) is the object of that [thoroughly imagining] mind, it lacks real self and phenomena; therefore, it is not an objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and thus it is not that which is thoroughly imagined.
Regarding the statement that "by way of successive explanation, it is also that which is thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita*)," this is like imagining a rope to be a snake;
it is precisely the imagining of the hemp as a snake. Although it is the object of that [imagination], it is not an objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

For instance, at the time one imagines a snake, a snake has never actually existed; there is only the rope. Therefore, the snake is not an objective condition, nor is it that which is thoroughly imagined. It should be understood thus.

One should know that the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of the parikalpita-svabhāva is exclusively the paratantra-svabhāva. For example, when one falsely imagines a snake, one is still imagining it with respect to a rope;

thus, the actual substance of the rope serves as the remote objective condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*), while the rope-aspect of the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna-nimitta-bhāga*) serves as the immediate objective condition (*sannikṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*).
Within this, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) falsely gives rise to the fear of a snake, which is termed "non-valid cognition" (*apramāṇa*).
This is called "thoroughly imagined attachment" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). △ Third, clarifying the thoroughly imagined nature in relation to the dependent nature:
What are the characteristics of the thoroughly imagined nature? Furthermore, how does it differ from the dependent-arising nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)?
This is also a provisional inquiry intended to provoke reflection. Its explanation has two meanings: the first meaning is incorrect, while the second meaning is correct.

According to one interpretation, the contaminated minds and mental factors (*citta* and *caitta*) comprised within the three realms, due to false habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) from beginningless time, appear as two—namely, the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) and the object-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*)—even though each is essentially one.
These are what are termed the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*). Thus, these two...

Because [the object] exists as a conceptual construction (*parikalpita*) of the mind but does not exist as a reality of the principle, these two aspects—the grasper and the grasped—are called the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the imagined nature). This refers to the aspect of the perceived (*nimitta*).

The essence that serves as the basis for these two [aspects], namely self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), truly arises in dependence upon conditions; this nature is not non-existent, and for this reason it is called the "dependent nature" (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Because it arises from the conditions of false conceptualization. How is this known to be so? Various sacred teachings state that false conceptualization is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), while the grasping of the two [subject and object] is termed the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

This delusion takes the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) as the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the two portions of the seeing and the seen (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*) as the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

According to another interpretation, all minds and mental factors— whether contaminated or uncontaminated, defiled or undefiled, mundane or supramundane— arise through the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*).
The two divisions [of appearance and seeing] are dependently originated; therefore, they are also the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Based upon these two divisions (appearance and seeing), one falsely clings to them as being determinately real—clinging to a self and phenomena, or to existence and non-existence, identity and difference, both and neither, and so forth. It is precisely these two (existence and non-existence, or identity and difference) and their like that are termed the "thoroughly imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
For various sacred teachings state that "only the measure" (*pramāṇa-mātra*) and "only the two" (*dvaya-mātra*) are all designated as the dependent nature.

Furthermore, since the treatises state that the four phenomena, such as the [three] characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and the eleven consciousnesses, etc., are all subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), this is the correct tenet of Dharmapāla.
"Both" means both existent and non-existent, or both identical and different.
"Not both" means neither existent nor non-existent, or neither identical nor different. These are the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of grasping at reality. Now...

This is termed the "thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). As for the two divisions of the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subject-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), since they originally arise from conditions, are they not the "dependent nature" (*paratantra-svabhāva*)?
Regarding the terms "only the measure" (*pramāṇa-mātra*) and "only the two," the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: first, "only the measure," because the object (*artha*) does not exist;
second, "only the two," meaning there is the consciousness of the object-aspect and the subject-aspect; third, "only the various [aspects]."

This means that various characteristics arise. Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "Only measure" (*pramāṇa-mātra*) means it is only the measure of consciousness, because the objects of cognition do not exist.
"Only two" establishes the existence of the aspect (*nimitta*) and the vision (*darśana*).
That is to say, within this single consciousness, one part constitutes the aspect and the second part constitutes the vision; these are the two divisions of the eye-consciousness and so forth.

"Only the various [aspects]" refers to this single consciousness itself. The six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) that arise from it constitute the "image-part" (*nimittabhāga*), while the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) constitutes the "seeing-part" (*darśanabhāga*).

Because the objects of the mental consciousness are not fixed, it is said to be "only the various [aspects]. Regarding the four factors such as the image-part and so forth, each mind and mental factor possesses four divisions:
namely, first, the image-part; second, the seeing-part; third, the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*); and fourth, the verifying-of-self-verifying part (*svasaṃvittisaṃvittibhāga*).

This is the section on realization (*adhigama-bhāga*). Regarding the eleven consciousnesses: first, the body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñapti*), which refers to the five internal bases (*dhātu*) such as the eye;

second, the "body-of-the-experiencer" consciousness (*kāyasya-vijñapti*), which refers to the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭa-manas*); third, the experiencer-consciousness (*vedaka-vijñapti*), which refers to the mind-base (*mano-dhātu*); fourth, the object-of-experience consciousness (*vedanīya-vijñapti*), which refers to the six external bases such as form;

fifth, the correctly experiencing consciousness (*samyag-vedaka-vijñapti*), which refers to the six consciousness-bases (*vijñāna-dhātu*); sixth, the temporal consciousness (*adhvan-vijñapti*), which refers to the uninterrupted continuity of successive births; seventh, the numerical consciousness (*saṃkhyā-vijñapti*), which refers to the calculation of "one."
...up to the immeasurable. Eighth is the consciousness of the environment, which refers to the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).

Ninth is the consciousness of verbal expression, which refers to the four kinds of verbal expression: seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. These nine arise from seeds perfumed by conventional designations (*nāma-vikalpa*).

Tenth is the consciousness of the distinction between self and others, which refers to the differentiation of bodies; this arises from seeds perfumed by the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). Eleventh is the wholesome...
The consciousness of the two evil paths of birth and death refers to the immeasurable varieties of rebirth destinies within saṃsāra;

these arise from the seeds of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*). Such consciousnesses are all described in the treatises as being subsumed under false discrimination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), and are termed the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

It is not so. The two parts—the aspect (*nimitta*) and the seeing aspect (*darśana*)—belonging to the category of subsequently attained uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) should also be designated as "thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita*).

If you accept this, then noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) would not arise by taking those two parts as its object; or alternatively, the category of wisdom that takes those two parts as its object would be the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) rather than the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).

If you do not accept that the two parts of the uncontaminated [wisdom] are thoroughly imagined, you should know that the same applies to the two parts of the contaminated [wisdom]: they too are merely dependent nature (*paratantra*).

[The nature of] arising). Furthermore, if these two parts were of the nature of the parikalpita (the imagined), they would be like a rabbit’s horns and so forth, and thus could not serve as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for ordinary beings.
This is because the substance of the parikalpita does not exist. Moreover, since these two parts would lack substantial existence, they could not infuse seeds [into the storehouse consciousness].

If no seeds were infused, then when subsequent consciousnesses and so forth arise, those two parts should not exist. Furthermore, these various habit-energies (*vāsanā*) are precisely the *nimitta* (aspect/image) of the eighth consciousness.
[If it were] subsumed [under the category of] non-existence, how could a non-existent dharma serve as the direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the manifesting consciousnesses?

Furthermore, if the internal image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) and seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) produced by conditions were not of the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), then what would be the essence that serves as the basis for these two parts?
The example should likewise be so (as both belong to the *parikalpita-svabhāva*, since both are produced from conceptual conditions), for there is no difference in cause.
This refutes the first position. The text is easily understood. The first explanation of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* is complete.

△ Second, the explanation of the *paratantra-svabhāva* has two parts: first, presenting the essence of the *paratantra* based on the preceding; second, a detailed explanation. First, [the presentation of the essence].
The aforementioned presentation of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) explains the fifth line of the verse.

According to this principle, the entities and aspects—the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subjective-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*)—of mind and mental factors produced by multiple conditions, whether contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), [are all of the dependent nature].
All are *paratantra* (dependent origination), because they arise in dependence upon various conditions.
△ Second, the specific explanation: this explains the sixth line of the verse (*vikalpa-pratyaya-ja*).

Regarding the verse’s statement that "that which is produced from conditions is conceptualized," one should understand that this refers, for the time being, to the defiled portion of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

However, the pure portion of the dependent nature may also be called the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Alternatively, all mental states and mental factors—whether defiled or pure—are termed "conceptualized" because they are capable of objective apprehension (since even subsequently attained wisdom involves conceptualization).
Thus, all defiled and pure dependent natures are included within this category of the dependent nature.

Regarding the section on "Arising and Inclusion": "The dependent nature of the pure division is also the perfected nature" refers, for example, to the four wisdoms of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and so forth.

Because these are qualities cultivated through practice, they are called the "pure dependent nature. Furthermore, because they accord with the true nature (*dharmatā*), they may also be called the "perfected real nature. This is the second interpretation.

The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is concluded. △ Third, the explanation of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) has three parts: first, the direct explanation of the actual substance and nature of the perfected;
second, clarifying its neither-identity-nor-difference from the dependent; third, clarifying that realizing this enables one to comprehend the dependent.
First, the direct explanation of the actual substance and nature of the perfected, which explains verses 7 and 8: "The perfected nature is therein / Always free from... [and so forth].

The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is so named because it is the thoroughly accomplished true nature of all phenomena, revealed by the two kinds of emptiness. It is shown to be pervasive and eternal,
its essence being non-erroneous, thereby distinguishing it from self-characteristics, common characteristics, space, and the self (*ātman*).

This first explains the meaning of the three characters *pariniṣpanna* (perfectly established). It is "perfect" (*pari*) because it is pervasive; it is "established" (*niṣpanna*) because it is eternal;

and it is called "real nature" (*sat*) because it is not false or erroneous. The self-characteristic of all phenomena refers to the conventional reality (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is the essence of phenomena free from all conceptual constructions such as names and categories—such as form, odor, taste, and touch—and so forth, each according to its own [nature].

Because they possess distinctions, they are not all-pervasive or universal. The common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena—such as impermanence, selflessness, and so forth—are those obtained through inference (*anumāna*) and constitute the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
They are revealed through names and conventions without error; however, because they are expressed by way of conceptual meanings, they are not established as eternal realities.
Space (*ākāśa*) is manifested through form (*rūpa*); it receives its name in contrast to that which possesses material obstruction (*sapratigha*).

I do not possess a truly existent intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Because it is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*) based upon the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), it is entirely false and deceptive.
Uncontaminated conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*), which are free from inversion, ultimate, and characterized by pervasive supreme function, also receive this name [of *pariniṣpanna*].
However, in the present verse, the first [meaning] is intended, not the latter.

This is the meaning of the verse that analyzes [the categories]. Uncontaminated conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*) are precisely the dependent nature of the pure portion (*śubha-āśraya-paratantra*), namely the four wisdoms of enlightenment (*catur-jñāna-bodhi*) and so forth.
Because they are free from inversion, they may be called "real" (*satya*); because they are ultimate, they may also be called "perfected" (*niṣpanna*).
Because its supreme function is all-pervasive, it may also be called "perfect" (*pariniṣpanna*).

However, the "perfectly established nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) mentioned in the verse refers only to that which is revealed by the two kinds of emptiness, and does not refer to conditioned uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*).
This [perfected nature] is that very [nature] which, upon that dependent origination, is eternally devoid of the aforementioned imagined nature.
Its essence is the suchness (tathatā) manifested by the two absences of self (pudgala- and dharma-nairātmya).

The mention of "upon that" in the verse serves to demonstrate that the perfected nature and the dependent nature are neither identical nor separate. The mention of "eternally devoid" in the verse serves to demonstrate the object of false attachment.

The nature of the apprehended object is eternally non-existent (as stated in the verse). The preceding statement [of the first line] clarifies that while the imagined nature is merely empty, the dependent nature is not empty (as stated in the verse).

The single phrase "nature" (svabhāva) reveals that the two kinds of emptiness are not themselves the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva); rather, it is that which is revealed by the two kinds of emptiness that is called the perfected nature, because suchness has a nature that is free from both existence and non-existence.
This is the correct explanation of the meaning of the seven characters "at all times far removed from that nature" (*nityaṃ tad-vivikta-svabhāvam*) within the verse. △ Second,
clarifying that [the perfected nature] is neither identical to nor different from the dependent nature (*paratantra*), which explains verses 90, 91, and 92 (therefore,
it is neither different nor not different from the dependent nature, just as with the nature of impermanence and so forth).
For the reasons stated above, this perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and that dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) are neither different nor non-different.

If one were to say they are different, then True Suchness (*tathatā*) would not be the actual nature of that [dependent nature]. If one were to say they are non-different, then this nature [the perfected] would be impermanent;

furthermore, both would then be objects that are simultaneously pure and impure, which would likewise apply to the functions of the fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms (*mūla- and prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
"There should be no distinction.
This first explains the ninth and tenth lines. That *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) pervades both the defiled and the pure;

it is the object of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). This *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature), however, is exclusively pure and not defiled; it is the object of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

Therefore, one cannot definitively state that they are not different. Viewed from this perspective, Asvaghosa’s claim that when ignorance perfumes [the mind], it is simultaneously the perfuming of True Suchness (tathatā), is based on their being different yet not different—just as when touching a wave, one touches the water entirely, yet it is not a case of absolute identity.
Dharmapāla’s claim that the ālayavijñāna receives perfuming while True Suchness is not involved, is based on their being not different yet different.
Just as when waves surge, the nature of moisture does not move; it is not a fixed difference [between them].
If one holds that *tathatā* (suchness) is a fixed reality that undergoes perfuming (*vāsanā*), then it must be subject to change; how then can it be called *tathatā*?

If one holds that *tathatā* is a fixed reality that does not undergo perfuming, then *tathatā* would not be omnipresent, and there would be various phenomena existing apart from the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena). How would this differ from the position that a portion [of reality] is non-existent?
Those non-Buddhist outsiders who hold that "a portion is eternal" and who practice two systems—how should they reflect deeply on this?
(Question: In what way are the two natures neither different nor identical? (Answer: It is like those dharmas such as impermanence and selflessness;

if one were to say that the nature of impermanence and so forth is different from the dharmas such as conditioned formations (which are subject to arising and ceasing), then those dharmas [the formations] would not be impermanent and so forth.
If one says they are not different, then this [impermanence and so forth] would not be the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of those [conditioned phenomena such as formations].

By means of this analogy, it is shown that this perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and that dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) are neither identical nor different—just as a phenomenon (*dharma*) and its true nature (*dharmatā*).
This must necessarily be so, because the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) exist only in mutual dependence.
This explains the eleventh phrase. Regarding the dharmas of impermanence, non-self, and so forth: it means that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and likewise without self.
For example, form (*rūpa*) is impermanent; feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are impermanent.

The eye is impermanent; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are impermanent. Visible forms are impermanent; sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharma*) are impermanent. Eye-consciousness is impermanent, and so on.

Up to the consciousness aggregate, all are impermanent. Being impermanent, they are without self (*anātman*). Because they are without self, they are empty (*śūnya*), impure, and subject to suffering and affliction.
Therefore, each of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) possesses its own intrinsic nature, which is termed the "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Impermanence, selflessness, suffering, emptiness, and impurity pervade all phenomena; these are termed the "common characteristics" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). These specific and common characteristics are neither identical nor different.
If one says they are definitely different, then the aggregates, bases, and elements would not be impermanent or non-self.
If one says they are definitely one, then for instance, since form and impermanence are one, sensation, perception, and so forth—being different from form—would consequently not be impermanent;
the same logic applies to other cases. Therefore, they are neither definitely one nor definitely different. Now, regarding the dependent nature and the perfected nature...
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is likewise so. The thoroughly established nature is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Since these two truths exist in mutual dependence, they are neither identical nor different.

Analogies such as waves and water, or rope and hemp, may all be applied accordingly for reflection. △ Third, the clarification of how realizing this enables the understanding of the dependent nature, which explains the second verse of the *kārikā*.
The twelve phrases [state that] it is not the case that one does not see this while seeing that.

It is not that one does not realize and see this *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) and yet can see that *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature). This is because one has not yet reached the emptiness of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature);
one does not know, as it truly is, that the dependent nature exists. Once non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) has realized suchness (*tathatā*), [the realization occurs].

It is only within the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that one is able to fully comprehend the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as being like illusory phenomena and the like.

Although from beginningless time the mind and mental factors have already been able to take their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), such as the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), as objects, because the grasping at self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-abhiniveśa*) has always accompanied them, [this comprehension does not occur prior to the subsequent attainment].
One does not know, as it truly is, that one's own mind and mental factors, induced by various conditions, are false manifestations,
like magical illusions, mirages, dreams, reflections in a mirror, shadows, echoes, the moon in water, or transformations produced by supernatural power— non-existent yet appearing to exist.

Based on this meaning, there is a verse that says: Without seeing suchness, one cannot understand that all conditioned phenomena are like magical illusions and the like—though they exist, they are not real.

Question: If one must realize and perceive *tathatā* (suchness) before fully understanding the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), then at the very first moment of practicing contemplation, one should immediately contemplate *tathatā*.

Why, then, does the *Mahāyāna-śamatha-vipaśyanā* instruct one to first contemplate the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), next the *paratantra-svabhāva*, and finally the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature)? Answer: *Tathatā* does not exist outside of the *paratantra-svabhāva*.
If a beginner contemplates *tathatā* (suchness), they will inevitably take that which is falsely conceptualized as being nameless, signless, and vast as empty space to be *tathatā*.
This then becomes a parikalpita-parikalpita (universally imputed) nature.

This ailment is most incurable, for it fails to realize that all phenomena are by their very essence devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), thereby falling into "badly grasped emptiness" (*durgṛhīta-śūnyatā*) and remaining ignorant of the true principle of emptiness that is the object of contemplation.
This is the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the sixth consciousness.

Even if an empty realm were to manifest before one at all times, provided that one does not violate the precepts nor repudiate the myriad practices, one may only be reborn among the gods of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
However, if because of seeing this emptiness one breaks the precepts and destroys right view, one will fall directly into the Avīci Great Hell. Therefore, all...
The Mahāyāna Dharma-gate causes all sentient beings to immediately observe, within the very presence of all phenomena, that they lack substantial reality.

Once they know they lack substantial reality, they understand them to be like illusions. Once they understand them to be like illusions, they awaken to their true nature. Having awakened to the true nature, [they realize...]
Only then can one give rise to function from the essence. Now, that which is forcibly observed as lacking reality is the observation of the *parikalpita* (imagined nature).

Understanding it to be like an illusion is the observation of the *paratantra* (dependent nature). Realizing its true nature is the *mūla-jñāna* (fundamental wisdom). Giving rise to function from the essence is the *prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna* (subsequently attained wisdom).
It is like using hemp to make a rope; a foolish child, lacking knowledge, falsely imagines it to be a snake. If not...
One then observes the snake as it was previously imagined according to its true nature. By what means is it known that the snake was originally non-existent?

Therefore, once the conceptualization of the snake has ceased, one subsequently knows that the rope is actually hemp. This knowledge that it is hemp is a metaphor for fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
One knows that hemp can be made into various ropes, both large and small; yet each and every rope lacks any inherent nature and is produced according to one’s will.

This serves as a metaphor for subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Therefore, it is known that there has never been a divergence between the two paths of the *Mahāyāna-śamatha-vipaśyanā* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, nor between these and the *Subtle Instructions on Contemplating the Mind*.
The first part, the detailed explanation of the verses, is concluded. △ Second, the general presentation of the meaning of the verses.
The meaning intended here is that the three natures are all inseparable from mind and mental factors—namely, the mind and mental factors themselves, as well as their manifested transformations.
Because they arise from a multitude of conditions, they are like magical illusions and the like: non-existent yet appearing to exist, deceiving and deluding the foolish.

All these are termed the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature). Upon this, the foolish superimpose the existence or non-existence, identity or difference, conjunction or non-conjunction of a self and phenomena;
like flowers in the sky and so forth, their nature and characteristics are entirely non-existent. All such [superimpositions] are termed the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).

Upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), both the self and phenomena falsely grasped therein are empty. The true nature of consciousness and so forth, which is revealed by this emptiness, is called the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Therefore, these three natures are not separate from the mind and its mental factors.
This is precisely what is meant by "one dependent nature is all dependent natures," "one imagined nature is all imagined natures," and "one perfected nature is all perfected natures.
The initial formal explanation of the verse is concluded. II. The Mutual Inclusion of Categories (in thirteen parts). 1.
Mutual inclusion with the six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). [End of section]. 13. Conclusion of the summary and indication of the extensive treatment. Now, the first part.

(Question: To what nature (*svabhāva*) are space (*ākāśa*), cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) subsumed? (Answer: All three may be subsumed [within the three natures].

If [space and so forth] are the appearances similar to space that arise from the mind and its associates, they are subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) because they arise following the mind.

If the ignorant falsely grasp these as being truly existent, this is subsumed under the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). If [they are] provisionally designated upon suchness (*tathatā*), [they are subsumed under the perfected nature].
If the objects such as space (*ākāśa*) are [unconditioned], they are subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

However, if the objects of impure minds (*sāsrava-citta*)—namely, the six unconditioned phenomena—are necessarily dependent on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*), then the objects of pure minds (*anāsrava-citta*)—namely, the six unconditioned phenomena—may be subsumed under both natures. Because they are produced by various conditions, they are subsumed under the dependent nature;
yet, because they are non-erroneous (*aviparyāsa*), they may also be subsumed under the perfected nature.
△ 2. The mutual inclusion of the three natures and the seven suchnesses.

(Question: How are these three natures mutually included within the seven suchnesses? As for the seven suchnesses: first, the suchness of phenomenal evolution (*pravṛtti-tathatā*), which refers to the true nature of the evolution of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*);
second, the suchness of the true aspect (*lakṣaṇa-tathatā*), which refers to the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*).

The reality (tattva) thus revealed is sevenfold: first, the suchness of all phenomena; second, the suchness of the nature of things; third, the suchness of representation-only, which refers to the reality of the nature of all defiled and pure phenomena as being representation-only;
fourth, the suchness of establishment, which refers to the reality of the truth of suffering; fifth, the suchness of false practice, which refers to the reality of the truth of origination;

sixth, the suchness of purification, which refers to the reality of the truth of cessation; and seventh, the suchness of correct practice, which refers to the reality of the truth of the path. (The answer says:)
These seven real natures are all subsumed under the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature), because they are the objects of both the fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms.

However, if categorized according to their specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the three types of *tathatā* (suchness) associated with the *pravṛtti* (evolving) aspect—namely, those of suffering and its origin—are subsumed under the first two natures (*parikalpita* and *paratantra*), because they involve the defilement of false attachment.
The remaining four are all subsumed under the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*.
Although there are seven names, there is only one true suchness (*tathatā*). This essence of true suchness is free from names and transcends all characteristics;

it is personally realized only by fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Based on this true essence, these seven names are established according to their distinct meanings through subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*);
therefore, they are all subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Alternatively, within the state of non-transmigration...

Deluded attachment to the cycle of transmigration falsely constitutes suffering and its origin within that which is neither suffering nor its origin; this is subsumed under the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).
Furthermore, when True Suchness (*tathatā*) remains unchanging yet follows conditions, its entire substance manifests as the various defiled phenomena of transmigration, suffering, and its origin;
this is subsumed under the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature). △ Third, the mutual inclusion of these with the six dharmas.
(Question: How are the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) subsumed within the six phenomena (*ṣaḍdharma*)? (Answer: Within those six phenomena, all three natures are fully present.
This is because form, sensation, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) all possess the nature of false attachment, dependent origination, and reality.

The six phenomena consist of the five aggregates and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). The false attachment to these six phenomena is the nature of universal imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);

the six phenomena arising through conditions are the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*); and the principle upon which these six phenomena depend is the nature of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

△ 4. The Mutual Inclusion of the Four and the Five Subjects (i.e., the five dharmas: 1. *lakṣaṇa* [characteristic]; 2. *nāman* [name]; 3. *vikalpa* [discrimination], also called *parikalpita* [false imagination]; 4. *samyagjñāna* [correct wisdom]; 5. *tathatā* [suchness], also called *tathatā* [thusness]).
(Question: How are the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) subsumed within the five categories (*pañcavastu*)? (Answer: The various sacred teachings state that their mutual subsumption is not fixed.

That is to say, in some places it is said that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) subsumes those [categories of] characteristics (*nimitta*), names (*nāman*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*); the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) subsumes true suchness (*tathatā*);

and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not subsume the five categories. This is because that [imagined nature] refers to the transformation of contaminated mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
That which resembles the signified is called the "characteristic" (*nimitta*); that which appears resembling the signifier is designated as the "name" (*nāman*).

The mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that undergo transformation are established as "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*). Because untainted minds and mental factors are free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), they are collectively termed "correct gnosis" (*samyagjñāna*).
It is not said that the signifier and the signified (above) [are included]. All four [factors] arise from conditions and are all subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Alternatively, in some places it is stated that the dependent nature subsumes the grasped aspect (*nimitta*) and the conceptualization (*vikalpa*), while the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) subsumes only their names.

Correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*) are subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). That [text] states that the "aspects" (*nimitta*) of the contaminated mind and mental factors are called the "aspect," and the remainder...

(The aspect of seeing and the substance of the transformative consciousness) are both termed "discrimination. Because that which is grasped through pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) has no substance whatsoever, in order to manifest its non-existence, it is merely designated by the name [of "name" itself].
Because they are non-erroneous, the two [aspects] are subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). In some places, it is said:

The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) comprises only the conceptualizing mind (*vikalpa*). The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) comprises its images (*nimitta*) and names (*nāman*). Correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*) are comprised within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

That [text] explains that the objective and subjective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga* and *darśana-bhāga*) of contaminated minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are collectively termed "conceptualization."

Because its intrinsic nature consists of false conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpa*), the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*)—which are the objects of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*)—are established as the two entities of "name" (*nāman*) and "characteristic" (*nimitta*) in accordance with conventional cognition.
Furthermore, there are passages stating that the name belongs to the dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*), while the meaning (or characteristic) belongs to the thoroughly imagined nature.

That [teaching] explains that the objective and subjective aspects (*grāhyagrāhakabhāga*) of the contaminated mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) are established as such through the power of names.

Because it is a pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*), it is called "name" (*nāman*). It is because one universally clings to that which is grasped (*parikalpya*) by following after names and arbitrarily conceptualizing their essence—that the essence is in fact non-existent.

Therefore, the name for the characteristics of the referent (*artha*) is established as a mere designation. Although the phrasing of these five things (*pañcavastu*) taught in various sacred scriptures (*āgama*) differs, their meaning is not contradictory.
However, the initial presentation is particularly excellent as it avoids confusion, as in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
The detailed exposition should be understood as follows.

△ Five: The Mutual Inclusion of the Five Characteristics (1. the characteristic of that which is signified; 2. the characteristic of that which signifies; 3. the characteristic of the relationship between these two; 4. the characteristic of being grasped through attachment; 5. the characteristic of non-attachment).
(Question: Furthermore, it is stated in the holy teachings that there are five characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). How do these relate to the inclusion within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*)? (Answer:

Both the signified (*lakṣya*) and the signifier (*lakṣaṇa*) each possess the three natures. That is to say: that which is falsely conceptualized belongs to the inclusion of the first nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

The signified and signifier of "characteristics, names, and discrimination," according to their respective applications, belong to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). True suchness (*tathatā*) and correct gnosis (*samyagjñāna*), according to their respective... [text ends]

The object to be expressed (*vācya*), the expression (*vācaka*), and that which belongs to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) [are so designated] because the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) manifests as the semblance of the expression when teaching the Dharma to others.
The characteristic of mutual dependence belongs exclusively to the first nature (the imagined nature), because it consists of the false attachment to the fixed relationship between object and name.

The characteristic of being grasped belongs exclusively to the dependent nature, because its intrinsic nature is false conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*). The characteristic of non-grasping belongs exclusively to the perfected nature.
It is established as such, because its intrinsic nature consists of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and so forth.
Six: The Subsumption of the Four Realities (1. Reality established by worldly consensus; 2. Reality established by reasoning; 3.
Reality as the object of knowledge purified of the afflictive obscurations; 4. Reality as the object of knowledge purified of the cognitive obscurations).
(Question: Furthermore, it is taught in the holy scriptures that there are four kinds of reality (*tattva*). How are these subsumed under the three natures (*trisvabhāva*)? (Answer:

The reality established by worldly convention (*loka-prasiddha-tattva*) is subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because it is comprised of the three factors [of name, appearance, and conceptualization]—namely, the afflictions and the objects of knowledge.

The reality that is the object of the purified wisdom of the two obstacles (*kleśa-jñeya-āvaraṇa-viśuddhi-jñāna-gocara-tattva*) is subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because it is comprised of the two factors [of correct cognition and suchness]. Thus it is stated in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*.
The first (worldly) reality is explained as being comprised solely of the first nature (the imagined), because it is that which is commonly grasped. The second (logical) reality...

They generally pertain to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*), because the principle [of reality] encompasses both the grasping and non-grasping, as well as the defiled and the pure. Regarding the latter two realities, they pertain exclusively to the third nature;

however, both interpretations are applicable. As for the second [truth] pertaining to all three natures: from the perspective of the principle of grasping, it belongs to the *parikalpita* (imagined) nature; from the perspective of non-grasping...
Thus, the defiled [nature] belongs to the dependent [nature], while the pure [nature] belongs to the perfected [nature]. △ Seventh:
The inclusion within the Four Noble Truths (suffering, origin, cessation, and the path).
(Question: How are the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) subsumed within the four truths (*catuḥsatya*)? (Answer: Each of the four [truths] possesses all three natures.

For instance, within the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), each of the four aspects of contemplation—impermanence and so forth—possesses its own three natures. Regarding the three types of impermanence:

first, impermanence as the absence of nature (*abhāva-anityatā*), because its nature is eternally non-existent (*parikalpita*); second, impermanence as arising and ceasing (*utpāda-vyaya-anityatā*), because it has birth and death (*pariniṣpanna*); third, impermanence as defilement and purity (*saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-anityatā*).
Impermanence: because there is transformation within the stages (*pariniṣpanna*). Regarding the three types of suffering:

first, observing that the grasped (the five aggregates) is suffering, because it is the basis for grasping at the two attachments to self and phenomena (*parikalpita*); second, because the phenomenal characteristics of conditioned things are themselves suffering (*paratantra*);
third, because the characteristics of suffering are themselves suffering, meaning that True Suchness is conjoined with suffering (*pariniṣpanna*). Regarding the three types of emptiness: first—

1. Contemplating the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*) refers to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the imagined nature), because its nature does not exist. 2. Contemplating the emptiness of other-nature (*anya-bhāva-śūnyatā*) refers to the *paratantra-dharma* (the dependent nature), because it is different from the self-nature falsely grasped.

3. Contemplating the emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) refers to the *pariniṣpanna* (the perfected nature), because its self-nature is *tathatā* (suchness) as revealed by the two [preceding] emptinesses.

Regarding the three kinds of selflessness (*anātman*): 1. Contemplating the selflessness of signlessness (*animitta-anātman*) refers to the *parikalpita-svabhāva*, because the characteristic of a self is absent.

Therefore, there are two [aspects of observing the dependent nature]: (1) the absence of self in terms of differing characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-nairātmya*), which means it differs from the characteristics of the self as falsely grasped;

and (2) the absence of self in terms of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-nairātmya*), which means that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)—namely, suchness (*tathatā*) revealed by the absence of self—is its own characteristic. Regarding the three aspects of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*):

first is the collection of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-samudaya*), which refers to the habitual tendencies of the grasping at the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as apprehended by the mind of universal conceptualization (*parikalpa*). This is grasping.

Because of those latencies (*vāsanā*), the name "accumulation of latencies" is provisionally established. Second is the accumulation of origination, which refers to karma and afflictions (i.e., the *paratantra-svabhāva*).

Third is the accumulation of non-separation from fetters, which refers to suchness that has not yet abandoned its obstructions (i.e., the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Regarding the three aspects of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*):

first is cessation by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-nirodha*), because [the *parikalpita*] is inherently unarisen. Second is the cessation of the two graspings, which refers to [cessation through] the wisdom of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Third is...
Because the two graspings of subject and object do not arise; third, because of essential extinction, as the nature of emptiness and true suchness is fundamentally quiescent.
Regarding the three aspects of the Truth of the Path: first, the path of universal knowledge, which is able to know that the nature of the imputed is empty;

second, the path of permanent abandonment, which is able to abandon the defiled portion of the dependent nature; third, the path of realization, which is able to realize the perfected nature. Furthermore, the path of universal knowledge also...
These correspond respectively to the two [natures] of the subsequent [section] (the dependent and the perfected), and to the three natures of the seven [categories].
One should understand, according to reason, whether the three natures assigned here are provisional or real.
"Thoroughly knowing the path also extends to the latter two" means that one who has attained complete penetration regarding all three natures (trisvabhāva) is said to "thoroughly know the path.
"The seven triads" refers to the four modes of contemplation regarding the truth of suffering, as well as the three truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
Each of these seven [categories] has three phrases. To explain them by assigning them respectively:

the first phrase in each belongs to the *parikalpita* (imagined nature), the second phrase belongs to the *paratantra* (dependent nature), and the third phrase belongs to the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature). Regarding "whether provisional or real":

This refers to the three natures (trisvabhāva) of the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*), which are assigned strictly according to their substantial reality. As for the remaining six truths, their three natures may be designated metaphorically.
△ Eight: The mutual inclusion of the [eight] liberations and the [three] gates of liberation.
(Question: How are the spheres of activity of the three gates of liberation subsumed within these three natures? (Answer: In principle, they all pertain to all three;

however, according to their specific characteristics, each corresponds to one. One should understand that emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apranihita*), and signlessness (*animitta*) correspond respectively [to the imagined, dependent, and perfected natures].

The gate of liberation of emptiness is the knowledge that the imputed nature is empty. The gate of liberation of wishlessness is the absence of any aspiration or seeking regarding phenomena of the dependent nature.
The gate of liberation of signlessness is the realization of the perfected nature, which is free from the signs of existence and non-existence.

Based on this, there further arise three types of the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*): first, the patience regarding the non-arising of intrinsic nature (because self and phenomena are fundamentally non-existent);

second, the patience regarding the non-arising of spontaneity (because dependent origination is without agency); and third, the patience regarding the non-arising of afflictions and suffering (because they ultimately do not arise).
These three [patiences] correspond respectively to those [three liberations], as they are their respective objects.
△ 9. The Subsumption by the Two Truths.

(Question: How are these three natures subsumed within those two truths (the ultimate and the conventional)? (Answer: It should be understood that the conventional truth possesses all three of these natures.

The ultimate truth (paramārtha) is exclusively the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva). There are three types of conventional truth (saṃvṛti): first, the conventional of designation (prajñapti-saṃvṛti), such as an army or a forest, which exist merely as provisional names.
Second is the conventional of practice (such as the aggregates, bases, and elements; it is also called the conventional of reasoning because it arises and ceases according to conditions).

Third is the conventional of clear manifestation (that is, the conventional of designation, because true suchness is designated by subsequently attained wisdom). These should be understood respectively as the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). There are three types of ultimate (*paramārtha*):
first, the ultimate of principle (*artha*), which refers to true suchness, because it is the most supreme object (*artha*) of principle. Second, the ultimate of attainment, which refers to nirvāṇa.

Because "ultimate" (*paramārtha*) means "supreme" (*parama*). Third is the ultimate as the object of realization (*prāpti-paramārtha*), namely the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), because it is supreme and is the object (*artha*).
These three types of ultimate are, as appropriate, all subsumed within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because they are unchanging and non-erroneous.
△ Ten: The Objects of Wisdom for Ordinary Beings and Sages.

(Question: Regarding these three natures, by which wisdoms are they traversed? (Answer: That which is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is entirely not an object of wisdom, because it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and thus cannot function as an objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Nevertheless, foolish worldlings (*bāla*) falsely cling to it as existing, whereas the noble ones (*ārya*) realize its fundamental non-existence.

It may also be described as the cognitive domain of both ordinary and noble beings. The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is the object of the two types of cognition belonging to both ordinary and noble beings, whereas the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is exclusively the cognitive domain of the noble ones.
△ 11. The Distinction between the Provisional and the Real. (Question:
Among these three natures, how many are provisional and how many are real? (Answer: Because the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) is falsely established, it may be said to be provisional;
because it lacks any substantial essence or characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it may also be said to be neither provisional nor real. The *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) is real.

There is the conventional (prajñapti). Because it is of the nature of a collection, a continuity, or a specific state, it is said to exist conventionally. Mind, mental factors, and matter are said to exist substantially because they arise from conditions.
If substantial dharmas did not exist, conventional dharmas would also not exist, because the conventional is designated based on substantial causes.
The perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) exists only substantially, because it is not designated in dependence upon other conditions.

"Aggregation" refers to the collective characteristics of the sense faculties, the body, and the vessel-world (the environment). "Continuity" refers to the characteristic of the uninterrupted succession of the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
"States" refers to the twenty-four types of formations dissociated from thought (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

Since none of these possess a separate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are termed "provisional. "Mind" refers to the eight consciousnesses as the sovereign minds (*citta-rāja*). "Mental factors" refers to the five... [text truncated]
The eleven mental factors (*caitta-dharma*). As for "form" (*rūpa*), it refers to the eleven types of form-dharmas consisting of the five sense-faculties and the six sense-objects.
Because they arise from seeds as manifest phenomena in the present moment, they are termed "real. Based upon these real minds, mental factors, and forms...
There is, however, a state of similarity through aggregation; therefore, it is said that the provisional is designated based upon real causes. Question:
In the second fascicle, you already refuted the claim that provisional designations depend on the real. Why do you now say that the provisional depends on what is substantially existent? Answer:
External phenomena truly existing apart from the mind are definitively non-existent; therefore, metaphorical designations do not necessarily depend upon a real basis.

Now, regarding all phenomena manifested by consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), some are real and some are metaphorical. The real corresponds to the conventional truth of principle (*yukti-saṃvṛti*), while the metaphorical corresponds to the conventional truth of designation (*prajñapti-saṃvṛti*).
Thus, there must first be the real for there to be the metaphorical; yet whether metaphorical or real, they are both termed conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
This is not like the real dharmas external to the mind as clung to by non-Buddhists and those of other vehicles. Question:

Previously it was said that the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) exist in mutual dependence; now it is said that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is not established based on other conditions.
How can these two statements be reconciled? Answer: Without relying upon the conventional, the name "ultimate" would not be established. Therefore, it is said that they are mutually dependent.
It exists dependently; for example, it is because water exists that waves can exist, and because there is the movement of waves that water is described as being "still.
However, one may only say that waves exist because of water, but one cannot say that water exists because of waves.
Therefore, the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) is not established based upon the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature). △ 12. Analysis of Difference and Non-difference.
(Question: Are these three natures different, or are they not different? (Answer: It is taught that they are neither. They are not different because they lack separate substantial entities;
yet they are not non-different because the objects of false attachment and the true meaning of dependent origination are distinct for each of the three.

This very inconceivable essence of reality, when grasped through deluded attachment, becomes the *parikalpita* (imagined nature); when arising in accordance with conditions, it becomes the *paratantra* (dependent nature);
and from the perspective of ultimate truth, it is the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature). Therefore, the five stages and one hundred dharmas of the ten dharma-realms are all *paratantra*.
To grasp these five stages and one hundred dharmas of the ten dharma-realms as a self or as substantial reality is [the imagined nature].
All real dharmas are the *parikalpita* (the imagined). The true meaning of the ten dharma-realms, the five stages, and the hundred dharmas is entirely the *pariniṣpanna* (the perfected).
The true source of nature and characteristics is hereby presented in its entirety. May readers reflect upon this with deep thought. △ Thirteen:
Concluding the Brief Exposition and Pointing toward the Extensive.
These three natures have infinite categories of meaning; fearing that excessive detail would weary the reader, I have briefly indicated the essential framework.

Within the section on resolving the difficulty regarding the three natures as being contrary to the sūtras, the first part—concluding the formal explanation that the three natures are not separate from consciousness—is finished.
