This is because one enters the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) by depending on this most excellent basis; thus, it relies solely on the wholesome states of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The body arises [in this state] because, within the other realms and destinies, the wisdom-mind and the mind of wearying detachment are not particularly sublime.

This stage is also subsumed under the Stage of Practice through Understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), as one has not yet realized the true ultimate reality of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*).

The "fortunate realms" (*sugati*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) refers to devas, humans, and asuras. However, while the asuras are currently in a state of anger and the devas are in the midst of pleasure, it is only the human path that is particularly capable [of this].
By means of a body belonging to a fortunate realm, one attains the fundamental fourth dhyāna.
Within the four dhyānas, one must simultaneously seal both types of emptiness in order to induce the true path of seeing and touch upon the non-established truths (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*).
If one is in the miserable realms (*apāya*), there is aversion but no superior wisdom; if one is in the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) heavens, there is wisdom but no superior aversion;
and if one is in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) heavens, there is neither wisdom nor aversion. Therefore, none of these [states] are capable [of inducing the path].

Thus these roots of goodness are accomplished. This concludes the second section, the explanation of the stage of application (*prayoga*). △ Third, the explanation of the stage of penetration (*prativedha*).
Part one: the citation of the verse; part two: the commentary’s explanation. Now, the first.

Next is the stage of thorough penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*). What are its characteristics? The verse says: "When, with respect to the object of cognition, wisdom perceives nothing at all, at that time one abides in representation-only (*vijñapti-mātra*), because one is free from the characteristics of the two graspings."

△ Second, the commentary on the treatise has two parts: first, a brief explanation; second, an extensive explanation. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, a general explanation of the verse text;
second, a detailed analysis of the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Now, the first section.

The Treatise says: When a bodhisattva, regarding the objects of perception, possesses non-conceptual wisdom that attains nothing at all—because it does not grasp at the various signs of conceptual proliferation—it is then said to truly abide in the ultimate nature of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*). This is the realization of *tathatā* (suchness).
Wisdom and suchness are equal and identical, for both are free from the characteristics of the grasper and the grasped. Because... [it is able to...]
The characteristics of the grasped and the grasper are both manifestations of the conceptual proliferation of a mind that possesses the notion of attainment.
There is no suchness external to wisdom that is realized by wisdom; there is no wisdom external to suchness that can realize suchness.
Therefore, it is said to be "equally equal. Both are free from the characteristics of the dual grasping of subject and object, and thus differ from a mind that possesses the notion of attainment.

This refers to the appearances manifested by the conceptual proliferation of discrimination. △ Second, the specific explanation of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). There are three schools of interpretation;
the first two meanings are incorrect, while the third meaning is correct.

One interpretation holds that this wisdom lacks both the objective (nimitta-bhāga) and subjective (darśana-bhāga) aspects, because it is taught to be devoid of the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper.

Another interpretation holds that this wisdom possesses both the objective and subjective aspects; for it is only by arising while bearing the aspect of that [Tathatā] that it is designated as "taking Tathatā as its object.

If one could be said to take Tathatā as its object without bearing its aspect, then a cognition of form and so forth (even though it lacks the aspect of sound and so on) would also have to be called "sound."

Regarding conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*): if it lacked a seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*), it would be unable to take an object. How then could it be said to be knowledge that takes suchness as its object?
One must not allow that the nature of suchness itself is also called a "grasper" (*ālambaka*). Therefore, one must admit that this knowledge definitely possesses a seeing portion.
This wisdom is precisely the fundamental wisdom of non-apprehension. The first refers to the absence of both the perceived object and the perceiving subject;
the second refers to the presence of both the perceived object and the perceiving subject. Both may be understood according to the text.

There is an interpretation that this [fundamental wisdom] possesses the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) but lacks the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect). It is said that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is "without aspect" (*animitta*) because it is apprehended by means of non-apprehension.
Although the *darśana-bhāga* exists, because it lacks conceptualization (*vikalpa*)—specifically the retrospective and deliberative types—it is described in the verse as "not an apprehender.

This does not mean that the apprehension of the *darśana-bhāga* is entirely absent. Furthermore, although the *nimitta-bhāga* is absent, it can be said that this fundamental, ultimate wisdom carries the essence of True Suchness.

[The aspects] arise together [by means of this wisdom]. Because it is not separate from suchness (the analogy), just as when the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) takes the seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object, it is a direct realization and does not take it as a transformed aspect (*pariṇāma*).
This [wisdom of suchness] must likewise be so. If it were to take [its object] as a transformed aspect, it would not be a direct realization;

like subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), it would necessarily involve conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Therefore, one must admit that this [fundamental, ultimate wisdom] has the seeing portion but lacks [the aspectual portion].
[This is] the characteristic. This is the third correct meaning. Although there is the "seeing portion" (darśana-bhāga) [below], it explains the objection. That is to say, an objection is raised:

"Since there is already a seeing portion, why does the verse state that it is not the 'appropriator' (grāhaka)? The answer and explanation are clear. Although there is no "characterized portion" (nimitta-bhāga) [below],...
Dispelling Doubts: It is said that some may have the following doubt: "If there is no objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*), then there should be no object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).

If there is no object, how can there be a solitary subjective cognizer? The explanation states: This is a case of "carrying along" (*sahānubandha*), not a case of "transforming and carrying" (*pariṇāmānubandha*).

Carrying along the essence and characteristics constitutes the object-condition; because it does not transform into a specific form, it is not the objective aspect. It is just like the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).

The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is taken as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), yet because it does not undergo transformation or carry [the image], it is not called the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).

If one were to transform the image-part of *tathatā* (suchness) and take it as an object, that would be the subsequently attained wisdom with conceptualization (*prsthalabdha-savikalpa-jñāna*), and not this fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*mūla-nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The brief explanation is concluded. △ Second, the detailed explanation has two parts: first, explaining the name of the stage; second, explaining the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).
First: at the moment immediately following the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), when this non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) arises, its essence realizes and accords with suchness (*tathatā*).

This is called the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*), because it is the first stage in which the principle [of reality] is illuminated; for this reason, it is also called the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
△ Second, the explanation of the path of seeing, which has three parts: first, the general presentation; second, the detailed explanation; third, the conclusion on the benefits. Now, the first:
This path of seeing, briefly stated, is of two kinds.

△ Second, the detailed explanation has two parts: first, the explanation of the two paths of seeing; second, the subsumption of the six clear realizations (*abhisamaya*). In the first part, there are two sections: first, the explanation of the meaning of the two paths;

second, the distinction between the two paths. In the first of these, there are again two sections: first, the explanation of the true path of seeing (*tattvadarśanamārga*); second, the explanation of the semblance path of seeing (*pratibhāsadarśanamārga*). This is the first.

First is the true path of vision (*darśana-mārga*). This refers to the aforementioned non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which directly realizes the ultimate truth revealed by the two kinds of emptiness and truly severs the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two obstacles associated with conceptualization.
Although it requires many moments for the task to be fully accomplished, it is designated as a single stage because its characteristics are uniform.

Regarding the general exposition of the single mind, there is one interpretation: herein, the two emptinesses and the two obstacles are realized and abandoned gradually, because there are differences in their depth and coarseness.

There is another interpretation: herein, the two emptinesses and the two obstacles are realized and abandoned instantaneously, because the power of the aspirational intention possesses such capability.

Regarding the phrase "because they are equal": this means that from beginning to end, one contemplates only the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*), which differs from the characteristics of the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the eight truths—superior and inferior—that are contemplated by the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Concerning the two meanings of gradual and sudden, the sudden meaning is the correct one.

The initial mention of "gradual" refers to the fact that the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is shallow and is thus realized first, whereas the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is deep and is thus realized later; furthermore, the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are coarse.

Therefore, the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are abandoned first; because they are subtle, they are abandoned later. Next, regarding the term "sudden": it is because, through the resolute intention for great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*), one possesses the capacity [to abandon them simultaneously].
△ Second, the explanation of the characteristics of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) has two parts:

first, the formal explanation of the Path of Vision; second, the conclusion showing that it is merely a provisional designation. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the heading; second, the explanation. Now, the first:
Second, the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*). This, in turn, has two parts:
△ Second, explaining it as twofold. First, explaining the three types of mind that contemplate the non-established truths (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*);
second, explaining the sixteen moments of mind that take the established truths (*pratiṣṭhita-satya*) as their object. Now, the first.
First is the contemplation of the non-established truths (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*). There are three grades of mind: 1.

The wisdom that takes the internal body as its object and eliminates the conceptualization of a "sentient being" (*sattva-prajñapti*) is able to eliminate the soft-grade latent tendencies of discrimination (*vikalpa-anuśaya*). 2.

The wisdom that takes internal phenomena (*dharma*) as its object and eliminates the conceptualization of "phenomena" (*dharma-prajñapti*) is able to eliminate the medium-grade latent tendencies of discrimination. 3. [The wisdom] that universally eliminates all sentient beings...

The wisdom that [realizes] all phenomena as being dependently originated can eliminate all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of conceptual construction. The first two are termed "dharma-knowledge" (*dharmajñāna*) because they take their objects individually;

the third is termed "subsequent knowledge" (*anvayajñāna*) because it takes its objects collectively (this is the model). Within the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the uninterrupted and liberated paths (*ānantaryamārga* and *vimuktimārga*) regarding the specific and general aspects of the two types of emptiness—which sever their respective obstacles—are established;
this is called the "path of seeing in terms of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇadarśanamārga*).
Non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*) is precisely suchness (*tathatā*). "Provisional conditions" refers to the conditions of provisional designations that lack intrinsic substance.

"Mild grade" refers to the inferior grade, spoken of solely in relation to the clinging to a self (*ātma-grāha*). "Medium grade" refers solely to the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). "All" refers to both types of clinging combined.
"Those of the same category as wisdom" refers to the subsequent manifestations of the two aforementioned wisdoms; they are so called because they emulate the [unconditioned].

The first two [stages] are established because they sever the two obstacles separately via the intervening paths (*antara-mārga*). The third is established because it severs the two obstacles collectively via the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*);

this is precisely the subsequently attained wisdom with conceptual differentiation (*prsthalabdha-savikalpa-jñāna*), and is therefore called the "Path of Vision with Aspects" (*sākāra-darśana-mārga*).
One interpretation holds that these three constitute the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because the path of seeing with images (*sākāra-darśanamārga*) takes the four truths as its objects.
Another interpretation holds that these three constitute the path of seeing with images, because the true path of seeing does not take [the truths] as distinct objects.
There are two interpretations for judging these three types of knowledge (*jñāna*); the latter interpretation is the correct one.

△ Second, the explanation of the sixteen moments of mind regarding the conventionally established truths (*prajñaptisatya*) also has three parts: first, the restatement of the two types; second, the individual explanation of the two types;
third, the conclusion that they constitute nine moments of mind. Now, the first part.
The second [category] consists of the sixteen moments of mind that take the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*) as their object.
This, in turn, has two parts: first, establishment based on the grasped and the grasper;
second, establishment based on the lower and higher realms of truth. Now, the first.
First, based on the observation of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), sixteen distinct types of mind are established in terms of their dharmas and categories.
That is to say, regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), there are four types of mind: first, the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*).

This refers to the contemplation of the suchness (*tathatā*) of the Truth of Suffering within the three realms, which correctly abandons the twenty-eight types of conceptual proclivities (*vikalpānuśaya*) to be abandoned at the time of seeing the Truth of Suffering within the three realms.
The object of apprehension (*grāhya*) is suchness (*tathatā*); the subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*) is correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*).

Because there are the patience regarding the dharma of the four truths (*catur-āryasatya-dharma-kṣānti*), the knowledge regarding the dharma of the four truths (*catur-āryasatya-dharma-jñāna*), the subsequent patience regarding the four truths (*catur-āryasatya-anvaya-kṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge regarding the four truths (*catur-āryasatya-anvaya-jñāna*), they are called the sixteen types of minds of dharma and subsequent [knowledge].

To speak of them specifically in terms of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*): "suffering" refers to the truth; "dharma" refers to suchness; and "knowledge" refers to the contaminated wisdom of the preparatory stage (*prayoga-mārga*).
Furthermore, "patience" (kṣānti) refers to the uninterrupted and untainted patience (*anantarya-anāsrava-kṣānti*). As for the twenty-eight types:
there are ten afflictions in the desire realm, and nine afflictions each in the form and formless realms, with anger excluded from both.

Second is the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*). This refers to the contemplation of the aforementioned suchness immediately following the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), whereby one realizes liberation from the afflictions previously abandoned.
"Dharma" here also refers to suchness; "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to untainted liberation (*anāsrava-vimukti*).

3. The Receptivity to the Subsequent Knowledge of Suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*): This refers to the arising of untainted wisdom immediately following the aforementioned [Dharma] Knowledge, wherein one internally realizes each of the Dharma-receptivities and Dharma-knowledges individually.

It is said that after these two moments of mind—the Dharma-receptivity and the Dharma-knowledge—up to all the noble dharmas of the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*), they are all of this same category.

4. The Subsequent Knowledge of Suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*): This refers to the arising of untainted knowledge immediately following this [receptivity], which definitively confirms and validates the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering.
Just as there are four types of mind regarding the Truth of Suffering, it should be understood that the same applies to the Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path.

These sixteen minds (consisting of the fourfold sets of Dharma-patience and Dharma-knowledge) observe True Suchness (tathatā) through eight types of anvaya-kṣānti and anvaya-jñāna; they observe Correct Knowledge (samyag-jñāna) through the other eight types. This is the model.

Within the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga), these are established through the distinctions of the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga), the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga), the seeing-portion (darśana-bhāga), and the self-verifying portion (svasaṃvedana-bhāga). This is termed the "aspectual seeing" (lakṣaṇa-darśana).
The Path refers to the four dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*), which are established according to the vision of the true uninterrupted path (*anantaryamārga*).

The four dharma-knowledge (*dharmanirvedha*) are established according to the vision of the true path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*). The four subsequent patience (*anvayakṣānti*) all emulate the self-nature of the true uninterrupted path.
The establishment based on realization consists of the four types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*); all are modeled after the self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*) of the true path of liberation.
△ Second, the establishment based on the objects of the lower and upper truths.
Second, based on the contemplation of the lower and higher truths (*satya*), sixteen distinct types of mind—comprising both phenomena (*dharma*) and categories (*anvaya*)—are established.

That is to say, when contemplating the four truths such as suffering (*duḥkha*) within both the manifest and non-manifest realms, there are two types of mind for each: first, the patience of clear realization (*abhisamayakṣānti*); second, the wisdom of clear realization (*abhisamayajñāna*).

In accordance with what is appropriate (as an emulation), within the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) and liberated (*vimukti*) aspects of the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) contemplate the truths (*satya*).
This severing of the one hundred and twelve types of conceptual proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by seeing is called the "path of seeing in terms of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-darśanamārga*).

The "lower" refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), which is called the "manifest realm. Based on the Four Noble Truths of this realm, the four *dharmakṣāntis* (receptivities to the dharma) and the four *dharmajñānas* (knowledges of the dharma) are established.

The "upper" refers to the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*), which are called the "non-manifest realm. Based on the Four Noble Truths of those realms, the four *anvayakṣāntis* (subsequent receptivities) and the four *anvayajñānas* (subsequent knowledges) are established.

The "receptivity of clear observation" (*abhisamayakṣānti*) is the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*). Regarding these, there are [receptivities] for each of the lower and upper [realms].
Regarding the Four Truths, there are thus eight patiences (*kṣānti*). The wisdom of clear observation (*abhisamaya-jñāna*) is itself the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Based on each of the four truths in both the lower and upper realms, there are eight knowledges (*jñāna*). The one hundred and twelve distinct latent dispositions (*anuśaya-vikalpa*) are the seeds of the fundamental afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the three realms.
This concludes the second section: the detailed explanation of the two types. △ Third, the summary into nine minds.
If one follows the principle of the extensive dissemination of the holy teachings, it is said that the path of insight (*darśanamārga*) consists of nine moments of mind.
This is established based on the previous two sets of sixteen types of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) directed toward the established truths (*vyavasthāpitasatya*).

That is to say, when the forbearances (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) of the categories of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) are combined into one, there are four insights each for the lower and upper realms, totaling eight moments of mind. These are the eight aspects of insight.

It should be understood that these are collectively explained as one [pair] (the combined exposition of śamatha and vipaśyanā; thus there are nine types). Although śamatha and vipaśyanā are necessarily practiced in tandem within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), [they are distinguished here].

Regarding the realization of the meaning (*artha*), contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) accords with it rather than cessation (*śamatha*). Therefore, this contemplation and cessation differ in their opening and closing. By means of these nine mental states, they are called the "Path of Seeing through Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-darśanamārga*).
This concludes the initial formal explanation of the Path of Seeing through Characteristics. II. Conclusion and Demonstration that [the Path] is Merely Provisionally Established.

All aspects of the path of seeing (darśanamārga) are likewise; based on the true path of seeing, it is conventionally designated as arising immediately after the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgradharma).

And although it is conventionally said that [this] severs the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), it is not actually so. This is because this aspectual path of seeing (*lakṣaṇa-darśanamārga*) can only arise after the true path of seeing (*tattva-darśanamārga*).
Furthermore, one does not first give rise to the contemplation of the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*) after [the contemplation of] the non-established truths (*avyavasthāna-satya*);
for the latent tendencies analyzed [in the latter] have already been severed within the true path of seeing.
The initial explanation of the meaning of the two paths is concluded. △ Second, distinguishing between the two paths:

the former, the True Path of Seeing (*tattva-darśana-mārga*), realizes the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*); the latter, the Phenomenal Path of Seeing (*nimitta-darśana-mārga*), realizes the appearances of consciousness-only. Between these two, the former is superior.

Therefore, the verse speaks specifically [of this] because wisdom (jñāna) has no apprehension whatsoever. The preceding true path of seeing (darśana-mārga) is subsumed under fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna), while the subsequent path of seeing with images (sākāra-darśana-mārga) is subsumed under subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna).
[Question: Do all subsequently attained wisdoms possess the two divisions of the perceiving subject and the perceived object?

This is the correct judgment and distinction. Next, the question is asked regarding the existence or non-existence of the two parts. Below, three answers are given; the third meaning is the correct one.

According to one interpretation, both [parts] are absent, because they are free from the two types of grasping (subject and object). According to another interpretation, this wisdom (the subsequently attained wisdom) has a seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) that exists, while its image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) is...

[No] [intrinsic nature]. This is because this category of wisdom is said to possess conceptual differentiation (*savikalpa*). Furthermore, since all noble wisdoms (*āryajñāna*) are able to directly illuminate their objects, they are said to be "free from the two graspings" (*dvaya-grāha-vivikta*) precisely because they do not cling [to them].
According to another interpretation, this [subsequently attained] wisdom possesses both parts—the seen (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*).

This is because it is said that this wisdom merely contemplates an image resembling *tathatā* (suchness), and does not perceive the true nature of *tathatā*. Moreover, it is stated that this wisdom involves conceptual differentiation.

This is because one teaches by observing the differences in the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings regarding the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
Furthermore, it is taught that this wisdom manifests bodies and lands in order to preach the True Dharma for sentient beings.

If it did not manifest as something resembling form, sound, and so forth, how could there be such matters as manifesting a body or preaching the Dharma? Even if one were to transform the basis of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), if form were not manifested, [how could these things occur]? It transforms...
If [the cognition] were the support for the four aggregates, there would be no feeling and so forth [as distinct entities].

Furthermore, if this cognition did not transform into the likeness of the object, then, being devoid of a dharma that constitutes its own nature, it could not be an object of cognition (*ālambana*). Alternatively, when cognizing form and so forth, it should also cognize sound and so forth.

Moreover, when cognizing non-existent dharmas and the like, there would be no object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), because the essence of those [past and future dharmas] is not substantially real and thus lacks the functional capacity to serve as an object. For these reasons, the subsequent cognition possesses both parts.

There is. Within the third meaning, five points are used to demonstrate that subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) possesses two aspects: first, because it observes the true nature through the transformation of appearances;
second, because it discriminates between specific and general characteristics and teaches the Dharma according to the faculties [of beings]; and third, because it is capable of...
Because it manifests in the body and the land; because the five outflow-tainted aggregates (*āsrava-skandha*) must be transformed into the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*);

fourth, even if the object were not transformed, there would be no object of cognition (*ālambana*); and even if it were not its own object yet could still be cognized, then by cognizing form (*rūpa*), one would likewise cognize sound (*śabda*) and so forth;
fifth, dharmas of the past, future, and so on lack substantiality in the present, and even if their characteristics were not transformed, they would [lack existence].
By way of the object of focus (*ālambana*). This concludes the first explanation of the two paths of vision (*darśanamārga*). △ Second, the inclusion of the six clear realizations (*abhisamaya*).
How are these two paths of vision subsumed within the six clear realizations? As for the six clear realizations: first, the clear realization through reflection (*cintā-abhisamaya*).

This refers to the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*) associated with the highest degree of pleasant feeling (*prīti-vedanā*). This [wisdom of reflection] is able to examine the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, such as impermanence and suffering;

because it induces the roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) of meditative wisdom (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, it examines all phenomena exclusively within the Path of Preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).

Because this volition (*cetanā*) is most intense, it alone is specifically designated by the term "clear observation" (*abhisamaya*). The stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth cannot extensively analyze phenomena, nor have they yet realized the principle;

therefore, they are not clear observation. Second is the clear observation of faith (*śraddhā-abhisamaya*); this refers to the definitive, pure faith directed toward the Three Jewels, both mundane and supramundane.
Because this assists clear observation by preventing regression, it is also designated by the name "clear observation. Third is the [clear observation] of ethical discipline (*śīla*).

1. *Abhisamaya* (Clear Realization): This refers to untainted (*anāsrava*) ethical discipline (*śīla*). It is called "clear realization" because it removes the stains of immoral conduct and causes clear observation to increase in brilliance. 2. *Catur-abhisamaya-jñāna-satya-abhisamaya* (Clear Realization of the Truths through the Wisdom of Clear Realization):
This refers to the fundamental and subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) that takes all aspects of the unestablished truths (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*) as its object.

3. *Abhisamaya-antika-jñāna-satya-abhisamaya* (Clear Realization of the Truths through the Wisdom at the Conclusion of Clear Realization): This refers to [the wisdom] regarding the clear realization of the truths through the wisdom of clear realization.

Subsequently, there are the wisdoms that establish the truths based on various conditions, both mundane and supramundane; and the sixth is the ultimate clear realization (*abhisamaya*), which refers to the wisdom at the final stage, such as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
This first establishes the inquiry to introduce the subject; next, it sets forth the names and characteristics of the six types of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Second is the clear realization of faith (*śraddhā-abhisamaya*), which consists of the four unshakable faiths: first, firm faith in the Buddha; second, firm faith in the Dharma;
third, firm faith in the Saṃgha; and fourth, firm faith in the Truths—namely, the respective causes and effects of the mundane and supramundane realms.

The second [set] consists of what are called the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. The third is the clear realization of the precepts (*śīla-abhisamaya*), which is the morality concomitant with the Path (*mārga-sahabhū-śīla*).

Once the untainted (*anāsrava*) state has arisen, the essence of the unmanifest precept (*avijñapti-śīla*) obtained therefrom can never again be violated. Because the precepts are pure, wisdom is rendered pure.
Regarding "all aspects" (*sarvākāra*): regardless of the stage, it refers only to the latter two [truths] of the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*).

All forms of wisdom are subsumed within this fourth clear realization (*abhisamaya*). Regarding the objects of perception: that which takes the truths of suffering and its origin as its object is mundane wisdom;

that which takes the truths of cessation and the path as its object is supramundane wisdom. The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) exist only at the stage of ultimate perfection;
therefore, it is called the "ultimate clear realization."

This true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) subsumes a portion of that fourth clear realization (*abhisamaya*). This inferential path of seeing (*anvayadarśanamārga*) subsumes portions of both the fourth and fifth [clear realizations].
Although those second (realization of faith) and third (realization of ethical discipline) arise simultaneously with this [path of seeing], [they are not included here].
[They] merely assist [one another] and do not constitute the nature of direct realization (*abhisamaya*); therefore, they are not mutually inclusive.
The true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the fourth direct realization; hence it is said to be "partial.

There are two types of the semblance path of seeing (*nimitta-darśanamārga*). If one contemplates the three categories of the non-established truths (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*), this occurs after the fourth direct realization.

Because it is subsumed under the attainment of wisdom, it is called "a small portion. If one takes the sixteen moments of mind regarding the established truths (*prajñaptisatya*) as the object, it is then subsumed under the fifth clear observation (*abhisamaya*).
However, while the fifth clear observation pertains to both the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), this [present case] pertains only to the path of seeing;
therefore, it is also called "a small portion. The second part, the detailed explanation, is concluded. △ Third, the conclusion on the benefits.

When a bodhisattva attains these two paths of vision (*darśanamārga*), they are born into the family of the Tathāgata, abide in the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), and thoroughly penetrate the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
They attain all forms of equality and are constantly born within the great assemblies of all Buddhas. Regarding hundreds of gateways [to the teachings], they have already attained mastery.
He knows for himself that before long he will realize great bodhi, being able to bring benefit and happiness to all throughout the future.
He attains various forms of equality: namely, the equality of all sentient beings, the equality of all bodhisattvas, and the equality of all Tathāgatas;
that is to say, the equality of ordinary beings and sages, the equality of cause and effect, and the equality of self and others. Furthermore—
This refers to what is called the non-differentiation of the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings. Regarding the "many hundreds of gates":

these pervade the five positions and one hundred dharmas, thoroughly penetrating the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*). Within each and every dharma, the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the two emptinesses is entirely equal;
thus, each one possesses all one hundred. Therefore, they are called "the many hundreds. Even if the five aspects were not fused as both the ultimate and the conventional, they would not be so named.

Attaining mastery. Therefore, although the paths of teaching differ, the path of realization is equally perfected. This concludes the third explanation: the stage of thorough penetration (prativedha-avasthā).
△ Fourth, the explanation of the stage of cultivation (bhāvanā-avasthā) has two parts: first, the citation of the verse; second, the commentary. Now, the first.
Next is the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*). What are its characteristics? The verse says: "Non-apprehension and inconceivable, This is supramundane wisdom.
Because it abandons the two types of grossness (*dauṣṭhulya*), One then realizes the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*)."
△ Second, the commentary on the treatise has two parts: first, a brief explanation of the verse; second, an extensive explanation of the meaning of the verse. Now, the first: The treatise says:

After the Bodhisattva has arisen from the preceding path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), in order to sever the remaining [two] innate obstacles (*sahaja-āvaraṇa*) and realize the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).

Furthermore, one repeatedly cultivates non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). Because this wisdom is far removed from the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), it is described as "non-attainment" (*anupalabdhi*) and "inconceivable" (*acintya*).
Alternatively, it is called "non-attainment" because it is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); its sublime function is difficult to fathom, and thus it is named "inconceivable."
This is supramundane non-conceptual wisdom. It is called "supramundane" because it severs the mundane.

The latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two-grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) are the root of the mundane; only this [wisdom of non-apprehension and inconceivability] can sever them. Therefore, it alone receives the name "supramundane."
Alternatively, the term "supramundane" is established based on two meanings: namely, that its essence is untainted (*anāsrava*), and that it realizes suchness (*tathatā*).
Because this wisdom possesses these two meanings, it alone is called "supramundane," whereas other forms of wisdom are not.
That is to say, through the repeated cultivation of non-conceptual wisdom within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one is able to abandon the two types of heavy obstructions (*dauṣṭhulya*).

The seeds of the two obstructions are designated by the term "heavy" because their nature is unserviceable and contrary to the subtle, light, and untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas. [Now, it is able to] cause...

Because those [two] are eternally extinguished, it is called "equanimity" (*upekṣā*). Since this wisdom of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi-jñāna*) is able to relinquish those two types of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), one is thereby able to realize the vast transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).

Regarding the arising of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*): the initial moment of mind that abandons the afflictions is the Path of Uninterruptedness (*ānantaryamārga*); the central moments of mind that realize the principle are the Path of Liberation (*vimuktimārga*);
and the subsequent moments of mind that give rise to cultivation are the Path of Superior Progress (*viśeṣamārga*). Here, the discussion specifically concerns the subsequent moments of mind.
"Support" refers to the basis, namely the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), because it serves as the support for both defiled and pure phenomena.
"Defiled" refers to the false and pervasive *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature); "pure" refers to the true and perfect *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).

"Transformation" refers to the transformation within the two parts of the *paratantra*—the relinquishing of the defiled part and the attaining of the pure part—through the repeated cultivation of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), whereby the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) is severed.

Because it eliminates the two types of coarse obstructions (*dausthulya*) within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), one is able to discard the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) that exists upon the dependent nature, and is able to realize the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) within the dependent nature.
By transforming the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one attains Great Nirvāṇa;

by transforming the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one realizes Unsurpassed Enlightenment. It is with this intent that this treatise establishes Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), so that sentient beings may realize these two states.
The fruit of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). This is first explained in terms of the transformation that sustains the seeds within the eighth consciousness.

The seeds of the two obstacles—afflictions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*) and the cognizable (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*)—are all maintained by the eighth consciousness; likewise, the two fruits of transformation, namely *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*, are also [maintained] by the eighth consciousness.

That which is fundamentally possessed [is obscured]: by the seeds of affliction (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*), great *nirvāṇa* is obstructed; by the seeds of the cognitive obstruction (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*), supreme enlightenment is obstructed.
Now, as these two obstructions are gradually abandoned part by part, their two fruits are likewise gradually realized part by part.

It may be said that this beginningless saṃsāra and the blissful, wondrous permanence are nothing other than these eight consciousnesses, and no other thing. Question: The School of Nature (*Xingzong*) maintains that...
"Transforming afflictions (*kleśa*) into bodhi; transforming birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) into nirvāṇa. How should this be reconciled? The answer is:
what is here termed the "afflictive hindrance" (*kleśāvaraṇa*) refers to the general delusions of both views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-mithyā-saṃjñā*).

What is here termed the "hindrance to the knowable" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) refers to the specific delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*). Since the nature school (*xingzong*) generally designates both these general and specific delusions as "afflictions," that which [is stated there]...

The statement that "afflictions (*kleśa*) are transformed into awakening (*bodhi*)" is identical to the present claim that "the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are transformed to realize unsurpassed enlightenment.

This is because, through the universal afflictions, one incurs the false fruit of *paricchinna-saṃsāra* (segmented birth and death), which obstructs *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder).
Through the particular afflictions, one incurs the false fruit of *pariṇāmi-saṃsāra* (transformative birth and death), which obstructs *prakṛti-viśuddha-nirvāṇa* (nirvana of intrinsic purity).
It also obstructs non-abiding nirvana. Therefore, what they say—that one transforms birth-and-death into nirvana—is stated in terms of the fruit;
whereas what is said here—that one transforms afflictions to attain nirvana—is stated in terms of the cause. Thus, there is no contradiction between them.

Furthermore, the meaning of afflictions giving rise to [rebirth] is manifest, while the meaning of the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa) veiling awakening is predominant; therefore, this [text] speaks specifically of the latter. Moreover, [the former]...

By severing the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one also attains the enlightenment of the two vehicles; because this is not the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is merely termed "nirvāṇa.

By severing the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one also attains non-abiding nirvāṇa; because one does not abide in the mark of nirvāṇa, it is merely termed "unsurpassed enlightenment" (*anuttara-bodhi*).
Alternatively, the "basis" refers to the suchness of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra-tathatā*), for it is the basis of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

Because foolish worldlings are inverted and deluded regarding this suchness, they have undergone the suffering of birth and death since beginningless time. Sages, free from inversion, realize this suchness and thereby attain nirvāṇa, which is ultimate peace and bliss.
Through the repeated cultivation of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), they sever [the afflictions] within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

Because of the two obstructions and their coarse latencies (*dausthulya*), one is able to transform and extinguish the two kinds of birth-and-death that depend upon suchness, and is able to transform and realize the non-abiding nirvāṇa that depends upon suchness.
This is precisely the nature of suchness as being free from defilement; although suchness is pure by nature, its characteristics may be defiled.

Therefore, at the time of becoming free from defilement, it is metaphorically described as "newly purified. This very state of being newly purified is called the *āśraya-parāvṛtti* (transformation of the basis).
Although within the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*) one attains this by severing hindrances and realizes awakening (*bodhi*), this is not what is intended to be expressed by the verse.

The intent of the verse merely reveals the transformation of the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*). Since the nature of consciousness-only is itself nirvāṇa, [it is so designated]; however, in the case of the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*) at their stage of fulfillment—[it is only]...
It is called the "Body of Liberation" (vimuktikāya); only when [attaining] the ultimate fruit of the Mahāyāna Sage does it receive the name of the "Dharma Body" (dharmakāya).

This further explains [the relationship] by way of the basis for the transformation of delusion and awakening. The true suchness (*tathatā*) of consciousness is the very essence of consciousness itself.
Saṃsāra is like ice; nirvāṇa is like water. True suchness is like the nature of moisture. Saṃsāra is like the state of changing; nirvāṇa is like the state of not changing.
True suchness is like the original house. Saṃsāra is like delusion; nirvāṇa is like awakening. True suchness...
It is as in the original parable: birth and death are like a frantic run; nirvana is like the cessation of that frenzy. True Suchness (Tathatā) is like the original head.
To be deluded by it is to undergo birth and death in vain; to awaken to it is to immediately attain nirvana. This is the unchanging that constantly accords with conditions.

The essence (*tǐ*) is itself the function (*yòng*). Abiding in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), it is not defiled; dwelling in nirvana, it is not pure. This is the constant unchanging nature that accords with conditions. The function is itself the essence.
The followers of the Two Vehicles realize only the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), yet they remain deluded regarding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);

thus, while they emerge from the cycle of birth-and-death in its segmented form (*paricchinna-saṃsāra*), they merely realize the nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), which is termed the "body of liberation" (*vimukti-kāya*). The Mahayana, however, fully awakens to both the self and...
Since phenomena and emptiness are co-existent, one emerges from the two kinds of birth-and-death and deeply realizes non-abiding nirvana; this is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
One should know that what is realized is precisely the *tathatā* (suchness) Dharma-body, and that which realizes it is unsurpassed bodhi.

Because the subject and object are non-dual, the intent of the verse merely reveals the transformation of the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*); it is not necessary to speak further of bodhi.

*Muni*. This is translated as "Silent Quiescence" (*jìmò*). It refers to the state of being well-attuned to the Middle Way through silent realization, having transcended the two extremes of existence and non-existence.
This concludes the initial brief explanation of the verse. II. The Detailed Explanation of the Verse’s Meaning has two parts: first, a general inquiry; second, the actual explanation. Now, the first.

How are the two kinds of transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) realized? It is by means of cultivating the ten superior practices within the ten stages (bhūmi), severing the ten heavy obstructions, and realizing the ten suchnesses (tathatā) that these two kinds of transformation of the basis are attained.

△ Second, the correct explanation has two parts: first, clarifying the causes of the ten stages; second, clarifying the fruit of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Within the first part, there are four sections: first, explaining the names of the ten stages;
second, explaining the ten superior practices; third, explaining the ten heavy obstacles; fourth, explaining the ten suchnesses (*tathatā*).

First, regarding the "Ten Grounds" (*daśabhūmi*): 1. **The Ground of Utmost Joy** (*pramuditā-bhūmi*): Because for the first time one attains the nature of a noble being (*āryatva*), fully realizes the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), and is able to benefit oneself and others, giving rise to great joy.
2. **The Ground of Purity** (*vimalā-bhūmi*): Because one possesses pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) and remains far removed from even subtle transgressions that could give rise to violation.

The third is the Ground of Luminous Radiance (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*), so called because one achieves superior meditative concentrations and great dhāraṇīs, thereby able to emit the light of boundless sublime wisdom.

The fourth is the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), so called because one dwells securely in the most excellent factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), and the flames of wisdom increase as they burn the fuel of afflictions.

The fifth is the Ground Extremely Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*), so called because the two types of knowledge—of the ultimate and the conventional—have mutually contradictory modes of activity, yet are joined and made to harmonize.
2. The Ground of Perfect Intellect (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*): Because it is extremely difficult to overcome. 3. The Ground of Manifestation (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*):

Because one dwells in the wisdom that thoroughly penetrates dependent origination with discrimination, thereby bringing forth the manifestation of non-conceptual, supreme *prajñā*. 4. The Ground of Far-Going (*Dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*):

Because one reaches the ultimate limit of the stage of effort within the dwelling of signlessness, transcending both the mundane path and the supramundane paths of the two vehicles. 5. The Ground of Immovability (*Acalā-bhūmi*): Because non-conceptual wisdom functions spontaneously...

The ninth is the Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*): because its characteristics and functions cannot be disturbed by afflictions, one attains the subtle and wondrous four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and is able to skillfully teach the Dharma throughout the ten directions. The tenth is the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*Dharmameghā*):

it is a great cloud of Dharma-wisdom that contains the waters of manifold virtues; it provides shade and protection for all things, rendering the heavy obstructions (*dausthulya*) as non-obstructive as space. Furthermore, by means of this great wisdom, it completely fills that which is realized and that upon which it relies.
Because it is the Dharma-body. Thus, these ten stages collectively encompass all conditioned and unconditioned merits as their intrinsic nature;
they serve as the supreme support for the practices cultivated, enabling them to grow and flourish. Therefore, they are called "stages" (bhūmi).
"Noble One" (*ārya*) means "correct. To be eternally free from error and inversion and to enter the assembly of those established in correctness is called "attaining the nature of a noble one.

"Subtle transgressions" refers to unintentional offenses. "Non-conceptual wisdom" is the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*). Its spontaneous continuity is the meaning of "effortless" (*anābhoga*).
"The great cloud of dharma-wisdom" refers to the wisdom that takes all phenomena as its collective object, containing all...
The "Virtuous Water" refers to the gateways of *dhāraṇī* and the gateways of *samādhi*, and so forth.
"Coarseness like space" refers to a portion of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as well as the seeds of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), which are as vast as space.

"Conditioned merits" refer to the *pratyavekṣaṇājñāna* (wonderful observation wisdom) and the *samatājñāna* (equality wisdom). "Unconditioned merits" refer to the *tathatā* (suchness) realized within each of the stages (*bhūmi*).
The rest may be understood accordingly. △ Second, the explanation of the ten superior practices consists of thirteen sections. The first clarifies the section on number (up to).
The thirteenth summarizes the essential points for distinguishing cultivation. Now, the first [section].

The ten superior practices are the ten *pāramitās*. Generosity (*dāna*) is threefold: namely, the gift of material wealth, the gift of fearlessness, and the gift of the Dharma. Ethical discipline (*śīla*) is threefold:
namely, the discipline of restraint, the discipline of gathering virtuous qualities, and the discipline of benefiting sentient beings.
Patience (*kṣānti*) is threefold: namely, patience in enduring enmity and harm, patience in accepting suffering, and patience in the discernment of phenomena. Diligence (*vīrya*)...

There are three kinds: namely, armor-like diligence (*saṃnāha-vīrya*), diligence in gathering virtue (*kuśala-saṃgrāhaka-vīrya*), and diligence in benefiting and bringing happiness to others (*sattvārtha-vīrya*).

There are three kinds of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*): concentration for abiding (*sthiti-dhyāna*), concentration for eliciting [supernormal powers] (*abhinirhāra-dhyāna*), and concentration for accomplishing tasks (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-dhyāna*). There are three kinds of wisdom (*prajñā*):

non-conceptual wisdom regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), non-conceptual wisdom regarding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), and non-conceptual wisdom regarding the emptiness of both. Skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*)...
Skillful means are of two kinds: namely, skillful means of dedication and skillful means of rescue. Aspirations are of two kinds:

namely, the aspiration for enlightenment and the aspiration for the benefit and happiness of others. Powers are of two kinds: namely, the power of analytical discernment and the power of cultivation. Wisdom is of two kinds:
namely, the wisdom that experiences the joy of the Dharma and the wisdom that brings sentient beings to maturity.
The gift of material wealth is also called the gift of the means of subsistence; it consists of relinquishing all articles of livelihood with a mind free from attachment.
The gift of fearlessness consists of not harming or vexing others and rescuing them from terror; it comprises the two perfections of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*).
The gift of Dharma consists of proclaiming the true Dharma with a mind free from attachment, acting in accordance with one’s words so as to bring benefit to others; it is...
This advances one through the three higher trainings of meditation and wisdom. Regarding the *śīla* of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*): it consists of ceasing evil and preventing wrongdoing;

it comprises all the categories of precepts for both laypeople and monastics. Regarding the *śīla* of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*): by the power of maintaining these precepts, one gathers all the merits that lead to Buddhahood;

this is the practice for one's own benefit. Regarding the *śīla* of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*): by the power of maintaining these precepts, [one gives rise to... one... (Note: The source text appears to be truncated at the end.)

All activities for the sake of delivering sentient beings constitute the practice of benefiting others. Patience toward enmity and harm is also called patience toward living beings (*sattva-kṣānti*), because one does not give rise to anger while bringing sentient beings to maturity.
Patience in enduring suffering is also called patience toward phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*), because one withstands toil and endures hardship in seeking the Buddha-dharma.

Patience through the discernment of phenomena is also called patience regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-kṣānti*), because one contemplates the emptiness of arising phenomena and remains unshakable.
Because it is transformative, there is the diligence of donning armor, which is the initial generation of the bodhicitta, as one dons the great armor of the vow and exerts oneself deeply.

Because it gathers what is wholesome, there is the diligence of gathering virtue, as one delights in accumulating the qualities of a Buddha. Because it brings benefit and happiness, there is the diligence of benefiting and gladdening others, as one delights in delivering all sentient beings.
Regarding "abiding in meditative concentration," this refers to attaining the blissful dwelling in the present life. Regarding "inducing meditative concentration," this refers to...

This refers to the elicitation of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and so forth. The meditative concentration for accomplishing tasks (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-dhyāna*) refers to accomplishing such matters as benefiting sentient beings.
The three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) may be understood according to the text. The skillful means of dedication (*pariṇāmanopāya*) refers to not abiding in saṃsāra.

The skillful means of deliverance (*uddharaṇopāya*) refers to not abiding in nirvāṇa. Furthermore, the skillful means of dedication causes others not to abide in nirvāṇa, while the skillful means of deliverance...
The skillful means [of the first vow] cause others not to dwell in saṃsāra. Furthermore, the skillful means of dedication lead directly toward unsurpassed bodhi.
The skillful means of rescue and deliverance cause one to equally transcend the two kinds of birth-and-death. The vow to seek bodhi corresponds to the Dharma-gate:

"I vow to learn all immeasurable dharmas" and "I vow to accomplish the unsurpassed Buddha-way. The vow to benefit and bring joy to others corresponds to "sentient beings... [I vow to deliver them all].
The vow to deliver all beings at the limits of existence; the vow to sever afflictions that are inexhaustible. "Discernment" refers to the power of the practice of wisdom (*prajñā*).

"Cultivation" refers to the power of the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "The knowledge that experiences the joy of the Dharma" is subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which is non-deluded and unerring regarding the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena.
"The knowledge that matures sentient beings" is also subsequently attained wisdom, which observes all...

[One must] administer medicine according to the illness, taking into account whether the faculties are sharp or dull, and whether they are mature or immature. △ Second, the section on defining the essential nature:
Regarding these ten natures, giving has non-attachment as its nature, along with the three types of action (body, speech, and mind) arising therefrom at the time of practicing generosity.

Ethical discipline has the three types of action at the time of receiving and training in the bodhisattva precepts as its nature. Patience has non-hatred as its nature, while diligence [is characterized by] clarity and discernment.

Wisdom (*prajñā*) and the three types of action (*karman*) arising from it have patience (*kṣānti*) as their nature at the time [of that patience]. Diligence (*vīrya*) has exertion (*vīrya*) and the three types of action arising from it as its nature at the time [of that diligence].
Meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) has meditative equipoise (*samādhi*) alone as its nature.

The latter five all have the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*)—one of the seven factors of enlightenment—as their nature, because [in the treatises] *prajñā* is said to be fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), while the other four [skillful means and so forth] are subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). According to another interpretation, the eighth [perfection] is the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).

It has as its nature (kuśala-) desire (chanda-), resolute conviction (adhimukti-), and faith (śraddhā-); for [the great vows of ordinary beings] necessarily have these three as their intrinsic nature.
This above explains the intrinsic nature. If taken together with their retinues, each one has as its nature all the qualities that function in conjunction with them.

At the time of receiving the Bodhisattva precepts, there are three types of action (*karman*): namely, the mind aspiring for unsurpassed enlightenment, taking the Three Jewels as its object, and performing the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*).
Through this volitional action, seeds are perfumed and established, which give rise to the spontaneous capacity to cease evil and practice good;
this is termed "unconditioned form" (*avijñapti-rūpa*). Until the end of the future, it functions to sever all evil and cultivate all goodness.
"Excellent! Delivering all sentient beings—this is the essential nature of the threefold pure precepts (tri-śikṣā-viśuddhi).

Samādhi is *samādhi* itself, the wholesome concentration (*samādhi*) among the specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-citta*). Dharma-discernment (*dharmapravicaya*) is the wholesome wisdom (*prajñā*) among the specific mental factors;
this is because both the fundamental and subsequent knowledges are subsumed under the mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā-cetasika*). If considered in terms of their retinue, then each *pāramitā*..."
Maitreya. It must necessarily be associated with faith, shame, and remorse—the three wholesome roots—as well as the wholesome specific-object, wholesome universal, and other mental factors;
these may all be inferred accordingly. △ Third, the section on the characteristics [of the mind].
These ten characteristics must be embraced by seven types of excellence (*paramatā*) before they can be established as *pāramitās*.
First, the excellence of abiding: this means one must abide in the bodhisattva lineage (*gotra*). Second, the excellence of reliance:
this means one must rely upon the great mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). Third, the excellence of intention: this means one must possess compassion for all sentient beings. Fourth...

First, the excellence of the undertaking (*karma*), which means it must be endowed with the excellence of performing all activities. Second, the excellence of skillful means (*upāya*), which means it must be embraced by signless wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*).
Third, the excellence of dedication (*pariṇāmana*), which means it must be dedicated toward unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Fourth, the excellence of purity (*viśuddhi*), which means it must not be interspersed with the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*). If [an action] is not embraced by these seven, then...

The practice of giving and so forth does not, by itself, constitute reaching the other shore (*pāramitā*). For this reason, each of these ten—giving and the rest—must be analyzed through four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) in relation to the *pāramitās*.
Since practitioners of the Two Vehicles and even worldly virtuous persons also possess practices such as giving and upholding the precepts, it is said that [the *pāramitās*] require seven [factors].
Only when embraced by the Most Victorious One (the Buddha) can it be called a *pāramitā*.
First, one must abide in the bodhisattva lineage, which refers to the two types of lineages previously mentioned.

If one lacks the bodhisattva lineage, then the virtues practiced, such as generosity and ethical discipline, will merely result in the fruits of the human and celestial realms or the two vehicles; they will not bring about unexcelled, great enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Second, relying on the great bodhicitta means that one must seek the Buddha-way above;

only by practicing the virtues of generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth will one not fall into the outflows (*āsrava*). Third, having the intention of compassion for sentient beings means that one must transform sentient beings below;
only by practicing the virtues of generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth will one not be biased toward self-interest alone. Fourth, being endowed with the practice of all [virtues].
Sixth, "virtuous deeds" refers to practicing virtues such as giving and ethical discipline with a mind free from partiality and without satiety;
for only in this way can one increase and fulfill the supreme provisions (*sambhāra*).

Fifth, "essential skillful means and non-conceptual wisdom" refers to practicing virtues such as giving and ethical discipline while realizing that the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are empty in essence; for only in this way do merit and virtue become equal to space. Sixth.

First, regarding dedication toward the unsurpassed path: this means that whatever practice one performs, each must be directed toward the ultimate fruit so as not to incidentally produce a ripening result (*vipāka-phala*).
Seventh, regarding being pure and free from intermixture:

this means that whatever practice one performs, it must be free from regret throughout the three times and not be interspersed with afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) or cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
This is because it alone enables one to swiftly reach the other shore. Regarding the "fourfold analysis," there are three types of fourfold sets.
First, concerning giving (*dāna*) alone: first, there is that which is giving but not a *pāramitā*, because it is practiced without being conjoined with the seven excellences.
Second, there is that which is a *pāramitā* but not giving, such as rejoicing (*anumodanā*) in the giving of others while possessing the seven excellences.

Therefore, the third category consists of both giving and *pāramitā*. The fourth category consists of neither giving nor *pāramitā*, because although one may rejoice in the giving of others, it is not conjoined with the seven excellences.

By analogy with this, the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) for each of the nine perfections, beginning with ethical discipline (*śīla*), can be understood. Second, regarding the four [categories] as explained by way of sequential cultivation: 1. Giving that is not yet a *pāramitā*. 2. Giving that is already a *pāramitā*. 3. That which is neither giving nor a *pāramitā*.
4. That which is both giving and a *pāramitā*. [The same applies to the other perfections. Regarding the second point, the four [categories] are clarified through sequential cultivation.
In the first [section], the Perfection of Giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), there are only two propositions: first, giving that is not a perfection; second, giving that is a perfection.

Next, within the Perfection of Ethics (*śīla-pāramitā*), four propositions are clarified in contrast to giving: first, ethics that is not a perfection, because it is not associated with the seven excellences;
second, a perfection that is not ethics, namely the aforementioned giving which possesses the seven excellences; third, that which is both ethics...

They are also "crossings" (*pāramitā*), because they maintain the precepts while being endowed with the seven excellences. Four are neither precepts nor crossings; this refers to the aforementioned generosity (*dāna*) because it is not endowed with the seven excellences.
Regarding patience (*kṣānti*) in relation to the precepts and so forth, one should understand it by analogy with this. Third, as for not restricting them to a fixed order:

when the various perfections are compared with one another, each forms four permutations (*catuṣkoṭika*), as can be understood from the usual [treatises]. Only the sixth, wisdom (*prajñā*), has only three.
This is because there is nothing that is a *pāramitā* which is not also *prajñā*. △ Fourth is the gate of neither increase nor decrease.
As for why there are only ten and neither more nor less: it means that within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one counteracts the ten obstacles and realizes the ten suchnesses (*tathatā*).

Because there is neither increase nor decrease. Furthermore, the reason why the first six [perfections] do not increase or decrease is that they eliminate six kinds of opposing obstacles, allow for the gradual cultivation of all Buddha-dharmas, and allow for the gradual maturation of all sentient beings;

this should be understood as it is explained at length in other treatises. Moreover, the three beginning with generosity (are called) the path of superior rebirth within the realms of humans and devas. (Generosity) brings about great wealth.
Because the essence [of morality] and its retinue [of patience] induce the Great [Vehicles], the three beginning with diligence are called the "definitive path of excellence" (*niyata-viśeṣa-mārga*).
Diligence can subdue the afflictions; based on meditative concentration, it brings forth supernormal powers; and through wisdom, it matures sentient beings and matures the Buddha-dharmas.

Thus, the paths of all Bodhisattvas consist of only these two types: the "superior birth" (*abhyudaya*) and the "definitive path of excellence. Furthermore, the first three types benefit sentient beings by providing them with material resources.

(1) Ethical discipline (*śīla*) [protects others]. (2) Patience (*kṣānti*) does not harm or afflict others, for it endures their afflictions while benefiting them. The latter three—diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)—are antidotes to the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Although diligence has not yet subdued and extinguished them, one is able to diligently cultivate the various virtuous applications that serve as their antidotes.

Meditative concentration can permanently subdue the afflictions, and wisdom can permanently extinguish all afflictions. Furthermore, by means of the [first] three perfections such as generosity, [the bodhisattva], through great compassion, benefits sentient beings without remaining [attached to them].

Nirvāṇa. Furthermore, the latter three [faculties, such as diligence] constitute great wisdom that suppresses and extinguishes all afflictions; they serve as the provisions for non-abiding nirvāṇa, ensuring one does not dwell in saṃsāra.
For this reason, the preceding six are neither more nor less. As for why there are only four of the latter, it is because they assist the preceding six.

They cause [the perfections] to be cultivated to fulfillment because they neither increase nor decrease. Through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they assist the first three [perfections], such as giving;

through aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), they assist diligence (*vīrya*); through power (*bala*), they assist meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); and through wisdom (*jñāna*), they assist insight (*prajñā*), thereby causing them to be cultivated to fulfillment. This should be understood as explained at length in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.

First, the ten [factors] are clarified as being without increase or decrease; next, the six [factors] are clarified as being without increase or decrease; finally, it is clarified that because the four assist the six, there is no increase or decrease.
The meaning of these points may be understood accordingly. △ Fifth, the Section on Sequence.
Regarding the tenfold sequence: it is because each preceding stage induces the succeeding one, and each succeeding stage sustains and purifies each preceding one;
furthermore, because the preceding stages are coarse while the succeeding ones are subtle, they differ in terms of ease and difficulty of cultivation. This is the sequence.
As for the explanation of the general name (*pāramitā*) and the specific names (*dāna*, *śīla*, etc.), it is as explained elsewhere.
Regarding the way each preceding stage induces each succeeding stage: through giving one induces ethical discipline; through ethical discipline one induces patience;

and so on, up to inducing wisdom through power. Regarding the way each succeeding stage maintains the purity of each preceding stage: because it is maintained by wisdom, power is purified; because it is maintained by power, aspiration is purified;
and so on, down to giving being purified because it is maintained by ethical discipline. Regarding the way each preceding stage is coarser: giving is coarser than [ethical discipline].
Regarding the precepts: the precepts are coarser than patience, and so on, up to power being coarser than wisdom. As for those that become progressively subtler:
wisdom is subtler than power, power is subtler than aspiration, and so on, down to the precepts being subtler than giving. Giving is easy to cultivate; the precepts are difficult to cultivate.

The precepts are easy to cultivate; patience is difficult to cultivate; and so on, up to aspiration being easy to cultivate and power being difficult to cultivate, and power being easy to cultivate while wisdom is difficult to cultivate.
Therefore, the sequence is established based on these various meanings. △ Sixth, the five gates of cultivation.
Regarding these ten cultivations, there are five types of cultivation: first, cultivation based on reliance and sustenance; second, cultivation based on mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Third is cultivation based on the resolute intention (*āśaya*); fourth is cultivation based on skillful means (*upāya*); and fifth is cultivation based on mastery (*vaśitā*).
By means of these five types of cultivation, one brings all ten perfections (*pāramitā*) to full completion. Their characteristics are explained in detail in such works as the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
First, regarding the cultivation based on reliance and sustenance, there are four types: first, reliance on the cause, which refers to the power of the spiritual lineage (*gotrabala*);
second, reliance on maturation, which refers to the power of one's superior physical constitution; third, reliance on aspiration, which refers to the power of original vows;

and fourth, reliance on discernment, which refers to the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*). Second, regarding the cultivation based on mental attention (*manasikāra*), there are likewise four types. First—

1. Mental attention of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*): because it gives rise to superior resolute conviction toward the scriptural teachings associated with the ten perfections (*pāramitā*).
2. Mental attention of relish (*āsvādana-manasikāra*): because it gives rise to deep relish upon seeing the excellent qualities of having attained the ten perfections.

3. Mental attention of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā-manasikāra*): because it generates profound sympathetic joy for all practices of the ten perfections. 4. Mental attention of delight (*abhirati-manasikāra*): [Because it gives rise to great joy regarding the ten perfections.]

Because one generates a profound aspiration and delight for the superior categories of the ten perfections for oneself and others in the future, there is thirdly, cultivation based on the intentional attitude (*āśaya*).
This, moreover, has six types: first, the attitude of non-contentment, because one practices generosity and the other perfections without ever being satisfied.
2. The vast intention (*udāra-āśaya*), because it is without retreat or interruption until reaching the ultimate goal. 3.
The joyful intention (*pramudita-āśaya*), because one gives rise to great joy toward the sentient beings one has gathered. 4.

The intention of gratitude and virtue (*upakāra-guṇa-āśaya*), because one regards all sentient beings as having great kindness and virtue, being able to assist one in attaining unsurpassed great enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). 5. The unstained intention (*asaṃkliṣṭa-āśaya*), because [it is] not...
Sixth is the superior intention (*āśaya*) for the sake of desiring to repay the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
Fifth is cultivation based on skillful means (*upāya*), which refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), because it observes that the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are all pure.
Fifth is cultivation based on mastery (*vaśitā*), which refers to the body...

Mastery (*vaśitā*). Mastery of conduct (*caryā-vaśitā*). Mastery of speech (*abhilāpa-vaśitā*). Regarding mastery of body (*kāya-vaśitā*), it refers to the two bodies: the self-nature body (*svābhāvika-kāya*) and the enjoyment body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*).

Regarding mastery of conduct, it refers to the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*). Regarding mastery of speech, it refers to the ability to proclaim all the distinctions of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) without any obstruction.
7. The Section on Mutual Inclusion of Similar Categories.
Regarding this inclusion of the ten: if one discusses their mutual inclusion in general terms, each and every one of these ten types of practice includes all the *pāramitās*.
Because they are mutually concordant, there are two further meanings when discussing their mutual inclusion:

First, regarding the induction of a subsequent stage by relying on the cultivation of a preceding stage, the former includes the latter because the latter necessarily depends upon the former (as that which is induced). However, the latter does not include the former, because the former does not depend upon the latter (for its production).

Second, regarding the purification of a preceding stage by relying on the cultivation of a subsequent stage, the latter includes the former because it is capable of purifying the former. However, the former does not include the latter.
(One is) able. This is not because it maintains purity (subsequently). If one practices according to the pure and the mixed, four permutations should be established in relation to one another.
First, pure and not mixed; second, mixed and not pure; third, both pure and mixed; fourth, neither pure nor mixed.
Furthermore, these may correspond to the three preceding sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). △ Eighth: The Section on the Mutual Inclusion of Six and Ten.
Although these actually consist of ten, they are spoken of as six; one should know that the latter four are all subsumed under the sixth.

As for their expansion into ten, the sixth subsumes only non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), whereas the latter four are all subsumed under subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), since [the wisdoms of] skillful means and so forth are all included therein.
Because they arise conditioned by the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
△ Ninth, the section on the ripening of results:

Regarding the results produced by these ten practices, those that are with outflows (*sāsrava*) have four [results]—namely, the result of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), the matured result (*vipāka-phala*), the dominant result (*adhipati-phala*), and the result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*)—but [the result of disconnection is excluded].

The fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*).
