For the ten untainted [paths of action], there are four [fruits]—namely, the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*), the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), and the fruit of disjunction—but with the exception of the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*).

As for the passages where it is said that [certain formations] possess five fruits, these are either stated in reference to their mutual support or by combining the two types of formations, namely the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
The permanent abandonment of that which is to be countered by each [perfection] is the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) of these perfections.

In the present life, the fact that one’s own and others’ welfare are sustained through this giving and so forth is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*). In future lives, their progressive increase and excellence is the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Arising successively is the *niṣyanda-phala* (fruit of outflow). Attaining great enlightenment is the *adhipati-phala* (dominant fruit).

To experience great wealth, rebirth in the happy realms (*sugati*), being without enmity, being indestructible, possessing much joy and happiness, being honored among sentient beings, having no physical injury, and belonging to a vast and noble lineage—these are the *vipāka-phala* (ripened fruits) of giving and the other perfections.
These [fruits] comprise both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Second, the King of Accumulated Merit Concentration; this refers to the fact that this concentration freely accumulates boundless [merit].
1. The concentration of merit (*puṇya-samādhi*). Because its power is peerless, it is like that of a king. 2. The concentration of guarding the noble (*ārya-rakṣa-samādhi*).

Regarding these three types of wisdom: in the first two stages—the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*) and the stage of application (*prayoga*)—the seeds possess all three [types], while the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) consist only of those of application.
In the stage of penetration (*prativedha*), there are two types of active manifestations (namely, both fundamental and subsequently attained), while the seeds possess all three;

this is because there are no active manifestations of application within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). In the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), prior to the seventh ground, both seeds and active manifestations encompass all three types.

From the eighth stage onward, there are two [types of] manifest [wisdom]—namely, the fundamental and the subsequently attained—and three [types of] seeds. This is because the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*) contradicts the preparatory application (*prayoga*);
therefore, all progress therein proceeds spontaneously within the subsequently attained uncontaminated contemplation (*anāsrava-vipaśyanā*), and is thus not subsumed under preparatory application.
In the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*), both manifest and seeds are of these two types, because the manifest and seeds of preparatory application have already been abandoned.
This further classifies the three types of training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*) based on the five categories. The first section concludes the explanation of the characteristics of the three trainings.
△ Second, the explanation of their mutual inclusion (*saṃgraha*).

If one were to include them solely by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), then ethical discipline (*śīla*) would include only ethical discipline; meditative concentration (*samādhi*) would include the dhyānas; and wisdom would include the latter five [categories]. If...

If one takes the associated factors (*sahāya*) into account, all [perfections] are mutually inclusive. If categorized according to their functional characteristics (*kāritra-lakṣaṇa*), ethical discipline (*śīla*) includes the first three:

giving is the equipment (*sambhāra*) for ethical discipline; ethical discipline is its essential nature (*svabhāva*); and patience is its retinue (*parivāra*). Concentration (*samādhi*) includes meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). Wisdom (*prajñā*) includes the latter five.

Diligence (*vīrya*) is included in all three, as it universally stimulates them all. If categorized according to their manifest characteristics (*vyakti-lakṣaṇa*), ethical discipline includes the first four.

The first three are as previously explained; [the fourth] is included in diligence because it guards the precepts; concentration includes meditative absorption (dhyāna); and wisdom includes the final five.

The Section on the Cultivation of All [Perfections] Throughout the Five Stages. Regarding these ten [perfections], if categorized by stage, they are present in all five stages; however, their characteristics are most manifest within the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Nevertheless, for the bodhisattva of sudden awakening during the first two stages—the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*) and the stage of application (*prayoga*)—the seeds of the ten perfections, though comprising both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) types, are nonetheless manifest.

As for those who practice [the path]: if they are *sāsrava* (with outflows)—as in the first two stages—then for a Bodhisattva of gradual realization, both seeds and manifestations belong to both types [of nature], because they have already attained the *anāsrava* (outflow-free) contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Within the stage of "thorough penetration" (*prativedha-avasthā*), seeds belong to both types, while manifestations are exclusively *anāsrava* (because they are correctly severing the seeds of the two obstacles of afflictions and cognizable objects, and have not yet emerged from contemplation).
As for the stage of "cultivation" (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), if it is prior to the seventh ground, then both seeds and manifestations belong to both types.

They encompass both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). (Whether it be the emptiness of persons or the emptiness of phenomena, whether emerging from or entering into them, because the sublime practices one cultivates should pertain to both.

From the eighth stage onward, the seeds pertain to both types, while the manifest [activity] is exclusively uncontaminated. Up to the ultimate state (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*), both the seeds and the manifest [activity] are exclusively uncontaminated.

that is, during the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa. At that time, the power of giving and the other perfections increases further, such that they are able to ultimately subdue all afflictions.

The Obstacle to Mastery.

First, the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*). This refers to that which arises from conceptual construction (*vikalpaja*) among the two obstacles—namely, the afflictive (*kleśa*) and cognitive (*jñeya*) obstacles—because the nature of an ordinary being is established based upon the seeds of those two conceptual obstacles.
When the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the Two Vehicles manifests, one severs only the [conceptual] afflictions.

The seeds [of the two obstacles] are termed "attaining the nature of an Ārya. When the Bodhisattva’s path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) manifests before him, he completely abandons these two kinds [of seeds], which is termed "attaining the nature of an Ārya.

When the two true paths of seeing manifest before him, those seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) can no longer be established, just as light and darkness certainly do not coexist, or like the two ends of a scale, where the rising and falling are simultaneous. This is because they are mutually contradictory.
This principle must necessarily be so. Therefore, there is no fault of the two natures [of wisdom and delusion] being established simultaneously.
First, I have distinguished that the severance of delusions in the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna is either extensive or narrow; next, I shall resolve the anticipated objection. The objection states:
Within the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), does one coexist with delusions, or does one not coexist with delusions? If one does not coexist with delusions, then...
If delusions were severed first and one subsequently attained the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), how could it be called "severing delusions through the Path of Seeing"?
If [the wisdom] coexisted with the delusions, then the Path of Seeing would come first and the severance of delusions later; this would constitute a "severance by opposition" (*pratipakṣa-prahāṇa*).

Furthermore, since wisdom and delusion would be simultaneous, there would be the fallacy of a single individual possessing both the natures of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and a noble one (*ārya*) at once. Now, we explain: it is also not the case that delusions are severed first and the Path of Seeing seen afterward.

The Path is also not such that one first perceives the Path and subsequently abandons the afflictions. Rather, at the very moment the two true paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) manifest, the seeds of the two obstacles necessarily cease to exist.
This is like the absence of darkness when there is light, or the absence of light when there is darkness;

it is also like the two ends of a balance scale, where one rises as the other falls, with no sequence between them. Therefore, it is not a case of affliction and wisdom meeting face-to-face as adversaries.

This is discussed in terms of "severance. Furthermore, it is not the case that one first severs the afflictions and only afterwards attains the Path of Vision; rather, at the very moment of correctly perceiving the Path, the afflictions do not arise.
Thus, while there is neither severing nor non-severing, it is spoken of as "severance."

(Question: If the seeds of affliction have already been eliminated at the time of the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*), what is the purpose of further arising the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)? (Answer:)

The path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is for the purpose of severing the afflictions; the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is for the purpose of realizing cessation. This is because their intentional orientations (*citta-āśaya*) differ.

Furthermore, it is in order to abandon the state of heavy dysfunction (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to that category of afflictions: although the seeds of the afflictions no longer exist during the time of the path of uninterrupted transition, one has not yet abandoned that state of unfitness (*akarmanyatā*).
In order to abandon this unfitness, and in order to realize the unconditioned analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of that category, the path of liberation arises.

The followers of the Hīnayāna falsely calculate that within the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), the seeds of affliction still exist, and that it is only upon reaching the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) that they are permanently severed.
This would entail the fallacy of both natures being simultaneously established. It is for this reason that the Mahāyāna refutes them, leading to this objection.
The answer and its explanation are as follows: "Coarseness" (*dausthulya*) is precisely the state of being unserviceable (*akarmanyatā*); it is the residue of the category of afflictions.
It is merely a matter of terminology.

however, for now, we speak of the afflictions that give rise to [those karmic results], because they are the root thereof. For this reason, it is said that in the first bhūmi, two [types of obstacles] are severed.

Why, however, are karma and its fruits also called "delusion"? [Answer: It should be understood that because karma and its fruits belong to the category of delusion (*moha-pakṣika*), they are also collectively designated as "delusion. [The following nine stages...]

The delusions regarding the commission of the three types of karma and so forth are all to be explained according to this principle. Alternatively, when it is said that two delusions are abandoned in the first bhūmi, this refers only to the two delusions associated with the category of obstacles consisting of the sharp proclivities (the five views) and the dull proclivities (greed and so forth), which arise simultaneously.
If it is said that the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) is severed, this refers only to the root [obstacle].

If it is said that two delusions (*moha*) are severed, this includes both karma and its fruit. Furthermore, if "delusion" is defined as a category of delusion, then the second delusion refers to karma and its fruit.

The term "delusion regarding the afflictions of the miserable realms" (*durgati-saṃkleśa-moha*) refers to the dull underlying tendencies (*mūla-anuśaya*).

The phrase "their coarse heaviness" (*dausthulya*) indicates the seeds of those two types of delusion; alternatively, it refers to the state of unserviceability (*akarmanyatā*) arising from those two delusions.

This is like the description of the abandonment of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkha-indriya*) upon entering the second dhyāna; although the faculty of suffering is abandoned there, [the seeds remain].

It is neither manifest activity—because such activity has already been suppressed—nor is it the seed—because the seeds have not yet been permanently severed—and yet it is termed "coarseness" (*dausthulya*).

This [coarseness] associated with the two delusions abandoned in the first stage should likewise be understood in this way; the term "coarseness" used for the subsequent nine stages should also be explained by analogy with this.

Because the seeds of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are severed gradually, part by part, whereas the seeds of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are merely suppressed and not yet severed, the meaning of "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) must be explained through these two interpretations: as seeds and as lack of functional capacity (*akarmanya*).

Although the afflictions abandoned during the path of seeing on the first bhūmi actually pertain to both obstacles—the afflictive and the cognitive—the "obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being" (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*) mentioned here refers specifically to the cognitive obstacle.

This is because the sūtras describe ten types of ignorance (*avidyā*) to be abandoned throughout the ten bhūmis as being non-afflictive in nature; thus, ignorance itself constitutes the delusions belonging to the category of the ten obstacles.
Furthermore, while the followers of the two vehicles are also able to abandon the afflictive obstacle, [the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being is not removed by them].

Because [these afflictions] are abandoned in common with the two vehicles, they are not what is being discussed here. Furthermore, the ten non-defiled types of ignorance are spoken of solely in reference to those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) on the ten stages (whereas the conceptual grasping at phenomena abandoned through seeing is indeed defiled).

Although within this stage [of the first bhūmi], one also suppresses a portion of the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) and abandons their coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*, i.e., the lack of functional capacity), this is not the primary intent; the primary intent lies solely in abandoning that which is to be abandoned through cultivation.
It is known that [the obstacle] is not severed; furthermore, because the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of those co-emergent afflictions are not abandoned, this is not mentioned.

In reality, even within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) of the first ground, a portion of the co-emergent cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is also severed. However, for now, only that which is severed at the very beginning (the path of seeing) is discussed;

therefore, it is said only that "the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*) is severed. One should understand that the severance in the subsequent nine grounds follows this same principle. Since the time spent dwelling in the perfected grounds is already long, [the obstacles are severed gradually].

It stands to reason that one must progress toward the abandonment of the obstacles that ought to be abandoned; otherwise, there would be no distinction between the three stages—the paths of uninterrupted continuity (*ānantarya-mārga*), liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and special advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*)—in the beginning, middle, and end.

Each of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) possesses three periods and three paths. The first period is called the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), which correctly severs the seeds of the afflictions of the stage itself.
The middle period is called the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), which correctly realizes the ultimate truth manifested by that stage.

The final period is called the path of advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*), wherein one again initiates preparatory application (*prayoga*) to sever the afflictions of the subsequent stages. Therefore, at the final moment of mind of the first stage...
It is subsumed under the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and also severs one portion of the innate (*sahaja*) objects of knowledge (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*).

Therefore, it is said that after a bodhisattva has attained clear realization (*abhisamaya*), they further cultivate only the path that eternally extinguishes the cognitive obscurations during the ten stages of the path of cultivation;
they retain the seeds of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*) to assist their aspirational vows (*praṇidhāna*) in taking birth within the three realms. This is not like...

The followers of the two vehicles quickly proceed toward parinirvāṇa; therefore, during the stage of cultivating the path, they do not sever the seeds of the afflictions, but only sever them suddenly at the time they are about to attain Buddhahood.
This statement clarifies that the final moment of mind (*cittakṣaṇa*) of the first stage (*bhūmi*) is precisely what is termed the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

It further clarifies the intention that one only severs the seeds of the innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), but does not sever the seeds of the innate afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Regarding "clear observation" (*abhisamaya*), it refers to the two types of clear observation mentioned previously in the fourth and fifth [sections].
The remainder may be understood accordingly. Question: Why do they retain the afflictive obstructions to assist their vows and undergo rebirth?
[Question: To which teaching and doctrine does this belong? [Answer: This meaning is profound and subtle; it cannot be hastily determined through superficiality.

Why is this so? Because in the *Hīnayāna* (Zàngjiào) system of the *Pāramitās*, one subdues the afflictions over three great eons (*tri-kalpa*) without having previously severed the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*).

If one follows the *Pratyekabuddha* and *Śrāvaka* paths of the *Common Teaching* (Tōngjiào), the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being severed at the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*) is identical to that of the two vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*), and there has never been...

Regarding the meaning of severing the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): by the time one reaches the Bodhisattva stages (*bodhisattvabhūmi*), even if these are completely severed, there is no principle of retaining afflictions as seeds for the purpose of sustaining habitual tendencies or moistening rebirth.
In the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna*), upon ascending the stages, one merely severs the seeds of the cognitive obstacles; furthermore, there is no principle of retaining afflictions.

This is even more unnecessary to mention in the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpannadharmaparyāya*). Now, speaking in terms of terminology, this [Perfect Teaching] generally encompasses the Separate Teaching.

This enters separately into the *sāmānya* (common) [category]. If one infers the underlying intent, it is a subtle revelation of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*). Please attempt to analyze this. The Treatise states:
"The grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) necessarily arises based on the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), just as at night one mistakes a tree stump for a person. Therefore...
Attachment to the self (*ātma-grāha*) is the afflictive obstruction (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*); attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) is the cognitive obstruction (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*).

How could it be that while the seeds of the cognitive obstruction have already been severed, the seeds of the afflictive obstruction still remain in actual existence? To say now that one "retains obstructions to assist vows" clearly refers to the skillful application of the dharma-gate of the inherent evil of nature (*prakṛti-pāpa-dvāra*).
Question: Why not state directly that on the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), one partially attains the single body of non-arising (*anutpāda-eka-kāya*)?
Regarding the measurement of capacity: what is called the Middle Way corresponds to the fundamental [nature]. It is like the moon reflected in a thousand rivers. One might then ask:

"Is it said that one retains the affliction-obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) to assist one’s vows for rebirth? The answer is: If this were so, it would mean that the Distinct (*byō*) is contained within the Perfect (*en*), and the Perfect enters the Distinct;
it is not a case of the Distinct entering the Shared (*tsū*). Rather, the Shared contains the meanings of both the Distinct and the Perfect. Question: To speak directly of the Distinct...
What is so wrong with including both the Perfect and the Shared Teachings? Why must they necessarily be accompanied by the provisional means of the Tripitaka and the Shared Teachings? The answer is:

since sentient beings are not yet capable of hearing the Distinct and the Perfect teachings directly, how could these not be accompanied by the provisional means of the Tripitaka and the Shared Teachings? Therefore, there are four teachings in the Dharma of Transformation.

All of these are the Tathāgata’s wondrous wisdom of provisional and ultimate truth, established in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings. How could one permit the partial abandonment of any? How could one permit partial attachment to any?

This treatise and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* share the same flavor as the Vaipulya sūtras; they primarily refute the clinging to dharmas in the Hīnayāna, while secondarily refuting the clinging to a self among ordinary people and non-Buddhists.
If the skillful means of the Shared Teaching were abandoned, those of Hīnayāna capacity would be cut off from their lot; by what means could they then be led in?

This is indeed the distinction between the Separate and the Perfect [Vehicles]. The first explanation of the obstacle of the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanatva*) is concluded. △ Second, the explanation of the obstacle of wrong conduct (*mithyāpratipatti*).

The second, the obstacle of wrong conduct, refers to a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the three karmas of body, speech, and mind that arise from it through transgressions.
This obstacle hinders the utterly pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) of the second stage (*bhūmi*); upon entering the second stage, one is able to sever it forever. By means of...
In this second stage (*bhūmi*), it is taught that two types of ignorance (*moha*) along with their corresponding heavy residues (*dausthulya*) are abandoned:

first, the ignorance of subtle transgressions, which is a portion of the innate [ignorance] mentioned here; and second, the ignorance regarding the various courses of action, which refers to the threefold karma of transgression arising from that [innate ignorance], or alternatively, the ignorance of initiating action without understanding its nature.

Question: Why are the three types of mistaken transgressions (*āpatti*) that arise also called "delusion" (*moha*)? Explanation: One is called deluded because, while initiating an action, one does not understand the nature of that action.
Due to this delusion regarding a portion of what is to be known (*jñeya*), one commits a mistaken transgression;
due to this delusion regarding the course of the action (*karmagati*), one is unable to immediately restore purity at that very moment. Question: Regarding the Śrāvaka at the beginning...
[Question: When one tills the soil, one immediately finds insects four inches away [from the blade]. Now, it is only upon reaching the second bhūmi that a Bodhisattva attains utterly pure śīla;
is this not nearly equal to the first fruit (srotāpanna)? [Answer: That the insects are four inches away is due to the power of the precepts associated with the Path (mārga-sahagata-śīla).

Regarding natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), one no longer commits them through error. As for subtle errors regarding prohibited transgressions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), even Arhats have not entirely avoided them;
thus, one knows that the sphere of the second stage is profoundly deep. △ Third, the explanation of the obstacle of dullness.

Third is the obscuration of dullness (*mṛdv-indriya-āvaraṇa*). This refers to a portion of the innate aspect of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) that causes one to forget what has been heard, reflected upon, and cultivated.

This obscuration obstructs the superior meditative concentrations and dhāraṇīs of the third stage (*bhūmi*), as well as the three types of sublime wisdom (*prajñā*) they produce. Upon entering the third stage, it can be permanently severed.

For this reason, it is said that at the third stage, two delusions (*moha*) and their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*) are abandoned: first, the desire for sensual pleasures (*kāma-rāga*).

Ignorance (*moha*) refers here to that which obstructs superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). It is a portion of the innate aspect of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that obstructs superior concentration and the wisdom born of cultivation.
Because it has long been associated with sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), it is termed "ignorance of sensual desire.

Now, having attained superior concentration and the wisdom born of cultivation, once that portion of the cognitive obscuration has been permanently severed, the sensual desire that was concomitant with it is likewise suppressed. This [sensual desire]...
Because it has operated in dependence upon that [a portion of the knowable] since beginningless time, there is the delusion regarding the perfection of the dhāraṇīs for hearing and retaining;

this is precisely that which can obstruct the wisdoms of hearing and reflection within this context (it does not fail to obstruct the wisdom of cultivation, but because it is proximate, it is mentioned specifically).
△ Fourth, the explanation of the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle afflictions.

The fourth is the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle afflictions. This refers to a portion of the innate aspect of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which is comprised of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth associated with the sixth consciousness.
Because it is of the lowest grade and because its conditions are not intentionally cultivated, it persists in accordance [with the mind] for a long time.
Because it functions [in these three ways], it is called "subtle. It obstructs the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) of the fourth stage;

upon entering the fourth stage, one is able to sever it forever. This cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is so designated as a "defilement" (*kleśa*) because, in the past, it frequently arose with the same substance as the spontaneously occurring grasping at a self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and other afflictions within the sixth consciousness.
Now, in the fourth stage, since one has attained [the realization of] non-existence...

The factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) that are associated with outflows (sāsrava) are thereby permanently extinguished; thus, this view of self (ātman-dṛṣṭi) and the like also never again arise.

On the first, second, and third stages, one practices generosity, ethical discipline, and cultivation, which are similar to those of worldly beings. On the fourth stage, one cultivates and attains the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Only then can it be called "transcending the world. Thus, it is able to permanently destroy this view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and other such views.

It is of the lowest grade, meaning it is exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*). It does not arise through deliberate attention (*amanasikāra-pratyaya*), but arises spontaneously (*svarasavāhin*). It persists by following along with current mental activity (*samudācāra*).

This refers to their mutual accompaniment since beginningless time. Because of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one is unable to cultivate the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and other such contemplations;

thus, they obstruct the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). Through the attainment of the factors conducive to enlightenment, those obstructions are severed accordingly, just as light and darkness, or like the rising and falling of the two ends of a scale.
[One practices] generosity in the first stage (*bhūmi*), ethical discipline in the second stage, and meditation in the third stage.

Regarding the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*): if one follows the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), they have long since transcended the world; if one relies on the Shared Teaching (*śrāvaka-yāna*), they are identical to those in the mundane world.

That is to say, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) corresponds to the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*); the Stage of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*) corresponds to the Stage of Nature (*gotra-bhūmi*);

the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*) corresponds to the Stage of the Eight Persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*); and the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*) corresponds to the Stage of Seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*), because in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* (or *Āgama-sūtra*), these are termed the stage of the *srotāpanna*.

However, in the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), the stage of "seeing the path" (*darśanamārga*) is designated as *srotāpanna*. This [Shared Teaching] merely eliminates the conceptualized view of self (*parikalpita-satkāyadṛṣṭi*), whereas this [Distinct Teaching] eliminates the subtle, innate view of self (*sahaja-satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
thus, they remain different. If one considers the ultimate meaning, it is simply the elimination of the subtle view of a dharma-self (*dharmātman-dṛṣṭi*) within the sixth consciousness.
Since the Distinct Teaching is elucidated by means of the Shared Teaching, how can there be any doubt?
(Question: How do we know that [the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth] are associated only with the sixth consciousness? (Answer:

The grasping at a self-view (*ātmagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and so forth associated with the seventh consciousness are contrary to the nature of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*); therefore, they cease to function forever from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward.

However, up until the seventh stage, they can still manifest, because the view of a self-body within that seventh consciousness serves as the support for the other afflictions, such as self-love (*ātmasneha*) and so forth. This...

(The sixth [consciousness] that is co-present with it) is coarse; that (the seventh consciousness that is co-present with it) is subtle. Because their subduing occurs sequentially, what is abandoned within this stage (the fourth bhūmi) is associated only with the sixth [consciousness].

The mention of "view of a self" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth also includes the attachment to meditative absorption (*samādhi-rāga*) and attachment to the Dharma (*dharma-rāga*), which are comprised within the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) from beginningless time.
Those attachments to absorption and the Dharma still increase even in the third stage; it is only upon entering the fourth stage that they can be permanently severed. Bodhi.

Regarding the method of classification: because it specifically contradicts that [previous state], the fourth stage (*caturthī bhūmiḥ*) is said to eliminate two delusions (*moha*) along with their corresponding heavy residues (*dausthulya*).

First is the delusion of craving for meditative attainment (*samāpatti-tṛṣṇā-moha*), which corresponds here to that associated with craving for concentration (*dhyāna-tṛṣṇā*). Second is the delusion of craving for phenomena (*dharma-tṛṣṇā-moha*), which corresponds here to that associated with craving for the teachings (*dharma-tṛṣṇā*).

Since these two delusions are subsumed under the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the two cravings—namely, craving for concentration and craving for the teachings—which are subsumed under the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), are likewise eliminated.

To never practice [the path] but instead to indulge in and take pleasure in various *dhyānas* and *samādhis* is called "craving for concentration" (*samāpatti-tṛṣṇā*). To indulge in and take pleasure in the cultivation of hearing, reflection, and meditation is called "craving for the Dharma" (*dharma-tṛṣṇā*).

Regarding "attainment" (*samāpatti*): in Sanskrit it is called *samāpatti*, which refers to the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and the four [immeasurables].

Form, the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and so forth. △ Fifth, the explanation of the obstacle to parinirvāṇa in the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

Regarding the fifth, the obstacle to parinirvāṇa in the Lesser Vehicle: it refers to a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that causes one to loathe cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and aspire to nirvāṇa, being identical to the aversion to suffering and longing for extinction found in the two lower vehicles. This obstacle [prevents] the [attainment of] non-differentiation in the fifth stage (*bhūmi*).

On the Path, when entering the fifth stage (*pañcamī bhūmi*), one is able to permanently sever [these delusions]. For this reason, it is said that in the fifth stage one severs two delusions (*moha*) along with their coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*):
first, the delusion of purely directing the mind away from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), which refers here to those who are weary of birth-and-death;
second, the delusion of purely directing the mind toward nirvāṇa, which refers here to those who delight in nirvāṇa.

Ordinary beings delight in birth and death while remaining ignorant of nirvana; they are certainly deluded. Those of the Two Vehicles delight in nirvana while utterly loathing birth and death; they too are deluded.
This is because they do not understand that both birth and death and nirvana are equally *paratantra* (dependently originated), lacking any substantial reality.
If there is no substantial reality, then as they share the same nature of *paratantra*, there is no distinction between them. If one realizes this...
Realizing that the ultimate is without differentiation, one is already distinct from ordinary beings; how then could one be willing to be the same as those of the Two Vehicles?

Therefore, while fully understanding the faults and afflictions of saṃsāra, one does not single-mindedly focus on turning away from it, because one desires to seek all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) within it.
While fully understanding the peace and bliss of nirvāṇa, one does not single-mindedly focus on heading toward it, because one desires to [bring benefit] to sentient beings...
Because they are born together and attain unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. △ Sixth, the explanation of the obstacle of the manifestation of coarse characteristics (*sthūla-nimitta-pravṛtti-āvaraṇa*).

The sixth obstacle of the manifestation of coarse characteristics refers to a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) cognitive obscuration (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*), which consists of the manifest adherence to the coarse characteristics of defilement and purity.
This obstructs the path free from defilement and purity in the sixth stage (*bhūmi*). Upon entering the sixth stage, one is able to sever it forever. By means of...
In this sixth stage, it is taught that two types of ignorance and their associated coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*) are abandoned:

first, the ignorance regarding the observation of the flow of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), which refers here to the clinging to the existence of a defiled agent, because all flowing conditioned phenomena are subsumed under the category of the defiled;

second, the ignorance regarding the frequent manifestation of signs (*nimitta*), which refers here to the clinging to the existence of a pure agent, because one grasps at the signs of purity within the gate of cessation (*nirodha*). This is the contemplation of signs.
One practices extensively, yet is unable to abide in the contemplation of signlessness for a long duration (being able to enter the contemplation of signlessness only for a short time).
In the sixth stage, the most excellent *prajñā* manifests before one; regarding the dependent origination of arising and ceasing, there is absolutely nothing to be apprehended.
One thus realizes the *tathatā* that is neither defiled nor pure. Therefore, the path by which this realization is attained is also called the "path of neither defilement nor purity. △ Seven.
This explains the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle characteristics.

The seventh obstacle is the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle characteristics. This refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that involves the manifestation of subtle characteristics, such as grasping at arising and ceasing.
It obstructs the sublime path of signlessness (*animitta*) of the seventh stage. Upon entering the seventh stage, one is able to sever it forever. Because...
In this seventh stage, it is said that two delusions and their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*) are abandoned:
first, the delusion of the manifestation of subtle signs, which is the grasping at existence within this [stage], because one still apprehends the subtle signs of arising in the process of *saṃsāra*;

second, the delusion of seeking the signless through exclusive mental attention, which is the grasping at cessation within this [stage], because one still apprehends the subtle signs of cessation in the process of returning to extinction. Regarding the exclusively... [in the signless]...
While diligently applying mental attention to signs, they are unable to skillfully initiate superior practices within signless emptiness.
△ The eighth [topic]: Obstacles to the application of effort regarding signlessness (*animitta*).

Regarding the application of effort toward the eight types of signlessness, this refers to a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which prevents the contemplation of signlessness from arising spontaneously.
In the first five stages (*bhūmi*), contemplation with signs (*nimitta*) is predominant and contemplation without signs is scarce; however, in the sixth [stage]...
In the [seventh] stage, there is little contemplation with signs (*sanimitta-bhāvanā*) and much contemplation without signs (*animitta-bhāvanā*).

Although in the seventh stage pure contemplation without signs continues uninterruptedly, it still involves applied effort (*prayoga*). Because there is applied effort within the signless state, one is not yet able to manifest forms and lands spontaneously (*anābhoga*).
Such applied effort constitutes an obstacle to the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*) in the eighth stage. Thus, when one enters the eighth stage...
At that time, one is able to permanently sever them. Because they are permanently severed, one attains two kinds of mastery.

For this reason, it is said that in the eighth stage one severs two delusions along with their coarse residues (*dausthulya*): first, the delusion of exerting effort regarding the signless (*animitta*); second, the delusion of lacking mastery over signs.
This is because [the latter] causes one to lack mastery over signs—and these "signs" do not refer solely to bodily signs, as they also include a portion of the signs of the [buddha-]lands.
From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, because the purely untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) arises spontaneously, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms never manifest again;

however, the subtle cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the seventh consciousness may still arise, as the fruit of the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*) has not yet been fully realized.
Because it does not contradict that [subtle cognitive obscuration].
Second, regarding mastery: it refers to the spontaneous manifestation of forms and the manifestation of buddha-fields. The rest may be understood.
△ Ninth, the explanation of the obstacle to the lack of desire to act for the benefit of others.

The ninth is the obstacle of being unwilling to engage in altruistic activity. This refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that causes one to be disinclined toward diligently engaging in activities for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, instead taking pleasure in cultivating one’s own welfare. This obstruction hinders the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) of the ninth stage;
upon entering the ninth stage, it can be permanently severed. For this reason, it is said that in the ninth stage, two delusions and their coarse residues are abandoned.

[This section concerns] the heavy [obstructions]: first, the ignorance regarding the mastery of the *dhāraṇī* of successive wisdom over the immeasurable names, phrases, and syllables within the immeasurable teachings that have been expounded.
Regarding "mastery over the *dhāraṇī* of the immeasurable teachings that have been expounded," this refers to the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
It is mastery over the retention (*dhāraṇī*) of what is signified, because one manifests all meanings within a single meaning. Regarding the immeasurable names...
Mastery over the dhāraṇī of phrases and syllables refers to the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*);
it is mastery over the retention of that which expresses, because within a single name, phrase, or syllable, all names, phrases, and syllables are manifested.

Mastery over the dhāraṇī of subsequent wisdom and eloquence refers to the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*); it is the retention of the successive explanations and etymological definitions of speech and sound.
Mastery (*vaśitā*). Because within a single sound one manifests all sounds, there is the delusion regarding mastery over eloquence (*pratibhāna-vaśitā-moha*).

Mastery over eloquence refers to the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*); it is the skillful ability to preach by thoroughly understanding the capacities and needs [of listeners].
This delusion obstructs these four kinds of mastery; all such obstructions are subsumed under this ninth hindrance.

Because its essential nature consists of the subtle cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the seventh consciousness, it prevents the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) from attaining mastery;
therefore, they are called the "two delusions. These can obstruct the ninth stage (*bhūmi*). Now that one has ascended to the ninth stage, these obstructions are forever severed.

Just as light and darkness, they certainly do not arise together. Regarding the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*): first is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), which refers to unimpeded mastery in comprehending that which is expressed;
second is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), which refers to unimpeded mastery in comprehending that which expresses.
Third is the unimpeded analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), which refers to the unimpeded mastery of verbal sounds and expressions.

Fourth is the unimpeded analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), which is what is here termed the "unimpeded analytical knowledge of discernment" (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*); it refers to the unimpeded and skillful exposition of the Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Now, that which obstructs the first three types is collectively designated as the first delusion, while that which obstructs the latter—eloquence—is named the second delusion. △ Ten Explanations.
Regarding the obstacles to attaining mastery over all phenomena, there are two further aspects: first, the direct explanation of this obstacle; second, the incidental explanation of other obstacles.
Now, for the first:
the obstacle to attaining mastery over all phenomena refers to a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) aspect within the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which causes...
One does not attain mastery over all phenomena. Those [obstructions] hinder the great cloud of dharma-knowledge of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) and the activities arising from what it contains;

upon entering the tenth stage, they can be permanently severed. For this reason, it is said that the tenth stage severs two delusions (*moha*) along with their coarse habitual tendencies (*dauṣṭhulya*):
first, the delusion regarding the great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which refers here to the hindrance to the activity of performing emanations for the sake of others (*parārtha*).
The second is the delusion regarding the subtle and secret [reality], which constitutes the obstacle here to the great dharma-cloud of wisdom and that which is contained within it.
The "great dharma-cloud of wisdom" refers to the wisdom that contains; "that which is contained" refers to the powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth.
This is the merit. △ Second, the simultaneous explanation of the remaining obstacles:
Although one has attained mastery over the dharmas in this stage, there remain further obstacles such that it is not yet called "ultimate.

Specifically, there exists a subtle, innate cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), as well as the seeds of spontaneously arising afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*). [One must wait] until the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) manifests.

At that time, they all suddenly sever [these obstacles] and enter the stage of the Tathāgata. For this reason, it is said that on the Buddha-stage one abandons two types of ignorance along with their coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*):
first, the ignorance of extremely subtle attachment toward all objects of knowledge, which is precisely the subtle cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) herein;
second, the ignorance of extremely subtle hindrance, which is precisely the seeds of all spontaneously arising afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) herein. Therefore...
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that at the moment of attaining enlightenment, one simultaneously abandons the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
thereby becoming an Arhat and a Tathāgata, as one realizes great nirvāṇa and great bodhi.
By severing the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one realizes great *nirvāṇa* and is called an *arhat*; this borrows the meaning of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*).

By severing the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one realizes great *bodhi* and is called a Tathāgata; this reveals the meaning of the Distinct and Perfect Teachings (*viśeṣa- and saṃpanna-yāna*).
However, even a Buddha of the Shared Teaching severs the cognitive hindrances within the realm of desire and form and realizes the *bodhi* of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
[The Buddha] said: "Tí. The Buddhas of the Separate and Perfect [Vehicles] likewise sever the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*) beyond the realms and realize non-abiding *nirvāṇa*.

Above, within the section on the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), the three explanations of the ten layers of obstacles have been completed: first, the formal introduction; second, the main explanation;

and third, the conclusion regarding their subsumption under the two obstacles. First, the formal conclusion on their inclusion within the two obstacles; second, the clarification of the meaning of the abandonment of the two obstacles. Now...
First:
These eleven hindrances are all comprised within the two obstacles—namely, the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Second: Clarifying the meaning of the abandonment of the two obstacles has two parts: first, the stages of abandoning the seeds and the manifest states; second, the sudden and gradual abandonment of the seeds.

First: Among the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the seeds to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) are severed at the very beginning of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) on the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

Their manifest activity (*samudācāra*) has already been suppressed prior to that stage. As for the seeds to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they are [severed] by the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) when it is present.
Previously, all [afflictions] were severed instantaneously; as for those obstacles that manifest, they are gradually suppressed prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
From the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward, one is able to suppress them entirely and instantaneously so that they never again arise—just like an Arhat.

Therefore, by the power of intentional effort (*abhiprāya*), even if they should temporarily manifest during the first seven stages, it does not constitute a fault. From the eighth stage upward, they are ultimately [eliminated].

It is not so. Among the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the seeds to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) are severed at the very beginning of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) on the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
The active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of those obstructions have already been suppressed prior to that stage.

As for the seeds to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they are gradually eliminated throughout the ten stages until, at the moment the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, they are finally and completely eradicated. Such is that obstruction.
As for their manifestation, they are gradually suppressed prior to the [first] bhūmi and are permanently and completely severed only upon reaching the tenth bhūmi.

From the eighth bhūmi upward, if they are associated with the six consciousnesses, they no longer manifest, because the continuum consists of the outflow-free contemplative mind and the fruit-aspect of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*).

Because it can oppose the manifestation of that [congenital cognitive obscuration within the sixth consciousness], if it were associated with the seventh consciousness, it would still be able to manifest;

however, it must be suppressed only at the stage when the fruit of the wisdom of dharma-emptiness arises. As for the first five evolving consciousnesses, even if they have not yet undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), because they are suppressed by untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-bhāvanā*), the obscuration does not arise.
This is the correct explanation of the stage where the seeds and active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of the two obstacles are correctly severed and eliminated.
Although within the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one does not sever the seeds of the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*), their coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*;
lack of functional capacity) is also gradually severed and eliminated. For this reason, it is said that for each of the two obstacles, there are three types of coarse heaviness.

This explains the meaning of "abandonment at the stages. This serves as a response to an objection. The objection states: "While the seeds of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are gradually abandoned throughout the ten stages, it may be said that the meaning of abandonment applies to all three stages.
However, as for the seeds of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), their conceptualized portion is..."

Those [afflictions] abandoned suddenly upon the Path of Seeing are abandoned all at once by the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*) for those that are innate (*sahaja*). Thus, there is only the sense of abandonment occurring in two stages.
Why, then, is it said that there is also a sense of abandonment occurring in three stages? The answer and its explanation can be understood as follows.

What are called the "three stages" are: first, the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*); second, the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*); and third, the stage of culmination (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*).

Although the heavy obscurations (*dausthulya*) are severed throughout all stages, they are specifically mentioned in three stages; this also serves as a response to an anticipated objection. The objection states: "If the term 'heavy obscuration' refers solely to the state of being unserviceable (*akarmanyatā*), then since there is also the sense of severing heavy obscurations during the stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and the application (*prayoga*), why are they not mentioned?

The answer may be explained as follows: [The answer: Although the heavy obscurations are indeed severed in those two stages, their severance is not explicitly taught because it is not yet complete. In the stage of the equipment, the heavy obscurations are severed only partially, and in the stage of the application, they are severed only to a limited extent.

It is only in the subsequent stages that they are severed in their entirety. Therefore, the teaching focuses on the stages where the severance is most prominent. Furthermore, the term "heavy obscuration" is used here to refer to the seeds (*bīja*) of the afflictions, which are the primary objects of abandonment. Since these seeds are severed in their entirety only in the three aforementioned stages, they are the ones specifically designated. Thus, the explanation is established.
[Understood. The section on the stage of severing the seeds and manifestations is concluded. △ Second, the sudden and gradual severance of the seeds. (Question:
Regarding the severance of the seeds of the two obstacles, what is the nature of their gradual or sudden occurrence? (Answer:

As for the seeds of the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*) associated with the seventh consciousness, when those of the three vehicles are about to attain the fruit of Arhatship, they are severed all at once across the three realms within a single moment. As for the seeds of the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), when...

At the time of attaining Buddhahood, all [afflictive obstructions] are severed instantaneously within a single *kṣaṇa*. This is because they arise spontaneously from within and lack the distinction between coarse and subtle.

As for the seeds of the afflictive obstructions associated with the remaining six consciousnesses: those belonging to what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) are all severed instantaneously within the True Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) during the stage of seeing of the Three Vehicles.
Those belonging to what is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are severed according to their respective conditions—either all at once or in two categories.

[Regarding] the afflictions co-arising with the three realms and nine stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*), each is gradually severed in nine distinct grades. Furthermore, there is a class of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* who combine the afflictions co-arising with the three realms and nine stages into a single aggregate and sever them in nine distinct grades.
As for Bodhisattvas, they must give rise to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) to suddenly sever all afflictions of the three realms in a single moment.
Regarding the seeds of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), [they are severed] at the first thought-moment of the first stage (*bhūmi*).

Those [afflictions] to be abandoned by seeing are all severed instantaneously; however, those to be abandoned by cultivation are severed gradually during the subsequent stage of the path of cultivation across the ten bhūmis, until they are finally exhausted entirely within a single moment when the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*) actually arises.

(This is because the cognitive obstructions associated with the six consciousnesses arise by taking both internal and external coarse and subtle objects as their general conditions, and there are distinctions among their categories.)
Because they are numerous, [it is impossible] to sever them all at once;
this precisely clarifies the seeds that are to be severed. Below, it further clarifies the path capable of severing them.

Because the faculties of those of the Two Vehicles are dull, when they gradually sever the afflictions co-arising with the six consciousnesses, they must each separately give rise to the Path of Uninterruptedness (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
(Regarding the two paths: If it concerns the preparatory (*prayoga*) and the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*), they may be either distinct or combined.
If the superior progress of the preceding stage serves as the preparatory stage for the subsequent one, this is termed "combined. Alternatively, they may not be simultaneous.
This is what is meant by "distinct.

Because Bodhisattvas possess sharp faculties, they do not need to separately give rise to the two paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) during the stage of gradually severing the cognitive obstructions (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) that arise simultaneously with the six consciousnesses;

rather, they are able to sever and realize [these obstructions] within each and every moment. Therefore, the four paths, such as the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), occur in every single moment.
When these preceding and succeeding moments are viewed in relation to one another, each is fully present.

To be able to sever [afflictions] in every moment is the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*); to be able to realize [the fruit] in every moment is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Not abiding in that liberation constitutes further progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*). This further progress in this stage is, moreover, the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the subsequent stage; it is precisely the application itself.
Furthermore, during the stage of practice, that which constitutes an obstruction or a principle in a subsequent state is capable of being severed or realized.

Therefore, within each moment of thought, in relation to what precedes it, it constitutes liberation and superior progress; in relation to what follows it, it constitutes preparatory application and immediate succession.
This concludes the third section: the explanation of the ten layers of obstructions. △ Fourth: the explanation of the ten suchnesses.

Regarding the ten kinds of suchness: first is the suchness of universal pervasion. This means that this suchness is revealed by the two kinds of emptiness, for there is not a single dharma that does not abide within it.

In the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), one deeply contemplates the emptiness of both self and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*) and permanently severs the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*).

Therefore, the true suchness (*tathatā*) realized within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is called "universal" (*sarvatraga*). This refers to [the realization] regarding the five categories and one hundred dharmas (*pañca-vastu śata-dharma*).
Each and every person (*pudgala*) lacks substantial reality, and likewise, phenomena (*dharma*) lack substantial reality.

The absence of a substantially real person is called the emptiness of living beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*), and it is also called the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*) or the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).

The absence of substantially real phenomena is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), and it is also called the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). To realize that neither self nor phenomena can be apprehended is what reveals that there is only...
The true nature of consciousness is not false; therefore, it is called "True" (Bhūta). This nature is unchanging; therefore, it is called "Suchness" (Tathatā).
Since beginningless time, ordinary worldlings have falsely clung to a real self and real dharmas. Although this True Suchness is omnipresent, they remain unaware of it in their daily lives.
While those of the Two Vehicles have severed the clinging to a self, they still do not understand the emptiness of dharmas.
The suchness that is revealed is omnipresent; yet, one still forms two distinct conceptualizations regarding the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Furthermore, some may falsely maintain that form, the non-associated formations, and unconditioned phenomena are not identical to consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

Only those possessing the Mahāyāna lineage, having first gained faith and understanding in this principle of consciousness-only, give rise to the profound and firm resolve for great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).

In the stage of accumulation and application, the mind forcefully contemplates that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, causing the two types of emptiness contemplation to gradually permeate and become firmly established.
This continues until the stage of penetration, where the seeds of the two obstacles of conceptualization are suddenly severed.
One then truly touches and realizes the principle of the *tathatā-dharmadhātu*. It pervades all five positions and one hundred dharmas, being present everywhere.
Consequently, one is able to attain the "Gate of Illumination of the One Hundred Dharmas. Within each and every dharma, one fully realizes the nature of *tathatā* which is omnipresent.
One should know that the nature of *tathatā* is inherently pervasive; it is not only pervasive now for the first time. However—
Because at the beginning of this stage one first realizes the essence of *tathatā* (suchness), which is fundamentally all-pervasive, it alone receives the name "all-pervading" (*sarvatraga*).
The designations for all subsequent stages do not go beyond being established according to their specific qualities; there is no second suchness.

Based on the true meaning of this all-pervading *tathatā*, it is said that the first stage is fully endowed with the merits of all stages. This is based on the subsequent [distinctions] according to their qualities.

This is the meaning established by the designation [of the stages]. Therefore, it is said that those in the first stage do not know the second stage, and so on, up to Bodhisattvas at the level of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi), who do not know such matters as the Tathāgata’s lifting and setting down of his feet.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "All worthy sages are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Now, how could there be distinctions within the unconditioned dharma itself? It is only in the realization of the unconditioned dharma that [distinctions arise].
There still remains a distinction. It is like how both the shallow and the deep are all the great ocean, yet upon entering the sea, one still speaks of "shallow" and "deep.
Or it is like using fathoms and inches to manifest space, while space itself is fundamentally not measured by fathoms or inches.

This pervasive true suchness (sarvatraga-tathatā) is likened to the new moon when it first begins to appear; although its entire form and great function are already visible, it is no different from the full moon after the fifteenth day.
Nor does one immediately expect it to be like the full moon at night. Reflect on this, reflect on this:
the two most supreme *tathatā*s (suchnesses). That is to say, this *tathatā* possesses boundless virtues and is the most supreme among all phenomena.
It is simply the principle of the universally pervasive true suchness (*sarvatraga-tathatā*) revealed by the two kinds of emptiness within the five categories and one hundred dharmas.
It has been inherently endowed with boundless virtues and has always been supreme; it is only due to delusion since beginningless time that it is obstructed by erroneous practices.

This supreme virtue was previously prevented from manifesting; now, because the Bodhisattva understands that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is untainted and practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) accordingly, they sever the obstacles of misconduct.

Therefore, the essence of the threefold pure precepts (*tri-koṭi-śīla*) arising from their entire being is a wondrously unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) entity, endowed with boundless merit, and is the most supreme among all phenomena.

Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "Because the mind is inexhaustible, the precepts are also inexhaustible. One should know that because the objects of focus (*ālambana*) are boundless, the precepts are also boundless.
For example, regarding the precept against killing, one attains the virtue of non-killing with respect to all phenomena within the five categories and one hundred dharmas.

Regarding the precept against stealing, one attains the virtue of non-stealing with respect to all phenomena within the five categories and one hundred dharmas. Regarding the precept against sexual misconduct, [it likewise applies] throughout...
One attains the virtue of non-deviance regarding the one hundred dharmas of the five categories, as with the precept against false speech.
One attains the virtue of non-falsity throughout all one hundred dharmas of the five categories; this applies to each of the ten wholesome paths of action in the same way.

Furthermore, there is the virtue of severing evil throughout all one hundred dharmas of the five categories, which is likewise the virtue of producing goodness throughout all one hundred dharmas of the five categories. This also applies universally to the five [categories].

The hundred dharmas possess the virtue of delivering sentient beings. Severing evil is called the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint); this constitutes the merit of severance (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) of the *dharmakāya*.

Generating goodness is called the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering wholesome dharmas); this constitutes the merit of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) of the *sambhogakāya*. Delivering sentient beings is called the *sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings);
this constitutes the merit of grace (*anugraha-guṇa*) of the *nirmāṇakāya*. Furthermore, these are precisely the *dharmakāya*, *prajñā*, and *vimukti*.
Virtue. One should know that the entire substance of True Suchness (tathatā) is raised as the threefold pure precepts (tri-śikṣā-saṃvara).

Furthermore, each and every one of these threefold pure precepts is none other than the entire substance of True Suchness. Therefore, they are universally boundless horizontally and supremely excellent vertically.
There is not a single dharma that is not infinite; there is not a single dharma that is not most excellent.
Regarding the "True Suchness of the Threefold Excellence": this refers to the teaching that flows from this True Suchness, for it is far more excellent than all other teachings.
This is also merely the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*) among the one hundred dharmas of the five stages, as revealed by the two kinds of emptiness.
Although it cannot be described through any of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), it can nevertheless be explained due to the conditions of the four *siddhāntas*.

However, because of the obstructions caused by beginningless dullness and ignorance, one has been unable to accord with the principle and the capacity of beings to preach in accordance with their nature. Now, by means of the Bodhisattva’s skillful...
Skillfully augmenting the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as well as supreme meditative concentration and dhāraṇī, one severs the obstacle of dullness.

Thus, from True Suchness (tathatā) flows forth right knowledge; from within right knowledge flows forth subsequently attained knowledge; from within subsequently attained knowledge flows forth the mind of great compassion;
and from the mind of great compassion flow forth the twelve divisions of the sūtras—this is most supremely wondrous. If...
The teachings spoken by others, such as those of the two vehicles and ordinary beings, do not flow forth from the realization of *tathatā* (suchness);
therefore, they are not superior.
Fourth is the *tathatā* that is without appropriation; this means that this *tathatā* has no point of attachment and is not the basis for the grasping of a self (*ātman*) and so forth.
Because it is grasped, it is likewise the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*) revealed by the two kinds of emptiness within the five positions and hundred dharmas;
it is fundamentally unattached and has never been the basis or object of appropriation for self-grasping, self-love, self-conceit, or self-delusion, and so forth. It is merely due to...
Since beginningless time, it has been obstructed by the manifestation of subtle afflictions, such that its fundamental nature of being without grasping could not be realized.

Now, through the Bodhisattva’s skillful cultivation of the untainted factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), once these obstructions of the manifestation of subtle afflictions have been severed, the true nature (*tathatā*)—which is fundamentally without attachment—is finally manifested; this is termed "non-grasping" (*anupādāna*).
The *tathatā* of sensation;
the *tathatā* of the non-distinction of the five categories. That is to say, this *tathatā* is without differentiation of category, unlike the eye and so forth, which possess distinct categories.
This is also simply the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*) revealed by the two kinds of emptiness within the hundred dharmas of the five stages;

fundamentally, there is no distinction between birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa. It is only due to delusion from beginningless time that birth-and-death falsely arises. In contrast to that birth-and-death, [nirvāṇa is established].
One provisionally establishes nirvāṇa based on this illusory dependent origination of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, giving rise to false longing for the former and aversion toward the latter;

this is called the "obstruction to the parinirvāṇa of the Hīnayāna. Now, by means of the Bodhisattva’s profound contemplation of the equality of the Four Noble Truths, once this obstruction has been severed, the principle of True Suchness (tathatā), which is without differentiation among categories, finally manifests. This is said to be unlike the eye and other [sensory organs].

Regarding the differentiation of categories: this refers to how True Suchness (tathatā), remaining immutable while following conditions, gives rise to the distinct categories of the five stages and one hundred dharmas.

For instance, within the single category of form-dharmas (rūpa-dharma), there is the distinction between the sense organ (indriya) and the object (viṣaya); or, within the single category of sense organs, there is the distinction between the eye and the ear.
All of these belong to the nature of dependence on others (paratantra-svabhāva), being like illusions and the like; fundamentally, they are neither real self nor real dharmas.
Since they are neither a real self nor real dharmas, they share the same essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*). This is what is meant by "changing according to conditions yet remaining unchanging.
The eye is not the eye; the ear is not the ear. How could there be any further categories? Therefore it is said:

the two wisdoms of the ultimate and the conventional have mutually opposing modes of activity; to bring them into union and accord is called the Ground of Difficult Victory (*durjayā-bhūmi*). If one explains this according to the text:

Regarding the meaning: if one falsely claims that the eyes and other faculties are categorically distinct while True Suchness (tathatā) is categorically without distinction, then their modes of activity (ākāra) would still remain mutually contradictory.
Let the reader reflect upon this.
Sixth is the *tathatā* (suchness) that is neither defiled nor pure. This means that this *tathatā* is by nature undefiled and cannot be said to become pure only later.

It is also simply the principle of *tathatā* within the five positions and hundred dharmas as revealed by the two kinds of emptiness; it exists within the cycle of birth and death, yet remains [unaffected].
Regarding defilement (*saṃkleśa*): the realization of *nirvāṇa* is not something newly purified; rather, it is due to beginningless delusion that one falsely undergoes cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Based upon this cyclic existence, the "returning and ceasing" (*pratyāvṛtti-nirodha*) is provisionally taught. Cyclic existence is termed "defilement," and returning and ceasing is termed "purity.

To grasp these defilement and purity as being substantially real is called the "obstruction of the manifestation of coarse characteristics. Now, by means of the Bodhisattva’s profound contemplation of the equality of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), [this obstruction is overcome].
Once these obscurations have been severed, the reality of *tathatā* (suchness), which is fundamentally free from both defilement and purity, finally manifests.
Seventh is the *tathatā* of the non-differentiation of phenomena; this means that although this *tathatā* is established in various ways through numerous teachings, it remains without distinction.

It is likewise merely the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*)—the reality of the five positions and one hundred dharmas revealed by the two kinds of emptiness—upon which various teachings are established.
Yet this ultimate truth is fundamentally without differentiation; its characteristics are themselves formless, and emptiness and existence are harmoniously integrated.

It is simply because one does not realize that signs are fundamentally signless that one applies mental attention to diligently seek signlessness; this is called the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle signs.
Now, by means of the Bodhisattva’s skillful means practiced in accordance with the nature of reality, all Buddha-dharmas are fulfilled.
Once this obstacle of the manifestation of subtle signs has been severed, the wondrous principle of True Suchness (tathatā), in which phenomena have no differentiation, finally manifests.

The eighth is the *tathatā* of neither increase nor decrease. This means that this *tathatā* is free from the grasping at increase and decrease, because it does not undergo increase or decrease according to defilement or purity.
Furthermore, this is also called the *tathatā* that is the basis for mastery over marks and lands;
this is because once this *tathatā* has been realized, one possesses mastery over both manifesting the [physical] marks and manifesting the [buddha-]lands.
It is likewise merely the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*) revealed by the two kinds of emptiness within the one hundred dharmas of the five stages;

because it remains unchanging while following conditions, it cannot be increased or diminished by defilement or purity. Because it follows conditions while remaining unchanging, the manifestation of the lands of form is everywhere sovereign.
However, because one has not yet realized that the nature is without increase or decrease, one still directs the mind toward *tathatā* (suchness);

this is called the "obstruction to the application of effort within the signless. Now, because the bodhisattva has skillfully attained the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*) and deeply realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), having severed this obstruction to application, the essence that remains unchanging amidst conditions manifests spontaneously. This is called...
The *tathatā* (suchness) neither increases nor decreases; its function of remaining unchanging while following conditions manifests spontaneously.

This is called the *tathatā* that is the basis for mastery over marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and lands (*kṣetra*). One should know that within the five dharmas and the hundred dharmas, whichever single dharma one may select, all are without increase or decrease, and all constitute mastery over marks and lands.
"Marks" refers to the manifested body, while "lands" refers to the receptacle world.

The ninth is the *tathatā* (suchness) that is the basis for mastery over the nine knowledges; this means that once one has realized this *tathatā*, one attains mastery over the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, it is simply the principle of *tathatā* within the five categories and one hundred dharmas as manifested by the two kinds of emptiness, because each and every dharma...
Because it is suchness (*tathatā*), each and every phenomenon is able to sustain the entirety of all signified meanings;
each and every phenomenon is able to sustain the entirety of all signifying names, phrases, and syllables;
each and every phenomenon is able to sustain the entirety of all speech-sounds, definitions, and explanations; and each and every phenomenon is able to universally accommodate [all beings].
The capacities and dispositions of all sentient beings are skillfully and inexhaustibly explained, enabling them to attain the four benefits;

for this reason, this True Suchness (tathatā) is called the basis for mastery over wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*). However, due solely to the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one does not realize that a single meaning is all meanings, or that all meanings are a single meaning;
nor does one realize that a single phenomenon (*dharma*) is all phenomena, or that all phenomena are a single phenomenon.
They do not realize that all vocal sounds are contained within a single vocal sound, nor that all vocal sounds are contained within a single vocal sound;
