The same [transforming consciousnesses] that are wholesome and untainted (anāsrava) arise from purely wholesome and untainted causes and conditions;

they are subsumed under the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya), as they are neither suffering nor its origin. However, although the transforming consciousnesses are untainted, the characteristics of the transformed aggregates (skandha) and so forth need not necessarily be identical [to them], because they are produced through the combined influence of the three types of causes and conditions—the aggregates, bases, and elements within the minds of sentient beings.

Regarding the causes and conditions of pure, wholesome, and untainted [dharmas]: the ten realms (daśadhātu) of nature and characteristics inherently present within the immaculate consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*) serve as the cause;

while compassion, wisdom, practice, vows, and the responsive resonance of the capacities of all sentient beings serve as the conditions. As for the statement that the characteristics of the aggregates and other consciousnesses need not necessarily be identical:

this refers to cases such as when sentient beings enter the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), whereby their mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the three [other] consciousnesses...

The *dhātus*. Thus, they share the same untainted (*anāsrava*) nature as all Buddhas. Furthermore, if one has not yet entered the wisdom of the contemplation of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*), then the three categories of aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are exclusively comprised within the tainted (*sāsrava*).

However, when the Buddhas rely upon this tainted and untainted substrate (*bimba*) of sentient beings, they themselves transform it into untainted objective images (*nimitta-bhāga*). Indeed, the Buddha’s transformation is pure.

As for the land, it being purely wholesome and untainted (*anāsrava*), goes without saying. When the Buddha transforms a defiled land, it is produced through the causal conditions of the three factors of sentient beings;
therefore, the characteristics of consciousness do not necessarily have to be identical.

Nevertheless, within the portion belonging to the Tathāgata, although the reflections of the nine realms of existence (*navadhātu*) appear, those reflections of the nine realms are likewise entirely subsumed under what is purely wholesome and untainted.
It is said that when the fruits of the three thousandfold world-systems are perfected, they are all termed "eternal and blissful.

How could one not believe this? (That is to say, whether these bodies and lands are pure or defiled, if they are manifestations produced upon the out-flowing consciousnesses (*āsrava-vijñāna*) of the nine realms, they share the same nature as the transforming consciousnesses and are all out-flowing.

Being produced solely from out-flowing causes and conditions, they are subsumed under Suffering (*duḥkha*) and its Origin (*samudaya*), and are therefore neither Cessation (*nirodha*) nor the Path (*mārga*). [However, as for the transforming consciousness...]

Although [the Buddhas] are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), the characteristics of the consciousnesses transformed by them—which possess the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*)—need not necessarily be identical, because they arise through the diverse drawing-forth of causes and conditions from the minds of sentient beings (as the Buddhas manifest in accordance with the good, evil, or indeterminate states of those beings).

Thus, the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth [of the manifested Buddhas] may be either the same or different. One should understand it in this way; otherwise, the manifested Buddhas would lack the five aggregates, the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and so forth.

Regarding the causes and conditions for that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*): the ten realms (*dhātu*) of nature and characteristics inherently present within the maturation consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) act as the cause;

while the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, along with various meritorious deeds, accompanied by the two hindrances (*āvaraṇa*), act as the conditions. As for the statement that one should understand the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth to be either identical or different:
this means that if the Buddhas are within the minds of sentient beings, then the aggregates, bases (*āyatana*), and realms are all exclusively wholesome and non-defiled.

Regarding outflows (*āsrava*): if sentient beings perceive within their minds the noble assemblies of the Three Vehicles, then consciousness and its mental factors (*dharma*) belong to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
The preceding fifteen realms (*dhātu*), however, still belong to the outflowing (*sāsrava*).

Sentient beings, relying upon these four noble outflow-free and outflowing essences, each transform them into their own outflowing objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*). Indeed, those born who perceive an impure land belong exclusively to...

As for the outflowing [dharmas], there is no need for further discussion. When one gives rise to visions of the two lands—pure and impure—as well as the bodies of the Buddhas, these arise from the causes and conditions of the three natures and three dharmas manifested by the Buddhas. Therefore, the characteristics of consciousness do not necessarily all coincide.

However, within the realm of sentient beings, although they behold the reflections of the Buddha’s body and land, these reflections of the Buddha’s body and land are all subsumed under the category of outflows (*āsrava*).
This is what is meant by "the three thousand worlds existing in principle are collectively termed ignorance. How could one not believe this?

The first section, which correctly distinguishes between the outflowing and the non-outflowing, is concluded. △ Second, the section on synthesizing the five contemplations based on the three natures, in five parts. First, the demonstration.

1. The contemplation of discarding the unreal to preserve the real; 2. The contemplation of showing the abandonment of the mixed to retain the pure; 3. The contemplation of showing the gathering of the branches back to the root;
4. The contemplation of showing the discarding of marks to realize the nature; 5. The contemplation of showing the concealment of the inferior to reveal the superior. Question:

For what reason is the contemplation of concealing the inferior and revealing the superior placed after the contemplation of discarding marks and realizing the nature? Answer: Because once one has attained the realization of True Suchness (tathatā), one immediately realizes consciousness...
Regarding the true nature (*dharmatā*): one then realizes that *tathatā* is precisely the true nature of mental factors (*caitta*).

Once it is understood that there is no *tathatā* apart from the nature of consciousness, one further realizes that there is likewise no *tathatā* apart from the nature of mental factors. Therefore, those who eliminate [conceptual] marks (*nimitta*)...

This dispels the deluded nature and the marks of false perceptions regarding distinctions. To "realize the nature" means to realize that these very marks are none other than the nature of universal equality.
Now, the first [section].

However, the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and so forth manifest based upon consciousness; they are not like the nature of consciousness itself, which is the real [within the dependent nature] (the subtle conventional truth).

If it were otherwise, the principle of "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) would necessarily fail to be established, because one would be admitting that both consciousness and its internal objects are equally substantially existent.
Regarding this "contemplation that discards the unreal and preserves the real," there are two schools of interpretation.

The first is the position of Master Sthiramati, which holds that the two divisions of the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) are unreal, while the nature of self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is real. The phrase "the objective aspect, etc. implies the subjective aspect as well;
"the nature of consciousness" refers to the division of self-cognition.

Alternatively, the aspects of the object and the perceiving subject within consciousness, and so forth, all arise from conditions; they are both of the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Their unreality and reality are like the very essence of consciousness itself. One must understand that the term "only" (*vijñapti-mātra*) merely excludes [the existence of] a self and dharmas external to consciousness;

it does not negate the objective realm of the internal image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*). If this were not the case, then even *tathatā* (suchness), the truly real objective realm perceived by fundamental wisdom, would likewise have to be unreal.
This is precisely the correct principle for protecting the Dharma. That is to say, it negates the notion that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is real;

rather, all four divisions are the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is real. Regarding the statement that "the unreal and the real are like consciousness": from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), since the essence of consciousness is already like an illusion or a dream, the two divisions of the grasped (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the grasper (*darśana-bhāga*) that it transforms are also unreal.
From the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), however, the essence of the dependent consciousness is not [unreal].

No. The two parts—the perceived (nimitta) and the perceiving (darśana)—that are transformed are also real. Indeed, what is called "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra) uses the word "only" merely to exclude the self and dharmas that are grasped by pervasive conceptual construction (parikalpita) as being external to consciousness;
it does not simultaneously exclude these internal aspects of the perceived and the perceiving within consciousness itself.

Furthermore, for example, when fundamental real wisdom (mūla-tattvajñāna) takes True Suchness (tathatā) as its object, although it does not manifest by assuming its characteristics (ākāra), it is admitted that it grasps its essence and characteristics.
If one were to claim that the two divisions of aspect (nimitta-bhāga) and vision (darśana-bhāga) are unreal, then fundamental wisdom and True Suchness would likewise have to be unreal;
how could this possibly be acceptable? The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states: "The seeing, the objects of seeing, and the imagined characteristics..."
Like flowers in the sky, they fundamentally do not exist; this is the negation of marks according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Master An-hui established the first interpretation based on this. Furthermore, he said: "This seeing and its objects are originally the wondrously pure and luminous essence of bodhi."
How can there be "is" and "is not" within this? This refers to the fact that the conventional is eternally true.
Master Hu (Huiyuan) established the subsequent meaning based on this; therefore, Master Xuanzang preserved both explanations, as they can mutually illuminate one another.
However, those who cling to the first meaning will inevitably lose the subsequent meaning, whereas those who understand the subsequent meaning will necessarily penetrate the first.
Therefore, the preceding interpretation remains the correct one. △ Second, showing the abandonment of the redundant and the retention of the pure contemplation. (Question:

Since both the internal object and consciousness are neither unreal, why do you speak only of "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) and not [of "only seeing" or "only objects"]? (Answer: The term "only" (*mātra*) is used to exclude the external object, which is grasped as something separate from consciousness. It does not exclude the nature of consciousness itself. Therefore, it is said that there is "only consciousness," meaning that there is no external object apart from the manifestation of consciousness. This is because the internal object is not distinct from the consciousness that perceives it; they are of a single substance. Thus, while the object is not ultimately real, it is not entirely non-existent either, for it arises through the power of karmic seeds. Consequently, the term "only" serves to negate the duality of subject and object, establishing that what appears is nothing other than the transformation of consciousness. Hence, it is correctly termed "consciousness-only."

Consciousness exists only internally, whereas its objects extend to the external as well. Fearing that this might be confused with the externally apprehended nature of parikalpita-svabhāva, it is said to be "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra).
Alternatively, because foolish worldlings are deludedly attached to external objects, they give rise to afflictions and karma, sinking into the cycle of birth and death;

failing to understand that one must contemplate the mind to diligently seek liberation, the Buddha, out of compassion for them, spoke the term "consciousness-only" so that they might contemplate their own minds and attain liberation from birth and death. It is not... [the case].
This means that internal objects are entirely non-existent, just like external ones.
Objects are transformations of the mind; there are no objects outside the mind. Yet, ignorant people do not realize this is mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*) and falsely give rise to attachments.

From the arising of views comes the arising of craving; thus one undergoes the cycle of rebirth. Therefore, it is said that there is "only consciousness" (vijñapti-mātra), so as to cause them to contemplate the mind.
What is called "contemplating the mind" is simply to forcefully observe that all phenomena lack substantial reality and arise entirely through the transformation of consciousness;
by doing so, one can subdue and extinguish the deluded attachments of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). △ Third, showing the contemplation of returning the branches to the root.

Alternatively, the objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) and so forth all have consciousness as their essential nature (*svabhāva*). Through the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*), they arise appearing as many parts;
yet, that which is essentially a single nature of consciousness arises through the power of perfuming as if there were four distinct parts.

To speak in terms of ultimate reality, how could these secondary aspects of the objective and subjective parts ever be separate from the substance of consciousness? Thus, the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* says: "This is originally..."
The wondrously luminous, unsurpassed Bodhi, the pure, perfect, true mind, is falsely perceived as form, emptiness, hearing, and seeing—like a second moon.
Which of these is the real moon, and which is not? △ Fourth: Showing the contemplation that eliminates marks to realize the nature.
Suchness (*tathatā*) is likewise the true nature of consciousness; therefore, apart from the nature of consciousness, there is no separate dharma.

If one wishes to know that there is no consciousness outside of Suchness, one must first observe that there is no Suchness outside of consciousness. Only when one knows that there is no Suchness outside of consciousness does one realize that there is no consciousness outside of Suchness.
That there is no Suchness outside of consciousness means that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is not separate from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Just as there is no consciousness externally, so too the absence of nature in the dependent (*paratantra*) is itself the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*). Thus, the preceding verse states:
"The perfected is always devoid of that former nature; therefore, it is neither different nor non-different from the dependent."
It is further stated: "This ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena is also precisely suchness (*tathatā*), because its nature is eternally as-it-is.

It is the very reality of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra-tattva*). Is it not a grievous error for later commentators to falsely claim that within the Dharma-character school (*dharmalakṣaṇa-vāda*), suchness is established as something static and unchanging?
△ Fifth, showing the contemplation that conceals the inferior and reveals the superior.
In this context, the term "consciousness" (vijñāna) also includes mental factors (caitta), because the mind and its factors are necessarily associated.
However, since the superior subsumes the inferior, it is called "mere consciousness" (vijñapti-mātra); it does not mean that there are no distinct mental factors apart from the mind.
Each and every mental factor possesses the four divisions of the *paratantra-svabhāva*.

Each and every *paratantra* is neither different nor non-different from *tathatā*. Therefore, even in a single moment of thought, the three thousand realms are fully present. Were it otherwise, [the three thousand would not be complete].
To not fall into excessive deliberation is to fall into fragmentation; how could this be the dharma-meaning of the Middle Way of the Mahāyāna?

Generally speaking, the dharma-gate of the cultivation and realization of Consciousness-Only does not, in its entirety, depart from these five contemplations. When compared with Nanyue’s *Mahāyāna Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, they follow the same track.
First, "expelling the false to preserve the real"; second, "abandoning the mixed to retain the pure"—this refers to the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

This is the contemplation of cessation (*nirodha-vipaśyanā*). Third is "subsuming the derivative back into the fundamental," which is the contemplation of cessation and insight regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Fourth is "dispelling appearances to realize the essence," which is the contemplation of cessation and insight regarding the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Fifth is "concealing the inferior to reveal the superior," which refers to the implicit and explicit presentation of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) for both the defiled and pure aspects; all of these may fully incorporate the preceding four types of contemplation. Why is this so? If...
If one discusses only the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), the distinctions between defilement and purity are not revealed;
it is only by discussing the associated mental factors (*caitta*) as well that one comes to know how the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) differ from one another.

Since the four contemplations can be discussed with respect to the mind-king, they may likewise be discussed with respect to the mental factors. For instance, taking any single phenomenon such as greed, hatred, or delusion: if one eliminates the unreal and preserves the real...
Thus one knows that the external objects of craving do not exist. If one discards the defiled and retains the pure, one knows that even the internal objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is empty.
If one reabsorbs the derivative into the fundamental, one knows that the subject who craves and the object craved originally have no dual substance.

If one eliminates appearances to realize the nature, one knows that the true nature of craving is itself the nature of *tathatā*. Hatred, delusion, pride, and so forth are to be understood by this same analogy.

This can be understood. If even unwholesome dharmas are thus, then the benefit of neutral and wholesome dharmas is all the more evident. If even tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas are thus, then the benefit of untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas is all the more evident.

Therefore, one is able to pervade the five categories and one hundred dharmas, penetrate the three natures and the three non-natures, and achieve the contemplative gate of the non-duality of the ultimate and the conventional.
This is the essential secret for transmitting the mind from Buddha to Buddha and from Patriarch to Patriarch.
This is the true source of the Dharma-nature and the characteristics of phenomena. I pray that those possessed of wisdom will reflect with care, discern clearly, and practice it with devotion.

Do not fall into the traps of merely seeking out passages or picking at phrases; do not invite the reproach of one who counts sands or tallies jewels; do not sacrifice yourself to worldly conventions by circulating stale words;
and do not commit the offense of stubbornly clinging to polemical disputes. In this way, you may hope not to fail Vasubandhu, the protector of the Dharma.

This also does not辜负 (fail to repay) the compassionate power of the great Bodhisattvas, nor the painstaking efforts of the masters and disciples, such as Śīlabhadra and Xuanzang, in the transmission of the teachings.
The above concludes the second major section: the extensive exposition based on the scriptures.

△ Third, the section on the commentary and the dedication of merit (the *śāstrasaṃgraha* and *pariṇāmanā*) is divided into two parts: first, the commentary; second, the dedication of merit. Regarding the first:
this treatise establishes Vijñaptimātra through its three sections; therefore, it is called the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
It is also called the *Viśuddhavijñapti*, because it reveals the principle of Vijñaptimātra with extreme clarity and purity.

This first explains the conclusion of the commentary. There are three divisions: namely, the three members of inference consisting of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*);

furthermore, the three stages of the concise and extensive [teachings]; the three divisions of object (*viṣaya*), practice (*pratipatti*), and fruition (*phala*); and the three divisions of characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), nature (*svabhāva*), and stage (*avasthā*). Thus, the *Kai-meng* says:

There are three types of threefold categories (*triskandha*). First, the threefold category of the concise and extensive stages: the first one and a half verses provide a concise answer to external objections and briefly indicate the characteristics of consciousness (*vijñāna*);
the next twenty-three and a half verses extensively clarify the characteristics of consciousness to manifest the meaning of the preceding verses;
and the final five verses clarify the stages of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Second, the threefold category of object, practice, and fruit: the former...

The twenty-five verses clarify the realm of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*). The subsequent four verses clarify the practice of consciousness-only. The final verse clarifies the fruit of consciousness-only.
Regarding the three characteristics, the natures, the stages, and the three categories: the preceding twenty-four verses clarify the characteristics of consciousness-only.
The twenty-fifth verse clarifies the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*). The final five verses clarify the stages of consciousness-only.
It should be understood that these three sections constitute the three parts [of the treatise].
This root treatise is titled *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratā* (The Thirty Verses on Consciousness-Only), as it elucidates consciousness-only through thirty verses composed by the Great Being Vasubandhu.
The principle is thus rendered complete, for there is neither addition nor subtraction from the root verses (*mūla-kārikā*).

This further explains and concludes the treatise of our own school. It is not that brevity is insufficient to provide a guiding framework, nor that extensiveness is insufficient to exhaust the meaning;
it is not that [the structural] stages are insufficient to clarify cultivation and realization. Therefore, the thirty verses admit of neither increase nor decrease. Furthermore—

Without the objective realm (*viṣaya*), it is insufficient to guide practice; without practice, it is insufficient to realize the fruit; and without the fruit, it is insufficient to verify the objective realm.
Therefore, the Thirty Verses admits neither addition nor subtraction. Furthermore, without characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is insufficient to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox;

without nature (*svabhāva*), it is insufficient to harmonize emptiness and existence; and without stages (*avasthā*), it is insufficient to verify nature and characteristics. Thus, the Thirty Verses...

There is no room for addition or subtraction. Now, based on these thirty verses, I shall provide an exposition. First, I will extensively refute the two attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*), briefly clarifying that there are only three transformations (*pariṇāma*).
Next, I will extensively explain the characteristics of these three transformations and clarify that what is transformed is consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Having thus refuted the two types of pervasive attachment—self and phenomena—within the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), [the text proceeds].
By calculation, one immediately knows that the *tathatā* (suchness) revealed by the two kinds of emptiness is neither different nor non-different from the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).

Thus, the principles of the ultimate and conventional truths become clear, and their natures and characteristics mutually penetrate. By relying on this to initiate practice, one may traverse the five stages and realize the two kinds of *āśraya-parāvṛtti* (transformation of the basis).
Although there are ten distinct commentaries totaling a hundred fascicles, I have meticulously examined and searched through them, synthesizing them into this work.
In ten fascicles, it likewise contains thirty verses; in meaning, there is neither addition nor subtraction.

It may be called the initial gateway for entering the Mahāyāna, the sharp axe that cleaves false attachments, the skillful means for receiving those of provisional and limited capacities, and the vanguard that reveals the inherent nature.
The first section, the "Exposition," concludes here. △ Second, the "Bestowal of Vows."

Having analyzed the meaning of the nature and characteristics of consciousness-only based upon the sacred teachings and correct reasoning, I dedicate the merit of this protection to all living beings;
may we together swiftly ascend to unsurpassed enlightenment.
"Scripture" refers to the words that express; "reasoning" refers to the meaning expressed. Words follow meaning, and meaning follows words;

how could scripture and reasoning ever be two separate things? Yet, fearing that interpreting meaning based solely on the literal text would constitute an offense against the Buddhas of the three periods, one must rely upon scripture while simultaneously employing correct reasoning as a compass. Furthermore, fearing...

To deviate from even a single word of the sūtras is to be identical to the teachings of Māra; therefore, while relying upon correct reasoning, one must still take the holy scriptures as the definitive authority.
Regarding the meaning of the characteristics of the nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*): if one does not understand its nature, one will likewise not understand its characteristics.
Their characteristics are themselves delusive. If one does not recognize their characteristics, one will likewise not recognize their nature; that nature would then remain isolated.

Therefore, it is necessary to penetrate both nature and characteristics simultaneously before one can benefit both oneself and others. Furthermore, nature and characteristics are simply phenomena and principle.

Without comprehending phenomena, principle is not complete; without understanding principle, how can phenomena be established? Thus, I shall now distinguish these meanings so that [the practitioner may...]
The two truths of the ultimate and the conventional are clearly and distinctly understood as the foundation for initiating practice, traversing the stages, and realizing the fruit.

Merely this single thought-moment of merit from propagating the Dharma can repay the profound kindness of the Buddhas of the ten directions and further bestow [benefits] upon all sentient beings, thereby acceding with great compassion.
By aspiring to attain Great Enlightenment, one accords with great wisdom. When compassion and wisdom are practiced in tandem, it is—
These are the armor of the four great vows; they are the authentic seal of the Mahāyāna Vijñaptimātratā.
*The Essential Dharma for Contemplating the Mind According to the Cheng weishi lun*, Fascicle Ten (End).
Postscript.
The *Zongjing lu* states: One must unite wisdom with extensive learning; one must never cling to the expression and mistake it for the finger.
One must employ extensive learning to refine wisdom, so as to avoid becoming narrow-minded and wall-eyed.
If there is even a single speck of dust that remains uncomprehended, ignorance still persists therein, for that point of non-comprehension acts as an obscuration. Why?
How much more so within the gates of one's own senses during daily life—where there are countless urgent Dharma-gates, yet not a single one has been clarified.
If you wish to teach others, on what basis can you analyze them? You will only end up deceiving yourself and, conversely, fall into ignorance.

If one’s own eyes have not yet become clear, how can one open the eyes of others? Therefore, one must employ the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to determine right from wrong, so that true cultivation is not confused with the false.
One must divide the essence and function into four parts so that correct principle remains unimpaired.

Only then can the ten causes and four conditions distinguish the locus of the arising of defilement and purity, and the three retributions and five fruits reflect upon where the ultimate and conventional truths converge. If one does not comprehend these three means of valid cognition...
How can one distinguish between the real and the false? If one does not understand these four divisions, both the essence and its function are lost.

Furthermore, it is said that the true mark of the one mind comprises all phenomena (*dharmas*). All phenomena that arise take the seeds stored within the eighth consciousness—perfumed by the manifestation of good and evil—as their cause;
they initiate the differentiated retributions of defilement and purity as their fruit. If one does not [understand this] minutely...

Analyze in detail through questions and answers to resolve doubts. By what means can one reach the source of the unity and diversity of the single mind and penetrate the boundary between the nature and characteristics of the eight consciousnesses?
As the ancient masters said, "The intent of grasping the main rope lies in spreading the net"; one must not discard the net while retaining only the rope.

Raising the collar is intended for wearing the robe; one must not discard the robe to grasp only the collar. Thus we know that only when both principle and phenomena are clearly elucidated does one penetrate the perfect purport;
only when teaching and contemplation operate in tandem does one finally reach the One Vehicle. Furthermore, it is said: "If one does not rely on what is pointed out by the teachings..."
By what means can one come to recognize one's own mind? Even if it were not for the illumination provided by the teachings, one must still rely on the teachings for confirmation.
Were it otherwise, all would become naturalistic non-Buddhists or Zen masters who attain realization in the dark; this remains true even if one were born with innate knowledge.
This is likely due to the seeds sown by hearing the sutras over many lifetimes, or perhaps the secret empowerment of the original vows of the various saints. Alas!
The Great Master Yongming, as a direct descendant of the Dharma-eye and one who realized the level of the patriarchs, exhorted us with such bitter heart and bitter mouth.
Who would say that the *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) is not the essential key for transmitting the mind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? Since I myself—

Regretting that my hindrances are deep and my delusions heavy, such that I am unable to subdue the active afflictions (*kleśa*) and have deeply failed the initial resolve of my renunciation, I have nonetheless gained a slight glimpse of the source of both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Truly, it may be due to the secret empowerment of the fundamental vows of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;

therefore, I dare not remain selfish or secretive. Exhausting whatever light I can find in my leisure moments, I have set forth this whole work in its entirety. I take up the brush on the year of Dinghai.
On the twenty-fifth day of the third month of this year, I began the draft; on the twenty-fifth day of the fifth month of this same year, I completed it.
Having taken two months in total, I have composed the *Ten Volumes of the Essentials of Contemplating the Mind*. I humbly pray that all who see or hear this may rejoice and never retreat from Bodhi.
Whether they believe or doubt, may they all become wondrous seeds and be born together in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, where they shall first behold [Amitābha].
Amitābha Buddha returns to the first assembly at Dragon Flower (Nāgapuṣpa) to serve as a spiritual influence for the World-Honored One Maitreya.
Throughout the entirety of the future, he will extensively deliver all sentient beings. Only when all beings have been fully delivered will he realize unsurpassed nirvana.
This concludes the brush of the Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu; written as an epilogue in his forty-ninth year.
The layman Cai Bingzhou, a man of pure virtue, has donated his wealth to carve this tenth fascicle of the *Essentials of Consciousness-Only*.
We humbly pray that his official rank and longevity may increase, and his merit and wisdom flourish;

that he may shatter attachments to manifest the ultimate principle, transform consciousness into wisdom, and together with all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, realize the same enlightenment.
Realizing the wondrous nature of Consciousness-Only, they suddenly awaken to the three bodies and perfectly purify the four lands.
They shall behold Amitābha in the Land of Bliss and assist Maitreya at the Dragon Flower Assembly.
Recorded at the Patriarchal Hall on the middle day of autumn in the year of Dinghai.
